The answer to this is plain from the words of the Master in the second book: The proud enemy, standing before the woman, did not dare to break out into words of persuasion, fearing to be detected; but he attacked her under the form of a question, so as to gather from her answer how he could proceed in tempting. And so the devil said: [[3:1|Why hath God commanded you, that you should not eat of every tree of paradise?|Cur præcepit vobis Deus, ut non comederetis de omni ligno paradisi]], that is, of the fruits of all the trees, one excepted?

paras.t: Postremo quidam hic scribit, quod diabolus non est permissus tentare hominem in specie gratiosa. Et addit: Aliqui tamen dicunt, quod serpens ille habuit faciem gratiosam ac virginalem, quod de Scriptura nullam habet auctoritatem. Quocirca sciendum quod Beda hoc dicit, et Bonaventura allegat. In Scholastica quoque historia additur, quod rectus seu erectus incessit, atque adhuc, ut traditur, pareas erectus incedit. In gestis quoque Alexandri habetur quod […] quibus consonare videtur textus mox explanandus, sicut patebit. Sicque dictum illud censetur satis authenticum.
paras.en: Lastly, a certain writer says here that the devil was not permitted to tempt man in a comely form. And he adds: Some, however, say that that serpent had a comely and maidenly face, which has no authority from Scripture. On this it should be known that Bede says this, and Bonaventure cites it. In the Scholastic History too it is added that it went upright or erect, and that the pareas [a kind of serpent named by ancient writers] still, as is handed down, goes erect. In the Deeds of Alexander too it is recorded that […] [the editors note in the margin that something is wanting here in the original]; with which the text soon to be explained seems to agree, as will appear. And so that saying is judged authentic enough.

paras.t: Denique locutus est diabolus per serpentem, formando verba per linguam serpentis, ita quod serpens non intellexit verba illa, quemadmodum loquitur per energumenos atque fanaticos, hoc est arrepticios et obsessos, quos intellectu rationeque privat, ut Strabus ait. Sic quoque angelus bonus loquebatur per asinam Balaam. Sed mirum apparet, quod mulier ex allocutione serpentis non timuit. Ad quod Magister libro secundo respondet, quod putavit eum accepisse a Deo loquendi officium. Et aliqui dicunt, quod æstimavit serpentem illum esse aliquam rationalem creaturam. Ex quibus prætacta positio de virgineo vultu et recto incessu serpentis illius, apparentiam habet majorem. Sed et Bonaventura super secundum testatur, quod mulier credidit eum, qui loquebatur in serpente, non esse adversarium, sed bonum consiliarium. Porro Thomas super secundum, distinctione 25, el[…]tur: Mulier credidit serpentem accepisse usum loquendi, non quidem per conditionem naturæ, sed per ministerium spiritualis creaturæ. Nec contulit, an hoc fieret virtute angeli boni, an mali; aut utrum fieret Deo permittente, an Deo jubente. Et istud dicit Thomas solvendo, et exponendo auctoritatem Magistri Sententiarum secundo libro, distinctione 21, dicentis: Mulier ideo serpentem non horruit, quoniam quem a Deo creatum scivit, usum loquendi ab eo accepisse credidit. Ex his sequitur, quod mulier non putavit serpentem illum esse rationalis naturæ. Verumtamen expositio ista non apparet consona intentioni Magistri. Si enim mulier æstimavit rationalem spiritum loqui per serpentem, habuisset causam horrendi. Nec horrendi causa fuisset ei ablata ex tali opinione, præsertim quia non erat assueta aliquid tale sentire, quemadmodum Balaam ariolus. Nec ex hoc dicitur creaturam proprie accepisse usum loquendi a Deo, quoniam ab extrinseco principio, scilicet angelo aut diabolo, ad loquendum movetur.
paras.en: Further, the devil spoke through the serpent, forming the words with the serpent's tongue, so that the serpent did not understand those words; just as he speaks through energumens and the frenzied, that is, through the possessed and obsessed, whom he deprives of understanding and reason, as Strabo says. So too the good angel spoke through Balaam's ass[[Num 22:28||]]. But it seems strange that the woman was not afraid at being addressed by the serpent. To which the Master replies, in the second book, that she thought it had received from God the office of speaking. And some say that she judged that serpent to be some rational creature. From these things the opinion mentioned above, about the maidenly face and upright gait of that serpent, has the greater likelihood. And Bonaventure too, on the second book, testifies that the woman believed that he who spoke in the serpent was not an adversary but a good counsellor. Further, Thomas, on the second book, distinction 25, says [the word is damaged in the print, el…tur, probably *eloquitur*, “declares”]: The woman believed that the serpent had received the use of speech, not indeed by the condition of its nature, but by the ministry of a spiritual creature. Nor did she consider whether this was done by the power of a good angel or a bad one, or whether it was done by God's permission or by God's command. And Thomas says this in resolving and expounding the authority of the Master of the Sentences, in the second book, distinction 21, who says: The woman did not shrink from the serpent, because she believed that the one she knew to have been created by God had received the use of speech from Him. From this it follows that the woman did not think that serpent to be of a rational nature. Yet this exposition does not seem to agree with the Master's meaning. For if the woman judged that a rational spirit was speaking through the serpent, she would have had cause to shrink from it. Nor would the cause of shrinking have been taken away from her by such an opinion, especially since she was not accustomed to perceive any such thing, as Balaam the soothsayer was. Nor on this account is a creature properly said to have received the use of speech from God, since it is moved to speak by an outside principle, namely an angel or the devil.

paras.t: Sed quum actualis recordatio præcepti soleat a peccato retrahere, mirum quod tentator a commemoratione divini præcepti tentationem illam exorsus est: Cur, inquiens, præcepit vobis Deus, etc.? Ad hoc Augustinus super Genesim ait, quatenus per hoc mulieris transgressio gravior et inexcusabilior redderetur. Quæsivit igitur, ut ex mulieris responsione inveniret occasionem ducendi illam ad malum intentum, quemadmodum factum est. Denique quidam hic scribit: Stante statu innocentiæ, non poterat esse deordinatio in viribus inferioribus, nisi prius esset in ratione. Istud consonat dictis authenticorum doctorum, sed ex isto concludit: Et ideo diabolus non tentavit hominem primo de comestione ligni, sed de restrictione præcepti. Hoc autem consequens non videtur. Primo, quoniam Christum qui erat in statu perfectioris innocentiæ quam primi parentes, tentavit primo de gula, dicendo: Si filius Dei es, dic ut lapides isti panes fiant. Secundo, quia quum gula sit ex suo genere peccatum mortale, poterat circa eam deordinari non solum inferior pars animæ hominis, sed item superior. Tertio, quia Gregorius dicit: Primum parentem diabolus tribus modis tentavit, videlicet gula, vana gloria, et avaritia. Gula, quum cibum vetitum comedendum suasit, etc.
paras.en: But since the actual remembrance of a precept usually draws one back from sin, it is strange that the tempter began that temptation by recalling the divine precept: [[3:1|Why|Cur]], he says, [[3:1|hath God commanded you|præcepit vobis Deus]], etc.? To this Augustine says, on Genesis, that it was so that by this the woman's transgression might be made graver and less excusable. He asked, then, so as to find in the woman's answer an occasion of leading her to the evil he intended, as came about. Further, a certain writer says here: While the state of innocence stood, there could be no disorder in the lower powers unless there were first disorder in the reason. This agrees with the sayings of the authoritative doctors; but from it he concludes: And therefore the devil did not tempt man first about eating of the tree, but about the restriction of the precept. This, however, does not seem to follow. First, because he tempted Christ, who was in a state of more perfect innocence than our first parents, first about gluttony, saying: [[Matt 4:3|If thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread|Si filius Dei es, dic ut lapides isti panes fiant]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are those of Matt 4:3]. Secondly, because, since gluttony is of its kind a mortal sin, not only the lower part of man's soul but the higher too could be disordered about it. Thirdly, because Gregory says: The devil tempted our first parent in three ways, namely by gluttony, vainglory and avarice. By gluttony, when he persuaded him to eat the forbidden food, etc.

paras.t: Cui respondit mulier: De fructu lignorum quæ sunt in paradiso, vescimur: hoc est, licentiam ac præceptum comedendi tempore opportuno habemus. Si autem tam modico tempore in paradiso fuerunt, ut communiter dicitur et infra tangetur, non videtur multum probabile quod ederint ex fructibus paradisi. De fructu vero ligni, quod est in medio paradisi, videlicet de fructu ligni scientiæ boni et mali, quæ arbor forsitan erat magis propinque stans ad medium paradisi, sive directe in medio ejus: vel ideo specialiter dicitur esse in medio paradisi, tanquam notabile aliquid, utpote singulariter vetitum: præcepit nobis Deus, vel immediate simul nobis ambobus, aut viro per se, et mihi per virum, ut tactum est supra: ne comederemus, et ne tangeremus illud ad comedendum, vel ad abstrahendum aliquid de fructibus ejus; ne forte moriamur in corpore, necessitatem moriendi incurrendo per inobedientiam, atque in anima per divini præcepti transgressionem. Istud adverbium, forte, adjecit mulier ex suo, quoniam Deus assertive fuerat comminatus: In quacumque die comederis, etc.: ubi Septuaginta pluraliter transtulerunt, comederitis. Itaque mulier addidit notam hanc dubietatis, non per respectum ad Dei præceptum, quia de illo jam assertive disseruit, De fructu ligni quod est in medio paradisi, præcepit nobis Deus, etc.; sed per respectum ad pœnam desuper comminatam.
paras.en: [[3:2|And the woman answered him|Cui respondit mulier]]: [[3:2|Of the fruit of the trees that are in paradise we do eat|De fructu lignorum quæ sunt in paradiso, vescimur]]: that is, we have leave and command to eat at the fitting time. But if they were in paradise for so short a time, as is commonly said and will be touched on below, it does not seem very probable that they ate of the fruits of paradise. [[3:3|But of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise|De fructu vero ligni, quod est in medio paradisi]], namely of the fruit of the tree of knowledge of good and evil, which tree perhaps stood nearer the middle of paradise, or directly in its middle; or else it is said in particular to be in the midst of paradise as something notable, being singularly forbidden: [[3:3|God hath commanded us|præcepit nobis Deus]], either immediately to both of us together, or to the man by himself and to me through the man, as was touched on above: [[3:3|that we should not eat; and that we should not touch it|ne comederemus, et ne tangeremus illud]] in order to eat, or to take away any of its fruits; [[3:3|lest perhaps we die|ne forte moriamur]] in the body, incurring the necessity of dying through disobedience, and in the soul through the transgression of the divine precept. This adverb, *perhaps*, the woman added of her own, since God had threatened assertively: [[Gen 2:17|in what day soever thou shalt eat|In quacumque die comederis]], etc.; where the Septuagint translated in the plural, *ye shall eat*. So the woman added this note of doubt not with respect to God's precept, since of that she had already spoken assertively, [[3:3|of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise, God hath commanded us|De fructu ligni quod est in medio paradisi, præcepit nobis Deus]], etc., but with respect to the penalty threatened for it.

paras.t: Ideo non est convenienter dictum quod quidam hic scribit: Apposuit de suo, forte, quod est adverbium dubitandi, quum tamen Deus assertive præcepisset. Ubi dicendum erat, Quum tamen Deus assertive comminatus fuisset. Est etenim quædam comminatio absolute affirmatoria, ut illa: Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis. Rursus idem scribit hoc loco: Ultimum istud, videlicet, Ne tangeremus illud, addidit mulier de suo. Non enim Deus prohibuerat tactum ligni, sed gustum tantum: ideo mulier addidit hoc ex displicentia præcepti, quoniam ille cui displicet præceptum impositum, libenter aggravat illud referendo. Aliqui tamen dicunt, quod etiam tactus ligni fuit eis prohibitus, ut magis elongarentur a gustu. Sed quia hoc non habetur ex littera, vel ex ejus circumstantia, prima expositio melior est. Et quia ad displicentiam præcepti quod reputatur indebitum, sequitur dubitatio de pœna imposita pro transgressione, ideo mulier subdidit: Ne forte moriamur. Hæc ille.
paras.en: Therefore what a certain writer says here is not fittingly said: She added of her own *perhaps*, which is an adverb of doubting, although God had commanded assertively. Where he ought to have said: although God had threatened assertively. For there is a kind of threat that is absolutely affirmative, like this one: [[Luke 13:3|unless you shall do penance, you shall all likewise perish|Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis]] [the margin gives Luke xiii, 3, 5; Denis's *egeritis* is the word of v. 5]. Again, the same writer says in this place: That last part, namely, [[3:3|that we should not touch it|Ne tangeremus illud]], the woman added of her own. For God had not forbidden the touching of the tree, but only the tasting; therefore the woman added this out of displeasure at the precept, since one who is displeased by a precept laid on him gladly makes it heavier in reporting it. Some, however, say that the touching of the tree was also forbidden them, so that they might be kept further from tasting. But since this is not had from the letter or from its circumstances, the first exposition is better. And because doubt about the penalty laid down for transgression follows on displeasure at a precept that is reckoned undue, the woman went on: [[3:3|lest perhaps we die|Ne forte moriamur]]. Thus he.

paras.t: In his verbis multa patent rationabili reprobationi. Primum est, quia si Deus tantum prohibuit gustum ligni et non tactum, ergo mulier mentiebatur, dicendo quod Deus prohibuit sibi ac viro etiam tactum. Mendacium autem omne, peccatum est. Et quia secundum doctores communiter, primum peccatum primorum parentum non fuit, imo nec esse potuit, veniale, mendacium illud fuisset mortale, et ita peccasset mortaliter ante suggestionem serpentis. Secundum est, quod dicit istud non haberi ex littera, scilicet quod Deus prohibuit tactum ligni; imo haberi videtur ex littera, eo quod littera dicat mulierem hoc dixisse ante suam ruinam. Denique, quod mulier dixit, Et ne tangeremus illud, non oportet exponi de solo tactu, sed accipi potest (ut tetigi) de tactu tendente ad esum. Tertium est, quod dicit mulieri displicuisse illud præceptum. Nam displicentia illa fuisset grande peccatum, et præcessisset suggestionem serpentis. Quartum est, quod asserit, Quia ad displicentiam præcepti quod reputatur indebitum: ubi insinuat quod mulier reputavit divinum præceptum indebitum; quod fuisset enormis blasphemia atque perfidia. Sicque omnia vitia ista fuissent in Eva ante suggestionem serpentis, dicentis, Nequaquam morte moriemini. Quintum est, quod ait mulierem ex divini præcepti displicentia addidisse, Et ne tangeremus illud: imo hoc potius dixisse videtur ex ponderatione jussionis divinæ, insinuando quam diligenter eis esset prohibitum vesci de ligno illo. Is quoque cui præceptum aliquod displicet, non semper aggravat illud dum recitat ipsum; imo sæpe extenuat, ut videatur minus culpabiliter illud infringere.
paras.en: In these words many things are open to reasonable rejection. The first is that, if God forbade only the tasting of the tree and not the touching, then the woman lied in saying that God had forbidden her and the man the touching too. But every lie is a sin. And since, according to the doctors generally, the first sin of our first parents was not venial, indeed could not be, that lie would have been mortal, and so she would have sinned mortally before the serpent's suggestion. The second is that he says this is not had from the letter, namely that God forbade the touching of the tree; on the contrary, it seems to be had from the letter, since the letter says that the woman said this before her fall. Further, what the woman said, [[3:3|and that we should not touch it|Et ne tangeremus illud]], need not be explained of touching alone, but can be taken (as I touched on) of a touching that tends to eating. The third is that he says this precept displeased the woman. For that displeasure would have been a great sin, and would have gone before the serpent's suggestion. The fourth is what he asserts: Because on displeasure at a precept that is reckoned undue: where he suggests that the woman reckoned the divine precept undue; which would have been enormous blasphemy and faithlessness. And so all these vices would have been in Eve before the suggestion of the serpent, who said, [[3:4|No, you shall not die the death|Nequaquam morte moriemini]]. The fifth is that he says the woman added out of displeasure at the divine precept, [[3:3|and that we should not touch it|Et ne tangeremus illud]]: rather she seems to have said this out of a weighing of the divine command, suggesting how carefully they had been forbidden to eat of that tree. Moreover, one who is displeased by some precept does not always make it heavier when he repeats it; rather he often lightens it, so as to seem less blameworthy in breaking it.

paras.t: Porro, quod mulier addidit, forte, non fuit ex hoc quod dubitavit de veritate verborum Dei, sed quia non scivit plenarie qualiter comminatio illa esset intelligenda, an scilicet solum ad perterrendum et refrenandum, an etiam ad absolutam assertionem, ut Thomas, Bonaventura, et alii scribunt super secundum. Ait enim Bonaventura super secundum, distinctione 22: Mulier non dubitavit verum esse quod Dominus dixerat, sed de hoc dubitabat, qualiter Dominus intelligebat, an scilicet intelligeret de morte corporali vel spirituali, aut alio quocumque modo.
paras.en: Further, that the woman added *perhaps* was not because she doubted of the truth of God's words, but because she did not know fully how that threat was to be understood, namely whether only to frighten and restrain, or also as an absolute assertion, as Thomas, Bonaventure and others write on the second book. For Bonaventure says on the second book, distinction 22: The woman did not doubt that what the Lord had said was true, but she was in doubt about this, how the Lord meant it, namely whether He meant bodily or spiritual death, or in some other way.

paras.t: Sed circa hoc argui potest, quia Magister ait libro secundo: Attende ordinem et progressum humanæ perditionis. Primo dixerat Deus, Quacumque hora ex eo comederis, morte morieris. Deinde mulier dixit, Ne forte moriamur. Novissime serpens dixit, Nequaquam morte moriemini. Deus affirmavit, mulier quasi ambigens dixit, serpens negavit. Quæ ergo dubitavit, a Deo affirmante recessit, et dæmoni neganti appropinquavit. Sed a Deo affirmante recedere, et diabolo verum neganti appropinquare, non caret culpa. Rursus, de verbis Dei ambigere, est peccatum: ergo in muliere fuit peccatum ante suggestionem serpentis; cujus oppositum Magister libro secundo determinat, et doctores concorditer scribunt. Et respondendum quod non omnis recessus a Deo est culpa, sed recessus a Deo per mentis aversionem. Recessus autem per solam dissimilitudinem, non est semper peccatum: et ita fuit in muliere, quæ pro tanto dicitur a Deo affirmante recessisse, quia a perfecta cognitione sensus verborum Dei defecit. Et quamvis de veritate verborum Dei ambigere, impium sit, non tamen semper iniquum est, dubitare de intellectu verborum ipsius: et quantum ad hoc, appropinquavit diabolo, quod a perfectione defecit. Hinc ait Bonaventura, quod dubitatio illa non fuit culpa nec pœna, sed nescientia tantum, quæ etiam in angelis locum habet.
paras.en: But against this it can be argued, since the Master says in the second book: Mark the order and progress of man's perdition. First God had said, [[Gen 2:17|in what day soever thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death|Quacumque hora ex eo comederis, morte morieris]] [the Master has *in what hour soever*]. Then the woman said, [[3:3|lest perhaps we die|Ne forte moriamur]]. Last of all the serpent said, [[3:4|No, you shall not die the death|Nequaquam morte moriemini]]. God affirmed, the woman spoke as one in doubt, the serpent denied. She, then, who doubted withdrew from God who affirmed and drew near to the demon who denied. But to withdraw from God who affirms, and to draw near to the devil who denies the truth, is not without fault. Again, to be in doubt of God's words is a sin; therefore there was sin in the woman before the serpent's suggestion; the opposite of which the Master lays down in the second book, and the doctors write with one accord. The answer must be that not every withdrawal from God is a fault, but only withdrawal from God by the turning away of the mind. Withdrawal by mere unlikeness is not always a sin; and so it was in the woman, who is said to have withdrawn from God who affirmed inasmuch as she fell short of a perfect knowledge of the sense of God's words. And although to doubt of the truth of God's words is impious, it is not always wicked to be in doubt about the understanding of His words; and in this respect she drew near to the devil, that she fell short of perfection. Hence Bonaventure says that that doubt was neither fault nor punishment, but only nescience [that is, a mere not-knowing, without blame], which has place even in the angels.

paras.t: Dixit autem serpens ad mulierem: Nequaquam morte moriemini. Circa hoc ait Magister libro secundo: Ut diabolus libere persuaderet mulieri malum culpæ quod intendebat, malum quod mulier timuit, scilicet mortem, negando removit, promissionemque addidit. Atque ut ejus promissio citius reciperetur, duplicavit promissionem. Unam namque comestionem vetiti ligni suadens, duo pro mercede proposuit, utpote similitudinem Dei, et scientiam boni ac mali. Nam subditur: Scit enim Deus, quod in quocumque die comederitis ex eo, aperientur oculi vestri, id est, corda vestra implebuntur scientia, et eritis sicut dii, id est divini, et angelis similes, imo et Deo, scientes bonum et malum. In quibus verbis, secundum Magistrum, imo secundum Gregorium in homilia, diabolus hominem tentavit de tribus: puta de gula, persuadendo cibum, quum dixit, In quacumque die comederitis; inani gloria, addens, Eritis sicut dii; avaritia, subdens, Scientes bonum et malum. Avaritia quippe non solum est aviditas pecuniæ, sed altitudinis quoque et scientiæ, dum sublimitas supra modum ambitur. Attamen avaritia sic accepta, non est vitium spirituale, nec proprie sumitur ita. Nam talis aviditas scientiæ, est curiositas magis quam avaritia proprie dicta.
paras.en: [[3:4|And the serpent said to the woman|Dixit autem serpens ad mulierem]]: [[3:4|No, you shall not die the death|Nequaquam morte moriemini]]. On this the Master says in the second book: So that the devil might freely persuade the woman to the evil of fault that he intended, he removed by denying it the evil that the woman feared, namely death, and added a promise. And so that his promise might be the more quickly received, he doubled the promise. For while urging one eating of the forbidden tree, he set forth two things as its reward, namely likeness to God and the knowledge of good and evil. For there follows: [[3:5|For God doth know that in what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened|Scit enim Deus, quod in quocumque die comederitis ex eo, aperientur oculi vestri]], that is, your hearts shall be filled with knowledge, [[3:5|and you shall be as Gods|et eritis sicut dii]], that is, divine, and like the angels, indeed like God, [[3:5|knowing good and evil|scientes bonum et malum]]. In which words, according to the Master, or rather according to Gregory in a homily, the devil tempted man on three things: on gluttony, urging the food, when he said, [[3:5|in what day soever you shall eat|In quacumque die comederitis]]; on vainglory, adding, [[3:5|you shall be as Gods|Eritis sicut dii]]; on avarice, going on, [[3:5|knowing good and evil|Scientes bonum et malum]]. For avarice is a greed not only for money but also for loftiness and knowledge, when eminence is sought beyond measure. Yet avarice taken in this way is not a spiritual vice, nor is the word properly taken so. For such a greed for knowledge is curiosity rather than avarice properly so called.

paras.t: Insuper circa hæc verba in Scholastica historia legitur: Quum mulier quasi dubitando dixisset, Ne forte moriamur, diabolus quasi securus de victoria, quoniam dubitans in utramque partem facile flectitur, dixit: Nequaquam morte moriemini, imo Deus volens vos et in scientia assimilari, et sciens quod quandocumque comederitis de hoc ligno, eritis sicut dii, scientes bonum et malum, quasi invidus prohibuit hoc: sed mirum apparet, quod mulier credere potuit tentatori, tam perverse de Deo loquenti. Et respondendum, quod mulier ex promissione serpentis, quamdam concepit elationem, quæ deinde corrupit rectæ rationis judicium. Et quamvis non crederet Deum falsa dixisse, credidit tamen vera esse verba serpentis, et verba Dei esse prolata ad perterrendum, vel ad aliquid designandum, ut super Genesim loquitur Augustinus. Hinc ait Magister libro secundo: Talis fuit processus tentationis: diabolus tentando dixit: Si comederitis, eritis sicut dii, scientes bonum et malum. Quo audito, statim subrepsit mulieri elatio quæ jam et amor propriæ potestatis, ex quo mulieri complacuit facere quod diabolus suadebat, et fecit; sicque elationem secutum est peccatum operis, et pœna peccati.
paras.en: Moreover, on these words we read in the Scholastic History: When the woman, as if doubting, had said, [[3:3|lest perhaps we die|Ne forte moriamur]], the devil, as though sure of victory, since one who doubts is easily bent to either side, said: [[3:4|No, you shall not die the death|Nequaquam morte moriemini]]; rather, God, not wishing you to be made like Him in knowledge too, and knowing that whenever you eat of this tree [[3:5|you shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil|eritis sicut dii, scientes bonum et malum]], forbade this as one who envies [the Latin reads *volens*, “wishing”; the sense seems to require “not wishing”, *nolens*]. But it seems strange that the woman could believe the tempter when he spoke so perversely of God. The answer must be that from the serpent's promise the woman conceived a certain elation, which then corrupted the judgement of right reason. And although she did not believe that God had spoken falsely, she yet believed that the serpent's words were true, and that God's words had been uttered to frighten, or to signify something, as Augustine says on Genesis. Hence the Master says in the second book: Such was the course of the temptation: the devil, tempting, said: If you eat, [[3:5|you shall be as Gods, knowing good and evil|eritis sicut dii, scientes bonum et malum]]. When she heard this, there at once crept into the woman an elation, which was already also a love of her own power, from which it pleased the woman to do what the devil urged, and she did it; and so on the elation followed the sin of deed, and the punishment of sin.

paras.t: Præterea Augustinus super Genesim ait: Constat, prætactis verbis diaboli, persuasum esse peccatum per elationem, quoniam dixit: Eritis sicut dii, etc. Ubi notatur tantum persuasum esse, ut sub Domino nollent esse, sed in propria potestate, ne legem Dei obtemperando servarent, qui invideret eis quod regerent semetipsos, non indigentes interno lumine Creatoris, sed utentes prudentia propria quasi oculis suis ad cognoscendum bonum et malum quod Deus prohibuisset; sicque persuasum est eis, ut propriam potestatem nimis amarent: ideo amiserunt quod acceperunt, quoniam usurpaverunt quod non acceperunt, videlicet ut per suam potestatem, Deo non regente, beati essent. Et quantum ad hoc, voluerunt esse Deo quodammodo pares. Hoc quippe est proprium Deo, propria potestate esse beatum, nullo alio se regente. Ex his Augustini eloquiis sumitur expositio hujus litteræ talis: Scit Deus quod in quocumque die comederitis ex eo, aperientur oculi vestri interiores per scientiam perfectiorem, et eritis sicut dii, hoc est Deo consimiles, quantum ad hoc, quod non eritis ita arctati aliqua prohibitione, nec subjecti alicui ad obediendum; scientes bonum et malum, id est, per vos ipsos scientes ac proprio corde intelligentes, quid expediat vobis, et item quid agere, quid respuere debeatis.
paras.en: Besides, Augustine says on Genesis: It is clear from the aforesaid words of the devil that the sin was urged on them through elation, since he said: [[3:5|you shall be as Gods|Eritis sicut dii]], etc. Where it is noted that they were persuaded so far as to be unwilling to be under the Lord, but to be in their own power, so as not to keep by obedience the law of God, who, as he made out, grudged them ruling themselves, not needing the inward light of the Creator, but using their own prudence as their own eyes to know the good and evil that God had forbidden; and so they were persuaded to love their own power too much. Therefore they lost what they had received, because they usurped what they had not received, namely to be blessed by their own power, without God ruling them. And in this respect they wished to be in a manner equal to God. For this is proper to God, to be blessed by His own power, with no other ruling Him. From these sayings of Augustine the exposition of this letter is taken thus: [[3:5|For God doth know that in what day soever you shall eat thereof, your eyes shall be opened|Scit Deus quod in quocumque die comederitis ex eo, aperientur oculi vestri]], your inward eyes, through a more perfect knowledge, [[3:5|and you shall be as Gods|et eritis sicut dii]], that is, like God, in this respect, that you will not be so straitened by any prohibition, nor subject to anyone to obey him; [[3:5|knowing good and evil|scientes bonum et malum]], that is, knowing by yourselves and understanding with your own heart what is expedient for you, and likewise what you ought to do and what to reject.

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit quidam: Secundum prædicta, mulier peccavit elatione et dubitatione, antequam comederet fructum prohibitum: quod videtur aliquibus falsum. Ad quod dico, quod nullus intelligens dicit hoc esse falsum, quia interior culpa exteriorem præcessit. Deinde tamen concedit, quod elatio mulieris secuta est suasionem serpentis. Verum per hoc non evadit ea, quæ jam in isto articulo contra eum inducta sunt.
paras.en: On these things a certain writer says: According to what has been said, the woman sinned by elation and doubt before she ate the forbidden fruit; which seems false to some. To which I say that no one of understanding says this is false, since the inward fault went before the outward. Afterwards, however, he grants that the woman's elation followed the serpent's persuasion. But by this he does not escape the points already brought against him in this article.

3.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus tertii capituli ab illo loco: Vidit igitur mulier
3.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this third chapter from the place: “And the woman saw”

paras.t: CONSEQUENTER describitur lapsus primorum parentum. Vidit igitur mulier quod bonum esset lignum ad vescendum. Hoc est, postquam verba serpentis audivit, atque elatione permota, eisdem verbis credidit, atque tentatori consensit, adspexit oculo corporali et etiam interiori arborem illam scientiæ boni ac mali, et consideravit quod fructus arboris illius, secundum se consideratus, seu ex sua natura, esset conveniens esui, quamvis fuerit primis parentibus nocivus et malus ex prohibitione. Vidit itaque quod fructus illius ligni esset conveniens ad vescendum: quod ex odore et tactu fructus illius perpendere potuit. Et pulchrum oculis ad intuendum aspectuque delectabile. Nam pulchrum naturaliter visum oblectat, sicut suave gustum. Et quamvis omnes arbores paradisi essent non mediocriter pulchræ ac delectabiles ad videndum, utpote paulo ante productæ cum fructibus et virore ac foliorum frondiumque ornatu, tamen hæc arbor exstitit specialiter pulchra ad intuendum, et dulcis ad comedendum. Et tulit de fructu ejus. Unde patet, quod decor, amabilitas, et dulcedo ligni et fructus sui, moverunt etiam feminam ad transgressionem præcepti. Et primo ad concupiscentiam malam, sicque tunc cœpit impleri illud Sapientiæ: Creaturæ Dei factæ sunt in muscipulam et laqueum pedibus insipientium, et in deceptionem animæ hominum. Et comedit.
paras.en: Next the fall of our first parents is described. [[3:6|And the woman saw that the tree was good to eat|Vidit igitur mulier quod bonum esset lignum ad vescendum]]. That is, after she had heard the serpent's words, and, stirred by pride, had believed those words and consented to the tempter, she looked with the bodily eye and with the inner eye also upon that tree of knowledge of good and evil, and considered that the fruit of that tree, considered in itself, or by its own nature, was fit for eating, although for our first parents it was harmful and evil by reason of the prohibition. So she saw that the fruit of that tree was fit to eat: which she could judge from the smell and touch of the fruit. [[3:6|and fair to the eyes|Et pulchrum oculis]] to look upon, [[3:6|and delightful to behold|aspectuque delectabile]]. For the beautiful naturally delights the sight, as the sweet delights the taste. And although all the trees of paradise were no little beautiful and delightful to see, having been brought forth a little before with their fruits and their greenness and the adornment of leaves and foliage, yet this tree was especially beautiful to look upon, and sweet to eat. [[3:6|and she took of the fruit thereof|Et tulit de fructu ejus]]. Whence it is plain that the comeliness, loveliness and sweetness of the tree and of its fruit also moved the woman to transgress the commandment; and first to evil desire; and so there began then to be fulfilled that saying of Wisdom: [[Wis 14:11|the creatures of God are turned|Creaturæ Dei factæ sunt]] into a trap and a snare [[Wis 14:11|to the feet of the unwise|pedibus insipientium]], and into a deceiving of the souls of men [Denis's wording differs from the Vulgate here, which reads "are turned to an abomination, and a temptation to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the unwise"; *muscipula* is literally a mousetrap]. [[3:6|and did eat|Et comedit]].

paras.t: Sed ubi fuit tunc Adam? Et plane apparet, quod per aliquod spatium absens fuit a femina, ita quod nec serpentem vidit eam affantem, nec eam de fructu arboris manducantem. Quia enim spirituali mente præditus fuit, Deo vacavit, nec tunc de corporali mulieris curavit præsentia, quamvis paulo ante fuisset ex eo formata, et ei adducta. Deditque viro suo, qui comedit. Nempe quum juxta suggestionem serpentis edisset, puto quod serpens mox ei suggesserat, ut virum ad idem alliceret. Ipsa quoque volens virum, quem valde amavit, habere facti sui socium et consortem, et quia ipsa jam delectata fuit in esu fructus prohibiti, atque ex hoc putavit se adepturam quæ serpens promisit, voluit virum suum hæc eadem obtinere. Estque probabile, quod retulit viro quæ a serpente audivit, et per verba consuluit viro suo, ut de fructu illo comederet. Cui vir consensit, quamvis non crederet verba serpentis esse vera, nec ex esu illo commoda adipisci.
paras.en: But where was Adam then? It plainly appears that he was away from the woman for some time, so that he neither saw the serpent speaking to her nor saw her eating of the fruit of the tree. For since he was endowed with a spiritual mind, he was giving himself to God, and did not then concern himself with the bodily presence of the woman, although a little before she had been formed from him and brought to him. [[3:6|and gave to her husband, who did eat|Deditque viro suo, qui comedit]]. For when she had eaten at the serpent's suggestion, I think the serpent at once suggested to her that she entice her husband to the same. She too, wishing to have her husband, whom she greatly loved, as companion and partner in her deed, and because she had already taken delight in eating the forbidden fruit and thought she would thereby obtain what the serpent had promised, wished her husband to obtain these same things. And it is probable that she told her husband what she had heard from the serpent, and in words counselled her husband to eat of that fruit. And the man consented to her, although he did not believe the serpent's words to be true, nor that he would gain any advantage from that eating.

paras.t: Cur ergo consensit et manducavit, et qualiter ipse per elationem peccavit? Ad quæ patet responsio ex verbis Magistri libro secundo, distinctione 22, dicentis: Solet etiam quæri, utrum talis elatio et amor propriæ potestatis in viro fuit. Ad quod dicimus, quod Adam non fuit seductus eo modo quo mulier, nec prior seductus est, nec in eo in quo mulier, ut crederet Deum prohibuisse tangere lignum illud idcirco, quia si tangerent, fierent sicut dii. Verumtamen prævaricator fuit Adam, ut testatur Apostolus. Potuit ergo aliqua elatio esse in mente ejus illico post tentationem, ex qua voluit lignum vetitum experiri, quum mulierem non videret mortuam esca illa percepta. Hinc super Genesim loquitur Augustinus: Non credidit Adam, quod Deus prohibuerit ideo tangi lignum illud a se et a muliere, quod Deus sciret eos quasi deos futuros, si tangerent illud, tanquam inviderat eis divinitatem, qui eos fecerat homines. Sed etsi virum ex aliqua mentis elatione sollicitavit quædam experiendi cupiditas quum mulierem videret, accepta esca illa, non esse mox mortuam: non tamen arbitror eum credidisse, quod suggerebat diabolus.
paras.en: Why then did he consent and eat, and how did he sin through pride? The answer to these is plain from the words of the Master [that is, Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences] in the second book, distinction 22, where he says: It is also commonly asked whether such pride and love of one's own power was in the man. To which we say that Adam was not seduced in the way the woman was[[1 Tim 2:14||]], nor was he seduced first, nor in the thing in which the woman was, so as to believe that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because, if they touched it, they would become as gods. Yet Adam was a transgressor, as the Apostle testifies[[Rom 5:14||]] [the margin note here cannot be read; Rom 5:14 speaks of "the transgression of Adam"]. There could therefore have been some pride in his mind immediately after the temptation, from which he wished to try the forbidden tree, when he did not see the woman dead after she had taken that food. Hence Augustine says on Genesis: Adam did not believe that God had forbidden that tree to be touched by himself and the woman because God knew they would be as gods if they touched it, as though he who had made them men begrudged them divinity. But even if, out of some pride of mind, a certain desire to make trial urged the man when he saw that the woman, having taken that food, had not died at once, yet I do not think he believed what the devil was suggesting.

paras.t: Rursus ait Magister libro secundo, ex verbis Augustini: Adam consensit persuasioni uxoris, tanquam morem ei gerens, et eam contristare non volens, nec a se alienatam relinquere, ne periret; putans utrumque fieri posse, ut scilicet et uxori morem gereret, et per pœnitentiam de sua culpa veniam impetraret. Hinc iterum Augustinus: Postquam, inquit, mulier seducta comedit, viroque dedit, noluit eam contristare, quam credebat sine suo solatio contabescere, atque a se alienatam penitus interire, non quidem carnali concupiscentia victus, quam nondum sensit, sed amicabili quadam benevolentia, qua plerumque fit, ut offendatur Deus, ne offendatur amicus. Ex his innotescit, quod Adam comedit ex fructu prohibito ex ea radice, qua Salomon idola adoravit: utpote ne suas contristaret delicias, id est uxorem. Unde quartodecimo de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus: Non est credibile, Salomonem ex errore putasse idolis esse serviendum, sed blanditiis feminæ esse inductum ad sacrificia illa: ita credendum est, quod Adam acquieverit Evæ ad Dei legem transgrediendam, non tanquam verum loquenti, sed sociali quadam necessitudine fecit hoc. Ideo dicit Apostolus, quod Adam non est seductus in prævaricationem, sed mulier.
paras.en: Again the Master says in the second book, from the words of Augustine: Adam consented to his wife's persuasion as though humouring her, not wishing to grieve her, nor to leave her estranged from himself, lest she perish; thinking that both things could be done, namely that he might humour his wife and through penance obtain pardon for his fault. Hence Augustine again: After the woman, being seduced, had eaten and given to her husband, he would not grieve her, who he believed would pine away without his comfort and, estranged from him, utterly perish; not indeed overcome by carnal concupiscence, which he had not yet felt, but by a certain friendly goodwill, through which it often happens that God is offended lest a friend be offended. From these things it becomes known that Adam ate of the forbidden fruit from the same root from which Solomon worshipped idols[[3 Kings 11:4||]] [the margin note here cannot be read; the passage is 3 Kings 11:4]: namely, so as not to grieve his delight, that is, his wife. Whence in the fourteenth book of the City of God Augustine declares: It is not credible that Solomon thought through error that idols were to be served, but that he was led to those sacrifices by a woman's blandishments: so it is to be believed that Adam yielded to Eve so far as to transgress God's law, not as to one speaking the truth, but he did this from a certain bond of fellowship. Therefore the Apostle says that [[1 Tim 2:14|Adam was not seduced|Adam non est seductus]] into transgression, [[1 Tim 2:14|but the woman|sed mulier]].

paras.t: Porro in Scholastica historia dicitur: Adam facile acquievit uxori, quia quum crederet statim morituram, et vidisset non esse mortuam, verba Dei de morte inferenda, æstimavit tantummodo ad terrorem prolata. Hinc etiam Thomas super secundum Sententiarum, distinctione 22, testatur: Non crediderunt primi parentes Deum dixisse falsum, sed verba ejus forte aliter esse intelligenda, aut metaphorice dicta, sive ad aliud significandum. Verumtamen difficultas hic oritur: Si enim Adam non credidit verbis diaboli quibus promisit, Eritis sicut dii, esse vera, ergo non peccavit ex elatione, neque ex desiderio inordinato assimilationis divinæ. Ad hoc Thomas respondet ibidem: Elatio quæ movit mulierem, major fuit quam quæ movit virum. In muliere namque talis fuit elationis progressus, quod ad verba serpentis tantum excellentiæ appetitum concepit, quod judicium rationis pervertit, et verum atque possibile credidit quod dixerat serpens: ideo dicitur fuisse seducta. In viro autem non tantum crevit in principio amor excellentiæ suæ, quod judicium suæ rationis pervertit, ita quod crediderit hoc esse futurum. Sed quia id voluit, si fuisset aut foret possibile, ideo dicitur non fuisse seductus; attamen talis elatio incitavit eum ad experiendum. Unde elatio ejus quamdam dubitationem in eo produxit, quæ in muliere firmam fecit æstimationem: idcirco voluntas mulieris, perfectum habuit appetitum divinæ assimilationis præfatæ; voluntas viri imperfectum et conditionatum, videlicet si esset possibile. Hæc Thomas. Verum, ut tactum est, in hoc Adam fuit aliquo modo deceptus, quod putavit peccatum illud non esse tam grave ut fuit, et post transgressionem suam veniam consequi, nec de paradiso expelli, atque in suo statu manere.
paras.en: Further, in the Scholastic History it is said: Adam readily yielded to his wife, because, although he believed she would die at once, yet when he saw that she had not died, he reckoned that God's words about inflicting death had been spoken only to frighten them. Hence too Thomas, on the second book of the Sentences, distinction 22, testifies: Our first parents did not believe that God had said what was false, but that his words were perhaps to be understood otherwise, or had been spoken metaphorically, or to signify something else. Yet a difficulty arises here. For if Adam did not believe the devil's words, in which he promised [[3:5|you shall be as Gods|Eritis sicut dii]], to be true, then he did not sin through pride, nor through an inordinate desire of likeness to God. To this Thomas answers in the same place: The pride that moved the woman was greater than that which moved the man. For in the woman pride went so far that at the serpent's words she conceived so great a craving for excellence that it perverted the judgment of her reason, and she believed what the serpent had said to be true and possible: therefore she is said to have been seduced. But in the man the love of his own excellence did not at first grow so great as to pervert the judgment of his reason, so that he believed this would come to pass. But because he wished it, if it had been or should be possible, he is therefore said not to have been seduced; yet such pride urged him to make trial. So his pride produced in him a certain doubt, where in the woman it produced a firm opinion: therefore the woman's will had a perfect craving for that likeness to God, the man's an imperfect and conditional one, namely, if it were possible. Thus far Thomas. Yet, as was touched on above, Adam was in some way deceived in this, that he thought that sin was not so grave as it was, and that after his transgression he would obtain pardon, and not be driven out of paradise, but remain in his state.

paras.t: Et aperti sunt oculi amborum. Hoc de corporalibus et spiritualibus seu interioribus et mentalibus primorum parentum oculis potest exponi, quum nec exteriores nec interiores eorum oculi fuerint ante penitus clausi, quia jam ante peccatum viderunt se invicem et fructum ligni, quem comederunt, utebanturque ratione; sed oculi eorum tam corporales quam intellectuales post transgressionem aperti dicuntur, quoniam per utrosque oculos aliter viderunt et cognoverunt, postquam peccaverunt, quam ante. Nam ante peccatum viderunt invicem corpora sua et genitalia membra sua absque erubescentia, eo quod nulla motio inhonesta oriretur in eis. Sed quum peccando privati fuissent originali justitia, cœperunt se mutuo cum verecundia intueri, quia senserunt in se ex mutuo adspectu motus libidinosos. Per habitum namque et virtutem originalis justitiæ eis concreatæ, fuit ratio eorum et voluntas Deo sine rebellione subjecta, sensitiva quoque pars rationi, et caro spiritui, nec poterat in eis oriri motus inordinatus aut culpa in sensitiva parte aut corpore, quamdiu superior pars animæ mansit Deo obediens ac subjecta. Quod autem ista expositio apta sit, patet ex consueto modo loquendi Scripturæ. Nam infra habetur, quod angeli percusserunt Sodomitas cæcitate, non quod penitus nil viderunt. Similiter quarto Regum Eliseus oravit: Domine, aperi oculos horum; quos etiam Dominus cæcitate quadam percusserat, qui tamen ante illam oculorum apertionem videbant, etiam durante illa eorum excæcatione; sed non eo modo, quo postquam aperti fuerunt oculi eorumdem, quamvis non sit per omnia simile.
paras.en: [[3:7|And the eyes of them both were opened|Et aperti sunt oculi amborum]]. This can be explained of the bodily and of the spiritual, that is, inward and mental, eyes of our first parents; since neither their outward nor their inward eyes had been altogether closed before, for already before the sin they saw one another and the fruit of the tree which they ate, and they used reason; but their eyes, bodily as well as intellectual, are said to have been opened after the transgression, because through both kinds of eyes they saw and knew otherwise after they had sinned than before. For before the sin they saw each other's bodies and their genital members without blushing, since no unseemly motion arose in them. But when by sinning they had been deprived of original justice, they began to look on one another with shame, because they felt lustful motions in themselves from looking at one another. For through the habit and virtue of original justice created together with them, their reason and will were subject to God without rebellion, the sensitive part too to reason, and the flesh to the spirit; nor could any inordinate motion or fault arise in them in the sensitive part or the body as long as the higher part of the soul remained obedient and subject to God. That this explanation is fitting is plain from Scripture's usual way of speaking. For below it is related that the angels struck the Sodomites with blindness[[Gen 19:11||]], not that they saw nothing at all. Likewise in the fourth book of Kings Eliseus prayed: [[4 Kings 6:20|Lord, open the eyes of these men|Domine, aperi oculos horum]]; men whom the Lord had also struck with a kind of blindness, who nevertheless saw before that opening of their eyes, even while that blinding of theirs lasted, but not in the way they saw after their eyes had been opened; though the case is not alike in every respect.

paras.t: Præterea, interiores oculi primorum parentum fuerunt aperti post culpam, quoniam post eam cœperunt aliter videre visione intellectuali, quam ante: quia quod ante sciebant simplici et speculativa notitia, tunc per experientiam cœperunt cognoscere, utpote quid intersit inter bonum obedientiæ, et malum inobedientiæ: quod ex propriis motibus inordinatis, et interiori rebellione carnis adversus animam, et sensitivæ partis contra rationis imperium, tunc scire cœperunt. Quumque cognovissent se esse nudos, hoc est, per experientiam jam præfatam considerassent nuditatem suam corporalem, confusibilem, inhonestam, quam et corporaliter apprehendere inceperunt, quia intellectiva cognitio ex sensitiva notitia sumit exordium. Nec dubium quin et ante transgressionem cognoverunt se esse nudos, quod viderunt ad oculum, sed non cognoverunt hoc eo modo quo postea.
paras.en: Moreover, the inward eyes of our first parents were opened after the fault, since after it they began to see by intellectual sight otherwise than before: for what they had known before by simple and speculative knowledge, they then began to know by experience, namely what difference there is between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience; which they then began to know from their own inordinate motions, and from the inner rebellion of the flesh against the soul, and of the sensitive part against the rule of reason. [[3:7|and when they perceived themselves to be naked|Quumque cognovissent se esse nudos]], that is, when through the experience just mentioned they had considered their bodily nakedness, shameful and unseemly, which they also began to apprehend bodily, since intellectual knowledge takes its beginning from the knowledge of the senses. Nor is there any doubt that before the transgression too they knew themselves to be naked, for they saw it with their eyes; but they did not know it in the way they did afterwards.

paras.t: Hinc ait super Genesim Augustinus: Aperti sunt oculi amborum ad concupiscendum invicem, et ad pœnam peccati, ut haberent non solum corpus animale, sed etiam corpus peccati, in quo lex, hoc est concupiscentia membrorum, repugnat legi mentis. Non enim cæci facti fuerunt, neque palpando decerpserunt fructus prohibitos: sed sicut in fractione panis aperti sunt oculi discipulorum, ita quod cognoverunt quem prius cognoscere non valebant, quamvis præsentem vidissent: sic horum oculi sunt aperti ad id quod ante non potuerunt; quoniam anima rationalis bestialem motum in carne sua erubuit, habuitque pudorem non solum, quia hunc sensit quem ante non senserat, sed et ideo, quoniam motus ille ex transgressione descendit. Ibi etenim eum sensit, ubi gratia ante vestiebatur, quum in nuditate nil indecens patiebatur. Hinc in Scholastica historia legitur: Sicut primi parentes inobedientes fuerunt suo superiori, sic et membra eorum cœperunt moveri contra suum superius, scilicet rationem: et primum concupiscentiæ motum rationi contrarium, senserunt in genitalibus: itaque membra circa se moveri videntes, erubuerunt. Ideo membra illa sunt dicta pudenda. Nam cetera membra ad nutum hominis stant aut moventur, non autem pudenda. Denique quia ista est porta propaginis, ideo inobedientia membrorum, quasi signum inobedientiæ primorum parentum, scripta est in porta præfata.
paras.en: Hence Augustine says on Genesis: [[3:7|the eyes of them both were opened|Aperti sunt oculi amborum]] to desire one another, and for the punishment of sin, so that they had not only an animal body but also a body of sin, in which the law, that is, the concupiscence of the members, fights against the law of the mind[[Rom 7:23||]]. For they had not been made blind, nor did they pluck the forbidden fruit by groping; but as at the breaking of bread the disciples' [[Luke 24:31|eyes were opened|aperti sunt oculi discipulorum]], so that they knew him whom before they could not know, although they had seen him present: so the eyes of these were opened to what they could not see before; since the rational soul blushed at the bestial motion in its flesh, and was ashamed not only because it felt this which it had not felt before, but also because that motion came down from the transgression. For it felt it there where before it was clothed with grace, when in nakedness it suffered nothing unseemly. Hence one reads in the Scholastic History: As our first parents were disobedient to their superior, so their members too began to move against their own superior, namely reason; and they felt the first motion of concupiscence contrary to reason in the genitals; and so, seeing those members move about them, they blushed. Therefore those members are called pudenda [that is, the parts to be ashamed of, from *pudor*, shame]. For the other members stand still or move at man's bidding, but not the pudenda. Lastly, because this is the gate of propagation, the disobedience of the members, as a sign of the disobedience of our first parents, is written on that gate.

paras.t: Quum itaque cognovissent se taliter nudos, conturbati et confusione operti, dolentes et deceptos se esse videntes, utpote pristina tranquillitate ac spiritualitate privati, consuerunt folia ficus, et fecerunt sibi perizomata, id est, succinctoria et velamenta, quibus cooperuerunt sua pudenda, fecerunt ex foliis ficus, ea connectendo. Dicunt quoque nonnulli, atque (ut fertur) Hebræi idem affirmant, quod arbor fici fuit arbor illa prohibita; et sicut sub ea comedendo peccaverunt, sic mox ejus foliis velamina sibi fecerunt.
paras.en: So when they had known themselves to be naked in this way, troubled and covered with confusion, grieving and seeing that they had been deceived, being deprived of their former tranquillity and spirituality, [[3:7|they sewed together fig leaves, and made themselves aprons|consuerunt folia ficus, et fecerunt sibi perizomata]], that is, girdles and coverings, with which they covered their shameful parts; they made them of fig leaves, by joining them together. Some also say, and (as is reported) the Hebrews affirm the same, that the fig tree was that forbidden tree; and as they sinned by eating under it, so they at once made themselves coverings from its leaves.

paras.t: Et quum audissent vocem Domini Dei deambulantis in paradiso ad auram post meridiem. Scriptura loquitur more humano de incircumscriptibili ac simplicissimo Deo. Ideo non est sic intelligendum, quod Deus in deitatis forma aut propria persona ita deambulaverit, sed per creaturam subjectam, ita quod angelus in Dei persona apparens, in forma sic ambulavit humana: quemadmodum Deus dicitur apparuisse Abrahæ in convalle Hebron, et Moysi, aliisque Prophetis ac Sanctis. Ideo Augustinus fatetur, quod deambulantis Dei vocem audierunt, non nisi per creaturam subjectam: quod factum est, ne substantia invisibilis et ubique tota, quæ est Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti, corporalibus sensibus locali temporalique motu apparuisse credatur. Denique Dominus deambulavit, quasi suo motu designans se recessisse ab eis, in quibus ante per gratiam mansit, quia in sua obedientia non steterunt. Abscondit se Adam et uxor ejus a facie Domini Dei in medio ligni paradisi, id est, inter arbores illas absconderunt se, quia male sibi conscii erant, et increpari ac castigari jam verebantur. Et quamvis scirent Deum in propria essentia invisibilem esse, et omnia intuentem nec quidquam se posse ab ejus adspectu abscondere; attamen quia in forma visibili audierunt eum deambulare, erubuerunt coram ejus præsentia apparere, quemadmodum modo nudus verecundatur coram venerabilibus apparere personis. Porro quod ait, In medio ligni paradisi, non est intelligendum, quod præ timore et pudore intraverint ipsum lignum, sed ponitur singulare pro plurali, juxta sensum prælatum.
paras.en: [[3:8|And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the afternoon air|Et quum audissent vocem Domini Dei deambulantis in paradiso ad auram post meridiem]]. Scripture speaks in human fashion of God, who is uncircumscribable and most simple. So it is not to be understood that God walked thus in the form of the Godhead or in his own person, but through a subject creature, so that an angel appearing in the person of God walked thus in human form: as God is said to have appeared to Abraham in the vale of Hebron[[Gen 18:1||]] [so Denis; the Douay-Rheims has "the vale of Mambre"], and to Moses, and to other Prophets and Saints. Therefore Augustine declares that they heard the voice of God walking only through a subject creature: which was done lest the invisible substance, wholly present everywhere, which is that of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, be believed to have appeared to the bodily senses by local and temporal motion. Further, the Lord walked as if signifying by his motion that he had withdrawn from them, in whom he had dwelt before by grace, because they did not stand firm in their obedience. [[3:8|Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God, amidst the trees of paradise|Abscondit se Adam et uxor ejus a facie Domini Dei in medio ligni paradisi]], that is, they hid themselves among those trees, because they were conscious of their wrongdoing, and now feared to be rebuked and punished. And although they knew God to be invisible in his own essence and beholding all things, and that they could hide nothing from his sight, yet because they heard him walking in visible form, they were ashamed to appear in his presence, as now a naked man is ashamed to appear before venerable persons. Further, where it says [[3:8|amidst the trees of paradise|In medio ligni paradisi]] [in the Latin, *ligni*, "of the tree", is singular], it is not to be understood that out of fear and shame they went into the tree itself; but the singular is put for the plural, according to the sense given above.

paras.t: Vocavitque Dominus Deus Adam, et dixit ei: Ubi es? Quasi compatiens dicat, Vide in quanta sis modo miseria constitutus: nec quasi ignorans quærit, sed ut juxta exigentiam responsionis Adæ, convenientius reprehendatur a Domino. Et quoniam angelus Dei personam repræsentavit, atque in ejus persona loquebatur, ideo quidquid Deus fecit et dixit per angelum illum, Deo adscribitur. Vocavitque Deus Adam magis quam Evam, quoniam principalior fuit, ad insinuandum quod superiores, dum peccant, specialiter fiant reprehensibiles apud Deum. Qui ait: Vocem tuam Domine, audivi in paradiso; et timui, eo quod nudus essem, id est, ex propria nuditate confusibilis factus per culpam; et abscondi me, metuens et verecundans coram te taliter præsentari. Verumtamen ista responsio, quantum ad formam verborum, fuit insipiens. Quum enim a Creatore nudus esset formatus, et in nuditate relictus sine pudore, non debuit dicere, Abscondi me, quoniam nudus sum; sed potius, quia peccando nunc habeo erubescibilem nuditatem. Cui dixit Deus: Quis enim indicavit tibi quod nudus esses, id est, qualiter nunc advertis et experimentaliter noscis ex proprio pudore et horrore, quod nudus sis, nisi quod ex ligno, id est fructu arboris, de quo tibi præceperam ne comederes, comedisti? id est, non aliunde accidit tibi cognitio ista experimentalis et pœnalis propriæ nuditatis, nisi quia transgressus es præceptum meum, per quod meruisti privari justitia originali et inordinationem incurrere passionum.
paras.en: [[3:9|And the Lord God called Adam, and said to him: Where art thou?|Vocavitque Dominus Deus Adam, et dixit ei: Ubi es?]] As if he said with compassion: See in how great misery thou art now set. Nor does he ask as one who does not know, but so that Adam might be more fittingly reproved by the Lord according to what his answer would call for. And since the angel represented the person of God and spoke in his person, whatever God did and said through that angel is ascribed to God. And God called Adam rather than Eve, because he was the more principal, to intimate that superiors, when they sin, become especially reprehensible before God. [[3:10|And he said: I heard thy voice in paradise; and I was afraid, because I was naked|Qui ait: Vocem tuam Domine, audivi in paradiso; et timui, eo quod nudus essem]] [Denis's text adds *Domine*, "O Lord", after "thy voice"], that is, made shameful by my own nakedness through the fault; [[3:10|and I hid myself|et abscondi me]], fearing and ashamed to be presented before thee in this state. Yet this answer, as to the form of the words, was foolish. For since he had been formed naked by the Creator, and left in nakedness without shame, he ought not to have said, [[3:10|I hid myself|Abscondi me]] because I am naked; but rather, because by sinning I now have a nakedness to blush for. [[3:11|And he said to him: And who hath told thee that thou wast naked|Cui dixit Deus: Quis enim indicavit tibi quod nudus esses]], that is, how dost thou now perceive and know by experience, from thy own shame and horror, that thou art naked, [[3:11|but that thou hast eaten of the tree|nisi quod ex ligno]], that is, of the fruit of the tree, [[3:11|whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldst not eat|de quo tibi præceperam ne comederes, comedisti]]? That is, this experiential and penal knowledge of thy own nakedness has come to thee from nowhere else than because thou hast transgressed my commandment, whereby thou hast deserved to be deprived of original justice and to fall into the disorder of the passions.

paras.t: Circa hæc loquitur Augustinus: Probabile est Deum per congruam creaturam in forma humana solere primis hominibus apparere, quos non permisit nuditatem suam advertere, in superna eos sustollens, nisi post peccatum eorum. Sic ergo pudore affecti, sicut solent homines nudi sub oculis hominum, quod erat de pœna peccati, utpote velle eum latere, quem nihil latere potest, et carnem ei abscondere quum corda inspiciat, volentesque esse sicut dii, evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis, et obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum, et Deo faciem avertente, stulti facti sunt. Erubescebant ergo se ipsos, et succinctoria faciebant, sed magis verebantur succincti videri ab illo, qui tanquam familiari temperamento per creaturam visibilem offerebat se videndum oculis humanis. Sic etenim apparebat, ut loqueretur hominibus tanquam homo, quemadmodum Abrahæ ad quercum Mambre. Et hac amicitia auxit et oneravit pudorem in eis post culpam, qui antea dabat fiduciam, nec audebant nuditatem suam ostendere talibus oculis, qui displicebant et oculis propriis. Dominus ergo nolens peccatorem punire, nisi pœna qua cogebatur erubescere, dixit: Quis enim indicavit tibi quod nudus esses, etc.?
paras.en: On these things Augustine says: It is probable that God was wont to appear to the first men through a fitting creature in human form, though he did not let them notice their nakedness, raising them up to things above, until after their sin. So then they were affected with shame, as men are wont to be when naked under the eyes of men, which belonged to the punishment of sin: namely, to wish to hide from him from whom nothing can be hidden, and to hide the flesh from him who sees into hearts; and wishing to be as gods, they [[Rom 1:21|became vain in their thoughts. And their foolish heart was darkened|evanuerunt in cogitationibus suis, et obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum]], and as God turned his face away, [[Rom 1:22|they became fools|stulti facti sunt]]. So they were ashamed of themselves, and made girdles; but still more they feared to be seen, even girded, by him who, as it were in a familiar condescension, offered himself through a visible creature to be seen by human eyes. For he appeared so as to speak with men as a man, as to Abraham at the oak of Mambre. And this friendship, which before gave them confidence, after the fault increased and weighed down their shame, and they did not dare to show their nakedness to such eyes, when it displeased even their own. So the Lord, not wishing to punish the sinner except with a punishment by which he was made to blush, said: [[3:11|And who hath told thee that thou wast naked|Quis enim indicavit tibi quod nudus esses]], etc.?

paras.t: Dixitque Adam, se ipsum inaniter excusando, sicque culpam culpæ adjiciendo, quia mortale peccatum mox pondere suo trahit ad aliud: Mulier quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi. Quasi dicat, Culpa mea imputanda est conjugi, imo et quodammodo tibi, qui mihi talem sociam præstitisti; sicque peccatum suum retorsit in mulierem, et ex obliquo aliqualiter in Creatorem. Josephus tamen ait, quod Adam peccati veniam postulavit, ac Deum rogavit, ne eum nimis affligeret. Et dixit Dominus Deus ad mulierem: Quare hoc fecisti? Quæ respondit, simili modo, sicut maritus, se excusando, et excessum suum serpenti imponendo: Serpens decepit me, et comedi. Erat autem excusatio Adæ irrationabilis valde, quia quum esset caput uxoris, et sapientior ac virtuosior ea fuisset, non solum non debuit ei consentire in malo, sed debuisset eam corripere. Debuit quoque culpam suam humiliter confiteri, veniamque precari; similiter femina. Præterea per hoc, quod Deus interrogavit Adam et Evam, et excusationem eorum, quamvis injustam, audivit, antequam tulit contra eos sententiam; designatur, quod nemo debeat condemnari antequam inquiratur, et locum respondendi accipiat. Unde in Actibus Apostolorum leguntur etiam Romani adhuc gentiles, hoc reservasse, dicente Festo: Non est consuetudo Romanis condemnare aliquem hominem, antequam is qui accusatur, præsentes habeat accusatores, et locum defendendi accipiat ad crimina abluenda.
paras.en: [[3:12|And Adam said|Dixitque Adam]], excusing himself in vain, and so adding fault to fault, because mortal sin by its own weight soon drags one into another: [[3:12|The woman, whom thou gavest me to be my companion, gave me of the tree, and I did eat|Mulier quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi]]. As if he said: My fault is to be imputed to my wife, nay in a way to thee, who gavest me such a companion. And so he turned his sin back upon the woman, and indirectly in some sort upon the Creator. Josephus, however, says that Adam asked pardon for his sin, and prayed God not to afflict him too much. [[3:13|And the Lord God said to the woman: Why hast thou done this? And she answered|Et dixit Dominus Deus ad mulierem: Quare hoc fecisti? Quæ respondit]], in like manner as her husband, excusing herself and laying her excess upon the serpent: [[3:13|The serpent deceived me, and I did eat|Serpens decepit me, et comedi]]. Now Adam's excuse was very unreasonable, because, since he was the head of his wife, and had been wiser and more virtuous than she, not only ought he not to have consented to her in evil, but he should have rebuked her. He ought also humbly to have confessed his fault and begged pardon; and so likewise the woman. Moreover, by the fact that God questioned Adam and Eve, and heard their excuse, unjust though it was, before he passed sentence on them, it is signified that no one ought to be condemned before inquiry is made and he has opportunity to answer. Whence in the Acts of the Apostles we read that even the Romans, still pagans, kept this, as Festus says: [[Acts 25:16|it is not the custom of the Romans to condemn any man, before that he who is accused have his accusers present and have liberty to make his answer, to clear himself of the things laid to his charge|Non est consuetudo Romanis condemnare aliquem hominem, antequam is qui accusatur, præsentes habeat accusatores, et locum defendendi accipiat ad crimina abluenda]].

paras.t: Et ait Dominus Deus ad serpentem. Cur non interrogavit serpentem? Et respondendum, quia serpens ex proprio motu non fecit hoc, nec capax fuit cognitionis intellectualis; et quia diabolus qui per serpentem id egerat, jam ante damnationis sententiam sumpsit. Serpens quoque confiteri nequivit, nec habuit facultatem se excusandi. Et rursus, quoniam serpens non peccavit revera, quamvis fuerit instrumentum peccandi, sicut et lapis seu ensis.
paras.en: [[3:14|And the Lord God said to the serpent|Et ait Dominus Deus ad serpentem]]. Why did he not question the serpent? It is to be answered: because the serpent did not do this of its own motion, nor was it capable of intellectual knowledge; and because the devil, who had done it through the serpent, had already before received the sentence of damnation. Also the serpent could not confess, nor had it the ability to excuse itself. And again, because the serpent did not really sin, although it was the instrument of sinning, as is a stone or a sword.

paras.t: Quia fecisti hoc, maledictus es inter omnia animantia et bestias terræ. Scriptura hic difficultatibus et quæstionibus plena est. Si etenim serpens non peccavit, quare maledicitur ac punitur tam dire? Cur etiam dictum est serpenti, Super pectus tuum gradieris, quasi hoc non fuerit ante naturale serpenti, quum a serpendo serpens vocatus sit? Cur item bruto locutus est Deus hæc verba, quod ea intelligere non valebat? Itaque propter has rationes quidam dixerunt, ista non posse exponi ad litteram de serpente, sed de diabolo sub appellatione serpentis. Verumtamen rationes istæ non convincunt hoc ipsum, idcirco exponenda sunt ista tam de serpente quam de diabolo.
paras.en: [[3:14|Because thou hast done this thing, thou art cursed among all cattle, and beasts of the earth|Quia fecisti hoc, maledictus es inter omnia animantia et bestias terræ]]. Here the Scripture is full of difficulties and questions. For if the serpent did not sin, why is it cursed and punished so dreadfully? Why too was it said to the serpent, [[3:14|upon thy breast shalt thou go|Super pectus tuum gradieris]], as if this had not been natural to the serpent before, since the serpent is named from creeping [*serpens*, from *serpere*, to creep]? Why again did God speak these words to a brute beast, since it could not understand them? So for these reasons some have said that these things cannot be explained literally of the serpent, but of the devil under the name of the serpent. Yet these reasons do not prove this; therefore these things are to be explained both of the serpent and of the devil.

paras.t: Itaque dixit Dominus ad serpentem. Nam, quia transgressio ista a serpente mulierem interrogante, cepit exordium, serpens primo punitur: non quia peccavit, sed in detestationem tanti peccati, ad insinuandum quantum displiceat Deo peccatum. Locutus est quoque Deus serpenti, non propter serpentem, ut intelligeret serpens, sed propter primos parentes, ut ipsi ex divina locutione et serpentis punitione addiscerent divinæ rigorem justitiæ, qui de misericordia Dei nimis præsumpserant. Quia hoc fecisti, id est, quoniam tantæ nequitiæ instrumentum fuisti, maledictus eris inter omnia animantia et bestias terræ, id est, præ omnibus brutis temporalibus pœnis eris addictus ac subditus, specialiterque contemptus, vilis et exhorrendus, quum ante habueris staturam erectam, faciem quasi virginalem ac gratiosam, prout præcedenti articulo est probatum. Super pectus tuum gradieris, id est, de cetero repende seu serpendo procedes, qui ante per pedes ambulasti erectus. Et terram comedes cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ, id est, tu qui antea vescebaris fructibus arborum, de cetero vesceris insipido cibo telluris. Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem, id est, specialiter odiosum te faciam mulieri, imo et viro, totique generi humano. Ideo subditur: Et semen tuum et semen illius, id est, inimicitiam istam inducam non solum inter te et feminam istam, sed et inter ceteros tuæ speciei serpentes, et filios primorum parentum. Unde in hac locutione magis exprimitur mulier quam vir, quoniam serpens mulierem immediate fefellit, specialiterque et directe in eam peccavit. Ipsa conteret caput tuum, id est, quia repende progredieris, mulieri conculcabilis eris, et suppeditare te poterit, quum tamen læsio capitis tui sit tibi singulariter periculosa. Unde serpens caput suum naturaliter valde custodit, tanquam sedem propriæ vitæ. Et tu insidiaberis calcaneo ejus, id est, mordere eam conaberis in inferiori parte pedis ipsius, qui erigere te nequibis ad mordendum et inferiendum eam superius.
paras.en: So [[3:14|the Lord God said to the serpent|dixit Dominus ad serpentem]]. For because this transgression took its beginning from the serpent questioning the woman, the serpent is punished first: not because it sinned, but in detestation of so great a sin, to intimate how much sin displeases God. God also spoke to the serpent, not for the serpent's sake, that the serpent might understand, but for the sake of our first parents, that from the divine speech and the punishment of the serpent they might learn the rigour of divine justice, they who had presumed too much on the mercy of God. [[3:14|Because thou hast done this thing|Quia hoc fecisti]], that is, since thou wast the instrument of so great wickedness, [[3:14|thou art cursed among all cattle, and beasts of the earth|maledictus eris inter omnia animantia et bestias terræ]] [Denis has *eris*, "thou shalt be", for *es*], that is, beyond all the brute beasts thou shalt be given over and subjected to temporal punishments, and especially despised, vile and abhorred, whereas before thou hadst an upright stature and a face as it were maidenly and graceful, as was proved in the preceding article. [[3:14|upon thy breast shalt thou go|Super pectus tuum gradieris]], that is, henceforth thou shalt go forward crawling, or creeping, who before didst walk upright on feet. [[3:14|and earth shalt thou eat all the days of thy life|Et terram comedes cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ]], that is, thou who before didst feed on the fruits of trees shalt henceforth feed on the tasteless food of the ground. [[3:15|I will put enmities between thee and the woman|Inimicitias ponam inter te et mulierem]], that is, I will make thee especially hateful to the woman, nay to the man too, and to the whole human race. Therefore it is added: [[3:15|and thy seed and her seed|Et semen tuum et semen illius]], that is, I will bring in this enmity not only between thee and this woman, but also between the other serpents of thy species and the children of our first parents. Whence in this saying the woman is named rather than the man, because the serpent deceived the woman directly, and sinned especially and directly against her. [[3:15|she shall crush thy head|Ipsa conteret caput tuum]], that is, because thou shalt go crawling, thou shalt be trodden down by the woman, and she will be able to trample thee underfoot; while a wound to thy head is singularly dangerous to thee. Whence the serpent by nature guards its head carefully, as the seat of its life. [[3:15|and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel|Et tu insidiaberis calcaneo ejus]], that is, thou shalt try to bite her in the lower part of her foot, since thou wilt be unable to raise thyself to bite and strike her higher up.

paras.t: Sed contra hanc expositionem argui potest, sicut præfatum est: Primo, quia videtur divinæ derogare justitiæ pœnam infligere sine prævia culpa, atque punire innoxium seu innocens animal. Secundo, quia non decet sapientem alloqui bestiam. Tertio, quia statura erecta soli videtur competere homini.
paras.en: But against this explanation it can be argued, as was said before: first, because it seems to derogate from divine justice to inflict punishment without preceding fault, and to punish a harmless or innocent animal; secondly, because it does not befit a wise man to address a beast; thirdly, because upright stature seems to belong to man alone.

paras.t: Ad primum horum est respondendum, quod quum mediis utendum sit secundum exigentiam finis, et omnia bruta propter hominem sint producta, nequaquam derogat divinæ justitiæ, sed congruit sapientiæ Dei, ut brutis utatur secundum quod expedit ad hominum instructionem, perterritionem aut punitionem. Ideo serpens ille taliter est punitus ad hominum, et specialiter protoplastorum, informationem. Porro, non infligere pœnam sine culpa patientis, fallit in casibus multis; imo Deus in veteri Testamento præcepit occidi jumenta, non solum si quis per ea peccaverit, sicut in Levitico jussit occidi pecus, cum quo quis coierit, sed etiam si ab homine repressa non essent ab actu solum exteriori, qui tamen in se non fuit culpabilis, sicut in Exodo præcepit interfici pecus si montem attingeret. Unde in epistola ad Hebræos ait Apostolus: Et si bestia tetigerit montem, lapidabitur. Vel in quantum pertinebant ad hominem, sicque mandavit non solum bruta, sed et inanimata propter hominum vitia destrui, ut patet in libro Josue de omnibus quæ erant in Jericho. De equis quoque et curribus Amorrhæorum, de quibus locutus est Dominus ad Josue: Equos eorum subnervabis, et currus igne combures. Et primo Regum, ubi Deus præcipit Sauli, occidere Amalecitas viros et feminas, infantes ac parvulos et jumenta, propter peccata parentum diu ante commissa: quæ omnia facta sunt ad commendationem divinæ justitiæ, ac hominum instructionem atque terrorem.
paras.en: To the first of these it must be answered that, since means are to be used according to what the end requires, and all brute animals were brought forth for man's sake, it in no way derogates from divine justice, but befits the wisdom of God, that he should use brute animals as is expedient for the instruction, frightening or punishment of men. Therefore that serpent was so punished for the instruction of men, and especially of the first-formed [that is, Adam and Eve, the *protoplasti*]. Further, the rule that punishment is not inflicted without fault in the one who suffers fails in many cases; nay, God in the Old Testament commanded beasts to be killed, not only if someone had sinned by means of them, as in Leviticus he ordered the beast to be killed with which anyone had lain[[Lev 20:15||]], but also if they had not been held back by man from a merely outward act, which yet in itself was not culpable, as in Exodus he commanded a beast to be killed if it touched the mountain[[Ex 19:13||]].
