Ad quod probandum allegant, quod Genesis primo legitur Deus dixisse, Crescite et multiplicamini: quod argumentum nil valet, quia quum hoc fuerit præceptum affirmativum, obligavit semper, sed non ad semper: idcirco executio illius præcepti fuit intelligenda pro tempore determinato, certo et apto. Unde Augustinus testatur, et præcedenti articulo tactum est, quod non genuerunt in paradiso, quia exspectabant præceptum Dei, quantum ad tempus gignendi. Et item, quod nondum acceperunt generandi præceptum, videlicet quoad temporis determinationem aut operis executionem. Illi autem errores tam stolidi sunt, textuique contrarii, ut contra eos arguere sit indignum.
paras.en: Having described the production of our first parents, their transgression and their expulsion from paradise, he next describes their generation and the multiplying of the human race. [[4:1|And Adam knew Eve his wife; who conceived and brought forth Cain|Adam vero cognovit uxorem suam Evam, quæ concepit et peperit Cain]]. By this passage a twofold error of the Jews is refuted. One is that by which they say that Adam had two wives: one, the first, whom they understand in that text of Genesis 1, [[Gen 1:27|male and female he created them|Masculum et feminam creavit eos]]; the other, the one who is read to have been made in paradise from Adam's rib. For they say that the first was made from the slime of the earth together with Adam. Hence Josephus too says that the woman was formed outside paradise and brought into paradise together with the man: "Into this garden," he says, that is, paradise, "God brought Adam and Eve, charging them to take care of its planting." And from these two wives of Adam they make up endless genealogies; indeed (so it is said) they say that apes were born of one of those wives. But their error is shown from the text, because in the course of the text no mention is made except of one wife of Adam and of the generation of men from her, and only one wife is read to have been tempted by the serpent, overcome, and expelled with Adam. And it is certain, and can very easily be proved, that apes differ from men in species. The second error of the Jews is that by which they say that Adam and Eve begot Cain and Abel in paradise. To prove this they allege that in Genesis 1 God is read to have said, [[Gen 1:28|Increase and multiply|Crescite et multiplicamini]]. This argument is worthless, because, since this was an affirmative precept, it bound always but not for always [that is, an affirmative precept is always in force, but does not oblige one to act at every moment, only at the due time]; and so the carrying out of that precept was to be understood for a determined time, fixed and fitting. Hence Augustine testifies, as was touched on in the preceding article, that they did not beget in paradise because they were awaiting God's command as to the time of begetting; and again, that they had not yet received the precept of generating, that is, as to the fixing of the time or the carrying out of the act. But those errors are so stupid and so contrary to the text that it is unworthy to argue against them.

paras.t: Cognovit itaque Adam uxorem suam Evam. Circa quod quidam scribit: Ejecti de deliciis paradisi, recurrerunt ad delicias carnis. Ex quo sequi videtur quod desiderii voluptatis carnalis fuerint moti ad commixtionem carnalem: quod non apparet consonum veritati, quoniam Adam et Eva post suam expulsionem, suam transgressionem non mediocriter deplanxerunt, atque in compunctione et contritione diu manserunt. Experti quoque poenam transgressionis divini præcepti de non edendo ex pomo, studuerunt implere præceptum Dei de generando ex zelo justitiæ et prolis amore. Nec dubitandum est, eos post expulsionem a paradiso, religiose vixisse. Peperit ergo Eva primogenitum suum Cain dicens: Possedi hominem per Deum, id est, naturali dono, virtute seu beneficio Dei, peperi et adepta sum ex viro meo filium istum: vocavitque eum Cain, quoniam Cain (secundum Hebraicam veritatem atque Hieronymum) interpretatur acquisitio sive possessio. Consuetudo autem fuit antiquis, imponere nomina pueris suis ex aliqua proprietate aut significatione. Dixit ergo, Possedi hominem per Deum, ac si gratulans et se ipsam consolans, dicat: Quamvis paradiso privata sum, et in exsilium istud projecta, ac multis ærumnis addicta, attamen Deo largiente, ex copula viri adepta sum fructum istum.
paras.en: [[4:1|And Adam knew Eve his wife|Cognovit itaque Adam uxorem suam Evam]]. On this someone writes: "Cast out of the delights of paradise, they ran back to the delights of the flesh." From this it seems to follow that they were moved to carnal union by desire of carnal pleasure; which does not appear consonant with the truth, since Adam and Eve after their expulsion lamented their transgression not a little, and remained long in compunction and contrition. Having also experienced the penalty for transgressing God's precept about not eating of the apple, they were eager to fulfil God's precept about generating, out of zeal for justice and love of offspring. Nor is it to be doubted that after their expulsion from paradise they lived religiously. Eve, then, brought forth her firstborn Cain, [[4:1|saying: I have gotten a man through God|dicens: Possedi hominem per Deum]]; that is: by the natural gift, power or kindness of God I have brought forth and obtained this son from my husband. And she called him Cain, since Cain (according to the Hebrew verity [that is, the original Hebrew text] and Jerome) is interpreted *acquisition* or *possession*. Now it was the custom of the ancients to give their children names from some property or signification. She said, then, [[4:1|I have gotten a man through God|Possedi hominem per Deum]], as if, rejoicing and consoling herself, she were to say: Although I am deprived of paradise and thrown into this exile and given over to many hardships, yet by God's bounty I have obtained this fruit from union with my husband.

paras.t: Rursumque peperit fratrem ejus Abel: in cujus ortu non legitur aliquid protulisse, quamvis forsitan protulerit, licet scriptum non sit. Moyses enim transilit multa, imo de multis scripsit perpauca. Porro Abel interpretatur uno modo luctus. Hinc in Scholastica historia legitur: Abel sonat luctus vel vapor, quasi cito hinc transiturus, tanquam ipso nomine fuerit prophetatum seu designatum, quod de ipso erat futurum. Abel tamen secundum Josephum, interpretatur, hoc nihil, quoniam non reliquit semen super terram. Hinc aliqui dicunt, quod vocatus sit Abel, id est luctus, ab eventu, quia ob ejus interfectionem fuerunt parentes ejus in gravissimo diuturnoque luctu. Aliqui quoque dicunt, quod vocatus sit Abel, id est vanitas, quia natura humana jam erat vanitati mortalitatis et instabilitatis subjecta. Abel quippe alio modo interpretatur vanitas, ut ait hic Lyra. Sed contra hoc scribit sic Rabbi Paulus: Abel, dum in Hebraico scribitur cum prima littera A, significat proprie luctum; sed dum scribitur cum littera H, ut dicatur Habel, non significat luctum, sed vanitatem dumtaxat, prout in principio Ecclesiastæ quo legitur, Vanitas vanitatum, habetur Habel, ut hic. Et ratio hujus nominationis potest accipi ex hoc, quod Abel non remansit posteritas, et ita quoad mundum sensibilem, videbatur quasi in vanum productus, quamvis quoad Deum, mansit in vita immortali. Sed ex his Rabbi Pauli verbis consequens videretur, quod in textu dici debeat Habel, quod communiter non tenetur.
paras.en: [[4:2|And again she brought forth his brother Abel|Rursumque peperit fratrem ejus Abel]]: at whose birth she is not read to have said anything, though perhaps she did, even if it is not written. For Moses passes over many things; indeed, of many he wrote very few. Now Abel is interpreted in one way *mourning*. Hence we read in the Scholastic History: "Abel means mourning or vapour, as one soon to pass hence," as though by his very name it had been foretold or signified what was to befall him. According to Josephus, however, Abel is interpreted *nothing*, since he left no seed upon the earth. Hence some say that he was called Abel, that is, mourning, from the event, because on account of his slaying his parents were in very grievous and long mourning. Some also say that he was called Abel, that is, vanity, because human nature was now subject to the vanity of mortality and instability. For in another way Abel is interpreted *vanity*, as Lyra says here. But against this Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, the converted rabbi whose Additions accompany Lyra's Postill] writes thus: "Abel, when it is written in Hebrew with the first letter A, properly signifies mourning; but when it is written with the letter H, so as to be read Habel, it signifies not mourning but only vanity, as at the beginning of Ecclesiastes, where we read [[Eccles 1:2|Vanity of vanities|Vanitas vanitatum]], it is Habel, as here." And the reason for this naming can be taken from the fact that no posterity remained to Abel, and so, as regards the world of sense, he seemed to have been brought forth as it were in vain, although as regards God he remained in immortal life. But from these words of Rabbi Paul it would seem to follow that the text ought to read Habel, which is not commonly held.

paras.t: Consequenter exprimitur diversitas officiorum horum fratrum. Fuit autem Abel pastor ovium, et Cain agricola. Abel tanquam vir simplex et innocens, elegit sibi officium simplex ac facile, scilicet pecora custodire ac pascere, quod et postea Patriarchæ fecerunt. Et possunt hoc loco nomine ovium, etiam alia pecora domestica designari. Unde et infra fratres Joseph leguntur dixisse: Pastores ovium sumus. De quibus constat, quod non solum oves, sed et alia diversa pecora aluerunt, puta camelos, capras, vaccas et boves. Cain autem tanquam versutus et cupidus, coluit terram tanquam rem magis lucrosam. Hinc in Scholastica fertur historia: Quum esset malignissimus, primus coluit terram, ut inde consuleret avaritiæ suæ. Porro Rabbi Paulus ait: Distinctio officiorum Cain et Abel, potest sic considerari. Sciens autem Abel Deum juste maledixisse terræ propter peccatum Adæ, separavit se a terræ cultura, tanquam a re maledicta a Deo, elegitque officium pastoris ovium, quoniam pecora non fuerant maledicta. Cain vero elegit sibi agriculturam, quasi non curans de Dei sententia, quod reputatum est et ad contemptum. Verumtamen istud non videtur idonee dictum. Deus enim non maledixit terræ secundum se, nec agriculturæ quasi rei illicitæ, præsertim quum in præcedenti capitulo scriptum sit: Emisit Dominus eum, videlicet Adam, de paradiso, ut operaretur terram de qua sumptus est. Unde ostenditur, quod et Adam coluit terram, quum dictum sit ei a Domino: In labore comedes ex ea. Et rursus alia littera habet: Quum operatus fueris terram, non dabit fructus suos. Idcirco, quod Cain dicitur primus terram coluisse, non videtur congrue dictum, nisi forte intelligatur quantum ad filios Adæ.
paras.en: Next the difference between the occupations of these brothers is expressed: [[4:2|And Abel was a shepherd, and Cain a husbandman|Fuit autem Abel pastor ovium, et Cain agricola]]. Abel, as a simple and innocent man, chose for himself a simple and easy occupation, namely to keep and feed cattle, which the Patriarchs too did afterwards. And in this place other domestic cattle can also be meant by the name of *sheep*. Hence below the brothers of Joseph are read to have said: We [[Gen 47:3|are shepherds|Pastores ovium sumus]] [literally "shepherds of sheep"]; of whom it is certain that they raised not only sheep but various other cattle as well, such as camels, goats, cows and oxen. Cain, on the other hand, as a crafty and covetous man, tilled the earth, as the more profitable thing. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History: "Since he was most wicked, he first tilled the earth, so as to serve his avarice from it." Rabbi Paul, again, says: "The difference between the occupations of Cain and Abel can be considered thus. Abel, knowing that God had justly cursed the earth for the sin of Adam, kept himself apart from tilling the earth, as from a thing cursed by God, and chose the occupation of a shepherd of sheep, since cattle had not been cursed. But Cain chose husbandry for himself, as if not caring about God's sentence; and this was reckoned as contempt." Yet this does not seem fitly said. For God did not curse the earth in itself, nor husbandry as an unlawful thing, especially since it is written in the preceding chapter: [[Gen 3:23|the Lord God sent him out|Emisit Dominus eum]], that is, Adam, [[Gen 3:23|of the paradise of pleasure, to till the earth from which he was taken|de paradiso, ut operaretur terram de qua sumptus est]]. From this it is shown that Adam too tilled the earth, since it was said to him by the Lord: [[Gen 3:17|with labour and toil shalt thou eat thereof|In labore comedes ex ea]]. And again another text has: [[4:12|When thou shalt till it, it shall not yield to thee its fruit|Quum operatus fueris terram, non dabit fructus suos]] [these are the words spoken to Cain in v. 12 below]. Therefore the saying that Cain was the first to till the earth does not seem fittingly said, unless perhaps it be understood with regard to the sons of Adam.

paras.t: Factum est autem post multos dies, ut offerret Cain de fructibus terræ munera Domino, quum scilicet fructus maturi erant et apti ad immolandum. Circa quod dicit quidam, quod obtulit de fructibus terræ vilioribus et corrosis. Quocirca loquitur Rabbi Paulus: Non habetur ex littera, quod Cain obtulit de pejoribus et corrosis. Simpliciter enim dicit Scriptura, quod obtulit Cain de fructibus terræ munera Domino. Sed ex providentia et diligentia Abel, intelligitur improvidentia et negligentia Cain. Verumtamen per hoc quod Scriptura manifeste testatur ipsum Abel obtulisse de primogenitis gregis sui, adipibusque eorum, probabiliter elici potest, quod Cain obtulit de vilioribus fructibus terræ: erat enim indevotus et cupidus.
paras.en: [[4:3|And it came to pass after many days, that Cain offered, of the fruits of the earth, gifts to the Lord|Factum est autem post multos dies, ut offerret Cain de fructibus terræ munera Domino]], namely when the fruits were ripe and fit to be offered. On this someone says that he offered of the poorer and gnawed fruits of the earth. Wherefore Rabbi Paul says: "It is not had from the letter that Cain offered of the worse and gnawed fruits. For Scripture says simply that Cain offered of the fruits of the earth gifts to the Lord. But from the foresight and diligence of Abel the improvidence and negligence of Cain is understood." Yet from the fact that Scripture plainly testifies that Abel offered [[4:4|of the firstlings of his flock, and of their fat|de primogenitis gregis sui, adipibusque eorum]], it can with probability be inferred that Cain offered of the poorer fruits of the earth: for he was undevout and covetous.

paras.t: Quocirca quæri potest, quis docuit filios Adæ Deo hæc immolare? Ad hoc communiter dicitur, quod Adam docuit eos. Unde in Scholastica historia fertur: Creditur Adam docuisse filios suos, ut Deo offerrent decimas atque primitias. Denique, sicut Thomas conscribit in secunda secundæ, quæstione 85: Offerre sacrificium Deo, est de lege naturæ. Naturalis enim ratio dictat, ut homo recognoscat se Deo esse subjectum, eamdemque recognitionem per exteriora signa aliqua protestetur. Naturale quippe est homini, sensibilibus signis uti ad spiritualia et interiora significanda. Hinc ex naturali ratione processit, quod homo sensibiles res obtulit Deo in signum debitæ subjectioni ac reverentiæ, atque ad protestandum se omnia sua a Domino suscepisse: talis autem oblatio sacrificium appellatur. Verumtamen determinatio sacrificiorum est ex institutione divina aut humana. Ideo quantum ad hoc, varia sunt sacrificia secundum temporum intervalla et hominum status. Hæc Thomas. Insuper, quoniam sacrificium exterius designat sacrificium illud interius, quo homo intus se ipsum offert Deo tanquam principio sui esse et fini suæ salutis: hinc quemadmodum Deo soli debetur sacrificium istud interius, ita et sacrificium illud exterius. Rursus, de qualibet re licite possessa, oblatio fieri potest in evangelica lege, similiter in lege naturæ, ut dicitur: in aliquibus tamen casibus non recipitur oblatio de re juste possessa.
paras.en: Here it may be asked who taught the sons of Adam to offer these things to God. To this it is commonly said that Adam taught them. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History: "Adam is believed to have taught his sons to offer tithes and first-fruits to God." Further, as Thomas writes in the Secunda Secundæ, question 85: "To offer sacrifice to God is of the law of nature. For natural reason dictates that man acknowledge himself subject to God, and declare this same acknowledgement by some outward signs. For it is natural to man to use sensible signs to signify things spiritual and inward. Hence it proceeded from natural reason that man offered sensible things to God in sign of due subjection and reverence, and to declare that he had received all he has from the Lord: and such an offering is called sacrifice. But the determination of sacrifices is by divine or human institution; and so in this respect sacrifices vary according to the intervals of time and the states of men." Thus Thomas. Moreover, since the outward sacrifice signifies that inward sacrifice by which man inwardly offers himself to God as the principle of his being and the end of his salvation, it follows that, just as that inward sacrifice is due to God alone, so too is that outward sacrifice. Again, an offering can be made of anything lawfully possessed, under the law of the Gospel, and likewise under the law of nature, as is said; yet in some cases an offering of a thing justly possessed is not received.

paras.t: Abel quoque obtulit de primogenitis gregis sui, id est optima et primitiva pecorum suorum, et de adipibus eorum, id est de pinguioribus ac melioribus partibus pecorum, ita quod sive integra animalia, sive animalium partes obtulerat, meliora obtulit semper. Josephus dicit quod obtulit primogenita agnorum et lac. Et respexit Dominus ad Abel et ad munera ejus, id est, approbavit et accepta habuit tam offerentem Abel quam oblationes ipsius, ita quod primo per approbationem respexit Abel propter ipsius devotionem, caritatem et gratiam, deinde ad munera ejus. Oblationes enim legis naturæ et etiam legis scriptæ, non erant ex se ipsis sanctæ aut acceptabiles Deo, sed solum ex offerentium dignitate aut bonitate. Unde communiter dicitur, quod placuerunt non ex opere operato, sed ex opere operante. Hinc Josephus: Abel, inquit, justitiam coluit, et in omnibus quæ gerebat, Deum putavit præsentem.
paras.en: [[4:4|Abel also offered of the firstlings of his flock|Abel quoque obtulit de primogenitis gregis sui]], that is, the best and first-born of his cattle, [[4:4|and of their fat|et de adipibus eorum]], that is, of the fatter and better parts of the cattle; so that whether he offered whole animals or parts of animals, he always offered the better. Josephus says that he offered the firstlings of lambs, and milk. [[4:4|and the Lord had respect to Abel, and to his offerings|Et respexit Dominus ad Abel et ad munera ejus]], that is, approved and held acceptable both Abel the offerer and his oblations; so that first, by approval, he had respect to Abel for his devotion, charity and grace, and then to his offerings. For the oblations of the law of nature, and also of the written law, were not holy or acceptable to God of themselves, but only from the worth or goodness of those offering them. Hence it is commonly said that they were pleasing not *ex opere operato* but *ex opere operante* [that is, not by the mere performance of the rite, as the sacraments of the New Law work, but by the merit of the one performing it]. Hence Josephus: "Abel," he says, "cultivated justice, and in all that he did thought God present."

paras.t: Ad Cain vero et ad munera illius non respexit: Quia nec ipse Cain Deo erat acceptus, sed reprobus propter suas malitias, idcirco nec sacrificia seu dona ipsius Deo complacuerunt. Iratusque est Cain vehementer, id est, contra fratrem suum innocentem indignabatur, inviditque ei, videns eum sibi esse prælatum in bonitate et gratia coram Deo: per quod reputavit sibi quasi primogenito ac seniori derogatum, sive injuriam factam a fratre juniore, idcirco optavit se vindicare de eo. Et concidit vultus ejus, id est, præ verecundia et tristitia tabescebat, non solum in corde, sed item in facie, quia in vultu passiones affectionesque animæ cito apparent. Propter quod in libro Proverbiorum scriptum est: Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem, in mœrore animi dejicitur spiritus. Et iterum ait Scriptura: Cor hominis immutat faciem ejus, sive in bonum, sive in malum.
paras.en: [[4:5|But to Cain and his offerings he had no respect|Ad Cain vero et ad munera illius non respexit]]: because Cain himself was not acceptable to God, but reprobate for his wickedness, neither did his sacrifices or gifts please God. [[4:5|and Cain was exceeding angry|Iratusque est Cain vehementer]], that is, he was indignant against his innocent brother and envied him, seeing him preferred to himself in goodness and grace before God; by which he reckoned that something had been taken from himself as the firstborn and elder, or a wrong done him by his younger brother, and so he desired to avenge himself on him. [[4:5|and his countenance fell|Et concidit vultus ejus]], that is, he pined away with shame and sadness, not only in heart but also in face, because the passions and affections of the soul quickly appear in the countenance. Wherefore it is written in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 15:13|A glad heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by grief of mind the spirit is cast down.|Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem, in mœrore animi dejicitur spiritus]] And again Scripture says: [[Ecclus 13:31|The heart of a man changeth his countenance, either for good, or for evil.|Cor hominis immutat faciem ejus, sive in bonum, sive in malum]]

paras.t: Sed quum nesciat homo, an amore sit dignus an odio, qualiter Cain cognovit fratrem suum cum oblationibus suis Deo esse acceptum, se autem reprobatum? Ad hoc patet responsio ex eo quod ait Hieronymus: Unde hoc potuit scire Cain, nisi vera esset interpretatio Theodotionis, qua dicitur, Et inflammavit Dominus super Abel et super sacrificium ejus: super Cain et super sacrificium ejus non inflammavit? Quorum verborum iste est sensus, quod ipso Abel offerente, descendit ignis, et incendit sacrificium ejus, quemadmodum factum legitur in Levitico de sacrificio Aaron, atque in libris Regum de sacrificiis Salomonis et Eliæ. In libro quoque Judicum legitur ignis consumpsisse sacrificium Gedeonis et Manue. Ex ista igitur inflammatione sensibili cognovit Cain quod dictum est.
paras.en: But since [[Eccles 9:1|man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|nesciat homo, an amore sit dignus an odio]], how did Cain know that his brother with his oblations was accepted by God, and he himself rejected? The answer to this is plain from what Jerome says: "Whence could Cain know this, unless the rendering of Theodotion were true, in which it is said: And the Lord set on fire over Abel and over his sacrifice, but over Cain and over his sacrifice he did not set on fire?" The sense of these words is that when Abel offered, fire came down and burned his sacrifice, as we read happened in Leviticus with the sacrifice of Aaron[[Lev 9:24||]], and in the books of Kings with the sacrifices of Solomon[[2 Par 7:1||]] [the margin gives II Par. vii, 1: the fire on Solomon's sacrifice is told in Paralipomenon] and of Elias[[3 Kings 18:38||]]. In the book of Judges too fire is read to have consumed the sacrifice of Gedeon and of Manue. From this sensible burning, then, Cain knew what has been said.

paras.t: Dixit quoque Dominus ad eum: Quare iratus es, et cur concidit facies tua? quasi dicat: Non habes rationabilem causam harum detestabilium passionum tuarum, videlicet iræ, impatientiæ, indignationis, invidiæ, et mœroris perversi, quia potius deberes congratulari fratri tuo in bonis, et gratiæ ejus cordialiter congaudere, imo et ædificari virtutibus ejus, atque ex acceptione et inflammatione munerum ejus, de tuis perversitatibus corrigi, atque ad meliora mox provocari. Nam gratia ejus tibi non noceat, et ego paratus sum tibi retribuere bona, quemadmodum ei, si egeris virtuose. Ideo subditur: Nonne si bene egeris, id est, devote obtuleris, virtuoseque vixeris, et fratri tuo favorabilis fueris, recipies? scilicet justam mercedem a me, qui non sum personarum acceptor, et inflammabo munera tua, sicut et fratris tui. Sin autem male, id est, si perverse te habeas, pejora et indevote immolando, ac fratrem innoxium odiendo, statim in foribus peccatum tuum aderit? id est, mox et evidenter coram te reus eris, ac pœnis obnoxius: quemadmodum id quod præ foribus seu ante januam stat, manifeste adspicitur. Rursus, peccatum tuum in foribus aderit, id est, iniquitas tua comitabitur te intrantem et exeuntem. Sed sub te erit appetitus ejus, id est, peccandi affectio et passio, ex qua inclinaris ad opus iniquum, esse debet rationi subjecta, ita quod potes resistere, quum liberi exsistas arbitrii. Et tu dominaberis illius, id est, dominari merito debes, quia ad hoc obligaris, ut vitiosis motibus domineris, non ipsi motus aut vitia tibi.
paras.en: [[4:6|And the Lord said to him: Why art thou angry? and why is thy countenance fallen?|Dixit quoque Dominus ad eum: Quare iratus es, et cur concidit facies tua?]] as if to say: Thou hast no reasonable cause for these detestable passions of thine, namely anger, impatience, indignation, envy and perverse grief; for thou oughtest rather to rejoice with thy brother in his goods and heartily share the joy of his grace, nay, to be edified by his virtues, and from the acceptance and burning of his gifts to be corrected of thy perversities and straightway roused to better things. For his grace would do thee no harm, and I am ready to repay thee good things, as I do him, if thou act virtuously. And so it is added: [[4:7|If thou do well|Nonne si bene egeris]], that is, offer devoutly, live virtuously and be well disposed to thy brother, [[4:7|shalt thou not receive|recipies]]? namely a just reward from me, who am no respecter of persons; and I will set thy gifts on fire, as I did thy brother's. [[4:7|but if ill|Sin autem male]], that is, if thou behave perversely, offering worse things and undevoutly, and hating thy innocent brother, [[4:7|shall not sin forthwith be present at the door?|statim in foribus peccatum tuum aderit?]] that is, thou shalt at once and evidently be guilty in thy own sight, and liable to punishment, just as what stands before the doors or at the gate is plainly seen. Again, thy sin shall be present at the door, that is, thy iniquity shall accompany thee going in and going out. [[4:7|but the lust thereof shall be under thee|Sed sub te erit appetitus ejus]], that is, the affection and passion for sinning, by which thou art inclined to a wicked deed, ought to be subject to reason, so that thou canst resist, since thou art of free will. [[4:7|and thou shalt have dominion over it|Et tu dominaberis illius]], that is, thou rightly oughtest to have dominion, because thou art bound to this, that thou rule over vicious motions, not the motions or vices over thee.

paras.t: Porro S. Hieronymus litteram LXX interpretum ponens, sic ait: Dixit Dominus ad eum: Quare concidit vultus tuus? Nonne si recte offeras, non recte autem dividas, peccasti? quiesce. Ad te conversio ejus, et dominaberis illius. Hæc est littera LXX. Deinde subdit Hieronymus: In Hebræo alius sensus est: Quare irasceris? et quare concidit vultus tuus? Nonne si bene egeris, dimittetur tibi? et si male egeris, ante fores peccatum tuum sedebit? Ad te societas ejus, sed tu magis dominare ejus. Quasi dicat: Quare irasceris, et invidia cruciatus, vultum in terram dimittis? Nonne si bene egeris, dimittetur tibi omne delictum? Vel secundum Theodotionem, Acceptabile erit, id est, munus tuum suscipiam, sicut suscepi munus fratris tui. Quod si male egeris, illico peccatum tuum ante vestibulum tuum sedebit, et tali janitore comitaberis. Sed quia liberi arbitrii es, moneo ut peccatum non tibi, sed tu peccato domineris. Hæc Hieronymus.
paras.en: Further, St Jerome, setting down the text of the Seventy translators, says thus: "The Lord said to him: Why is thy countenance fallen? If thou offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, hast thou not sinned? Be still. To thee shall be its turning, and thou shalt rule over it. This is the text of the Seventy." Then Jerome adds: "In the Hebrew the sense is otherwise: Why art thou angry? and why is thy countenance fallen? If thou do well, shall it not be forgiven thee? and if thou do ill, shall not thy sin sit before the doors? To thee shall be its fellowship, but do thou rather rule over it. As if to say: Why art thou angry, and, tormented by envy, dost cast thy countenance to the ground? If thou do well, shall not every offence be forgiven thee? Or, according to Theodotion, It shall be acceptable, that is, I will receive thy gift as I received thy brother's gift. But if thou do ill, forthwith thy sin shall sit before thy porch, and thou shalt be accompanied by such a doorkeeper. But since thou art of free will, I warn thee that sin be not master of thee, but thou of sin." Thus Jerome.

paras.t: Circa hæc verba in Scholastica historia dicitur: Recte obtulerat Cain, quia Deo; sed non recte diviserat, quia se ipsum, qui erat dignior sua oblatione, dedit diabolo. Vel, non recte divisit, quia meliora sibi retinuit. Spicas vero attritas et secus viam corrosas, obtulit Deo. Porro quod LXX transtulerunt, Ad te conversio ejus, sic potest intelligi, id est, peccatum se vertet ad te, blandieturque tibi, quoniam sua voluptate et prava libertate delectat et allicit atque impugnat.
paras.en: On these words it is said in the Scholastic History: "Cain had offered rightly, because to God; but he had not divided rightly, because himself, who was worthier than his offering, he gave to the devil. Or, he did not divide rightly, because he kept the better things for himself, and offered to God ears of corn trodden down and gnawed beside the way." Further, what the Seventy translated, *To thee shall be its turning*, can be understood thus: that is, sin will turn itself towards thee and flatter thee, since by its pleasure and wicked liberty it delights and entices and assails.

paras.t: Quæritur circa prædicta, qualiter Deus loquebatur ad Cain. Ad hoc beatus Augustinus quintodecimo de Civitate Dei, capitulo 7, breviter dat responsum: Locutus est, inquiens, Deus ad Cain eo modo, quo cum primis parentibus, per creaturam subjectam, velut eorum socius, congrua forma, id est, per angelum in humana effigie apparentem. In eodem quoque capitulo Augustinus hunc passum eleganter et prolixe exponit, inter cetera dicens: Obscuritas hujus verbi, Nonne si recte offeras, recte autem non dividas, peccasti? multos peperit sensus, quia non elucet, cur vel unde sit dictum ad Cain. Recte quippe offertur sacrificium, quum vero Deo offertur, cui soli est offerendum. Non recte autem dividitur, dum non discernuntur recte loca et tempora, in quibus est offerendum, vel res ipsæ quæ offeruntur; vel qui offert, non discernit se ipsum, et eum cui offert, aut eos quibus distribuitur ad vescendum quod oblatum est, aut electiora sibi reservat, ut per divisionem intelligamus hic discretionem. In quo autem horum Cain displicuerit Deo, non potest faciliter inveniri. Sed quia Joannes apostolus in prima sua epistola de his duobus fratribus loquens: Diligatis, inquit, alterutrum, non sicut Cain, qui ex maligno erat, et occidit fratrem suum. Et propter quid occidit eum? Quoniam opera ejus maligna erant, fratris autem justa. Ex quibus datur intelligi, ob hoc Deum non respexisse munera Cain, quia in eo male divisit, quod dedit Deo aliquid sui, et se ipsum sibimetipsi, imo et dæmoni: quod faciunt omnes iniqui, qui non Dei, sed propriam voluntatem sectantur, per quod se ipsos tradunt diabolo. Hæc sententialiter Augustinus.
paras.en: It is asked, concerning what has been said, how God spoke to Cain. To this blessed Augustine, in the fifteenth book of the City of God, chapter 7, gives a brief answer: "God spoke to Cain," he says, "in the way in which he spoke with our first parents, through a subject creature, as their companion, in a fitting form": that is, through an angel appearing in human likeness. In the same chapter, too, Augustine expounds this passage elegantly and at length, saying among other things: "The obscurity of this saying, If thou offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, hast thou not sinned? has given rise to many senses, because it is not clear why or whence it was said to Cain. For sacrifice is rightly offered when it is offered to the true God, to whom alone it is to be offered. But it is not rightly divided when the places and times in which it is to be offered, or the very things that are offered, are not rightly discerned; or when he who offers does not discern himself and him to whom he offers, or those to whom what has been offered is distributed to be eaten; or keeps the choicer things for himself: so that by *division* we are to understand here *discernment*. But in which of these Cain displeased God cannot easily be found. But since John the apostle, speaking of these two brothers in his first epistle, says: [[1 John 3:11|that you should love|Diligatis]], he says, [[1 John 3:11|one another|alterutrum]]; [[1 John 3:12|Not as Cain, who was of the wicked one and killed his brother. And wherefore did he kill him? Because his own works were wicked: and his brother's just|non sicut Cain, qui ex maligno erat, et occidit fratrem suum. Et propter quid occidit eum? Quoniam opera ejus maligna erant, fratris autem justa]] [the margin gives 1 John iii, 12; the opening words, *Diligatis alterutrum*, are the end of v. 11]: from this we are given to understand that God did not have respect to Cain's gifts because he divided wrongly in this, that he gave God something of his own, but himself to himself, nay, to the demon; which all the wicked do, who follow not God's will but their own, and thereby hand themselves over to the devil." Thus Augustine, in substance.

paras.t: Dixitque Cain ad Abel fratrem suum: Egrediamur foras. Complexum istud, Egrediamur foras, non habetur in Hebræo. Unde ait Hieronymus: Dixitque Cain ad Abel, subaudi ea quæ locutus est Dominus. Superfluum est ergo quod in Samaritanorum et nostrorum voluminibus reperitur, Transeamus in agrum. Hæc Hieronymus. Quocirca sciendum, quod Samaritani a rege Assyriorum missi, eorumque posteri, receperunt Pentateuchum, id est quinque libros Moysis, et aliqua addiderunt ac mutarunt in eis, atque ex hoc devenit additio ista ad fideles. Porro Hieronymus in libro de Hebraicis quæstionibus ait, quod Cain dixit fratri suo Abel, verba increpationis et exhortationis sibi a Domino dicta. Hebræi vero affirmant, quod dixit sibi verba injuriosa.
paras.en: [[4:8|And Cain said to Abel his brother: Let us go forth abroad|Dixitque Cain ad Abel fratrem suum: Egrediamur foras]]. That phrase, *Let us go forth abroad*, is not in the Hebrew. Hence Jerome says: "And Cain said to Abel: understand, the things which the Lord had spoken. It is superfluous, then, what is found in the volumes of the Samaritans and in ours: Let us pass into the field." Thus Jerome. On this it is to be known that the Samaritans sent by the king of the Assyrians, and their descendants, received the Pentateuch, that is, the five books of Moses, and added and changed some things in them; and from this that addition came to the faithful. Further, Jerome in the book of Hebrew Questions says that Cain spoke to his brother Abel the words of rebuke and exhortation that the Lord had spoken to him. But the Hebrews affirm that he spoke insulting words to him.

paras.t: Quumque essent in agro. Secundum Hieronymum, Cain blande induxit sanctum Abel ad exeundum secum in agrum, recitando ei verba præfata divinitus sibi dicta. Hebræi autem, qui dicunt ipsum Cain dixisse verba dura ad Abel, asserunt impium Cain observasse, quando et qualiter reperiret fratrem suum in agro solum.
paras.en: [[4:8|And when they were in the field|Quumque essent in agro]]. According to Jerome, Cain coaxingly led holy Abel to go out with him into the field, by reciting to him the aforesaid words spoken to him by God. But the Hebrews, who say that Cain spoke harsh words to Abel, assert that the wicked Cain watched when and how he might find his brother alone in the field.

paras.t: Consurrexit Cain adversus fratrem suum Abel, et interfecit eum. Ecce quanta malignitas, et quanta obstinatio hujus infelicissimi Cain, qui visibiliter ac sensibiliter ac dignantissime informatus, admonitus et blande increpatus a Deo, nequaquam pœnituit, neque compunctus est, sed auxit contemptum in Dominum. Hinc quintodecimo de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus: In electis operatur Spiritus Sanctus intrinsecus, ut valeat aliqua medicina, id est exhortatio seu increpatio, quæ adhibetur extrinsecus. Alioqui etiam si Deus ipse utens creatura sibi subjecta, in aliqua specie humana alloquatur sensus humanos, sive exteriores, sive quæ intus simillimos istis habemus in somnis, nec tamen interiori gratia mentem regat et agat, nil proficit homini omnis prædicatio veritatis. Facit autem hoc Deus a vasis misericordiæ, vasa iræ discernens, dispensatione sibi nota, multum occulta, sed justa. Deinde sequenti ibi capitulo Augustinus applicat istud ad Cain, ostendens qualiter ex Dei admonitione non sit correctus, sed potius pejoratus.
paras.en: [[4:8|Cain rose up against his brother Abel, and slew him|Consurrexit Cain adversus fratrem suum Abel, et interfecit eum]]. Behold how great the malice and how great the obstinacy of this most unhappy Cain, who, though visibly and sensibly and most graciously instructed, admonished and gently rebuked by God, did not repent at all, nor was pricked to compunction, but increased his contempt of the Lord. Hence Augustine says in the fifteenth book of the City of God: "In the elect the Holy Ghost works within, so that some medicine," that is, exhortation or rebuke, "which is applied from without, may avail. Otherwise, even if God himself, using a creature subject to him, should speak in some human form to human senses, whether the outward ones or those most like them that we have within in dreams, and yet does not rule and move the mind by inward grace, all preaching of the truth profits a man nothing. But God does this, distinguishing the vessels of wrath from the vessels of mercy[[Rom 9:22||]], by a dispensation known to himself, very hidden, but just." Then in the following chapter Augustine applies this to Cain, showing how by God's admonition he was not corrected but rather made worse.

paras.t: Præterea et alibi Rabbi Paulus ait: Notanda est hic Glossa seu translatio Chaldaica ipsius Jonathæ, quæ apud Hebræos quasi tantæ auctoritatis est sicut textus, in qua legitur: Dixit Cain ad Abel: Non est justitia neque judex, neque sæculum aliud, neque remuneratio justis, neque punitio impiis. Quumque Abel hæc omnia remisset, consurrexit Cain, et occidit eum. Ex quibus patet, quod Abel fuit primus martyr, et primus sacerdos, et primus virgo. Unde Augustinus in libro de Mirabilibus sacræ Scripturæ: Triplex justitia primo in Abel fuit, qui et munera placita Deo obtulit, ut sacerdos; et prosapiam generis, id est posteros, non reliquit in sæculo; et coronam martyrii proprii sanguinis effusione promeruit. Merito ergo Dominus Jesus commisit ei primatum justitiæ hominum: A sanguine, inquiens, Abel justi, etc. Hæc Augustinus. Hinc aliqui dicunt, quod in Abel refulsit et commendatur triplex primatus, utpote sacerdotii, virginitatis, martyrii.
paras.en: Again, Rabbi Paul says elsewhere: "Here is to be noted the Gloss, or Chaldee translation, of Jonathan himself, which among the Hebrews is of almost as great authority as the text, in which we read: Cain said to Abel: There is no justice and no judge, no other world, no reward for the just and no punishment for the wicked. And when Abel had rejected all these things, Cain rose up and killed him." From which it is plain that Abel was the first martyr, and the first priest, and the first virgin. Hence Augustine, in the book On the Wonders of Holy Scripture: "A threefold justice was first in Abel, who both offered gifts pleasing to God, as a priest; and left no lineage of his race, that is, descendants, in the world; and merited the crown of martyrdom by the shedding of his own blood. Rightly, then, did the Lord Jesus commit to him the primacy of justice among men: [[Matt 23:35|from the blood|A sanguine]], he says, [[Matt 23:35|of Abel the just|Abel justi]], etc." Thus Augustine. Hence some say that in Abel a threefold primacy shines forth and is commended, namely of priesthood, of virginity and of martyrdom.

paras.t: Verumtamen circa hoc oritur quæstio, quia (ut Hugo de S. Victore et alii concorditer protestantur) in lege naturæ primogeniti erant sacerdotes. Cain autem fuit primogenitus Adæ, vel saltem senior ipso Abel, ergo potius fuit sacerdos quam Abel. Rursus, si ideo fuit sacerdos, quoniam obtulit sacrificium Deo, ergo et simili ratione Cain. Adam quoque indubitanter obtulit Deo oblationes frequenter ante filios suos, ergo ipse fuit primus sacerdos. Ad istud videtur mihi posse responderi, quod inter filios ac posteros primorum parentum, Abel vocatur primus sacerdos, vel quia bonus fuit sacerdos, et primus sacerdotum bonorum; vel quia jus sacerdotale fuit et desuper datum, et a Cain in ipsum translatum, quemadmodum primo libro Paralipomenon, primogenita dicuntur translata a Ruben, eo quod violasset torum patris sui, et data filiis Joseph. Vel Abel vocatus est sacerdos, ab actu et devotione immolandi. Nam et filii David dicuntur fuisse sacerdotes secundo Regum.
paras.en: Yet on this point a question arises, because (as Hugh of St Victor and others agree in declaring) under the law of nature the firstborn were priests. But Cain was Adam's firstborn, or at least older than Abel; therefore he, rather than Abel, was a priest. Again, if Abel was a priest because he offered sacrifice to God, then by the same reasoning so was Cain. Adam too, without doubt, often offered oblations to God before his sons; therefore he himself was the first priest. To this it seems to me it can be answered that among the sons and descendants of our first parents Abel is called the first priest, either because he was a good priest and the first of good priests; or because the priestly right was both given him from above and transferred to him from Cain, just as in the first book of Paralipomenon the birthright is said to have been transferred from Ruben, because he had defiled his father's bed, and given to the sons of Joseph[[1 Par 5:1||]]. Or Abel is called a priest from the act and devotion of offering sacrifice. For the sons of David too are said to have been priests, in the second book of Kings[[2 Kings 8:18||]] [the Vulgate there has *sacerdotes*, priests, which the Douay-Rheims renders "princes"].

paras.t: Et ait Dominus ad Cain: Ubi est Abel frater tuus? Interrogat Dominus non quasi ignorans, sed quasi redarguendo, fratricidium improperans, atque ut impium ex sua responsione directius justiusque convincat. Qui respondit: Nescio. Ecce manifestum mendacium. Nam scivit ubi corpus ejus remansit, quod secundum Josephum occultavit: et de anima ejus poterat scire per fidem, quod in refrigerio esset. Deinde sceleratam et falsam excusationem subjungit: Numquid custos fratris mei sum ego? quasi dicat, Ego non teneor curam habere de fratre meo, nec eum ab adversis tueri aut custodire, quum tamen ex naturali lege fuerit obligatus ad ista saltem in casu, quoniam tenebatur eum diligere, sicut se ipsum. O quanta fuit duritia et impudentia Cain, qui tam frontose et quasi imperterrite ausus est respondere, quasi crimen suum posset Deum latere! Sicque impletum fuit in Cain quod Salomon ait: Impius quum in profundum peccatorum venerit, contemnit.
paras.en: [[4:9|And the Lord said to Cain: Where is thy brother Abel?|Et ait Dominus ad Cain: Ubi est Abel frater tuus?]] The Lord asks, not as if ignorant, but by way of reproof, charging him with fratricide, and so as to convict the wicked man more directly and justly from his own answer. [[4:9|And he answered: I know not|Qui respondit: Nescio]]. Behold a manifest lie. For he knew where his body remained, which, according to Josephus, he hid; and of his soul he could know by faith that it was in refreshment. Then he adds a wicked and false excuse: [[4:9|am I my brother's keeper?|Numquid custos fratris mei sum ego?]] as if to say: I am not bound to take care of my brother, nor to protect or guard him from harm; though by the natural law he was obliged to these things, at least in case of need, since he was bound to love him as himself. O how great was the hardness and shamelessness of Cain, who so brazenly and as it were fearlessly dared to answer, as if his crime could be hidden from God! And so there was fulfilled in Cain what Solomon says: [[Prov 18:3|The wicked man, when he is come into the depths of sins, contemneth|Impius quum in profundum peccatorum venerit, contemnit]].

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad eum: Quid fecisti? quasi diceret, Enorme nimis facinus perpetrasti. Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra. Ista est metaphorica et tanquam figurativa locutio, in qua non oportet singula verba accipere juxta primam et propriam significationem eorum. Est itaque sensus: Manifestum est quod fecisti: quia ipsa effusio sanguinis fratris tui hoc indicat et testatur, et quasi contra te clamat, ultionem tantæ tuæ impietatis exigens a me.
paras.en: [[4:10|And he said|Dixitque]] the Lord [[4:10|to him: What hast thou done|ad eum: Quid fecisti]]? as if he said: Thou hast committed an exceedingly enormous crime. [[4:10|the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth|Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra]]. This is a metaphorical and as it were figurative way of speaking, in which one need not take each word according to its first and proper meaning. The sense, then, is: What thou hast done is manifest; for the very shedding of thy brother's blood shows and witnesses it, and as it were cries out against thee, demanding of me vengeance for thy so great impiety.

paras.t: Qui autem curiosius investigat, quid per vocem sanguinis Abel designetur, audire potest, quod vox sanguinis dicitur sanguis ipse vociferans et vindictam expostulans. Quod totum attribuitur sanguini, non effective, sed materialiter, juxta quem modum irrationalia et inanimata dicuntur Deum benedicere et laudare. Vel vox sanguinis, appellatur jus seu debitum ultionis in sanguinis effusorem. Denique, quatuor peccata leguntur in Scripturis ad Deum pro ultione clamare, quæ et peccata clamantia nominantur. Primum est homicidium, et præsertim fratricidium, ut patet hoc loco. Secundum est vitium contra naturam, ut infra habetur: Clamor Sodomorum venit ad me. Tertium est detentio mercedis operariorum, de quo Jacobus: Clamor, inquit, eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introiit. Quartum est oppressio infirmorum. De hoc clamore sanguinis Abel, ad Hebræos scriptum est: Accessistis ad montem Sion, et sanguinis adspersionem, melius clamantem quam Abel.
paras.en: But whoever inquires more curiously what is meant by the voice of Abel's blood may hear that the voice of the blood is the name given to the blood itself crying out and demanding vengeance. All of which is attributed to the blood not effectively but materially [that is, not as the agent that cries, but as the thing that gives cause for the cry], in the way in which irrational and inanimate things are said to bless and praise God[[Dan 3:57||]][[Ps 148:1||]] [the margin gives Dan. iii, 56 and following, and Ps. cxlviii]. Or the voice of the blood is the name given to the right or debt of vengeance on the shedder of blood. Lastly, four sins are read in the Scriptures to cry to God for vengeance, which are also called the crying sins. The first is homicide, and above all fratricide, as appears in this place. The second is the vice against nature, as is found below: [[Gen 18:20|The cry of Sodom|Clamor Sodomorum]] [[Gen 18:21|is come to me|venit ad me]] [Denis joins the start of Gen 18:20 to words of 18:21]. The third is withholding the wages of labourers, of which James says: [[Jas 5:4|the cry|Clamor]], he says, [[Jas 5:4|of them hath entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth|eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introiit]] [the margin gives Jac. v, 1; the words are v. 4]. The fourth is oppression of the weak. Of this cry of Abel's blood it is written to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:22|you are come to mount Sion|Accessistis ad montem Sion]], [[Heb 12:24|and to the sprinkling of blood which speaketh better than that of Abel|et sanguinis adspersionem, melius clamantem quam Abel]] [Denis has *clamantem*, crying, where the Vulgate has *loquentem*, speaking].

paras.t: Insuper, ut refert Lyra, in Hebræo habetur: Vox sanguinum fratris tui: et dicunt Hebræi, quod ait pluraliter, sanguinum, quoniam Cain interficiendo Abel justum, factus est reus non solum sanguinis Abel, sed etiam omnium quos generaturus erat, si vivus mansisset. Ex hoc passu Scripturæ accipitur, quod evidentia patrati facinoris, non indiget accusatore seu probatione. Circa quod in Scholastica historia additur: Inde est, quod suspecti in Ecclesia de effusione sanguinis, etiamsi nemo accuset, trahuntur in causam. Quod si negaverint, judicio Dei examinentur. Hæc ibi. Porro quod ait, Judicio Dei examinentur, exponitur sic, id est, juramento, vel per ignem aut aquam. Verumtamen judicia ista per ignem et aquam, sunt modo prohibita, quoniam potius pertinere videntur ad Dei tentationem, quam hominis examinationem seu probationem. Postremo, per vocem sanguinis Abel, quidam intelligunt parentes et propinquos ipsius, qui ejusdem sanguinis […] fuerunt, et contra Cain clamaverunt ad Dominum vel directe, vel occasionaliter; quia aut ultionem […] criminis optaverunt, aut ex eorum planctu, dolore ac gemitu, Deus magis provocatus fuit ad punitionem fratricidii Cain.
paras.en: Moreover, as Lyra reports, the Hebrew has: *The voice of the bloods of thy brother*; and the Hebrews say that it speaks in the plural, *bloods*, because Cain, by killing the just Abel, became guilty not only of Abel's blood but also of the blood of all whom he would have begotten had he remained alive. From this passage of Scripture it is gathered that the evidence of a crime committed needs no accuser or proof. On which it is added in the Scholastic History: "Hence it is that those suspected in the Church of shedding blood, even if no one accuse them, are brought to trial. And if they deny it, let them be examined by the judgement of God." Thus that work. Now what it says, *Let them be examined by the judgement of God*, is explained thus: that is, by oath, or by fire or water. Yet these ordeals by fire and water are now forbidden, since they seem rather to belong to the tempting of God than to the examination or proof of man. Lastly, by the voice of Abel's blood some understand his parents and kinsfolk, who were of the same blood […], and who cried to the Lord against Cain, either directly or occasionally [that is, not by asking for it, but by giving occasion]: because either they desired vengeance […] of the crime, or from their lamentation, grief and groaning God was the more provoked to punish Cain's fratricide.

paras.t: Deinde describitur punitio Cain: Nunc igitur maledictus eris super terram. Maledictus fuit Cain de cetero super terram a Deo et coram Deo, itemque ab hominibus et coram hominibus: a Deo, quoniam plus quam ante fuit deinceps a Deo reprobatus, relictus, et a donis gratiæ elongatus. Quemadmodum autem benedictio Dei vocatur collatio gratiæ ejus, sic maledictio ejus, uno modo accipitur retractio seu denegatio gratiæ suæ. Fuit quoque maledictus coram Deo, hoc est, vero ac justo judicio Dei. Fuit recte ab hominibus maledictus, quoniam zelo justitiæ maledixerunt ei frequenter propter tantum excessum in proprium fratrem, et quia tam ineffabiliter contristavit suos parentes. Sed et coram hominibus exstitit maledictus, quoniam reputaverunt eum maledictione et omni aspernatione dignissimum. Sed si verba hæc ita erant intelligenda, videtur quod Cain desperaverit juste, utpote qui ab ineffabili Judice se damnandum audivit. Et respondendum, quod non oportebat Cain ita intelligere verba ista per omnia, sicut modo exposita sunt, quamvis sint ita in eo impleta, et secundum prædestinationem Dei sic erat decretum; imo potuit ea intelligere per modum comminationis, et quantum ad temporalem maledictionem seu pœnam. Verum et Alexander de Hales, et Guillelmus Antisiodorensis, testantur in Summis suis, quod Deus non posset de potentia ordinata alicui viatori suam damnationem absolute prædicere: quia si sic, homo viator haberet seu teneretur desperare, nec videretur desperando peccare.
paras.en: Then Cain's punishment is described: [[4:11|Now therefore cursed shalt thou be upon the earth|Nunc igitur maledictus eris super terram]]. Cain was thenceforth cursed upon the earth by God and before God, and likewise by men and before men: by God, since from then on he was more than before reprobated by God, abandoned, and removed far from the gifts of grace. For as God's blessing is the name for the bestowal of his grace, so his curse in one way is taken as the withdrawing or denial of his grace. He was also cursed before God, that is, by the true and just judgement of God. He was rightly cursed by men, since out of zeal for justice they often cursed him for so great an outrage against his own brother, and because he had grieved his parents so unspeakably. And he was also cursed before men, since they thought him most worthy of curse and of all contempt. But if these words were to be understood thus, it seems that Cain despaired justly, as one who heard from the ineffable Judge that he was to be damned. And it must be answered that Cain did not need to understand these words in every respect as they have now been explained, although they were so fulfilled in him and so decreed by God's predestination; rather, he could understand them by way of threat, and with regard to a temporal curse or penalty. Indeed both Alexander of Hales and William of Auxerre testify in their Summas that God could not, by his ordained power [that is, his power as it acts within the order he has freely established], absolutely foretell to any wayfarer [that is, a man still in this life, on the way to his end] his damnation: for if so, the wayfarer would have, or be bound, to despair, and would not seem to sin by despairing.

paras.t: Itaque maledictus eris super terram in vita præsenti, deinde sub terra in inferno, in statu futuro; quæ aperuit os suum, hoc est, intra se recepit, et deglutivit fratris tui cruorem. Unde quasi expositorie subditur: Et suscepit sanguinem fratris tui de manu tua, hoc est effusum per manus tuas sceleratissimas. Itaque Cain maledictus est in propria persona a Deo, et cum hoc in re sibi concessa ad usum, scilicet in terræ maledictione. Sicque punitus est gravius multo quam Adam, quia gravius valde deliquit, quoniam sciens patris sui justam punitionem, non timuit Deum, sed fratricidium addidit. Quum operatus fueris eam per agriculturam, non dabit tibi fructus suos, id est, sterilis erit pro parte, et frequenter, ac magis quam ex maledictione ei illata propter peccatum Adæ. Vagus per diversa et incerta loca eundo, et profugus ab hominibus fugiendo, eris super terram.
paras.en: Thus [[4:11|cursed shalt thou be upon the earth|maledictus eris super terram]] in the present life, and then beneath the earth in hell, in the state to come; [[4:11|which hath opened her mouth|quæ aperuit os suum]], that is, received within itself and swallowed thy brother's blood. Hence, as if by way of explanation, it is added: [[4:11|and received the blood of thy brother at thy hand|Et suscepit sanguinem fratris tui de manu tua]], that is, shed by thy most wicked hands. Thus Cain was cursed by God in his own person, and with this in the thing granted him for his use, namely in the curse of the earth. And so he was punished much more heavily than Adam, because he sinned much more heavily, since, knowing his father's just punishment, he did not fear God, but added fratricide. [[4:12|When thou shalt till it|Quum operatus fueris eam]] by husbandry, [[4:12|it shall not yield to thee its fruit|non dabit tibi fructus suos]], that is, it shall be barren in part, and often, and more than from the curse laid upon it for the sin of Adam. A [[4:12|vagabond|Vagus]], by going through various and uncertain places, and [[4:12|a fugitive|profugus]], by fleeing from men, [[4:12|shalt thou be upon the earth|eris super terram]].

4.title: Expositio residuæ partis hujus capituli, ab eo loco quo habetur: Dixitque Cain ad Dominum
4.title_en: Exposition of the remaining part of this chapter, from the place where it says: “And Cain said to the Lord”

paras.t: INIQUI semper ad commoda propria sunt reflexi, idcirco non timent directe Dei offensam et elongationem ab eo, sed proprias pœnas. Et quia non habent affectum ad Deum, nec eum sincere contemplantur, aut nimis præsumunt de misericordia ejus, quasi et male vivendo possint salvari, aut nimis diffidunt de illa, quasi et pœnitendo nequeant veniam promereri : quod totum ita fuit in Cain, sicut subjungitur : Dixitque Cain ad Dominum : Major est iniquitas mea, quam ut veniam merear, hoc est, tam magna est, ut veniam promereri non valeam. Hæc fuit desperatio ejus, in qua gravius Deum offendit, quam in fratricidio, præsertim quum et Judas secundum Hieronymum gravius peccavit desperando, quam Christum tradendo. Hebræi tamen (ut dicitur) exponunt verbum istud interrogative, et negative. Quasi dicat : Estne iniquitas mea tam gravis, ut non queam veniam obtinere? quasi dicat, non. Per quod innuisse videtur, quod Deus nimis dure egit secum. Unde et Josephus dicit, quod Cain sacrificavit, et Deum rogavit, ne iram, hoc est ultionem, susciperet. Et ob hoc sæviorem homicidii pœnam ei Dominus relaxavit. Sed prima expositio, quæ est Sanctorum, est melior ; quia subjungitur : Ecce ejicis me hodie a facie terræ, hoc est, a loco isto expellis me, vel a consortio hominum me repellis : et a facie tua abscondar, id est, ab adspectu misericordiæ tuæ, et a protectione tua ero alienus. Quocontra S. Job exoravit : Ne abscondas me a facie tua. Peccatum enim est medium inter Deum et peccatorem, et quasi absconditum unum ab alio, quemadmodum loquitur Isaias : Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos, et peccata vestra absconderunt faciem ejus a vobis. Vel, A facie tua abscondar, hoc est, a præsentia tua me subtraham, nec coram te apparere audebo timore pœnarum ; quemadmodum Adam et Eva, voce Dei audita, se absconderunt. Quamvis enim omnipotens Deus omnia jugiter intueatur, impii tamen quantum in ipsis est, ab eo se subtrahunt, et quærunt latere. Non enim recogitant Dei præsentiam.
paras.en: The wicked are always turned back upon their own advantage; therefore they do not fear directly the offence of God and estrangement from Him, but their own punishments. And because they have no love for God, nor contemplate Him sincerely, they either presume too much on His mercy, as though they could be saved even while living wickedly, or despair too much of it, as though even by repenting they could not merit pardon: all of which was so in Cain, as is added: [[4:13|And Cain said to the Lord: My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon|Dixitque Cain ad Dominum : Major est iniquitas mea, quam ut veniam merear]], that is, it is so great that I am not able to merit pardon. This was his despair, in which he offended God more gravely than in the fratricide; especially since Judas too, according to Jerome, sinned more gravely by despairing than by betraying Christ. The Hebrews, however (as is said), expound this saying as a question, and in the negative; as if he were saying: Is my iniquity so grave that I cannot obtain pardon? as if to say, No. By which he seems to have hinted that God dealt too harshly with him. Hence Josephus too says that Cain offered sacrifice and besought God not to take up His anger, that is, vengeance; and for this the Lord remitted to him the more savage punishment of homicide. But the first exposition, which is that of the Saints, is the better; for it is added: [[4:14|Behold thou dost cast me out this day from the face of the earth|Ecce ejicis me hodie a facie terræ]], that is, Thou drivest me out of this place, or Thou thrustest me away from the fellowship of men; [[4:14|and from thy face I shall be hid|et a facie tua abscondar]], that is, I shall be shut out from the sight of Thy mercy, and a stranger to Thy protection. Against this holy Job prayed: Hide me not from thy face[[Job 13:24||]] [the margin gives Job xiii, 24; Denis's words are not there word for word: Job 13:24 has "Why hidest thou thy face", and Job 13:20 "then from thy face I shall not be hid"]. For sin is a medium between God and the sinner, and as it were hides the one from the other, as Isaias says: [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you|Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos, et peccata vestra absconderunt faciem ejus a vobis]]. Or, [[4:14|from thy face I shall be hid|A facie tua abscondar]], that is, I shall withdraw myself from Thy presence, and shall not dare to appear before Thee for fear of punishment; as Adam and Eve, when they had heard the voice of God, hid themselves. For although almighty God beholds all things continually, yet the wicked, as far as in them lies, withdraw themselves from Him and seek to lie hidden; for they do not reflect upon the presence of God.

paras.t: Et ero vagus et profugus in terra, juxta sensum expositum. Omnis igitur qui invenerit me, occidet me ; quasi dicat : Quicumque primo occurrerit mihi, me trucidabit, tanquam a te maledictum, et omnibus odiosum. Hoc dixit, timendo ne sic eveniret. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod ex desperatione hoc dixit, quasi optando hoc ipsum, quatenus brevi ac celeri morte multas ac diuturnas calamitates sibi imminentes evaderet.
paras.en: [[4:14|and I shall be a vagabond and a fugitive on the earth|Et ero vagus et profugus in terra]], according to the sense already set out. [[4:14|every one therefore that findeth me, shall kill me|Omnis igitur qui invenerit me, occidet me]]; as if to say: Whoever first meets me will slaughter me, as one cursed by Thee and hateful to all. He said this fearing that it would so turn out. But some say that he said this out of despair, as though wishing for this very thing, so that by a brief and swift death he might escape the many and long-lasting calamities hanging over him.

paras.t: Dixitque ei Dominus : Nequaquam ita fiet, hoc est, tam austerus tibi non ero, sed tempus pœnitendi præstabo, nec te omnium occisioni expono, quasi possis a quocumque impune occidi. Vel, Nequaquam ita fiet, id est, miserias tibi instantes non evades celeri morte, sed omnis qui occiderit Cain, septuplum punietur. Verbum hoc, secundum superficiem suam, facile esse videtur, ut puta si quis occiderit ipsum Cain, punietur septies plusquam Cain pro fratricidio suo. Sed iste sensus non videtur posse defendi. Quum enim pœna correspondeat culpæ, sequetur quod occisor ipsius Cain, septies plus peccasset occidendo Cain, quam ipsemet Cain peccavit, occidendo proprium fratrem, justum ac innocentem, ex deliberatione ac mera malitia : quod nequaquam apparet, nec aliquis dicit hoc : imo communiter dicitur, quod Lamech sagittando occidit Cain nescienter, putans occidere bestiam.
paras.en: [[4:15|And the Lord said to him|Dixitque ei Dominus]]: [[4:15|No, it shall not so be|Nequaquam ita fiet]], that is, I shall not be so severe to thee, but I shall grant thee a time for repentance, nor do I expose thee to be slain by all, as though thou couldst be slain by anyone with impunity. Or, [[4:15|No, it shall not so be|Nequaquam ita fiet]], that is, thou shalt not escape by a swift death the miseries that press upon thee; [[4:15|but whosoever shall kill Cain, shall be punished sevenfold|sed omnis qui occiderit Cain, septuplum punietur]]. This saying, on its surface, seems to be easy: namely, that if anyone kills Cain himself, he will be punished seven times more than Cain for his fratricide. But this sense does not seem defensible. For since punishment corresponds to guilt, it would follow that the slayer of Cain would have sinned seven times more in killing Cain than Cain himself sinned in killing his own brother, a just and innocent man, deliberately and out of sheer malice: which by no means appears, nor does anyone say it; rather, it is commonly said that Lamech, shooting with arrows, killed Cain unknowingly, thinking he was killing a beast.

paras.t: Hinc diversi diversimode exposuerunt hoc verbum, tam Hebræi quam doctores catholici. Itaque sanctus Hieronymus ait : Quod Aquila transtulit, Septempliciter, et Symmachus, Septimus ulciscetur : majores ita intellexerunt, quod Cain interfectus est a Lamech septima generatione post Adam. Alii, quia septenarius numerus plenus est et perfectus, ita dicunt : Qui occiderit Cain, septem vindictas exsolvet. Sicque ab ingenti pœna et omni transeunti supplicio liberavit eum, scilicet Cain. Alii de septem peccatis Cain suspicantur. Primum peccatum ejus dicunt, quod non recte divisit. Secundum, quod fratri invidit. Tertium, quod dolose egit, dicendo, Transeamus in agrum. Quartum, quod eum occidit. Quintum, quod procacriter negavit seu excusavit se. Sextum, quod desperavit. Septimum, quod nec postea se correxit. Inde dicunt eum usque ad septimam generationem dilatum seu a morte protractum, ut saltem adversis compulsus, pœnitentiam ageret, et absolvi mereretur. Sed ex verbis his non videtur haberi manifesta expositio et intelligentia hujus textus.
paras.en: Hence different men have expounded this saying in different ways, Hebrews as well as Catholic doctors. Thus St. Jerome says: Where Aquila translated *Sevenfold*, and Symmachus *The seventh shall be avenged*, our elders understood it thus, that Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation after Adam. Others, because the number seven is full and perfect, say thus: He who kills Cain will pay seven penalties; and so he freed him, namely Cain, from an immense punishment and from every passing torment. Others conjecture that it is about seven sins of Cain. His first sin, they say, was that he did not divide rightly [that is, did not rightly divide his offering; the Septuagint at 4:7 reads: If thou offerest rightly, but dost not divide rightly, hast thou not sinned?]. The second, that he envied his brother. The third, that he acted deceitfully, saying, Let us pass over into the field[[4:8||]]. The fourth, that he killed him. The fifth, that he insolently denied or excused himself. The sixth, that he despaired. The seventh, that not even afterwards did he amend. Hence they say that he was put off, or kept back from death, until the seventh generation, so that at least, driven by adversities, he might do penance and merit to be absolved. But from these words no clear exposition and understanding of this text seems to be had.

paras.t: Porro in Glossa introducitur alia expositio plana et bona, quæ etiam adscribitur sancto Hieronymo : Omnis qui occiderit Cain, septuplum, hoc est valde gravi ultione, punietur. Non enim debuit homo occidere eum, cui Deus reservavit vitam vel ad pœnam ipsius, vel ad aliorum correctionem. Porro Septuaginta sic transtulerunt : Omnis qui occiderit Cain, septem pœnas exsolvet. Quod aliqui sic exponunt : Qui occiderit Cain, imponet finem pœnis temporalibus Cain, quæ usque ad generationem septimam duraverunt. Porro Lyra dicit, quod verbum istud, Septuplum punietur, non possit intelligi de interfectore ipsius Cain, propter motiva superius tacta, ideo addit : Propter quod aliter exponunt Hebræi, dicentes quod ista punitio septupla, refertur ad mortem Cain, exponendo sic litteram : Omnis qui occiderit Cain. Ibi est punctus et finis sententiæ, et subintelligitur, Graviter punietur. Sed modus punitionis non exponitur. Quod autem subditur, Septuplum punietur, secundum proprietatem sermonis Hebraici, tantum est dicere, Septennis punietur. Et intelligitur de ipso Cain, qui in fine septem generationum a Lamech occisus est.
paras.en: Further, in the Gloss another exposition is brought in, plain and good, which is also ascribed to St. Jerome: [[4:15|whosoever shall kill Cain|Omnis qui occiderit Cain]], [[4:15|sevenfold|septuplum]], that is, with very grave vengeance, [[4:15|shall be punished|punietur]]. For man ought not to kill him for whom God reserved life, either for his own punishment or for the correction of others. Further, the Septuagint translated thus: Whosoever shall kill Cain shall pay seven penalties. Which some expound thus: He who kills Cain will put an end to the temporal punishments of Cain, which lasted until the seventh generation. Further, Lyra says that this saying, [[4:15|shall be punished sevenfold|Septuplum punietur]], cannot be understood of the slayer of Cain, for the reasons touched on above; therefore he adds: For this reason the Hebrews expound it otherwise, saying that this sevenfold punishment refers to the death of Cain, expounding the letter thus: [[4:15|whosoever shall kill Cain|Omnis qui occiderit Cain]]. There is the full stop and end of the sentence, and *shall be gravely punished* is understood; but the manner of the punishment is not set out. And what is added, [[4:15|shall be punished sevenfold|Septuplum punietur]], is, according to the idiom of the Hebrew tongue, as much as to say, *He shall be punished for seven* [*septennis*, that is, through seven generations]. And it is understood of Cain himself, who at the end of seven generations was killed by Lamech.

paras.t: Sed contra istud Rabbi Paulus scribit prolixe. Primo dicit, quod ista sit expositio Rabbi Salomonis, et valde importuna textui, utpote quod ibi sit finis sententiæ, Omnis qui occiderit Cain, et subintelligatur, Graviter puniendus, et quod subticetur modus punitionis. Totum hoc, inquit, fundatur in vacuo, et contra litteram, quæ statim exprimit quantitatem punitionis illius, qui occiderit ipsum Cain : sequitur enim immediate, Septuplum punietur. Idcirco ab aliis expositoribus Hebræorum magis authenticis, aliter exponitur littera ab isto loco, Major est iniquitas mea. Ad quod sciendum, quod sententia Dei contra Cain lata, fuit gravior quam sententia contra Adam lata, in tribus. Primo, quoniam Deus non maledixit Adæ, sed terræ: Maledixit autem Deus ipsi Cain. Secundo, quoniam in sententia contra Adam lata non dicitur quod terra non daret et fructus, sed quod in labore et sudore perciperet fructus ejus. Sed contra Cain dictum est: Quum operatus fueris terram, non dabit tibi fructus suos. Tertio, quoniam Deus dedit Adæ congruum locum ad habitandum, videlicet terram, ubi formatus est. Sed ad Cain locutus est: Vagus et profugus eris super terram: quibus auditis, Cain desperavit. Petivit tamen ne puniretur plusquam audivit a Deo, utpote, ne occideretur. Et in hoc Dominus condescendit suæ petitioni tanquam justæ, et duo fecit ad tuitionem ipsius Cain. Primo, quia magnam pœnam minabatur cuicumque occisori ipsius, quod scilicet septuplum puniretur, prout littera tam Hebraica quam Latina plane sonat. Secundo, quoniam posuit signum in Cain, quod esset ab occisione securus, sicut in textu subjungitur: ideo expositio ista consonat rationi et textui, quod scilicet septies plus puniretur, qui occideret ipsum Cain, quam erat ipse Cain punitus. Hæc Rabbi Paulus.
paras.en: But against this Rabbi Paul writes at length. First he says that this is the exposition of Rabbi Solomon, and very ill suited to the text: namely that the end of the sentence is there, at [[4:15|whosoever shall kill Cain|Omnis qui occiderit Cain]], and that *is to be gravely punished* is understood, and that the manner of punishment is passed over in silence. All this, he says, is founded on nothing, and against the letter, which at once expresses the measure of the punishment of him who should kill Cain; for there follows immediately, [[4:15|shall be punished sevenfold|Septuplum punietur]]. Therefore by other expositors of the Hebrews, of more authority, the letter is expounded otherwise from this place, [[4:13|My iniquity is greater|Major est iniquitas mea]]. For which it must be known that the sentence passed by God against Cain was heavier than the sentence passed against Adam, in three respects. First, because God did not curse Adam, but the earth; whereas God cursed Cain himself. Second, because in the sentence passed against Adam it is not said that the earth would not give its fruits, but that in labour and sweat he would gather its fruits; but against Cain it was said: [[4:12|When thou shalt till it, it shall not yield to thee its fruit|Quum operatus fueris terram, non dabit tibi fructus suos]]. Third, because God gave Adam a fitting place to dwell in, namely the land where he was formed; but to Cain He said: [[4:12|a fugitive and a vagabond shalt thou be upon the earth|Vagus et profugus eris super terram]]: having heard which, Cain despaired. Yet he asked not to be punished more than he had heard from God, namely, not to be killed. And in this the Lord condescended to his petition as a just one, and did two things for the protection of Cain. First, He threatened a great punishment to whoever should kill him, namely that he would be punished sevenfold, as the letter, Hebrew as well as Latin, plainly sounds. Second, He set a mark on Cain, that he might be safe from being slain, as is added in the text. Therefore this exposition agrees with reason and with the text: namely that he who killed Cain would be punished seven times more than Cain himself had been punished. Thus far Rabbi Paul.

paras.t: Denique ad objectiones contra hoc introductas, respondet dupliciter: Primo, quod iste qui occidisset ipsum Cain, fuisset septies plus punitus, in quantum fecisset hoc contra specialem assecurationem, qua Deus assecuravit ipsum Cain ab occisione, cum appositione signi assecurationis. Secundo, quia interdum majores pœnæ taxantur minoribus criminibus, ad quæ homines sunt proniores: et ita in proposito fuit, quia ad ipsius Cain occisionem multi fuissent proniores, propter ipsius malitiam excessivam, quam ad interficiendum homines alios. Deinde Rabbi Paulus fortiter dicit et tenet, quod Cain non fuit occisus a Lamech, nec ab aliquo alio homine. Ad quod primo allegat Hieronymum in libro de Quæstionibus novi ac veteris Testamenti, dicentem: Frustra putant qui arbitrantur, quod Lamech dixerit de Cain: Occidi virum in furore meo, et juvenem in vulnere meo. Deinde probat istud ex textu, quia quum Cain dixisset Deo, Omnis igitur qui invenerit me, occidet me, Deus statim respondit: Nequaquam ita fiet. Unde non videtur rationabiliter dictum, quod divina assertio frustraretur. Ideo secundum expositionem istam tenetur quod Cain nunquam fuit occisus, sed solum punitus juxta divinam sententiam contra eum latam usque diluvium, in quo diluvio secundum quosdam de antiquis Hebræis, submersus fuit cum omni sua posteritate. Ideo dicunt, quod Scriptura non dicit, quanto tempore vixerit Cain, nec etiam aliquis de successoribus suis, sicut de aliis, eo quod omnes pariter sint submersi. Et probabiliter dici potest, quod Deus voluit ipsum Cain ab occisione tueri, ut pœna sui facinoris ab hominibus diutius videretur, propter quod etiam voluit eum vagum et profugum per mundum discurrere, ut in pluribus locis justitia Dei circa ipsum ostenderetur. Hæc Rabbi Paulus.
paras.en: Then to the objections brought against this he replies in two ways. First, that he who had killed Cain would have been punished seven times more inasmuch as he would have done it against the special assurance by which God assured Cain against being slain, with the addition of a sign of that assurance. Second, because sometimes greater penalties are fixed for lesser crimes, to which men are more prone; and so it was in the case before us, because many would have been more prone to kill Cain, on account of his excessive wickedness, than to kill other men. Then Rabbi Paul says and firmly holds that Cain was not killed by Lamech, nor by any other man. For this he first alleges Jerome in the book of Questions on the New and Old Testament, who says: They think in vain who suppose that Lamech said of Cain: [[4:23|I have slain a man|Occidi virum]] in my fury, and a youth in my wound [Denis's text reads *in furore meo … in vulnere meo*; the Vulgate has *in vulnus meum … in livorem meum*, "to the wounding of myself … to my own bruising"]. Then he proves this from the text: for when Cain had said to God, [[4:14|every one therefore that findeth me, shall kill me|Omnis igitur qui invenerit me, occidet me]], God at once answered: [[4:15|No, it shall not so be|Nequaquam ita fiet]]. Hence it does not seem reasonably said that the divine assertion was made void. Therefore according to this exposition it is held that Cain was never killed, but only punished according to the divine sentence passed against him, until the flood; in which flood, according to some of the ancient Hebrews, he was drowned with all his posterity. And so they say that Scripture does not say how long Cain lived, nor any of his successors either, as it does of the others, because all were drowned together. And it can probably be said that God willed to protect Cain from being slain so that the punishment of his crime might be seen by men for a longer time; for which reason also He willed him to roam as a vagabond and fugitive through the world, so that the justice of God concerning him might be shown in many places. Thus far Rabbi Paul.

paras.t: Præterea circa hæc verba primo pensandum est, quod expositio ista, quam acriter reprobat Rabbi Paulus, non solum est Rabbi Salomonis et Lyræ, sed etiam multorum catholicorum et antiquorum doctorum fidelium. Ait enim auctor Scholasticæ historiæ: Omnis qui occiderit Cain, supplendum est, Liberabit eum a laboribus atque miseria. Et tunc additur impersonaliter, Septuplum punietur, id est, punitio fiet de eo, id est de Cain, dum vivit in pœna usque ad septimum Lamech. Hæc expositio convenit cum præfata in hoc, quod facit punctum et finem sententiæ ibi, Omnis qui occiderit Cain; et aliquid ibidem subaudit, et deinde de ipso Cain exponit, Septuplum punietur. Quod autem subaudit, Liberabit eum, potius quam, Graviter punietur, procedit secundum expositionem, qua Cain dicitur optando dixisse: Omnis qui invenerit me, occidet me. Sicque habetur in Glossa: Non morieris cito sicut vis, quia punietur (impersonaliter, id est, punitio fiet de te) septuplum, quoniam vives in cruciatu usque ad septimam generationem, in qua a Lamech occideris. Ergo, Omnis qui occiderit, subaudis, Liberabit te ab illo male conscientiæ cruciatu. Hæc Glossa. Simili autem ratione, secundum expositionem qua Cain dicitur timendo dixisse, Omnis qui invenerit me, subintelligendum est post verbum istud, Omnis qui occiderit Cain, graviter punietur. Propter quod etiam non oportuit illam expositionem Hebræis adscribere, quasi ipsi in hoc melius exponerent litteram istam, quam doctores catholici.
paras.en: Besides this, concerning these words it must first be weighed that the exposition which Rabbi Paul so sharply rejects is not only that of Rabbi Solomon and of Lyra, but also of many Catholic, ancient and faithful doctors.
