And at first either they themselves or their fathers were devout: so they were called sons of God, or angels, in the way that in the Scriptures certain men are named angels by reason of their life or office, as priests are called in the prophet Malachias [[Mal 2:7|the angel of the Lord of hosts|angeli Domini exercituum]]. And of the most blessed John the Baptist it was foretold: [[Mal 3:1|Behold I send my angel|Ecce mitto angelum meum]]. They are also called sons of the gods, that is, of godly men. And by the daughters of men are understood the daughters born of the seed of Cain, who were wanton, proud, vain and fair; taken with love of them, the sons of Seth married them; and then vices prevailed everywhere upon the earth, so that very few good men remained.

paras.t: Quocirca quæri potest, quo tempore, seu quamdiu ante diluvium factum sit istud. Ad hoc in Scholastica historia respondetur : Tempus quando hoc factum fuit, utrum sub Noe, an ante ; et utrum diu aut parum ante, non determinat Scriptura. Porro Josephus dicit, quod filii Seth usque ad septimam generationem boni manserunt. Post ad vitia sunt delapsi a patribus solennitatibus, id est, ritibus seu observantiis recedentes. Methodius vero causam diluvii et tempus vitiorum illorum diffusius exsequitur dicens : Anno quingentesimo primæ chiliadis, hoc est primi millenarii, filii Cain abutebantur uxoribus fratrum suorum nimiis fornicationibus : sexcentesimo anno, mulieres in amentiam versæ, supergressæ seu superjacentes viris abutebantur. Mortuo Adam, Seth separavit cognationem suam a cognatione Cain. De isto multa dicuntur in prælata Scholastica historia, quæ requirantur ibidem. Alibi legitur, quod anno sexcentesimo vitæ Adæ, cœperunt filii Cain abuti uxoribus fratrum suorum per nimias fornicationes. Octingentesimo anno vitæ Adæ, dilatatæ sunt fornicationes super terram nimis et immunditiæ a filiis Cain. Præceperat autem Adam filio suo Seth, ne cognatio sua misceretur nationi Cain. Quadragesimo anno Jared, in secundo millenario sæculi, fuerunt viri malefici, et artis pessimæ inventores de filiis Cain, et omnis immunditia atque spurcitia filiorum Lamech post annos septingentos sub tempore vitæ Jared, cœpit multa malitia pejor priore crescere super terram, quæ a nobis est omittenda. Tunc concupierunt filii Dei filias hominum, et genuerunt ex eis gigantes, qui erant atrocissimi præ cunctis hominibus.
paras.en: Here it may be asked at what time, or how long before the flood, this took place. To this the Scholastic History answers: The time when this was done, whether under Noe or before, and whether long or a little before, Scripture does not determine. Josephus, further, says that the sons of Seth remained good up to the seventh generation. Afterwards they fell away into vices, departing from the solemnities of their fathers, that is, from their rites or observances. But Methodius sets out the cause of the flood and the time of those vices at greater length, saying: In the five hundredth year of the first chiliad, that is, of the first thousand years, the sons of Cain abused the wives of their brethren with excessive fornications; in the six hundredth year the women, turned to madness, overstepping, or lying upon, the men, abused them. When Adam was dead, Seth separated his kindred from the kindred of Cain. Of this much is said in the Scholastic History already cited, which may be sought there. Elsewhere it is read that in the six hundredth year of Adam's life the sons of Cain began to abuse the wives of their brethren by excessive fornications. In the eight hundredth year of Adam's life fornications and uncleannesses were spread exceedingly over the earth by the sons of Cain. Now Adam had commanded his son Seth that his kindred should not be mingled with the nation of Cain. In the fortieth year of Jared, in the second millennium of the world, there were among the sons of Cain evil-doers and inventors of a most wicked art, and all the uncleanness and filth of the sons of Lamech; after seven hundred years, in the time of Jared's life, much wickedness, worse than the former, began to grow upon the earth, which we must pass over. Then the sons of God desired the daughters of men, and begot of them giants, who were the most savage of all men.

paras.t: Dixitque Deus. Cui vel qualiter dixit, hoc Scriptura non exprimit. Itaque dixit vel in se ipso hæc cogitans, ac decernens sive definiens, vel per inspirationem internam, aut angelicam revelationem ac apparitionem, locutus est alicui sancto viro, potissime sancto Noe : Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est. Hoc multis modis exponitur. Primo sic : Non permanebit spiritus meus, hoc est ira seu indignatio mea, in hominem, id est contra homines, in æternum, hoc est absque fine. Quasi dicat : Temporaliter puniam eum, non æternali supplicio, quia caro est, id est pronus ad vitia, fragilis, atque multiplici infirmitate circumdatus. Ita exponit Hieronymus, dicens : Quia fragilis est hominum conditio, non eos æterno cruciatui reservabo, sed hic eis retribuam quod merentur. Clementia ergo est, non severitas, quod peccator hic pro scelere visitatur. Unde secundum Hieronymum, in Hebræo est : Non judicabit spiritus meus hominem in æternum. Quidam exponunt sic : Non permanebit spiritus meus, hoc est, anima humana a me creata non perseverabit in homine in æternum ; quia per diluvium animæ hominum auferentur a suis corporibus. Alii ita exponunt : Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine, hoc est, Spiritus Sanctus non permanebit de cetero in istis hominibus, in quibus erat, quamdiu filii Dei erant. Quia caro sunt, id est, totaliter carnales et turpes effecti sunt. Hunc sensum sæpe tangit S. Bernardus.
paras.en: [[6:3|And God said|Dixitque Deus]]. To whom or in what way He said it, Scripture does not express. So He said it either within Himself, thinking it and decreeing or determining it, or He spoke, by inward inspiration or by an angel's revelation and appearance, to some holy man, above all to holy Noe: [[6:3|My spirit shall not remain in man for ever, because he is flesh|Non permanebit spiritus meus in homine in æternum, quia caro est]]. This is expounded in many ways. First thus: [[6:3|My spirit shall not remain|Non permanebit spiritus meus]], that is, My wrath or indignation, [[6:3|in man|in hominem]], that is, against men, [[6:3|for ever|in æternum]], that is, without end. As if He said: I will punish him in time, not with eternal punishment, [[6:3|because he is flesh|quia caro est]], that is, prone to vices, frail, and beset with manifold infirmity. So Jerome expounds it, saying: Because the condition of men is frail, I will not keep them for eternal torment, but will repay them here what they deserve. It is therefore clemency, not severity, that the sinner is visited here for his crime. Hence according to Jerome the Hebrew has: My spirit shall not judge man for ever. Some expound it thus: My spirit shall not remain, that is, the human soul created by Me shall not continue in man for ever; for through the flood the souls of men will be taken from their bodies. Others expound it thus: My spirit shall not remain in man, that is, the Holy Ghost shall not henceforth remain in these men, in whom He was as long as they were sons of God. Because they are flesh, that is, they have become wholly carnal and foul. St Bernard often touches on this sense.

paras.t: Eruntque dies illius centum viginti anni : id est, hominibus istis dabo adhuc tempus pœnitendi, et dilationem debitæ pœnæ, ut corrigant se per centum et viginti annos. Hoc addidit Deus, ne quasi crudelis, videretur locum et tempus pœnitendi non præstitisse peccatoribus illis. Denique Strabus ait, quod Deus hæc dixit eodem anno quo arca cœpit ædificari. Sed quia iniqui illi non correxerunt se, Deus per viginti annos anticipavit vindictam, inducendo diluvium per tot annos citius quam prædixit. Hieronymus vero circa hæc verba dicit, quod Deus dixit ea ad Noe per viginti annos antequam arca cœpta est fieri. Verumtamen alibi tangit et approbat sensum, qui secundum Strabum jam tactus est. Itaque Deus non dixit hæc verba, præscribendo spatium vitæ humanæ post diluvium, sed determinando tempus pœnitendi, et ad inundationem diluvii, secundum Hieronymum. Idem ait Augustinus quintodecimo de Civitate Dei, ubi ait, aliquos post diluvium excessisse quingentesimum annum. Et infra habetur, quod plurimi post diluvium plusquam ducentis annis vixerunt. Verumtamen Josephus opinatus est, Deum dixisse hæc verba, statuendo terminum vitæ humanæ post diluvium.
paras.en: [[6:3|and his days shall be a hundred and twenty years|Eruntque dies illius centum viginti anni]]: that is, I will still give these men time for repentance, and a delay of the punishment due, that they may amend themselves, for a hundred and twenty years. God added this lest He should seem cruel, as if He had not afforded those sinners place and time for repentance. Strabo, further, says that God said this in the same year in which the ark began to be built. But because those wicked men did not amend themselves, God hastened the vengeance by twenty years, bringing on the flood so many years sooner than He had foretold. Jerome, on the other hand, says on these words that God said them to Noe twenty years before the ark was begun. Yet elsewhere he touches on and approves the sense already given after Strabo. So God did not say these words to prescribe the span of human life after the flood, but to fix the time for repentance, up to the overflowing of the flood, according to Jerome. Augustine says the same in the fifteenth book of The City of God, where he says that some after the flood passed their five hundredth year. And below we find that very many after the flood lived more than two hundred years. Yet Josephus was of the opinion that God said these words to fix the term of human life after the flood.

paras.t: Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis, in quibus filii Dei acceperant filias hominum in uxores ; idcirco mox subditur, qualiter factum sit, quod gigantes tunc erant in terra. Postquam autem ingressi sunt filii Dei ad filias hominum, id est, viri nati ex Seth, qui ad tempus erant devoti, cognoverunt conjuges suas ex semine Cain ortas ; […]que filiæ gestarunt, isti sunt potentes robore corporali et dominatione terrena aliis præsidendo, a sæculo, id est a prima mundi ætate, seu ab antiquis temporibus, et viri famosi, id est multum nominati, quos excessiva sua malitia fecit famosos, et etiam in quibusdam naturalibus donis ac bonis fortunæ fuerant excellentes. Erant namque gigantes valde proceræ staturæ, excellentis potentiæ ac pluribus præsidentes ; erant et mente feroces, superbissimi corde, incircumcisique moribus, carnales, violenti, ac vitiis pleni. Quum itaque filiæ istæ genuissent, Isti sunt potentes, hoc est, nati ex illis, sunt potentes a sæculo ac famosi, puta gigantes.
paras.en: [[6:4|Now giants were upon the earth in those days|Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis]], in which the sons of God had taken the daughters of men as wives; therefore it is at once added how it came about that there were giants on the earth then. [[6:4|For after the sons of God went in to the daughters of men|Postquam autem ingressi sunt filii Dei ad filias hominum]], that is, the men born of Seth, who for a time were devout, knew their wives sprung from the seed of Cain; [[6:4|and they brought forth children|filiæ gestarunt]] [a word is lost in the transcription before 'filiæ gestarunt', 'the daughters bore'; the Vulgate has 'illæque genuerunt'], [[6:4|these are the mighty men|isti sunt potentes]] in bodily strength and in earthly dominion, ruling over others, [[6:4|of old|a sæculo]], that is, from the first age of the world, or from ancient times, and [[6:4|men of renown|viri famosi]], that is, much spoken of, whom their excessive wickedness made renowned, and who were also excellent in certain natural gifts and goods of fortune. For the giants were of very tall stature, of surpassing might, and ruling over many; they were also fierce of mind, most proud of heart, uncircumcised in their ways, carnal, violent and full of vices. When therefore these daughters had borne, These are the mighty men: that is, those born of them are mighty from of old and renowned, namely the giants.

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit Rabbi Paulus, quod ex quo in Hebræo habetur, Nephilim, quod interpretatur cadentes, ideo per gigantes primo ac proprie atque ad litteram dæmones designantur, qui corruerunt de cœlo. Sed sicut præhabitum est, istud non valet, et est contra Augustinum aperte aliosque doctores, imo et scripturæ huic non consonat, quæ loquitur de gigantibus istis tanquam de hominibus, et asserit eos in concubitu natos, ita quod non sunt spirituales substantiæ, nec dæmones incubi. Argumentum quoque ipsius infirmum est. Non enim ex nominum interpretatione potest semper sumi expositio litteralis, imo sensus qui ex interpretatione hujusmodi sumitur, est communiter spiritualis, ex quo argumentum sumi non valet. Denique casus est multiplex : idcirco quod dicitur Cadentes, multipliciter accipi potest, imo in bono et malo. Nam et Prophe[…] quando […] aliquid contemplabantur, cadebant in terram et super faciem suam, ut Origenes disserunt, et ipsi Prophetæ insinuant, Ezechiele dicente : Vidi, et cecidi in faciem meam. Isaias quoque : Corrui, inquit, quum viderem. Quemadmodum autem dæmones appellantur cadentes, quoniam ceciderunt de cœlo, atque ad spiritualia vitia corruerunt ; ita gigantes vocantur cadentes, quoniam ad carnalia, imo ad omnia pene corruerunt facinora. Unde in Scholastica historia fertur : Gigantes dicuntur a geos, quod est terra, quasi terreni. Cui concordat quod ait Glossa : Gigantes filii terræ dicuntur.
paras.en: On this Rabbi Paul writes that, since the Hebrew has Nephilim, which is interpreted falling ones, the giants therefore designate first, properly and according to the letter the demons who fell from heaven. But, as was said before, this does not hold, and is openly against Augustine and other doctors; nay, it does not agree with this Scripture either, which speaks of these giants as of men, and asserts that they were born of intercourse, so that they are not spiritual substances, nor incubus demons. His argument, too, is weak. For the literal exposition cannot always be taken from the interpretation of names; nay, the sense taken from an interpretation of this kind is commonly a spiritual one, from which an argument cannot be drawn. Lastly, falling is of many kinds: so what is called falling ones can be taken in many ways, in a good sense as well as a bad. For the Prophets too, when they contemplated something […], used to fall to the ground and upon their face, as Origen […] explain [the transcription has lost words here ('Nam et Prophe[…] quando […] aliquid contemplabantur'), and the plural 'disserunt' suggests that a name after Origen is lost too], and as the Prophets themselves intimate, Ezechiel saying: [[Ezech 2:1|I saw, and I fell upon my face|Vidi, et cecidi in faciem meam]] [the margin note is unreadable; the words are those of Ezech 2:1, numbered 1:28 in the Vulgate]; Isaias too: I fell down, he says, when I saw[[Is 21:3||]] [the margin note is unreadable; the nearest words are Is 21:3, 'I fell down at the hearing of it, I was troubled at the seeing of it']. And just as the demons are called falling ones because they fell from heaven and rushed into spiritual vices, so the giants are called falling ones because they rushed into carnal crimes, nay into almost all crimes. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History: Giants are so called from geos, which is earth, as if earthly. With this agrees what the Gloss says: Giants are called sons of the earth.

paras.t: Primo quæri potest, anne in terra fuerunt gigantes ante concubitum filiorum Seth cum filiabus Cain. Ad quod beatus Augustinus manifeste respondet, quod imo, et probat hoc ex littera ista. Verumtamen probatio Augustini procedit secundum litteram Septuaginta interpretum. Unde Augustinus ita allegat hunc textum : Factum est postquam cœperunt homines multi fieri super terram, videntes angeli Dei filias hominum, etc. Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis. Et post illud : Quum intrarent filii Dei ad filias hominum, et generabant sibi, illi erant gigantes a sæculo homines nominati. Ex his verbis litteræ Augustinus concludit : Hæc verba Libri divini satis indicant, jam illis diebus fuisse gigantes super terram, quando filii Dei acceperunt uxores filias hominum. Deinde addit : Sed et postquam hoc factum est, nati sunt gigantes. Sic enim ait Scriptura : Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis. Et post illud : Quum intrarent filii Dei ad filias hominum. Ergo et ante, et illis diebus, et post illud tempus fuerunt. Porro ex nostra translatione istud non sequitur, saltem tam evidenter : quia quum dictum est, Gigantes erant super terram in diebus illis, mox subditur : Postquam enim ingressi sunt filii Dei, etc. In quibus verbis redditur causa, cur dictum sit, quod gigantes tunc erant super terram. Quod tamen posset exponi de causa a posteriori, quæ dicitur causa effectus. Verbis autem Augustini concordat quod ait Methodius martyr : Natus est Adæ filius nomine Seth, vir gigas magnus. Ex quo sequeretur, quod non omnes gigantes mali fuerunt.
paras.en: First it may be asked whether there were giants on the earth before the union of the sons of Seth with the daughters of Cain. To this blessed Augustine plainly answers that there were, and proves it from this very text. Yet Augustine's proof proceeds according to the text of the Septuagint translators. So Augustine cites this text thus: It came to pass, after men began to be many upon the earth, the angels of God seeing the daughters of men, etc. [[6:4|Now giants were upon the earth in those days|Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis]]. And after that: When the sons of God went in to the daughters of men, and begot for themselves, those were the giants, men of renown from of old. From these words of the text Augustine concludes: These words of the divine Book show clearly enough that there were already giants on the earth in those days when the sons of God took the daughters of men to wife. Then he adds: But after this was done, too, giants were born. For thus says Scripture: [[6:4|Now giants were upon the earth in those days|Gigantes autem erant super terram in diebus illis]]. And after that: When the sons of God went in to the daughters of men. Therefore they existed both before, and in those days, and after that time. But from our translation this does not follow, at least not so evidently: for when it has been said, [[6:4|giants were upon the earth in those days|Gigantes erant super terram in diebus illis]], there is at once added: [[6:4|For after the sons of God went in|Postquam enim ingressi sunt filii Dei]], etc. In these words the reason is given why it was said that the giants were then upon the earth. This, however, could be expounded of a cause a posteriori, which is called the cause of the effect [that is, a reason from which the thing is known, not one by which it comes to be]. With Augustine's words agrees what Methodius the martyr says: There was born to Adam a son named Seth, a man, a great giant. From which it would follow that not all the giants were wicked.

paras.t: Præterea, sicut loquitur Augustinus, hoc movet quosdam, quod ex filiis Dei et filiabus hominum, non quasi homines nostri generis, sed gigantes legimus esse natos. Ad quod ibidem Augustinus respondet : Quasi etiam non nostris temporibus nata sint corpora hominum, longe excedentia modum nostrum. Nonne ante paucos annos nata est Romæ puella, quæ fuit ibi cum suis parentibus, et corpore giganteo longe ceteris præminebat ? Ad quam videndam fiebat mirabilis populorum concursus. Et hoc erat maximæ admirationis, quod ambo parentes ejus non erant tam magnæ quantitatis, sicut quosdam videmus. Hæc Augustinus. Insuper infra in libro Numerorum et Deuteronomio, et in Paralipomenon scribuntur fuisse gigantes, quos ipsa Scriptura docet ex hominibus natos, quamvis Rabbi Paulus scribat circa hunc passum, etiam gigantes qui fuerunt post diluvium, ex dæmonibus incubis natos, quod nec Scripturis, nec doctoribus consonat, prout Deo præstante, suis locis plenius ostenditur. Unde in Scholastica historia legitur : Post diluvium nati sunt alii gigantes in Hebron, et post in Tanis civitate Ægypti, a qua Titanes vocati sunt. De quorum stirpe fuit Enac, cujus filii habitaverunt in Hebron, de quibus ortus est Goliath, et alii quidam. Ex quibus omnibus innotescit, gigantes naturaliter generari, quamvis ad eorum generationem concurrant cœlestes influentiæ naturalesque causæ satis speciales atque occultæ, nec ad eorum generationem requiritur cooperatio dæmonum, seu adhibitio quorumdam seminum occultorum per dæmones, ut Rabbi Paulus affirmat, quamvis fortassis interdum ita contingere queat. Postremo, qui dicuntur esse homines parvuli naturaliter, distant valde a nostrorum corporum quantitate : […]ste gigantes possunt naturaliter nostram quantitatem multum excedere.
paras.en: Moreover, as Augustine says, some are troubled by this: that we read that there were born of the sons of God and the daughters of men not men, as it were, of our own kind, but giants. To which Augustine answers in the same place: As if even in our own times there had not been born bodies of men far exceeding our measure! Was there not born at Rome a few years ago a girl, who lived there with her parents, and with a giant's body far surpassed all others? A marvellous concourse of people came to see her. And what caused the greatest wonder was that neither of her parents was of such great size as some we see. Thus Augustine. Besides, further on, in the book of Numbers[[Num 13:33||]] and in Deuteronomy[[Deut 2:20||]], and in Paralipomenon[[1 Par 11:23||]], giants are written of whom Scripture itself teaches that they were born of men; although Rabbi Paul writes on this passage that even the giants who lived after the flood were born of incubus demons, which agrees neither with the Scriptures nor with the doctors, as will be shown more fully in its places, God granting. Hence it is read in the Scholastic History: After the flood other giants were born in Hebron, and afterwards in Tanis, a city of Egypt, from which they were called Titans. Of their stock was Enac, whose sons dwelt in Hebron, from whom sprang Goliath and certain others. From all of which it is known that giants are begotten naturally, although special and hidden heavenly influences and natural causes concur in their begetting; nor is the cooperation of demons, or the application of certain hidden seeds by demons, required for their begetting, as Rabbi Paul affirms, though perhaps it might sometimes happen so. Lastly, those who are said to be little men by nature differ greatly from the size of our bodies: […] these giants can naturally far exceed our size [the first word or two of this line, at the top of a column (PDF 258), are lost in the transcription; the sense is 'so also these giants'].

paras.t: Videns autem Deus quod multa malitia hominum esset in terra, hoc est, quod homines multa et magna facinora perpetrarent, et cuncta cogitatio cordis humani intenta esset ad malum omni tempore, hoc est, quod homines illius temporis indesinenter excogitabant studiose, qualiter possent sua pravissima desideria adimplere, atque ad libitum prævaricari ac delectari, ita quod ex proposito et certa malitia, non ex ignorantia et infirmitate, seu passione solummodo peccaverunt, quemadmodum scriptum est de quibusdam, Scrutati sunt iniquitates ; pœnituit eum, quod hominem fecisset in terra, id est, per modum pœnitentis se habuit circa hoc. Non enim mutatio aliqua, nec passionum affectus, nec pœnitudo de facto præterito cadere potest in Deo absolute perfecto, in quo est sapientia infinita, beatitudo immensa, invariabilitasque æterna. Unde per Malachiam testatur : Ego Dominus, et non mutor. Et præcavens in futurum, id est, præfatis malitiis hominum obicem ponere, ac finem imponere proponens, et tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus, hoc est, suis effectibus, præsertim hominibus ad suam imaginem conditis, quasi intime condolens instar piissimi patris, utpote per modum contristatissimi habens se, quum tamen in se ipso incommutabiliter infinita jucunditate superplenissimus esset : juxta quem modum loquendi scriptum est in libro Judicum, Dominus doluit super miseriis eorum : de quo nihilo minus primo Regum Samuel ait : Triumphator in Israel pœnitudine non flectetur ; neque enim homo est ut agat pœnitentiam. Delebo, inquit, hominem quem creavi, a facie terræ, id est, universum genus humanum, perpaucis demptis, occidam diluvio : ab homine usque ad animantia, id est tam homines quam animalia terrestria ; a reptili usque ad volucres cœli, hoc est tam reptilia terræ quam aves cœli aerei : pœnitet enim me fecisse eos, id est, per modum ejus quem pœnitet ea fecisse quæ destruit, habeo me, in eo quod intendo præfata opera mea occidere.
paras.en: [[6:5|And God seeing that the wickedness of men was great on the earth|Videns autem Deus quod multa malitia hominum esset in terra]], that is, that men were committing many and great crimes, [[6:5|and that all the thought of their heart|et cuncta cogitatio cordis]] [[6:5|was bent upon evil at all times|intenta esset ad malum omni tempore]], that is, that the men of that time were ceaselessly and studiously devising how they might fulfil their most depraved desires, and transgress and take their pleasure at will, so that they sinned of set purpose and certain malice, not merely of ignorance and infirmity or passion, as it is written of some: [[Ps 63:7|They have searched after iniquities|Scrutati sunt iniquitates]]; [[6:6|It repented him that he had made man on the earth|pœnituit eum, quod hominem fecisset in terra]], that is, He bore Himself in this after the manner of one repenting. For no change, no feeling of passion, no repentance for a past deed can befall God, who is absolutely perfect, in whom is infinite wisdom, immeasurable beatitude and eternal unchangeableness. Hence He testifies by Malachias: [[Mal 3:6|I am the Lord, and I change not|Ego Dominus, et non mutor]]. And providing for the future [Denis's text has here 'Et præcavens in futurum', which the Clementine Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims do not have], that is, purposing to set a bar to the aforesaid wickedness of men and to put an end to it, [[6:6|And being touched inwardly with sorrow of heart|et tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus]], that is, as it were grieving inwardly over His works, above all over men made to His image, like a most loving father, bearing Himself after the manner of one most saddened, though in Himself He was unchangeably overflowing with infinite joy: according to which manner of speaking it is written in the book of Judges, The Lord [[Judg 10:16|was touched with their miseries|doluit super miseriis eorum]]; while of the same Lord Samuel nonetheless says in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 15:29|the triumpher in Israel|Triumphator in Israel]] [[1 Kings 15:29|will not be moved to repentance: for he is not a man that he should repent|pœnitudine non flectetur ; neque enim homo est ut agat pœnitentiam]]. [[6:7|I will destroy man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth|Delebo, inquit, hominem quem creavi, a facie terræ]], that is, I will slay with the flood the whole human race, a very few excepted; [[6:7|from man even to beasts|ab homine usque ad animantia]], that is, both men and land animals; [[6:7|from the creeping thing even to the fowls of the air|a reptili usque ad volucres cœli]], that is, both the creeping things of the earth and the birds of the airy heaven; [[6:7|for it repenteth me that I have made them|pœnitet enim me fecisse eos]], that is, I bear Myself after the manner of one who repents of having made the things he destroys, in that I intend to slay these works of Mine.

paras.t: Quamvis autem irrationalia non peccarunt, nihilo minus justo Dei judicio sunt punita, in detestationem excessuum hominum, propter quos facta erant, sicut hoc diffuse expositum est supra. Sed cur tunc pisces non fuerunt deleti, quum et ipsi propter homines essent facti ? Respondetur quod terra et aër quodammodo inquinati fuerunt per scelera hominum, qui in terra et aëre, non in aquis morantur. Ideo animalia ad ornatum terræ aërisque spectantia, sunt necata. Natura etiam piscium est, aquis non mergi et perire, sed foveri et delectari. Quid autem dicendum sit de avibus, quarum natura est super aquas natare, infra patebit.
paras.en: Now although the irrational creatures had not sinned, they were nonetheless punished by the just judgment of God, in detestation of the excesses of men, for whose sake they had been made, as has been set out at length above. But why were the fishes not destroyed then, since they too had been made for men's sake? The answer is that the earth and the air were in a manner defiled by the crimes of men, who dwell on the earth and in the air, not in the waters. Therefore the animals belonging to the adornment of the earth and the air were slain. Also it is the nature of fishes not to be drowned in the waters and perish, but to be cherished and delighted by them. What is to be said of the birds whose nature is to swim upon the waters will appear below.

paras.t: Præterea Scriptura non sine grandi pondere ac rationabilissima causa ita de invariabili Deo locuta est, utpote quod pœnituit eum, et præcaverit in futurum, atque interno cordis dolore sit tactus, quum tamen providissimi sit auctoris, universa futura sic prævidere, ut prorsus nil agat de quo postmodum doleat. Cur ergo Spiritus Sanctus per Moysen ita locutus est, nisi ut addiscamus et contemplemur, quantum displiceant Deo, essentialiter sancto, justo et bono, peccata nostra, et diligentius ea vitemus ? Hinc loquitur gratiosissimus Augustinus : Ira Dei, non perturbatio animi ejus est, sed judicium quo irrogatur pœna peccati. Cogitatio vero cordis ipsius, est immutabilis ratio rerum mutandarum. Neque enim Deum cujusquam facti sui proprie pœnitet, cujus est de omnibus rebus tam fixa sententia, quam certa præscientia. Sed nisi Scriptura uteretur talibus verbis, non tam familiariter insinuaret se omni generi hominum quibus vult esse consultum, ut et perterreat superbientes, et excitet negligentes, exerceatque quærentes, et alat intelligentes : quod non faceret, si non prius inclinaret se, et quodammodo descenderet ad jacentes. Porro quod et interitum animalium terrenorum, volatiliumque denuntiat, magnitudinem cladis designat.
paras.en: Further, it is not without great weight and a most reasonable cause that Scripture has spoken thus of the unchangeable God, namely that it repented Him, and that He provided for the future, and was touched with inward sorrow of heart, though He is the most provident author, who so foresees all things to come that He does nothing at all for which He afterwards grieves. Why then did the Holy Ghost speak thus through Moses, if not that we may learn and contemplate how much our sins displease God, who is essentially holy, just and good, and may shun them the more diligently? Hence the most gracious Augustine says: The wrath of God is not a disturbance of His mind, but the judgment by which punishment is inflicted on sin. And the thought of His heart is the unchangeable reason of changing things. For God does not properly repent of any deed of His, whose sentence on all things is as fixed as His foreknowledge is certain. But if Scripture did not use such words, it would not make itself known so familiarly to every kind of men whom it wishes to help, so as to terrify the proud, rouse the negligent, exercise the seekers and feed those who understand: which it would not do unless it first stooped and in a manner came down to those lying low. Further, that it announces the destruction of the land animals and the birds as well shows the greatness of the disaster.

6.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus capituli, a loco: Noe vero invenit gratiam coram Domino
6.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this chapter, from the place: “But Noe found grace before the Lord”

paras.t: Noe vero invenit gratiam coram Domino, hoc est, Deo acceptus fuit ac placens, et gratiam quam optavit, a Domino impetravit. Hæ sunt generationes Noe. Noe vir justus atque perfectus fuit in generationibus suis, id est, inter homines sui temporis suique generis fuit notabiliter justus, dando unicuique quod ei debebat, Deo cultum, sibi ipsi custodiam, proximis suis virtuosum exemplum. Fuit quoque perfectus, secundum quod viatori et viro heroico competere solet perfectio. Fuit ergo justus, servando præcepta : et perfectus, per multa supererogationis virtuosæ opera. Rursus justus fuit, se ipsum debite gubernando : perfectus, pro communi bono curam gerendo, et aliis pro posse benefaciendo.
paras.en: [[6:8|But Noe found grace before the Lord|Noe vero invenit gratiam coram Domino]], that is, he was acceptable and pleasing to God, and obtained from the Lord the grace he desired. [[6:9|These are the generations of Noe|Hæ sunt generationes Noe]]: [[6:9|Noe was a just and perfect man in his generations|Noe vir justus atque perfectus fuit in generationibus suis]], that is, among the men of his time and of his race he was notably just, giving to each what he owed him: worship to God, watchfulness to himself, a virtuous example to his neighbours. He was also perfect, in the way that perfection is wont to belong to a wayfarer [that is, one still on the way, in this life, not yet in the homeland] and to a heroic man. He was just, then, in keeping the commandments, and perfect through many virtuous works of supererogation [that is, works beyond what the commandments require]. Again, he was just in governing himself as he ought; perfect in taking care for the common good and doing good to others as far as he could.

paras.t: Porro quod additur, In generationibus suis, exponi solet dupliciter. Primo, depressive, ita ut sonet in minorationem sui præconii : quasi dicatur, perfectus fuit inter suos et tempore isto, quando pene omnes pessimi erant, quamvis tempore evangelicæ legis conversatio sua non fuisset magnæ reputationis. Alio modo promotivé : ita ut sonet in excellentiam suæ laudis : quasi diceretur, Tempore illo quo sic abundavit iniquitas, fuit perfectus, et inter pessimos optimus : quod præcipui meriti est, utpote non vinci a malo, nec a perversis perverti, sed contrario constanter persistere in omni virtute. Sicque de beato Loth ait princeps Apostolorum : Quod vita et adspectu justus erat, habitans apud eos, qui de die in diem animam justi iniquis operibus affligebant. Et ita intelligendum est istud de Noe, per quem Deus fecit tam grande bonum. Unde de eo scriptum est : Noe inventus est perfectus et justus, et in tempore iracundiæ factus est reconciliatio : ideo dimissum est reliquum terræ, quum factum est diluvium. Testamenta sæculi posita sunt apud illum, ne deleri possit diluvio omnis caro. Hinc Josephus narrat : Noe graviter ferens actus et consilia iniquorum illorum, agebat ut ad meliora mentem eorum actusque transferret : quos quum videret sibi non acquiescentes, sed vehementer libidine detineri, metuens ne ipsum cum uxoribus et filiis suis occiderent, discessit a terra illa.
paras.en: Further, what is added, [[6:9|in his generations|In generationibus suis]], is commonly expounded in two ways. First, as lessening, so that it tends to diminish his praise: as if it said, He was perfect among his own and in that time, when almost all were very wicked, although in the time of the law of the Gospel his manner of life would not have been of great account. In another way, as heightening, so that it tends to the excellence of his praise: as if it said, In that time when iniquity so abounded he was perfect, and the best among the worst; which is of singular merit, namely not to be overcome by evil nor perverted by the perverse, but on the contrary to persevere steadfastly in every virtue. So the prince of the Apostles says of blessed Lot that in life and in sight [[2 Pet 2:8|he was just, dwelling among them who from day to day vexed the just soul with unjust works|justus erat, habitans apud eos, qui de die in diem animam justi iniquis operibus affligebant]] [Denis reads *vita*, “in life”, where the Vulgate has *auditu*, “in hearing”]. And so this is to be understood of Noe, through whom God wrought so great a good. Hence it is written of him: [[Ecclus 44:17|Noe was found perfect, just, and in the time of wrath he was made a reconciliation|Noe inventus est perfectus et justus, et in tempore iracundiæ factus est reconciliatio]]: [[Ecclus 44:18|Therefore was there a remnant left to the earth, when the flood came|ideo dimissum est reliquum terræ, quum factum est diluvium]]. [[Ecclus 44:19|The covenants of the world were made with him, that all flesh should no more be destroyed with the flood|Testamenta sæculi posita sunt apud illum, ne deleri possit diluvio omnis caro]]. Hence Josephus relates: Noe, taking grievously the deeds and counsels of those wicked men, strove to turn their minds and deeds to better things; and when he saw that they would not heed him, but were held fast by lust, fearing lest they should kill him together with the wives and his sons, he departed from that land.

paras.t: Cum Deo ambulavit, secundum Dei beneplacitum conversando, et ei fideliter adhærendo, quemadmodum præcedenti capitulo dictum fuit de Enoch.
paras.en: [[6:9|he walked with God|Cum Deo ambulavit]]: that is, living according to God’s good pleasure and cleaving faithfully to him, as was said of Enoch in the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Corrupta est autem terra coram Deo, id est, habitatores terræ per carnalia vitia exteriora infecti sunt ; et repleta est iniquitate, hoc est, etiam per vitiosos affectus, cogitationesque pessimas intus corrupti sunt. Quumque vidisset Deus terram esse corruptam, juxta sensum inductum : omnis quippe caro, id est omnis homo, paucissimis demptis, loquendo de hominibus adultæ ætatis, corruperat viam suam super terram, hoc est, ordinem legitimæ generationis, per quam generabilia intrant in mundum, et pertingunt ad esse specificum, subvertit per fornicationes, adulteria, et innaturalem modum coeundi, ut tactum est supra, quod mulieres ascenderant viros, et item per vitia contra naturam. Potest quoque per viam intelligi tota eorum vita, quæ fuit vitiis plena. Est autem consuetudo Scripturæ, per omnem carnem, omnem hominem designare, juxta illud in Isaia : Videbit omnis caro salutare Dei nostri. Aliqui quoque dicunt, quod homines ex perversitate fecerunt bruta innaturaliter commisceri, contra id quod in Levitico dicitur : Jumenta tua non facies cum alterius generis jumentis coire.
paras.en: [[6:11|And the earth was corrupted before God|Corrupta est autem terra coram Deo]], that is, the inhabitants of the earth were infected outwardly with carnal vices; [[6:11|and was filled with iniquity|et repleta est iniquitate]], that is, inwardly too they were corrupted by vicious affections and very wicked thoughts. [[6:12|And when God had seen that the earth was corrupted|Quumque vidisset Deus terram esse corruptam]], in the sense just given; [[6:12|for all flesh|omnis quippe caro]], that is, every man, a very few excepted, speaking of men of grown age, [[6:12|had corrupted its way upon the earth|corruperat viam suam super terram]]: that is, overturned the order of lawful generation, by which things that are generated come into the world and attain their specific being [that is, the being proper to their species], by fornications, adulteries and an unnatural manner of coupling (as was touched on above, that the women mounted the men), and likewise by vices against nature. By *way* may also be understood their whole life, which was full of vices. Now it is the custom of Scripture to signify every man by *all flesh*, according to that in Isaias: [[Luke 3:6|all flesh shall see the salvation of God|Videbit omnis caro salutare Dei]][[Is 40:5||]] [Denis adds *nostri*, “our God”; his wording is that of Luke 3:6, where the Evangelist quotes Isaias; Is 40:5 itself reads “all flesh together shall see, that the mouth of the Lord hath spoken”]. Some also say that men out of perversity made brute beasts mate unnaturally, against what is said in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:19|Thou shalt not make thy cattle to gender with beasts of any other kind|Jumenta tua non facies cum alterius generis jumentis coire]].

paras.t: Dixit Dominus ad Noe, per subjectam creaturam, seu angelum in humana specie, ut creditur, apparentem ; Finis universæ carnis venit coram me, id est, justo judicio instat mors cunctis mortalibus propter eorum excessus. Repleta est terra iniquitate a facie eorum, id est, habitatores terræ propria iniquitate repleti sunt. Vel ipsa terra dicitur vitiis suorum habitatorum impleta, quemadmodum locus dicitur adimpleri operatione et culpa locati. Et ego disperdam eos cum terra, hoc est, tam habitatores terræ, quam ipsam eorum terram, diversimode perdam : homines hinc inde fugando, terrendo, ac submergendo, ipsamque terram suis fructibus ac solita fecunditate et fructuum suorum virtute privando, superiora etiam terræ loca per aquas diluvii corrumpendo, secundum quod unum elementum est alterius corruptivum. Hinc in Scholastica historia fertur, et idem habetur in Glossa : Tradunt doctores, vigorem fecunditatemque terræ longe inferiorem, seu multo minorem post diluvium esse, quam ante : et ideo esum carnium hominibus esse concessum, quum ante solis terræ fructibus sustentarentur. Denique Lyra refert, quemadmodum Judæi dicunt, quod terra in superficie sua per quantitatem trium palmorum fuerit per aquas diluvii tabefacta, et in aquam conversa. Verumtamen istud de quantitate trium palmorum reor incertum, præsertim quum terra non fuerit ubique ad talem corruptionem æque disposita, nec æque diu aquis operta. Est quoque probabile, quod per salsedinem aquarum abyssi, quæ pro magna parte causaverunt diluvium, terra fuerit vitiata.
paras.en: The Lord [[6:13|said to Noe|Dixit Dominus ad Noe]], through a subject creature, that is, an angel appearing, as is believed, in human form: [[6:13|The end of all flesh is come before me|Finis universæ carnis venit coram me]], that is, by a just judgement death is at hand for all mortals because of their excesses. [[6:13|the earth is filled with iniquity through them|Repleta est terra iniquitate a facie eorum]], that is, the inhabitants of the earth are filled with their own iniquity. Or the earth itself is said to be filled with the vices of its inhabitants, as a place is said to be filled with the doing and the guilt of what is in it. [[6:13|and I will destroy them with the earth|Et ego disperdam eos cum terra]]: that is, I will destroy, in different ways, both the inhabitants of the earth and their earth itself: the men by driving them hither and thither, terrifying and drowning them; the earth by depriving it of its fruits, of its wonted fruitfulness and of the strength of its fruits, and by spoiling the upper parts of the earth through the waters of the flood, inasmuch as one element is corruptive of another. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History, and the same is in the Gloss: The doctors teach that the vigour and fruitfulness of the earth are far lower, or much less, after the flood than before; and that for this reason the eating of flesh was granted to men, whereas before they were sustained by the fruits of the earth alone. Lastly Lyra relates that, as the Jews say, the earth was dissolved on its surface by the waters of the flood to a depth of three palms, and turned into water. But this about the depth of three palms I think uncertain, especially since the earth was not everywhere equally disposed to such corruption, nor covered equally long by the waters. It is also probable that the earth was spoiled by the saltness of the waters of the abyss, which in great part caused the flood.

paras.t: Fac tibi, hoc est ad præservationem tui ipsius atque tuorum a submersione diluvii, arcam de lignis lævigatis, id est complanatis, dolatis, et alleviatis, seu bene siccatis, ut facilius super aquas levetur. Porro in Glossa dicitur, de lignis lævigatis, videlicet fortioribus et imputribilibus ac bene coarctatis, quæ alia translatio vocat quadrata, ut arca nec vi ventorum, nec inundatione aquarum posset dissolvi. Hanc arcam aliqui vocant navem, quod verum est, quantum ad hoc, quod instar navis super aquas ferebatur, et contenta in se, a submersione protexit. Verumtamen non habuit formam navis, sed erat quadrata, latera tamen ipsius inæqualia erant.
paras.en: [[6:14|Make thee|Fac tibi]], that is, for the preservation of thyself and thine from drowning in the flood, [[6:14|an ark of timber planks|arcam de lignis lævigatis]] [*lævigatis*, “smoothed”, where the Douay-Rheims has “timber planks”], that is, planed, hewn and lightened, or well dried, so that it might be lifted the more easily on the waters. Further, the Gloss says: [[6:14|of timber planks|de lignis lævigatis]], that is, of the stronger kinds, that do not rot, and well fitted together, which another translation calls *squared*, so that the ark could be broken up neither by the force of the winds nor by the flooding of the waters. Some call this ark a ship, which is true in so far as it was borne on the waters like a ship and protected what it held from drowning. Yet it did not have the form of a ship, but was squared [that is, rectangular], though its sides were unequal.

paras.t: Mansiunculas in ea facies, id est distincta loca, ut diversa reponantur in eis. Et bitumine linies eam intrinsecus et extrinsecus. Hoc fuit, ne arca aquarum impetu læderetur. Dicitur namque in Scholastica historia ; Bitumen est glutinum ferventissimum ac tenacissimum, quo ligna lita, non dissolvuntur aliqua vi vel arte, id est, non nisi difficillime, nec sine menstruo solvi potest materia bituminata. Augustinus quoque testatur, quod ligna arcæ cohærebant sibi invicem partim bitumine, per epirosque et clavos atque testudines.
paras.en: [[6:14|thou shalt make little rooms in the ark|Mansiunculas in ea facies]], that is, separate places, so that different things may be stored in them. [[6:14|and thou shalt pitch it within and without|Et bitumine linies eam intrinsecus et extrinsecus]]. This was so that the ark should not be harmed by the force of the waters. For it is said in the Scholastic History: Bitumen is a very hot and very tenacious glue; timbers smeared with it are not loosened by any force or art, that is, only with the greatest difficulty; nor can matter bound with bitumen be loosened without menstrual blood [an old belief, found in Josephus and Tacitus, that this alone dissolves bitumen]. Augustine also testifies that the timbers of the ark held together partly by bitumen, and by *epiri* [a word of uncertain sense, perhaps pegs or dowels], nails and vaulted coverings.

paras.t: Et sic facies eam : Trecentorum cubitorum erit longitudo arcæ, quinquaginta cubitorum erit latitudo ipsius, et triginta cubitorum altitudo illius. De qualibus cubitis istud dicatur, infra tractabitur.
paras.en: [[6:15|And thus shalt thou make it. The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits: the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits.|Et sic facies eam : Trecentorum cubitorum erit longitudo arcæ, quinquaginta cubitorum erit latitudo ipsius, et triginta cubitorum altitudo illius]]. With what kind of cubits this is meant will be treated below.

paras.t: Fenestram in arca facies. Ista fenestra stetit altius ipso ostio arcæ. Atque ut Scholastica ait historia, Hebræi dicunt eam fuisse crystallinam, quæ copiose lumen solis reciperet, et aquas repelleret : sed tamen aquæ usque ad eam ascenderant, quod non videtur, nisi forsan ex vehementia impulsionis interdum ; et vocatur in Hebræo meridiana, a Symmacho autem diluculum. Lyra dicit, quod Hebræi dicant, Lucernam facies in ea : quam lucernam aliqui putant fuisse lapidem pretiosum ac splendidum, arcam suo lumine illustrantem, ut facit carbunculus ; sed primum melius sonat. Aliqui quoque opinantur, quod fenestra ponitur hic pluraliter, pro fenestra, quoniam dicunt, tantum ædificium non potuisse per unam fenestram satis illuminari.
paras.en: [[6:16|Thou shalt make a window in the ark|Fenestram in arca facies]]. This window stood higher than the door of the ark itself. And, as the Scholastic History says, the Hebrews say that it was of crystal, so as to receive the sunlight abundantly and keep out the waters; and yet the waters had risen up to it, which does not seem likely, unless perhaps at times from the violence of their surging. In Hebrew it is called *noonday*, and by Symmachus *daybreak*. Lyra says that the Hebrews read: Thou shalt make a lamp in it; and some think this lamp was a precious and shining stone, lighting the ark with its brightness as a carbuncle does; but the first sounds better. Some also are of opinion that *window* is put here for *windows* [the print has *pluraliter, pro fenestra*, “in the plural, for window”; the sense wants the singular put for the plural], since they say that so great a building could not be lit well enough by one window.

paras.t: Et in cubito consummabis summitatem ejus. Fuit namque hæc arca in fundamento quadrata, atque in forma longiori altera parte ab angulis in altum conscendens, quousque tectum incepit se angulariter stringere, donec summitas ejus in cubito complebatur : ita quod latera tecta superiora non distabant ab invicem, nisi per cubitum : sicque per spatium cubitale fuit arca superius plana, quatenus pluvia super tectum descendens, deflueret facilius extra arcam, ipsaque firmius staret inter undarum impulsus.
paras.en: [[6:16|and in a cubit shalt thou finish the top of it|Et in cubito consummabis summitatem ejus]]. For this ark was squared at its base, and oblong in form [*longiori altera parte*, longer on one side], rising straight up from its corners until the roof began to draw in at an angle, until its top was finished in a cubit: so that the upper sides of the roof were no more than a cubit apart; and thus for the space of a cubit the ark was flat on top, so that the rain falling on the roof might run off the ark more easily, and the ark itself stand more firmly amid the beating of the waves.

paras.t: Ostium autem arcæ pones in latere deorsum. Ostium istud factum est in latere arcæ, in ea parte, in qua jungebantur mansio animalium et apotheca, seu victualium locus, ita quod fuit in horum confinio et supra duas cameras inferiores, ut infra plenius exponetur. Ideo dicit Strabus, quod ostium fuit inter apothecariam et animalium habitationem.
paras.en: [[6:16|and the door of the ark thou shalt set in the side|Ostium autem arcæ pones in latere]] below [Denis takes *deorsum*, “below”, with the door; the Douay-Rheims takes it with what follows, “with lower, middle chambers”; see below]. This door was made in the side of the ark, in the part where the dwelling of the animals and the storeroom, or place for provisions, met, so that it was on the border between them and above the two lower chambers, as will be explained more fully below. So Strabus says that the door was between the storeroom and the dwelling of the animals.

paras.t: Cœnacula et tristega facies in ea. Secundum Bedam, στέγη, Græce, Latine dicitur tectum. Inde tristega dicuntur triplicia tecta, id est interstitia seu operimenta. Unde Septuaginta transtulerunt, Bicamerata et tricamerata facies in ea, hoc est, locum habentem cameras duas inter se distinctas, et alium locum habentem tres cameras.
paras.en: [[6:16|middle chambers, and third stories shalt thou make it|Cœnacula et tristega facies in ea]] [*cœnacula*, upper rooms, and *tristega*, third stories]. According to Bede, *stege* (στέγη) in Greek is called *tectum*, a roof, in Latin. Hence *tristega* means threefold roofs, that is, storeys or coverings. So the Septuagint translated: Thou shalt make it two-chambered and three-chambered; that is, a place having two chambers distinct from each other, and another place having three chambers.

paras.t: Circa quod scribit Strabus : Bicamerata facies in inferioribus, et tricamerata in superioribus. Quinque enim mansiones distinctæ fuerunt in arca. Infima fuit stercoraria, ad quam stercora defluebant, ne exsistentes in arca, læderentur fœtore. Secunda, apothecaria. Tertia, immitium animalium et serpentium. Quarta, animalium mansuetorum. Quinta, hominum et animalium. Verumtamen diversi diversimode disponunt has mansiones. Nam aliqui dicunt, quod una fuit directe super aliam, secundum totam longitudinem ac latitudinem arcæ, absque hoc quod aliqua earum esset divisa seu distincta in duas aut tres cameras : et dicunt quod infima fuit sentina seu stercoraria ; secunda, apothecaria ; tertia, habitatio animalium immitium ; quarta, mitium ; quinta, hominum et avium. Porro alii dicunt, quod in arca erant ascendendo tres mansiones, una super aliam sita, ita quod infima fuit (ut dictum est) stercoraria seu sentina, ad quam fæces defluebant, quam dicunt non fuisse interclusam, seu in aliquas mansiones divisam. Secunda fuit apotheca, quam dicunt fuisse in cameras duas distinctam, ita quod in una camera erant fructus quibus quædam bruta vescuntur, in alia herbæ quibus vescuntur ceteræ bestiæ. Tertia fuit tricamerata, seu tres cameras habens collaterales, quarum duæ extremæ erant pro bestiis, una pro mitibus, alia pro immitibus, media pro avibus atque hominibus.
paras.en: On this Strabus writes: Thou shalt make it two-chambered in the lower parts and three-chambered in the upper. For there were five distinct dwellings in the ark. The lowest was the dung-room, into which the dung ran down, so that those who were in the ark should not be harmed by the stench. The second, the storeroom. The third, that of the wild animals and serpents. The fourth, that of the tame animals. The fifth, that of men and animals. Yet different writers arrange these dwellings differently. For some say that one was directly above another, through the whole length and breadth of the ark, without any of them being divided or parted into two or three chambers; and they say that the lowest was the bilge or dung-room; the second, the storeroom; the third, the dwelling of the wild animals; the fourth, of the tame; the fifth, of men and birds. Others again say that there were three dwellings in the ark going upward, one set above another, so that the lowest was (as has been said) the dung-room or bilge, into which the filth ran down, and which they say was not partitioned or divided into any dwellings. The second was the storeroom, which they say was parted into two chambers, so that in one chamber were the fruits on which some beasts feed, in the other the herbs on which the other beasts feed. The third was three-chambered, that is, it had three chambers side by side, of which the two at the ends were for the beasts, one for the tame, the other for the wild, and the middle one for the birds and men.

paras.t: Insuper in Scholastica historia dicitur : Arca habuit cameras quinque, quas Augustinus etiam præter sentinam dicit ibi fuisse, asserens super tabulatum sentinæ eam fuisse bicameratam per longum. Una camerarum erat stercoraria, alia apothecaria, et super hanc mansionem fuit alia mansio tricamerata per longum, ita quod laterales cameræ erant una immitium animalium, alia mansuetorum, media hominum et avium. Alii has cameras in altitudine sola disponunt, inferiorem et sentinam vocantes stercorariam ; secundam super illam, apothecariam ; tertiam, immitium ; quartam, mitium animalium ; quintam, hominum et avium. Josephus tamen ait, arcam quatuor cameras habuisse, quia stercorariam seu sentinam forsitan non includit nec computat. Hæc ibi. Itaque cœnacula possunt referri ad bicamerata, tristega ad tricamerata.
paras.en: Moreover it is said in the Scholastic History: The ark had five chambers, which Augustine too says were there, besides the bilge, asserting that above the floor of the bilge it was two-chambered lengthwise. One of the chambers was the dung-room, the other the storeroom; and above this dwelling was another dwelling, three-chambered lengthwise, so that of the side chambers one was for the wild animals, the other for the tame, and the middle one for men and birds. Others arrange these chambers by height alone, calling the lowest, the bilge, the dung-room; the second, above it, the storeroom; the third, that of the wild animals; the fourth, of the tame; the fifth, of men and birds. Josephus, however, says that the ark had four chambers, perhaps because he does not include or count the dung-room or bilge. Thus far the History. So the [[6:16|middle chambers|cœnacula]] can be referred to the two-chambered storey, the [[6:16|third stories|tristega]] to the three-chambered.

paras.t: Præterea præinductum textum quidam sic punctuat : Ostium autem arcæ pones in latere : dicens quod ibi sit punctus secundum Hebræos, ita quod verbum istud, Deorsum, refertur ad textum sequentem : quia (ut dicunt) ostium arcæ non poterat conveniente poni in inferiori parte, quoniam arca fuit multum profundata in aqua, et expositores catholici dicunt ostium illud fuisse in confinio habitationis animalium et apothecæ. Sed istud non videtur valere, et punctatio catholicorum probatur aptior esse. Nam et expositores catholici, qui dicunt ostium fuisse in latere arcæ in præfato confinio, textum sic punctuant : Ostium autem arcæ pones in latere deorsum. Ex hoc enim quod fuit deorsum, non sequitur quod fuit in infima parte, sed quod fuit infra habitationem omnium animalium et hominum ac avium. Quod si Hebræi et eos sequentes, intelligunt per Deorsum, infimam partem, non possunt hoc verbum, Deorsum, referre ad litteram sequentem, qua dicitur : Cœnacula et tristega facies in ea ; quia tristega fuerunt sursum et supra ostium, sicut jam patuit.
paras.en: Further, a certain writer punctuates the text quoted above thus: [[6:16|and the door of the ark thou shalt set in the side|Ostium autem arcæ pones in latere]], saying that according to the Hebrews the stop comes there, so that the word *deorsum*, “below”, belongs to the text that follows; because (as they say) the door of the ark could not fittingly be put in the lower part, since the ark sat very deep in the water; and the Catholic expositors say that the door was on the border between the dwelling of the animals and the storeroom. But this does not seem to hold, and the punctuation of the Catholics is shown to be the more fitting. For the Catholic expositors too, who say that the door was in the side of the ark at the border mentioned, punctuate the text thus: [[6:16|and the door of the ark thou shalt set in the side|Ostium autem arcæ pones in latere]] below. For from its being *below* it does not follow that it was in the lowest part, but that it was beneath the dwelling of all the animals, men and birds. And if the Hebrews and those who follow them understand the lowest part by *below*, they cannot refer this word *below* to the letter that follows, where it is said: [[6:16|middle chambers, and third stories shalt thou make it|Cœnacula et tristega facies in ea]]; for the third stories were up above the door, as has already appeared.

paras.t: Ecce ego adducam aquas diluvii super terram, et interficiam omnem carnem in qua spiritus vitæ est, id est omne animatum sensitivum habens spiritum seu animam vitalem, sive rationalem sive irrationalem. Et universa quæ in terra sunt, consumentur, id est, omnia viventia in terra, occidentur, demptis his quæ in arca ducentur. Pisces autem morantur in aquis, nec proprie habent carnem, quamvis dicat Apostolus, Alia caro piscium, large accipiens nomen carnis.
paras.en: [[6:17|Behold, I will bring the waters of a great flood upon the earth|Ecce ego adducam aquas diluvii super terram]], [[6:17|to destroy all flesh, wherein is the breath of life|et interficiam omnem carnem in qua spiritus vitæ est]] [Denis reads *et interficiam*, “and I will destroy”; the margin gives the variant *subter cœlum*, “under heaven”, as the Vulgate has it], that is, every animate sentient thing that has spirit or a living soul, whether rational or irrational. [[6:17|All things that are in the earth shall be consumed|Et universa quæ in terra sunt, consumentur]], that is, all living things on the earth shall be killed, except those that will be brought into the ark. But fish live in the waters and do not properly have flesh, although the Apostle, speaking of flesh, says: [[1 Cor 15:39|another of fishes|Alia caro piscium]], taking the word *flesh* broadly.

paras.t: Ponamque fœdus meum tecum, id est, pactum amicitiæ specialis tecum inibo et demonstrabo in te, utpote quod te et eos qui tecum arcam intrabunt, præservabo ab imminenti periculo ex aquarum diluvio, et quod per te reparaturus sum sæculum. Ideo ait Glossa : Ponam fœdus meum tecum, de te et familia tua conservanda ad humani generis reparationem. Infra autem legitur Dominus aliud fœdus pepigisse cum Noe.
paras.en: [[6:18|And I will establish my covenant with thee|Ponamque fœdus meum tecum]], that is, I will enter into a pact of special friendship with thee and show it in thee: namely that I will preserve thee and those who will enter the ark with thee from the danger that threatens from the flood of waters, and that through thee I am to restore the world. So the Gloss says: [[6:18|I will establish my covenant with thee|Ponam fœdus meum tecum]], concerning thee and thy household, to be preserved for the restoring of the human race. Below, however, the Lord is read to have made another covenant with Noe.

paras.t: Et ex cunctis animantibus universæ carnis bina, id est combinata seu duo, induces in arcam, ut vivant tecum in arca, masculini sexus et feminini, hoc est unum masculum et unam femellam. Qualiter factum sit istud, videlicet qualiter animalia ista ad arcam venerunt, et de quibus animalibus istud intelligatur, infra diligentius exponetur.
paras.en: [[6:19|And of every living creature of all flesh|Et ex cunctis animantibus universæ carnis]] [[6:19|two of a sort|bina]], that is, paired, or two, [[6:19|thou shalt bring|induces]] [[6:19|into the ark, that they may live with thee|in arcam, ut vivant tecum]] in the ark, [[6:19|of the male sex, and the female|masculini sexus et feminini]], that is, one male and one female. How this was done, namely how these animals came to the ark, and of which animals it is to be understood, will be explained more carefully below.

paras.t: Sed quid est quod Dominus nunc legitur præcepisse, ut Noe tolleret secum de cunctis animalium speciebus duo, quum sequenti capitulo Deus legatur jussisse ut Noe tolleret ex omnibus animalibus mundis septena et septena, masculum et feminam, de animalibus vero immundis duo et duo, sed et de volatilibus cœli septena et septena? Et respondendum quod ista commissio legitur facta ipsi Noe a Deo, antequam cœpit arcam ædificare, et tunc facta est ei in generali et indistincte : postmodum vero arca jam præparata, facta est ei jussio illa secunda, in qua in speciali atque distincte Deus expressit, quod ante in communi et confuse mandavit. Numerus autem minor non excludit majorem. Si autem objiciatur, necessarium aut statim congruum exstitisse, ut ante fabricationem arcæ Dominus exprimeret omnia illa distincte, quatenus juxta hoc faceret mansiones arcæ majores sive minores : dicendum, quod Dominus ante hanc jussionem satis exposuit sancto Noe magnitudinem arcæ fiendæ. Potest quoque responderi, quod ante fabricationem Dominus forsan insinuavit Noe istud præceptum distincte, sicut et postea : Moyses tamen non curavit hoc in isto capitulo plene exprimere, quia in sequenti capitulo fuit hoc distincte expressurus ac plene, propter quod satis reputavit nunc dicere in communi.
paras.en: But how is it that the Lord is read here to have commanded Noe to take with him two of every species of animals, when in the following chapter God is read to have bidden Noe take of all clean animals [[Gen 7:2|seven and seven, the male and the female|septena et septena, masculum et feminam]], but of the unclean animals [[Gen 7:3|two and two|duo et duo]], and also [[Gen 7:3|Of the fowls also of the air seven and seven|sed et de volatilibus cœli septena et septena]]? It must be answered that this charge is read to have been given to Noe by God before he began to build the ark, and was then given him in general and without distinction; but afterwards, when the ark was already prepared, that second command was given him, in which God expressed in particular and distinctly what he had before commanded in common and confusedly. And a smaller number does not exclude a greater. But if it is objected that it was necessary, or at least fitting [the print has *statim*, “at once”; *saltem*, “at least”, seems meant], that before the building of the ark the Lord should express all this distinctly, so that Noe might make the rooms of the ark larger or smaller accordingly: it must be said that before this command the Lord had sufficiently set out to holy Noe the size of the ark to be made. It can also be answered that before the building the Lord perhaps made this command known to Noe distinctly, as he did afterwards; but Moses did not trouble to express it fully in this chapter, because he was going to express it distinctly and fully in the following chapter, for which reason he thought it enough to speak in general now.

paras.t: Bina induces in arcam de volucribus juxta genus suum, hoc est de qualibet specie specialissima avium duo ; et de jumentis in genere suo, id est de qualibet tali specie jumentorum duo. Jumenta autem proprie appellantur animalia domita atque domestica, hominibus accommoda, quæ dicuntur jumenta quasi juvamenta, ut supra inductum est. Nunc tamen per jumenta intelligi possunt bruta in generali, de quibus nunc fit hic mentio specialis. Et ex omni reptili terræ, id est ex qualibet reptilium terrestrium specie, secundum genus suum, id est secundum suam naturam. Sumitur enim hic genus pro specie. Bina de omnibus jam prælatis, utpote duo de singulis speciebus, ingredientur tecum in arcam, ut possint vivere.
paras.en: [[6:19|thou shalt bring two of a sort into the ark|Bina induces in arcam]]: [[6:20|Of fowls according to their kind|de volucribus juxta genus suum]], that is, two of each most special species of birds [that is, of each lowest species, below which there is no further division]; [[6:20|and of beasts in their kind|et de jumentis in genere suo]], that is, two of each such species of beasts. Now *jumenta* [beasts] properly means tamed and domestic animals useful to men, which are called *jumenta* as if *juvamenta* [helps], as was brought forward above. Here, however, by *jumenta* may be understood brute beasts in general, of which special mention is now made here. [[6:20|and of every thing that creepeth on the earth|Et ex omni reptili terræ]], that is, of each species of land reptiles, [[6:20|according to its kind|secundum genus suum]], that is, according to its nature: for *genus*, kind, is taken here for species. [[6:20|two of every sort|Bina de omnibus]] of those already named, namely two of each species, [[6:20|shall go in with thee|ingredientur tecum]] into the ark, [[6:20|that they may live|ut possint vivere]].

paras.t: Tolles igitur tecum ex omnibus escis quæ mandi possunt, id est, aliqua accipies de omnibus rebus aptis esui hominum ac brutorum. Utrum vero intelligendum sit hoc etiam de animalibus illis, quibus homines et quædam bruta naturaliter nutriuntur, infra discutietur. Et comportabis apud te, id est, in apotheca arcæ repones, adjuvantibus te filiis tuis ac ceteris tuis domesticis, quantum oportet. Et erunt tam tibi quam illis in escam ; id est, tu ipse cum domesticis tuis tecum ingressuris, et irrationalia animalia in arca nutriemini comestibilibus illis. Unumquodque individuum secundum congruentiam et dispositionem suæ naturæ, seu singuli singulis cibis sibi competentibus nutrientur. Erant autem comestibilia ista valde multa, quia per integrum annum fuerunt in arca ipse Noe cum suis ac bruta.
paras.en: [[6:21|Thou shalt take unto thee of all food that may be eaten|Tolles igitur tecum ex omnibus escis quæ mandi possunt]], that is, thou shalt take some of all things fit to be eaten by men and beasts. Whether this is to be understood also of those animals by which men and certain beasts are naturally nourished will be discussed below. [[6:21|and thou shalt lay it up with thee|Et comportabis apud te]], that is, thou shalt store it in the storeroom of the ark, with the help of thy sons and the rest of thy household, as much as is needed. [[6:21|and it shall be food for thee and them|Et erunt tam tibi quam illis in escam]]; that is, thou thyself, with thy household who will go in with thee, and the irrational animals, shall be fed in the ark with those foods: each individual according to what befits and suits its nature, or each shall be fed with the food proper to it. And these foods were very many, since Noe himself with his own, and the beasts, were in the ark for a whole year.

paras.t: Fecit igitur omnia quæ præceperat illi Deus. Non quod per se solum exsecutus sit omnia, sed per adjutoria opportuna.
paras.en: Therefore he [[6:22|did all things which God commanded him|Fecit igitur omnia quæ præceperat illi Deus]]: not that he carried out everything by himself alone, but with fitting helpers.

6.title: De objectionibus infidelium contra prædicta, et de quæstionibus concernentibus præsens capitulum, ac solutionibus earumdem. De figura quoque seu forma et quantitate, dispositioneque arcæ
6.title_en: On the objections of unbelievers against what has been said, and on the questions concerning the present chapter, and their solutions. Also on the figure or shape, the size and the arrangement of the ark

paras.t: Quemadmodum super Genesim in homilia de Arca Noe recitat Origenes, quidam, præsertim Apelles hæreticus, discipulus Marcionis hæresiarchæ, qui Apelles fuit inventor alterius hæresis, ultra eam quam didicerat a suo magistro, cum quo intendebat probare, Scripturam veteris Testamenti non esse a Deo : hic ergo Apelles dixit, nullo modo fieri potuisse, ut tam breve spatium arcæ contineret tot animalium genera, eorumque cibos qui illis per totum annum sufficerent, imo non poterat continere saltem quatuor elephantes, quum tamen dicantur in arca fuisse ex immundis animalibus bina et bina, hoc est duo masculi, duæque feminæ, secundum quod indicat sermo repetitus. Ex mundis vero septena et septena, id est paria septena, videlicet quatuordecim talia. Et postea quasi per singulas species sic refragatur Apelles, puta de gryphis. Ex quibus concludit. Constat ergo fictam esse hanc fabulam. Quod si est, constat hanc a Deo non esse Scripturam.
paras.en: As Origen relates in his homily on Genesis concerning the Ark of Noe, certain men, and above all the heretic Apelles, a disciple of the heresiarch Marcion (this Apelles was the inventor of a further heresy, beyond the one he had learned from his master, with whom he set out to prove that the Scripture of the Old Testament is not from God): this Apelles, then, said that it could in no way have come about that so small a space as the ark should hold so many kinds of animals, and the food to suffice them for a whole year; indeed, it could not hold even four elephants, though it is said that of the unclean animals there were in the ark two and two, that is, two males and two females, as the repeated word shows [*bina et bina*, ‘two and two’, taken as two pairs], and of the clean seven and seven, that is, seven pairs, namely fourteen of each. And afterwards Apelles argues in the same way species by species, for instance about the griffins. From which he concludes: It is plain, then, that this story is made up; and if so, it is plain that this Scripture is not from God.

paras.t: Insuper Augustinus tangit alias quorumdam objectiones. Quidam enim dixerunt Moysen non descripsisse rem gestam hoc loco, sed ea quæ scribit de arca, esse intelligenda dumtaxat spiritualiter et figurative. Ad quod aliqua induxerunt motiva. Primo, quia non potuit tam magnum esse diluvium, quod altissimis montibus altius esset quindecim cubitis, propter altitudinem montis Olympi, ad cujus verticem nequeunt nubes ascendere, nec est in vertice isto aer hic crassior, in quo nebulæ, venti ac nubes gignuntur. Secundo, quia ut eis apparet, non poterat tantæ magnitudinis arca compingi. Tertio, quia quum Deus omnipotens omnia possit solo imperio reparare, non videtur ad litteram quod jussit animalia reservari propter destructorum reparationem.
paras.en: Augustine moreover touches on other objections of certain men. For some have said that Moses did not in this place write down a thing that was really done, but that what he writes of the ark is to be understood only spiritually and figuratively. For this they brought forward some reasons. First, that the flood could not have been so great as to stand fifteen cubits higher than the highest mountains, because of the height of Mount Olympus, to whose summit the clouds cannot rise; nor is there on that summit this thicker air in which mists, winds and clouds are formed. Second, that, as it seems to them, an ark of such size could not have been put together. Third, that since almighty God can restore all things by his command alone, it does not seem that he literally ordered animals to be kept for the restoring of those destroyed.

paras.t: Ad ista objecta responderunt viri catholici, atque ad primum acceperunt responsionem ex Origene, qui ait : Quæ a prudentioribus viris et Hebraicarum traditionum gnaris, atque a veteribus magistris didicimus, ad auditorum notitiam deferemus. Dixerunt ergo majores, quod Moyses, qui (teste Scriptura) doctus erat omni sapientia Ægyptiorum, posuit in hoc loco numerum cubitorum secundum geometricam artem, qua præcipue callent Ægyptii. Unus autem cubitus apud geometras, continet sex cubitos nostros. Hanc Origenis responsionem Augustinus allegat et approbat, quam etiam tangit Hugo de S. Victore in libro suo de Arca Noe. Sic itaque quantitatem cubitorum accipiendo, arca tantæ fuit extensionis, quod capere poterat omnia quæ in textu scribuntur fuisse in ea.
paras.en: To these objections Catholic men have replied, and to the first they took the answer from Origen, who says: What we have learned from wiser men, versed in the Hebrew traditions, and from the masters of old, we will bring to the knowledge of our hearers. The elders, then, said that Moses, who (as Scripture witnesses) [[Acts 7:22|was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians|doctus erat omni sapientia Ægyptiorum]], set down in this place the number of cubits according to the art of geometry, in which the Egyptians are especially skilled. Now one cubit among the geometers contains six of our cubits. This answer of Origen Augustine cites and approves, and Hugh of St Victor also touches on it in his book on the Ark of Noe. Taking the measure of the cubits in this way, then, the ark was of such extent that it could hold everything that the text records to have been in it.

paras.t: Ad secundum respondet Augustinus, admirando cæcitatem adducentium illud objectum. Si enim terra quæ est gravior aqua, potuit tam alte ascendere in monte Olympo, cujus suprema pars terra est, et tamdiu in tanta elevatione persistere, cur aqua non potuit ad tempus breve omni monte ascendere altius per quindecim cubitos ?
paras.en: To the second Augustine replies, marvelling at the blindness of those who bring that objection. For if earth, which is heavier than water, could rise so high in Mount Olympus, whose topmost part is earth, and stay so long at such a height, why could not water, for a short time, rise fifteen cubits higher than every mountain?

paras.t: Ad tertium quoque respondet : Illud quod disputant tantæ magnitudinis arcam non potuisse compingi, ineptissime calumniantur, quum sciant maximas urbes esse constructas, nec attendunt centum annos quibus arca illa est fabricata, nisi forte lapis lapidi cohærere potest sola calce conjunctus, ut murus per tot milliaria circumducatur, et lignum ligno per testudines, epuros, clavos, glutem bituminis adhærere non valet, ut fabricetur arca longe lateque porrecta, non curvis, sed lineis rectis, quam humanus conatus non misit in mare, sed veniens unda levavit, magisque divina providentia quam humana prudentia gubernavit.
paras.en: To the third also he replies: In arguing that an ark of such size could not have been put together they cavil most foolishly, since they know that very great cities have been built; nor do they consider the hundred years in which that ark was made. Unless perhaps stone can cleave to stone joined by lime alone, so that a wall may be carried round for so many miles, and yet timber cannot hold to timber by joints [*testudines*; Augustine's own text has *subscudes*, dovetails], pegs [*epuros*], nails and the glue of pitch, so that an ark may be built stretching far in length and breadth, not with curved lines but with straight ones: an ark which no human effort launched into the sea, but the coming wave lifted, and which divine providence more than human prudence steered.

paras.t: Ad quartum respondet, quod propter designandum mysterium Deus jussit animalia reservari in arca, sicut in sequenti articulo in spirituali hujus capituli expositione patebit.
paras.en: To the fourth he replies that God ordered the animals to be kept in the ark in order to signify a mystery, as will appear in the next article, in the spiritual exposition of this chapter.

paras.t: Præterea Augustinus : Quæritur, inquit, utrum tam magna arca poterat fabricari infra centum annos a quatuor viris, videlicet Noe et tribus filiis ejus : quod si non poterat, non erat magnum adhibere et alios fabros, quamvis accepta laboris sui mercede, non curaverint utrum Noe sapienter an inaniter ageret, nec eam ingressi sunt, quia non crediderunt quod credidit ille.
paras.en: Augustine also says: It is asked whether so great an ark could be built within a hundred years by four men, namely Noe and his three sons. If it could not, it was no great matter to bring in other workmen as well, though, once they had taken the wages of their labour, they did not care whether Noe acted wisely or foolishly, and did not go into it, because they did not believe what he believed.

paras.t: At vero de forma seu figura arcæ Origenes sic ait : Primo quæritur, qualem oporteat intelligi formam arcæ. Quam ego, inquit, quantum datur intelligi ex Scriptura, puto consurgentem quatuor angulis ex imo, eisdemque angulis paulatim usque ad summum contractis in angustum, ipsam arcam in spatium unius cubiti fuisse collectam. Sic enim refertur, quod in fundamento ejus trecenti cubiti erant in longitudine, quinquaginta in latitudine, in altitudine vero triginta. Sicque collecta est in angustum cacumen, ita ut cubitus sit longitudo et latitudo ipsius.
paras.en: Of the shape or figure of the ark, Origen speaks thus: First it is asked what shape the ark should be understood to have. As far, he says, as can be understood from Scripture, I think that it rose from the bottom with four corners, and that, these corners being drawn in little by little to a narrow point up to the top, the ark itself was gathered into the space of one cubit. For it is related that at its base it was three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty in height; and so it was gathered into a narrow peak, so that its length and breadth there were one cubit.
