Ex quibus concludit: Ideo Glossa nostra mentionem non facit de hoc, nec (ut credo) aliquis Sanctorum, nec etiam Hebræorum doctorum, nisi solus Rabbi Salomon, qui in hujusmodi vanis quæstionibus longam facit altercationem. Deinde reprobat argumentum primi dicti Nicolai de Lyra, quoniam etsi arca intrasset aquam quindecim cubitis, non sequeretur quod montium capita tetigisset, nec flotare quivisset. Potuisset enim flotare in terris planis, quæ multo plures et majores sunt montuosis. Deinde reprobat secundum dictum illius. Nam quando arca requievit super montes Armeniæ, non intravit tantum præcise aquas, quantum aquæ erant montibus altiores: nisi quis dicat, quod montes illi Armeniæ fuissent altissimi montes totius terræ, quod non apparet, præsertim propter altitudinem montis Olympi. Et ideo potuit aqua alibi altior esse quam fuit spatium profunditatis, qua arca intravit aquas, quando primo super montes quievit. Consequenter reprobat tertium dictum illius. Quod, prolixitatem vitans, prosequi cesso. Ultimo addit: Hæc introduxi, ad ostendendum ineptitudinem Rabbi Salomonis in expositione Scripturæ, licet Lyra eum frequenter alleget. Hæc Rabbi Paulus.
paras.en: On this Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi, in his Additions to Lyra] writes that this inquiry is more curious than useful, because it brings no useful knowledge in matters of belief, nor is it required for a full exposition of the letter. From which he concludes: Therefore our Gloss makes no mention of this, nor (as I believe) does any of the Saints, nor even of the Hebrew doctors, save only Rabbi Salomon [that is, Rashi], who makes a long dispute in vain questions of this sort. Then he refutes the argument of Nicholas of Lyra's first statement: for even if the ark had entered the water by fifteen cubits, it would not follow that it touched the tops of the mountains, nor that it could not float; for it could have floated over the level lands, which are far more numerous and larger than the mountainous ones. Then he refutes his second statement. For when the ark rested upon the mountains of Armenia, it did not enter the waters by exactly as much as the waters were higher than the mountains, unless one were to say that those mountains of Armenia were the highest mountains of the whole earth, which does not appear, especially because of the height of Mount Olympus. And therefore the water could elsewhere have been higher than the depth to which the ark entered the waters when it first rested on the mountains. Next he refutes his third statement, which, to avoid prolixity, I forbear to follow. Lastly he adds: I have brought these things in to show the ineptitude of Rabbi Salomon in expounding Scripture, though Lyra often cites him. Thus far Rabbi Paul.

paras.t: Verumtamen Hugo de S. Victore in libro suo de Arca Noe, aliquid tangit de quantitate profundationis arcæ in aqua, dicendo: Verisimile est quod duæ inferiores mansiones arcæ, arca natante, premebantur inter aquas deorsum, videlicet mansio infima in qua recipiebantur superfluitates naturæ, et secunda in qua continebantur cibaria. Tertia vero in qua animalia erant, quæ spiramento aperti aeris eguerunt, prima super aquas eminebat. Sed juxta hanc positionem dici non potest, quod arca intraverit tredecim cubitis aquas, quoniam Hugo dicit infimam mansionem arcæ, habuisse in altitudine cubitos quatuor, secundum cubitos quinque, et ita arca non intrasset aquam nisi per cubitos circiter novem. Attamen magna et exquisita inquisitio de quantitate profundationis arcæ in aqua, videtur inutilis. Unde nec Hugo multum super hoc tractat.
paras.en: Yet Hugh of St Victor, in his book on Noe's Ark, touches somewhat on how deep the ark sank in the water, saying: It is likely that the two lower storeys of the ark, while the ark floated, were pressed down below the waters, namely the lowest storey, in which the superfluities of nature were received, and the second, in which the food was kept; but the third, in which were the animals, which needed the breath of the open air, was the first to stand out above the waters. But according to this position it cannot be said that the ark entered the waters by thirteen cubits, since Hugh says that the lowest storey of the ark was four cubits high and the second five cubits; and so the ark would not have entered the water by more than about nine cubits. Nevertheless a great and minute inquiry into how deep the ark sank in the water seems useless. Hence Hugh too does not treat much of this.

8.title: De spirituali intelligentia ejusdem capituli octavi
8.title_en: On the spiritual understanding of the same eighth chapter

paras.t: Per recordationem, qua Dominus recordatus est ipsius Noe et exsistentium secum in arca, designatur quod Deus permittit electos suos in Ecclesia militante ad tempus affligi, tentari, et variis tribulationibus exerceri, sed non supra vires eorum, neque in finem deserit eos, sed per misericordiæ suæ effectus ostendit se memorem eorumdem, pie visitando, consolando ac confortando, ita ut dicant: Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala. Itemque: Benedictus Deus qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra. Et denuo: Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam. Ideo non debemus in adversis deficere, nec pusillanimitate tabescere, nec unquam de gratiosa Dei subventione diffidere.
paras.en: By the remembering with which the Lord remembered Noe himself and those who were with him in the ark, it is signified that God permits his elect in the Church militant [that is, the Church on earth, still fighting, as against the Church triumphant in heaven] to be afflicted for a time, tempted, and exercised by various tribulations[[Jdt 8:22||]], yet not beyond their strength; nor does he forsake them to the end, but by the effects of his mercy he shows himself mindful of them, lovingly visiting, consoling and strengthening them, so that they say: [[Ps 89:15|We have rejoiced for the days in which thou hast humbled us: for the years in which we have seen evils|Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala]]. And again: [[2 Cor 1:3|Blessed be the God|Benedictus Deus]] [[2 Cor 1:4|Who comforteth us in all our tribulation|qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra]]. And once more: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam]]. Therefore we ought not to fail in adversity, nor waste away in faint-heartedness, nor ever lose trust in God's gracious help.

paras.t: Præterea recordatus est Dominus Noe, id est Christi, cujus in tantum videbatur oblitus tempore passionis, ut Christus ipse clamaverit: Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me? et rursus in Psalmo: Repleta est malis anima mea; Æstimatus sum cum descendentibus in lacum: Sicut vulnerati dormientes in sepulcris, quorum non es memor amplius. Unde de ipso dictum est in Isaia: Vidimus eum quasi leprosum et percussum a Deo et humiliatum. Itaque recordatus est Deus Pater hominis Christi, quando ipso Domino Jesu Christo in cruce clamante, Pater, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum, Deus Pater spiritum Christi suscepit, et paulo post eumdem spiritum seu animam reunivit corpori ejus, illud mox glorificando, et jam corpus quam animam Christi ab omni passibilitate penitus exaltando. Tunc quoque recordatus est Dominus cunctorum animantium quæ erant cum eo, hoc est omnium discipulorum Christi, qui in ejus societate et congregatione fuerunt ante passionem ipsius.
paras.en: Moreover, [[8:1|God remembered Noe|recordatus est Dominus Noe]], that is, Christ, whom he seemed to have forgotten so far in the time of the passion that Christ himself cried out: [[Matt 27:46|My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken me?|Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me]]? and again in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:4|my soul is filled with evils|Repleta est malis anima mea]]; [[Ps 87:5|I am counted among them that go down to the pit|Æstimatus sum cum descendentibus in lacum]]: [[Ps 87:6|Like the slain sleeping in the sepulchres, whom thou rememberest no more|Sicut vulnerati dormientes in sepulcris, quorum non es memor amplius]]. Hence it was said of him in Isaias: [[Is 53:4|we have thought him as it were a leper, and as one struck by God and afflicted|Vidimus eum quasi leprosum et percussum a Deo et humiliatum]] [Denis reads "we have seen him", where the Vulgate has "we have thought him"]. So God the Father remembered the man Christ when, as the Lord Jesus Christ himself cried out on the cross, [[Luke 23:46|Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit|Pater, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum]], God the Father received Christ's spirit, and a little after reunited that same spirit, or soul, to his body, at once glorifying the body, and raising both the body and the soul of Christ wholly above all capacity to suffer. Then too the Lord remembered [[8:1|all the living creatures|cunctorum animantium]] which were with him, that is, all the disciples of Christ, who were in his company and fellowship before his passion.

paras.t: Et adduxit spiritum super terram, id est, Spiritum Sanctum misit illis in signo sensibili in die sacratissimo Pentecostes, per cujus charismata illos excellentissime vivificavit, exhilaravit et sublimavit. Et imminutæ sunt aquæ, id est, tribulationes atque formidines quas ante habuerunt discipuli, tunc cessarunt, quemadmodum de sacratissima illa Ecclesia primitiva Actuum secundo scriptum est: Omnes qui credebant, erant pariter, et erant eis omnia communia, sumebantque cibum cum exsultatione et simplicitate cordis, collaudantes Deum, et habentes gratiam ad omnem plebem. Ceterorum autem nemo audebat se conjungere eis, sed beatificabat eos populus, et metus magnus erat in omnibus aliis.
paras.en: And he [[8:1|brought a wind upon the earth|adduxit spiritum super terram]] [the Latin *spiritus* means both "wind" and "spirit"], that is, he sent them the Holy Ghost under a sign perceptible to the senses on the most sacred day of Pentecost, by whose gifts he most excellently quickened, gladdened and raised them up. [[8:1|and the waters were abated|Et imminutæ sunt aquæ]], that is, the tribulations and fears that the disciples had before then ceased, as is written in the second chapter of the Acts of that most sacred primitive Church: [[Acts 2:44|And all they that believed were together and had all things common|Omnes qui credebant, erant pariter, et erant eis omnia communia]], [[Acts 2:46|they took their meat with gladness and simplicity of heart|sumebantque cibum cum exsultatione et simplicitate cordis]], [[Acts 2:47|Praising God and having favour with all the people|collaudantes Deum, et habentes gratiam ad omnem plebem]]. [[Acts 5:13|But of the rest no man durst join himself unto them: but the people magnified them|Ceterorum autem nemo audebat se conjungere eis, sed beatificabat eos populus]] [Denis reads "called them blessed", where the Vulgate has "magnified them"], and great fear was upon all the others [this last clause is not in Acts 5:13; compare Acts 2:43 and 5:11].

paras.t: Et clausi sunt fontes abyssi magnæ. Per fontes abyssi intelliguntur Scribæ et Pharisæi, sacerdotes atque pontifices Synagogæ, quæ erat instar abyssi repleta aqua sapientiæ legis, et doctrina Prophetarum, legaliumque doctorum; sed omnes fontes isti clausi sunt, Christo sermocinante, et ejus Apostolis atque discipulis post susceptionem Spiritus Sancti, quando non potuerunt resistere et contradicere Spiritui Sancto qui loquebatur per os Christi, discipulorumque ejus, quibus ante passionem promisit: Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri. Hinc de Christo Evangelista testatur, quod erat docens sicut potestatem habens, non sicut Scribæ et Pharisæi, ita quod omnes mirabantur in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus: propter quod quidam ex adversariis Christi, evidentia veritatis compulsi, dixerunt: Nunquam locutus est homo sicut hic loquitur.
paras.en: And [[8:2|The fountains also of the deep|fontes abyssi magnæ]] (the great deep) [[8:2|were shut up|Et clausi sunt]]. By the fountains of the deep are understood the scribes and Pharisees, the priests and high priests of the Synagogue, which was like a deep filled with the water of the wisdom of the Law and with the teaching of the Prophets and of the doctors of the Law. But all these fountains were shut up when Christ preached, and his Apostles and disciples after receiving the Holy Ghost[[Acts 2:4||]], when they were not able to resist and gainsay the Holy Ghost who spoke through the mouth of Christ and of his disciples[[Acts 6:10||]], to whom before the passion he promised: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]]. Hence the Evangelist testifies of Christ that [[Matt 7:29|he was teaching them as one having power, and not as the scribes and Pharisees|erat docens sicut potestatem habens, non sicut Scribæ et Pharisæi]] [the margin gives Matt. xii, 29], so that all [[Luke 4:22|wondered at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth|mirabantur in verbis gratiæ quæ procedebant de ore ejus]]; for which reason some of Christ's adversaries, compelled by the evidence of the truth, said: [[John 7:46|Never did man speak like this man|Nunquam locutus est homo sicut hic loquitur]].

paras.t: Et cataractæ cœli. Cataractæ cœli id est fenestræ Synagogæ, erant præcepta cæremonialia legis, per quæ olim sol sapientiæ splenduit et refulsit in Synagoga: quæ fenestræ Evangelio divulgato sunt clausæ, quia tunc finem sumpserunt, et per eorum observantiam non fiebat illuminatio, sed excæcatio et condemnatio observantium ea, sicut dixit Apostolus: Quia si circumcidamini, Christus nihil proderit vobis. Et prohibitæ sunt pluviæ de cœlo: id est, gratia atque auctoritas prædicandi, ablata est Synagogæ, in qua Deus olim per gratiam quasi in cœlo regnavit, quemadmodum nunc in Ecclesia regnat. Tota autem gratia, sapientia, et multiplex eminentia, quæ olim in Synagoga fuerunt, ad Ecclesiam Christi per gloriosos Apostolos sunt translatæ cum ineffabili superabundantia et profectu.
paras.en: [[8:2|and the floodgates of heaven|Et cataractæ cœli]]. The floodgates of heaven, that is, the windows of the Synagogue, were the ceremonial precepts of the Law, through which the sun of wisdom once shone and gleamed in the Synagogue. These windows were shut once the Gospel had been spread abroad, because then they came to their end, and their observance brought not enlightenment but blinding and condemnation to those who kept them, as the Apostle said: [[Gal 5:2|if you be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing|si circumcidamini, Christus nihil proderit vobis]]. And [[8:2|the rain from heaven was restrained|prohibitæ sunt pluviæ de cœlo]]: that is, the grace and authority of preaching was taken away from the Synagogue, in which God once reigned by grace as in a heaven, as he now reigns in the Church. And all the grace, wisdom and manifold eminence that were once in the Synagogue were carried over to the Church of Christ by the glorious Apostles, with unspeakable superabundance and increase.

paras.t: Reversæque sunt aquæ de terra euntes et revertentes: id est, vera intelligentia Scripturarum et sapientia salutaris, fideique doctrina reliquerunt Judæam seu Synagogam, euntes ad Christi Ecclesiam et gentilitatem conversam. Et cœperunt minui post centum quinquaginta dies. Per hos dies insinuatur tempus evangelicæ prædicationis usque ad ejus divulgationem: qua facta, legalia erant mortifera. Ideo extunc cœperunt præfatæ aquæ a Judæis deficere et abire. Tuncque requievit arca super montes Armeniæ: id est, congregatio ecclesiastica innitebatur Apostolorum doctrinis. Tunc quoque apparuerunt cacumina montium: id est, dignitas, sanctitas et eminentia multiformis Apostolorum et apostolicorum virorum ac ceterorum Ecclesiæ prælatorum cœpit undique declarari atque agnosci, et a fidelibus latissime honorari ac allegari, de quibus ait Psalmista: Fundamenta ejus in montibus sanctis. Et Isaias: Erit in novissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Domini in vertice montium.
paras.en: [[8:3|And the waters returned from off the earth going and coming|Reversæque sunt aquæ de terra euntes et revertentes]]: that is, the true understanding of the Scriptures, saving wisdom and the teaching of the faith left Judea, or the Synagogue, going to the Church of Christ and to the converted Gentiles. [[8:3|and they began to be abated after a hundred and fifty days|Et cœperunt minui post centum quinquaginta dies]]. By these days is suggested the time of the preaching of the Gospel until it was spread abroad; once that was done, the legal observances [that is, the ceremonies of the Old Law] were deadly. And so from then on the waters mentioned began to fail the Jews and depart from them. And then [[8:4|the ark rested|requievit arca]] [[8:4|upon the mountains of Armenia|super montes Armeniæ]]: that is, the gathering of the Church rested upon the teachings of the Apostles. Then too [[8:5|the tops of the mountains appeared|apparuerunt cacumina montium]]: that is, the dignity, holiness and manifold eminence of the Apostles and apostolic men and the other prelates of the Church began to be made known and acknowledged everywhere, and to be honoured and appealed to far and wide by the faithful; of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 86:1|The foundations thereof are the holy mountains|Fundamenta ejus in montibus sanctis]]. And Isaias: [[Is 2:2|in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of mountains|Erit in novissimis diebus præparatus mons domus Domini in vertice montium]].

paras.t: Quumque transissent quadraginta dies, aperiens Noe fenestram arcæ, quam fecerat, dimisit corvum. Per quadraginta dies, tempus luctus ac pœnitentiæ designatur, post quod Christus emittit corvum, id est, homines sæculares permittit ad exteriora sua redire negotia qui frequenter remanent extra, inordinate adhærendo rebus terrenis, et obliviscuntur devotionis et compunctionis præhabitæ. Tuncque Salvator emittit post eos columbam, id est viros innocentes ac simplices prædicatores et contemplativos, ut revocent illos ad viam salutis obedientiamque et caritatem Ecclesiæ, denuntiando eis sæculi vanitates, impiorumque clades ac futura supplicia. Quumque columba hæc non invenit sibi quietem in exterioribus rebus et actibus, nec pedem suum figere potest in eis, fructificando in conversione pravorum, et reducendo eos juxta desiderium suum ad Dominum, redit in arcam, hoc est ad interna exercitia ecclesiasticæ politiæ, et suscipit eam Christus ac introducit in sanctuarium suum, in contemplationis secretum, in cellam vinariam, quæ est spiritualis ebriatio, et suavis refectio ex copiosa degustatione increatæ dulcedinis, copiosaque participatione supernorum charismatum ac valida inflammatione Spiritus Sancti.
paras.en: [[8:6|after that forty days were passed, Noe opening the window of the ark, which he had made, sent forth a raven|Quumque transissent quadraginta dies, aperiens Noe fenestram arcæ, quam fecerat, dimisit corvum]]. By the forty days is signified the time of mourning and penance, after which Christ sends forth the raven: that is, he lets worldly men go back to their outward affairs, and they often stay outside, clinging inordinately to earthly things, and forget the devotion and compunction they had before. And then the Saviour sends forth the dove after them, that is, innocent and simple men, preachers and contemplatives, to call them back to the way of salvation and to the obedience and charity of the Church, proclaiming to them the vanities of the world, the ruin of the wicked and the punishments to come. And when this dove finds no rest for herself in outward things and doings, and cannot set her foot in them by bearing fruit in the conversion of the wicked and bringing them back to the Lord as she desires, she returns into the ark, that is, to the inward exercises of the Church's way of life; and Christ receives her and brings her into his sanctuary, into the secret place of contemplation, into the wine cellar [compare Cant 2:4, "He brought me into the cellar of wine"], which is spiritual inebriation and sweet refreshment from a plentiful tasting of uncreated sweetness, a plentiful sharing in heavenly gifts, and a strong kindling of the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Aquæ enim erant super universam terram. Istæ sunt aquæ mundanæ prudentiæ, quæ superfusa est cordibus hominum mundanorum; quia ut ait Salvator, Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores sunt filiis lucis in sua generatione. Sed et aquæ, id est multitudo et inquietudo tentationum, vitiorum, passionum, atque multiplicium tribulationum abundant in terrenis et corporalibus istis hominibus.
paras.en: [[8:9|for the waters were upon the whole earth|Aquæ enim erant super universam terram]]. These are the waters of worldly prudence, which is poured over the hearts of worldly men; for, as the Saviour says, [[Luke 16:8|the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light|Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores sunt filiis lucis in sua generatione]]. And the waters too, that is, the multitude and restlessness of temptations, vices, passions and manifold tribulations, abound in these earthly and fleshly men.

paras.t: Exspectatis autem ultra septem diebus aliis, rursus dimisit columbam ex arca. Sic Christus non semel dumtaxat, sed iterum ac frequenter mittit prædicatores et vicarios suos ac servos ferventes ad pravorum conversionem; nec frustra, quia interdum aliqui convertuntur: sicque redit columba ad Christum ad vesperam, portans ramum olivæ virentibus foliis in ore suo, id est, devoti prædicatores et fideles prælati, ac fervidi famuli Creatoris, dum fructum fecerunt in aliis, ad Dominum se convertunt, et ei omne bonum cum gratiarum actione præcordiali adscribunt, ramumque olivæ, id est meritum quod assecuti sunt, et pietatis opus quod exercuerunt, Deo præsentant humiliter ac devote, ad vesperam, hoc est post expletionem occupationis suæ circa exteriora, in quibus quamdam obscurationem splendidæ contemplationis quandoque incurrunt: sed redeuntes ad domum, mox recuperare amissa conantur, et magis quam ante illuminantur. Intellexit ergo Noe quod cessassent aquæ super terram. Sic Christus in tali casu videt, quod præfatæ aquæ vitiorum, passionum ac mundanæ prudentiæ, ablatæ sunt a cordibus horum qui vere ad ipsum conversi sunt. Deinde emittit rursus columbam, quæ ultra non redit ad eum. Per hoc designatur, quod tales viri virtutum per columbam expressi, post frequentem suam emissionem et administrationem circa exteriora agenda ac alios convertendos, tandem relicta Ecclesia militante, triumphantem ingrediuntur.
paras.en: [[8:10|And having waited yet seven other days, he again sent forth the dove out of the ark|Exspectatis autem ultra septem diebus aliis, rursus dimisit columbam ex arca]]. So Christ, not once only but again and often, sends his preachers and vicars and fervent servants to convert the wicked; and not in vain, for at times some are converted. And so the dove returns to Christ in the evening, [[8:11|carrying a bough of an olive tree, with green leaves, in her mouth|portans ramum olivæ virentibus foliis in ore suo]]: that is, devout preachers and faithful prelates and fervent servants of the Creator, when they have borne fruit in others, turn to the Lord and ascribe every good to him with heartfelt thanksgiving; and [[8:11|a bough of an olive tree|ramumque olivæ]], that is, the merit they have gained and the work of piety they have done, they present to God humbly and devoutly in the evening, that is, after finishing their busy work with outward things, in which they sometimes incur a certain darkening of their bright contemplation; but returning home, they at once strive to recover what was lost, and are enlightened more than before. [[8:11|Noe therefore understood that the waters were ceased upon the earth|Intellexit ergo Noe quod cessassent aquæ super terram]]. So Christ, in such a case, sees that the waters of vices, passions and worldly prudence mentioned above have been taken away from the hearts of those who are truly converted to him. Then he sends forth the dove again, and she returns to him no more. By this is signified that such men of virtue, represented by the dove, after being often sent out and busied with outward affairs and with converting others, at last leave the Church militant and enter the Church triumphant.

paras.t: Igitur sexcentesimo primo anno vitæ Noe, imminutæ sunt aquæ super terram: hoc est, infra unum annum designatum per annum quo Noe fuit in arca, quum haberet annos sexcentos, aquæ sapientiæ et gratiarum fluenta totaliter sunt subtracta Judæis incredulis. Deinde Judæa arefacta est, id est indurata in sua perfidia atque ab omni humore gratiæ desiccata. Denique, per tectum arcæ, puta Ecclesiæ, potest intelligi divina protectio seu evangelica theoria, qua teguntur ac defenduntur credentes. Tectum quoque Ecclesiæ, sunt prælati et viri perfecti: hoc tectum aperit Christus, dum corda eorum revelat ad intuendum cœlestia ac divina seu abdita Scripturarum, dum item per eos considerat, seu eos ad considerandum inducit, qualiter corda subditorum ac infirmorum disposita sint.
paras.en: [[8:13|Therefore in the six hundredth and first year|Igitur sexcentesimo primo anno]] of Noe's life, [[8:13|the waters were lessened upon the earth|imminutæ sunt aquæ super terram]]: that is, within one year, signified by the year Noe was in the ark when he was six hundred years old, the waters of wisdom and the streams of graces were wholly withdrawn from the unbelieving Jews. Then Judea was dried up, that is, hardened in its unbelief and dried out of all the moisture of grace. Lastly, by [[8:13|the covering of the ark|tectum arcæ]], that is, of the Church, may be understood God's protection, or the contemplation of the Gospel, by which believers are covered and defended. The roof of the Church is also its prelates and perfect men: this roof Christ opens when he lays open their hearts to behold heavenly and divine things, or the hidden things of the Scriptures, and again when through them he considers, or leads them to consider, how the hearts of their subjects and of the weak are disposed.

paras.t: Locutus est autem Deus ad Noe, dicens: Egredere de arca, tu et uxor tua, et filii tui, etc.: id est, obstinatis Judæis, voluit Deus ut Christus et primitiva ejus Ecclesia, quæ fuit sponsa ipsius, hoc est sancti Apostoli et plurimi Judæorum ab eis conversi, ad totius mundi informationem atque conversionem processerunt. Non quod Christus in cœlo tunc residens, corporaliter cum suis discipulis, sed spiritualiter tantum profectus sit, quibus jam ante promiserat: Ego vobiscum sum cunctis diebus; et, Non relinquam vos orphanos. Sed quomodo tunc de arca, id est de Ecclesia, exierunt? Dicendum, quod exierunt de ea, non eam relinquendo, sed dilatando: sicque ejus angustias deserendo, et ipsam ubique terrarum plantando: sicque creverunt et multiplicati sunt in toto orbe super numerum.
paras.en: [[8:15|And God spoke to Noe, saying|Locutus est autem Deus ad Noe, dicens]]: [[8:16|Go out of the ark, thou and thy wife, thy sons|Egredere de arca, tu et uxor tua, et filii tui]], etc.: that is, the Jews being obstinate, God willed that Christ and his primitive Church, which was his bride, that is, the holy Apostles and very many of the Jews converted by them, should go forth to instruct and convert the whole world. Not that Christ, then dwelling in heaven, went forth bodily with his disciples, but only spiritually; to whom he had already promised before: [[Matt 28:20|I am with you all days|Ego vobiscum sum cunctis diebus]]; and, [[John 14:18|I will not leave you orphans|Non relinquam vos orphanos]]. But how did they then go out of the ark, that is, of the Church? It must be said that they went out of it not by leaving it but by enlarging it: by leaving behind its narrow bounds and planting it everywhere on earth; and so they increased and were multiplied beyond number in the whole world.

paras.t: Ædificavit autem Noe altare Domino, et tollens de cunctis pecoribus et volucribus mundis, obtulit holocausta super altare. Dominus noster Jesus Christus constantissime prædicando, justissime conversando, strenuissime increpando pontifices, Scribas et Pharisæos Judæorum, ædificavit sibi altare, id est, crucis patibulum sibi parari ab illis ac erigi procuravit, quia ex actibus illis præfatis, moti fuerunt ad interfectionem ipsius. Ædificavit quoque sibi altare, id est, aram crucis voluit sibi parari, in qua obtulit semetipsum Deo Patri. Tollens de cunctis pecoribus et volucribus mundis, hoc est, universos suos electos activos ac contemplativos, et potissimum eos quos ex Judæis collegit, cordi suo inscribens, ac suæ memoriæ imprimens, eos secum Patri offerens ac præsentans.
paras.en: [[8:20|And Noe built an altar unto the Lord: and taking of all cattle and fowls that were clean, offered holocausts upon the altar|Ædificavit autem Noe altare Domino, et tollens de cunctis pecoribus et volucribus mundis, obtulit holocausta super altare]]. Our Lord Jesus Christ, by preaching most steadfastly, living most justly, and rebuking most boldly the high priests, scribes and Pharisees of the Jews, built himself an altar: that is, he brought it about that the gibbet of the cross was made ready for him by them and set up, since those deeds of his moved them to kill him. He also built himself an altar, that is, he willed the altar of the cross to be made ready for him, on which he offered himself to God the Father. [[8:20|taking of all cattle and fowls that were clean|Tollens de cunctis pecoribus et volucribus mundis]]: that is, all his elect, active and contemplative, and above all those he gathered from the Jews, writing them in his heart and pressing them into his memory, offering and presenting them with himself to the Father.

paras.t: Odoratusque est Dominus odorem suavitatis, id est, passionem Christi gratissimam et superacceptissimam habuit, et caritatem animæ Christi, ex qua sponte omnia protulit, maxime approbavit, et vere suavissimam judicavit. Nam passio Christi ex parte patientis, summe complacuit Patri; propter quod ait Apostolus: Christus dilexit nos, et tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis. Et Isaias: Oblatus est, inquit, quia ipse voluit. Unde et ipsemet fassus est: Animam meam pono pro ovibus meis. Et ait ad eum: Nequaquam ultra maledicam terræ propter homines: hoc est, virtute et merito tuæ passionis, o Christe unigenite mi dilecte, propitiabor hominibus, et piissimus ero tempore evangelicæ legis, ultra omne tempus præteritum. Etenim propter Christum, et merito suæ sanctissimæ conversationis, ardentissimæ caritatis, et acerbissimæ passionis, summe et incomparabiliter propitiatus est Deus Pater, imo Trinitas tota superbenedicta hominibus.
paras.en: [[8:21|And the Lord smelled a sweet savour|Odoratusque est Dominus odorem suavitatis]]: that is, he held the passion of Christ most pleasing and acceptable beyond all, and he approved above all, and judged truly most sweet, the charity of Christ's soul, out of which he freely brought forth everything. For the passion of Christ, on the part of the one suffering, pleased the Father supremely; for which reason the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:2|Christ also hath loved us and hath delivered himself for us, an oblation and a sacrifice to God for an odour of sweetness|Christus dilexit nos, et tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis]]. And Isaias: [[Is 53:7|He was offered|Oblatus est]], he says, [[Is 53:7|because it was his own will|quia ipse voluit]]. Hence he himself also declared: [[John 10:15|I lay down my life for my sheep|Animam meam pono pro ovibus meis]]. [[8:21|and said|Et ait]] to him: [[8:21|I will no more curse the earth for the sake of man|Nequaquam ultra maledicam terræ propter homines]]: that is, by the power and merit of thy passion, O Christ, my only-begotten and beloved, I will be propitious to men, and will be most merciful in the time of the law of the Gospel, beyond all time past. For on account of Christ, and by the merit of his most holy life, his most ardent charity and his most bitter passion, God the Father, nay the whole Trinity, blessed above all, was supremely and incomparably appeased towards men.

paras.t: Sensus enim et cogitatio humani cordis in malum prona sunt, etc. Non solum ex originalis peccati infectione consurgit pronitas ista ad vitia. Nam et primi parentes, quum essent in gratia et originali justitia conditi, ante suam transgressionem tam proni fuerunt ad malum, quod Eva ex una persuasione serpentis, Dei mandatum transgressa est, similiter Adam occasione uxoris. Et quid dicam de primis parentibus aliunde ad malum inductis, quum et creatura illa altissima atque dignissima, angelus primus ac summus, ex se ipso ad tantam impietatem inductus sit, tamque sceleratissime lapsus, cui et alii angeli multi tam faciliter consenserunt? Itaque creatura rationalis et intellectualis, secundum se accepta, et sibi ipsi relicta, ad malum est prona. Et eo ipso quo ex nihilo facta est, et ad finem alium a se ordinata, potest deficere et peccare, nisi desuper adjuvetur; et sicut indiget Creatoris conservatione ut in esse suo subsistat, ita voluntas ejus indiget incessanter adjutorio gratiæ Dei, ut in bono permaneat et non peccet. Quod semper pensare debemus, et humiliare ac aspernari nosmetipsos, et jugiter timorati consistere, ac in solo Creatore confidere, ipsumque indesinenter invocare; et quidquid boni agimus aut habemus, ipsi cum omni gratiarum actione et profundissima humilitate adscribere.
paras.en: [[8:21|for the imagination and thought of man's heart are prone to evil|Sensus enim et cogitatio humani cordis in malum prona sunt]], etc. This proneness to vices does not arise only from the infection of original sin. For our first parents too, when they had been created in grace and original justice, were before their transgression so prone to evil that Eve broke God's commandment at a single persuasion of the serpent, and Adam likewise on his wife's occasion. And what shall I say of our first parents, who were led to evil from outside, when even that highest and worthiest creature, the first and highest angel, was led of himself to such great impiety, and fell so very wickedly[[Is 14:12||]], and many other angels so easily consented to him? So the rational and intellectual creature, taken in itself and left to itself, is prone to evil. And by the very fact that it was made out of nothing and ordered to an end other than itself, it can fail and sin unless it is helped from above; and as it needs the Creator's preserving in order to go on in its being, so its will needs ceaselessly the help of God's grace in order to remain in good and not sin. This we ought always to weigh, and to humble and despise ourselves, and to stand ever in fear, and to trust in the Creator alone and call on him unceasingly; and whatever good we do or have, to ascribe it to him with all thanksgiving and the deepest humility.

paras.t: Non igitur ultra percutiam omnem animam viventem, sicut feci. Ante adventum Christi, Deus pene omnem animam viventem vita naturæ, percussit plaga justæ derelictionis et excæcationis internæ, sicut in Actibus loquitur Paulus: Deus in præteritis generationibus dimisit omnes gentes ingredi vias suas. Et Isaias: Nos omnes, inquit, quasi oves erravimus; unusquisque in viam suam declinavit. Sed per Christum et ejus discipulos cunctis hominibus annuntiata est via salutis, neque deinceps reliquit genus humanum Deus, ut prius: Cunctis diebus terræ, sementes, hoc est seminatio verbi cœlestis, et messis, id est fructificatio inde proveniens, frigus, hoc est infrigidatio a concupiscentiæ, iræ ceterarumque passionum fervore, et æstus, hoc est ardor vehemens divini amoris, æstas, hoc est sinceritas contemplationis et gratiæ, et hiems, id est rigor compunctionis ac pœnitentiæ, nox, hoc est tribulatio seu tentatio electos exercens, et dies, id est gratiosa illuminatio eorumdem, non requiescent, hoc est, in Ecclesia esse non desinent, in vasis misericordiæ usque in finem mundi.
paras.en: [[8:21|therefore I will no more destroy every living soul as I have done|Non igitur ultra percutiam omnem animam viventem, sicut feci]]. Before the coming of Christ, God struck almost every soul living the life of nature with the stroke of just abandonment and of inward blinding, as Paul says in the Acts: God [[Acts 14:15|in times past, suffered all nations to walk in their own ways|in præteritis generationibus dimisit omnes gentes ingredi vias suas]] [the margin gives Acts xiv, 6]. And Isaias: [[Is 53:6|All we|Nos omnes]], he says, [[Is 53:6|like sheep have gone astray, every one hath turned aside into his own way|quasi oves erravimus; unusquisque in viam suam declinavit]]. But through Christ and his disciples the way of salvation was proclaimed to all men, and from then on God did not abandon the human race as before. [[8:22|All the days of the earth, seedtime|Cunctis diebus terræ, sementes]], that is, the sowing of the heavenly word, [[8:22|and harvest|et messis]], that is, the bearing of fruit that comes from it; [[8:22|cold|frigus]], that is, the cooling from the heat of concupiscence, of anger and of the other passions, [[8:22|and heat|et æstus]], that is, the vehement ardour of divine love; [[8:22|summer|æstas]], that is, the clearness of contemplation and grace, [[8:22|and winter|et hiems]], that is, the rigour of compunction and penance; [[8:22|night|nox]], that is, tribulation or temptation exercising the elect, [[8:22|and day|et dies]], that is, their gracious enlightening, [[8:22|shall not cease|non requiescent]]: that is, they will not cease to be in the Church, in the vessels of mercy, until the end of the world.

paras.t: Postremo, spiritualis intelligentia hujus capituli posset trahi ad tempus Antichristi, sub cujus persecutione silebit Ecclesia pro maxima sui parte, et multi fidelium se abscondent, et quasi in arca in abscondito remanebunt. Deinde impiissimo interfecto, recordabitur Deus suæ Ecclesiæ, adducetque spiritum super terram, quia fideles exibunt ad prædicandum liberrime, et totus quasi mundus convertetur ad Christum, ac Spiritu Sancto implebitur. Longum esset totum hoc per singula prosequi. Hoc quoque prædictis adjiciendum, quia per hoc quod columba emissa non potuit in montium cacuminibus propter eorum lutositatem quiescere, designatur quod Spiritus Sanctus qui per columbam sæpe exprimitur, non invenit sibi quietem in multis doctoribus, prædicatoribus, sacerdotibus, principibus ac prælatis, propter carnalem et turpem eorum vitam.
paras.en: Lastly, the spiritual understanding of this chapter could be drawn to the time of Antichrist, under whose persecution the Church will for the most part be silent, and many of the faithful will hide themselves and remain in hiding as if in the ark. Then, when that most wicked one has been slain, God will remember his Church and will bring a wind [or spirit] upon the earth, since the faithful will go out to preach most freely, and almost the whole world will be converted to Christ and filled with the Holy Ghost. It would be long to follow all this out point by point. To what has been said this too must be added: that by the dove, when sent forth, not being able to rest on the tops of the mountains because of their muddiness, is signified that the Holy Ghost, who is often represented by the dove, finds no rest for himself in many doctors, preachers, priests, princes and prelates, because of their fleshly and shameful life.

9.title: Declaratio litteralis capituli noni: Benedixitque Deus Noe, etc.
9.title_en: Literal explanation of the ninth chapter: And God blessed Noe, etc.

paras.t: Benedixitque Deus Noe et filiis ejus. Hoc de spirituali benedictione a quibusdam exponitur: ut sit sensus, quod dona gratiæ ac virtutum eis infudit, aut infusa auxit, et fructuosa effecit. Aliqui tamen dicunt, quod Cham filius Noe fuit semper iniquus, quamvis propter merita patris sui fuerat a diluvio præservatus. Credendum est etiam, quod Deus benedixit uxoribus Noe, filiorumque ejus. Et dixit ad eos: Crescite et multiplicamini, id est, generando augete et multiplicate individua vestræ speciei; et replete terram vestra posteritate, hoc est, incipite eam implere hominibus. Istud tamen præceptum refertur ad filios Noe, non ad ipsum Noe, nisi dicatur post diluvium genuisse: de qua re infra quæretur. Et terror ac tremor vester sit super cuncta animantia terræ, et super omnes volucres cœli, cum universis quæ moventur super terram, id est, omnia animalia terrestria, cunctæque aves cœli aerei, et universa reptilia terræ, timeant vos, et ad vestrum tremant adspectum.
paras.en: [[9:1|And God blessed Noe and his sons|Benedixitque Deus Noe et filiis ejus]]. Some expound this of a spiritual blessing, so that the sense is that he poured into them the gifts of grace and of the virtues, or increased those already poured in, and made them fruitful. Some, however, say that Cham the son of Noe was always wicked, although he had been preserved from the flood for the merits of his father. It is to be believed, too, that God blessed the wives of Noe and of his sons. [[9:1|And he said to them: Increase, and multiply|Et dixit ad eos: Crescite et multiplicamini]], that is, by begetting, increase and multiply the individuals of your species; [[9:1|and fill the earth|et replete terram]] with your posterity, that is, begin to fill it with men. This precept, however, refers to the sons of Noe, not to Noe himself, unless he is said to have begotten children after the flood: a matter which will be inquired into below. [[9:2|And let the fear and dread of you be upon all the beasts of the earth, and upon all the fowls of the air, and all that move upon the earth|Et terror ac tremor vester sit super cuncta animantia terræ, et super omnes volucres cœli, cum universis quæ moventur super terram]], that is, let all the animals of the land, and all the birds of the airy heaven, and all the creeping things of the earth fear you, and tremble at the sight of you.

paras.t: Quæritur, an dictum sit hoc Noe et filiis ejus pro ipsis dumtaxat, an etiam pro eorum posteris universis. Respondetur, quod sic specialiter dictum est hoc Noe et filiis ejus, ut nihilo minus in eorum personis dictum sit aliqualiter cunctis hominibus. Dictum est enim ad illos specialiter, ne, quia pauci erant, timerent a multis ferocibus bestiis lædi. In eorum quoque personis dictum est hoc ad omnes homines, quoniam irrationabilia naturaliter metuunt homines, […] humanam. Et raro aut nunquam invaderent hominem, nisi provocata aut fame impulsa. Præfata tamen irrationabilia non fuerunt Noe et filiis ejus tam plene subjecta ac obedientia, sicut primis parentibus in statu innocentiæ.
paras.en: It is asked whether this was said to Noe and his sons for themselves alone, or also for all their posterity. The answer is that it was said to Noe and his sons specially, yet in such a way that in their persons it was none the less said in some manner to all men. It was said to them specially lest, being few, they should fear to be harmed by the many fierce beasts. And in their persons it was said to all men as well, since irrational creatures naturally fear men, […] human. And they would rarely or never attack a man unless provoked or driven by hunger. Yet these irrational creatures were not so fully subject and obedient to Noe and his sons as they were to our first parents in the state of innocence.

paras.t: Circa hæc verba dicit Gregorius: Homo non hominibus, sed irrationabilibus est prælatus natura, id est naturali dignitate et ordine. Ideo dicitur ei: Ut ab animalibus, non ab hominibus, timeatur: quoniam ab æquali velle timeri, est contra naturam superbire. Unde antiqui patres non reges hominum, sed pastores pecorum fuisse dicuntur. Natura ergo omnes homines æquales genuit; sed pro varietate meritorum, dispensatio Dei justa, sed occulta, alios aliis præponit, ut humana formidine peccare metuant, qui divina judicia non formidant. Præpositi autem ex hoc timore nequaquam superbiant, in quo non suam gloriam, sed subditorum quærant justitiam. Non enim hominibus, sed bestiis, dominantur; quia ex qua parte bestiales sunt, id est carnales seu proni ad malum, ex ea parte formidini sunt substrati.
paras.en: On these words Gregory says: Man has been set by nature over the irrational creatures, not over men (that is, by natural dignity and order). Therefore he is told that he is to be feared by the animals, not by men; for to wish to be feared by one's equal is to be proud against nature. Hence the ancient fathers are said to have been not kings of men but shepherds of flocks. Nature, then, has brought forth all men equal; but according to the variety of their merits the dispensation of God, just though hidden, sets some over others, so that those who do not dread the judgements of God may fear to sin through dread of men. Yet let superiors by no means grow proud of this fear, in which they should seek not their own glory but the righteousness of their subjects. For they rule not over men but over beasts; since in so far as their subjects are bestial, that is, carnal or prone to evil, in so far are they made subject to fear.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæri potest, qualiter ista sint vera, et utrum post originale peccatum inductum sit dominium unius super alium, ex solo demerito culpæ, ita quod non sit de jure naturali atque divino. Et objici potest contra verba Gregorii, quia Paulus apostolus præcipit servis, ut cum timore et tremore dominis suis obediant: ergo et domini hoc a servis exigere possunt ut debitum, et præsertim prælati a sibi commissis exigere possunt ac debent, ut debite timeantur: imo princeps Apostolorum jubet in sua Canonica: Servi, subditi estote in omni timore dominis, non tantum bonis et modestis, sed etiam dyscolis. Jus ergo divinum seu Deus prætulit hominem homini, vultque hominem ab homine formidari. Antiqui etiam patres, non solum pecoribus, sed et hominibus præfuerunt, videlicet Abraham trecentis servis suis, et Moyses Israelitis ac David populo Judæorum. Verum ad omnia ista patet solutio ex his quæ dicta sunt supra, articulo vicesimo septimo; ubi quæsitum atque tractatum est, quomodo in statu innocentiæ fuisset dominium, et qualiter non. Tale enim dominium, quale fuisset in innocentiæ statu, etiam nunc est ex ordinatione divina, non in pœnam culpæ, sed propter subditorum profectum. Dominium vero quod est in commodum dominantis, non subditorum, ex culpa inductum est. De duplici isto dominio dictum est ibi diffusius.
paras.en: On this it may be asked how these things are true, and whether the lordship of one man over another was brought in after original sin solely through the guilt deserved, so that it is not of natural and divine right. And it may be objected against Gregory's words that the Apostle Paul commands servants to obey their masters [[Eph 6:5|with fear and trembling|cum timore et tremore]] [the margin reads Ephes. xi, 5, a misprint for vi, 5]: therefore masters too may require this of their servants as their due, and above all prelates may and ought to require of those committed to them that they be duly feared. Indeed the prince of the Apostles commands in his canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 2:18|Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward|Servi, subditi estote in omni timore dominis, non tantum bonis et modestis, sed etiam dyscolis]]. Divine right, then, or God, has set man over man, and wills that man be feared by man. The ancient fathers, too, were set not only over flocks but over men as well: Abraham, namely, over his three hundred servants[[Gen 14:14||]] [the margin note here cannot be read; Abraham's servants are numbered in Gen 14:14], Moses over the Israelites, and David over the people of the Jews. But the answer to all this is plain from what was said above, in the twenty-seventh article, where it was asked and discussed how there would have been lordship in the state of innocence, and how not. For such lordship as there would have been in the state of innocence exists even now by divine ordinance, not as a punishment for guilt but for the profit of the subjects; whereas the lordship that is for the advantage of the one who rules, not of the subjects, was brought in by guilt. Of this twofold lordship more was said there at length.

paras.t: Omnes pisces maris manui vestræ traditi sunt, id est, vestræ potestati et usui vestro eos subjicio, ut vel arte, vel vi eos capere valeatis, et vesci eisdem. Interdum tamen belluæ quædam marinæ evertunt naves, et devorant homines: quod consecutum est ex peccato: ideo pisces et cetera bruta non sunt ita perfecte subjecta potestati humanæ in statu naturæ corruptæ, sicut in statu innocentiæ. Et omne quod movetur et vivit, erit vobis in cibum. Non est hoc absolute intelligendum de omni animato ac mobili ex se ipso: non enim venenosa et alia quædam turpissima data sunt homini ad edendum: sed intelligendum est de universis animalibus humano esui aptis. Quasi olera virentia tradidi vobis omnia, hoc est, volatilia cœli, bestias terræ, et pisces maris vobis concedo in usum et esum, nunc post diluvium, quemadmodum ante diluvium contuli vobis ad edendum olera, et terræ nascentia cetera. Vel, Quasi olera, hoc est, ut eis tam libere vescamini, sicut oleribus.
paras.en: [[9:2|all the fishes of the sea are delivered into your hand|Omnes pisces maris manui vestræ traditi sunt]], that is, I subject them to your power and to your use, so that you may be able to catch them, whether by skill or by force, and to feed on them. Yet at times certain monsters of the sea overturn ships and devour men: this has followed from sin. Therefore the fishes and the other brute beasts are not so perfectly subject to human power in the state of fallen nature as in the state of innocence. [[9:3|And every thing that moveth, and liveth shall be meat for you|Et omne quod movetur et vivit, erit vobis in cibum]]. This is not to be understood absolutely of every animate thing that moves of itself: for poisonous things and certain other most foul things were not given to man to eat; but it is to be understood of all the animals fit for man to eat. [[9:3|even as the green herbs have I delivered them all to you|Quasi olera virentia tradidi vobis omnia]], that is, I grant you the birds of the air, the beasts of the earth and the fishes of the sea for your use and for food, now after the flood, as before the flood I gave you herbs to eat and the other things that grow from the earth. Or, [[9:3|as the green herbs|Quasi olera]], that is, that you may feed on them as freely as on herbs.

paras.t: Excepto quod carnem cum sanguine non comedetis, id est suffocatum seu strangulatum, submersum et omne tale quod moritur sine sanguinis effusione. Vel, Carnem cum sanguine, hoc est, non comedetis sanguinem seorsum, seu separatum a carnalibus, utpote aliquid confectum ex sanguine, sicut potestis comedere carnem sanguine ejus fuso. Istud quoque in Actibus Apostolorum sanxerunt Apostoli: Visum est, inquiunt, Spiritui Sancto et nobis, nihil aliud imponere vobis, nisi ut abstineatis ab immolatis simulacrorum, et suffocato, et sanguine, et fornicatione. Potest quoque ita exponi: Carnem cum sanguine non comedetis, id est morticinum et captum a bestia seu aucupio, nisi ejus quod ita capitur, sanguis primo fundatur. Unde Ezechiel ait: Omne morticinum et captum a bestia non comedent sacerdotes. Itaque post diluvium concessit Deus hominibus carnes et pisces ad manducandum: tum quia natura humana de cetero fuit fragilior et pluribus indigens, tum quia fecunditas terræ exstitit minorata, et terræ nascentia minus vigorosa minusque nutritiva; ideo ait Glossa: Esus carnium videtur concessus post diluvium propter infecunditatem terræ, et hominis fragilitatem. Hinc cantat Psalmographus Deo: Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus, videlicet hominis, oves et boves universas, etc.
paras.en: [[9:4|Saving that flesh with blood you shall not eat|Excepto quod carnem cum sanguine non comedetis]], that is, what has been choked or strangled, or drowned, and everything of the kind that dies without the shedding of its blood. Or, [[9:4|flesh with blood|Carnem cum sanguine]]: that is, you shall not eat blood by itself, or separated from the flesh, such as something made from blood, as you may eat flesh once its blood has been poured out. This too the Apostles decreed in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 15:28|it hath seemed good|Visum est]], they say, [[Acts 15:28|to the Holy Ghost and to us to lay no further burden upon you|Spiritui Sancto et nobis, nihil aliud imponere vobis]], except that [[Acts 15:29|you abstain from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication|abstineatis ab immolatis simulacrorum, et suffocato, et sanguine, et fornicatione]]. It may also be expounded thus: [[9:4|flesh with blood you shall not eat|Carnem cum sanguine non comedetis]], that is, what has died of itself, and what has been caught by a beast or in fowling, unless the blood of what is so caught be first poured out. Hence Ezechiel says: [[Ezech 44:31|The priests shall not eat of any thing that is dead of itself or caught by a beast|Omne morticinum et captum a bestia non comedent sacerdotes]]. And so after the flood God granted men flesh and fish to eat: both because human nature was thenceforth frailer and in need of more things, and because the fruitfulness of the earth was lessened, and what grows from the earth was less vigorous and less nourishing. Hence the Gloss says: The eating of flesh seems to have been granted after the flood because of the barrenness of the earth and the frailty of man. Hence the Psalmist sings to God: [[Ps 8:8|Thou hast subjected all things under his feet|Omnia subjecisti sub pedibus ejus]], that is, man's, [[Ps 8:8|all sheep and oxen|oves et boves universas]], etc.

paras.t: Quæri potest, an istud præceptum obliget modo. Respondetur, quod non omnifarie, neque in quantum fuit cærimoniale. Et quod in Actibus Apostolorum leguntur instituisse Apostoli, fuit solum ex certa ratione servandum ad tempus, quantum ad id quod tangitur ibi de observatione quorumdam legalium, quatenus conversi ex Judaismo et gentilitate, coalescerent simul pacifice, nec scandalizarent se invicem, sicut de hoc super Actus Apostolorum plenius scripsi.
paras.en: It may be asked whether this precept binds now. The answer is: not in every respect, nor in so far as it was ceremonial. And what the Apostles are read in the Acts of the Apostles to have laid down[[Acts 15:29||]] was to be kept only for a time and for a definite reason, as regards what is touched on there concerning the observance of certain legal precepts [that is, observances of the Law of Moses]: namely, so that those converted from Judaism and from among the Gentiles might grow together in peace and not scandalize one another, as I have written more fully on this in my commentary on the Acts of the Apostles [the editors note in the margin that Denis wrote on the Acts before this work].

paras.t: Deinde subjungitur ratio, cur caro cum sanguine non sit edenda. Sanguinem enim animarum vestrarum, hoc est sanguinem vestrum, intelligendo totum pro parte, seu Sanguinem animarum vestrarum, id est corporum vestrorum animatorum, utpote effusionem injustam sanguinis humani, requiram de manu cunctarum bestiarum, hoc est bestialium atque ferocium ac fortium hominum. Vel, De manu bestiarum, id est actu feroci brutorum, quia in detestationem homicidii, quandoque occidatur bestia illud committens, ne amplius illud committat, quemadmodum Deus præcepit occidi pecus, cum quo homo coierit. Vel sic: Requiram sanguinem vestrum, supple effusum, de manu, hoc est operatione seu violentia bestiarum, et de manu hominis, hoc est, sive homo per se ipsum immediate, sive per bestiam occiderit hominem, puniam hujusmodi homicidam.
paras.en: Next is added the reason why flesh with blood is not to be eaten: [[9:5|For I will require the blood of your lives|Sanguinem enim animarum vestrarum]], that is, your blood, taking the whole for the part; or, [[9:5|the blood of your lives|Sanguinem animarum vestrarum]], that is, of your living bodies, namely the unjust shedding of human blood, [[9:5|at the hand of every beast|requiram de manu cunctarum bestiarum]], that is, of bestial, fierce and violent men. Or, [[9:5|at the hand of every beast|De manu bestiarum]], that is, by the savage act of brute beasts; because, in detestation of murder, a beast that commits it is sometimes to be killed, lest it commit it again, as God commanded that the beast with which a man had lain be killed[[Lev 20:15||]]. Or thus: [[9:5|I will require|Requiram]] your blood (supply: that has been shed) [[9:5|at the hand|de manu]], that is, by the doing or violence, of the beasts, [[9:5|and at the hand of man|et de manu hominis]], that is, whether a man kill a man by himself, directly, or by means of a beast, I will punish such a murderer.

paras.t: De manu viri et de manu fratris ejus requiram animam hominis; id est, extinctionem injustam vitæ humanæ, videlicet homicidium, requiram et vindicabo, sive occidatur homo a viro extraneo, sive a propinquo ac proximo, et sive hoc fiat a proposito et rancore ab inimico, sive a casu et ignoranter a quocumque propinquo. Quamvis enim utrumque horum non sit æque enorme, tamen et illud quod fit a casu, non evadit omnimodam pœnam, nisi forte in aliquo casu, ut si occisor propinquus et amicus, in nullo fuerit negligens circa ea vitanda per quæ proximum interemit.
paras.en: [[9:5|at the hand of every man, and of his brother, will I require the life of man|De manu viri et de manu fratris ejus requiram animam hominis]]; that is, the unjust extinguishing of human life, namely murder, I will require and avenge, whether a man be slain by a stranger or by a kinsman and neighbour, and whether this be done of set purpose and in rancour by an enemy, or by chance and unknowingly by any kinsman whatever. For although these two are not equally grievous, yet even what is done by chance does not escape all punishment, except perhaps in some case, as when the slayer, a kinsman and friend, was in no way negligent in avoiding the things through which he killed his neighbour.

paras.t: Quicumque fuderit humanum sanguinem, contra processum et ordinem juris, fundetur sanguis illius. Videtur hoc concordare verbo Christi, dicentis: Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit. Sed objici potest, quia et ipse Moyses sanguinem fudit, occidendo Ægyptium, nec tamen effusus est sanguis ejus. Et multi sceleratissimi homicidæ obierunt in pace naturalique morte. Est itaque sensus: Quicumque effuderit sanguinem humanum, fundetur sanguis illius, hoc est, occidi meretur secundum juris rigorem. Sicque quod dicitur, Fundetur, non est assertio aut prænuntiatio, quod semper sic fiat, sed jussio, ut sic fiat de lege communi. Vel, Sanguis ejus fundetur, hoc est, spiritualiter morietur et propria iniquitate peribit, nec mortem æternam effugiet, nisi forte vere, id est condigne pœniteat. Causa quoque cur tam facinorosum, atque tam acriter ulciscendum sit homicidium, subditur: Ad imaginem quippe Dei factus est homo. Quum ergo tantæ sit dignitatis, impiissimum est eum occidere, prætermisso ordine juris; et propter conformitatem naturæ, propter quam est naturaliter diligendus, quia homicidium est contra legem naturalem itemque divinam.
paras.en: [[9:6|Whosoever shall shed man's blood|Quicumque fuderit humanum sanguinem]], against the process and order of law, [[9:6|his blood shall be shed|fundetur sanguis illius]]. This seems to agree with the word of Christ, who says: [[Matt 26:52|all that take the sword shall perish with the sword|Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit]]. But it may be objected that Moses himself shed blood by slaying the Egyptian[[Ex 2:12||]], and yet his blood was not shed; and many most wicked murderers have died in peace and by a natural death. The sense, then, is: [[9:6|Whosoever shall shed man's blood, his blood shall be shed|Quicumque effuderit sanguinem humanum, fundetur sanguis illius]], that is, he deserves to be slain according to the rigour of the law. And so what is said, [[9:6|shall be shed|Fundetur]], is not an assertion or a foretelling that it will always so happen, but a command that it be so done by the common law. Or, [[9:6|his blood shall be shed|Sanguis ejus fundetur]], that is, he will die spiritually and perish by his own iniquity, and will not escape eternal death, unless perhaps he repent truly, that is, worthily. The reason too why murder is so heinous, and to be so sharply avenged, is added: [[9:6|for man was made to the image of God|Ad imaginem quippe Dei factus est homo]]. Since, then, he is of such dignity, it is most impious to kill him, setting aside the order of law; and also because of the likeness of nature, on account of which he is naturally to be loved; for murder is against the natural law and likewise against the divine.

paras.t: Præterea quæritur, quid ista ratio pertineat ad præfatum præceptum, quo Deus prohibuit manducare carnem cum sanguine. Prohibitio namque homicidii seu ultio ejus, non videtur aliquo modo causa seu ratio, cur caro animalis non sit cum sanguine comedenda. Respondetur, quod causa accipitur hic pro motivo vel signo, ita quod Deus in ampliorem homicidii detestationem ac prohibitionem, prohibuit animalia atrocius suffocari aut edi, quam ratio dictat. Aut quod tanta prohibitio ac ultio homicidii, signum est quod Deus non vult animalia crudelius strangulari, laniari, ac comedi, quam oportet seu expedit. Unde in Deuteronomio prohibet Deus hœdum coqui in lacte matris suæ, et avem capi cum pullis suis, et consimilia quædam, quæ quamvis spiritualem habeant rationem, habent tamen et litteralem, ut scilicet homo circa bruta quamdam exhibeat pietatem, quatenus sic discat eam amplius exhibere hominibus, prout Rabbi Moyses scribit, et suo loco, Deo præstante, dicetur. Et ex inductis etiam constat, non esse satis idonee dictum, quod Rabbi Paulus hoc loco in reprobationem Nicolai de Lyra, scribit, dicendo: Qualitercumque littera exponatur, ex hoc quod Deus prohibuit homicidium, non habetur ratio ad hoc, quod caro animalis non comedatur cum sanguine. Hoc enim non consonat textui, in quo quum Dominus jussit, Carnem cum sanguine non comedetis, protinus subditur, Sanguinem enim animarum vestrarum requiram: quod tanquam causa prohibitionis illius inseritur. Dicit autem Rabbi Paulus, quod pro hac conjunctione causali, Enim, in Hebræo habetur, Verumtamen, ut sit sensus: Verumtamen sanguinem animarum vestrarum requiram, id est, quamvis concesserim occisionem et esum animalium, non tamen hominum. Et quamvis hæc littera planior esset, littera tamen nostræ translationis videtur secundior, potestque esse quod dictio Hebraica sit ad utramque æquivoca.
paras.en: It is further asked what this reason has to do with the aforesaid precept by which God forbade the eating of flesh with blood. For the forbidding of murder, or its punishment, does not seem in any way to be a cause or reason why the flesh of an animal is not to be eaten with its blood. The answer is that *cause* is taken here for a motive or a sign: so that God, for a fuller detestation and prohibition of murder, forbade animals to be choked or eaten more cruelly than reason dictates; or that so great a prohibition and punishment of murder is a sign that God does not wish animals to be strangled, torn and eaten more cruelly than is fitting or expedient. Hence in Deuteronomy God forbids us to [[Deut 14:21|boil a kid in the milk of his dam|hœdum coqui in lacte matris suæ]], and to take the mother bird with her young[[Deut 22:6||]], and certain like things; which, though they have a spiritual reason, have also a literal one: namely, that man should show a certain kindness toward the brute beasts[[Ex 23:5||]], so that he may thus learn to show it the more toward men, as Rabbi Moses [that is, Moses Maimonides] writes, and as will be said in its place, God granting. And from what has been brought forward it is also plain that what Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, in his Additions to Lyra's Postilla] writes on this place, in refutation of Nicholas of Lyra, is not said fittingly enough, when he says: However the letter be expounded, from God's forbidding murder no reason is to be had why the flesh of an animal is not to be eaten with its blood. For this does not agree with the text, in which, as soon as the Lord has commanded, [[9:4|flesh with blood you shall not eat|Carnem cum sanguine non comedetis]], there is added at once, [[9:5|For I will require the blood of your lives|Sanguinem enim animarum vestrarum requiram]]: which is put in as the cause of that prohibition. Rabbi Paul, however, says that in place of this causal conjunction *For* [Latin *enim*], the Hebrew has *Nevertheless*, so that the sense is: Nevertheless I will require the blood of your lives; that is, although I have granted the killing and eating of animals, yet not of men. And although this reading would be plainer, yet the reading of our translation seems more apt; and it may be that the Hebrew word can bear either sense.

paras.t: Consequenter describitur, qualiter Deus assecuravit ipsum Noe, quod diluvium de cætero non veniet: quod quamvis jam per verba ei promiserat, jam tamen per signum sensibile idem ei insinuat. Nempe ut Josephus recitat, homines maxime tunc timebant, ne rursus inundaret diluvium. Noe quoque quum quotidie Dominum exoraret, ne hoc amplius fieret, ideo Dominus pepigit pactum cum Noe de hoc, sicut subjungitur: Ecce ego statuam pactum meum vobiscum, hoc est, cum te ac filiis tuis inibo et ponam fœdus seu ordinationem, et quamdam spontaneam obligationem, per signum sensibile de diluvio amplius non venturo: et cum semine vestro post vos, id est, pactum istud concernet etiam posteros vestros usque in finem mundi, ita quod et ipsi erunt de diluvio assecurati: et ad omnem animam viventem quæ est vobiscum, id est ad omne irrationale animal vobiscum exsistens, tam in volucribus, quam in jumentis et pecudibus terræ, cunctisque aliis, puta reptilibus, quæ egressa sunt de arca, et universis bestiis terræ, quæ vel nunc sunt, vel postea erunt.
paras.en: Next it is described how God assured Noe that the flood would not come again: which, though he had already promised it to him in words[[Gen 8:21||]] [the margin note here cannot be read; the promise in words is presumably Gen 8:21], he now also makes known to him by a sign that can be perceived by the senses. For, as Josephus relates, men then greatly feared lest the flood should overflow again; and since Noe also prayed the Lord daily that this should happen no more, the Lord therefore made a covenant with Noe about it, as is added: [[9:9|Behold I will establish my covenant with you|Ecce ego statuam pactum meum vobiscum]], that is, with thee and thy sons I will enter into and set a covenant or ordinance, a kind of freely undertaken obligation, by a sign perceptible to the senses, that the flood shall come no more; [[9:9|and with your seed after you|et cum semine vestro post vos]], that is, this covenant will concern your posterity also, until the end of the world, so that they too will be assured against the flood; [[9:10|And with every living soul that is with you|et ad omnem animam viventem quæ est vobiscum]], that is, to every irrational animal that exists with you, [[9:10|as well in all birds, as in cattle and beasts of the earth|tam in volucribus, quam in jumentis et pecudibus terræ]], and all the others, for instance the creeping things, [[9:10|that are come forth out of the ark|quæ egressa sunt de arca]], [[9:10|and in all the beasts of the earth|et universis bestiis terræ]], whether those that are now or those that shall be hereafter.

paras.t: Statuam pactum meum præfatum, ita quod istud etiam irrationalia ista concernet, sic quod non peribunt diluvio; vobiscum, scilicet sicut constitui istud tecum, atque cum filiis ac posteris tuis. Neque erit deinceps diluvium dissipans omnem terram, id est, universos habitatores et bruta ac fructus terræ evertens, quasi dicat: Non erit ultra universale diluvium. Particularia tamen diluvia interim sæpius contigerunt, in quibus multa millia hominum ac brutorum submersa sunt.
paras.en: [[9:11|I will establish my covenant|Statuam pactum meum]], the aforesaid, so that it will concern these irrational creatures too, so that they shall not perish by a flood; [[9:11|with you|vobiscum]], that is, as I have made it with thee, and with thy sons and posterity. [[9:11|neither shall there be from henceforth a flood to waste the earth|Neque erit deinceps diluvium dissipans omnem terram]], that is, overthrowing all the inhabitants, and the brute beasts and the fruits of the earth; as if he said: There shall be no more a universal flood. Particular floods, however, have often happened meanwhile, in which many thousands of men and beasts have been drowned.

paras.t: Dixitque Deus : Hoc est signum fœderis quod do inter me et vos, et ad omnem animam viventem quæ est vobiscum in generationes sempiternas : id est, sensibile indicium pacti, quod statuo inter me et homines ac jumenta usque ad finem mundi, est istud quod sequitur : Arcum meum, id est iridem quæ habet formam arcus extenti, videlicet semicirculi, ponam, id est apparere faciam, in nubibus, et erit signum fœderis […] inter me et inter terram, id est habitatores terræ. Quumque obduxero nubibus cœlum, apparebit arcus meus in nubibus : non quod semper appareat aut sit iris, quando sunt nubes, sed interdum : et recordabor fœderis mei facti vobiscum : id est, per effectum monstrabo me memorem pacti hujus, et per modum recordantis habebo me pie vobiscum agendo.
paras.en: [[9:12|And God said: This is the sign of the covenant which I give between me and you, and to every living soul that is with you, for perpetual generations|Dixitque Deus : Hoc est signum fœderis quod do inter me et vos, et ad omnem animam viventem quæ est vobiscum in generationes sempiternas]]: that is, the token, perceptible to the senses, of the pact which I establish between me and men and beasts until the end of the world is this which follows: [[9:13|my bow|Arcum meum]], that is, the rainbow, which has the shape of a bow drawn taut, namely of a semicircle, [[9:13|I will set|ponam]], that is, I will make to appear, [[9:13|in the clouds, and it shall be the sign of a covenant|in nubibus, et erit signum fœderis]] […] [[9:13|between me and between the earth|inter me et inter terram]], that is, the dwellers on the earth. [[9:14|And when I shall cover the sky with clouds, my bow shall appear in the clouds|Quumque obduxero nubibus cœlum, apparebit arcus meus in nubibus]]: not that the rainbow always appears, or exists, when there are clouds, but at times; [[9:15|And I will remember my covenant|et recordabor fœderis mei]] made [[9:15|with you|vobiscum]]: that is, I will show by the effect that I am mindful of this pact, and after the manner of one who remembers I will bear myself toward you by dealing kindly with you.

paras.t: Circa hæc dicunt Glossa et Scholastica historia, item Strabus et alii : Arcus est signum duorum judiciorum, unius per aquam facti, ac præteriti, ne timeatur ; et alterius quod fiet per ignem, ut exspectetur : ideo iris duos habet colores, unum ceruleum, qui aqueus est atque exterior, et designat judicium jam diluvio factum : alium rubeum, qui igneus est et interior, significatque judicium per ignem futurum. Et tradunt Sancti, quod quadraginta annis ante judicium non videbitur arcus : quod etiam naturaliter demonstrabit desiccationem aeris tunc inceptam. Hæc ibi.
paras.en: On these words the Gloss and the Scholastic History, and also Strabo and others, say: The bow is the sign of two judgments: of one made by water, and past, that it may not be feared; and of the other, which shall be made by fire, that it may be awaited. Therefore the rainbow has two colours: one blue, which is watery and on the outside, and betokens the judgment already made by the flood; the other red, which is fiery and on the inside, and signifies the judgment to come by fire. And the Saints hand down that for forty years before the judgment the bow will not be seen: which will also show, in the course of nature, the drying of the air begun at that time. Thus far they.

paras.t: Sed istis objicitur : Quum iris sit naturalis effectus, et ante diluvium fuit, quemadmodum nubes et pluviæ, non ergo est signum pacti præfati, supernaturaliumque judiciorum. Ad hoc quidam dixerunt, quod ante diluvium non fuerunt nubes, nec pluviæ, neque iris. Unde in Scholastica fertur historia : Usque diluvium non fuerunt aquæ collectæ in nubes. Alcuinus etiam ait : Quoniam arcus non est, nisi ex radiis solis et humida nube, videtur quod ante diluvium non fuerint pluviæ. Poterat autem ex rore et fontium inundatione terra fecundari.
paras.en: But against these it is objected: since the rainbow is a natural effect, and existed before the flood, as did clouds and rains, it is not, then, a sign of the aforesaid pact and of supernatural judgments. To this some have said that before the flood there were no clouds, nor rains, nor rainbow. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History: Until the flood the waters were not gathered into clouds. Alcuin too says: Since there is no bow except from the rays of the sun and a moist cloud, it seems that before the flood there were no rains. But the earth could be made fruitful by the dew and by the overflowing of springs.

paras.t: Sed istud non placet aliis, quoniam sufficientes totalesque causæ nubium et pluviarum ac iridis, fuerunt ante diluvium, sicut et nunc, videlicet calor solis, influentia siderum, dispositio aeris, aqua maris ac fluminum et indigentia terræ. Iris autem fit ex repercussione radiorum solis ad nubem aquosam : quæ repercussio fuit tunc naturaliter ut nunc, nisi quis dicat quod miraculose et supernaturaliter tunc prohibebatur : contra quod loquitur Augustinus, quod Deus res creatas sic administrat ac regit, ut eas agere sinat proprias operationes et motus. Nec terra poterat ubique sufficienter irrigari ex rore et fontibus : imo sicut quibusdam terris irrigatio pluvialis noxia est, ut patet de terra Ægypti, ita quibusdam terris noxia est irrigatio fluvialis. Propter quod in Deuteronomio scriptum est : Terra ad quam ingredieris, videlicet terra promissionis, non est sicut terra Ægypti, ubi jacto semine aquæ ducuntur irriguæ, sed montuosa est et campestris, de cœlo exspectans pluviam. Denique, supra dictum est. Non enim pluerat Dominus super terram : quod dictum est pro tempore illo, antequam primi parentes peccaverunt, quod tempus erat brevissimum, et vix unius hebdomadæ : per quod satis insinuari videtur, quod postea infra duo millia annorum, qui ante diluvium erant, sæpius pluit.
paras.en: But this does not please others, since the sufficient and complete causes of clouds and rains and of the rainbow existed before the flood, as they do now: namely the heat of the sun, the influence of the stars, the disposition of the air, the water of the sea and of the rivers, and the need of the earth. Now the rainbow is made by the reflection of the sun's rays on a watery cloud; and that reflection took place then by nature, as it does now, unless someone says that it was then prevented miraculously and supernaturally: against which Augustine says that God so governs and rules created things as to let them carry out their own operations and motions. Nor could the earth everywhere be watered sufficiently by dew and springs; rather, just as watering by rain is harmful to some lands, as is plain in the land of Egypt, so watering by rivers is harmful to some lands. For which reason it is written in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 11:10|the land, which thou goest|Terra ad quam ingredieris]], namely the land of promise, [[Deut 11:10|is not like the land of Egypt|non est sicut terra Ægypti]], [[Deut 11:10|where, when the seed is sown, waters are brought in to water it|ubi jacto semine aquæ ducuntur irriguæ]]; [[Deut 11:11|But it is a land of hills and plains, expecting rain from heaven|sed montuosa est et campestris, de cœlo exspectans pluviam]]. Finally, it was said above: [[Gen 2:5|for the Lord God had not rained upon the earth|Non enim pluerat Dominus super terram]]; which was said of that time before our first parents sinned, a time that was very short, scarcely a week: and by this it seems to be implied clearly enough that afterwards, within the two thousand years that were before the flood, it rained often.

paras.t: Alii ergo dicunt ante diluvium fuisse nubes, pluvias et iridem. Nihilo minus asserunt, iridem post diluvium datam in signum diluvii non futuri, non in signum pure ad placitum, sicut nomina significant rem, sed in signum quodammodo naturale, sicut urina signum est sanitatis. Iris namque generatur tempore non multum sicco, nec multum pluvioso, quia fit in nube rorida soli opposita : ad quam iridem requiritur etiam nubes densa, sic tamen, ut vapores non sint in tanta abundantia, quin solis calor queat eos resolvere, ita quod ex eis non sequitur pluvia magna. Sicque iris naturaliter signat diluvium non cito futurum. Sed contra hanc responsionem arguit quidam, cujus dicta Rabbi Paulus satis reprobat in hoc loco. Nec enim positionem illam satis idonee et integre recitare censetur, et contra verba magis quam contra mentem ponentium arguit. Non enim positio illa vult dicere, quod apparitio iridis sit signum pure naturale, et necessarium ex se diluvii nunquam futuri ; sed quantum ad hoc dicitur signum naturale illius rei, in quantum designat ex sua natura diluvium non cito futurum, per quod habet congruentiam naturalem designandi ex beneplacito Dei diluvium nunquam futurum. Nec huic positioni contrariatur positio tertia, et clarior, dicens quod iris est signum ad placitum diluvii non futuri, in quantum Deus ex beneplacito suo sic ordinavit et voluit, ut apparitio hujus naturalis effectus, videlicet iridis, sit signum rememorativum fœderis Dei cum hominibus initi de diluvio non futuro, seu signum diluvii nunquam venturi. Quemadmodum interdum lapis jacens in agro, ex beneplacito hominum fit signum divisionis hereditatum seu dominiorum. Et hanc positionem induxit Rabbi Moyses Gerundensis, quam et sanctus Thomas in quodam approbat loco. Nec inconveniens est, ut naturalis effectus sit signum ad placitum supernaturalis aut voluntariæ rei, quam naturaliter designare non valet.
paras.en: Others, then, say that before the flood there were clouds, rains and the rainbow. Nevertheless they assert that the rainbow was given after the flood as a sign that there would be no more flood: not as a sign purely at will [that is, *ad placitum*: a sign by convention or choice, as opposed to a natural sign], as names signify a thing, but as a sign in some way natural, as urine is a sign of health. For the rainbow is produced in weather neither very dry nor very rainy, since it is formed in a dewy cloud opposite the sun; and for the rainbow a dense cloud is also needed, yet such that the vapours are not so abundant that the heat of the sun cannot dissolve them, so that no great rain follows from them. And so the rainbow by nature signifies that a flood is not soon to come. But against this answer a certain writer argues [probably Lyra, to whose Postill Rabbi Paul wrote his Additions], whose words Rabbi Paul refutes well enough in this place.
