Hence Josephus says more plainly: The sons of Japheth held the northern region, from Taurus and Amanus, mountains of Cilicia and Syria, as far as the river Tanais, and in Europe as far as Gadira [that is, Cadiz]. The sons of Cham held all the lands from the province of Syria and the mountains Amanus and Libanus, whatever lie toward the sea, taking in also those that reach to the Ocean. The sons of Sem dwelt apart, beginning from the Euphrates.

paras.t: Præterea, in Scholastica historia recitatur, quod Cham vixit usque ad tempus Nini, et regnavit in Bractia, dicebaturque Zoroastres, qui fuit magister astrorum et inventor magicæ artis, qui et septem liberales artes scripsit in quatuordecim columnis, videlicet in septem æreis atque in septem latericiis, totas in utrisque septenis, contra utrumque diluvium, scilicet aquæ et ignis. Augustinus quoque testatur, quod ante diluvium scripsit eas in columnis, et post diluvium eadem curiositate quæsivit. Ex quo apparet, quod semper exstitit malus. Insuper Philo disertissimus Judæorum, testatur in libro Quæstionum super Genesim, quod ex tribus filiis Noe, ipso vivente, viginti quatuor millia virorum et centum, præter mulieres et parvulos, nata sunt.
paras.en: Further, it is related in the Scholastic History that Cham lived until the time of Ninus and reigned in Bractia [that is, Bactria], and was called Zoroaster; he was a master of the stars and the inventor of the magic art, and he also wrote the seven liberal arts on fourteen pillars, namely on seven of bronze and seven of brick, the whole of them on each set of seven, against both floods, that is, of water and of fire. Augustine too testifies that before the flood he wrote them on pillars, and after the flood sought them out with the same curiosity; from which it appears that he was always wicked. Moreover Philo, the most eloquent of the Jews, testifies in his book of Questions on Genesis that from the three sons of Noe, while Noe himself was living, twenty-four thousand one hundred men were born, besides women and little children.

paras.t: Postremo, ut tactum est, Judæi dicti sunt Hebræi ab Heber patriarcha. Augustinus tamen quæstionem inducit, an potius dicti sint Hebræi ab Heber, vel ab Abraham, quasi Habræi, quoniam Abraham fuit principalior pater eorum. Tenendum est autem, quod ab Heber sic dicti sint, præsertim quum et ipse Abraham infra vocetur Hebræus, quod et Josephus asserit. Attamen Rabbi Paulus dicit oppositum, quod alibi reprobavi.
paras.en: Lastly, as was touched on above, the Jews were called Hebrews from the patriarch Heber. Augustine, however, raises the question whether they were rather called Hebrews from Heber or from Abraham, as if Habræi, since Abraham was their more principal father. But it is to be held that they were so called from Heber, especially since Abraham himself is called a Hebrew further on[[Gen 14:13||]], as Josephus also asserts. Yet Rabbi Paul says the opposite, which I have refuted elsewhere.

11.title: Expositio litteralis capituli undecimi: Erat autem terra labii unius
11.title_en: Literal exposition of the eleventh chapter: And the earth was of one tongue

paras.t: Quod præcedenti capitulo dictum est de gentium divisione, nunc declaratur, videlicet cur et qualiter factum sit. Erat autem terra labii unius et sermonum eorumdem: id est, universi habitatores terræ erant tunc ejusdem loquelæ, quantum ad habitualem facultatem loquendi; eorumdem quoque verborum, quantum ad loquendi usum seu actum. Fuitque lingua illa idioma Hebræum, primis parentibus dinitum, et in eorum posteris universis relictum, usque ad tempus unde nunc agitur. Quemadmodum enim homines universi ejusdem sunt speciei et conformis ingenii, sic rationabile fuit, ut eisdem uterentur sermonibus, per quod etiam poterant sibi invicem facilius communicare, succurrere, et prodesse.
paras.en: What was said in the preceding chapter about the division of the nations is now made plain, namely why and how it came about. [[11:1|And the earth was of one tongue, and of the same speech|Erat autem terra labii unius et sermonum eorumdem]]: that is, all the inhabitants of the earth were then of the same language as regards the habitual faculty of speaking, and of the same words as regards the use or act of speaking. And that tongue was the Hebrew idiom, given [the print reads *dinitum*, apparently a misprint for *inditum*, "implanted", or *traditum*, "handed down"] to our first parents and left to all their descendants down to the time now being treated. For just as all men are of the same species and of like mind, so it was reasonable that they should use the same words; by this, too, they could more easily communicate with one another, help one another and do one another good.

paras.t: Quumque proficiscerentur de oriente, recedendo de orientali plaga terræ, invenerunt campum in terra Sennaar, quæ postea dicta est terra Babylonis et Chaldæa, in qua postmodum Nabuchodonosor rex Chaldæorum regnavit: et habitaverunt in eo, id est, habitare cœperunt ibidem. Fuit enim campus ille planus, pulcher, longissimus atque latissimus, et per consequens aptus ad cohabitationem eorum, et constructionem urbis ac turris, per quam possent evadere diluvium, si veniret, cujus inundationem vehementer timebant, non credentes pacto Dei cum Noe peracto de diluvio amplius non futuro. Hinc in Scholastica historia legitur: Post obitum Noe moventes pedes suos ab oriente, convenerunt duces in campum unum Sennaar, et timentes diluvium, consilio Nemrod volentis regnare super eos, cœperunt ædificare. Dicitur autem in eadem Historia, quod exemplo Nemrod regnantis super filios Cham, cœpit et Jectan regnare super filios Sem, et Sufene super filios Japhet. Itaque duces illi convenerunt in campum præfatum cum populis suis, ad providendum sibi contra diluvium. Circa hoc Josephus narrat, quod filii Noe primo de montibus ad campestria descenderunt, posteri vero eorum præ timore diluvii non audebant descendere, sed filii Noe induxerunt eos ad descendendum.
paras.en: [[11:2|And when they removed from the east|Quumque proficiscerentur de oriente]], withdrawing from the eastern region of the earth, [[11:2|they found a plain in the land of Sennaar|invenerunt campum in terra Sennaar]], which was afterwards called the land of Babylon and Chaldea, where Nabuchodonosor king of the Chaldeans later reigned: [[11:2|and dwelt in it|et habitaverunt in eo]], that is, they began to dwell there. For that plain was level, beautiful, very long and very broad, and so suited to their living together and to the building of a city and a tower by which they might escape a flood if one came; for they greatly feared its inundation, not believing the covenant God had made with Noe, that there would be no more flood. Hence we read in the Scholastic History: After the death of Noe, moving their feet from the east, the chiefs came together into one plain of Sennaar, and fearing a flood, they began to build on the counsel of Nemrod, who wished to reign over them. It is also said in the same History that, after the example of Nemrod reigning over the sons of Cham, Jectan too began to reign over the sons of Sem, and Sufene over the sons of Japhet. So those chiefs came together with their peoples into the plain spoken of, to provide for themselves against a flood. On this Josephus relates that the sons of Noe first came down from the mountains to the plains, but their descendants did not dare to come down for fear of the flood, and the sons of Noe induced them to come down.

paras.t: Dixitque alter ad proximum suum, id est mutuo se hortabantur: Venite, faciamus lateres, et coquamus eos igni, ut indurata materia non valeat aquis dissolvi, nec habuerunt lapides tunc ad manum. Habueruntque lateres pro saxis, et bitumen pro cæmento. Unde infra legitur de puteis bituminis, sicque bitumen poterant copiose acquirere. Dicitur quoque in Glossa, quod non potest aquis dissolvi postquam siccatum est, nec potest aliqua re dissolvi nisi menstruo sanguine.
paras.en: [[11:3|And each one said to his neighbour|Dixitque alter ad proximum suum]], that is, they urged one another on: [[11:3|Come let us make brick, and bake them with fire|Venite, faciamus lateres, et coquamus eos igni]], so that the hardened material could not be dissolved by water; and they had no stones at hand then. [[11:3|And they had brick instead of stones, and slime instead of mortar|Habueruntque lateres pro saxis, et bitumen pro cæmento]]. Hence we read further on of pits of bitumen [the Douay-Rheims calls it "slime"], and so they could get bitumen in plenty. The Gloss also says that once it has dried it cannot be dissolved by water, nor by anything else except menstrual blood.

paras.t: Et dixerunt: Venite, et faciamus nobis, utpote ad commodum et honorem nostrum, non ad gloriam Dei, civitatem et turrim, cujus culmen pertingat ad cœlum, id est, tam altam sicut fieri potest. Hoc dixerunt ex consilio Nemrod, volueruntque turrim in medio construere civitatis, tanquam fortalitium et consistorium seu prætorium dominorum, tam altum, ut aquis quantumlibet erumpentibus operiri non posset. Circa quod tangit Augustinus, quod per turrim singulariter nominatam, intelliguntur turres pluraliter, ita quod vel omnes turres civitatis intendebant altissimas facere, vel unam inter eas præcipue altam. Verum (ut loquitur Augustinus) quid fecisset eorum vana præsumptio, quando aquæ excessissent montes altissimos, nebulosumque aerem, pertingendo ad aerem tam subtilem, quod in eo homines vivere nequeunt? Et celebremus nomen nostrum, id est, nomen famosum ac inclytum procuremus ac relinquamus nobismetipsis, antequam dividamur in universas terras. Videbant enim posteros suos universos non posse habitare in loco illo, sed undique diffundendos, quibus voluerunt præbere exemplum ædificandi talem confugii turrim. Itaque incitati fuerunt ad ædificandum urbem illam turrimque, non tantum timore diluvii, sed et desiderio famæ humanæ ac gloriæ temporalis, in quo patet eorum elatio.
paras.en: [[11:4|And they said: Come|Et dixerunt: Venite]], [[11:4|let us make|et faciamus nobis]] for ourselves, that is, for our own advantage and honour, not for the glory of God, [[11:4|a city and a tower, the top whereof may reach to heaven|civitatem et turrim, cujus culmen pertingat ad cœlum]], that is, as high as can be done. This they said on the counsel of Nemrod, and they meant to build the tower in the middle of the city, as a fortress and the council-house or seat of government of the lords, so high that it could not be covered by the waters, however far they might break forth. On this Augustine remarks that by the tower, named in the singular, towers in the plural are to be understood: so that either they meant to make all the towers of the city very high, or one among them especially high. But (as Augustine puts it) what would their vain presumption have done, when the waters had gone beyond the highest mountains and the cloudy air, reaching up to air so thin that men cannot live in it? [[11:4|and let us make our name famous|Et celebremus nomen nostrum]], that is, let us win and leave for ourselves a famous and renowned name, [[11:4|before we be scattered abroad into all lands|antequam dividamur in universas terras]]. For they saw that all their descendants could not live in that place but must be spread abroad everywhere, and they wished to give them an example of building such a tower of refuge. So they were moved to build that city and tower not only by fear of the flood but also by desire for human fame and temporal glory, and in this their pride is plain.

paras.t: Descendit autem Dominus, ut videret civitatem et turrim quam ædificaverant, id est ædificare cœperant, filii Adam, qui in hoc secuti sunt transgressionem Adæ. Porro Septuaginta transtulerunt, Filii hominum. Nam isti fuerunt filii hominum, non filii Dei. Loquitur autem Scriptura de incircumscriptibili, invariabili et supersapientissimo Deo more humano, non quod ipse in sua deitate descendat aut videre incipiat seu aliquid discat, sed quia ipse qui præsidet cœlis, aliquid de novo agit in terris, seque per effectum demonstrat attendere ea quæ in terris geruntur. Ideo loquitur Augustinus: Non loco movetur qui semper ubique est totus, sed descendere dicitur, quum aliquid facit in terra, quod præter usitatum naturæ cursum mirabiliter factum, ostendit nobis præsentiam ejus; atque (ut ait Gregorius) descendere Dei, est humanorum actuum attendere pravitatem. Utitur quoque Scriptura hoc modo loquendi, ad innuendum quod prælati et judices non debent aliquid judicare, nisi illud prius diligenter considerent.
paras.en: [[11:5|And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower|Descendit autem Dominus, ut videret civitatem et turrim]], which [[11:5|the children of Adam|filii Adam]] had built, that is, had begun to build: in this they followed the transgression of Adam. The Septuagint, for its part, translated: The sons of men. For these were sons of men, not sons of God. Now Scripture speaks in a human way of God, who cannot be circumscribed, who does not change and who is wise above all wisdom: not that he comes down in his Godhead, or begins to see, or learns anything, but because he who presides over the heavens does something new on earth, and shows by its effect that he attends to what is done on earth. So Augustine says: He who is always whole everywhere is not moved from place to place; but he is said to come down when he does something on earth which, being done wonderfully beyond the usual course of nature, shows us his presence. And (as Gregory says) God's coming down is his attending to the wickedness of human deeds. Scripture also uses this manner of speaking to intimate that prelates and judges ought not to judge anything without first considering it carefully.

paras.t: Et dixit Dominus: Ecce unus est populus, unus inquam, in generali et unus consensu malo ac cohabitatione, imo et unitate naturæ specificæ, et unum est labium, id est idioma, omnibus. Cœperuntque hoc facere, scilicet urbem et turrim istam construere, nec desistent, quantum in ipsis est, et nisi impediantur virtute divina, a cogitationibus suis, quibus firmiter proposuerunt ista ædificare, donec eas opere compleant. Venite igitur, descendamus, et confundamus ibi linguam eorum. Jam dictum est semel, Descendit autem Dominus ut videret civitatem: quomodo ergo nunc denuo dicitur, Venite igitur, descendamus? Ad hoc Augustinus respondet dupliciter. Primo, ut istud quod dicitur, Venite, descendamus, sit recapitulatio, pandens qualiter factum sit quod prius dictum est, Descendit Dominus. Secundo, ut istud sit verbum Dei ad angelos, qui in destructione turris fuerunt divinæ executores justitiæ, in quibus Deus descendit, quia in ipsis fuit. Itaque Dominus dixit, Confundamus linguam eorum, id est, linguis eorum inferamus diversas loquelas, non plures eidem, sed uni linguæ istam loquelam, alii illam.
paras.en: [[11:6|And he said|Et dixit Dominus]]: [[11:6|Behold, it is one people|Ecce unus est populus]]; one, I say, in a general way, and one in evil agreement and in living together, and indeed in the unity of their specific nature [that is, as being of one species]; [[11:6|and all have one tongue|et unum est labium]], that is, one idiom, common to [[11:6|all|omnibus]]. [[11:6|and they have begun to do this|Cœperuntque hoc facere]], namely to build this city and tower, [[11:6|neither will they leave off|nec desistent]] (as far as in them lies, and unless they are hindered by divine power) [[11:6|from their designs|a cogitationibus suis]], in which they have firmly resolved to build these things, [[11:6|till they accomplish them in deed|donec eas opere compleant]]. [[11:7|Come ye, therefore, let us go down, and there confound their tongue|Venite igitur, descendamus, et confundamus ibi linguam eorum]]. It has already been said once, [[11:5|And the Lord came down to see the city|Descendit autem Dominus ut videret civitatem]]: how then is it said again now, [[11:7|Come ye, therefore, let us go down|Venite igitur, descendamus]]? To this Augustine gives two answers. First, that this saying, [[11:7|Come ye, therefore, let us go down|Venite, descendamus]], is a recapitulation, showing how there came about what was said before, [[11:5|And the Lord came down|Descendit Dominus]]. Second, that it is the word of God to the angels, who were the executors of divine justice in the destruction of the tower; in them God came down, because he was in them. So the Lord said: Let us [[11:7|confound their tongue|Confundamus linguam eorum]], that is, let us put different speech into their tongues: not several into the same tongue, but this speech into one tongue, that into another.

paras.t: Circa hoc scribit Alcuinus: In hac divisione linguarum nil novum fecit Dominus, sed dicendi modos et formas loquelarum gentibus diversis divisit. Unde easdem syllabas, et ejusdem potestatis litteras, aliter et aliter conjunctas, in diversis linguis invenimus, quod in Scholastica habetur historia: quod intelligi potest quantum ad verborum materiam, præsertim remotam, quæ sunt syllabæ ipsæ: sed quantum ad formam verborum, utpote quoad litterarum et syllabarum proximam connexionem ac propriam contemperationem, fecit Dominus in divisione illa aliquid novum, imo rem valde mirabilem et supernaturalem, ita quod homines cœperunt subito linguis uti, et verba proferre quæ nunquam antea audierunt nec didicerunt. Propter quod Augustinus fatetur: Per linguas divisæ sunt gentes, sicut placuit Deo, qui hoc modis occultis, nobisque incomprehensibilibus fecit. Insuper verbum hoc, Venite, descendamus, etc., potest esse verbum totius superdignissimæ Trinitatis ad se ipsam, cujus indivisa sunt opera, seu Patris ad Filium ac Spiritum Sanctum.
paras.en: On this Alcuin writes: In this division of tongues the Lord made nothing new, but divided among different nations the manners of speaking and the forms of speech. Hence we find the same syllables, and letters of the same value [*potestas*, the sound a letter stands for], joined now one way and now another in different languages; and this is found in the Scholastic History. This can be understood of the matter of words, especially their remote matter [in the language of the schools, the material furthest removed from the finished thing], which is the syllables themselves. But as to the form of words, that is, as to the proximate joining of letters and syllables and their proper ordering together, the Lord did make something new in that division, indeed something most wonderful and supernatural: men suddenly began to use tongues and to utter words they had never heard or learned before. For this reason Augustine owns: The nations were divided by their tongues as it pleased God, who did this in hidden ways that are beyond our grasp. Further, this saying, [[11:7|Come ye, therefore, let us go down|Venite, descendamus]], etc., can be a word of the whole most worthy Trinity to itself, whose works are undivided, or of the Father to the Son and the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Ut non audiat unusquisque vocem proximi sui, hoc est, ne unus eorum intelligat verba alterius. Attamen non fuerunt ibi inductæ tot linguæ, quot homines ibi fuerunt, sed plures manserunt ejusdem loquelæ. Nihilo minus Deus (ut reor) ita disposuit, quod in pertinentibus ad ædificationem inceptam, nullus eorum alium intellexit; vel quia hi qui in ædificando erant permixti, fuerunt differentium loquelarum, seu alio modo, Deo omnipotente id disponente.
paras.en: [[11:7|that they may not understand one another's speech|Ut non audiat unusquisque vocem proximi sui]]: that is, so that none of them should understand the words of another. Yet not as many tongues were brought in there as there were men there; many remained of the same speech. Nevertheless God (as I think) so ordered it that in what concerned the building they had begun, none of them understood another: either because those who were mixed together in the building were of different speech, or in some other way, as almighty God ordered it.

paras.t: Atque ita divisit eos Dominus ex illo loco in universas terras, videlicet quosdam in unam provinciam, quosdam in aliam. Qui enim ejusdem erant loquelæ, sibi invicem cohærebant. Et cessaverunt ædificare civitatem et turrim. In primis enim quum cœpissent loqui diversis linguis, nec se invicem intelligerent, nescientes quid eis acciderit, putabant se ab invicem derideri, cœperuntque indignari et corrixari. Uno etiam hoc aut illud postulante, alter aliud porrigebat. Deinde advertentes plagam et ultionem sibi a Deo inflictam, exterriti sunt, formidantes graviorem vindictam, propter quod cessaverunt ab opere illo.
paras.en: [[11:8|And so the Lord scattered them from that place into all lands|Atque ita divisit eos Dominus ex illo loco in universas terras]], namely some into one province, some into another; for those who were of the same speech kept together. [[11:8|and they ceased to build the city|Et cessaverunt ædificare civitatem]] and the tower. For at first, when they had begun to speak in different tongues and did not understand one another, not knowing what had happened to them, they thought they were being mocked by one another, and began to grow angry and to quarrel. And when one asked for this or that, another would hand him something else. Then, noticing the stroke and punishment inflicted on them by God, they were terrified, fearing a heavier vengeance, and for this reason they ceased from that work.

paras.t: Idcirco vocatum est nomen ejus, videlicet civitatis illius, Babel, seu Babylon aut Babylonia, quod interpretatur confusio; quia ibi confusum est labium universæ terræ, id est, cuncti habitatores terræ incurrerunt ibi confusionem et perturbationem ex varietate idiomatum suorum: quod intelligendum est de his, qui ibi fuerunt et peccaverunt in ædificio illo per consensum, suggestionem, vel actum. Heber vero et boni viri qui fuerunt cum ipso, nec consenserunt operi illi, manserunt in pristina lingua, quæ ante fuerat cunctis communis, et vocabatur humana, atque extunc mansit eis eorumque posteris propria, et Hebræa vocata est. Et inde dispersit eos Dominus super faciem cunctarum regionum: non quod illi soli poterant omnes mundi regiones implere aut occupare, sed per eos inceptum est hoc, et per eorum posteros consummatum. Unusquisque autem recessit ab eo quem intelligere non valebat, tanquam non potens conversari et loqui cum eo.
paras.en: [[11:9|And therefore the name thereof was called|Idcirco vocatum est nomen ejus]], namely of that city, [[11:9|Babel|Babel]], or Babylon or Babylonia, which is interpreted *confusion*; [[11:9|because there the language of the whole earth was confounded|quia ibi confusum est labium universæ terræ]]: that is, all the inhabitants of the earth fell there into confusion and disorder through the variety of their idioms. This is to be understood of those who were there and sinned in that building by consent, suggestion or deed. But Heber, and the good men who were with him and did not consent to that work, kept the original tongue, which before had been common to all and was called human; from then on it remained proper to them and their descendants, and was called Hebrew. [[11:9|and from thence the Lord scattered them abroad upon the face of all countries|Et inde dispersit eos Dominus super faciem cunctarum regionum]]: not that they alone could fill or occupy all the regions of the world, but this was begun through them and completed through their descendants. And each one withdrew from the man he could not understand, as being unable to live and talk with him.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur primo, quot novæ loquelæ fuerunt inductæ ibi. Secundo, an omnes loquelæ quæ sunt in mundo, fuerunt inductæ ibidem, dempta Hebræa. Tertio, an omnes qui erant ejusdem gentis, facti sint linguæ ejusdem. Ad ista patet aliqualis responsio ex verbis Augustini, dicentis: Ex tribus filiis Noe, septuaginta duæ gentes ac totidem linguæ per terras esse cœperunt, quæ gentes crescendo etiam insulas impleverunt. Auctus est autem numerus gentium multo amplius quam linguarum. Nam et in Africa novimus multas barbaras gentes esse in una lingua.
paras.en: On these things it is asked, first, how many new kinds of speech were brought in there; second, whether all the kinds of speech in the world, Hebrew excepted, were brought in there; third, whether all who were of the same nation were made of the same tongue. Some answer to these is plain from the words of Augustine, who says: From the three sons of Noe seventy-two nations, and as many tongues, began to be on the earth, and these nations as they grew filled even the islands. But the number of nations has grown far more than that of tongues; for in Africa too we know of many barbarous nations having one tongue.

paras.t: Præterea circa hæc movet Augustinus tres quæstiones. Prima est, qualiter feræ prorsus indomitæ, quæ ex sola commixtione nascuntur, potuerunt venire et esse in insulis. Ad quod dicit: Credi possunt natando venisse ad proximas insulas. Sunt autem quædam insulæ tam longe positæ a terris feras tales continentibus, ut nulla fera videatur potuisse natando venisse ad insulas illas. Quod si homines adduxerunt eas secum captas, non est incredibile venandi studio id fieri potuisse, quamvis negandum non sit, eas transferri potuisse jussu Dei et opera angelorum. Si vero ex terra exortæ sunt, quemadmodum in principio mundi, quando dixit Deus, Producat terra animam viventem, clarissime patet, omnia animalia fuisse in arca, non tam reparandorum animalium causa, quam gratia figurandarum variarum gentium propter Ecclesiæ sacramentum.
paras.en: Augustine also raises three questions about these things. The first is how wholly untamed wild beasts, which are born only from the mating of their kind, could come to be in the islands. To this he says: They can be believed to have come to the nearer islands by swimming. But some islands lie so far from the lands that have such beasts that no beast seems able to have reached them by swimming. And if men caught them and brought them over, it is not incredible that this could have been done out of zeal for hunting; though it is not to be denied that they could have been carried across at God's command and by the work of angels. But if they sprang from the earth, as at the beginning of the world, when God said, [[Gen 1:24|Let the earth bring forth the living creature|Producat terra animam viventem]], it is very plain that all the animals were in the ark not so much for the sake of renewing the animals as to figure the various nations, for the sake of the sacrament of the Church.

paras.t: Secundo quæritur, an ex Adam seu filiis Noe, propagata sint monstruosa hominum genera, quæ gentium narrat historia, quorum quidam dicuntur habere oculum in media fronte; quidam plantas habere versas post crura; quidam habere naturam utriusque sexus, dexteramque mamillam virilem, sinistram femineam, vicibus quoque inter se coeundo et gignere et parere; alii ora non habere, sed per nares solo halitu vivere; alii cubitalem habere staturam, qui Pygmæi vocantur, et octavum vitæ non excedere annum. Item dicunt gentem esse, ubi singula crura in pedibus habent, nec poplitem flectunt, et sunt mirabilis celeritatis, quos Sciopodas vocant, quod tempore æstus resupini in terra jacentes, umbra pedum se protegunt a calore. Et quid de Cynocephalis dicam, quorum canina capita atque latratus, magis videntur ostendere bruta, quam homines? Ad istud Augustinus non dat certam responsionem; sed primo ait, quod non sit necesse credere omnia hujusmodi hominum genera esse. Secundo, quod si homines sunt, indubitanter ex primis parentibus nati sunt. Tertio, quod eadem ratio potest assignari de monstruosis talibus gentibus, qualis apud nos redditur de monstruosis hominum membris seu partibus. Et circa hoc quibusdam interpositis, ait: Absurdum nobis videri non debet, quod sicut in singulis gentibus sunt aliqua particularium hominum monstra, ita in toto genere humano sint gentes aliquæ monstruosæ. Quarto refert de quodam, qui natus est non diu ante tempora sua, lunatas habens manus ac pedes, et binos tantummodo digitos in eisdem. Refert quoque de alio monstro non diu ante sua tempora nato, quod superioribus membris fuit duplex homo, inferioribus simplex: nam habuit duo capita, duoque pectora et quatuor manus, sed unum ventrem et duos pedes. Quinto concedit esse Hermaphroditos, quamvis paucissimi sint, in quibus ita uterque sexus apparet, ut incertum sit ex quo potius debeant nominari. Deinde finaliter sic respondet, quod præfata hominum aut quasi hominum monstra omnino non sunt, aut si sunt, homines non sunt: aut si homines sunt, ex Adam sunt. Præterea Joannes Mandevillæ in itinerario suo multa scribit de præfatis et aliis quampluribus talibus monstruosis gentibus, asserens eas esse. Alexander quoque de Hales in scripto suo super secundum Sententiarum, præfatam movens quæstionem, multa circa eam induxit, non tamen certitudinaliter ac plene eam determinat, magis tamen videtur declinare ad hoc, quod credendum sit eas esse. Qualiter vero talia naturaliter fieri possunt, longum est pertractare: ideo hoc in præfato doctore et in libro Guillelmi Parisiensis de Universo, potest inquiri. Verumtamen certum est, esse Cynocephalos ac Pygmæos, quum de Pygmæis in Ezechiele dicatur: Sed et Pygmæi qui erant in turribus tuis, pharetras suas suspenderunt in muris tuis; ipsi compleverunt decorem tuum. An tamen sint homines, vertitur nonnullis in dubium.
paras.en: The second question is whether the monstrous races of men that the history of the nations tells of are descended from Adam, or from the sons of Noe. Of these some are said to have one eye in the middle of the forehead; some to have the soles of their feet turned back behind their legs; some to have the nature of both sexes, the right breast a man's and the left a woman's, and, coupling with one another by turns, both to beget and to bear; others to have no mouths, but to live by breathing alone through the nostrils; others to be a cubit tall, who are called Pygmies, and not to live beyond their eighth year. They also say there is a race that has a single leg to its feet [that is, one leg for both feet] and cannot bend the knee, yet is of wonderful speed; these they call Sciopodes, because in the heat of summer they lie on their backs on the ground and shield themselves from the heat with the shade of their feet. And what shall I say of the Cynocephali [the dog-headed men], whose dogs' heads and barking seem to show them beasts rather than men? To this Augustine gives no certain answer. First he says that it is not necessary to believe that all such races of men exist. Second, that if they are men, they are without doubt born of our first parents. Third, that the same reason can be given for such monstrous races as is given among us for monstrous limbs or parts of men; and on this, after some other words, he says: It ought not to seem absurd to us that, as there are some monsters among individual men in each nation, so in the whole human race there are some monstrous nations. Fourth, he tells of a man born not long before his own time who had crescent-shaped hands and feet, with only two fingers or toes on each. He tells too of another monster born not long before his time, who was a double man in his upper members and a single man in his lower: he had two heads, two breasts and four hands, but one belly and two feet. Fifth, he grants that there are hermaphrodites, though very few, in whom both sexes so appear that it is uncertain from which they should rather be named. Then at last he answers thus: the monsters spoken of, men or as it were men, either do not exist at all; or, if they exist, they are not men; or, if they are men, they are from Adam. Further, John Mandeville in his Travels writes much of these and of very many other such monstrous races, asserting that they exist. Alexander of Hales too, in his writing on the second book of the Sentences, raises this question and brings forward much on it; he does not settle it with certainty or fully, yet he seems rather to incline to the view that they are to be believed to exist. How such things can come about naturally would take long to treat; so it can be looked into in that doctor and in the book of William of Paris On the Universe. It is certain, however, that there are Cynocephali and Pygmies, since it is said of the Pygmies in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 27:11|the Pygmeans also that were in thy towers, hung up their quivers on thy walls|Sed et Pygmæi qui erant in turribus tuis, pharetras suas suspenderunt in muris tuis]]: [[Ezech 27:11|they perfected thy beauty|ipsi compleverunt decorem tuum]]. Whether they are men, however, is doubted by some.

paras.t: Tertio quærit Augustinus, an (sicut narratur) sint homines antipodes, id est, ex adverso sub terra contra nos gradientes: quod Augustinus dicit nequaquam esse credendum, nec ab historiis recitatum, sed a quibusdam quasi ratiocinando opinatum, eo quod terra sphæricæ sit figuræ, ideo partem terræ quæ infra nos est, habitatione hominum carere non posse. Ad quod Augustinus respondet, quod licet terra sit sphærica, non tamen est certum, quod terra in parte illa quæ infra est, sit discooperta ab aquis. Et quamvis discooperta consisteret, tamen contra Scripturam hanc esset dicere, quod ibi homines habitent, eo quod nimis absurdum sit dicere aliquos homines ex hac terra in illam partem navigare ac pervenire potuisse, immensitate Oceani peragrata. Verumtamen ex his quæ in sphæra mundi probantur, constat qualiter partes terræ in quibus homines commorantur, multipliciter differunt situ, qualitate, distinctioneque temporum.
paras.en: Third, Augustine asks whether (as is told) there are antipodes, that is, men walking on the opposite side, beneath the earth, with their feet against ours. Augustine says this is by no means to be believed: it is not related by any histories, but some have supposed it by a kind of reasoning, because the earth is spherical in shape and so the part of the earth that is below us cannot lack men to dwell in it. To this Augustine answers that though the earth is spherical, it is still not certain that the earth in that lower part is uncovered by the waters; and even if it stood uncovered, it would still be against this Scripture to say that men dwell there, since it is too absurd to say that any men could have sailed from this land to that part and reached it, crossing the immensity of the Ocean. Yet from what is proved in the treatise on the sphere of the world, it is clear how the parts of the earth where men dwell differ in many ways, in situation, in quality and in the division of the seasons.

paras.t: Præterea de turre Babel Josephus scribit, quod latitudo ejus fuit tam magna, ut prope eam adspicientibus longitudo ejus videretur minor quam latitudo. Dii vero, utpote angeli, ventum miserunt, et turrim everterunt. De hac turre dixit Sibylla: Quum omnes homines unius vocis exsisterent, quidam turrim ædificaverunt excelsam, tanquam per eam ascensuri in cælum. Estius quoque historiographus scribit de campo Sennaar, dicens: Quidam in Sennaar Babylonis venerunt, qui deinde divisi sunt diversitate linguarum et emigrantes apprehenderunt mediterranea atque maritima.
paras.en: Further, Josephus writes of the tower of Babel that its breadth was so great that to those who looked at it close by its length [that is, its height] seemed less than its breadth. But the gods, that is, the angels, sent a wind and overthrew the tower. Of this tower the Sibyl said: When all men were of one voice, some built a lofty tower, as if they would climb up by it into heaven. The historian Estius [probably Hestiæus, whom Josephus quotes in the same place] also writes of the plain of Sennaar, saying: Some came into Sennaar of Babylon, who were then divided by the diversity of tongues, and going forth they took possession of the inland places and the coasts.

paras.t: Consequenter reditur ad generationem Sem. Quemadmodum autem asserit Augustinus, omissis ceteris filiis Sem, illi describuntur et connectuntur in ordine generationis, per quos directe veniretur ad Abram, sicut in his qui ante diluvium erant, connectuntur nati ex Seth, per quos ad Noe perventum est. Itaque dicitur: Hæ sunt generationes Sem, id est filii generati ex Sem. Sem centum erat annorum quando genuit Arphaxad, biennio post diluvium. Sexto capitulo dictum est, quod Noe genuit Sem, Cham et Japhet, quum esset quingentorum annorum ante diluvium, quod inundavit sexcentesimo anno Noe. Ergo Sem fuit centum annorum dum venit diluvium, seu in ipso diluvio. Ergo dum genuit Arphaxad, biennio post diluvium evoluto, fuit ad minus centum et duorum annorum, si tamen fuit primogenitus Noe. Quomodo ergo nunc dicitur fuisse centum annorum quando genuit Arphaxad, quod fuit duobus post diluvium annis? Ex hac ratione (ut refert Lyra) dicunt Hebræi, quod Sem non fuit primogenitus Noe, sed Japhet, quod nec textui nostro, nec sanctis doctoribus consonat. Jam enim Japhet vocatus est junior filius Noe, et si primogenitus exstitisset, Scriptura non nominasset eum post Cham vitiosum, dato quod nominasset eum post Sem virtuosum et magis electum. Dicendum ergo cum Augustino, Beda et aliis, quod Sem primogenitus Noe fuit. Ad objectionem vero dicendum, quod consuetudo est Scripturæ, non exprimere minutias aut modicum excrementum numerorum et temporum. Vel forsitan ipse Noe non fuit præcise quingentorum annorum dum genuit Sem, nec sexcentorum erumpente diluvio, quia in tanta ætate non computabatur biennium supercrescens sive deficiens. Vixitque Sem postquam genuit Arphaxad, quingentis annis.
paras.en: Next the text returns to the generation of Sem. As Augustine asserts, the other sons of Sem are passed over, and those are described and linked together in the order of generation through whom the line comes straight down to Abram; just as, among those who lived before the flood, the sons of Seth are linked together through whom it came down to Noe. So it says: [[11:10|These are the generations of Sem|Hæ sunt generationes Sem]], that is, the sons begotten of Sem. [[11:10|Sem was a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the flood|Sem centum erat annorum quando genuit Arphaxad, biennio post diluvium]]. It was said in the sixth chapter [the words are at Gen 5:31] that Noe begot Sem, Cham and Japhet when he was five hundred years old, before the flood, which came in Noe's six hundredth year. So Sem was a hundred years old when the flood came, or during the flood itself. So when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the flood had passed, he was at least a hundred and two, if indeed he was Noe's firstborn. How then is he now said to have been a hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, which was two years after the flood? For this reason (as Lyra reports) the Hebrews say that Sem was not Noe's firstborn, but Japhet; which agrees neither with our text nor with the holy doctors. For Japhet has already been called Noe's younger son; and had he been the firstborn, Scripture would not have named him after Cham the wicked, granted that it might have named him after Sem, the virtuous and more chosen. So we must say with Augustine, Bede and others that Sem was Noe's firstborn. To the objection we must say that it is the custom of Scripture not to set down small details or a slight surplus in numbers and times. Or perhaps Noe himself was not exactly five hundred years old when he begot Sem, nor six hundred when the flood broke forth, since at so great an age two years over or under were not counted. [[11:11|And Sem lived after he begot Arphaxad, five hundred years|Vixitque Sem postquam genuit Arphaxad, quingentis annis]].

paras.t: Deinde littera expositione non indiget usque ibi, Vixitque Thare septuaginta annis, et genuit Abram et Nachor et Aran. Qualiter verum est hoc, quum paulo post habeatur in littera, quod Thare mortuus est in Haran, quum esset ducentorum et quinque annorum, atque quod Abram post mortem Thare patris sui egressus est de Haran, quum esset septuaginta quinque annorum, ex quibus concluditur, quod Thare erat centum triginta annorum quum genuit Abram? Respondetur secundum Augustinum et eum sequentes, quod Thare septuagenarius generavit, id est generare cœpit, præfatos filios suos, ita quod primogenitum inter eos genuit septuagenarius, et ille primogenitus non erat Abram, sed multis annis postmodum Abram natus est, quum scilicet Thare esset centum triginta annorum, secundum unum modum loquendi tactum ab Augustino, qui etiam tangit alium modum, secundum quem Abram dicitur genitus, quum Thare esset septuaginta annorum: sicque Abram diceretur primogenitus Thare, quod tamen non videtur posse teneri. Nam infra habetur, quod Abraham centenario exsistente, Sara uxor sua nonagenaria fuit, quæ tamen fuit filia Aran fratris ipsius Abrahæ, sicque Aran junior Abraham fratre suo, genuisset filiam suam Saram, quum vix decem esset annorum. Hinc etiam alii dicunt, quod sexaginta anni fluxerunt inter nativitatem primogeniti filii hujus Thare et nativitatem Abræ, qui inter filios Thare primo exprimitur propter multiplicem eminentiam ejus. Unde et Augustinus fatetur, et idem in Glossa habetur, quod in enumeratione filiorum Thare non attenditur ordo nativitatis seu temporis, sed significatio futuræ dignitatis. In Scholastica quoque fertur historia, quod in enumeratione filiorum Thare in littera est ordo præposterus, quoniam Aran fuit primogenitus, Nachorque medius, et Abram ultimus.
paras.en: After this the text needs no explanation as far as: [[11:26|And Thare lived seventy years, and begot Abram, and Nachor, and Aran|Vixitque Thare septuaginta annis, et genuit Abram et Nachor et Aran]]. How is this true, since a little later the text has it that Thare died in Haran at two hundred and five years of age, and that Abram went out of Haran after the death of his father Thare when he was seventy-five years old, from which it follows that Thare was a hundred and thirty years old when he begot Abram? The answer, according to Augustine and those who follow him, is that Thare at seventy begot, that is, began to beget, the sons named; so that at seventy he begot the firstborn among them, and that firstborn was not Abram: Abram was born many years later, namely when Thare was a hundred and thirty. This is according to one way of speaking touched on by Augustine, who also touches on another, by which Abram is said to have been begotten when Thare was seventy, so that Abram would be called Thare's firstborn; but this does not seem tenable. For further on we find that when Abraham was a hundred his wife Sara was ninety; yet she was the daughter of Aran, Abraham's own brother; and so Aran, younger than his brother Abraham, would have begotten his daughter Sara when he was barely ten years old. Hence others too say that sixty years passed between the birth of this Thare's firstborn son and the birth of Abram, who is named first among the sons of Thare because of his manifold eminence. So Augustine owns, and the Gloss has the same, that in the list of Thare's sons it is not the order of birth or of time that is followed, but the meaning of their future dignity. And the Scholastic History says that in the list of Thare's sons in the text the order is reversed, since Aran was the firstborn, Nachor the middle one and Abram the last.

paras.t: Porro Aran genuit Lot, et etiam filias duas, quæ paulo post nominantur. Mortuusque est Aran ante patrem suum in Ur Chaldæorum. Hoc dupliciter explanatur. Nam aliqui dicunt, quod Nemrod rex Sennaar seu Chaldææ, projecit Aran et Abram in ignem, quia nolebant juxta ejus præceptum adorare et colere ignem, et quod Aran fuit combustus in igne, Abram vero tanquam majoris fidei, exivit divina virtute illæsus, præsertim quia de semine ejus Christus fuerat nasciturus. Et ita per Ur intelligitur ignis. Unde et infra Dominus ait ad Abram: Ego sum qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum. In Esdra vero Dominus ait apertius: Ego sum qui eduxi Abram de igne Chaldæorum. Dicunt quoque aliqui, quod factum sit istud in præsentia Thare, imo et ex accusatione ipsius qua accusavit filium suum Aran vel Abram aut ambos ipsi Nemrod de hoc, quod ignem adorare spreverunt, sicque mortuus sit Aran ante patrem suum, hoc est in præsentia ejus. Unde Septuaginta transtulerunt, Coram patre suo. Secundo exponitur, intelligendo per Ur, locum in Chaldæa, in quo dicunt obiisse hunc Aran ante patrem suum, id est diu ante obitum patris sui. Hinc Josephus dicit, quod Ur sit hic nomen civitatis, in qua hactenus sepultura ipsius Aran ostenditur. Hoc idem Rabbi Manahen protestatur.
paras.en: [[11:27|And Aran begot Lot|Porro Aran genuit Lot]], and also two daughters, who are named a little later. [[11:28|And Aran died before|Mortuusque est Aran ante]] [[11:28|his father|patrem suum]] [[11:28|in Ur of the Chaldees|in Ur Chaldæorum]]. This is explained in two ways. Some say that Nemrod, king of Sennaar or Chaldea, cast Aran and Abram into the fire because they would not adore and worship fire as he commanded; and that Aran was burned in the fire, but Abram, as being of greater faith, came out unharmed by divine power, especially since Christ was to be born of his seed. And so by *Ur* fire is understood [in Hebrew *ur* means fire]. Hence further on the Lord says to Abram: It is I [[Gen 15:7|who brought thee out from Ur of the Chaldees|qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum]]. And in Esdras the Lord says more plainly: It is I who brought Abram [[2 Esd 9:7|out of the fire of the Chaldeans|de igne Chaldæorum]] [in 2 Esdras these are the words of the Levites' prayer to God: "Thou … broughtest him forth out of the fire of the Chaldeans"]. Some also say that this was done in Thare's presence, and indeed on his own accusation, when he accused his son Aran, or Abram, or both, to Nemrod of scorning to worship fire; and so Aran died *before* his father, that is, in his presence. Hence the Septuagint translated: In the presence of his father. In the second way it is explained by taking *Ur* for a place in Chaldea where they say this Aran died *before* his father, that is, long before his father's death. Hence Josephus says that *Ur* here is the name of a city in which Aran's tomb is shown to this day. Rabbi Manahen bears witness to the same.

paras.t: Duxerunt autem Abram et Nachor frater ejus uxores, id est, quilibet eorum unam, videlicet: Nomen uxoris Abram, Sarai: et nomen uxoris Nachor, Melcha filia Aran patris Melchæ et Jeschæ. Aran namque frater Abræ et Nachor, genuit filiam unam nomine Sarai seu Sara, quæ alio nomine dicta est Jescha, vel secundum Hieronymum cognominata est Jescha. Harum duarum unam, scilicet Sarai, accepit Abram in uxorem, aliam Nachor: imo secundum Scholasticam historiam ipse Thare dedit unam Abræ, alteram Nachor.
paras.en: [[11:29|And Abram and Nachor|Duxerunt autem Abram et Nachor]] his brother [[11:29|married wives|uxores]], that is, each of them one, namely: [[11:29|the name of Abram's wife was Sarai: and the name of Nachor's wife, Melcha, the daughter of Aran, father of Melcha and father of Jescha|Nomen uxoris Abram, Sarai: et nomen uxoris Nachor, Melcha filia Aran patris Melchæ et Jeschæ]]. For Aran, the brother of Abram and Nachor, begot a daughter named Sarai or Sara, who by another name was called Jescha, or, according to Jerome, had Jescha as a surname. Of these two, Abram took one, namely Sarai, to wife, and Nachor the other; indeed, according to the Scholastic History, Thare himself gave one to Abram and the other to Nachor.

paras.t: Tulit itaque Thare Abram filium suum, et Lot filium Aran, et Sarai nurum suam, id est uxorem filii sui, et eduxit eos de Ur Chaldæorum, juxta sensum expositum, ut irent in terram Chanaan. Ex quo videtur constare, quod Thare non accusavit filium suum Aran aut Abram, de hoc quod ignem non voluit adorare: imo concors fuit cum eis, atque (ut alii dicunt) idcirco sumpsit secum Abram et Lot et Sarai, ut irent simul in terram Chanaan, quia non voluit sustinere molestias Chaldæorum, incitantium eum ad ignis adorationem. Veneruntque usque ad Haran civitatem Mesopotamiæ, et habitaverunt ibi: mutato proposito eundi in terram Chanaan. Et facti sunt dies Thare ducentorum quinque annorum, et mortuus est in Haran urbe præfata, quam Septuaginta vocant Charan, sicque in Actibus Apostolorum vocatur.
paras.en: [[11:31|And Thare took Abram his son|Tulit itaque Thare Abram filium suum]], [[11:31|and Lot the son of Aran|et Lot filium Aran]], [[11:31|and Sarai his daughter in law|et Sarai nurum suam]], that is, the wife of his son, [[11:31|and brought them out of Ur of the Chaldees|et eduxit eos de Ur Chaldæorum]], in the sense explained, [[11:31|to go into the land of Chanaan|ut irent in terram Chanaan]]. From this it seems clear that Thare did not accuse his son Aran, or Abram, of refusing to worship fire; rather, he was of one mind with them, and (as others say) he took Abram, Lot and Sarai with him, to go together into the land of Chanaan, for this reason: that he would not put up with the harassment of the Chaldeans, who were urging him to worship fire. [[11:31|and they came as far as Haran|Veneruntque usque ad Haran]], a city of Mesopotamia, [[11:31|and dwelt there|et habitaverunt ibi]], having changed their purpose of going into the land of Chanaan. [[11:32|And the days of Thare were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran|Et facti sunt dies Thare ducentorum quinque annorum, et mortuus est in Haran]], the city spoken of, which the Septuagint calls Charan; and so it is called in the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 7:2||]].

paras.t: Quæritur, cur de Thare nunc dicitur quod mortuus sit, quod in isto capitulo de nullo exprimitur a Sem inclusive usque ad Thare. Respondent Alcuinus et alii, quod de aliis non dicitur in isto capitulo, quod mortui sunt sicut de his qui præcesserunt diluvium, quoniam nullus horum de lege mortis exemptus est, quemadmodum inter illos Enoch de morte est præservatus. Cur vero Thare mortuus scribitur, dici potest, quod non absolute dicitur mortuus sine additamento, sed mortuus in Haran, ne putaretur ingressus terram Chanaan sicut proposuit, quia præmisit Scriptura, Ut irent in terram Chanaan.
paras.en: It is asked why it is now said of Thare that he died, when in this chapter this is said of no one from Sem (Sem included) down to Thare. Alcuin and others answer that it is not said of the others in this chapter that they died, as it is said of those who lived before the flood, because none of these was exempted from the law of death, whereas among those Enoch was preserved from death[[Gen 5:24||]]. As for why Thare is written to have died, it can be said that he is not said to have died simply, without anything added, but to have died *in Haran*, lest he be thought to have entered the land of Chanaan as he had purposed; for Scripture had said before, [[11:31|to go into the land of Chanaan|Ut irent in terram Chanaan]].

paras.t: Insuper constat ex dictis, quod tempore Abræ non erat matrimonium inter patruum et neptem prohibitum, quum Sarai fuerit filia fratris sui mariti, et hoc idem ait Hieronymus.
paras.en: Further, it is clear from what has been said that in Abram's time marriage between an uncle and his niece was not forbidden, since Sarai was the daughter of her husband's brother; and Jerome says the same.

paras.t: Quæritur, an Thare fuerit idololatra. Et ex prædictis apparet, quod non. Oppositum vero apparet ex eo, quod Josue locutus est filiis Israel: Trans fluvium habitaverunt patres vestri, Thare pater Abrahæ et Nachor, servieruntque diis alienis. Ad hoc aliqui dicunt, quod Thare et Nachor ad idololatriam lapsi sunt in terra Haran seu Mesopotamia: verumtamen hoc loco non legitur quod Thare duxerit secum filium suum Nachor in Haran. Infra tamen satis patebit, quod Nachor habitaverit ibi, vel saltem posteritas ejus, et si non ivit illuc cum patre suo, forsan secutus est eum, imo (secundum Augustinum) secutus est ipsum. Opinatur enim Augustinus, quod ideo Thare non dicitur secum duxisse filium suum Nachor, quoniam Nachor adhæsit idololatriæ Chaldæorum, et post vel inde pœnitendo, aut persecutionem fugiendo, secutus sit Thare patrem suum, habitavitque secum cum conjuge sua in Haran.
paras.en: It is asked whether Thare was an idolater. From what has been said it appears that he was not. But the opposite appears from what Josue said to the children of Israel: [[Jos 24:2|Your fathers dwelt of old on the other side of the river|Trans fluvium habitaverunt patres vestri]], [[Jos 24:2|Thare the father of Abraham, and Nachor: and they served strange gods|Thare pater Abrahæ et Nachor, servieruntque diis alienis]]. To this some say that Thare and Nachor fell into idolatry in the land of Haran, or Mesopotamia. Yet it is not read in this place that Thare took his son Nachor with him to Haran. Further on, however, it will be plain enough that Nachor lived there, or at least his descendants; and if he did not go there with his father, perhaps he followed him; indeed (according to Augustine) he did follow him. For Augustine supposes that Thare is not said to have taken his son Nachor with him because Nachor clung to the idolatry of the Chaldeans, and afterwards, either repenting of it or fleeing persecution, followed his father Thare, and lived with him in Haran together with his wife.

11.title: Spiritualis explanatio ejusdem capituli undecimi
11.title_en: Spiritual explanation of the same eleventh chapter

paras.t: Erat autem terra labii unius et sermonum eorumdem. Per terram designantur homines carnales et vani, rebus terrenis potius quam divinis intenti. Quorum unum est labium, quoniam omnes verba iniqua loquuntur, et frequenter concordant in vitiis atque erroribus.
paras.en: [[11:1|And the earth was of one tongue, and of the same speech|Erat autem terra labii unius et sermonum eorumdem]]. By the earth are signified carnal and vain men, intent on earthly things rather than divine. Their lip [Latin *labium*, where the Douay-Rheims has "tongue"] is one, since all of them speak wicked words, and they often agree together in vices and errors.

paras.t: Quumque proficiscerentur de oriente, id est, verum et æternale lumen ac Christi doctrinam dereliquissent, de quo loquitur Zacharias, Ecce vir, Oriens nomen ejus : invenerunt campum in terra Sennaar, et habitaverunt in eo. Sennaar interpretatur fœtor seu excussio dentium, per quod intelligitur abundantia iniquitatum, quibus nihil fœtidius coram Deo et angelis ejus : quibus iniquitatibus desunt dentes, hoc est vis et diligentia terendi semen verbi cœlestis pro interiori refectione. In hac terra Sennaar, id est terrenis cordibus quæ subjecta sunt vitiis et erroribus istis, est campus, id est lata via perditionis, planaque quies impiæ voluptatis. In quo campo morantur præfati terreni, qui per lata perditionis itinera gradiuntur, et delectantur in rebus pravissimis. Contra quos scriptum est : Post concupiscentias tuas non eas, et a voluntate tua avertere.
paras.en: [[11:2|when they removed from the east|Quumque proficiscerentur de oriente]], that is, when they had forsaken the true and eternal light and the doctrine of Christ, of whom Zacharias speaks: [[Zach 6:12|BEHOLD A MAN, THE ORIENT IS HIS NAME|Ecce vir, Oriens nomen ejus]]: [[11:2|they found a plain in the land of Sennaar, and dwelt in it|invenerunt campum in terra Sennaar, et habitaverunt in eo]]. Sennaar is interpreted *stench* or *the shaking out of teeth*, by which is understood the abundance of iniquities, than which nothing is more foul before God and His angels; and these iniquities lack teeth, that is, the strength and diligence to grind the seed of the heavenly word for inward refreshment. In this land of Sennaar, that is, in earthly hearts that are subject to these vices and errors, there is a plain, that is, the broad way of perdition and the level rest of impious pleasure. In this plain dwell the aforesaid earthly men, who walk the broad roads of perdition and delight in the most depraved things. Against them it is written: [[Ecclus 18:30|Go not after thy lusts, but turn away from thy own will.|Post concupiscentias tuas non eas, et a voluntate tua avertere.]]

paras.t: Dixitque alter ad proximum suum : Venite, faciamus lateres, et coquamus eos igni. Per lateres designantur magnificæ cogitationes de se ipso, quæ igni coquuntur, dum privati amoris fervore durantur et roborantur. Ex his construunt impii turrim superbiæ, propriam excellentiam, præsidentiam, laudem et gloriam hominum appetendo : præfatosque lateres bitumine, id est sensuali viscositate seu fœditate, quasi inseparabiliter nectunt, quando et carnalium oblectamentorum affectione pravas cogitationes elationis continuant et defendunt, ita ut corripi ac corrigi dedignentur. Hanc turrim volunt erigere usque ad cœlum, quoniam Dei voluntati atque præceptis suas superbas ac improbas præferunt voluntates, nec subjici volunt, tanquam filii ejus qui dixit : In cœlum conscendam, et similis ero Altissimo. Ideo scriptum est de superbo in Job : Tetendit contra Deum manum suam, et cucurrit adversus eum erecto collo.
paras.en: [[11:3|And each one said to his neighbour: Come let us make brick, and bake them with fire|Dixitque alter ad proximum suum : Venite, faciamus lateres, et coquamus eos igni]]. By the bricks are signified high-flown thoughts about oneself, which are baked with fire when they are hardened and strengthened by the heat of private love [that is, love of self]. Out of these the wicked build the tower of pride, by seeking their own excellence, their own pre-eminence, and the praise and glory of men; and they bind the aforesaid bricks together, as though inseparably, with [[11:3|slime|bitumine]], that is, with sensual stickiness or filthiness, when through their attachment to carnal delights they keep up and defend their wicked thoughts of self-exaltation, so that they disdain to be rebuked and corrected. This tower they wish to raise up to heaven, since they set their own proud and wicked wills above the will and commandments of God and will not be subject to them, as sons of him who said: [[Is 14:13|I will ascend into heaven|In cœlum conscendam]], and [[Is 14:14|I will be like the most High|similis ero Altissimo]] [the margin gives only Is. xiv, 14; the first words are from v. 13]. Therefore it is written of the proud man in Job: [[Job 15:25|he hath stretched out his hand against God|Tetendit contra Deum manum suam]], and [[Job 15:26|He hath run against him with his neck raised up|cucurrit adversus eum erecto collo]].

paras.t: Et celebremus nomen nostrum. Hoc est quod homines vani, superbi, ac stolidi præcipue cupiunt procurare et habere in hac vita et post mortem, ab hominibus reputari, laudari, ac late famari, non obstante quod scriptum est : Soli Deo honor et gloria. Itemque : Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur.
paras.en: [[11:4|and let us make our name famous|Et celebremus nomen nostrum]]. This is what vain, proud and foolish men above all desire to procure and to have, in this life and after death: to be esteemed, praised and spoken of far and wide by men; notwithstanding that it is written: To [[1 Tim 1:17|the only God, be honour and glory|Soli Deo honor et gloria]]. And again: [[2 Cor 10:17|he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord|Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur]].

paras.t: Descendit autem Dominus ut videret civitatem et turrim quam ædificabant filii Adam. Hæc civitas est impiorum societas, ecclesia malignorum, congregatio infructuosorum reprobórumque hominum, qui sunt corpus diaboli, et spiritu elationis, magis autem privato sui ipsius amore nectuntur, moventur ac agitantur ad opera mala ac pessima. Nempe duo amores, duas constituunt civitates, quoniam amor Dei crescens usque ad contemptum sui, Dei constituit civitatem ; amor vero sui, crescens usque ad contemptum Dei, efficit civitatem diaboli, quæ Babylon appellatur, cujus constructor et princeps est Nemrod, id est diabolus, adeo potens ut non sit potestas super terram quæ ei valeat comparari. Estque animarum venator ac devorator, nam esca ejus electa, et habet fiduciam quod influat Jordanis in os ejus. Ille est primus iste apostata, totius elationis inventor. De hac civitate Deus loquitur per Osee prophetam : Non ingrediar civitatem. Longe quippe est Dominus ab impiis. Hanc civitatem ædificant filii transgressoris Adæ ex semetipsis, tanquam ex putridis saxis : quia peccando faciunt se ipsos membra diaboli, ac mortuos lapides Babyloniæ urbis. Hanc civitatem et turrim considerat Deus, qui loquitur per Prophetam : Cognovi scelera vestra. Oculi etenim Domini multo lucidiores sole, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum.
paras.en: [[11:5|And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of Adam were building|Descendit autem Dominus ut videret civitatem et turrim quam ædificabant filii Adam]]. This city is the society of the wicked, the church of the malignant, the congregation of fruitless and reprobate men, who are the body of the devil, and are bound together, moved and driven to evil and most wicked works by the spirit of pride, or rather by their private love of themselves. For two loves make two cities: the love of God, growing even to contempt of self, makes the city of God; but the love of self, growing even to contempt of God, makes the city of the devil [this is Augustine's saying, City of God XIV, 28], which is called Babylon. Its builder and prince is Nemrod, that is, the devil, so mighty that [[Job 41:24|There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him|non sit potestas super terram quæ ei valeat comparari]] [the margin gives Job xli, 25; these words are Job 41:24, and v. 25 calls him king over all the children of pride]. He is the hunter and devourer of souls, for his food is choice [compare Hab 1:16, "his meat dainty"], and [[Job 40:18|he trusteth that the Jordan may run into his mouth|habet fiduciam quod influat Jordanis in os ejus]]. He is that first apostate, the inventor of all pride. Of this city God speaks by the prophet Osee: [[Osee 11:9|I will not enter into the city|Non ingrediar civitatem]] [the margin gives Osee x, 9; the words are in Osee 11:9]. For [[Prov 15:29|The Lord is far from the wicked|Longe quippe est Dominus ab impiis]]. This city the sons of the transgressor Adam build out of themselves, as out of rotten stones: for by sinning they make themselves members of the devil and dead stones of the city of Babylon. This city and tower God beholds, who speaks by the Prophet: [[Amos 5:12|I know your manifold crimes|Cognovi scelera vestra]]. For [[Ecclus 23:28|the eyes of the Lord are far brighter than the sun, beholding round about all the ways of men|Oculi etenim Domini multo lucidiores sole, circumspicientes omnes vias hominum]].

paras.t: Et dixit : Venite igitur, descendamus, et confundamus linguam eorum, ut non audiat unusquisque vocem proximi sui. Hoc facit Omnipotens, quando impedit pravos ab exsecutione conceptæ elationis atque malitiæ, et male concordes facit discordes, ac contra se invicem incitari permittit, quemadmodum inter habitatores Sichem et Abimeleech misit spiritum pessimum. Ipse enim apprehendit astutos in astutia eorum, de quo testatur Scriptura : Qui dissipat cogitationes malignorum, ne manus eorum possint implere quæ cœperant.
paras.en: And he said: [[11:7|Come ye, therefore, let us go down, and there confound their tongue, that they may not understand one another's speech|Venite igitur, descendamus, et confundamus linguam eorum, ut non audiat unusquisque vocem proximi sui]]. This the Almighty does when He hinders the wicked from carrying out the pride and malice they have conceived, makes those who agree in evil disagree, and permits them to be stirred up against one another; as between the inhabitants of Sichem and Abimelech He [[Judg 9:23|sent a very evil spirit|misit spiritum pessimum]]. For He catches the crafty in their craftiness [an echo of Job 5:13], He of whom Scripture testifies: [[Job 5:12|Who bringeth to nought the designs of the malignant, so that their hands cannot accomplish what they had begun|Qui dissipat cogitationes malignorum, ne manus eorum possint implere quæ cœperant]].

paras.t: Atque ita divisit eos Dominus ex illo loco in universis terris, hoc est per diversos errores ac vitia permittit impios, præsertim hæreticos, ab invicem separari, quamvis ad resistendum Catholicis sint unanimes.
paras.en: [[11:8|And so the Lord scattered them from that place into all lands|Atque ita divisit eos Dominus ex illo loco in universis terris]]: that is, He permits the wicked, especially heretics, to be separated from one another through diverse errors and vices, although they are of one mind in resisting Catholics.

paras.t: Idcirco vocatum est nomen ejus Babel, quia ibi confusum est labium universæ terræ. Civitas diaboli, seu congregatio iniquorum, recte vocatur Babel, hoc est confusio: quoniam corda malorum omni confusione vitiorum et deordinatione propriarum perversitatum sunt plena, quorum mens a Deo aversa est, in quibus caro dominatur spiritui, imo eorum corpori et animæ dominatur diabolus, cui infelices deserviunt: propter quod sacratissimus princeps Apostolorum Petrus fatetur: Iniqui sunt servi corruptionis; a quo enim quis superatus est, hujus et servus est. Idcirco et Romam appellat Babylonem, dicendo: Salutat vos Ecclesia quæ est in Babylone coelecta. Quorum et labia sunt confusa, quia loquuntur verba iniqua, et invicem corrixantur. Quod si aliquando bona pronuntiant, non tamen eorum verbis opera propria correspondent. Et dicitur unicuique talium: Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam.
paras.en: [[11:9|therefore the name thereof was called Babel, because there the language of the whole earth was confounded|Idcirco vocatum est nomen ejus Babel, quia ibi confusum est labium universæ terræ]]. The city of the devil, or the congregation of the wicked, is rightly called Babel, that is, *confusion*: since the hearts of the wicked are full of every confusion of vices and of the disorder of their own perversities; their mind is turned away from God, in them the flesh rules the spirit, nay, the devil rules their body and soul, and the unhappy men are his slaves. Wherefore the most holy Peter, prince of the Apostles, declares: The wicked [[2 Pet 2:19|are the slaves of corruption. For by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave|sunt servi corruptionis; a quo enim quis superatus est, hujus et servus est]]. And so he also calls Rome Babylon, saying: [[1 Pet 5:13|The church that is in Babylon, elected together with you, saluteth you|Salutat vos Ecclesia quæ est in Babylone coelecta]]. Their lips too are confounded, because they speak wicked words and wrangle with one another. And if at times they utter good things, their own works do not answer to their words. And to each of them it is said: [[Luke 19:22|Out of thy own mouth I judge thee, thou wicked servant|Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam]].

paras.t: Postremo, per hoc quod Deus eduxit Abram de Ur seu igne Chaldæorum, figuratum est, quod Deus servos suos fideles liberat a tentationibus carnalium desideriorum, et inflammationibus dæmonum. Per hoc quoque, quod Thare tulit Abram, Lot et Sarai de populo Chaldæorum, ut iret in Chanaan, designatur quod bonus prælatus debet sibi commissos a pravis pro posse separare consortiis, seque cum illis applicare et associare bonis ac justis.
paras.en: Lastly, by this, that God brought Abram out of Ur, or the fire, of the Chaldeans [*Ur* means "fire"; compare 2 Esd 9:7, "broughtest him forth out of the fire of the Chaldeans"], it was figured that God sets His faithful servants free from the temptations of carnal desires and from the burning assaults of the demons. By this also, that [[11:31|Thare took Abram|Thare tulit Abram]], Lot and Sarai from the people of the Chaldeans, to go into Chanaan, it is signified that a good prelate ought, as far as he can, to separate those committed to him from wicked company, and to join and associate himself, together with them, with the good and the just.

12.title: Expositio litteralis capituli duodecimi: Dixit autem Dominus ad Abram: Egredere de terra tua
12.title_en: Literal exposition of the twelfth chapter: “And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth out of thy country”

paras.t: SANCTUS Moyses in præsenti capitulo incipit gesta præcipui Patriarchæ, videlicet Abrahæ, prosequi ac singulatim describere. Dixit autem Dominus ad Abram. Si quæratur, qualiter et in qua forma locutus sit Deus ad Abram, dici potest quod per angelum in humana specie apparentem, quemadmodum dictum est de apparitionibus et locutionibus factis a Deo ad Adam et Noe. Egredere de terra tua. Quando et ubi locutus sit Deus ista ad Abram, diversi diversimode opinantur, quibusdam dicentibus, quod ante mortem Thare patris sui, aliis autem quod postea. Sic et de loco varie æstimatur. Ait enim beatus Stephanus protomartyr: Deus gloriæ apparuit patri nostro Abraham, quum esset in Mesopotamia, priusquam moraretur in Charan, et dixit ad illum: Exi de terra tua, et de cognatione tua, et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi. Tunc exiit de terra Chaldæorum, et habitavit in Charan. Et inde postquam mortuus est pater ejus, transtulit illum in terram istam, videlicet Chanaan.
paras.en: Holy Moses in the present chapter begins to follow out and describe one by one the deeds of the chief Patriarch, namely Abraham. [[12:1|And the Lord said to Abram|Dixit autem Dominus ad Abram]]. If it be asked how and in what form God spoke to Abram, it can be said: through an angel appearing in human form, as was said of the apparitions and speeches made by God to Adam and Noe. [[12:1|Go forth out of thy country|Egredere de terra tua]]. When and where God said these things to Abram, different men hold different opinions: some say it was before the death of Thare his father, others that it was after. So too there are various views about the place. For blessed Stephen the protomartyr says: [[Acts 7:2|The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham, when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charan|Deus gloriæ apparuit patri nostro Abraham, quum esset in Mesopotamia, priusquam moraretur in Charan]], [[Acts 7:3|And said to him: Go forth out of thy country and from thy kindred: and come into the land which I shall shew thee|et dixit ad illum: Exi de terra tua, et de cognatione tua, et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi]]. [[Acts 7:4|Then he went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan. And from thence, after his father was dead, he removed him into this land|Tunc exiit de terra Chaldæorum, et habitavit in Charan. Et inde postquam mortuus est pater ejus, transtulit illum in terram istam]], namely Chanaan.

paras.t: Hæc autem narratio S. Stephani, imo et Lucæ evangelistæ, discordare videtur a littera ista Geneseos in tribus: Primo, in hoc quod dicit, Dominum ista locutum ad Abram ante mortem patris sui. In fine enim præcedentis capituli legitur, quemadmodum Thare pater Abræ in Haran defunctus sit, et nunc in exordio hujus capituli legitur, quod dixit Dominus Abræ verba prætacta, quasi juxta ordinem rei gestæ dictum sit hoc, ipso Thare defuncto. Porro secundum beati Stephani recitationem, Deus locutus est istud ad Abram, ante patris sui decessum, quod etiam in sequentibus clarius innotesceret. Secundo, quod Stephanus dicit ista a Domino dicta ad Abram, antequam moraretur in Charan: præcedenti autem capitulo scriptum est, quod Thare cum filio suo Abram de Chaldæa veniens, venit in Haran, id est Charan, et habitavit ibidem cum Abram. Deinde in isto capitulo scribitur, quod ipso Thare defuncto in Haran, Dominus locutus est ista ad Abram. Tertio, quod Stephanus ait ipsum Abram de Chaldæa egressum, postquam audivit a Domino verba præscripta. Moyses autem præcedenti capitulo scripsit, quod Thare cum Abram exiit de Chaldæa, et habitavit in Haran Mesopotamiæ urbe, et obiit ibi. Deinde in isto refert capitulo, quemadmodum Thare defuncto, Deus dixerit Abræ verba hæc: Exi de terra tua, etc.
paras.en: Now this account of St. Stephen, or rather of Luke the Evangelist [that is, as the writer of the Acts], seems to disagree with this text of Genesis in three ways. First, in that it says the Lord spoke these words to Abram before the death of his father. For at the end of the preceding chapter we read how Thare, the father of Abram, died in Haran, and now at the beginning of this chapter we read that the Lord said to Abram the words quoted above, as though, following the order of events, this was said after Thare was dead. But according to blessed Stephen's account, God said this to Abram before his father's death, as would also become clearer in what follows. Second, in that Stephen says these words were spoken by the Lord to Abram before he dwelt in Charan; whereas in the preceding chapter it is written that Thare, coming out of Chaldea with his son Abram, came into Haran, that is Charan, and dwelt there with Abram; then in this chapter it is written that, after Thare had died in Haran, the Lord said these things to Abram. Third, in that Stephen says Abram went out of Chaldea after he had heard the aforesaid words from the Lord. But Moses wrote in the preceding chapter that Thare went out of Chaldea with Abram, dwelt in Haran, a city of Mesopotamia, and died there; then in this chapter he relates how, after Thare's death, God spoke these words to Abram: [[12:1|Go forth out of thy country|Exi de terra tua]], etc. [Denis gives the command here in St. Stephen's wording.]

paras.t: Ad ista a diversis diversimode respondetur, estque prolixum omnia recitare. Augustinus namque ista concordat et solvit per modos loquendi Scripturæ, quibus multa per anticipationem et recapitulationem dicuntur. Hieronymus vero circa hoc dicit, veram esse relationem Hebræorum, dicentium, quod Abram liberatus sit de igne, in quem projecerant eum Chaldæi, eo quod ignem noluerit adorare, et quod tempus vitæ suæ computetur ei ex illo die. Planius autem loquendo, dicendum, quod Deus locutus est verba hæc Abræ in Mesopotamia, venienti cum patre suo Thare ex Chaldæa, antequam intravit aut inhabitavit civitatem, quæ dicitur Haran seu Charan, ut Stephanus refert, quod fuit ante obitum Thare. Quod vero nunc legitur, post mortem Thare Deum ista dixisse ad Abram, dupliciter solvitur: Primo, ut istud nunc dictum intelligatur per recapitulationem, quia Scriptura non semper refert res gestas eo ordine quo sunt factæ. Secundo, ut credamus Deum bis dixisse verba ista ad Abram: primo ante obitum patris sui, et antequam habitavit secum in Haran, videlicet quando de Chaldæa veniens, Mesopotamiam est ingressus, ut tactum est. Secundo, post patris sui decessum, ut legitur hic. Nec repetitio ista fuit ob inobedientiam aut negligentiam Abræ, quia præceptum affirmativum non obligat, nisi pro tempore opportuno. Et istam solutionem tangit auctor Scholasticæ historiæ circa Actus Apostolorum, quam et Lyra sequitur ibi.
paras.en: To these points different answers are given by different men, and it would be lengthy to recount them all. For Augustine reconciles and resolves them by the Scripture's ways of speaking, in which many things are said by anticipation and by recapitulation [that is, told before their time, or told again later out of the order of events]. Jerome, however, says on this point that the account of the Hebrews is true, who say that Abram was delivered from the fire into which the Chaldeans had thrown him because he would not worship fire, and that the time of his life is reckoned to him from that day. To speak more plainly, however, it must be said that God spoke these words to Abram in Mesopotamia[[Acts 7:2||]], as he was coming with his father Thare out of Chaldea, before he entered or dwelt in the city called Haran or Charan, as Stephen relates; and this was before Thare's death. As for what we now read, that God said these things to Abram after Thare's death, this is resolved in two ways. First, that what is said now is to be understood by recapitulation, since Scripture does not always relate things done in the order in which they were done. Second, that we believe God said these words to Abram twice: first before his father's death, and before he dwelt with him in Haran, namely when, coming from Chaldea, he entered Mesopotamia, as was touched on above; and a second time after his father's death, as we read here. Nor was this repetition on account of any disobedience or negligence of Abram, since an affirmative precept does not bind except at the fitting time [the scholastic rule: a positive command, unlike a prohibition, does not oblige at every moment, but only when the occasion calls for it]. And the author of the Scholastic History touches on this solution on the Acts of the Apostles, and Lyra follows it there.

paras.t: Præterea, quod Stephanus narrat ipsum Abram de Chaldæa exisse, postquam audivit verba ista a Domino, duobus solvitur modis. Primo, ut Mesopotamia dicatur pars Chaldææ, sicque dicatur Abram tunc de Chaldæa exisse, quia de Mesopotamia, quæ est pars Chaldææ, exivit. Hanc autem solutionem Rabanus ponit, quæ et in Scholastica historia tangitur, et ex verbis Augustini elicitur. Secundo, ut Abram dicatur primo de Chaldæa corporaliter exivisse, sed cum proposito redeundi: nunc autem præceptum sit ei, ut etiam mente inde exiret, id est, Mesopotamiam deserens, eundo ad terram promissionis, abjiceret propositum revertendi in Chaldæam. Hanc solutionem ponunt Strabus, Beda, Scholastica historia, imo et Glossa hoc loco, Augustinus quoque.
paras.en: Further, the point that Stephen relates that Abram went out of Chaldea after he had heard these words from the Lord is resolved in two ways. First, that Mesopotamia may be called a part of Chaldea, and so Abram may be said to have gone out of Chaldea then, because he went out of Mesopotamia, which is a part of Chaldea. This solution Rabanus gives; it is touched on also in the Scholastic History, and is drawn from the words of Augustine. Second, that Abram may be said to have gone out of Chaldea first in body, but with the intention of returning; and that now he was commanded to go out of it in mind also: that is, that leaving Mesopotamia and going to the land of promise, he should cast away the intention of returning to Chaldea. This solution is given by Strabus, Bede, the Scholastic History, and indeed the Gloss on this place, and by Augustine too.

paras.t: Sed quidam tam super Actus Apostolorum, quam circa hunc locum, solutionem hanc reprobat, eo quod non videatur rationabile æstimare, quod Abram proposuerit in Chaldæam redire, in qua Nemrod tyrannus regnavit. Verum hæc ratio modici est vigoris, nec propter eam oportet tantorum reprobare verba doctorum. Siquidem probabiliter dici potest, quod quia Abram fuit multo junior ipso Nemrod, intendebat redire in Chaldæam, si contingeret Nemrod ante se mori, et istud est multum apparens. Abram namque, quando cum patre suo Thare exivit Chaldæam, nullum habuit præceptum a Deo relinquendi Chaldæam seu terram natalem: ideo, sicut naturale est hominibus ad natalem affici terram, verisimile est eum habuisse propositum et affectum redeundi ad eam occasione oblata. Denique præfatus ita exponit hunc passum: Egredere, id est longius recede, de terra tua, scilicet de Chaldæa, videlicet quoniam de Mesopotamia exeundo versus terram promissionis, longius quam ante abiit a Chaldæa. Probat quoque convenientiam expositionis istius, quia (ut ait) in Hebræo habetur: Vade tibi de terra tua. Quasi dicatur: Pro utilitate tua longius vade ab ea. Ad quod dicendum videtur, quod expositio illa sit multum impropria et inusitata. Non enim proprie aut usitate loquendo, dicitur quis egredi de aliqua provincia, regione aut urbe, quia recedendo de alia provincia, regione aut urbe, longius recedit ab illa. Littera quoque Hebraica quam inducit, non est plus pro expositione ipsius, quam eorum quos reprobat, sed potius minus.
