Sive enim dicatur Abram de Chaldæa exisse, quia longius recessit ab ea, sive quia reliquit propositum redeundi ad illam, totum hoc fuit pro utilitate ipsius: imo magis videtur fuisse pro salute animæ suæ, quod spiritualiter eam reliquit et exiit, utpote deponendo propositum redeundi ad ipsam, quam quod corpore longius recessit ab ea, quum ratio virtutis ac meritum magis consistant in interioribus, quam exterioribus rebus et actibus.
paras.en: But a certain writer, both on the Acts of the Apostles and on this place, rejects this solution, on the ground that it does not seem reasonable to suppose that Abram purposed to return to Chaldea, where the tyrant Nemrod reigned. But this reason has little force, nor ought the words of such great doctors to be rejected on account of it. For it can be said with probability that, since Abram was much younger than Nemrod, he intended to return to Chaldea should Nemrod happen to die before him; and this is very likely. For Abram, when he went out of Chaldea with his father Thare, had no command from God to leave Chaldea, the land of his birth; therefore, as it is natural to men to have an affection for the land of their birth, it is likely that he had the intention and the desire of returning to it when occasion offered. Lastly, the writer just mentioned expounds this passage thus: [[12:1|Go forth|Egredere]], that is, withdraw further, [[12:1|out of thy country|de terra tua]], namely out of Chaldea: because, going out of Mesopotamia towards the land of promise, he went further away from Chaldea than before. He proves the fitness of this exposition, too, because (as he says) the Hebrew has: Go for thyself out of thy country; as if to say: For thy own good go further away from it. To this it seems one must say that this exposition is very improper and unusual. For in proper or ordinary speech a man is not said to go out of some province, region or city because, in leaving another province, region or city, he withdraws further from the first. Nor does the Hebrew text that he brings in tell more for his own exposition than for that of those he rejects, but rather less. For whether Abram be said to have gone out of Chaldea because he withdrew further from it, or because he gave up the intention of returning to it, all this was for his own good; indeed it seems to have been more for the salvation of his soul that he left it and went out of it spiritually, by laying aside the intention of returning to it, than that he withdrew further from it in body, since the ground of virtue, and merit, consist more in inward than in outward things and acts.

paras.t: Amplius, Rabbi Paulus circa hunc locum reprobat Lyram, qui per terram, de qua Dominus ait, Egredere de terra tua, Chaldæam intelligit, dicens Abram natum esse in terra Chaldææ: quod Paulus iste redarguit, asserens Abram esse in Mesopotamia natum. Quocirca sciendum, quod Paulus hoc dicens, non solum contradicit Nicolao de Lyra, sed et sancto Hieronymo, Augustino, Strabo, Bedæ, ceterisque doctoribus catholicis communiter, imo et Josepho, multis quoque doctoribus Hebræorum. Hieronymus quippe in multis locis testatur, quod Abram in Chaldæa sit natus, et inde in Mesopotamiam cum patre suo profectus. Denique Augustinus sic ait: Sicut Scriptura sancta indicante didicimus, in regione Chaldæorum natus est Abram. Deinde Augustinus probat hoc per ea quæ scripta sunt in Judith historia, ubi Achior de filiis Israel protestatur: Populus iste ex progenie Chaldæorum est, et primum in Mesopotamia habitavit, quoniam noluerunt sequi deos patrum suorum qui erant in terra Chaldæorum, et Deus præcepit eis ut exirent inde, et habitarent in Charan. In littera quoque præcedentis capituli apertissime scribitur: Tulit Thare Abram filium suum, et eduxit de Ur Chaldæorum, ut irent in terram Chanaan.
paras.en: Moreover, Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, who wrote additions to Lyra], on this place, finds fault with Lyra, who by the land of which the Lord says, [[12:1|Go forth out of thy country|Egredere de terra tua]], understands Chaldea, saying that Abram was born in the land of Chaldea; this Paul refutes, asserting that Abram was born in Mesopotamia. Wherefore it is to be known that Paul, in saying this, contradicts not only Nicholas of Lyra, but also St. Jerome, Augustine, Strabus, Bede and the Catholic doctors generally, and indeed Josephus too, and many of the Hebrew doctors as well. For Jerome testifies in many places that Abram was born in Chaldea and went thence into Mesopotamia with his father. And Augustine says thus: As we have learned from the showing of Holy Scripture, Abram was born in the region of the Chaldeans. Then Augustine proves this from what is written in the history of Judith, where Achior bears witness of the children of Israel: [[Jdt 5:6|This people is of the offspring of the Chaldeans|Populus iste ex progenie Chaldæorum est]], [[Jdt 5:7|They dwelt first in Mesopotamia, because they would not follow the gods of their fathers, who were in the land of the Chaldeans|et primum in Mesopotamia habitavit, quoniam noluerunt sequi deos patrum suorum qui erant in terra Chaldæorum]]; and God [[Jdt 5:9|commanded them to depart from thence, and to dwell in Charan|præcepit eis ut exirent inde, et habitarent in Charan]]. In the text of the preceding chapter, too, it is written most plainly: [[Gen 11:31|Thare took Abram his son|Tulit Thare Abram filium suum]], [[Gen 11:31|and brought them out of Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Chanaan|et eduxit de Ur Chaldæorum, ut irent in terram Chanaan]].

paras.t: Argumenta quoque Rabbi Pauli non prævalent, sed falsa includunt. Primo enim sic arguit: Constat quod Babylonia cum tota terra Sennaar, quæ est Chaldæa, pertinebat ad Cham filium Noe, et posteritatem ejus. Abram autem descendit de Sem, cujus posteritas in aliis regionibus habitavit. Error istius verbi, ex præinductis verbis Augustini et Judith, jam patet: quia de filiis Israel universaliter dictum est, quod sint de progenie Chaldæorum. Textus quoque præcedentis capituli manifeste sic loquitur, quasi Thare genuerit tres filios suos, videlicet Abram, Nachor et Aran, in Chaldæa, præsertim quum Aran dicatur mortuus in terra nativitatis suæ in Ur Chaldæorum. Denique decimo capitulo scriptum est, quod Sem genuit Arphaxad, a quo secundum expositores, descenderunt Chaldæi, ut ibi expositum est. In ejusdem etiam expositione capituli dicebatur, quod Assur filius Cham, egressus est de terra Sennaar seu Chaldæa, expulsus inde a Nemrod, quum tamen terra illa hereditario jure pertineret ad ipsum Assur: quo patet, quod Nemrod terram illam violenter obtinuit, prout ex Scholastica est ibi allegatum historia. Secundo arguit Rabbi Paulus, quoniam infra legitur Abraham præcepisse servo suo, ut iret in terram cognationis suæ, ad accipiendum inde uxorem filio suo Isaac, et dicit quod in Hebræo habetur, Ad terram nativitatis meæ, ubi nostra translatio continet, Ad terram cognationis meæ. Ad quod dici potest, quod dictio Hebraica illa sit forte ad utrumque æquivoca. Tertio arguit, quoniam in libro Josue habetur, qualiter ipse Josue locutus est filiis Israel: Trans fluvium habitaverunt patres vestri ab initio, Thare pater Abrahæ et Nachor. Constat autem quod trans fluvium est Mesopotamia. Et quum dicit, Ab initio, satis insinuat, quod inde sint oriundi. Ad quod respondetur, quod per terram trans fluvium, intelligitur ibi non Mesopotamia, sed Chaldæa. Et per fluvium, ibi intelligitur Euphrates, secundum expositores, qui per Chaldæam decurrit, ut dictum est plenius in expositione secundi capituli. Denique Mesopotamia non sortitur hoc nomen, quia trans fluvium sita est, sed quia in medio duorum est fluminum. Dicitur enim a meso, quod est medium, et potamos aqua, quasi in aquarum medio posita, quemadmodum dicitur Aquilegia, quasi aquis ligata, prout in Scholastica fertur historia. Hæc omnia dicta sunt circa exordium hujus capituli.
paras.en: Nor do Rabbi Paul's arguments prevail; rather, they contain falsehoods. For first he argues thus: It is certain that Babylonia, with the whole land of Sennaar, which is Chaldea, belonged to Cham the son of Noe and his posterity; but Abram descended from Sem, whose posterity dwelt in other regions. The error of this statement is already plain from the words of Augustine and of Judith brought in above, since it is said of the children of Israel universally that they are of the offspring of the Chaldeans. The text of the preceding chapter also plainly speaks as though Thare begot his three sons, namely Abram, Nachor and Aran, in Chaldea, especially since Aran is said to have died [[Gen 11:28|in the land of his nativity in Ur of the Chaldees|in terra nativitatis suæ in Ur Chaldæorum]]. Then in the tenth chapter it is written that Sem begot Arphaxad, from whom, according to the expositors, the Chaldeans descended, as was explained there. And in the exposition of that same chapter it was said that Assur the son of Cham [so the Latin; at Gen 10:22 Assur is named among the sons of Sem] went out of the land of Sennaar, or Chaldea, driven out of it by Nemrod, although that land belonged by right of inheritance to Assur himself; from which it is plain that Nemrod held that land by violence, as was alleged there from the Scholastic History. Second, Rabbi Paul argues that further on we read that Abraham commanded his servant to go to the land of his kindred to take a wife thence for his son Isaac, and he says that the Hebrew has, To the land of my nativity, where our translation has, To the land of my kindred. To this it can be said that that Hebrew word perhaps bears either meaning. Third, he argues that in the book of Josue we read how Josue himself spoke to the children of Israel: [[Jos 24:2|Your fathers dwelt of old on the other side of the river, Thare the father of Abraham, and Nachor|Trans fluvium habitaverunt patres vestri ab initio, Thare pater Abrahæ et Nachor]]. Now it is certain that beyond the river is Mesopotamia; and when he says, [[Jos 24:2|of old|Ab initio]], he gives enough to understand that they came from there. To this it is answered that by the land beyond the river is understood there not Mesopotamia but Chaldea, and by the river is understood there the Euphrates, according to the expositors, which runs through Chaldea, as was said more fully in the exposition of the second chapter. Lastly, Mesopotamia does not get this name because it lies beyond the river, but because it is in the middle of two rivers. For it is named from meso, which is "middle", and potamos, "water" [that is, river], as if set in the middle of waters; just as Aquilegia [Aquileia] is so called as if bound by waters, as is told in the Scholastic History. All these things have been said about the beginning of this chapter.

paras.t: Egredere de terra tua, id est, sic ab Haran civitate Mesopotamiæ vade ad terram Chanaan, ut propositum et affectum redeundi ad Chaldæam omnino abjicias; et de cognatione tua, id est a consanguineis tuis, quos in Chaldæa et Mesopotamia habes; et de domo, id est habitaculo et domesticis seu familia, patris tui, et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi, videlicet in terram Chanaan: quæ non exprimitur in speciali a Domino, ut per hoc obedientia Abræ major monstraretur, dum obedit pergendo ad locum, cujus nomen et qualitatem nondum a Domino didicit. Unde ad Hebræos Apostolus: Fide, inquit, qui vocatur Abraham, obedivit exire in locum quem accepturus erat, nesciens quo iret.
paras.en: [[12:1|Go forth out of thy country|Egredere de terra tua]], that is, go from Haran, a city of Mesopotamia, to the land of Chanaan in such a way that thou cast away altogether the intention and the desire of returning to Chaldea; [[12:1|and from thy kindred|et de cognatione tua]], that is, from thy kinsfolk, whom thou hast in Chaldea and Mesopotamia; [[12:1|and out of thy father's house|et de domo]], that is, out of the dwelling, and the household or family, of thy father; [[12:1|and come into the land which I shall shew thee|et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi]], namely into the land of Chanaan. This land is not named in particular by the Lord, so that by this the obedience of Abram might be shown to be the greater, in that he obeyed by going to a place whose name and nature he had not yet learned from the Lord. Whence the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 11:8|By faith|Fide]], he says, [[Heb 11:8|he that is called Abraham obeyed to go out into a place which he was to receive|qui vocatur Abraham, obedivit exire in locum quem accepturus erat]], [[Heb 11:8|not knowing whither he went|nesciens quo iret]].

paras.t: Faciamque te in gentem magnam, id est, copiosum populum faciam nasci ex te successive et mediate, non obstante quod uxor tua sit naturaliter infecunda: et benedicam tibi, id est, spiritualia dona gratiæ ac virtutum, temporalium quoque abundantiam tibi præstabo; et magnificabo nomen tuum, dando tibi famam præclaram, memoriamque perpetuam in hoc mundo, juxta illud Proverbiorum, Memoria justi cum laudibus; erisque benedictus sublimiter valde.
paras.en: [[12:2|And I will make of thee a great nation|Faciamque te in gentem magnam]], that is, I will cause a numerous people to be born of thee, successively and mediately [that is, through generations of thy descendants, not from thee directly], although thy wife is by nature barren; [[12:2|and I will bless thee|et benedicam tibi]], that is, I will bestow on thee the spiritual gifts of grace and of the virtues, and an abundance of temporal goods as well; [[12:2|and magnify thy name|et magnificabo nomen tuum]], by giving thee a glorious fame and a perpetual memory in this world, according to that of the Proverbs: [[Prov 10:7|The memory of the just is with praises|Memoria justi cum laudibus]]; [[12:2|and thou shalt be blessed|erisque benedictus]] in a very high degree.

paras.t: Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, et maledicam maledicentibus tibi. Aliter Deus benedicit hominibus, aliter unus homo alteri benedicit. Deus etenim hominibus benedicit, dona gratiæ dando et multiplicando; homo autem homini benedicit, bona de ipso dicendo, seu eum laudando. Prælati tamen dicuntur interdum subditos benedicere consecrando, seu ad divina deputando eosdem. Constat autem quod multi infideles ac reprobi benedixerint Abrahæ in hac vita, ipsum laudando, quemadmodum infra de Hemor habetur, qui dixit: Princeps Dei es apud nos. Similiter Sarraceni nunc usque magnifice laudant eum, sicut et impiissimus ac diabolicus Mahometus, qui in Alcorano suo vocat Abraham virum sanctissimum. Quomodo ergo verum est quod Dominus ait, Benedicam benedicentibus tibi? Et respondendum, quod quum Deus nullum bonum deserat irremuneratum, et ipsa laudatio justorum sit quoddam bonum ex genere, Deus aliquo modo remunerat eam, saltem in vita hac, quæ remuneratio benedictio Dei vocatur. Si vero exponatur de fidelibus, qui ex caritate benedicunt Abrahæ, certum est, quod talis benedictio, quum sit actus meritorius, augmentum gratiæ et gloriam promeretur: juxta quem modum dicit Apostolus, quod nemo potest dicere Dominus Jesus, nisi in Spiritu Sancto.
paras.en: [[12:3|I will bless them that bless thee, and curse them that curse thee|Benedicam benedicentibus tibi, et maledicam maledicentibus tibi]]. God blesses men in one way, and one man blesses another in another. For God blesses men by giving and multiplying the gifts of grace; but man blesses man by speaking good of him, or by praising him. Prelates, however, are sometimes said to bless their subjects by consecrating them, or by setting them apart for divine things. Now it is certain that many unbelievers and reprobate men have blessed Abraham in this life by praising him, as we read further on of Hemor, who said: [[Gen 23:6|thou art a prince of God among us|Princeps Dei es apud nos]] [the two margin notes here are unreadable. These words are spoken to Abraham by the children of Heth at Gen 23:6; Hemor appears at Gen 34]. Likewise the Saracens to this day praise him magnificently, as did also the most impious and diabolical Mahomet, who in his Alcoran calls Abraham a most holy man. How then is what the Lord says true: [[12:3|I will bless them that bless thee|Benedicam benedicentibus tibi]]? And it must be answered that, since God leaves no good unrewarded, and the very praising of the just is a kind of good by its kind [that is, good in the kind of act it is, even when not done from charity], God rewards it in some way, at least in this life; and this reward is called the blessing of God. But if it be expounded of the faithful, who bless Abraham out of charity, it is certain that such blessing, since it is a meritorious act, merits an increase of grace, and glory: in the way in which the Apostle says that [[1 Cor 12:3|no man can say The Lord Jesus, but by the Holy Ghost|nemo potest dicere Dominus Jesus, nisi in Spiritu Sancto]].

paras.t: Atque in te, id est in Christo ex tuo semine nascituro, jam nato, benedicentur universæ cognationes terræ: hoc est, universæ gentes, tribus et linguæ, credendo in Christum, gratiam in præsenti, et gloriam in futuro consequentur, juxta illud Psalmi: Benedicentur in ipso omnes tribus terræ, omnes gentes magnificabunt eum. Unde ab Isaia dictum est: Servos suos vocabit Dominus nomine alio, in quo qui benedictus est super terram, benedicetur in Deo, amen.
paras.en: [[12:3|and IN THEE|Atque in te]], that is, in Christ, who was to be born of thy seed and is now born, [[12:3|shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed|benedicentur universæ cognationes terræ]]: that is, all nations, tribes and tongues, by believing in Christ, shall obtain grace in the present and glory in the future, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 71:17|in him shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed: all nations shall magnify him|Benedicentur in ipso omnes tribus terræ, omnes gentes magnificabunt eum]]. Whence it was said by Isaias that the Lord shall [[Is 65:15|call his servants by another name|Servos suos vocabit Dominus nomine alio]], [[Is 65:16|In which he that is blessed upon the earth, shall be blessed in God, amen|in quo qui benedictus est super terram, benedicetur in Deo, amen]].

paras.t: Porro Judæi, ut dicitur, ita exponunt: Benedicentur in te, etc., id est, forma et exemplar benedicendi omni populo eris, ita quod dum quis voluerit alteri benedicere, dicet: Benedicat seu faciat tibi Deus sicut benedixit Abrahæ. Sed istud inconvenienter dictum censetur, quum innumerabiles gentes exstiterint, et innumerabiles tribus sint in quibus non observatur forma aut modus hujusmodi benedictionis. Circa hoc Rabbi Paulus scribit, licet vera sit expositio illa prima, videlicet, quod benedictio Christi fit super omnem nationem terræ, hoc tamen non fuit Abræ promissum hoc loco. Verum in hoc Rabbi Paulus non solum contradicit Lyræ, sed etiam Augustino et Isidoro, aliisque catholicis doctoribus communiter. Ait enim B. Augustinus: Advertendum est, duas res esse promissas Abrahæ, in verbis præhabitis, quod semen ejus possessurum esset terram Chanaan: aliam quoque multo præstantiorem, non de carnali, sed spirituali semine, scilicet Christo, per quod pater est non tantum unius Israeliticæ gentis, sed omnium gentium quæ fidei hujus vestigia consequentur. Idem dicit Isidorus et habetur in Glossa.
paras.en: But the Jews, as is said, expound it thus: [[12:3|IN THEE shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed|Benedicentur in te]], etc., that is, thou shalt be the form and pattern of blessing for every people, so that when anyone wishes to bless another he will say: May God bless thee, or do to thee, as he blessed Abraham. But this is judged to be said unfittingly, since there have been countless nations, and there are countless tribes, among whom the form or manner of such a blessing is not observed. On this Rabbi Paul writes that, although that first exposition is true, namely that the blessing of Christ comes upon every nation of the earth, yet this was not promised to Abram in this place. But in this Rabbi Paul contradicts not only Lyra but also Augustine and Isidore and the Catholic doctors generally. For blessed Augustine says: It is to be noted that two things were promised to Abraham in the words above: one, that his seed should possess the land of Chanaan; and another, far more excellent, concerning not the carnal but the spiritual seed, namely Christ, through which he is the father not of the one Israelite nation only, but of all the nations that follow in the footsteps of this faith. Isidore says the same, and it is in the Gloss.

paras.t: Egressus est itaque Abram de Haran urbe Mesopotamiæ, sicut præceperat ei Deus, et ivit cum eo Lot, qui magis elegit adhærere suo patruo justo, videlicet Abræ, quam inter ceteros consanguineos suos injustos aut minus justos manere. Tulitque uxorem suam Sarai, et Lot filium fratris sui, universamque substantiam quam possederant, et animas quas fecerant in Haran, id est animantia quæ acquisierant ibi, et dispositive produxerant, applicando activa passivis, videlicet mares femellis. Vel, animas, hoc est familiam quam ibi acceperant, seu servos et ancillas quos emerant, aut eos quos forsan ad unius Dei cultum attraxerant, quorum animas dispositive produxerant, quantum ad esse gratiæ.
paras.en: [[12:4|So Abram went out|Egressus est itaque Abram]] from Haran, a city of Mesopotamia, [[12:4|as the Lord had commanded him|sicut præceperat ei Deus]], [[12:4|and Lot went with him|et ivit cum eo Lot]], who chose rather to cleave to his righteous uncle, namely Abram, than to remain among his other kinsmen, who were unrighteous or less righteous. [[12:5|And he took Sarai his wife|Tulitque uxorem suam Sarai]], [[12:5|and Lot his brother's son, and all the substance which they had gathered|et Lot filium fratris sui, universamque substantiam quam possederant]], [[12:5|and the souls which they had gotten in Haran|et animas quas fecerant in Haran]], that is, the living creatures which they had acquired there and had brought forth dispositively [that is, by arranging the conditions for their generation, not by giving them being], by applying actives to passives, namely males to females. Or, *souls*, that is, the household which they had taken on there, or the menservants and maidservants whom they had bought, or those whom perhaps they had drawn to the worship of the one God, whose souls they had brought forth dispositively as regards the being of grace.

paras.t: Quumque venissent in terram Chanaan, pertransivit Abram terram illam usque ad locum Sichem, hoc est usque ad urbem sic appellatam, quæ in Evangelio dicitur Sichar, quod nomen venit ex corrupta prolatione; et usque ad convallem Illustrem, id est delectabilem et præclaram, ubi erat Pentapolis, seu regio quinque civitatum postea subversarum, videlicet Sodomæ, Gomorrhæ, etc., ut infra dicetur, quæ regio fuit ante suam eversionem valde amœna atque præcipua. Chananæus autem tunc erat in terra, id est, Chananæi orti ex Cham filio Noe, tunc habitaverunt in terra illa, quæ ordinatione divina et dispositione ipsius Noe, ut dicunt Hebræi, danda fuit semini Abrahæ. Nam et Melchisedech, qui creditur fuisse Sem filius Noe, ut infra magis patebit, habitavit atque regnavit in Salem urbe terræ Chanaan.
paras.en: [[12:5|And when they were come into it|Quumque venissent in terram Chanaan]], [[12:6|Abram passed through the country unto the place of Sichem|pertransivit Abram terram illam usque ad locum Sichem]], that is, as far as the city so called, which in the Gospel is called Sichar[[John 4:5||]], a name that came from a corrupt pronunciation; [[12:6|as far as the noble vale|usque ad convallem Illustrem]], that is, the delightful and splendid vale, where the Pentapolis was, or the region of the five cities afterwards overthrown, namely Sodom, Gomorrha, etc., as will be said below[[Gen 13:10||]], which region before its overthrow was exceedingly pleasant and choice; [[12:6|now the Chanaanite was at that time in the land|Chananæus autem tunc erat in terra]], that is, the Chanaanites, sprung from Cham the son of Noe, were dwelling at that time in that land which, by God's ordinance and by the disposition of Noe himself, as the Hebrews say, was to be given to the seed of Abraham. For Melchisedech too, who is believed to have been Sem the son of Noe, as will appear more fully below, dwelt and reigned in Salem, a city of the land of Chanaan.

paras.t: Apparuitque Dominus Abram in loco præfato, et dixit ei: Semini tuo dabo terram hanc. Qui ædificavit ibi altare Domino qui apparuit ei, et invocavit nomen ejus, gratias agens ei de beneficiis ac promissis ipsius, propter quod construxit ibi illud altare, super quod obtulit hostias ei, prout consuetudinis erat in lege naturali, sicut prædictum est de Abel et Noe.
paras.en: [[12:7|And the Lord appeared to Abram|Apparuitque Dominus Abram]] in the aforesaid place, [[12:7|and said to him: To thy seed will I give this land|et dixit ei: Semini tuo dabo terram hanc]]. [[12:7|And he built there an altar to the Lord, who had appeared to him|Qui ædificavit ibi altare Domino qui apparuit ei]], [[12:8|and called upon his name|et invocavit nomen ejus]], giving him thanks for his benefits and promises; for which reason he built that altar there, upon which he offered victims to him, as was the custom in the law of nature, as was said above of Abel[[Gen 4:4||]] and Noe[[Gen 8:20||]].

paras.t: Et inde transgrediens ad montem, qui est, vel, ut aliqui habent, vadit, id est vergit seu situs est, contra orientem Bethel, hoc est ex opposito orientalis plagæ, per respectum ad urbem nomine Bethel, tetendit ibi tabernaculum suum inter Bethel et oppidum Hai. Propter quod subditur: ab occidente habens Bethel, et ab oriente Hai. Itaque sanctus Patriarcha cum sua familia in tabernaculis quæ secum detulit, et hinc inde expandit, moratus est, quemadmodum ad Hebræos scribit Apostolus: Fide moratus est in terra repromissionis, tanquam in aliena, in casulis habitando, cum Isaac et Jacob coheredibus repromissionis ejusdem. Exspectabat enim fundamenta habentem civitatem, cujus artifex et conditor Deus. Ædificavit quoque ibi altare Domino. In quo patet fervor suæ devotionis. Perrexitque Abram vadens et ultra progrediens ad meridiem, hoc est ad partem terræ Chanaan, respicientem Ægyptum, quæ est ad meridiem respectu Judææ. Non ex animi levitate tantus Patriarcha, tam frequenter locum mutavit, sed ex divino instinctu, ut terram semini suo promissam circumspiciens, et perpendens, gratias Deo ageret ampliores.
paras.en: [[12:8|And passing on from thence to a mountain|Et inde transgrediens ad montem]], [[12:8|that was|qui est]] (or, as some have it, *that goes*, that is, inclines or is situated) [[12:8|on the east side of Bethel|contra orientem Bethel]], that is, over against the eastern quarter, with respect to the city named Bethel, [[12:8|he there pitched his tent|tetendit ibi tabernaculum suum]] between Bethel and the town of Hai. For which reason it is added: [[12:8|having Bethel on the west, and Hai on the east|ab occidente habens Bethel, et ab oriente Hai]]. So the holy Patriarch with his household abode in the tents which he brought with him and spread out here and there, as the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: [[Heb 11:9|By faith he abode in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in cottages, with Isaac and Jacob, the co-heirs of the same promise|Fide moratus est in terra repromissionis, tanquam in aliena, in casulis habitando, cum Isaac et Jacob coheredibus repromissionis ejusdem]]. [[Heb 11:10|For he looked for a city that hath foundations: whose builder and maker is God|Exspectabat enim fundamenta habentem civitatem, cujus artifex et conditor Deus]]. And [[12:8|he built there also an altar to the Lord|Ædificavit quoque ibi altare Domino]]. In this the fervour of his devotion is plain. [[12:9|And Abram went forward, going and proceeding on to the south|Perrexitque Abram vadens et ultra progrediens ad meridiem]], that is, to the part of the land of Chanaan that looks toward Egypt, which lies to the south with respect to Judea. It was not from fickleness of mind that so great a Patriarch changed his place so often, but by divine prompting, so that, viewing and weighing the land promised to his seed, he might give God more abundant thanks.

paras.t: Facta est autem fames in terra Chanaan, hoc est caristia, sive ex causa naturali, sive ob vitia Chananæorum, vel propter utrumque; descenditque Abram in Ægyptum, ut peregrinaretur, id est, ut tanquam peregrinus habitaret ibi ad tempus, quousque scilicet fame sublata, rediret ad terram ad quam desuper jussus fuit accedere. Descendit itaque, id est descendere cœpit in Ægyptum, eundo ad illam, quæ in bassiori est situ, quam terra promissionis. Circa hoc Josephus scribit: Audiens Abram Ægyptios feliciter vivere, adiit eos, ut eorum abundantia participaretur, et sacerdotum auditor esset, atque cognosceret quæ de diis exponerent, ut aut meliores inveniens sequeretur, aut sua prudentia eos in ornatum meliorem transponeret.
paras.en: [[12:10|And there came a famine in the country|Facta est autem fames in terra Chanaan]], that is, a dearth [Latin *caristia*, a medieval word for scarcity and dearness of food], whether from a natural cause, or because of the vices of the Chanaanites, or for both; [[12:10|and Abram went down into Egypt, to sojourn|descenditque Abram in Ægyptum, ut peregrinaretur]], that is, to dwell as a pilgrim [[12:10|there|ibi]] for a time, until, that is, the famine being lifted, he should return to the land to which he had been bidden from on high to go. So he [[12:10|went down|Descendit itaque]], that is, began to go down into Egypt, travelling to it, since it lies lower than the land of promise. On this Josephus writes: Abram, hearing that the Egyptians lived prosperously, went to them, to share in their abundance, and to be a hearer of their priests and learn what they set forth about the gods, so that either, finding them better, he might follow them, or by his own wisdom bring them over to a better state.

paras.t: Dixitque uxori suæ: Novi quod pulchra sis mulier, et quod quum viderint te Ægyptii, dicturi sunt, Uxor illius est, et interficient me, nisi tu acquiescas petitioni meæ, et te reservabunt. Quomodo sanctus Patriarcha, cui Deus promiserat quod semini suo daret terram Chanaan, hoc dicere potuit, aut occidi expavit, quum nondum haberet prolem, quasi divina promissio posset frustrari in eo? Ad hoc dici potest, quod dixit hoc secundum inferiorum causarum considerationem. Attenta enim libidine Ægyptiorum, probabile erat sic esse venturum, loquendo modo humano. Sic et David cui Deus regnum Israel jam promiserat, timuit a Saul occidi, et semel desperavit se posse evadere, tandemque dixit: Aliquando una die incidam in manus Saul. Iterum dici potest, quod sicut Abraham paratus fuit filium suum Isaac immolare, non obstante quod Deus ei spoponderat, In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen, nec tamen hæsitavit diffidentia de veritate promissionis divinæ, sciens quia a mortuis potens est Deus suscitare: sic poterat cogitare de semetipso, et nihilo minus mortem naturaliter formidare, violentamque mortem velle evadere.
paras.en: [[12:11|he said to Sarai his wife|Dixitque uxori suæ]]: [[12:11|I know that thou art a beautiful woman|Novi quod pulchra sis mulier]], [[12:12|And that when the Egyptians shall see thee, they will say: She is his wife|et quod quum viderint te Ægyptii, dicturi sunt, Uxor illius est]]: [[12:12|and they will kill me|et interficient me]], unless thou consent to my request, [[12:12|and keep thee|et te reservabunt]]. How could the holy Patriarch, to whom God had promised that he would give the land of Chanaan to his seed, say this, or be afraid of being killed, when he did not yet have offspring, as though the divine promise could be made void in him? To this it can be said that he said this according to a consideration of the lower causes [that is, the natural course of things, leaving aside God's promise]. For, the lust of the Egyptians being considered, it was probable that it would come about so, speaking in human fashion. So too David, to whom God had already promised the kingdom of Israel, feared to be killed by Saul, and once despaired of being able to escape, and at length said: [[1 Kings 27:1|I shall one day or other fall into the hands of Saul|Aliquando una die incidam in manus Saul]]. Again it can be said that, just as Abraham was ready to sacrifice his son Isaac, notwithstanding that God had pledged to him, [[Gen 21:12|in Isaac shall thy seed be called|In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen]], and yet did not waver through distrust of the truth of the divine promise, knowing that God is able to raise up even from the dead: so he could think of himself, and none the less fear death naturally, and wish to escape a violent death.

paras.t: Circa hunc locum quidam ait, quod Ægyptii reputabant adulterium majus esse peccatum, quam homicidium. Hoc tamen reor incertum, neque ex littera sequitur. Potuissent quippe Ægyptii amore libidinis maritum aliquando occidisse, ut ejus conjuge liberius fruerentur, quamvis scirent homicidium adulterio esse gravius. Sicut et nunc aliqui impii Christiani, non obstante quod sciant homicidium esse enormius adulterio, interdum occidunt maritum, ut ejus uxore fruantur: imo vir bonus posset tentationem talem incidere, ut patet in David, qui fecit occidi Uriam, sive ut ejus haberet uxorem, sive ut crimen quod cum illa commiserat, celaretur, vel potius propter utrumque. Denique, quam grave reputabant Ægyptii homicidium, quod item illud morte puniebant, constat ex hoc quod sicut in Exodo legitur, quum Moyses audisset publicatum esse, qualiter ipse occidit Ægyptium, fugit: quia et Pharao ob hoc voluit eum occidere, non obstante quod talis ac tantus esset in Pharaonis palatio. Præterea idem ait circa hunc passum, quod Deus permisit famem fieri in terra Chanaan, ut ostenderetur fides Abræ, qui ex illo eventu non diffidebat de veritate divinæ promissionis, qua dictum erat ad eum, quod tam sublimiter esset benedicendus in terra illa, quum tamen jam ex indigentia victualium cogeretur eam exire. Sed quamvis hoc poterat esse aliqua causa præfatæ permissionis, non tamen apparet, quod propter ostensionem fidei Abræ, Deus induxerit plagam famis super gentem illam, tam longe ac late.
paras.en: On this place someone says that the Egyptians reckoned adultery a greater sin than homicide. This, however, I think uncertain, nor does it follow from the letter. For the Egyptians, out of the love of lust, could at times have killed a husband in order to enjoy his wife more freely, although they knew homicide to be graver than adultery; just as now too some impious Christians, notwithstanding that they know homicide to be more enormous than adultery, sometimes kill a husband in order to enjoy his wife: indeed, even a good man might fall into such a temptation, as is plain in David, who had Urias killed[[2 Kings 11:15||]], whether to have his wife, or so that the crime he had committed with her might be hidden, or rather for both. Finally, how grave a thing the Egyptians reckoned homicide, so that they likewise punished it with death, is clear from this, that, as we read in Exodus, when Moses heard that it had been made known how he had killed the Egyptian, he fled[[Ex 2:15||]]: because Pharao too wished to kill him for this, notwithstanding that he was so great a man, and of such standing, in Pharao's palace. Moreover, the same writer says on this passage that God permitted the famine to come about in the land of Chanaan so that the faith of Abram might be shown, who did not, because of that event, distrust the truth of the divine promise, by which it had been said to him that he would be so sublimely blessed in that land, when yet he was now forced by want of victuals to leave it. But although this could be some cause of the permission aforesaid, yet it does not appear that God brought the scourge of famine upon that people, so far and wide, for the sake of showing Abram's faith.

paras.t: Dic ergo, obsecro te, quod soror mea sis. Per hoc Abram non est mentitus, nec persuasit uxori ut mentiretur, sed ut veritatem caute celaret, bona æquivocatione, non fallacia perniciosa, utendo. Multis etiam modis dicuntur homines fratres simul sive sorores, utpote propter identitatem naturæ specificæ, propter amicitiam specialem, propter consanguinitatem, propter fidei et religionis communionem: sicque Sarai fuit soror sui mariti pluribus modis: quia valde propinqua, ejusdemque speciei, et quia carissima est, et quia ejusdem religionis ac fidei. Et bene sit mihi propter te, hoc est, quatenus amore tui et propter talem assertionem, quod scilicet soror mea sis, bene faciant mihi Ægyptii: et vivat anima mea, id est, ego ipse in vita permaneam, nec occidar, ob gratiam tuam, hoc est propter hanc beneficentiam tuam circa me, seu propter gratiositatem et amabilitatem tuam, qua complacebis Ægyptiis.
paras.en: [[12:13|Say, therefore, I pray thee, that thou art my sister|Dic ergo, obsecro te, quod soror mea sis]]. By this Abram did not lie, nor did he persuade his wife to lie, but to hide the truth cautiously, using a good equivocation [that is, words true in the sense meant, used to conceal the truth without asserting anything false], not a harmful deceit. Moreover, men are called brothers, or sisters, to one another in many ways: for example, because of sameness of specific nature [that is, of belonging to the same species], because of special friendship, because of kinship, because of communion in faith and religion; and so Sarai was her husband's sister in several ways: because she was very near of kin, and of the same species, and because she is most dear, and because of the same religion and faith. [[12:13|that I may be well used for thee|Et bene sit mihi propter te]], that is, so that for love of thee, and because of such an assertion, namely that thou art my sister, the Egyptians may treat me well: [[12:13|and that my soul may live|et vivat anima mea]], that is, that I myself may remain in life and not be killed, [[12:13|for thy sake|ob gratiam tuam]], that is, because of this kindness of thine towards me, or because of thy graciousness and lovableness, by which thou wilt please the Egyptians.

paras.t: Circa hoc quærit quidam, quomodo Abraham per tale mendacium exposuit conjugem suam periculo adulterii: quæ quæstio non videtur congrue mota, quoniam sicut nunc patuit, verba ista non erant falsa, nec exposuit conjugem suam directe periculo adulterationis. Denique, ex hoc quod Ægyptii æstimabant feminam illam non esse alicui maritatam, non fuisset ibi formalis ratio adulterii, ex parte ipsorum, velut si quis accedat alienam quam putat suam uxorem. Abram quoque quum esset vir sanctus atque propheta, confidebat in Domino, quod conjugem suam servaret intactam. Attamen fecit et facere debuit quod in se erat, utendo bona ac humana industria, et sibi ac suis de necessariis providendo: quia ut asserit Augustinus, qui periculum non cavet, quantum potest, magis tentat Deum quam sperat in eo.
paras.en: On this someone asks how Abraham by such a lie exposed his wife to the danger of adultery: a question which does not seem fittingly raised, since, as has just been made plain, those words were not false, nor did he expose his wife directly to the danger of adultery. Further, since the Egyptians reckoned that the woman was not married to anyone, there would not have been the formal ratio of adultery there [that is, what makes the act adultery in its essence] on their part; as when someone goes in to another man's wife whom he thinks to be his own wife. Abram too, being a holy man and a prophet, trusted in the Lord that he would keep his wife untouched. Yet he did, and was bound to do, what lay in him, using good and human industry, and providing necessaries for himself and his own: because, as Augustine asserts, he who does not guard against danger as far as he can tempts God rather than hopes in him.

paras.t: Circa hoc quidam scribit, quod homo in periculis positus, semper agere debet ad sui liberationem, quod potest secundum viam humanam, ut non tentet Deum. Istud non est satis idonee dictum, nec universaliter verum, quum certum sit, quod plures martyres utriusque sexus noluerunt imminentem occisionem evadere, quum et apertis carceribus possent et rogarentur abire: imo quum beatissimus Petrus apostolus ad instantiam fratrum Romam exisset ad evadendum persecutionem tyranni, occurrit ei Salvator: Vado, inquiens, Romam iterum crucifigi. Quo dicto, disparuit Christus, et Petrus reversus est.
paras.en: On this someone writes that a man placed in dangers must always do what he can for his own deliverance by human means, so as not to tempt God. This is not said fitly enough, nor is it universally true, since it is certain that many martyrs of both sexes refused to escape the death that threatened them, even when the prisons were open and they could go away and were begged to: indeed, when the most blessed apostle Peter, at the urging of the brethren, had gone out of Rome to escape the persecution of the tyrant, the Saviour met him, saying: I go to Rome to be crucified again. Having said this, Christ vanished, and Peter went back.

paras.t: Rursus idem scribit hoc loco: Sciebat Abram quod reges tempore illo non accedebant ad uxores suas de novo acceptas, nisi post anni circulum; quia ut dicitur in libro Esther, sex mensibus ungebantur oleo myrtino, et aliis sex mensibus utebantur quibusdam pigmentis variisque unguentis. Istud nec verum videtur, nec apparentiam habet, nec allegatio libri Esther est ad propositum, nec recte adducta. Fuisset enim tunc regibus id et nunc molestum tamdiu differri, et carere cupitis amplexibus. Ex multis quoque antiquis historiis posset probari oppositum, imo et ex historia Esther. In libro etenim Esther non legitur, sicut iste allegat, quod uxores de novo acceptæ, totidem mensibus ungerentur: sed quod puellæ ad cubiculum regis Assueri ducendæ, sic ungebantur, quousque rex unam ex illis eligeret in uxorem: et illæ puellæ erant concubinæ, non conjuges regis. Et dato quod hoc fuisset consuetudo apud reges Persarum et Medorum, et tempore Assueri, qui plusquam per mille quingentos annos fuit post Pharaonem istum Ægypti regem, non tamen sequeretur quod apud reges Ægypti, et tempore Abrahæ fuerat talis consuetudo. Insuper in libro Esther habetur, quod dum Assuerus rex elegisset eam in conjugem, statim dedit requiem in universo regno suo ac munera, et jussit parari convivium pro conjunctione et nuptiis Esther, nec fit ibi aliqua mentio de protractione carnalis copulæ, postquam in conjugem est assumpta. Similiter in libro primo Machabæorum, ubi describitur connubium initum inter Alexandrum regem Asiæ, et Cleopatram filiam regis Ægypti, non fit mentio de tali dilatione carnalis conjunctionis; sed quod Ptolemæus rex in Ptolemaide celebravit nuptias filiæ suæ in gloria magna: nec in aliqua scriptura authentica invenitur, quod consuetudinis fuerit regibus post nuptiarum celebrationem abstinere per annum a conjugali accessu.
paras.en: Again, the same writer says in this place: Abram knew that kings at that time did not go in to their newly taken wives except after the round of a year; because, as is said in the book of Esther, for six months they were anointed with oil of myrtle [Denis writes *myrtino*, of myrtle; the Vulgate has *myrrhino*, of myrrh], and for the other six months they used certain perfumes and various ointments[[Esth 2:12||]]. This seems neither true nor even likely, nor is the citing of the book of Esther to the purpose, nor rightly brought in. For it would have been irksome to kings then, as it would be now, to be put off so long and to go without the embraces they desired. From many ancient histories too the opposite could be proved, and indeed from the history of Esther itself. For in the book of Esther we do not read, as he alleges, that newly taken wives were anointed for so many months, but that the girls who were to be brought to the chamber of king Assuerus were anointed in this way until the king should choose one of them for his wife: and those girls were concubines, not wives of the king. And granted that this had been the custom among the kings of the Persians and Medes, and in the time of Assuerus, who lived more than fifteen hundred years after this Pharao king of Egypt, it would still not follow that such a custom had existed among the kings of Egypt and in the time of Abraham. Moreover, the book of Esther has it that when king Assuerus had chosen her for his wife, he at once gave rest throughout his whole kingdom, and gifts, and commanded a feast to be prepared for the marriage and wedding of Esther[[Esth 2:18||]]; and no mention is made there of any putting off of carnal union after she had been taken as his wife. Likewise in the first book of Machabees, where the marriage made between Alexander king of Asia and Cleopatra the daughter of the king of Egypt is described, no mention is made of such a delay of carnal union, but only that king Ptolemee celebrated his daughter's marriage at Ptolemais in great glory[[1 Mach 10:58||]]: nor is it found in any authentic writing that it was the custom for kings, after the celebration of their marriage, to abstain for a year from conjugal approach.

paras.t: Quumque ingressus esset Abram Ægyptum, viderunt Ægyptii mulierem quod pulchra esset nimis. Ad corporalem autem pulchritudinem tria requiruntur, secundum Philosophum: Primum est elegans statura, seu condecens magnitudo: ideo homines parvæ staturæ non dicuntur proprie pulchri, quamvis dici possint decori. Secundum est proportionata cohabitudo membrorum. Tertium, superfusio naturalis vividique coloris.
paras.en: [[12:14|And when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians saw the woman that she was very beautiful|Quumque ingressus esset Abram Ægyptum, viderunt Ægyptii mulierem quod pulchra esset nimis]]. Now for bodily beauty three things are required, according to the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle]: the first is a comely stature, or a becoming size; therefore men of small stature are not properly called beautiful, though they may be called comely. The second is a proportioned arrangement of the limbs. The third, the overspreading of a natural and lively colour.

paras.t: Et nuntiaverunt principes Pharaoni, id est regi Ægypti, cujus reges tunc cognominabantur Pharaones, sicut et postea Ptolemæi, et sicut reges Franciæ cognominantur Delphim, quum tamen aliud habeant proprium nomen. Quidam per principes, intelligit custodes passagii: quod ineptum videtur, quum passagii custodia non sit tam altum officium. Idcirco principes rectius intelliguntur quidam præcipui et majores regis officiati, qui quod ab inferioribus forsitan perceperunt, regi denuntiaverunt ad complacendum eidem. Et laudaverunt illam apud illum, id est Sarai apud Pharaonem, dicendo quod esset pulchra, morigerata, honesta: et sublata est mulier in domum Pharaonis, id est, Pharao jussit ut sibi adduceretur. Abram vero bene usi sunt propter illam, id est, bene fecerunt ei amore Sarai, quam putabant ipsius sororem. Fueruntque ei oves et boves, asini et asinæ et cameli, servi et famulæ. Ægyptii namque contulerunt ei munera, honoraveruntque eum ob causam prætactam. Et quoniam in aliquibus eos instruxit, ditatus est ibi in his.
paras.en: [[12:15|And the princes told Pharao|Et nuntiaverunt principes Pharaoni]], that is, the king of Egypt, whose kings were then surnamed Pharaos, as afterwards Ptolemees, and as the kings of France are surnamed Dauphin [Denis's *Delphim*; properly the title of the French king's eldest son], though they have another proper name. Some take *the princes* to mean the keepers of the frontier passage: which seems unfitting, since the keeping of a passage is not so high an office. Therefore *the princes* are more rightly understood as certain chief and greater officers of the king, who reported to the king, to please him, what they had perhaps learned from those beneath them. [[12:15|and praised her before him|Et laudaverunt illam apud illum]], that is, Sarai before Pharao, saying that she was beautiful, well-mannered, modest: [[12:15|and the woman was taken into the house of Pharao|et sublata est mulier in domum Pharaonis]], that is, Pharao ordered that she be brought to him. [[12:16|And they used Abram well for her sake|Abram vero bene usi sunt propter illam]], that is, they did him good for love of Sarai, whom they thought his sister. [[12:16|And he had sheep and oxen and he asses, and men servants, and maid servants, and she asses, and camels|Fueruntque ei oves et boves, asini et asinæ et cameli, servi et famulæ]]. For the Egyptians bestowed gifts on him and honoured him for the cause already touched on. And since he instructed them in some things, he was enriched there in these.

paras.t: Nempe, ut Josephus refert, et in Scholastica recitatur historia, arithmeticam et astrologiam docuit eos. Quæ scientiæ postea ab Ægyptiis pervenerunt ad Græcos. Ipseque Abram, secundum Josephum, primus ausus est pronuntiare, Deum unum esse omnium creatorem, quod conjiciebat per mutationes terræ et maris, per ea quæ contingunt circa solem et lunam, atque ex omnibus quæ circa cœlum semper eveniunt. De eodem quoque refert Berosus: Post diluvium decima generatione, fuit apud Chaldæos vir justus et magnus, in cœlestibus rebus expertus. Verumtamen reor, quod Noe et Melchisedech et alii justi ante Abram, publice docuerunt subditos et posteros suos, unum esse omnium Creatorem ac Deum: et item, quod Abram ex supernaturali illuminatione magis quam ex astronomia cognovit hoc ipsum.
paras.en: For, as Josephus relates, and as is recounted in the Scholastic History [the *Historia Scholastica* of Peter Comestor], he taught them arithmetic and astrology [that is, the science of the stars, astronomy]. These sciences afterwards passed from the Egyptians to the Greeks. And Abram himself, according to Josephus, was the first who dared to declare that God is one, the creator of all things, which he inferred from the changes of land and sea, from the things that happen about the sun and moon, and from all that ever comes to pass about the heavens. Berosus too relates of him: In the tenth generation after the flood there was among the Chaldeans a just man and a great one, skilled in heavenly things. Yet I think that Noe and Melchisedech and other just men before Abram publicly taught their subjects and descendants that there is one Creator and God of all; and also that Abram knew this very thing by supernatural illumination rather than by astronomy.

paras.t: Si præterea quæratur, cur Pharao non cognovit conjugem Abræ, quum esset in domum suam deducta: respondet Augustinus, quod flagellationibus divinis fuit super hoc impeditus. Verumtamen in Glossa tangitur, quod ex libro Esther est allegatum de præparatione puellarum, quæ ad thalamum regis perducebantur. In Scholastica historia scribitur, quod Deus impedivit desiderium Pharaonis ægritudine et tumultu causarum. Hinc subditur: Flagellavit autem Dominus Pharaonem et domum, id est familiam, ejus plagis maximis, propter uxorem Abram, id est, ob hoc, quod eam injuste abstulerant, et Pharao detinere proponeret. Si quæratur, quæ fuerunt maximæ plagæ istæ: jam tactum est, quod ægritudines erant, seu impossibilitas pariendi, puta uxorum Pharaonis, et servarum ejus conclusio, sicut infra habetur de domo Abimelech: aut seminis fluxus, seu terror somniorum, apparitioque monstrorum.
paras.en: If it is asked further why Pharao did not know Abram's wife, since she had been brought into his house: Augustine answers that he was hindered in this by divine scourgings. In the Gloss, however, mention is made of what is cited from the book of Esther about the preparing of the girls who were brought to the king's bedchamber[[Esth 2:12||]]. In the Scholastic History it is written that God hindered Pharao's desire by sickness and by a turmoil of affairs. Hence it is added: [[12:17|But the Lord scourged Pharao|Flagellavit autem Dominus Pharaonem]] [[12:17|and his house|et domum]], that is, his household, [[12:17|with most grievous stripes|plagis maximis]], [[12:17|for Sarai, Abram's wife|propter uxorem Abram]], that is, because they had unjustly taken her away and Pharao meant to keep her. If it is asked what these most grievous stripes were: it has already been touched on that they were sicknesses, or an inability to bring forth, that is, a closing up of Pharao's wives and of his maidservants, as is told below of the house of Abimelech[[Gen 20:18||]]; or a flux of seed, or terror in dreams, and the appearing of monsters.

paras.t: Vocavitque Pharao Abram, et dixit ei: Quidnam est hoc quod fecisti mihi? Quasi dicat: Cur exposuisti me huic periculo, et his plagis? Quare non indicasti quod uxor tua esset? Quam ob causam dixisti sororem tuam esse, ut tollerem eam mihi in uxorem? An Abram ad ista responderit, textus non exprimit. Potuit autem causam rationabilem assignare, quæ tacta est, ne videlicet propter uxorem suam occideretur a plebe Ægypti. Sed unde cognovit Pharao, quod Sarai esset uxor Abræ? Dicunt aliqui, quod ex revelatione. Porro Scholastica historia dicit, quod dum sacerdotes Ægypti sacrificarent pro regis sanatione, acceperunt responsum, quod Pharao propter injuriam peregrino illatam in sublatione suæ uxoris, esset punitus. Sed mirum, quod tantus rex voluit uxorem simplicis peregrinæ, quam putavit ejus sororem, accipere conjugem. Ad quod dici potest, quod pulchritudo et modestia mulieris traxerunt eum ad hoc; honestas quoque et sapientia Abræ quem fratrem illius credebat.
paras.en: [[12:18|And Pharao called Abram, and said to him: What is this that thou hast done to me?|Vocavitque Pharao Abram, et dixit ei: Quidnam est hoc quod fecisti mihi?]] As if to say: Why hast thou exposed me to this danger, and to these stripes? [[12:18|Why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?|Quare non indicasti quod uxor tua esset?]] [[12:19|For what cause didst thou say, she was thy sister, that I might take her to my wife?|Quam ob causam dixisti sororem tuam esse, ut tollerem eam mihi in uxorem?]] Whether Abram answered these things the text does not say. He could, however, have given a reasonable cause, the one already touched on: namely, lest he be killed by the common people of Egypt on account of his wife. But how did Pharao know that Sarai was Abram's wife? Some say, by revelation. The Scholastic History, again, says that while the priests of Egypt were sacrificing for the king's healing, they received the answer that Pharao was being punished for the wrong done to a stranger in the taking away of his wife. But it is a wonder that so great a king wished to take to wife a simple foreign woman, whom he thought to be that man's sister. To which it can be said that the beauty and modesty of the woman drew him to this; and also the uprightness and wisdom of Abram, whom he believed to be her brother.

paras.t: Præterea, circa illud: Flagellavit Dominus Pharaonem propter uxorem Abræ, recitat Lyra, quod in Hebræo habetur, Propter verbum Sarai uxoris Abræ; quia ut dicunt Hebræi, Sarai habuit angelum sanctum corporis sui custodem. Unde Sarai dicente ad angelum, ut percuteret Pharaonem, percussit eum. Sic sancta Cæcilia dixit ad sponsum suum: Habeo angelum corporis mei custodem. Et simile legitur de beata Agnete.
paras.en: Moreover, on the words, [[12:17|the Lord scourged Pharao|Flagellavit Dominus Pharaonem]] [[12:17|for Sarai, Abram's wife|propter uxorem Abræ]], Lyra relates that in the Hebrew it reads, For the word of Sarai, Abram's wife; because, as the Hebrews say, Sarai had a holy angel as the guardian of her body. Hence, when Sarai told the angel to strike Pharao, he struck him. So Saint Cecilia said to her bridegroom: I have an angel as the guardian of my body. And the like is read of blessed Agnes.

paras.t: Nunc ergo ecce conjux tua, accipe eam, et vade. Præcepitque Pharao super Abram viris, id est, ministris suis præcepit de Abram, ut eum et domesticos ejus cum securitate ex Ægypto deducerent; ideo subditur: Et deduxerunt eum et uxorem ejus, et omnia quæ habebat, puta familiam, pecora, et cetera quæ habebat.
paras.en: [[12:19|Now therefore there is thy wife, take her, and go thy way|Nunc ergo ecce conjux tua, accipe eam, et vade]]. [[12:20|And Pharao gave his men orders concerning Abram|Præcepitque Pharao super Abram viris]], that is, he gave orders to his ministers concerning Abram, that they should lead him and his household out of Egypt in safety; therefore it is added: [[12:20|and they led him away and his wife, and all that he had|Et deduxerunt eum et uxorem ejus, et omnia quæ habebat]], that is, his household, his cattle, and the other things that he had.

12.title: Expositio spiritualis ejusdem capituli duodecimi
12.title_en: Spiritual exposition of the same twelfth chapter

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Abram: Egredere de terra tua, et de cognatione tua, et de domo patris tui, et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi. Abram nomine et virtute Christum præfiguravit. Abram namque per duas syllabas, interpretatur pater excelsus, Abraham vero, pater multarum gentium. Porro Christus, in quantum Deus, est pater excelsus creatione, gubernatione, justificatione; imo sic tota superadoranda, supersubstantialisque Trinitas est unus pater excelsus, sicut et unus creator, unus gubernator, unus justificator, prædestinator et glorificator. Sic quoque Christus est multarum gentium pater.
paras.en: [[12:1|And the Lord said to Abram: Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and out of thy father's house, and come into the land which I shall shew thee|Dixit autem Dominus ad Abram: Egredere de terra tua, et de cognatione tua, et de domo patris tui, et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi]]. Abram prefigured Christ in name and in virtue. For Abram, in two syllables, is interpreted *high father*, but Abraham *father of many nations*. Now Christ, inasmuch as he is God, is a high father by creation, governance and justification; indeed in this way the whole Trinity, to be adored above all and supersubstantial, is one high father, just as it is also one creator, one governor, one justifier, predestinator and glorifier. So too Christ is the father of many nations.

paras.t: Itaque Christo, prout est Verbum æternum, dixit Pater non præcipiendo tanquam minori, sed volendo et quasi practice intelligendo, seu per generationem æternam dando et communicando ei totam sapientiam suam, sicut et deitatem atque essentiam: Egredere de terra tua, id est, per Incarnationis mysterium de cœlo in terram descende, hominibusque appare, quemadmodum scriptum est: A summo cœlo egressio ejus. Unde et Christus: Exivi, inquit, a Patre, et veni in mundum. Cœlum quippe est terra vivorum, et patria Beatorum. Et de cognatione tua, id est multitudine supernorum spirituum, qui (in quantum intellectualis simplicisque naturæ sunt, et Deo beatifice perfruuntur) quamdam cum Verbo æterno, a quo conditi sunt, cognationem sortiri videntur. A quibus quasi egressus est, inter homines conversando, non illis divinam præsentiam subtrahendo, sicut nec locum mutando egressus est. Et de domo patris tui, de qua ait: In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt. Et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi, hoc est in terram mortalium, et in Judæam seu Synagogam. Descendit enim in inferiores partes terræ, secundum Apostolum: quam terram Pater Christo secundum naturam divinam monstravit, non de novo aut temporaliter ei aliquid ostendendo seu instruendo, sicut prætactum est, per divinam generationem, totam suam increatam sapientiam ei communicando. Hinc apud Joannem locutus est: Pater diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit.
paras.en: Accordingly the Father said to Christ, as he is the eternal Word, not by commanding him as one lesser, but by willing and, as it were, by practical understanding [that is, a knowing that brings about what it knows], or by giving and communicating to him through the eternal generation all his wisdom, as also his Godhead and essence: [[12:1|Go forth out of thy country|Egredere de terra tua]], that is, through the mystery of the Incarnation come down from heaven to earth and appear to men, as it is written: [[Ps 18:7|His going out is from the end of heaven|A summo cœlo egressio ejus]]. Whence Christ too: [[John 16:28|I came forth|Exivi]], he says, [[John 16:28|from the Father and am come into the world|a Patre, et veni in mundum]]. For heaven is the land of the living and the fatherland of the Blessed. [[12:1|and from thy kindred|Et de cognatione tua]], that is, from the multitude of the heavenly spirits, who (inasmuch as they are of an intellectual and simple nature, and enjoy God in beatitude) seem to have a certain kinship with the eternal Word, by whom they were made. From them he as it were went forth by living among men, not by withdrawing his divine presence from them, just as he did not go forth by changing place either. [[12:1|and out of thy father's house|Et de domo patris tui]], of which he says: [[John 14:2|In my Father's house there are many mansions|In domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt]]. [[12:1|and come into the land which I shall shew thee|Et veni in terram quam monstravero tibi]], that is, into the land of mortals, and into Judea or the Synagogue. For he [[Eph 4:9|descended first into the lower parts of the earth|Descendit enim in inferiores partes terræ]], according to the Apostle: which land the Father shewed to Christ according to his divine nature, not by shewing or teaching him anything anew or in time, but, as was touched on above, by communicating to him through the divine generation all his uncreated wisdom. Hence he said in John: [[John 5:20|the Father loveth the Son and sheweth him all things which himself doth|Pater diligit Filium, et omnia demonstrat ei quæ ipse facit]].

paras.t: Præterea, Christus secundum naturam assumptam, est pater excelsus, et multarum gentium, in quantum summus pontifex et prælatus ac legislator Ecclesiæ. Cum ergo Pater præcepit, ut egrederetur de terra sua, id est, Apostolos faceret ire ad gentium conversionem, relicta Judæa, Synagoga ac templo, in quibus Deus ante per gratiam habitavit. Apostoli namque Christum spiritualiter ad gentes undique portaverunt. Sicque venit ad terram gentilitatis, imo ad corda gentium electarum, et hoc Christus homo, Deo Patre jubente, significavit Apostolis ante eorum divisionem. Unde Paulus Barnabasque dixerunt Judæis: Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei, sed quoniam repulistis illud, ecce convertimur ad gentes. Sic enim præcepit nobis Dominus. Hinc Pater per Isaiam locutus est Christo: Posui te in lucem gentium, ut sis salus mea usque ad ultimum terræ.
paras.en: Moreover Christ, according to the nature he assumed, is a high father, and the father of many nations, inasmuch as he is the high priest, prelate and lawgiver of the Church. So the Father commanded him to go forth out of his country, that is, to make the Apostles go to the conversion of the Gentiles, leaving Judea, the Synagogue and the temple, in which God had dwelt before by grace. For the Apostles carried Christ spiritually to the Gentiles on every side. And so he came to the land of the heathen, nay rather to the hearts of the chosen Gentiles; and this Christ as man, at the bidding of God the Father, made known to the Apostles before they were dispersed. Whence Paul and Barnabas said to the Jews: [[Acts 13:46|To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God: but because you reject it|Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei, sed quoniam repulistis illud]], [[Acts 13:46|behold we turn to the Gentiles|ecce convertimur ad gentes]]. [[Acts 13:47|For so the Lord hath commanded us|Sic enim præcepit nobis Dominus]]. Hence the Father spoke to Christ through Isaias: [[Is 49:6|I have given thee to be the light of the Gentiles, that thou mayst be my salvation even to the farthest part of the earth|Posui te in lucem gentium, ut sis salus mea usque ad ultimum terræ]] [Denis's *Posui te* is the wording of Acts 13:47, where the Apostles quote this verse].

paras.t: Faciamque te in gentem magnam, etc. Istud totum incomparabiliter plenius in Christo, quam in Abraham est completum. Itaque Christum fecit Deus Pater seu Trinitas summa, in gentem magnam, convertendo ad ipsum innumerabiles populos nationum ubique terrarum, qui in Christo sunt regenerati, et filii ejus effecti. Et benedicam tibi. Humanitati Christi Deus Pater plenissime benedixit, totam ipsius capacitatem implendo supernaturalibus donis gratiæ et gloriæ, omnique sapientia ac virtute, quemadmodum scriptum est: Benedixit te Deus in æternum. Itemque: Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, etc. Et magnificabo nomen tuum. Deus etenim exaltavit Christum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine ejus omne genu flectatur, cœlestium, terrestrium, et infernorum. Benedixit quoque benedicentibus Christum, et maledicentibus ei, puta Judæis, hæreticis, ceterisque incredulis ac blasphemis, maledixit.
paras.en: [[12:2|And I will make of thee a great nation|Faciamque te in gentem magnam]], etc. All this was fulfilled incomparably more fully in Christ than in Abraham. For God the Father, or the most high Trinity, made Christ into a great nation by turning to him countless peoples of the nations throughout the world, who have been born again in Christ and made his children. [[12:2|and I will bless thee|Et benedicam tibi]]. God the Father blessed the humanity of Christ most fully, filling its whole capacity with the supernatural gifts of grace and glory, and with all wisdom and virtue, as it is written: [[Ps 44:3|God blessed thee for ever|Benedixit te Deus in æternum]]. And again: [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus]], etc. [[12:2|and magnify thy name|Et magnificabo nomen tuum]]. For [[Phil 2:9|God also hath exalted him and hath given him a name which is above all names|Deus etenim exaltavit Christum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen]], [[Phil 2:10|That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth|ut in nomine ejus omne genu flectatur, cœlestium, terrestrium, et infernorum]]. He also blessed them that bless Christ, and cursed them that curse him, such as the Jews, heretics, and the other unbelievers and blasphemers.

paras.t: Egressus est itaque Abram, etc., id est, Christus per Apostolorum prædicationem ad gentes transivit. Et uxorem suam, id est primitivam Ecclesiam, ac Lot, eos videlicet qui secundum carnem ei propinqui erant, fecit secum ad gentes procedere, et per prædicatores suos terram eorum perambulavit, in qua tunc morabatur Chananæus, id est incredulus populus, Chanæorum antiquorum vitiis plenus. Illam igitur terram dedit Deus semini Christi, utpote populo christiano, de quo ab Isaia est prædictum: Si posuerit animam suam pro peccato, videbit semen longævum. Et alibi: Omnes qui viderint eos, cognoscent illos, quia isti sunt semen cui benedixit Dominus.
paras.en: [[12:4|So Abram went out|Egressus est itaque Abram]], etc., that is, Christ passed over to the Gentiles through the preaching of the Apostles. And [[12:5|his wife|uxorem suam]], that is, the primitive Church, and [[12:5|Lot|Lot]], namely those who were his kin according to the flesh, he made to go forth with him to the Gentiles; and through his preachers he passed through their land, in which [[12:6|the Chanaanite|Chananæus]] then dwelt, that is, the unbelieving people, full of the vices of the ancient Chanaanites. That land, then, God gave to the seed of Christ, that is, to the Christian people, of whom it was foretold by Isaias: [[Is 53:10|if he shall lay down his life for sin, he shall see a longlived seed|Si posuerit animam suam pro peccato, videbit semen longævum]]. And elsewhere: [[Is 61:9|all that shall see them, shall know them, that these are the seed which the Lord hath blessed|Omnes qui viderint eos, cognoscent illos, quia isti sunt semen cui benedixit Dominus]].

paras.t: Qui ædificavit ibi altare Domino. Christus enim ubique ædificari fecit ecclesias, atque in eis altaria, quæ et spiritualiter ædificavit per fidem et caritatem in corde fidelium, in quibus et per quos offert sacrificium laudis Patri indesinenter, imo et se ipsum facit offerri. Et invocavit nomen ejus, quoniam interpellat pro nobis, et pro nostra offertur salute. Unde per Malachiam Dominus contestatur: In omni loco offertur nomini meo oblatio munda.
paras.en: [[12:7|And he built there an altar to the Lord|Qui ædificavit ibi altare Domino]]. For Christ caused churches to be built everywhere, and altars in them; and these he also built spiritually, through faith and charity, in the hearts of the faithful, in whom and through whom he offers the sacrifice of praise to the Father unceasingly; nay, he causes himself also to be offered. [[12:8|and called upon his name|Et invocavit nomen ejus]], since he intercedes for us and is offered for our salvation. Whence the Lord declares by Malachias: [[Mal 1:11|in every place|In omni loco]] [[Mal 1:11|there is offered to my name a clean oblation|offertur nomini meo oblatio munda]].

paras.t: Et inde transgrediens ad montem qui est contra orientem Bethel, hoc est, ad Romanum imperium et ad excellentiam philosophorum, qui erant per elationem erecti contra veræ et salutaris sapientiæ ortum ac lucem, quæ sapientia est in Bethel, id est in domo Dei. Tetendit ibi tabernaculum suum, hoc est, Ecclesiam dilatavit ibidem, subjiciendo illos fidei christianæ. Unde ad Corinthios fatetur Apostolus: Arma militiæ nostræ non carnalia sunt, sed potentia Deo ad destructionem munitionum, consilia destruentes, et omnem altitudinem extollentem se adversus scientiam Dei, et in captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi. Ab occidente habens Bethel, et ab oriente Hai. Per occidentem intelligi potest adversitatum eventus, seu obscura Dei cognitio per speculum in ænigmate; per orientem vero, prosperitatis et felicitatis præsentia, caritatisque fervor, et clara cognitio deitatis per speciem. Bethel vero interpretatur domus Dei, per quam Ecclesia militans designatur; Hai vero, oculus seu fons, per quod triumphans insinuatur Ecclesia. Christus itaque habet Bethel, id est Ecclesiam militantem ab occidente, hoc est, in his qui adversitatibus exercentur, et per fidem ambulantes Deum ænigmatice vident; Hai autem, id est Ecclesiam triumphantem in suis electis, qui plena felicitate et omni prosperitate replentur. Inter hos Christus est medius, unus (videlicet militantis) Ecclesiæ membra triumphanti conjungens.
paras.en: [[12:8|And passing on from thence to a mountain, that was on the east side of Bethel|Et inde transgrediens ad montem qui est contra orientem Bethel]], that is, to the Roman empire and to the eminence of the philosophers, who were raised up by pride against the rising and the light of the true and saving wisdom [Denis takes *contra orientem*, "on the east side", in the sense "against the rising"], which wisdom is in Bethel, that is, in the house of God. [[12:8|he there pitched his tent|Tetendit ibi tabernaculum suum]], that is, he enlarged the Church there, subjecting them to the Christian faith. Whence the Apostle avows to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 10:4|the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty to God, unto the pulling down of fortifications, destroying counsels|Arma militiæ nostræ non carnalia sunt, sed potentia Deo ad destructionem munitionum, consilia destruentes]], [[2 Cor 10:5|And every height that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God: and bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ|et omnem altitudinem extollentem se adversus scientiam Dei, et in captivitatem redigentes omnem intellectum in obsequium Christi]]. [[12:8|having Bethel on the west, and Hai on the east|Ab occidente habens Bethel, et ab oriente Hai]]. By the west may be understood the coming of adversities, or the dim knowledge of God through a glass in a dark manner; by the east, the presence of prosperity and happiness, the fervour of charity, and the clear knowledge of the Godhead by sight. Now Bethel is interpreted *house of God*, by which the Church militant is signified; but Hai *eye* or *fountain*, by which the Church triumphant is suggested. Christ therefore has Bethel, that is, the Church militant, on the west, that is, in those who are exercised by adversities and, walking by faith, see God darkly; but Hai, that is, the Church triumphant, in his elect, who are filled with full happiness and all prosperity. Between these Christ stands in the middle, joining the members of the one Church (namely the militant) to the triumphant.

paras.t: Facta est autem fames in terra, id est omnium spiritualium alimentorum defectus, Synagoga quærente terrena, præsertim quando Judæi prædicationem Apostolorum abjecerunt animo obstinato. Descenditque Abram in Ægyptum, id est, Christus per Apostolos suos ingressus est gentilitatem: ut peregrinaretur ibi, id est, tanquam hospes et peregrinus habitaret in cordibus credulorum, de quo Jeremias prædixit: Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum?
paras.en: [[12:10|there came a famine in the country|Facta est autem fames in terra]], that is, a want of all spiritual nourishment, the Synagogue seeking earthly things, especially when the Jews rejected the preaching of the Apostles with obstinate mind. [[12:10|and Abram went down into Egypt|Descenditque Abram in Ægyptum]], that is, Christ entered the heathen world through his Apostles: [[12:10|to sojourn there|ut peregrinaretur ibi]], that is, that he might dwell as a guest and pilgrim in the hearts of believers; of which Jeremias foretold: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?|Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum?]]

paras.t: Dixitque uxori suæ, id est primitivæ Ecclesiæ, quam pro magna et præcipua parte misit ad gentes convertendas: Novi quod pulchra sis mulier, id est congregatio et sponsa mea omni virtute et gratia perornata; et quod quum viderint te Ægyptii, dicturi sunt, Uxor illius est, et interficient me, et te reservabunt. Ægyptii isti sunt dæmones, qui visa Christi Ecclesia, contulerunt dicentes: Ecce ista est Christi sponsa; et nisi sunt eam a Christo avertere, ac spiritualiter constuprare ac perdere, imo et Christum in credentium cordibus enecare, ita ut ibi amplius non esset per gratiam, nec regnaret per fidem. Dic ergo, obsecro te, quod soror mea sis, id est, constanter me confitere, et me veraciter incarnatum testare, ita quod per assumptam humanitatem tuus sim frater; ut bene sit mihi propter te, id est, regnem in populo christiano usque ad finem mundi, et vivam in credentium mente per fidem.
paras.en: [[12:11|he said to Sarai his wife|Dixitque uxori suæ]], that is, to the primitive Church, the great and chief part of which he sent to convert the Gentiles: [[12:11|I know that thou art a beautiful woman|Novi quod pulchra sis mulier]], that is, a congregation and my bride, adorned with every virtue and grace; [[12:12|And that when the Egyptians shall see thee, they will say: She is his wife: and they will kill me, and keep thee|et quod quum viderint te Ægyptii, dicturi sunt, Uxor illius est, et interficient me, et te reservabunt]]. These Egyptians are the demons, who, on seeing Christ's Church, conferred together, saying: Behold, this is the bride of Christ; and they strove to turn her away from Christ, and to defile and destroy her spiritually, nay, and to kill Christ in the hearts of believers, so that he should no longer be there by grace, nor reign by faith. [[12:13|Say, therefore, I pray thee, that thou art my sister|Dic ergo, obsecro te, quod soror mea sis]], that is, confess me steadfastly and bear witness that I am truly incarnate, so that through the humanity I assumed I am thy brother; [[12:13|that I may be well used for thee|ut bene sit mihi propter te]] [literally "that it may be well with me for thee"], that is, that I may reign in the Christian people until the end of the world, and live in the mind of believers by faith.

paras.t: Quumque ingressus esset Abram Ægyptum, id est, Christus in gentilitate conversa regnaret, viderunt Ægyptii, utpote dæmones, mulierem, id est Ecclesiam, quod pulchra esset nimis, et nuntiaverunt Pharaoni, hoc est principi tenebrarum; et laudaverunt illam apud illum, virtutes, signa et opera Ecclesiæ recitando principi suo; et sublata est mulier in domum Pharaonis: id est, Ecclesia electorum in medio hominum iniquorum qui sunt domus diaboli, posita est in hoc mundo, cui et Christus dixit: Ecce ego mitto vos sicut oves in medio luporum. Abram vero bene usi sunt propter illam: id est, Christi misericordiam magnificam esse dixerunt et infinitam, ut per hoc facilius allicerent ad peccandum fideles: fueruntque ei oves et boves, asini et asinæ et cameli, servi et famulæ: hoc est, non solum innocentes et simplices, sed et grossi, rudes, duri et male laboriosi, corporaliterque robusti, ad Christum conversi sunt, quorum et plurimi de misericordia Dei temerarie præsumentes, carnales et bestiales effecti sunt.
paras.en: [[12:14|And when Abram was come into Egypt|Quumque ingressus esset Abram Ægyptum]], that is, when Christ reigned among the converted heathen, [[12:14|the Egyptians saw|viderunt Ægyptii]], namely the demons, [[12:14|the woman|mulierem]], that is, the Church, [[12:14|that she was very beautiful|quod pulchra esset nimis]], and [[12:15|told Pharao|nuntiaverunt Pharaoni]], that is, the prince of darkness; [[12:15|and praised her before him|et laudaverunt illam apud illum]], reciting the virtues, signs and works of the Church to their prince; [[12:15|and the woman was taken into the house of Pharao|et sublata est mulier in domum Pharaonis]]: that is, the Church of the elect has been set in this world in the midst of wicked men, who are the house of the devil; to which Christ also said: [[Matt 10:16|Behold I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves|Ecce ego mitto vos sicut oves in medio luporum]]. [[12:16|And they used Abram well for her sake|Abram vero bene usi sunt propter illam]]: that is, they said that Christ's mercy is magnificent and infinite, so as by this to entice the faithful the more easily to sin. [[12:16|And he had sheep and oxen and he asses, and men servants, and maid servants, and she asses, and camels|fueruntque ei oves et boves, asini et asinæ et cameli, servi et famulæ]]: that is, not only the innocent and simple, but also the gross, the rude, the hard and the drudging, and the bodily strong, were converted to Christ; and very many of these, presuming rashly on the mercy of God, became carnal and beastly.

paras.t: Flagellavit autem Dominus Pharaonem et domum ejus plagis maximis, propter uxorem Abram. Dominus enim per angelos sanctos et homines virtuosos, graviter ac multipliciter tribulat dæmones, eorumque principem, refrenando eos ac superando et deridendo, eo quod Christi Ecclesiam sic tentare non cessent; et tandem eorum miseria multum augebitur, dum juxta Isaiæ oraculum congregabuntur congregatione unius fasciis, et claudentur in carcere. Vocavitque Pharao Abram, etc. Hoc fit, quando diabolus videt et confitetur se victum a membris Christi, et dimittit victores in pace, ut serviant Christo.
paras.en: [[12:17|But the Lord scourged Pharao and his house with most grievous stripes for Sarai, Abram's wife|Flagellavit autem Dominus Pharaonem et domum ejus plagis maximis, propter uxorem Abram]].
