Not that any inordinate fear could be in Christ, who according to the nature he assumed was perfectly confirmed in good; but that he should not dwell long in natural fear, which at times he took on of his own will, and should not take it on more often than was fitting. Hence the Church sings in the person of Christ: [[Lam 3:57|in the day, when I called upon thee|In die qua invocavi te]], O Lord, [[Lam 3:57|thou saidst: Fear not|dixisti, Ne timeas]] [an antiphon of the Church's office, taken from Lamentations]. This word, [[15:1|Fear not|Noli timere]], can also be expounded not as urging him not to be afraid, but as rejoicing with him in his perfection, by which he feared nothing inordinately; as we sing: [[Ps 148:2|Praise ye him, all his angels|Laudate eum omnes angeli ejus]] [not to urge the angels, but rejoicing with them in their praise].

paras.t: Ego protector tuus sum. Nam Deus Pater, seu Verbum æternum, fuit in omnibus humanitatis Christi defensor ab omni malo culpæ, et item a malis pœnalibus, ita quod animæ Christi nullam læsionem nocivam inducere potuerunt, propter quod apud Isaiam Christus testatur: In umbra manus suæ protexit me.
paras.en: [[15:1|I am thy protector|Ego protector tuus sum]]. For God the Father, or the eternal Word, was in all things the defender of Christ's humanity from every evil of fault, and likewise from the evils of punishment, in such wise that these could inflict no harmful injury on the soul of Christ; wherefore in Isaias Christ testifies: [[Is 49:2|in the shadow of his hand he hath protected me|In umbra manus suæ protexit me]].

paras.t: Et merces tua magna nimis. Beatificam deitatis fruitionem, quæ est essentiale præmium omnium Beatorum, habuit anima Christi a suæ creationis et incarnationis Verbi exordio, nec eam promeruit. Postmodum vero promeruit sibi præmium accidentale, videlicet sui corporis glorificationem et judiciariam potestatem, suique nominis honorificentissimam dilatationem per totum orbem terrarum. Et de hoc præmio quod Christus sua humiliatione, patientia, labore, et passione sibi ipsi promeruit, potest exponi quod dictum est, Merces tua magna nimis. Vel, merces Christi vocatur magnitudo gratiæ, plenitudoque gloriæ, quam meruit suis electis, quibus tota sua conversatio et passio in hoc mundo meritoria fuit, in quantum ex ardentissima caritate pro eorum salute omnia gessit ac pertulit.
paras.en: [[15:1|and thy reward exceeding great|Et merces tua magna nimis]]. The beatific enjoyment of the Godhead, which is the essential reward of all the Blessed, the soul of Christ had from the beginning of its creation and of the incarnation of the Word, and did not merit it. But afterwards he merited for himself an accidental reward [that is, a joy added to the essential reward, the vision of God], namely the glorification of his body, the power of judging, and the most honourable spreading of his name through the whole world. And of this reward, which Christ merited for himself by his humiliation, patience, labour and passion, can be expounded what is said: [[15:1|thy reward exceeding great|Merces tua magna nimis]]. Or else the reward of Christ is the name for the greatness of grace and fullness of glory which he merited for his elect, for whom his whole life and passion in this world were meritorious, inasmuch as he did and bore all things for their salvation out of most ardent charity.

paras.t: Dixitque Abram, id est Christus: Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi pro mercede laborum meorum ? Ego vadam absque liberis, hoc est Judæis, propter quos veni in mundum, et quibus specialiter missus sum: eos non converti, non fructificavi in eis pro maxima parte eorum, in tantum quod tempore passionis pene omnes corruerunt a fide; et in cruce moriens, non reliqui semen ex eis, nisi perpaucum. Hinc in Isaia loquitur Christus affectu dolentis de Judæorum perditione: Ego dixi, In vacuum laboravi, sine causa et vane fortitudinem meam consumpsi. Et filius procuratoris mei iste Damascus. Procurator Christi, potest intelligi Moyses, qui tanquam Dei dispensator præfuit Synagogæ, et multos convertit: sicque filius ejus fuit populus sibi subjectus atque obediens, præsertim qui terram promissionis intravit.
paras.en: [[15:2|And Abram said|Dixitque Abram]], that is, Christ: [[15:2|Lord God, what wilt thou give me|Domine Deus, quid dabis mihi]] as the wages of my labours? [[15:2|I shall go without children|Ego vadam absque liberis]], that is, without the Jews, for whose sake I came into the world[[John 5:43||]], and to whom I was especially sent[[Matt 15:24||]]: I have not converted them, I have not borne fruit in them for the greatest part of them, so much so that at the time of the passion almost all fell away from the faith; and dying on the cross I left no seed of them, save very little. Hence in Isaias Christ speaks with the feeling of one grieving over the perdition of the Jews: [[Is 49:4|I said: I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength without cause and in vain|Ego dixi, In vacuum laboravi, sine causa et vane fortitudinem meam consumpsi]]. [[15:2|and the son of the steward of my house is this Damascus|Et filius procuratoris mei iste Damascus]] [Denis reads *procuratoris mei*, ‘of my steward’, without ‘house’]. The steward of Christ can be understood as Moses, who as God's dispenser was over the Synagogue and converted many; and so his son was the people subject and obedient to him, especially those who entered the land of promise.

paras.t: Et ecce vernaculus meus erit heres meus. Hereditas Christi fuit populus Synagogæ, sicut per Isaiam fatetur, Hereditas mea Israel; vernaculus vero Christi, fuit cœtus sacerdotum et ceterorum, qui tempore Christi præfuit Synagogæ. Ille etenim cœtus, natus fuit in lege divini obsequii, atque in domo seu populo Dei. Ille itaque impiissimus cœtus, voluit esse heres ac dominus Synagogæ seu vineæ Christi, ipso Christo expulso. Nam eo viso, locuti sunt: Hic est heres, venite, occidamus eum, et nostra erit hereditas, prout Christus in evangelica docet parabola: Homo, inquiens, paterfamilias plantavit vineam, et locavit eam agricolis, etc.
paras.en: [[15:3|and lo my servant born in my house, shall be my heir|Et ecce vernaculus meus erit heres meus]]. The inheritance of Christ was the people of the Synagogue, as he declares through Isaias: [[Is 19:25|Israel is my inheritance|Hereditas mea Israel]]; but the servant born in Christ's house was the body of the priests and of the others who at the time of Christ were over the Synagogue. For that body was born under the law of divine service, and in the house, that is, the people, of God. And so that most impious body wished to be heir and lord of the Synagogue, or of the vineyard of Christ, with Christ himself cast out. For when they saw him they said: [[Matt 21:38|This is the heir: come, let us kill him|Hic est heres, venite, occidamus eum]], [[Matt 21:38|and we shall have his inheritance|et nostra erit hereditas]] [Denis's *et nostra erit hereditas* is the wording of Mark 12:7], as Christ teaches in the Gospel parable: [[Matt 21:33|a man|Homo]], he says, [[Matt 21:33|an householder, who planted a vineyard|paterfamilias plantavit vineam]] [[Matt 21:33|and let it out to husbandmen|et locavit eam agricolis]], etc.

paras.t: Statimque sermo Domini factus est ad eum, dicens : Non erit hic hæres tuus, id est, impius cœtus iste non diu præsidebit Synagogæ, imo cito post tuam passionem penitus vastabitur, quemadmodum factum est per Romanos, et a Daniele prædictum est : Civitatem et sanctuarium dissipabit populus cum duce venturo, et usque in finem perseverabit desolatio ; sed qui egredietur de utero tuo, ipsum habebis hæredem, id est, Judæos electos, quos proprii cordis tui doctrina docebis et convertes, habebis filios atque discipulos, et per eos convertes innumerabiles alios.
paras.en: [[15:4|And immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying|Statimque sermo Domini factus est ad eum, dicens]]: [[15:4|He shall not be thy heir|Non erit hic hæres tuus]], that is, this impious body will not long preside over the Synagogue, but soon after thy passion will be utterly laid waste, as was done by the Romans, and as was foretold by Daniel: [[Dan 9:26|a people, with their leader, that shall come, shall destroy the city, and the sanctuary|Civitatem et sanctuarium dissipabit populus cum duce venturo]], [[Dan 9:27|and the desolation shall continue even to the consummation, and to the end|et usque in finem perseverabit desolatio]] [these last words are from Dan 9:27, where Denis has only *usque in finem*, ‘even to the end’]; [[15:4|but he that shall come out of thy bowels, him shalt thou have for thy heir|sed qui egredietur de utero tuo, ipsum habebis hæredem]], that is, the chosen Jews, whom thou shalt teach and convert by the doctrine of thine own heart, thou shalt have as sons and disciples, and through them thou shalt convert countless others.

paras.t: Eduxitque eum foras, id est, Deus eduxit Christum hominem a præfata consideratione, ad considerationem conversionis gentium universarum ; et ait illi : Suspice cælum, et numera stellas, si potes, id est, quia potes. Nam anima Christi cuncta creata distincte cognovit. Et dixit ei : Sic erit semen tuum, id est, tam innumerabilis erit populus qui a te Christo vocabitur christianus, et tanquam stellæ splendidus erit per gratiam in Ecclesia militante, et sicut sol fulgebit in Ecclesia triumphante. Hinc in Isaia Pater loquitur Christo : Parum est ut sis mihi servus ad suscitandas tribus Jacob, et fæces Israel convertendas. Dedi te in lucem gentium, ut sis salus mea usque ad extremum terræ.
paras.en: [[15:5|And he brought him forth abroad|Eduxitque eum foras]], that is, God brought Christ the man out of the consideration just spoken of to the consideration of the conversion of all the nations; [[15:5|and said to him: Look up to heaven and number the stars if thou canst|et ait illi : Suspice cælum, et numera stellas, si potes]], that is, since thou canst [Denis takes *si potes*, ‘if thou canst’, as *quia potes*]. For the soul of Christ knew all created things distinctly. [[15:5|And he said to him: So shall thy seed be|Et dixit ei : Sic erit semen tuum]], that is, so countless will be the people that will be called Christian after thee, Christ; and like the stars it will be bright by grace in the Church militant, and as the sun it will shine in the Church triumphant. Hence in Isaias the Father speaks to Christ: [[Is 49:6|It is a small thing that thou shouldst be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to convert the dregs of Israel|Parum est ut sis mihi servus ad suscitandas tribus Jacob, et fæces Israel convertendas]]. [[Is 49:6|I have given thee to be the light of the Gentiles, that thou mayst be my salvation even to the farthest part of the earth|Dedi te in lucem gentium, ut sis salus mea usque ad extremum terræ]].

paras.t: Credidit Abram Deo, et reputatum est illi ad justitiam, id est, Christus cognovit promissionem hanc veram esse, non tamen per fidem, quæ est theologica virtus, quæ non fuit in eo, quoniam fuit comprehensor perfectus secundum supremam suæ animæ portionem.
paras.en: [[15:6|Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice|Credidit Abram Deo, et reputatum est illi ad justitiam]], that is, Christ knew this promise to be true, yet not by faith, which is a theological virtue and was not in him, since in the highest part of his soul he was a perfect comprehensor [that is, one who already sees God, as the Blessed do, not a wayfarer who walks by faith].

paras.t: Dixitque ad eum : Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum, id est de passione et persecutionibus infidelium Judæorum, resuscitando te tertia die ad impassibilem et beatissimam vitam : ut darem tibi terram, et possideres eam, id est, totum mundum legi ac ditioni tuæ subjicerem, juxta illud : Reminiscentur et convertentur ad Dominum universi fines terræ. Itemque : Et dominabitur a mari usque ad mare, et a flumine usque ad terminos orbis terræ.
paras.en: [[15:7|And he said to him: I am the Lord who brought thee out from Ur of the Chaldees|Dixitque ad eum : Ego Dominus qui eduxi te de Ur Chaldæorum]], that is, out of the passion and the persecutions of the unbelieving Jews, by raising thee up on the third day to a life impassible and most blessed: [[15:7|to give thee this land, and that thou mightest possess it|ut darem tibi terram, et possideres eam]], that is, that I might subject the whole world to thy law and dominion, according to that: [[Ps 21:28|All the ends of the earth shall remember, and shall be converted to the Lord|Reminiscentur et convertentur ad Dominum universi fines terræ]]. And again: [[Ps 71:8|And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth|Et dominabitur a mari usque ad mare, et a flumine usque ad terminos orbis terræ]].

paras.t: At ille ait : Domine Deus, unde scire possum, etc., id est, experimentalem modum ac processum hujus rei mihi ostende. Hoc Christus non ait ex ignorantia aut diffidentia, sed ex superabundantia quadam, qua id quod scitur, libenter prospicitur.
paras.en: [[15:8|But he said: Lord God, whereby may I know|At ille ait : Domine Deus, unde scire possum]], etc., that is, show me by experience the manner and course of this thing. Christ did not say this out of ignorance or distrust, but out of a certain superabundance, by which what is known is gladly looked upon.

paras.t: Respondens Dominus : Sume, inquit, mihi vaccam triennem, et capram trimam, et arietem annorum trium, id est, lascivum, petulantem, ac contumacem populum Judæorum applica tibi, prædicando eisdem ; turturem quoque et columbam, hoc est, quosdam etiam virtuosos, pudicos et simplices ex plebe illa tibi assume. Hoc Christus fecit omnibus talibus evangelizando, divisitque vitiosos illos, quoniam quosdam ex eis pie convertit, et alios juste reliquit, propter quod dixit : Nunc judicium est mundi. Ceteros non divisit, sed recollegit in unum, et fecit ex eis primitivam Ecclesiam.
paras.en: [[15:9|And the Lord answered|Respondens Dominus]]: [[15:9|Take|Sume]], he says, [[15:9|me a cow of three years old, and a she-goat of three years. and a ram of three years|mihi vaccam triennem, et capram trimam, et arietem annorum trium]], that is, take to thyself the wanton, petulant and stubborn people of the Jews, by preaching to them; [[15:9|a turtle also, and a pigeon|turturem quoque et columbam]], that is, take to thyself also some of that people who are virtuous, chaste and simple. This Christ did by preaching the Gospel to all such; and he divided those vicious ones, since some of them he mercifully converted and others he justly left, for which reason he said: [[John 12:31|Now is the judgment of the world|Nunc judicium est mundi]]. The others he did not divide, but gathered them into one, and made of them the primitive Church.

paras.t: Descenderuntque volucres, id est dæmones, super cadavera, quoniam passione instante Christus locutus est Petro : Simon, ecce Satan expetivit vos ut cribraret sicut triticum, ego autem oravi pro te. Christus quoque eos abegit, sicut dixit ad Patrem : Pater, quos dedisti mihi, non perdidi ex eis quemquam.
paras.en: [[15:11|And the fowls came down|Descenderuntque volucres]], that is, the demons, [[15:11|upon the carcasses|super cadavera]], for when the passion was at hand Christ said to Peter: Simon, [[Luke 22:31|behold Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat|ecce Satan expetivit vos ut cribraret sicut triticum]], [[Luke 22:32|but I have prayed for thee|ego autem oravi pro te]]. And Christ drove them away, as he said to the Father: Father, [[John 18:9|of them whom thou hast given me, I have not lost any one|quos dedisti mihi, non perdidi ex eis quemquam]] [the margin gives John 17:12, where Christ says this to the Father; Denis's words are those of John 18:9, which recalls it].

paras.t: Quum sol occumberet, pavor irruit super Abram, et horror magnus, etc. Tunc sol quasi occubuit, quando Verbum æternum solitam consolationis internæ redundantiam humanitati Christi, quantum ad partem ejus sensitivam, subtraxit, tempore scilicet passionis, in tantum quod dixit : Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me ? Tunc intensissimus pavor et maximus horror Christum invasit, quando et sudor ejus factus est quasi guttæ sanguinis decurrentis in terram. Cœpit etenim contristari et pavere, dixitque : Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem.
paras.en: [[15:12|And when the sun was setting|Quum sol occumberet]], dread [[15:12|fell upon Abram|irruit super Abram]], [[15:12|and a great and darksome horror|et horror magnus]], etc. Then the sun as it were set, when the eternal Word withdrew from the humanity of Christ, as to its sensitive part, the wonted overflowing of inward consolation, namely at the time of the passion, so much so that he said: [[Ps 21:2|O God my God|Deus meus, Deus meus]], [[Ps 21:2|why hast thou forsaken me?|ut quid dereliquisti me ?]] [Denis's wording is that of Matt 27:46, the words on the cross]. Then the most intense dread and the greatest horror seized upon Christ, when also [[Luke 22:44|his sweat became as drops of blood, trickling down upon the ground|sudor ejus factus est quasi guttæ sanguinis decurrentis in terram]]. For [[Matt 26:37|he began|Cœpit]] [[Matt 26:37|to grow sorrowful|contristari]] and to fear [*pavere*, as in Mark 14:33], and said: [[Matt 26:38|My soul is sorrowful even unto death|Tristis est anima mea usque ad mortem]].

paras.t: Dictumque est ad eum : Scito prænoscens, quod peregrinum futurum sit semen tuum in terra non sua. Tunc enim Deo volente Christus actualiter consideravit omnem adversitatem, tribulationem et passionem, quam universi electi in sæculo isto pro fide ipsius ac sua salute erant passuri : quod utique ab incarnationis exordio scivit ; sed tunc cum vehementissima compassione hoc ipsum intuebatur.
paras.en: [[15:13|And it was said unto him: Know thou beforehand that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own|Dictumque est ad eum : Scito prænoscens, quod peregrinum futurum sit semen tuum in terra non sua]]. For then, by God's will, Christ actually considered all the adversity, tribulation and suffering which all the elect in this world were to suffer for faith in him and for their own salvation: which indeed he knew from the beginning of the incarnation, but then he beheld it with most vehement compassion.

paras.t: Tu autem ibis ad patres tuos in pace, descendendo in limbum patrum, ut eos inde educas, sepultus in senectute bona, non annorum, sed omni maturitate virtutum. Senectus enim venerabilis est, non annorum numero computata, etc. Necdum enim completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum. Amorrhæi isti, sunt reprobi qui affligunt et exercent electos usque ad tempus præfinitum a Domino.
paras.en: [[15:15|And thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace|Tu autem ibis ad patres tuos in pace]], by going down into the limbo of the fathers, to lead them out from there; [[15:15|and be buried in a good old age|sepultus in senectute bona]], not of years, but of every ripeness of the virtues. [[Wis 4:8|For venerable old age is|Senectus enim venerabilis est]] not [[Wis 4:8|counted by the number of years|annorum numero computata]], etc. [[15:16|for as yet the iniquities of the Amorrhites are not at the full|Necdum enim completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum]]. These Amorrhites are the reprobate, who afflict and exercise the elect until the time fixed beforehand by the Lord.

paras.t: Quum ergo occubuisset sol, id est, dum Christus expallescens penderet in cruce, facta est caligo tenebrosa, quia tunc tenebræ factæ sunt super universam terram ab hora sexta usque ad nonam ; et apparuit clibanus fumans, id est, tribulatio summe angustians, invasit eos qui cruci Christi assistebant, et pertinebant ad eum : et lampas ignis, transiens inter divisiones illas, hoc est fervor doloris penetrans corda eorum, quos Christus divisit a reprobis et reposuit sibi.
paras.en: [[15:17|And when the sun was set|Quum ergo occubuisset sol]], that is, while Christ, growing pale, hung upon the cross, [[15:17|there arose a dark mist|facta est caligo tenebrosa]], because then [[Luke 23:44|there was darkness over all the earth|tenebræ factæ sunt super universam terram]] from the sixth hour [[Luke 23:44|until the ninth hour|usque ad nonam]] [Denis's wording is closer to Matt 27:45]; [[15:17|and there appeared a smoking furnace|et apparuit clibanus fumans]], that is, a tribulation of extreme anguish seized upon those who stood by the cross of Christ and belonged to him; [[15:17|and a lamp of fire passing between those divisions|et lampas ignis, transiens inter divisiones illas]], that is, the fervour of sorrow piercing the hearts of those whom Christ divided from the reprobate and set apart for himself.

paras.t: In die illo pepigit Dominus fœdus cum Abram, dicens : Semini tuo dabo terram hanc. Quum enim Christus passione instante factus in agonia prolixius oraret, sanguinemque sudaret, apparuit illi angelus de cœlo confortans eum, id est per modum confortantis se habens, verba confortativa et consolatoria proferendo, commemorando videlicet fructuositatem passionis instantis, et qualiter propter eam Deus Pater totum mundum evangelicæ legi subjiceret, et cunctis propitiaretur hominibus, sicut per Zachariam Pater testatur de Christo : Auferam iniquitatem terræ illius in die una, et potestas ejus a mari usque ad mare, et a fluminibus usque ad fines terræ.
paras.en: [[15:18|That day God made a covenant with Abram, saying: To thy seed will I give this land|In die illo pepigit Dominus fœdus cum Abram, dicens : Semini tuo dabo terram hanc]]. For when Christ, with his passion at hand, being [[Luke 22:43|in an agony|in agonia]], [[Luke 22:43|prayed the longer|prolixius oraret]] and sweated blood, [[Luke 22:43|there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him|apparuit illi angelus de cœlo confortans eum]], that is, bearing himself in the manner of one who strengthens, uttering words of strength and consolation: recalling, namely, the fruitfulness of the passion at hand, and how because of it God the Father would subject the whole world to the law of the Gospel and be propitious to all men; as the Father testifies of Christ through Zacharias: [[Zach 3:9|I will take away the iniquity of that land in one day|Auferam iniquitatem terræ illius in die una]], [[Zach 9:10|and his power shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers even to the end of the earth|et potestas ejus a mari usque ad mare, et a fluminibus usque ad fines terræ]].

16.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli sextidecimi: Igitur Sarai uxor Abram non genuerat liberos
16.title_en: Literal explanation of the sixteenth chapter: “Now Sarai, the wife of Abram, had brought forth no children”

paras.t: Prolificatio Abræ consequenter describitur. Igitur Sarai uxor Abram non genuerat sibi liberos, imo nullam prolem hucusque, quoniam naturali sterilitate impediebatur concipere. Sed habens ancillam Ægyptiam natione, nomine Agar, dixit marito suo: Ecce conclusit me Dominus ne parerem, id est, fecunditatem uteri non contulit mihi. Opera enim naturæ, sunt opera Creatoris. Et dicitur Deus Sarai conclusisse, quia non aperiebatur uterus ejus ad fructuosam seminis susceptionem. Ingredere ad ancillam meam, id est, in conjugem accipe eam, et cognosce: si forte saltem ex illa suscipiam filios, hoc est, quatenus Deo præstante, ipsa ex te concipiat, et proles nata ex ea, sit mea per adoptionem seu jure dominii.
paras.en: Next is described how Abram came to have offspring. [[16:1|Now Sarai, the wife of Abram|Igitur Sarai uxor Abram]] [[16:1|had brought forth no children|non genuerat sibi liberos]], indeed no offspring at all up to this time, since she was kept from conceiving by natural barrenness. [[16:1|But having a handmaid, an Egyptian|Sed habens ancillam Ægyptiam]] by nation, [[16:1|named Agar|nomine Agar]], [[16:2|She said to her husband: Behold, the Lord hath restrained me from bearing|dixit marito suo: Ecce conclusit me Dominus ne parerem]], that is, He has not granted me fruitfulness of the womb. For the works of nature are the works of the Creator; and God is said to have restrained Sarai because her womb was not opened to receive seed fruitfully. [[16:2|go in unto my handmaid|Ingredere ad ancillam meam]], that is, take her as wife and know her: [[16:2|it may be I may have children of her at least|si forte saltem ex illa suscipiam filios]]; that is, so that by God's gift she may conceive by thee, and the child born of her may be mine by adoption, or by right of ownership.

paras.t: Refert Lyra, quod Hebræi dicant hanc Agar fuisse filiam regis Ægypti, ita quod una conjugum Pharaonis considerans sanctitatem Sarai, et qualiter propter eam Deus flagellavit Pharaonem et domum ipsius, tradidit filiam suam Sarai in ancillam, potius cupiens filiam suam servire in domo matronæ tam virtuosæ, quam honorari in domo paterna. Additque Lyra, istud non esse absonum rationi, quum in libro Esther legatur, quod multi gentilium videntes qualiter Deus liberavit Judæos de insidiis Aman, transtulerunt se ad legem et cærimonias Judæorum. Sed Rabbi Paulus dicit istud de Agar esse fictitium, et quod allegatio ista ex libro Esther non probet intentum, quia gentiles illi non subjecerunt se Domino, sed ritui Judæorum. Verumtamen reor probabile, quod Agar ista erat valde proba, notabilisque puella, eo quod Sarai quæ multas habebat ancillas, dedit eam suo marito præ ceteris.
paras.en: Lyra relates that the Hebrews say this Agar was the daughter of the king of Egypt: one of Pharao's wives, seeing the holiness of Sarai, and how God had scourged Pharao and his house on her account, gave her daughter to Sarai as a handmaid, wishing rather that her daughter should serve in the house of so virtuous a lady than be honoured in her father's house. And Lyra adds that this is not unreasonable, since we read in the book of Esther that many of the gentiles, seeing how God had delivered the Jews from the plots of Aman, went over to the law and ceremonies of the Jews. But Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos, a converted rabbi who wrote additions to Lyra] says that this about Agar is made up, and that the argument from the book of Esther does not prove the point, because those gentiles did not submit themselves to the Lord, but to the rite of the Jews. Yet I think it probable that this Agar was a very upright and remarkable girl, since Sarai, who had many handmaids, gave her to her husband rather than the others.

paras.t: Sed circa hæc oriuntur difficultates. Primo, cur Sarai rogavit virum suum, ut duceret aliam conjugem, quum Deus jam ante promiserit Abræ quod esset sobolem habiturus? Respondetur, quod Sarai ignoravit an promissio illa esset implenda per se, et timuit ne ex sua sterilitate frustraretur effectu, idcirco optavit eam impleri per aliam. Sed tunc rursus oritur difficultas, cur Abram acquievit precibus Sarai in isto; nam scire poterat quod promissio illa erat per Sarai adimplenda. Ad quod dicendum, quod hucusque non legitur hoc Abræ revelatum. Rabanus quoque dicit, Abram semen suum multiplicandum audierat, sed per quam feminam, nesciebat. Et quoniam primam conjugem noverat sterilem, duxit secundam, quam speravit fecundam. Præterea quæritur, qualiter licuit Abræ, ad instantiam conjugis suæ, accipere conjugem aliam, sicque inducere bigamiam, quum Lamech de bigamia reprehendatur, et naturalis lex dictet, ut unicus unicæ copuletur, nec aliquis Sanctorum ante Abram legatur ita fecisse. Ad istud Guillelmus Parisiensis respondet, quod nunquam licuit sine dispensatione divina uni viro simul habere plures uxores. Nam primæ uxori tradidit sui corporis potestatem: ideo Abram et ceteri qui plures uxores sine peccato duxerunt, quos scilicet a culpa in hoc excusare oportet, creduntur id egisse ex dispensatione divina, quam vel ipsi per occultam inspirationem aut modo alio acceperunt. Abram etiam multipliciter excusatur in facto isto, quia non movebatur libidine, nec contra uxoris primæ consensum, imo ex ejus petitione hoc fecit. Nondum quoque promulgata fuit lex evangelica de una sola uxore simul habenda. Qualiter vero sit de lege naturali unam habere, infra dicetur.
paras.en: But some difficulties arise about this. First, why did Sarai ask her husband to take another wife, when God had already promised Abram before that he would have offspring[[Gen 15:4||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the promise meant is presumably that of Gen 15:4]? The answer is that Sarai did not know whether that promise was to be fulfilled through her, and she feared that because of her barrenness it would fail of its effect; therefore she wished it to be fulfilled through another. But then a further difficulty arises: why did Abram give in to Sarai's entreaties in this, for he could have known that the promise was to be fulfilled through Sarai? To this it must be said that we do not read that this had yet been revealed to Abram. Rabanus also says: Abram had heard that his seed was to be multiplied, but he did not know by which woman. And since he knew his first wife to be barren, he took a second, whom he hoped would be fruitful. It is further asked how it was lawful for Abram, at his wife's urging, to take another wife and so bring in bigamy [that is, having two wives at once], since Lamech is blamed for bigamy, and the natural law dictates that one man be joined to one woman, nor do we read that any of the Saints before Abram did so. To this William of Paris replies that it was never lawful, without divine dispensation, for one man to have several wives at once; for he has given the power over his body to his first wife. Therefore Abram and the others who took several wives without sin (those, that is, whom we must excuse from fault in this) are believed to have done it by divine dispensation, which they received either by a hidden inspiration or in some other way. Abram is also excused in this deed on many counts: he was not moved by lust, nor did he act against the consent of his first wife, but did it at her request. Nor had the law of the Gospel, of having only one wife at a time, yet been promulgated. How far it belongs to the natural law to have one wife will be said below.

paras.t: Hinc loquitur Augustinus: Nullo modo inferendum est crimen Abræ de hac muliere. Usus quippe est ea ad generandum prolem, non ad explendam libidinem, nec insultans, sed magis obediens conjugi suæ, quæ suæ sterilitatis credidit esse solatium, si fecundum ancillæ uterum faceret suum. Ab utroque non culpæ luxus, sed naturæ fructus exquiritur. Verumtamen Augustinus hanc Agar vocat Abræ concubinam: quod non est intelligendum, quasi non fuerit ejus legitima uxor, quum paulo post in textu habeatur oppositum; sed quia consuetudo Scripturæ est, uxorem, præsertim minus principalem et secundariam, dicere concubinam, prout infra sæpe patebit.
paras.en: Hence Augustine says: In no way is a crime to be charged against Abram on account of this woman. For he used her to beget offspring, not to satisfy lust; not insulting his wife, but rather obeying her, who believed it a comfort for her barrenness if she made her handmaid's fruitful womb her own. Neither of them sought the indulgence of sin, but the fruit of nature. Yet Augustine calls this Agar Abram's concubine. This is not to be understood as though she were not his lawful wife, since the contrary is stated in the text a little later; but because it is the custom of Scripture to call a wife, especially a lesser and secondary one, a concubine, as will often be seen below.

paras.t: Quumque ille, videlicet Abram, acquiesceret deprecanti, tulit ipsa Sarai Agar Ægyptiam ancillam suam post decem annos, quam habitare cœperant in terra Chanaan, ab egressu de Mesopotamia: nam infra tantum tempus poterat sterilitas Sarai satis experimentaliter cognosci; et dedit eam viro suo uxorem. Et tunc erat Abram octoginta quinque annorum, quoniam septuaginta quinque annorum erat quando Deo jubente ex Mesopotamia venit ad habitandum in terra Chanaan, ut dictum est. Imo (ut fertur) Hebræi dicunt, quod decennium est tempus, infra quod maritus experiri debet de conjuge sua, an sterilis sit, et utrum propter sterilitatem ipsius accipere aliam possit. Verumtamen Ecclesia determinavit brevius tempus pro experientia hujus rei, videlicet tempus triennii, ut in cap. final. extra de frigid. et malef. Et dedit eam viro suo uxorem, ita quod Abram de consensu Sarai conjugis suæ, accepit Agar ancillam in conjugem per verba de præsenti, sive per modum tunc consuetum. Tamen ut patet ex dictis, ex sola uxoris auctoritate ac voluntate non licuit viro accipere conjugem aliam.
paras.en: [[16:2|And when he|Quumque ille]], namely Abram, [[16:2|agreed to her request|acquiesceret deprecanti]], [[16:3|She took Agar the Egyptian her handmaid|tulit ipsa Sarai Agar Ægyptiam ancillam suam]], Sarai herself, [[16:3|ten years after they first dwelt in the land of Chanaan|post decem annos, quam habitare cœperant in terra Chanaan]], from their going out of Mesopotamia; for within so long a time Sarai's barrenness could be known well enough by experience; [[16:3|and gave her to her husband to wife|et dedit eam viro suo uxorem]]. Abram was then eighty-five years old, since he was seventy-five years old when at God's command he came from Mesopotamia to dwell in the land of Chanaan, as was said. Indeed (as it is reported) the Hebrews say that ten years is the time within which a husband must find out about his wife, whether she is barren, and whether because of her barrenness he may take another. The Church, however, has set a shorter time for testing this, namely three years, as in the last chapter of the title *De frigidis et maleficiatis* in the Extra [that is, the Decretals of Gregory IX, on marriages hindered by impotence or sorcery]. [[16:3|and gave her to her husband to wife|Et dedit eam viro suo uxorem]], so that Abram, with the consent of his wife Sarai, took the handmaid Agar as wife by words of present consent [that is, words by which a marriage is contracted then and there, not a promise of marriage to come], or in the manner then customary. Yet, as is clear from what has been said, it was not lawful for a man to take another wife on the authority and will of his wife alone.

paras.t: At illa, scilicet Agar, concepisse se videns, id est cognoscens, seu ex tumore ventris sui corporaliter cernens, despexit dominam suam, tanquam infœcundam, reputans se digniorem nomine consortalis quam illam, eo quod fructum matrimonii gestaret in utero: atque (ut aliqui dicunt) putabat promissiones divinas Abræ factas de multiplicatione et benedictione seminis sui, complendas in prole sua concepta. Prosperitas quippe interdum incitat etiam bonos ad quamdam elationem, audaciam et gloriam vanam. Idcirco humilitas in prosperis præcipue commendatur.
paras.en: [[16:4|But she|At illa]], namely Agar, [[16:4|perceiving that she was with child|concepisse se videns]], that is, knowing it, or seeing it bodily from the swelling of her womb, [[16:4|despised her mistress|despexit dominam suam]] as unfruitful, thinking herself worthier than she of the name of consort, because she bore the fruit of the marriage in her womb; and (as some say) she thought that the divine promises made to Abram of the multiplying and blessing of his seed were to be fulfilled in the child she had conceived. For prosperity sometimes stirs even the good to a certain elation, boldness and vainglory. That is why humility in prosperity is especially commended.

paras.t: Dixitque Sarai ad Abram: Inique agis contra me, id est, reprehensibilis es, fovendo ancillæ meæ audaciam, seu dissimulando et non corrigendo ejus elationem qua spernit me. Et potest esse, quod Abram fuit in hoc venialiter culpabilis ex negligentia aut aliquantula sensuali affectione ad uxorem imprægnatam recenter acceptam, de cujus conceptu gaudebat, unde invite contristavit eamdem. Porro secundum Augustinum, Sarai ex quadam muliebri suspicione elationem suæ ancillæ imputavit suo marito. Ego dedi ancillam meam in sinum tuum, id est, admonui et consensi, quod fieret uxor tua, et tibi legitime misceretur: quasi dicat, Tu es causa meæ despectionis, et reddis mihi malum pro bono. Quæ, scilicet ancilla, videns quod conceperit de te, despectui me habet, gerens se circa me, quasi ego sim ejus ancilla potius quam econtra. Judicet Dominus inter me et te, unicuique nostrum reddendo quod promeretur in istis. Hoc Sarai dixit ex quodam zelo justitiæ.
paras.en: [[16:5|And Sarai said to Abram: Thou dost unjustly with me|Dixitque Sarai ad Abram: Inique agis contra me]], that is, thou art to blame, by encouraging my handmaid's boldness, or by overlooking and not correcting the elation with which she scorns me. And it may be that Abram was venially at fault in this, through negligence or some slight sensual affection for the wife he had lately taken and who was now with child, at whose conceiving he rejoiced, so that he was unwilling to grieve her. But according to Augustine, Sarai, out of a certain womanly suspicion, laid her handmaid's elation to her husband's charge. [[16:5|I gave my handmaid into thy bosom|Ego dedi ancillam meam in sinum tuum]], that is, I advised and consented that she should become thy wife and lawfully lie with thee; as if to say: Thou art the cause of my being despised, and thou renderest me evil for good. [[16:5|and she perceiving herself to be with child|Quæ, scilicet ancilla, videns quod conceperit]], namely the handmaid, by thee, [[16:5|despiseth me|despectui me habet]], behaving towards me as if I were her handmaid rather than the other way about. [[16:5|The Lord judge between me and thee|Judicet Dominus inter me et te]], rendering to each of us what we deserve in these things. Sarai said this out of a certain zeal for justice.

paras.t: Cui respondens Abram: Ecce, ait, ancilla tua in manu, id est potestate, tua est: utere ea ut libet, id est, fac ei quod tibi placet. Per hoc tamen Abram non dedit Sarai licentiam affligendi injuste ancillam suam, sed sciens Sarai esse virtuosam et timoratam, commisit rem istam suæ discretioni, seque monstravit immunem ab immoderata affectione, saltem mortali, ad Agar. Circa hæc loquitur Augustinus: O virum viriliter utentem feminis, conjuge temperanter, ancilla obtemperanter, nulla intemperanter!
paras.en: [[16:6|And Abram made answer|Cui respondens Abram]]: [[16:6|Behold thy handmaid is in thy own hand|Ecce, ait, ancilla tua in manu]], that is, power, [[16:6|use her as it pleaseth thee|utere ea ut libet]], that is, do to her what thou pleasest. By this, however, Abram did not give Sarai leave to afflict her handmaid unjustly; but knowing Sarai to be virtuous and God-fearing, he left the matter to her discretion, and showed himself free of any immoderate affection, at least of any mortal one, for Agar. On this Augustine says: O man, who used women manfully: his wife temperately, his handmaid compliantly, neither intemperately! [Augustine's play on *temperanter*, *obtemperanter*, *intemperanter* is lost in English.]

paras.t: Affligente igitur eam Sarai, id est, dum Sarai assidue humiliaret et increparet hanc Agar, castigando ejus præsumptionem: quod Sarai juste fecit, quamvis fortassis in hoc aliquantulum interdum excesserit. Nec enim oportet Sarai a venialibus excusare. Fugam iniit, quia volebat ad Ægyptum reverti. Quumque invenisset eam angelus, non casu aut post quæstionem reperit eam, sed invenit, id est præsentialiter ei occurrit, juxta fontem aquæ in solitudine, juxta quem fontem forsitan sedit et repausavit se Agar, atque in solitudine illa erexit cor suum ad Dominum, quum esset tribulatione et lassitudine plena, propter quod Dominus naturaliter infiniteque bonus ac pius, consolabatur eam per angelum sanctum. Qui dixit ad eam: Agar ancilla Sarai, unde venis, et quo vadis? Utrumque horum cognoverat angelus, sed interrogavit, quatenus ex qualitate responsionis ipsius Agar informaret eamdem. Quæ respondit: A facie Sarai dominæ meæ ego fugio. Dicunt aliqui quod Agar recessit a Sarai non solum ex quadam impatientia, sed item ex aliquanta superbia. Ideo angelus volens eam humiliare, vocavit eam ancillam Sarai: quo audito, etiam ipsa Agar humiliavit se, et conformans se verbo angelico, ipsam Sarai vocavit dominam suam, quam paulo ante contempsit velut ancillam. Nec legitur Agar respondisse ad secundum, puta quo tenderet, quia fortassis erubuit confiteri, quod a domo fidelis mariti virtuosæque dominæ, ad Ægyptios rediret idololatras. Vel ex vehementia suæ desolationis præscidit verba.
paras.en: [[16:6|And when Sarai afflicted her|Affligente igitur eam Sarai]], that is, while Sarai kept humbling and rebuking this Agar, chastising her presumption (which Sarai did justly, though perhaps at times she went somewhat too far in it; for we need not excuse Sarai from venial sins), [[16:6|she ran away|Fugam iniit]], because she wished to go back to Egypt. [[16:7|And the angel of the Lord having found her|Quumque invenisset eam angelus]]: he did not come on her by chance or after searching, but *found* her, that is, met her in person, [[16:7|by a fountain of water in the wilderness|juxta fontem aquæ in solitudine]]; beside which fountain Agar perhaps sat and rested, and in that wilderness lifted up her heart to the Lord, being full of trouble and weariness; and for this the Lord, who is by nature infinitely good and kind, comforted her through a holy angel. [[16:8|He said to her|dixit ad eam]]: [[16:8|Agar, handmaid of Sarai, whence comest thou? and whither goest thou?|Agar ancilla Sarai, unde venis, et quo vadis?]] The angel knew both of these, but he asked so that by the manner of Agar's answer he might instruct her. [[16:8|And she answered: I flee from the face of Sarai, my mistress|Quæ respondit: A facie Sarai dominæ meæ ego fugio]]. Some say that Agar left Sarai not only from a certain impatience but also from some pride. So the angel, wishing to humble her, called her the handmaid of Sarai; and on hearing this Agar too humbled herself and, conforming herself to the angel's word, called Sarai her mistress, whom a little before she had despised as a handmaid. Nor do we read that Agar answered the second question, namely where she was going, perhaps because she was ashamed to admit that from the house of a faithful husband and a virtuous mistress she was going back to the idolatrous Egyptians; or else the vehemence of her desolation cut her words short.

paras.t: Dixitque ei angelus Domini: Revertere ad dominam tuam, et humiliare sub manu ipsius, id est, te ipsam sponte sub ea humilia, ut decet ancillam, et æquanimiter tolera quidquid Sarai fecerit tibi. Angelus iste in forma humana visibiliter apparuit Agar. Scriptura vero ista non exprimit, an ex prima angeli apparitione fuerit Agar perterrita, et an statim cognovit quod angelus esset. Porro angeli quandoque apparent cum vultu jam igneo ac splendenti, quod prima facie grandem incutiunt eis quibus apparent, timorem; aliquando vero sic apparent, quod prima facie æstimantur homines esse. Unde mater Samsonis dixit: Vir Dei venit ad me, etc.
paras.en: [[16:9|And the angel of the Lord said to her: Return to thy mistress, and humble thyself under her hand|Dixitque ei angelus Domini: Revertere ad dominam tuam, et humiliare sub manu ipsius]], that is, humble thyself willingly under her, as befits a handmaid, and bear patiently whatever Sarai does to thee. This angel appeared visibly to Agar in human form. But this scripture does not say whether Agar was terrified at the angel's first appearing, and whether she knew at once that he was an angel. Now angels sometimes appear with a fiery and shining countenance, so that at first sight they strike great fear into those to whom they appear; but sometimes they appear in such a way that at first sight they are thought to be men. Hence the mother of Samson said: [[Judg 13:6|A man of God came to me|Vir Dei venit ad me]], etc.

paras.t: Et rursum: Multiplicans, inquit, multiplicabo semen tuum. Hoc angelus in persona Dei locutus est. Et est sensus: Ex prole quam paries, plurimi valde generabuntur per temporum successiones. Et non numerabitur præ multitudine, id est, posteritas filii tui erit innumerabilis hominibus præ multitudine sua. Promissio ista in Sarracenis impleta est, qui rectius Agareni quam Sarraceni essent vocandi, quia de Agar, non de Sara, sunt nati. Qui præ multitudine sua innumerabiles fuerunt et sunt; sed cognomen hoc quo Sarraceni vocantur, sibi mendaciter usurpasse censentur, quasi de principali et libera conjuge Abrahæ Sara geniti essent, se cognominantes, quum de ancilla et minus principali sint nati uxore.
paras.en: [[16:10|And again he said|Et rursum]]: [[16:10|I will multiply thy seed exceedingly|Multiplicans, inquit, multiplicabo semen tuum]] The angel said this in the person of God. And the sense is: From the child thou shalt bear, very many will be begotten as the ages follow one another. [[16:10|and it shall not be numbered for multitude|Et non numerabitur præ multitudine]], that is, the posterity of thy son will be beyond men's counting for its multitude. This promise was fulfilled in the Saracens, who would more rightly be called Agarenes than Saracens, since they are born of Agar, not of Sara. They have been and are past counting for their multitude; but they are held to have falsely usurped the name by which they are called Saracens, naming themselves as though they were born of Sara, Abraham's principal and free wife, when they are born of the handmaid, the lesser wife.

paras.t: Ac deinceps: Ecce, ait, concepisti et paries filium. Quod conceperat, patebat ad oculum; sed quod proles concepta exstitit filius, excessit naturalem cognitionem humanam, sed angelum non latebat. Vocabisque nomen ejus Ismael, id est, imponendo filio tuo nomen, vocabis eum hoc nomine. Ismael quippe interpretatur exauditio Domini; idcirco ratio nominationis hujus subjungitur: eo quod audierit Dominus afflictionem tuam, et orationem tuam quam in afflictione magna fudisti ad eum. Hinc in Deuteronomio habetur: Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum, si tamen toto corde tuo quæsieris eum, et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ. Afflictio ista est vera cordis contritio, seu quævis punitio pro peccatis aut aliis causis inflicta, æquanimiter tolerata. Talem etenim afflictionem audit seu pie respicit Deus, non illam quæ impatienter suscipitur et invite suffertur. Fuit autem magna afflictio Agar in fuga ista.
paras.en: [[16:11|And again: Behold, said he, thou art with child, and thou shalt bring forth a son|Ac deinceps: Ecce, ait, concepisti et paries filium]] That she had conceived was plain to the eye; but that the child conceived was a son was beyond natural human knowledge, though it was not hidden from the angel. [[16:11|and thou shalt call his name Ismael|Vocabisque nomen ejus Ismael]], that is, in giving thy son his name, thou shalt call him by this name. For Ismael is interpreted *the Lord's hearing*; therefore the reason for this name is added: [[16:11|because the Lord hath heard thy affliction|eo quod audierit Dominus afflictionem tuam]], and thy prayer, which thou didst pour out to Him in thy great affliction. Hence it is said in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 4:29|And when thou shalt seek there the Lord thy God, thou shalt find him: yet so, if thou seek him with all thy heart, and all the affliction of thy soul|Quum quæsieris Dominum Deum tuum, invenies eum, si tamen toto corde tuo quæsieris eum, et tota tribulatione animæ tuæ]]. This affliction is true contrition of heart, or any punishment inflicted for sins or for other causes and borne patiently. Such affliction God hears, or looks on with kindness; not that which is received impatiently and borne unwillingly. And Agar's affliction in this flight was great.

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit Lyra, quod in Hebræo habetur, Ecce concipies, sicut et in libro Judicum de Samsone prædictum est matri ejus: Ecce concipies. Nam idem verbum ponitur utrobique. Ideo dicunt Hebræi, quod Agar fuit aborsum passa, ita quod proles fuit in utero suo exstincta, et hoc forsan ex labore itineris et acerbitate mœroris, aut propter priorem ejus superbiam in dominam suam. Quumque pœnituisset, et angelo obtemperare disponeret, revivificavit Dominus prolem exstinctam. Quæ revivificatio vocatur conceptio. Sed Rabbi Paulus his contradicit, et dicit in Hebræo haberi: Ecce concepisti, quoniam dictio omnino similis ponitur hic et infra, ubi Thamar testatur: De viro cujus sunt hæc, concepi. Sicque, ut ait, non oportet aborsum et revivificationem confingere.
paras.en: On this Lyra writes that in the Hebrew it reads *Behold, thou shalt conceive*, just as in the book of Judges it was foretold to the mother of Samson concerning him: [[Judg 13:7|Behold thou shalt conceive|Ecce concipies.]] For the same word is used in both places. So the Hebrews say that Agar suffered a miscarriage, so that the child died in her womb, perhaps from the toil of the journey and the bitterness of her grief, or on account of her earlier pride against her mistress; and when she had repented and was disposed to obey the angel, the Lord brought the dead child back to life; and this bringing back to life is called a conception. But Rabbi Paul contradicts this, and says that the Hebrew reads *Behold, thou hast conceived*, since an altogether similar expression is used here and below, where Thamar declares: [[Gen 38:25|By the man, to whom these things belong, I am with child|De viro cujus sunt hæc, concepi]]. And so, as he says, there is no need to invent a miscarriage and a return to life.

paras.t: Denique hic primo legitur nomen a Deo impositum homini ante ipsius nativitatem, quod perrarum est. Sunt quoque tres alii, quibus in veteri Testamento nomen ita impositum est, scilicet Isaac, Samson et Josias. De Isaac patet capitulo sequenti, de Samsone in Judicum libro, de Josia in tertio libro Regum. In novo autem Testamento sunt duo hujusmodi, videlicet Christus et Joannes Baptista. Verumtamen nomen Cyri regis Persarum, diu ante ejus conceptionem fuit per Isaiam prædictum, juxta illud Isaiæ: Hæc dicit Dominus christo meo Cyro. In quibus verbis nomen Cyri dicitur potius prophetatum, quam vocatum aut institutum.
paras.en: Further, here for the first time we read of a name given by God to a man before his birth, which is very rare. There are also three others in the Old Testament to whom a name was given in this way, namely Isaac, Samson and Josias: of Isaac it is plain in the next chapter[[Gen 17:19||]], of Samson in the book of Judges[[Judg 13:24||]], of Josias in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 13:2||]]. In the New Testament there are two such, namely Christ[[Luke 1:31||]] and John the Baptist[[Luke 1:13||]]. The name of Cyrus king of the Persians, however, was foretold by Isaias long before his conception, according to the word of Isaias: [[Is 45:1|Thus saith the Lord to my anointed Cyrus|Hæc dicit Dominus christo meo Cyro]]. In these words the name of Cyrus is said rather to be prophesied than given or appointed.

paras.t: Insuper, quia in aliis jam præfatis, contigit miraculum aliquod quando prædicta sunt nomina eorum a Deo, aut paulo post (in nativitate enim Isaac et Samsonis fuit miraculum, quia eorum matres naturaliter steriles erant; item quando nomen Josiæ prædictum fuit, scissum fuit altare sacrilegum, et arefactum regis impii brachium; Jesus vero sine virili conceptus est semine, et Joannes de sterilibus senibusque parentibus natus), hinc aliqui dicunt, quod etiam in Ismaele contigit prætactum revivificationis miraculum, quando prædictum est nomen ejus ab angelo. Sed contra hoc scribit Rabbi Paulus, quia vita Ismaelis fuit valde dissimilis a vita illorum jam prælatorum. Et rursus, quia miraculum istud circa Ismaelem fuisset occultum, et ita non induceret utilitatem. Præterea, quidquid sit de veritate dicti illius, reprobationes istæ prorsus infirmæ sunt. Miracula namque communiter fiunt a bonis et malis, et utrisque communia sunt secundum doctores, sicut et cetera dona gratiæ gratis datæ. Miraculum etiam istud Ismaeli impensum, fuisset in primis utile matri suæ ac sibi, deinde his ad quorum devenisset notitiam. Innumerabilia quoque miracula Dei manserunt occulta, imo plurimi Sancti absconderunt pro posse miracula sua. Et beatissimis eremitis animalia illa silvatica fuerunt assidue innocua, imo quodammodo familiaria et sæpe obsequiosa.
paras.en: Moreover, since in the others already named some miracle took place when their names were foretold by God, or shortly after (for at the birth of Isaac and of Samson there was a miracle, because their mothers were naturally barren; again, when the name of Josias was foretold, the sacrilegious altar was split and the arm of the wicked king withered; Jesus was conceived without the seed of man[[Luke 1:34||]], and John was born of barren and aged parents[[Luke 1:7||]]), some therefore say that in Ismael too the miracle of bringing back to life, mentioned above, took place when his name was foretold by the angel. But Rabbi Paul writes against this, because the life of Ismael was very unlike the life of those already mentioned; and again, because this miracle concerning Ismael would have been hidden, and so would have brought no benefit. Yet, whatever be the truth of that saying, these refutations are quite weak. For miracles are commonly done by good and bad alike, and according to the doctors they are common to both, like the other gifts of grace freely given [that is, *gratia gratis data*, graces given for the good of others, such as prophecy or miracles, which do not of themselves make the one who has them holy]. And this miracle done for Ismael would have been useful first to his mother and to himself, then to those who came to know of it. Countless miracles of God, too, have remained hidden; indeed very many Saints hid their miracles as far as they could. And to the most blessed hermits the wild beasts were always harmless, indeed in a way friendly and often obliging.

paras.t: Hic erit ferus homo. Ismael enim fuit vir durus et satis feralis, abundans in irascibili etiam ex naturali dispositione, quemadmodum quidam ex naturali dispositione in concupiscibili magis abundant. Unde et infra habetur: Quum vidisset Sara Ismaelem ludentem cum filio suo Isaac, dixit: Ejice ancillam hanc et filium ejus. Siquidem ludus ille erat feralis. Verumtamen secundum Hieronymum in Hebræo habetur, Phara: quod interpretatur onager, atque ut alius ait, in Hebræo habetur, silvestris. Nam dictio ista Hebraica, forsitan æquivoca est ad omnia ista. Dictus est itaque Ismael onager: primo, ad insinuandum ferocitatem tam suam quam suæ posteritatis. Secundo, ad innuendum, quod habitaturus esset tam ipse quam ejus posteritas in locis deserti; specialiter quoque Ismael nemora et venationes dilexit, quoniam factus est juvenis sagittarius, ut infra habetur. Manus ejus contra omnes, et manus omnium contra eum. Iste est hyperbolicus sermo, ad designandum quod posteri Ismaelis essent multum bellicosi et inquieti, de quibus ait Hieronymus: Sarraceni incertis sedibus vagi, incursantes omnes gentes quibus desertum ex latere jungitur, impugnantur ab omnibus; imo usque in præsens Sarraceni legem suam gladio protegunt, et universos adversarios suæ legis impugnant. Et e regione, id est ex opposito, universorum fratrum suorum figet tabernacula, id est tentoria sua, in quibus morari consueverunt Ismaelitæ in solitudine hinc inde dispersi. Vel, figent tabernacula sua, ut fieri solet in præliis, quasi parati ad resistendum adversariis suis. Porro per universos fratres suos, intelligi possunt gentes natæ ex ceteris filiis Abrahæ, vel quicumque homines Sarracenis contrariantes, qui per conformitatem naturæ, et ratione primæ originis, dicuntur eorum fratres. Circa hæc allegantur in Scholastica historia verba Methodii martyris, de generali persecutione mundo per Ismaelitas futura. Futurum est, inquit, ut exeant adhuc semel, et obtinebunt orbem terræ per octo hebdomadas annorum. In sacris locis interficient sacerdotes, et ibi cum mulieribus dormient, ac sua jumenta ad sepulcra ligabunt Sanctorum, et hoc propter malitiam Christianorum, qui tunc erunt, de quibus prædixit Paulus: In novissimis diebus erunt homines se amantes, etc.
paras.en: [[16:12|He shall be a wild man|Hic erit ferus homo.]] For Ismael was a hard and rather savage man, abounding in the irascible appetite even by natural disposition, just as some by natural disposition abound more in the concupiscible. Hence it is said below: [[Gen 21:9|when Sara had seen|Quum vidisset Sara]] Ismael [[Gen 21:9|playing with Isaac, her son|ludentem cum filio suo Isaac]], she said: [[Gen 21:10|Cast out this bondwoman and her son|Ejice ancillam hanc et filium ejus]][[Gal 4:30||]]. For that play was savage. According to Jerome, however, the Hebrew has *Phara*, which is interpreted *wild ass*; and as another says, the Hebrew has *of the woods*. For this Hebrew word is perhaps ambiguous and covers all of these. So Ismael was called a wild ass: first, to suggest the fierceness both of himself and of his posterity; secondly, to hint that both he and his posterity would dwell in desert places. Ismael also especially loved the forests and hunting, since he [[Gen 21:20|became a young man, an archer|factus est juvenis sagittarius]], as is said below. [[16:12|his hand will be against all men, and all men's hands against him|Manus ejus contra omnes, et manus omnium contra eum]] This is a hyperbolic saying, to show that the descendants of Ismael would be very warlike and restless; of whom Jerome says: The Saracens, wandering without fixed abode, raiding all the nations whose borders touch the desert, are attacked by all. Indeed, to this day the Saracens defend their law with the sword and attack all the opponents of their law. [[16:12|and he shall pitch his tents over against all his brethren|et e regione universorum fratrum suorum figet tabernacula]]: *over against*, that is, opposite; *tents*, that is, the pavilions in which the Ismaelites were wont to dwell, scattered here and there in the wilderness. Or: they shall pitch their tents as is usually done in battle, as if ready to resist their adversaries. By *all his brethren* may be understood the nations born of Abraham's other sons, or any men at all opposed to the Saracens, who are called their brethren by likeness of nature and by reason of their first origin. On this the *Scholastic History* cites the words of Methodius the martyr about a general persecution of the world to come through the Ismaelites: It shall be, he says, that they will go forth once more and will hold the world for eight weeks of years. In the holy places they will kill the priests and lie there with women, and tie their beasts to the tombs of the Saints; and this because of the wickedness of the Christians who will be living then, of whom Paul foretold: [[2 Tim 3:1|in the last days|In novissimis diebus]] [[2 Tim 3:2|Men shall be lovers of themselves|erunt homines se amantes]], etc.

paras.t: Vocavit autem Agar nomen Domini qui loquebatur ad eam, Tu Deus qui vidisti me: id est, per aliquod nomen complexum seu incomplexum tantumdem significans, Deum vocavit. Deus enim solet cognosci et nominari per suos effectus: idcirco Deum se misericorditer intuentem, consolantem ac roborantem, femina ista vocavit hujusmodi nomine, sicut et David in Psalmo: Deus meus, misericordia mea. Quasi dicat: Tu Deus universorum, qui tam pie me adspexisti, es Deus meus, per specialem providentiam et pietatem tuam ad me. Hinc subditur ratio hujus nominis: Dixit enim hæc Agar: Profecto hic vidi posteriora videntis me.
paras.en: [[16:13|And she called the name of the Lord that spoke unto her|Vocavit autem Agar nomen Domini qui loquebatur ad eam]]: [[16:13|Thou the God who hast seen me|Tu Deus qui vidisti me]]: that is, she called God by some name, compound or simple [that is, a phrase or a single word], meaning as much. For God is wont to be known and named by His effects: therefore this woman called God, who looked on her mercifully, comforted and strengthened her, by a name of this kind; as David too says in the Psalm: [[Ps 58:18|my God my mercy|Deus meus, misericordia mea]] [the margin gives Ps. lxviii, 18; the words are Ps 58:18]. As if to say: Thou, God of all things, who hast looked on me so kindly, art my God, by Thy special providence and kindness towards me. Then the reason for this name is added: [[16:13|For she said|Dixit enim]], this Agar: [[16:13|Verily, here have I seen the hinder parts of him that seeth me|Profecto hic vidi posteriora videntis me]].

paras.t: Circa hoc scribit Lyra: Dicunt expositores nostri, quod angelus iste apparuit in similitudine assumpta, quasi habens faciem aversam ab Agar, ita quod vidit eum a dorso: ideo dixit: Vidi posteriora videntis me. Circa quod dico, verum esse quod plures dicunt, angelum istum apparuisse in forma humana, quod arbitror verum. Sed non videtur quod apparuit ei quasi vultum habens ab ea aversum. Non enim consueverunt angeli taliter apparere; imo in pluribus locis apparuisse leguntur vultu ad eos, quibus loquebantur, converso. Nec legi aliquem expositorem authenticum hoc dicentem. Cur igitur Agar non dixit, Vidi anteriora videntis me? Ad quod primo dici potest, quod præ claritate et majestate vultus angelici non audebat, aut forsitan vix poterat eum ab ante inspicere, nisi valde confuse; sed quum averteret angelus se ab illa, quasi volens mox disparere, respexit post eum, et vidit eum determinate a tergo. Unde in Scholastica historia legitur: Quumque loqueretur Dominus cum Agar, pertransiit in turbine. In Hebræo quoque secundum quosdam habetur: Hic vidi post videntem me, id est, post angelum a me recedentem, cum admiratione adspexi. Nec istud mirum de Agar et angelo, quum in Exodo scriptum sit, quod filii Israel adspiciebant tergum Moysis, donec ingrederetur tentorium. Et tam Aaron quam principes Synagogæ, videntes cornutam faciem Moysis, timuerunt accedere, et recesserunt ab eo. Secundo dici potest, quod Agar sciens angelum istum in Dei persona sibi apparere ac loqui, formam humanam assumptam ab angelo seu etiam angelum taliter apparentem, vocavit posteriora Dei, tanquam effectum ipsius, multum distantem a plena Dei repræsentatione. Nam et Moysi dixit Dominus: Videbis posteriora mea, faciem autem meam videre non poteris.
paras.en: On this Lyra writes: Our expositors say that this angel appeared in an assumed likeness, as if with his face turned away from Agar, so that she saw him from behind; therefore she said: [[16:13|here have I seen the hinder parts of him that seeth me|Vidi posteriora videntis me]] [the transcription is garbled here, giving only “videntis me”; the words of v. 13 are supplied]. On which I say: it is true, as many say, that this angel appeared in human form, and I think it true. But it does not seem that he appeared to her as if with his face turned away from her. For angels are not wont to appear in that way; on the contrary, in many places they are read to have appeared with the face turned towards those to whom they spoke. Nor have I read any authoritative expositor who says this. Why then did Agar not say, I have seen the fore parts of him that seeth me? To this it may be said, first, that because of the brightness and majesty of the angel's face she did not dare, or perhaps was scarcely able, to look at him from in front except very confusedly; but when the angel turned away from her, as if about to vanish, she looked after him and saw him distinctly from behind. Hence we read in the *Scholastic History*: And when the Lord spoke with Agar, He passed by in a whirlwind. In the Hebrew too, according to some, it reads: Here have I seen after him that seeth me; that is, I looked with wonder after the angel as he went away from me. Nor is this strange of Agar and the angel, since it is written in Exodus that the children of Israel beheld the back of Moses until he went into the tent[[Ex 33:8||]]; and both Aaron and the princes of the Synagogue, seeing the horned face of Moses, were afraid to come near and drew back from him[[Ex 34:30||]]. Secondly, it may be said that Agar, knowing that this angel appeared and spoke to her in the person of God, called the human form taken by the angel, or the angel himself appearing in this way, the hinder parts of God, as being His effect, falling far short of a full representation of God. For the Lord also said to Moses: [[Ex 33:23|thou shalt see my back parts: but my face thou canst not see|Videbis posteriora mea, faciem autem meam videre non poteris]].

paras.t: Iterum quæri potest, cur Agar vocavit eum qui loquebatur secum, Tu Deus, etc., quum sciret angelum secum loqui. Ad quod patet ex dictis responsio, quia in Dei persona angelus ei apparuit, et Dominus per angelum loquebatur ad eam. Refert hic Lyra, quod secundum quosdam Hebræos, iste est verus textus, Vidi per visum meum: ut sit sensus, Vidi angelum in hoc deserto, postquam vidi eum in domo Abræ, cujus angelus iste fuit visitator et custos: idcirco non fuit territa ex angeli visione, quia assueta fuit eum in Abræ domo videre. Nec mirum, quod hic atque in aliis pluribus locis veteris Testamenti littera pluribus modis ac sensibus sumitur, etiam secundum Hebræos doctores: quia Hebræi non habent grammaticam ita distinctam et dearticulatam per declinationes nominum et verborum, sicut Latini et Græci. Hæc Lyra. Circa quæ dico, incertum esse quod angelus ille fuit custos visitatorque Abræ. Simili enim et forsan majori apparentia dici posset, quod fuerit custos Agar, aut certe filii ejus Ismaelis, qui in utero matris habuit angelum, sicut et ceteri fetus. Nam ea quæ angelus iste dixit, magis pertinebant ad Agar et filium ejus, quam ad Abram. Deinde incertum est, quod Agar solita fuit angelum in Abræ domo videre, quia nec tantæ sanctitatis videtur fuisse, ut assidue cerneret sensibiliter angelum, nec putandum quod angelus Abræ ambulaverit in domo ejus visibiliter domesticis ejus. Nec certum est, quod angelus qui interdum apparuit Abræ, fuerit custos ejus, ei specialiter deputatus: nam simili ratione dici posset, quod angeli qui ceteris Prophetis et Patriarchis apparuerunt, fuerint illorum, quibus apparuerunt ac loquebantur, speciales custodes, quum tamen Daniel propheta scribat sibi Gabrielem apparuisse. Verumtamen non negatur, quin interdum angeli qui apparuerunt, fuerunt custodes horum quibus apparuisse leguntur.
paras.en: It may be asked again why Agar called him who spoke with her *Thou the God*, etc., when she knew that an angel was speaking with her. The answer is plain from what has been said: the angel appeared to her in the person of God, and the Lord spoke to her through the angel. Lyra relates here that according to some Hebrews the true text is: I have seen by my sight; so that the sense is: I have seen the angel in this desert after I saw him in the house of Abram, whose visitor and guardian this angel was; and so she was not frightened at the sight of the angel, because she was used to seeing him in Abram's house. Nor is it strange that here and in many other places of the Old Testament the letter is taken in several ways and senses, even by the Hebrew doctors; for the Hebrews do not have a grammar so distinct and articulated by the declensions of nouns and verbs as the Latins and Greeks. Thus far Lyra. On which I say that it is uncertain that this angel was Abram's guardian and visitor. For with like, and perhaps greater, likelihood it could be said that he was the guardian of Agar, or rather of her son Ismael, who had an angel in his mother's womb, as other unborn children do; for what this angel said concerned Agar and her son more than Abram. Then it is uncertain that Agar was used to seeing the angel in Abram's house; for she does not seem to have been of such holiness as to see an angel with her senses continually, nor is it to be thought that Abram's angel walked visibly in his house before his household. Nor is it certain that the angel who sometimes appeared to Abram was his guardian, specially appointed to him: for by the same reasoning it could be said that the angels who appeared to the other Prophets and Patriarchs were the special guardians of those to whom they appeared and spoke; whereas the prophet Daniel writes that Gabriel appeared to him[[Dan 8:16||]][[Dan 9:21||]]. Yet it is not denied that sometimes the angels who appeared were the guardians of those to whom they are read to have appeared.

paras.t: Propterea appellavit puteum illum, qui paulo ante vocatus est fons: siquidem omnis puteus, fons est, secundum Augustinum super Joannem: puteum Viventis et videntis me; hoc est, puteum illum appellavit hujusmodi nomine, quod designat puteum illum esse specialiter puteum Dei, qui omnia intuetur, et essentialiter vita ac vivens est, a quo omnis vita descendit; et propter specialem operationem pietatis divinæ, exhibitam huic Agar juxta puteum istum, vocavit hunc puteum nomine isto, quum tamen omnia Dei sint, tanquam summi creatoris universalisque domini. Ipse est inter Cades et Barad, id est, puteus iste situs est inter duo hæc loca: quocirca scribit Hieronymus, Usque hodie puteus Agar monstratur in deserto Arabiæ inter Cades et Barad.
paras.en: [[16:14|Therefore she called that well|Propterea appellavit puteum illum]], which a little before was called a fountain; for every well is a fountain, according to Augustine on John[[John 4:6||]] [Augustine comments on the well of Jacob at John 4:6, where the Gospel calls it both *fons* and *puteus*]: [[16:14|the well of him that liveth and seeth me|puteum Viventis et videntis me]]; that is, she called that well by this name, which shows that well to be in a special way the well of God, who beholds all things, and is life and living by His essence, from whom all life comes down; and because of the special working of the divine kindness shown to this Agar beside that well, she called this well by that name, though all things are God's, as the supreme Creator and universal Lord. [[16:14|The same is between Cades and Barad|Ipse est inter Cades et Barad]], that is, this well lies between these two places; on which Jerome writes: To this day the well of Agar is shown in the desert of Arabia, between Cades and Barad.

16.title: De spirituali ejusdem capituli sextidecimi intellectu
16.title_en: On the spiritual understanding of the same sixteenth chapter

paras.t: Igitur Sarai uxor Abram, non genuerat sibi liberos. Quid duæ uxores Abræ spiritualiter signent, docet Apostolus ad Galatas: Scriptum est, inquiens, quoniam Abraham duos filios habuit, unum de ancilla, et unum de libera: quæ sunt per allegoriam dicta. Hæc enim sunt duo Testamenta. Itaque per Saram principalem Abrahæ conjugem, designatur novum Testamentum, seu evangelica lex vel Ecclesia Christi. Per hoc itaque quod Sarai diu sterilis fuit, atque deinceps maritum suum rogavit, ut ancillam suam acciperet contoralem, quatenus ex ea susciperet filios: figuratum est, quod Ecclesia Christi seu novum Testamentum, tempore legis naturalis ac legis scriptæ, nondum genuit filios spirituales per fontem Baptismi et gratiam Christi. Nondum etenim fuerat propagata tunc evangelica lex, sed latebat et figurabatur in veteri lege. Ipsa quoque Ecclesia in prædestinatione erat divina, et in præscientia Dei fuerat Christo per Abraham figurato sponsata. Et ita quodammodo supplicavit Sponso cœlesti, ut ex Synagoga filios procrearet. Nam Sponsus ille, scilicet Verbum æternum, prævidit quod Ecclesia sua erat omnium hominum desideratura salutem.
paras.en: Now [[16:1|Sarai, the wife of Abram, had brought forth no children|Sarai uxor Abram, non genuerat sibi liberos]]. What the two wives of Abram signify spiritually, the Apostle teaches in writing to the Galatians: [[Gal 4:22|it is written|Scriptum est]], he says, [[Gal 4:22|that Abraham had two sons: the one by a bondwoman and the other by a free woman|quoniam Abraham duos filios habuit, unum de ancilla, et unum de libera]]: [[Gal 4:24|Which things are said by an allegory. For these are the two testaments|quæ sunt per allegoriam dicta. Hæc enim sunt duo Testamenta]]. Thus by Sara, the principal wife of Abraham, is designated the New Testament, or the law of the Gospel, or the Church of Christ. So by this, that Sarai was long barren, and afterwards asked her husband to take her handmaid as his bedfellow, so that she might have children of her, it was figured that the Church of Christ, or the New Testament, in the time of the law of nature and of the written law, did not yet bring forth spiritual children through the font of Baptism and the grace of Christ. For the law of the Gospel had not yet been spread abroad at that time, but lay hidden and was figured in the Old Law. The Church herself, too, was in the divine predestination, and in the foreknowledge of God she had been espoused to Christ, who was figured by Abraham. And so in a manner she besought the heavenly Bridegroom to beget children of the Synagogue. For that Bridegroom, namely the eternal Word, foresaw that his Church would desire the salvation of all men.

paras.t: Peperitque Agar Abræ filium, postquam ad domum Abræ reversa est, Qui vocavit nomen ejus Ismael. Dicunt nonnulli quod Abram ex revelatione cognovit, quod angelus dixerat Agar de sui filii nomine: ideo Abram vocavit eum nomine illo. Verumtamen Abram poterat ex relatione Agar cognoscere, quæ et dicta erant ab angelo.
paras.en: [[16:15|And Agar brought forth a son to Abram|Peperitque Agar Abræ filium]], after she had returned to Abram's house: [[16:15|who called his name Ismael|Qui vocavit nomen ejus Ismael]]. Some say that Abram learned by revelation what the angel had told Agar about the name of her son, and that for this reason Abram called him by that name. Yet Abram could have learned from Agar's own account the things that had been said by the angel.

paras.t: At illa se concepisse videns, despexit dominam suam. Synagoga quippe quæ erat tempore Christi, perpendens quam multos habuerat sub veteri Testamento filios spirituales, contempsit primitivam Ecclesiam, quæ veraciter erat domina Synagogæ per eminentiam gratiæ ac virtutum, imo et per ecclesiasticam potestatem, quoniam Christus commisit beatissimo Petro totum genus humanum tempore suo exsistens, specialiter quoque populum circumcisionis, sicut testatur Paulus apostolus: Qui operatus est, inquiens, Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est et mihi inter gentes.
paras.en: [[16:4|But she perceiving that she was with child, despised her mistress|At illa se concepisse videns, despexit dominam suam]]. For the Synagogue that existed in the time of Christ, weighing how many spiritual children she had had under the Old Testament, despised the primitive Church, which was truly the mistress of the Synagogue by the eminence of grace and of virtues, nay, by ecclesiastical power as well, since Christ committed to most blessed Peter the whole human race living in his time[[Matt 16:18||]][[Matt 16:19||]], and especially the people of the circumcision[[John 21:15||]][[John 21:16||]][[John 21:17||]], as Paul the apostle testifies: [[Gal 2:8|he who wrought|Qui operatus est]], he says, [[Gal 2:8|in Peter to the apostleship of the circumcision wrought in me also among the Gentiles|Petro in apostolatum circumcisionis, operatus est et mihi inter gentes]].

paras.t: Dixitque Sarai ad Abram, id est, primitiva Ecclesia, a Synagoga sic aspernata et injuriata, conquesta est Christo hoc ipsum zelo justitiæ, dicens: Inique agis contra me, id est, non æque te habes quantum ad hoc, quod ita permittis me a Synagoga incredula et superba despici et affligi ac trucidari. Non æque, inquam, respiciendo ad merita mea atque illius, quamvis alio respectu permissum sit hoc justo Dei judicio. Juxta quem sensum S. Job dixit: Intelligite quia Deus non æquo judicio afflixerit me. Ego dedi ancillam meam in sinum tuum, id est, Synagogam a te fecundari optavi.
paras.en: [[16:5|And Sarai said to Abram|Dixitque Sarai ad Abram]], that is, the primitive Church, thus spurned and wronged by the Synagogue, complained of this very thing to Christ out of zeal for justice, saying: [[16:5|Thou dost unjustly with me|Inique agis contra me]], that is, thou dost not deal fairly [Latin *non æque*, "not evenly", glossing *inique*, "unjustly"; Job's *non æquo judicio* below takes up the same word] in this, that thou dost so permit me to be despised and afflicted and slaughtered by the unbelieving and proud Synagogue. Not fairly, I say, if one looks to my merits and to hers, although in another respect this is permitted by the just judgment of God. In this sense holy Job said: [[Job 19:6|understand, that God hath not afflicted me with an equal judgment|Intelligite quia Deus non æquo judicio afflixerit me]]. [[16:5|I gave my handmaid into thy bosom|Ego dedi ancillam meam in sinum tuum]], that is, I wished the Synagogue to be made fruitful by thee.

paras.t: Cui re[…] Abram, videlicet Christus, Ecce, ait, ancilla tua in manu tua est, hoc est, Synagogam […] subjecto. Quotidie namque crevit Ecclesia merito et numero, quousque infideles Judæi Christianis subjecti sunt, in tantum quod utuntur Judæis ad […]atum, a quibus tulerunt Scripturas veteris Testamenti et terram promissionis.
paras.en: [[16:6|to her|Cui]] […] [[16:6|Abram|Abram]], namely Christ: [[16:6|Behold thy handmaid is in thy own hand|Ecce, ait, ancilla tua in manu tua est]], that is, the Synagogue […] I subject. For daily the Church grew in merit and in number, until the unbelieving Jews were made subject to Christians, so much so that they use the Jews for […]atum [the word is partly lost], the Jews from whom they took the Scriptures of the Old Testament and the land of promise.

paras.t: […] Sarai, fugam iniit. Ecclesia Christi Synagogam afflixit, eamdem rationabiliter convincendo per miracula et Scripturas, ita quod Synagoga arripuit fugam, evasiones quærendo, et comparere non audens ad disputandum ac confligendum adversus Christifideles.
paras.en: […] [[16:6|Sarai|Sarai]], [[16:6|she ran away|fugam iniit]]. The Church of Christ afflicted the Synagogue, convincing her by reason through miracles and the Scriptures, so that the Synagogue took to flight, seeking evasions, and not daring to appear to dispute and contend against the faithful of Christ.

paras.t: Quumque invenisset eam angelus Domini juxta fontem aquæ in solitudine, etc. Fons aquæ in solitudine, est Scriptura derelictæ Judææ, juxta quem fontem plebs illa sedet et occupat se, intendens sensui litterali, seu potius litteræ occidenti, non sensui spirituali, neque spiritui vivificanti. Ibi itaque inveniunt eam angeli sancti, qui Judæorum incredulorum custodes sunt, et suggerunt eis, ut pensent unde et quare in istas sint devoluti miserias; persuadentque eis, ut revertantur ad dominam suam, fidem Ecclesiæ amplectendo, et humilientur sub manu ipsius, obtemperando præceptis ejusdem.
paras.en: [[16:7|And the angel of the Lord having found her, by a fountain of water in the wilderness|Quumque invenisset eam angelus Domini juxta fontem aquæ in solitudine]], etc. The fountain of water in the wilderness is the Scripture of forsaken Judea, beside which fountain that people sits and busies itself, attending to the literal sense, or rather to the letter that killeth, not to the spiritual sense nor to the spirit that quickeneth[[2 Cor 3:6||]]. There, then, the holy angels who are the guardians of the unbelieving Jews find her, and suggest to them that they consider whence and why they have fallen into these miseries; and they persuade them to return to their mistress by embracing the faith of the Church, and to be humbled under her hand by obeying her precepts.

paras.t: Et rursum: Multiplicans, inquit, multiplicabo semen tuum, et non numerabitur præ multitudine. Hoc in fine mundi implebitur, quando Synagoga per prædicationem Enoch atque Eliæ convertetur ad Dominum.
