paras.en: [[17:15|God said also to Abraham: Sarai thy wife thou shalt not call Sarai, but Sara|Dixit quoque Deus ad Abraham: Sarai uxorem tuam non vocabis Sarai, sed Saram]]. By Abraham's wife is signified the Church of Christ, which could be called Sarai so long as she flourished in Judea alone, being then, as it were, Christ's princess [that is, *my princess*, the meaning of *Sarai*, as against *Sara*, "princess" without qualification]. But when she began to be spread through the whole world, and to be proclaimed and to hold sway everywhere, she was rightly called Sara, that is, princess absolutely; for according to the oracle of Isaias, [[Is 60:12|the nation and the kingdom that will not serve thee, shall perish|Gens et regnum quod non servierit ei, peribit]]. [[17:16|And I will bless her|Et benedicam ei]]: for God has filled the Church of Christ most abundantly with every heavenly gift. [[17:16|and of her I will give thee a son, whom I will bless|Et ex illa dabo tibi filium cui benedicturus sum]]. By this son is understood the Christian people, converted from the Gentiles through the early Church and spiritually begotten, on whom God has bestowed an unspeakable abundance of graces.

paras.t: Cecidit Abraham in faciem, et risit, quia Christus de his cum ingenti lætitia regratiatus est Patri, dicens in corde suo: Putasne centenario nascetur filius, et Sara nonagenaria pariet? Per centenarium numerum perfectio designatur; per nonagenarium autem, imperfectio quædam. Christus ergo spiritualiter centenarius fuit, quia mente plenissime canus, et maturitate virtutum senex. Ecclesia vero comparatione ipsius imperfecta consistit. Christus itaque non diffidendo, sed divinæ promissioni applaudendo hæc dicit, præsertim hæc referendo ad tempus suæ passionis, quando nubilo afflictionum quasi senio quodam videbatur confectus et Ecclesia ejus instar vetulæ, multiplici calamitate contabescebat, ita quod tunc pene incredibile apparebat quod totus mundus converteretur ad fidem Christi ita suspensi, et quod ipsa Ecclesia ejus tanta impleretur fecunditate, quod converteret omne genus humanum ad Crucifixum. Unde in Isaia scriptum est: Generationem ejus quis enarrabit? quia abscissus est de terra viventium. Quasi dicat: Idcirco spiritualis generatio Christi est inenarrabilis, quoniam ipse instar iniqui occisus est.
paras.en: [[17:17|Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed|Cecidit Abraham in faciem, et risit]]: for Christ thanked the Father for these things with great joy, [[17:17|saying in his heart: Shall a son, thinkest thou, be born to him that is a hundred years old? and shall Sara that is ninety years old bring forth?|dicens in corde suo: Putasne centenario nascetur filius, et Sara nonagenaria pariet?]] By the number one hundred perfection is signified, but by ninety a certain imperfection. Christ, then, was spiritually a hundred years old, for He was fully grey-haired in mind and an old man in the maturity of His virtues; but the Church, compared with Him, remains imperfect. So Christ says these words not in distrust but in applause of the divine promise, especially as He refers them to the time of His Passion, when under the cloud of afflictions He seemed, as it were, worn out with a kind of old age, and His Church, like an old woman, was wasting away under manifold calamity; so that it then seemed almost incredible that the whole world should be converted to the faith of Christ, hanged as He was, and that His Church should be filled with such fruitfulness as to convert the whole human race to the Crucified. Hence it is written in Isaias: [[Is 53:8|who shall declare his generation? because he is cut off out of the land of the living|Generationem ejus quis enarrabit? quia abscissus est de terra viventium]]. As though he were saying: Christ's spiritual generation is past telling precisely because He was put to death like a wicked man.

paras.t: Dixitque ad Dominum: Utinam Ismael vivat coram te! Per Ismael qui vocatur filius carnis, intelligitur carnalis populus Judæorum, pro cujus conversione Christus oravit. Cujus orationem Pater audivit, quia in primo Christi adventu et deinceps multa millia Judæorum conversa sunt. Interim quoque valde multiplicantur, et tandem in fine sæculi omnes tunc victuri, credent in Christum. Porro filius natus ex Sara, id est populus christianus, recte vocatur Isaac, hoc est risus, quia spirituali jucunditate perfunditur, et de ejus conversione angeli sancti lætantur. Christus quoque gavisus est. Ad quem populum Deus statuit pactum suum, videlicet evangelicam legem, novumque Testamentum.
paras.en: [[17:18|And he said to God|Dixitque ad Dominum]]: [[17:18|O that Ismael may live before thee|Utinam Ismael vivat coram te]]! By Ismael, who is called the son of the flesh, is understood the carnal people of the Jews, for whose conversion Christ prayed. And the Father heard His prayer, for at Christ's first coming and afterwards many thousands of Jews were converted. Meanwhile, too, they are greatly multiplied, and at last, at the end of the world, all who are then alive will believe in Christ. Further, the son born of Sara, that is, the Christian people, is rightly called Isaac, that is, laughter, for he is filled with spiritual gladness, and the holy angels rejoice at his conversion; Christ also rejoiced. With this people God established His covenant, namely the Gospel law and the New Testament.

paras.t: Tulit autem Abraham Ismaelem filium suum et omnes vernaculos, etc. Per hoc figuratum est, quod Christus in sua Ecclesia universos fideles cujuscumque sint status, gradus, dignitatis aut ordinis, spiritualiter circumcidit.
paras.en: [[17:23|And Abraham took Ismael his son, and all that were born in his house|Tulit autem Abraham Ismaelem filium suum et omnes vernaculos]], etc. By this it was prefigured that Christ, in His Church, spiritually circumcises all the faithful, of whatever state, rank, dignity or order they may be.

paras.t: Nunc breviter est tangendus tropologicus hujus capituli sensus, quo per Abraham intelligitur quicumque Christifidelis, præsertim prælatus aut religiosus, cui loquitur Dominus: Ambula coram me, juste et timorate vivendo, atque sollicite in Dei præsentia te custodiendo, ut cum Propheta psallere queas: Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo. Et esto perfectus, juxta illud: Estote perfecti, sicut et Pater vester cælestis perfectus est. Status autem prælatorum majorum, videlicet præsulum, est status perfectionis acquisitæ: status autem religiosorum, est status perfectionis acquirendæ.
paras.en: Now the tropological [that is, moral] sense of this chapter must be touched on briefly. In it Abraham stands for any one of Christ's faithful, especially a prelate or a religious, to whom the Lord says: [[17:1|walk before me|Ambula coram me]], by living justly and in fear of God, and by keeping thyself carefully in God's presence, so that thou mayest sing with the Prophet: [[Ps 118:168|I have kept thy commandments and thy testimonies: because all my ways are in thy sight|Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo]]. And [[17:1|be perfect|esto perfectus]], according to the saying: [[Matt 5:48|Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect|Estote perfecti, sicut et Pater vester cælestis perfectus est]]. Now the state of the greater prelates, namely bishops, is the state of perfection acquired; but the state of religious is the state of perfection to be acquired [a distinction of the schools: a bishop is bound to exercise a perfection he is presumed already to have, a religious binds himself by vow to strive for it].

paras.t: Præterea verbum istud, Ambula coram me, Nicolaus de Lyra exponit sic, id est, ac si me præsentialiter semper videres: quæ expositio Rabbi Paulo non placet, quia (ut ait) qui ambulat coram alio, non semper eum videt, sed potius qui sequitur eum. Ideo dicit quod Sancti qui fuerunt ante Christi adventum, dicuntur ambulasse coram Deo, quoniam exemplar perfectionis, videlicet Christum Deum incarnatum, habuerunt post se. Hinc David, Ezechias et tales scribuntur coram Domino ambulasse. Porro Sancti novi Testamenti dicuntur Deum esse secuti, juxta illud: Qui mihi ministrat, me sequatur: quoniam exemplar perfectionis præfatum ante se habuerunt. Sed istud non videtur magni valoris, quia et justi veteris Testamenti, frequenter leguntur Deum secuti, quemadmodum in Numerorum libro Deus testatur: Servum meum Caleb, qui plenus Spiritu secutus est me, inducam in terram quam circuivit. Et idem de Josue ait Scriptura. Rursusque in libro Josue Caleb fatetur: Fratres mei subverterunt cor populi, et nihilo minus ego secutus sum Dominum Deum meum. Sed et S. Job: Vestigia, inquit, ejus secutus est pes meus. Et de David rege Dominus contestatur: David secutus est me in toto corde suo. Præterea Rabbi Paulus affirmat, quod Abraham imitator fuit perfectionis Christi: ergo et Abraham secutus est Christum. Quid enim est imitari nisi sequi? Amplius, quod etiam justis novi Testamenti conveniat coram Domino ambulare, probatur ex cantico evangelici Zachariæ, qui causam incarnationis, adventusque Christi exprimens, ait: Visitavit et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ, ut sine timore serviamus illi in sanctitate et justitia coram ipso. Certumque est, quod Deo servire in sanctitate et justitia coram ipso, aliud nihil sit quam coram ipso ambulare. Postremo, qui ambulat coram alio, melius potest eum inspicere seu vultum ejus attendere, quam qui ambulat retro eum.
paras.en: Further, Nicholas of Lyra expounds this word, [[17:1|walk before me|Ambula coram me]], thus: that is, as if thou wert always seeing me present. This exposition does not please Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos, the converted rabbi whose Additions to Lyra's Postill Denis often cites], because (as he says) he who walks before another does not always see him; rather, he who follows him does. So he says that the Saints who lived before Christ's coming are said to have walked before God because they had the exemplar of perfection, namely Christ, God incarnate, behind them. Hence David[[2 Kings 7:9||]], Ezechias[[4 Kings 20:3||]] and such men are written to have walked before the Lord. But the Saints of the New Testament are said to have followed God, according to the saying: [[John 12:26|minister to me, let him follow me|Qui mihi ministrat, me sequatur]], since they had that exemplar of perfection before them. But this does not seem of much weight, for the just of the Old Testament too are often read to have followed God, as God testifies in the book of Numbers: [[Num 14:24|My servant Caleb, who being full of another spirit hath followed me, I will bring into this land which he hath gone round|Servum meum Caleb, qui plenus Spiritu secutus est me, inducam in terram quam circuivit]] [where the Douay-Rheims and the Vulgate have "full of another spirit", Denis reads "full of the Spirit"]. And Scripture says the same of Josue. And again in the book of Josue Caleb declares: [[Jos 14:8|my brethren|Fratres mei]] [[Jos 14:8|discouraged the heart of the people: and I nevertheless followed the Lord my God|subverterunt cor populi, et nihilo minus ego secutus sum Dominum Deum meum]]. And holy Job too: [[Job 23:11|his steps|Vestigia]], he says, [[Job 23:11|my foot hath followed|ejus secutus est pes meus]]. And of King David the Lord bears witness: David [[3 Kings 14:8|followed me with all his heart|secutus est me in toto corde suo]]. Further, Rabbi Paul affirms that Abraham was an imitator of Christ's perfection: therefore Abraham too followed Christ; for what is it to imitate, if not to follow? Moreover, that it befits the just of the New Testament also to walk before the Lord is proved from the canticle of Zachary in the Gospel, who, setting forth the reason for the Incarnation and coming of Christ, says: [[Luke 1:68|he hath visited and wrought the redemption of his people|Visitavit et fecit redemptionem plebis suæ]], [[Luke 1:74|we may serve him without fear|sine timore serviamus illi]] [[Luke 1:75|In holiness and justice before him|in sanctitate et justitia coram ipso]]. And it is certain that to serve God in holiness and justice before Him is nothing other than to walk before Him. Lastly, he who walks before another can look at him, or attend to his face, better than he who walks behind him.

paras.t: Ponamque fœdus meum inter me et te. Hoc facit Deus unicuique vere fideli, dum eum induit ad actualem divinæ legis memoriam, et in Scripturis ei promittit vitam beatam. Et multiplicabo te vehementer. Hoc fit, dum Deus meritis et precibus seu prædicationibus et exemplis servorum suorum alios multos convertit. Et item, dum servo suo ferventi præstat quotidie augmentum bonorum actuum copiosum.
paras.en: [[17:2|And I will make my covenant between me and thee|Ponamque fœdus meum inter me et te]]. This God does for every truly faithful soul when He leads him to keep the divine law actually in mind, and promises him in the Scriptures the life of bliss. [[17:2|and I will multiply thee exceedingly|Et multiplicabo te vehementer]]. This comes about when God converts many others by the merits and prayers, or the preaching and examples, of His servants; and also when He daily grants His fervent servant an abundant increase of good acts.

paras.t: Erisque pater multarum gentium. Hoc præcipue competit sanctis episcopis, qui verbo et exemplo generant Christo plures filios spirituales, ita quod vehementissime crescunt meritis, spiritualique sobole. Ex quibus episcopis et prælatis reges egrediuntur, dum eorum spirituales filii, discipuli ac subditi, tantæ perfectionis consistunt, quod aliis digne præficiuntur, et se ipsos ac illos efficaciter regunt. Vel, reges uniuscujusque boni fidelis, sunt actus contemplativi et considerationes sapientiales, per quos inferiora opera regulantur ac judicantur.
paras.en: [[17:4|and thou shalt be a father of many nations|Erisque pater multarum gentium]]. This belongs above all to holy bishops, who by word and example beget many spiritual sons for Christ, so that they [[17:6|increase exceedingly|vehementissime crescunt]] in merits and in spiritual offspring. And from these bishops and prelates [[17:6|kings shall come out|reges egrediuntur]], when their spiritual sons, disciples and subjects are of such perfection that they are worthily set over others, and rule both themselves and those others effectively. Or else the kings of each good faithful soul are its acts of contemplation and its considerations of wisdom, by which its lower works are ruled and judged.

paras.t: Deinde Dominus præcipit unicuique Christifideli, præsertim prælato, ut pactum suum, scilicet circumcisionis præceptum, spiritualiter impleat, non unum dumtaxat membrum corporaliter circumcidendo, sed universa corporis membra et animæ vires ab omni vitiorum abusu, vel ab omni opere pravo totaliter refrenando, quatenus juxta Apostolum: Exhibeamus membra nostra arma justitiæ Deo, et serviamus per ea justitiæ in sanctificationem: avertamusque oculos nostros, ne videant vanitatem; et aures nostras sepiamus spinis ne audiant linguam nequam: ostiumque circumstantiæ ponamus labiis nostris, ne loquamur verbum illicitum; sed et manum et pedem, et quodcumque membrum nostrum nos scandalizaverit, abscidamus, non quantum ad substantiam, sed quoad usum perversum. Hoc est quod ait Apostolus: Mortificate membra vestra, quæ sunt super terram. Hæc est vera spiritualis Deoque placens et figurata circumcisio populi christiani, cujus umbra et typus fuit circumcisio illa legalis. Unde per Jeremiam Dominus dixit: Circumcidite præputia cordium vestrorum. Paulus quoque apostolus: Nos, ait, sumus circumcisio qui spiritu Deo servimus, et non in carne fiduciam habemus. Itemque: Non enim qui in manifesto Judæus, neque quæ in carne circumcisio est, sed qui in occulto Judæus, et circumcisio cordis in spiritu, et non in littera.
paras.en: Then the Lord commands every one of Christ's faithful, especially a prelate, to fulfil His covenant, that is, the precept of circumcision, spiritually: not by circumcising one member only, in the body, but by wholly restraining all the members of the body and the powers of the soul from every abuse of vice, or from every evil work; so that, as the Apostle says, we may yield our members [[Rom 6:13|as instruments of justice unto God|arma justitiæ Deo]], and through them [[Rom 6:19|serve justice, unto sanctification|serviamus per ea justitiæ in sanctificationem]] [the margin gives Rom. xv, 19; the words are from Rom 6:13 and 6:19]; and turn away our eyes, [[Ps 118:37|that they may not behold vanity|ne videant vanitatem]]; and hedge in our ears [[Ecclus 28:28|with thorns|spinis]], that they hear not [[Ecclus 28:28|a wicked tongue|linguam nequam]]; and set [[Ps 140:3|a door round about|ostiumque circumstantiæ]] our lips, that we speak no unlawful word; and also that we cut off hand and foot and whatever member of ours shall scandalize us[[Matt 5:29||]][[Matt 5:30||]] [hand and foot together are named at Matt 18:8], not as to its substance but as to its perverse use. This is what the Apostle says: [[Col 3:5|Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth|Mortificate membra vestra, quæ sunt super terram]]. This is the true, spiritual circumcision of the Christian people, pleasing to God and prefigured, whose shadow and type was that circumcision of the Law. Hence the Lord said through Jeremias: Circumcise [[Jer 4:4|the foreskins of your hearts|præputia cordium vestrorum]] [the Vulgate has *auferte*, "take away", where Denis writes *Circumcidite*]. And Paul the Apostle: [[Phil 3:3|we|Nos]], he says, [[Phil 3:3|are the circumcision, who in spirit serve God|sumus circumcisio qui spiritu Deo servimus]], [[Phil 3:3|not having confidence in the flesh|et non in carne fiduciam habemus]]. And again: [[Rom 2:28|For it is not he is a Jew, who is so outwardly: nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh|Non enim qui in manifesto Judæus, neque quæ in carne circumcisio est]], [[Rom 2:29|But he is a Jew that is one inwardly and the circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit not in the letter|sed qui in occulto Judæus, et circumcisio cordis in spiritu, et non in littera]].

paras.t: Dixit quoque Deus ad Abraham: Sarai uxorem tuam non vocabis Sarai, sed Saram. Uxor viri virtuosi, potest dici anima ejus, seu sensitiva pars animæ, aut etiam mens rationalis, quorum unumquodque fecundatur ab homine, et recte Sara vocatur, dum motibus vitiorum et passionibus dominatur, paritque filium cui Dominus benedicit, id est actum meritorium æterno præmio dignum.
paras.en: [[17:15|God said also to Abraham: Sarai thy wife thou shalt not call Sarai, but Sara|Dixit quoque Deus ad Abraham: Sarai uxorem tuam non vocabis Sarai, sed Saram]]. The wife of a virtuous man may be called his soul, or the sensitive part of the soul, or again the rational mind; each of these is made fruitful by the man, and is rightly called Sara [that is, princess] when it rules over the motions of the vices and the passions, and bears a son whom the Lord blesses, that is, a meritorious act worthy of eternal reward.

paras.t: Denique dum Dominus per Scripturas et suos vicarios seu alios bonos viros hortatur nos ad viam perfectionis, et actus præcipuos contemplationis, non debemus diffidere aut pusillanimes esse, sed sperando in adjutorio Altissimi, ardua viriliter aggredi, atque in caritatis fervore et omni puritate interna infatigabiliter crescere; nihilo minus tamen orare, ut Ismael coram Domino vivat, id est, exercitatio vitæ activæ non pereat, sed potius crescat assidue loco et tempore opportuno, ut generet duces duodecim, disponendo et cooperando ad observantiam duodecim evangelicorum Christi consiliorum. Pactum vero Dei, videlicet familiaris confœderatio, statuatur ad Isaac, id est ad apicem mentis, qui non delectatur nisi in Domino, et fertur ad optima.
paras.en: Again, when the Lord, through the Scriptures and through His vicars or other good men, urges us to the way of perfection and to the chief acts of contemplation, we must not distrust or be faint-hearted, but, hoping [[Ps 90:1|in the aid of the most High|in adjutorio Altissimi]], manfully take on hard things, and grow tirelessly in the fervour of charity and in all inward purity; yet none the less we must pray [[17:18|that Ismael may live|ut Ismael coram Domino vivat]] before the Lord, that is, that the practice of the active life may not perish, but rather grow steadily in due place and time, so that [[17:20|he shall beget twelve chiefs|generet duces duodecim]], by preparing for and helping toward the keeping of Christ's twelve evangelical counsels [the counsels of perfection, which some medieval writers counted as twelve]. But let God's covenant, that is, His familiar alliance with the soul, be established with Isaac, that is, with the apex of the mind [that is, the highest point of the soul, where it meets God in contemplation], which delights in nothing but the Lord and is borne toward the best things.

paras.t: Postremo Richardus: Tres, inquit, sunt circumcisiones: Una tantum in carne, alia spiritualis in vita præsenti per depositionem iniquitatum, tertia erit in corpore et spiritu, in resurrectione futura per depositionem totius corruptionis et pronitatis in malum.
paras.en: Lastly Richard says: There are three circumcisions. One is in the flesh only; another is spiritual, in the present life, by the putting away of iniquities; the third will be in body and spirit, at the resurrection to come, by the putting away of all corruption and of the proneness to evil.

18.title: Declaratio litteralis capituli octavidecimi: Apparuit autem ei Dominus in convalle
18.title_en: Literal declaration of the eighteenth chapter: And the Lord appeared to him in the vale

paras.t: SCRIPTURA consequenter narrat, qualiter Deus nativitatem Isaac plenius prænuntiavit, et suam justitiam in impiis, suamque misericordiam in bonis ac piis monstravit. Apparuit autem ei, videlicet Abrahæ, Dominus in convalle Mambre. Circa hæc scribit Lyra : Aliter exponitur littera ista a doctoribus catholicis, et aliter ab Hebræis. Utraque tamen expositio consonat fidei. Dicunt ergo Hebræi, quod hic describitur apparitio duplex. Una ipsius Dei quum dicitur, Apparuit ei Dominus, etc. : alia angelorum, dum subditur, Quumque elevasset oculos, apparuerunt ei tres viri. Doctores autem catholici asserunt hic unam visionem conscribi. Circa hoc dico, quod nec omnes doctores Hebræi dicunt hic duas apparitiones describi, nec omnes doctores catholici dicunt hic describi unam tantummodo visionem. Nempe ut recitat Rabbi Paulus, Rabbi Moyses in libro de Directione perplexorum testatur, quod hic describitur visio una, ita quod per hoc quod dictum est, Quumque elevasset oculos, explicatur quod ante generaliter dictum fuit, Apparuit ei Dominus, utpote qualiter Dominus apparuit Abrahæ. Josephus quoque idem sentire videtur. Præterea quidam doctores catholici senserunt hic duas apparitiones describi : unam ipsius Dei, videlicet Verbi æterni seu Unigeniti Patris, quum dicitur, Apparuit ei Dominus, quoniam ipsum Verbum æternum testatur in Joanne : Abraham exsultavit ut videret diem meum ; vidit, et gavisus est. Quod secundum doctores in hac visione peractum est. Ait quippe Eusebius : Quum Verbum Dei primo omnium Prophetarum apparuisset Abrahæ in forma humana, vocationem gentium ei promisit. Sicque apparuit ei Dei Filius quem adoravit. Alcuinus quoque fatetur, et habetur in Glossa, quod duo viri Filium Dei comitabantur, Moyses scilicet, qui Christi adventum annuntiavit in lege, et Elias, qui secundum Christi adventum præveniet, et ejus Evangelium prædicabit : qui duo cum Christo in ejus transfiguratione sunt visi. Sed verba ista intelligi nequeunt ita, quod duo viri fuerunt realiter Moyses et Elias, quum ex consequentibus pateat evidenter eos angelos fuisse : quod et Apostolus ad Hebræos effatur : Hospitalitatem, inquiens, nolite oblivisci ; per hanc enim placuerunt quidam angelis hospitio receptis. Et per quosdam, intelliguntur ibi Abraham et Lot, secundum omnes expositores catholicos. Hinc in Scholastica habetur historia : Duo angeli apparuerunt, in designatione duorum præconum, Moysis scilicet et Eliæ. Unde auctor illius Historiæ videtur sentire, quod tertius ibi apparens, fuit angelus in persona Filii Dei se repræsentans et loquens, quod et glossa illius Historiæ ait aperte.
paras.en: Scripture next relates how God foretold the birth of Isaac more fully, and shewed His justice upon the wicked and His mercy towards the good and devout. [[18:1|And the Lord appeared to him|Apparuit autem ei]], that is, to Abraham, [[18:1|in the vale of Mambre|Dominus in convalle Mambre]]. On this Lyra writes: This text is expounded one way by the Catholic doctors and another way by the Hebrews; yet both expositions agree with the faith. The Hebrews say, then, that a twofold apparition is described here: one of God Himself, where it says, [[18:1|the Lord appeared to him|Apparuit ei Dominus]], etc.; the other of angels, where it adds, [[18:2|And when he had lifted up his eyes, there appeared to him three men|Quumque elevasset oculos, apparuerunt ei tres viri]]. The Catholic doctors, however, assert that one vision is set down here. On this I say that neither do all the Hebrew doctors say that two apparitions are described here, nor do all the Catholic doctors say that only one vision is described here. For, as Rabbi Paul relates, Rabbi Moses, in the book of the Guide of the Perplexed [the *Moreh Nebuchim* of Moses Maimonides], testifies that one vision is described here, so that by the words [[18:2|And when he had lifted up his eyes|Quumque elevasset oculos]] is explained what was said before in general, [[18:1|the Lord appeared to him|Apparuit ei Dominus]]: namely, in what way the Lord appeared to Abraham. Josephus too seems to hold the same. Moreover, some Catholic doctors held that two apparitions are described here: one of God Himself, namely of the eternal Word or Only-begotten of the Father, where it says, [[18:1|the Lord appeared to him|Apparuit ei Dominus]], since the eternal Word Himself testifies in John: Abraham [[John 8:56|rejoiced that he might see my day: he saw it and was glad|exsultavit ut videret diem meum ; vidit, et gavisus est]]. And this, according to the doctors, came to pass in this vision. For Eusebius says: When the Word of God, first of all the Prophets, had appeared to Abraham in human form, He promised him the calling of the Gentiles. And so the Son of God appeared to him, and he adored Him. Alcuin also states, and it is found in the Gloss, that two men accompanied the Son of God: namely Moses, who announced the coming of Christ in the law, and Elias, who will go before the second coming of Christ and will preach His Gospel; which two were seen with Christ in His transfiguration[[Matt 17:3||]]. But these words cannot be understood as though the two men were really Moses and Elias, since it is plain from what follows that they were angels; which the Apostle too declares to the Hebrews: [[Heb 13:2|hospitality|Hospitalitatem]], he says, [[Heb 13:2|do not forget|nolite oblivisci]]: [[Heb 13:2|for by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels|per hanc enim placuerunt quidam angelis hospitio receptis]] [Denis reads *placuerunt quidam*, "some have pleased the angels they received as guests", where the Vulgate has *latuerunt quidam*, "some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels"]. And by *some* are meant there Abraham and Lot, according to all Catholic expositors. Hence it is found in the Scholastic History [the *Historia scholastica* of Peter Comestor]: Two angels appeared, signifying the two heralds, namely Moses and Elias. Whence the author of that History seems to hold that the third who appeared there was an angel representing the person of the Son of God and speaking in His person; which the gloss on that History also says openly.

paras.t: Porro B. Augustinus, eorum quæ fidei sunt acutissimus et fidelissimus considerator, istud quod de apparitione Filii Dei in forma humana prædictum est, reprobat dicendo : Apparuit Deus Abrahæ ad quercum Mambre in tribus viris, quos fuisse angelos non est dubitandum, quamvis quidam existiment unum ex eis fuisse Dominum Christum, asserentes eum ante indumentum carnis fuisse visibilem, id est, ante incarnationem suam visibiliter apparuisse. Sed si ideo aliquem horum trium affirmant fuisse Christum, quia quum tres vidisset, ad unum singulariter est locutus, eumque adoravit : cur non advertunt duos ex angelis illis venisse ad Sodomam subvertendam, quum Abraham adhuc loqueretur cum uno illo, quem singulariter Dominum appellavit, et ne Sodoma subverteretur, eumdem rogavit ? Alii duo a Lot suscepti sunt, et unum eorum singulariter est affatus, Dominumque vocavit, et pro sua salvatione deprecatus est illum. Scriptum est enim sequenti capitulo : Dixit Lot ad eos : Quæso, Domine mi, quia invenit servus tuus gratiam coram te, etc. Multo ergo credibilius est, quod Abraham in tribus viris illis, et Lot in duobus ex eis, Dominum cognoscebant, cui per singularem numerum loquebantur, quum angelos illos esse homines arbitrabantur : in quibus tamen aliquid tantæ eminentiæ considerabant, ut non dubitarent Dominum esse in eis, sicut fuit in sanctis Prophetis ; ideo alloquebantur eos quandoque pluraliter, atque interdum in eis Dominum singulariter appellabant. Hæc Augustinus.
paras.en: But Blessed Augustine, a most acute and most faithful considerer of the things of faith, rejects what has been said above about the apparition of the Son of God in human form, saying: God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mambre in three men, who, it is not to be doubted, were angels; although some think that one of them was the Lord Christ, asserting that He was visible before He put on the garment of flesh, that is, that He appeared visibly before His incarnation. But if they affirm that one of these three was Christ because, when Abraham had seen three, he spoke to one in the singular and adored him, why do they not notice that two of those angels came to overthrow Sodom while Abraham was still speaking with that one whom he called Lord in the singular, and whom he begged that Sodom should not be overthrown? The other two were received by Lot, and he addressed one of them in the singular, and called him Lord, and besought him for his deliverance. For it is written in the following chapter: [[Gen 19:18|And Lot said to them: I beseech thee, my Lord|Dixit Lot ad eos : Quæso, Domine mi]], [[Gen 19:19|Because thy servant hath found grace before thee|quia invenit servus tuus gratiam coram te]], etc. It is therefore much more credible that Abraham in those three men, and Lot in two of them, recognized the Lord, to whom they spoke in the singular number, while they thought those angels to be men; in whom nevertheless they perceived something of such eminence that they did not doubt that the Lord was in them, as He was in the holy Prophets. So they addressed them sometimes in the plural, and at times called upon the Lord in them in the singular. Thus far Augustine.

paras.t: Ex cujus etiam verbis jam elucescit, quod in exordio hujus capituli usque ibi, Quos quum vidisset, etc., non duæ visiones, sed una dumtaxat visio describatur. Etenim ait, Apparuit Deus Abrahæ ad quercum Mambre in tribus viris, etc. His consonat quod in Scholastica fertur historia : Nunquam legitur Pater apparuisse in creatura subjecta ante primum Christi adventum. Ex quo ibi innuitur, quod nec Filius ante Incarnationis mysterium visibiliter apparuit in aliqua creata similitudine sensibili ipsum immediate repræsentante. Hinc quoque Thomas super primum Sententiarum, distinctione 16, aliique quamplures determinant, quod ad Patres veteris Testamenti non sit facta visibilis missio alicujus divinæ Personæ. Verumtamen quidam dicunt, quod Augustinus istud non approbet, scilicet Patrem non apparuisse in veteri Testamento in subjecta creatura, propter id quod in Daniele legitur : Antiquus dierum sedit. In qua etiam visione Daniel protestatur se quasi Filium hominis vidisse, videlicet Christum. Sed isti imperite loqui videntur. Nam visio illa Danielis imaginaria fuit in nocte et somno ostensa, sicut ibidem plenius scripsi. In tali autem visione non proprie res ipsa, sed similitudo rei ostenditur per species in vi imaginativa formatas, ita quod res quæ apparet, non ita, sicut apparet, extra imaginationem vere realiterque consistit. Idcirco in tali apparitione non dicitur Deus seu divina apparuisse Persona in creatura subjecta, sed in similitudine repræsentativa.
paras.en: From his words, too, it is now clear that from the beginning of this chapter as far as [[18:2|as soon as he saw them|Quos quum vidisset]], etc., not two visions but only one vision is described. For he says, God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mambre in three men, etc. With this agrees what is said in the Scholastic History: The Father is never read to have appeared in a subject creature [that is, in a created thing made use of to represent Him] before the first coming of Christ. From which it is implied there that neither did the Son, before the mystery of the Incarnation, appear visibly in any created sensible likeness representing Him immediately. Hence too Thomas on the first book of the Sentences, distinction 16, and very many others determine that no visible mission of any divine Person was made to the Fathers of the Old Testament [a *visible mission*: the sending of a divine Person made known by a visible sign, as of the Holy Ghost in the form of a dove]. Some, however, say that Augustine does not approve this, namely that the Father did not appear in the Old Testament in a subject creature, because of what is read in Daniel: [[Dan 7:9|the ancient of days sat|Antiquus dierum sedit]]. In that same vision Daniel declares that he saw as it were the Son of man, namely Christ. But these seem to speak unskilfully. For that vision of Daniel was imaginary [that is, seen in the imagination, not with the bodily eyes], shown at night and in sleep, as I have written more fully in that place. In such a vision it is not properly the thing itself but a likeness of the thing that is shown, through images formed in the imaginative power, so that the thing which appears does not truly and really exist outside the imagination as it appears. Therefore in such an apparition God, or a divine Person, is not said to have appeared in a subject creature, but in a representative likeness.

paras.t: His præmissis, exponenda est littera. Apparuit ei Dominus in convalle Mambre : Abraham namque tunc habitavit in valle, quæ a viro nomine Mambre vocata est vallis Mambre, ut supra diffusius dictum est ; sedenti in ostio tabernaculi sui, in quo sedebat ad circumspiciendum an videret aliquos peregrinos aut inopes pertranseuntes, quatenus eos ad suam deduceret domum, et bene tractaret : in quo patet, quam devotissima mente intentus erat hospitalitati et actibus pietatis, ita quod arbitrabatur donum Dei, si peregrinis et pauperibus curam impenderet hospitalem ; in ipso fervore diei : ita quod nec propter solis æstum cessavit a tali occupatione tam pia, et circa meridiem specialiter circumspexit, quia tunc aptum est tempus reficiendi personas hujusmodi. His verbis descripta est visio ista in generali ; consequenter in speciali describitur, utpote qualiter facta sit.
paras.en: With this premised, the letter is to be expounded. [[18:1|the Lord appeared to him in the vale of Mambre|Apparuit ei Dominus in convalle Mambre]]: for Abraham was then dwelling in the valley which, after a man named Mambre, was called the vale of Mambre, as was said more at length above; [[18:1|as he was sitting at the door of his tent|sedenti in ostio tabernaculi sui]], where he sat to look about, whether he might see any pilgrims or poor people passing by, so as to bring them to his house and treat them well. In this it is plain with how devout a mind he was intent on hospitality and works of piety, so that he counted it a gift of God if he could bestow hospitable care on pilgrims and the poor; [[18:1|in the very heat of the day|in ipso fervore diei]]: so that not even because of the heat of the sun did he leave off so pious an occupation; and about midday he looked about especially, because that is the fitting time for refreshing such persons. In these words this vision is described in general; next it is described in particular, namely how it took place.

paras.t: Quumque elevasset, etc. Circa hæc scribit Lyra : Quædam glossa Hebraica dicit hic, quod Abraham voluit surgere ex reverentia apparitionis divinæ, sed Dominus dixit : Sede, tu es enim signum filiis tuis, quia futurum est ut filii tui sedeant tanquam judices in concilio, et ego stem. Quæ glossa consonat fidei nostræ, atque impleta est quando Salvator noster Deus et homo, stetit coram principibus sacerdotum, consedentibus in concilio ad ipsum dijudicandum. Nescio tamen quid intellexerit iste glossator per verba præhabita. Contingit enim interdum, Deo sic disponente, ut loquens præter propriam intentionem verba sua sic proferat, quod consonant fidei orthodoxæ, quemadmodum in Joanne legitur Caiphas protulisse : Expedit ut unus moriatur homo pro populo et non tota gens pereat. Hæc Lyra.
paras.en: [[18:2|And when he had lifted up|Quumque elevasset]], etc. On this Lyra writes: A certain Hebrew gloss says here that Abraham wished to rise out of reverence for the divine apparition, but the Lord said: Sit, for thou art a sign to thy sons, since it shall come to pass that thy sons sit as judges in council, and I stand. This gloss agrees with our faith, and was fulfilled when our Saviour, God and man, stood before the chief priests as they sat together in council to judge Him. Yet I do not know what this glossator understood by the words given above. For it sometimes happens, by God's disposing, that a speaker utters his words, beyond his own intention, in such a way that they agree with the orthodox faith; as we read in John that Caiphas said: [[John 11:50|it is expedient|Expedit]] [[John 11:50|that one man should die for the people and that the whole nation perish not|ut unus moriatur homo pro populo et non tota gens pereat]]. Thus far Lyra.

paras.t: Itaque apparuit Dominus Abrahæ per angelos, sicut subjungitur : Quumque elevasset oculos, ad circumspiciendum ex causa præfacta apparuerunt ei tres viri, id est tres angeli in specie habituque virili, stantes prope eum, id est non remote ab eo. Septuaginta transtulerunt, Propter eum : quoniam propter eum venerunt, quamvis non tantum propter eum. Denique quum esset tanta devotione hospitalitati intentus, meruit pro hominibus angelos sanctos suscipere. Origenes utitur littera tali, Stantes super eum. Et dicit quod Scriptura sic loquitur, ad insinuandum præcipua merita Abrahæ, cui angeli spiritualiter propinquissimi erant, eo quod ipse vitam angelis quamplacentissimam duceret. Ait equidem Origenes : Conferamus visionem hanc Abrahæ, cum illa quæ facta est Lot. Tres angeli veniunt ad Abraham, et stant super eum. Ad Lot veniunt duo, et sedent in platea. Vide si non dispensatione Spiritus Sancti, pro meritis res geruntur. Etenim Lot longe inferior erat Abraham ; alias terra et habitatio Sodomorum ei non placuisset. Veniunt ergo tres viri ad Abraham meridie, ad Lot duo de vespere. Non enim capiebat Lot magnitudinem lucis meridianæ, cujus Abraham capax fuit. Hæc Origenes. Quos quum vidisset, cucurrit in occursum eorum : putavit quippe quod homines peregrini essent, ideo acceleravit ad ipsos, ut ipsos ad suam deduceret mansionem, et bene reficeret eos. In quo innotescit mirabilis fervor, devotio, humilitas, pietas et liberalitas hujus beatissimi Patriarchæ.
paras.en: So the Lord appeared to Abraham through angels, as is added: [[18:2|And when he had lifted up his eyes|Quumque elevasset oculos]], to look about, for the reason given before, [[18:2|there appeared to him three men|apparuerunt ei tres viri]], that is, three angels in the form and dress of men, [[18:2|standing near to him|stantes prope eum]], that is, not far from him. The Seventy translated, *Because of him* [*propter eum* for *prope eum*, "near him"]: since they came because of him, though not only because of him. For since he was intent on hospitality with such devotion, he deserved to receive holy angels in place of men. Origen uses this text, *Standing over him*. And he says that Scripture speaks so in order to suggest the special merits of Abraham, to whom the angels were spiritually very near, because he led a life most pleasing to the angels. For Origen says: Let us compare this vision of Abraham with that which took place with Lot. Three angels come to Abraham, and stand over him; to Lot come two, and sit in the street. See whether things are not done according to merits, by the dispensation of the Holy Ghost. For Lot was far inferior to Abraham; otherwise the land and dwelling of the Sodomites would not have pleased him. So three men come to Abraham at midday, two to Lot at evening. For Lot could not take in the greatness of the midday light, of which Abraham was capable. Thus far Origen. [[18:2|as soon as he saw them, he ran to meet them|Quos quum vidisset, cucurrit in occursum eorum]]: for he thought they were pilgrims, and so he hastened to them, to bring them to his dwelling and refresh them well. In this is made known the wonderful fervour, devotion, humility, piety and liberality of this most blessed Patriarch.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, cur tres angeli simul apparuerunt. Ad hoc Sancti respondent, quod Deus altissimus, unus in essentia, et trinus in personis, misit angelos tres ad superbeatissimæ Trinitatis mysterium designandum. Unde et Abraham in tribus uni singulariter est locutus, unumque adoravit : propter quod cantat Ecclesia : Abraham tres vidit, et unum adoravit. Josephus vero et alii multi dicunt, quod unus angelorum illorum missus fuit annuntiare futuram Isaac conceptionem ; alii duo, ut everterent Sodomam. Porro, ut recitat Lyra, Hebræi dicunt, quod isti tres angeli fuerunt Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, atque quod Michael missus fuit ad denuntiandum de Isaac nascituro, Gabriel ad Sodomam evertendam, Raphael ad sanandum Abraham adhuc dolentem ex circumcisione (nam dicunt apparitionem istam contigisse tertia die post circumcisionem illius), et ad eripiendum ipsum Lot cum suis de periculo Sodomorum. Ista pro majori parte videntur incerta, an scilicet tres angeli illi, fuerunt personæ tres istæ præfatæ, et an apparitio ista contigerit tertio die post Abrahæ circumcisionem. Itemque, an unus missus fuit ad Abraham de illo dolore curandum, quia de hoc textus nil loquitur, et etiam an unus specialiter venit ad Sodomæ eversionem, præsertim quum sequenti capitulo duo angeli protestentur : Delebimus locum istum. Et iterum : Misit nos Dominus ut perdamus illos. Quo constat, quod ambo missi erant ad hoc. Ambo quoque admonuerunt Lot ad exeundum de Sodomis, imo cogebant eum, et apprehenderunt manum ejus et conjugis suæ, etc., et posuerunt eum extra civitatem.
paras.en: On this it is asked why three angels appeared together. To this the Saints answer that God most high, one in essence and three in Persons, sent three angels to signify the mystery of the most blessed Trinity. Whence Abraham too spoke to one of the three in the singular, and adored one; for which reason the Church sings: Abraham saw three, and adored one. But Josephus and many others say that one of those angels was sent to announce the coming conception of Isaac, the other two to overthrow Sodom. Further, as Lyra relates, the Hebrews say that these three angels were Michael, Gabriel and Raphael: that Michael was sent to announce Isaac who was to be born, Gabriel to overthrow Sodom, Raphael to heal Abraham, who was still in pain from his circumcision (for they say that this apparition happened on the third day after his circumcision), and to rescue Lot with his household from the peril of the Sodomites. These things seem for the most part uncertain: namely whether those three angels were the three persons named, and whether this apparition happened on the third day after Abraham's circumcision; likewise whether one was sent to Abraham to cure that pain, since the text says nothing of this; and also whether one came specially for the overthrow of Sodom, especially since in the following chapter the two angels declare: [[Gen 19:13|we will destroy this place|Delebimus locum istum]]. And again: [[Gen 19:13|the Lord, who hath sent us to destroy them|Misit nos Dominus ut perdamus illos]] [Denis's wording: "The Lord hath sent us to destroy them"]. From which it is clear that both were sent for this. Both too urged Lot to go out of Sodom, nay, [[Gen 19:15|pressed him|cogebant eum]], and [[Gen 19:16|took his hand, and the hand of his wife|apprehenderunt manum ejus et conjugis suæ]], etc., and [[Gen 19:17|set him without the city|posuerunt eum extra civitatem]].

paras.t: Et adoravit in terra. Quidam dicunt quod adoravit omnes tres angelos adoratione duliæ, quæ impenditur rationalibus creaturis, quemadmodum Nathan et Bethsabee adoraverunt regem David, ut legitur tertio Regum. Putavit enim quod homines essent. Alii dicunt quod unum specialiter adoravit, et quod adoravit eumdem adoratione latriæ ; quod salvari potest, dicendo quod adoravit Dominum Deum in angelo. Verumtamen secundum Augustinum et Gregorium, in adoratione hac et postea ad tempus Abraham æstimavit, quod angeli isti homines essent : ideo verius creditur, quod de adoratione duliæ istud intelligatur, præsertim quum sequenti capitulo Lot legatur angelos adorasse. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus dicit, quod intelligendum sit de adoratione latriæ, quoniam scriptum est, quod adoravit pronus in terram : quæ argumentatio non procedit, quoniam Josue adoravit angelum pronus in terram, et Nathan David. Joannes quoque in Apocalypsi : Cecidi, inquit, ad pedes ejus, videlicet angeli, ut adorarem eum. Quæ omnia certum est de adoratione duliæ dici.
paras.en: [[18:2|and adored down to the ground|Et adoravit in terra]]. Some say that he adored all three angels with the adoration of dulia [that is, the honour shown to creatures, as distinct from *latria*, the worship due to God alone], which is paid to rational creatures, as Nathan and Bethsabee adored King David[[3 Kings 1:16||]][[3 Kings 1:23||]], as we read in the third book of Kings. For he thought that they were men. Others say that he adored one in particular, and that he adored him with the adoration of latria; which can be upheld by saying that he adored the Lord God in the angel. Yet according to Augustine and Gregory, in this adoration and for a time afterwards Abraham thought that these angels were men; therefore it is more truly believed that this is to be understood of the adoration of dulia, especially since in the following chapter Lot is read to have adored the angels. Rabbi Paul, however, says that it is to be understood of the adoration of latria, since it is written that he adored prone upon the ground. But this argument does not hold, since Josue adored the angel prone upon the ground[[Jos 5:15||]], and Nathan adored David. John too in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 19:10|I fell down|Cecidi]], he says, [[Apoc 19:10|before his feet|ad pedes ejus]], that is, of the angel, [[Apoc 19:10|to adore him|ut adorarem eum]][[Apoc 22:8||]]. All of which, it is certain, is said of the adoration of dulia.

paras.t: Et dixit : Domine, si inveni gratiam in oculis tuis, id est, si coram te placeo, et pietatem tuam ostendis in me, ne transeas servum tuum, hoc est, non tam cito pertranseas me, quin primo utaris obsequio et beneficiis meis : de quibus subjungitur, sed afferam pauxillum aquæ, et lavate pedes vestros. Circa hoc quæritur, quid sibi velit iste modus loquendi, quod scilicet tribus visis, singulariter loquitur uni quem et specialiter Dominum vocat : deinde mox rursus pluraliter eos alloquitur, Lavate, inquiens, pedes vestros. Ad hoc Glossa respondet, quod Abraham Deum in angelis sentiens, maluit Deo loqui quam angelis. Augustinus vero : Abraham, inquit, et Lot in viris illis agnoscebant Dominum, cui per singularem numerum loquebantur, quum viros illos esse homines arbitrarentur. His consonat, quod quum dixisset numero singulari, Domine ne transeas servum tuum, quum de humanis obsequiis subderet, statim pluraliter addidit, Lavate, etc. Alii dicunt, quod tres angeli sic apparuerunt, quod unus videbatur principalior inter eos, is scilicet qui ad annuntiandum nativitatem Isaac venerat, quem dicunt Hebræi Michaelem fuisse, ut tactum est. Ideo quamvis Abraham æstimavit quod homines essent, illum tamen principalem singulariter est affatus, arbitrans si ille acquiesceret suæ petitioni, alii quoque duo non denegarent. Et dicunt nonnulli, quod principalis ille angelus ivit in medio, scilicet inter alios duos : quia tunc dicunt consuetudinem exstitisse, quod principalis inter tres gradientes, pergebat in medio, et quod Abraham per hoc principalem illum cognoverat. Asserunt quoque, quod homines non ibant tunc calceati neque equestres ut modo : ideo rogaverat Abraham quatenus pedes suos lavarent. Et quamvis probabile sit, quod angeli illi non apparuerunt calceati, incertum tamen videtur quod generaliter homines tunc incesserint non calceati : imo constat quod tempore egressionis filiorum Israel ex Ægypto, homines utebantur equis ad equitandum, et calceis ad eundum, quum de filiis Israel pro tempore illo dicatur : Nec calceamenta pedum vestrorum vetustate consumpta sunt : atque de Pharaonis ministris : Equum et ascensorem projecit in mare. Itemque : Ingressus est eques Pharao cum curribus et equitibus ejus in mare. Denique lotio competit etiam calceatis, præsertim itinerantibus.
paras.en: [[18:3|And he said: Lord, if I have found favour in thy sight|Et dixit : Domine, si inveni gratiam in oculis tuis]], that is, if I please thee, and thou shewest thy kindness to me; [[18:3|pass not away from thy servant|ne transeas servum tuum]], that is, do not pass me by so quickly without first making use of my service and my kindnesses; of which it is added, [[18:4|But I will fetch a little water, and wash ye your feet|sed afferam pauxillum aquæ, et lavate pedes vestros]]. On this it is asked what this manner of speaking means: that, having seen three, he speaks in the singular to one, whom he also calls Lord in particular, and then at once addresses them again in the plural, saying, [[18:4|wash ye|Lavate]], [[18:4|your feet|pedes vestros]]. To this the Gloss answers that Abraham, perceiving God in the angels, chose to speak to God rather than to the angels. But Augustine says: Abraham and Lot recognized the Lord in those men, to whom they spoke in the singular number, while they thought those men to be human. With this agrees the fact that when he had said in the singular number, [[18:3|Lord|Domine]], [[18:3|pass not away from thy servant|ne transeas servum tuum]], then, as he went on to human services, he at once added in the plural, [[18:4|wash ye|Lavate]], etc. Others say that the three angels so appeared that one seemed the chief among them, namely he who had come to announce the birth of Isaac, whom the Hebrews say was Michael, as was touched on above. So, although Abraham thought they were men, he yet addressed that chief one in the singular, thinking that if he agreed to his request, the other two would not refuse either. And some say that the chief angel walked in the middle, that is, between the other two, since they say it was then the custom that the chief of three walking together went in the middle, and that Abraham knew the chief one by this. They assert also that men did not go shod or on horseback then as now; and so Abraham asked them to wash their feet. And although it is probable that those angels did not appear shod, yet it seems uncertain that men in general went unshod at that time; indeed it is certain that at the time of the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt men used horses for riding and shoes for walking, since it is said of the children of Israel for that time: [[Deut 29:5|neither are the shoes of your feet consumed with age|Nec calceamenta pedum vestrorum vetustate consumpta sunt]]; and of Pharao's officers: [[Ex 15:21|the horse and his rider he hath thrown into the sea|Equum et ascensorem projecit in mare]] [the margin gives Exod. xv, 21; the same words stand in Exod 15:1]. And again: [[Ex 15:19|Pharao went in on horseback with his chariots and horsemen into the sea|Ingressus est eques Pharao cum curribus et equitibus ejus in mare]]. Lastly, washing befits even those who are shod, especially travellers.

paras.t: Et requiescite sub arbore : quia delectabile est, tempore calido sub ramis arborum repausare ac refici, et contra æstum solis refrigerativum. Arbor vero hæc, quercus fuit. Nam alia translatio habet : Apparuit Deus Abrahæ ad quercum Mambre. Origenes etiam utitur littera tali, Declina ad puerum tuum, et refrigera te sub arbore. De hac arbore in Scholastica recitatur historia : Habitavit Abraham circa quercum vel terebinthum, cujus radices adhuc apparent, quam Josephus proprio nomine expressit, dicendo : Habitavit Abraham circa ilicem quæ vocatur Agyga. Arborque illa, secundum Hieronymum, usque ad tempus Theodosii Imperatoris duravit, et ex ea orta perhibetur quæ nunc est, quæ quamvis sit arida, tamen medicinalis exsistit, de qua qui tulerit secum, non se ei infundit venenum. Hæc in præfata Historia.
paras.en: [[18:4|and rest ye under the tree|Et requiescite sub arbore]]: because in hot weather it is pleasant to rest and be refreshed under the branches of trees, and it is cooling against the heat of the sun. Now this tree was an oak. For another translation has: God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mambre. Origen too uses this text: Turn aside to thy servant, and refresh thyself under the tree. Of this tree it is related in the Scholastic History: Abraham dwelt by an oak or terebinth, whose roots still appear, which Josephus named by its own name, saying: Abraham dwelt by the holm-oak which is called Agyga. And that tree, according to Jerome, lasted until the time of the Emperor Theodosius, and from it is said to have sprung the one which is there now, which, though it is dry, is yet medicinal: whoever carries some of it with him, poison does not enter into him. Thus far the aforesaid History.

paras.t: Ponamque buccellam panis, id est cibum et potum, quæ nomine panis in Scripturis frequenter signantur. Loquitur quoque Abraham humiliter ac modeste, per minus significans majus. Et confortate cor vestrum, comedendo. Ex quibus probatur, quod Abraham æstimavit eos homines esse, qui ambulando et jejunando fatigarentur ac debilitarentur. Cor demum quandoque pro corporali parte ac membro accipitur, de quo Philosophus contestatur, quod sit primum vivens, et ultimum moriens : quod cibo et potu directe confortatur. Interdum vero accipitur cor pro mente, intellectu seu voluntate, de quo Psalmista fatetur. Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo : quod cibo et potu indirecte confortatur, sicut et fame nimia et corporali lassitudine debilitatur, in quantum ex bona et naturali corporis dispositione, mens magis idonea redditur ad actus intellectuales, in quibus corpus atque organicæ vires menti subserviunt. Idcirco enim declinastis ad servum vestrum, ut scilicet exhiberem vobis ista pietatis obsequia. Illa tamen non fuit principalis ratio quod illuc venerunt, sed Abraham dixit hoc blande loquendo, et ex quadam pia fiducia, ut moris est invitantium, ut sic magis alliceret illos.
paras.en: [[18:5|And I will set a morsel of bread|Ponamque buccellam panis]], that is, food and drink, which are often signified in the Scriptures by the name of bread. Abraham also speaks humbly and modestly, signifying the greater by the less. [[18:5|and strengthen ye your heart|Et confortate cor vestrum]], by eating. From which it is proved that Abraham thought them to be men, who would be wearied and weakened by walking and fasting. Further, *heart* is sometimes taken for the bodily part and member, of which the Philosopher [Aristotle] testifies that it is the first thing living and the last dying; and this is strengthened directly by food and drink. But sometimes *heart* is taken for the mind, understanding or will, of which the Psalmist says: [[Ps 9:2|I will give praise to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo]]; and this is strengthened indirectly by food and drink, just as it is weakened by excessive hunger and bodily weariness, inasmuch as from a good and natural disposition of the body the mind is made more fit for intellectual acts, in which the body and the organic powers serve the mind. [[18:5|for therefore are you come aside to your servant|Idcirco enim declinastis ad servum vestrum]], that is, so that I might shew you these services of piety. That, however, was not the chief reason why they came there; but Abraham said this speaking winningly, and out of a certain devout confidence, as is the way of those who invite, so as to draw them the more.

paras.t: Qui dixerunt : Fac ut locutus es. Cur statim acquieverunt Abrahæ, quum sequenti capitulo legantur duo angeli dixisse Lot eos invitanti, Nequaquam, sed in platea manebimus ? Respondet Petrus Alphonsi, vir christianissimus atque doctissimus ex Judaismo conversus, quod propter reverentiam et excellentiam Abrahæ patriarchæ mox acquiescebant : Lot vero minoris fuit auctoritatis, idcirco prima facie denegabant. Ex quibus idem Petrus concludit, quod quando quis invitatur a persona multum excellenti, debet acquiescere sine renisu.
paras.en: [[18:5|And they said: Do as thou hast spoken|Qui dixerunt : Fac ut locutus es]]. Why did they agree with Abraham at once, when in the following chapter the two angels are read to have said to Lot when he invited them, [[Gen 19:2|No, but we will abide in the street|Nequaquam, sed in platea manebimus]]? Peter Alphonsi, a most Christian and most learned man converted from Judaism, answers that because of the reverence and excellence of the patriarch Abraham they agreed at once; but Lot was of lesser authority, and so at first they refused. From which the same Peter concludes that when anyone is invited by a person of great excellence, he ought to agree without resistance.

paras.t: Festinavit Abraham in tabernaculum ad Saram, dixitque ei : Accelera, et tria sata similæ commisce. Satum mensuram quamdam significat. Unde secundum Isidorum, satum continet modium unum cum medio. Simila vero est farina purissima. Hinc Origenes utitur littera ista : Consperge tres mensuras similaginis. Et fac subcinericios panes ex tanta simila sic conspersa. Nonne Abraham habebat in domo panes sufficientes ? Respondendum, quod utique, sed voluit tam venerandis hospitibus recentia ac specialia proponere fercula. Idcirco in Scholastica fertur historia : Paravit eis encænia, id est peregrina, pretiosaque fercula. Propter quod subditur : Ipse vero ad armentum, id est pecorum gregem, cucurrit, et tulit inde vitulum tenerrimum et optimum, id est novellum, esuique aptissimum, et in suo genere valde bonum : deditque puero, id est ministro, et forsitan coquo : nam subditur : Qui festinavit et coxit illum. Puer ille secundum Hebræos (ut refert Lyra) Ismael fuit, cui Abraham vitulum dedit coquendum, ut ipsum ad opera hospitalitatis faceret assuetum. Sed si ista (ut dicunt Hebræi) acciderunt tertia die post Abrahæ circumcisionem, in qua Ismael tredecim erat annorum, non videtur Ismael in tantilla ætate aptus fuisse ad vituli coctionem. Tulit quoque butyrum et lac, et vitulum quem coxerat, id est coqui fecerat : et sicut Scholastica dicit historia, vitulus fuit assatus, forsan enim pars ejus fuit assata ; et posuit coram eis, ita quod personaliter ministravit ad mensam. De potu nihil hic dicitur, neque exprimitur quod pedes suos laverunt, sed ex aliis datur hoc satis intelligi.
paras.en: [[18:6|Abraham made haste into the tent to Sara, and said to her: Make haste, temper together three measures of flour|Festinavit Abraham in tabernaculum ad Saram, dixitque ei : Accelera, et tria sata similæ commisce]]. A *satum* signifies a certain measure. Hence according to Isidore a satum holds one modius and a half. And *simila* is the purest flour. Hence Origen uses this text: Knead three measures of fine flour. [[18:6|and make cakes upon the hearth|Et fac subcinericios panes]] [*subcinericios panes*: loaves baked under the ashes], from so much flour thus kneaded. Had not Abraham bread enough in the house? It must be answered that he certainly had, but he wished to set fresh and special dishes before such venerable guests. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History: He prepared for them *encænia* [the editors refer here to Du Cange's Glossary, under *Encænium*], that is, rare and costly dishes. For which reason it is added: [[18:7|And he himself ran to the herd|Ipse vero ad armentum]], that is, the herd of cattle, [[18:7|and took from thence a calf, very tender and very good|cucurrit, et tulit inde vitulum tenerrimum et optimum]], that is, young, most fit for eating, and very good in its kind; [[18:7|and gave it to a young man|deditque puero]], that is, to a servant, and perhaps a cook; for it is added: [[18:7|who made haste and boiled it|Qui festinavit et coxit illum]]. This young man, according to the Hebrews (as Lyra reports), was Ismael, to whom Abraham gave the calf to cook, so as to accustom him to the works of hospitality. But if these things happened (as the Hebrews say) on the third day after Abraham's circumcision, at which Ismael was thirteen years old, Ismael does not seem at so tender an age to have been fit to cook a calf. [[18:8|He took also butter and milk, and the calf which he had boiled|Tulit quoque butyrum et lac, et vitulum quem coxerat]], that is, had caused to be cooked; and, as the Scholastic History says, the calf was roasted, for perhaps a part of it was roasted; [[18:8|and set before them|et posuit coram eis]], so that he waited at table in person. Nothing is said here of drink, nor is it stated that they washed their feet, but this is given to be understood well enough from other things.

paras.t: Ex prædictis patent liberalitas, fervor, pietas atque alacritas Abrahæ jam centenarii, in caritatis et misericordiæ actibus. Hinc Origenes disseruit : Considera protinus impigrum et alacrem senem. Occurrit obviam, refestinat ad domum, et dixit uxori, Festina, etc. Vide in omnibus quanta sit suscipientis alacritas : festinatur in omnibus, omnia perurgentur, nihil per otium geritur. Abraham currit, uxor accelerat, puer festinat, nullus piger est in domo sapientis.
paras.en: From what has been said appear the liberality, fervour, piety and eagerness of Abraham, now a hundred years old, in works of charity and mercy. Hence Origen discoursed: Consider straightway the unwearied and eager old man. He runs to meet them, hastens back to the house, and said to his wife, Make haste, etc. See in all things how great is the eagerness of the host: there is haste in everything, everything is pressed forward, nothing is done at leisure. Abraham runs, his wife makes haste, the servant hastens; no one is slothful in the house of the wise man.

paras.t: Ipse vero stabat juxta eos sub arbore. Adstabat edentibus, paratus ad ministrandum, et propter reverentiam hospitum, atque ad intuendum ne quid deesset, negligenterve fieret. Sed mirum quod non invitabant tantum Patriarcham ad consedendum et reficiendum cum ipsis ; ad quod dici potest, quod non omnia scripta sunt, ideo quamvis non sit scriptum quod eum ad hoc invitaverint, non tamen sequitur quod non fecerunt hoc. Vel forsitan tam humiliter se gesserunt, quod non intromiserunt se de hoc, præsertim quum reficerentur gratis ut peregrini.
paras.en: [[18:8|but he stood by them under the tree|Ipse vero stabat juxta eos sub arbore]]. He stood by them as they ate, ready to serve, both out of reverence for his guests and to watch that nothing should be lacking or be done carelessly. But it is surprising that they did not invite so great a Patriarch to sit down and eat with them. To which it can be said that not everything is written; so, although it is not written that they invited him to this, it does not follow that they did not do it. Or perhaps they bore themselves so humbly that they did not concern themselves with this, especially since they were being refreshed without charge as pilgrims.

paras.t: Quumque comedissent, dixerunt ad eum: Ubi est Sara uxor tua? Verisimile est quod unus eorum quæsivit hoc, sed adscribitur eis communiter, secundum quod societati aut communitati solet attribui quod convenit parti ejus. Nec ex ignorantia venit interrogatio ista, sed ut aptius veniretur ad prænuntiandum Isaac. Ille respondit: Ecce in tabernaculo est. Quia ex virtuoso pudore et castimonia conjugali subtraxit se a virorum præsentia. Cui dixit angelus ille, ut communiter dicitur, qui venerat nuntiare de Isaac nascituro: Revertens veniam ad te tempore isto, hoc est, eodem die anno revoluto, vita comite. Hoc addit, loquendo more humano, quia adhuc homo æstimabatur, et ut homines talem in loquendo observent modestiam, ne incaute asseramus nos hoc aut illud facturos in posterum, sed sub conditione, videlicet Deo volente, et si vixerimus, secundum quod Jacobus apostolus in sua docet Canonica: Ut dicatis, si Dominus voluerit, et si vixerimus, faciemus hoc aut illud. Itemque, ut innuat, etiam esse et vivere supernorum civium, incessabiliter dependere a Deo, quamvis certi sint se nunquam amissuros quod habent. Et habebit filium Sara uxor tua, infra hunc annum.
paras.en: [[18:9|And when they had eaten, they said to him|Quumque comedissent, dixerunt ad eum]]: [[18:9|Where is Sara thy wife?|Ubi est Sara uxor tua?]] It is likely that one of them asked this, but it is ascribed to them in common, in the way that what belongs to a part is commonly attributed to the company or community. Nor did this question come from ignorance, but so that they might come more fittingly to the foretelling of Isaac. [[18:9|He answered: Lo she is in the tent|Ille respondit: Ecce in tabernaculo est]]: for out of virtuous modesty and conjugal chastity she had withdrawn from the presence of the men. [[18:10|And he said to him|Cui dixit]], that is, that angel, as is commonly said, who had come to announce Isaac who was to be born: [[18:10|I will return and come to thee at this time|Revertens veniam ad te tempore isto]], that is, on the same day when the year has come round, [[18:10|life accompanying|vita comite]]. He adds this speaking in human fashion, because he was still thought to be a man, and so that men may keep such modesty in speaking that we do not rashly assert that we shall do this or that in time to come, but under a condition, namely God willing, and if we live, as the apostle James teaches in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jas 4:15|that you should say: If the Lord will, and, If we shall live, we will do this or that|Ut dicatis, si Dominus voluerit, et si vixerimus, faciemus hoc aut illud]]. And also to suggest that even the being and life of the citizens on high depend unceasingly on God, though they are certain never to lose what they have. [[18:10|and Sara, thy wife, shall have a son|Et habebit filium Sara uxor tua]], within this year.

paras.t: Quo audito, Sara risit post ostium tabernaculi. Qui risus, secundum Augustinum, fuit dubitationis: ideo Sara est reprehensa. Risus autem Abrahæ fuit admirationis et gaudii. Itaque Sara dubitavit, et non credidit, quia ad naturales causas respexit, propter quod subditur: Erant autem ambo senes, provectæque ætatis. Et senium istud fuit in Sara una causa infecunditatis. Alia fuit suæ infecunditatis ratio naturalis, qua et in juventute sua erat naturaliter infecunda seu frigida. Et desierant Sara fieri muliebria, id est, menstrua amplius non fiebant in ea, ideo fuit infecunda. Et ista ratio senectutem consequebatur. Circa hoc loquitur Augustinus: Sara erat sanguine menstruo destituta, propter quod parere jam non posset, etiam si sterilis non fuisset. Porro, si femina ita sit provectioris ætatis, ut ei solita muliebria adhuc fluant, de juvene parere potest; de seniore non potest, quamvis senior ille adhuc de adolescentula gignere possit, quemadmodum Abraham post mortem Saræ de Cetura aliquos generavit. Hæc Augustinus.
paras.en: [[18:10|Which when Sara heard, she laughed behind the door of the tent|Quo audito, Sara risit post ostium tabernaculi]]. This laughter, according to Augustine, was the laughter of doubt: therefore Sara was reproved. But Abraham's laughter was of wonder and joy. So Sara doubted and did not believe, because she looked to natural causes; and for this reason it is added: [[18:11|Now they were both old, and far advanced in years|Erant autem ambo senes, provectæque ætatis]]. And this old age was in Sara one cause of barrenness. Another, natural, reason for her barrenness was that even in her youth she was by nature barren, or cold. [[18:11|and it had ceased to be with Sara after the manner of women|Et desierant Sara fieri muliebria]], that is, the menses no longer came upon her; therefore she was barren. And this reason followed upon old age. On this Augustine says: Sara was without the monthly blood, so that she could no longer bear, even if she had not been barren. Moreover, if a woman is so far advanced in age that her accustomed courses still flow, she can bear by a young man, but not by an older one; although that older man can still beget by a young girl, as Abraham after Sara's death begot some children of Cetura. Thus Augustine.

paras.t: Quare risit occulte, dicens, quasi arguendo de impossibilitate divinæ promissionis: Postquam consenui, et dominus meus vetulus est: maritum suum ex humilitate dominum suum appellat, quod beatissimus princeps Apostolorum in prima sua commemorans Canonica, proponit mulieribus imitandum. Mulieres, inquiens, viris suis subjectæ sint, sicut Sara obediebat Abrahæ, dominum eum vocans; voluptati operam dabo? quasi dicat. Non decet. Et verum est, quod non decuit propter voluptatem marito conjungi, sed propter prolem desuper repromissam. Præterea ex istis elicitur verbis, quod Sara jam diu a viri continuerat copula, præsertim a tempore quo naturale tempus concipiendi effluxerat.
paras.en: [[18:12|And she laughed secretly, saying|Quare risit occulte, dicens]], as though arguing the impossibility of the divine promise: [[18:12|After I am grown old, and my lord is an old man|Postquam consenui, et dominus meus vetulus est]]: out of humility she calls her husband her lord, which the most blessed prince of the Apostles, recalling it in his first Canonical Epistle, sets before women to imitate. [[1 Pet 3:1|let wives|Mulieres]], he says, [[1 Pet 3:1|be subject to their husbands|viris suis subjectæ sint]], [[1 Pet 3:6|As Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord|sicut Sara obediebat Abrahæ, dominum eum vocans]]; [[18:12|shall I give myself to pleasure|voluptati operam dabo]]? As if to say: It is not fitting. And it is true that it was not fitting to be joined to her husband for pleasure, but for the offspring promised from above. Further, it is gathered from these words that Sara had long refrained from intercourse with her husband, especially from the time when the natural time of conceiving had passed.

paras.t: Dixit autem Dominus ad Abraham. Per Dominum intelligitur angelus, qui ex persona Dei Abrahæ filium ex Sara promisit. Quare risit Sara uxor tua, ex diffidentia dicens: Num vere paritura sum anus? Quasi dicat, Ego jam vetula parere non potero; respiciens ad vim ordinemque naturæ, non ad efficaciam gratiæ ac virtutis divinæ. Et in hoc erat culpabilis. Nesciebat tamen quod iste promissor angelus esset. Numquid Deo quidquam est difficile? Tanquam dicat: Quum Deus omnipotens sit, cui omnia non solum possibilia, sed et facilia exstant, non debuit Sara hæc dubitare de veritate divini promissi. Juxta condictum, id est, sicut jam dixi. […] ad te, etc. Sara dubitando et ridendo peccavit, et tamen angelus non statim increpavit eam immediate, sed primo sciscitatus est ejus maritum, cur ipsa risisset, ad innuendum quod vir caput est mulieris, ad quem pertinet uxorem dirigere, et in moribus informare, ac delinquentem corripere, ita quod culpa conjugis in ipsum redundat, nisi in prædictis juste se habeat circa illam.
paras.en: [[18:13|And the Lord said to Abraham|Dixit autem Dominus ad Abraham]]. By *the Lord* is understood the angel who, in the person of God, promised Abraham a son by Sara. [[18:13|Why did Sara laugh|Quare risit Sara]] thy wife, out of distrust, [[18:13|saying: Shall I, who am an old woman, bear a child indeed?|dicens: Num vere paritura sum anus?]] As if to say: I, now an old woman, shall not be able to bear; looking to the force and order of nature, not to the efficacy of the grace and power of God. And in this she was blameworthy. She did not know, however, that this promiser was an angel. [[18:14|Is there any thing hard to God?|Numquid Deo quidquam est difficile?]] As if to say: Since God is almighty, to whom all things are not only possible but easy, Sara ought not to have doubted the truth of the divine promise. [[18:14|According to appointment|Juxta condictum]], that is, as I have already said. […] [[18:14|to thee|ad te]], etc. Sara sinned by doubting and laughing, and yet the angel did not rebuke her at once and directly, but first asked her husband why she had laughed, to suggest that the husband is the head of the wife, whose part it is to direct his wife, to form her in her conduct and to correct her when she does wrong; so that the wife's fault redounds upon him, unless he behaves justly towards her in these things.

paras.t: Negavit Sara, dicens: Non risi. Et in hoc more femineo auxit culpam mentiendo, seque non vere excusando. Mendacium tamen illud fuit veniale, non ex malitia, sed passione timoris, ad quem mulieres naturaliter pronæ sunt, prodiens. Timore perterrita: timuit quippe, quum audisset quod Dominus risum suum secretum tam cito deprehendisset. Dominus autem: Non est, inquit, ita, sed risisti. Circa hoc quæri potest, cur Deus Saram pro sua dubitatione, risu et diffidentia, non punivit, quemadmodum Zachariam. Dicunt aliqui, quod femineæ levitati pepercit, vel quia in dubitatione non exstitit pertinax, sed correpta pœnituit, confestimque credidit. Vel multum excusabilis erat, et magis quam Zacharias, quia non scivit eum qui promittebat, esse angelum Dei, neque distinctam habuit de ejus persona notitiam.
paras.en: [[18:15|Sara denied, saying: I did not laugh|Negavit Sara, dicens: Non risi]]. And in this, in womanly fashion, she increased her fault by lying and by not truly excusing herself. That lie, however, was venial [that is, a lesser sin, which does not destroy charity in the soul], proceeding not from malice but from the passion of fear, to which women are by nature prone. [[18:15|for she was afraid|Timore perterrita]]: she was afraid, indeed, when she heard that the Lord had so quickly detected her secret laughter. [[18:15|But the Lord|Dominus autem]]: [[18:15|Nay|Non est]], he said, [[18:15|but thou didst laugh|sed risisti]]. Here it may be asked why God did not punish Sara for her doubt, laughter and distrust, as he did Zachary[[Luke 1:20||]]. Some say that he spared womanly lightness; or that she was not obstinate in her doubt, but, once rebuked, repented and at once believed. Or she was very excusable, and more so than Zachary, because she did not know that he who made the promise was an angel of God, nor had she a distinct knowledge of his person.

paras.t: Quum ergo surrexissent inde viri, id est, angeli isti qui facta refectione, promissione et collocutione, more hominum surrexerunt a loco illo, direxerunt oculos suos contra Sodomam, quasi indignantes sceleratissimæ civitati, et eam adspicientes ad puniendum; et Abraham simul gradiebatur, cum illis videlicet angelis, deducens eos, quemadmodum moris est, quod hospites multum cari sive notabiles, deducantur ad spatium aliquod. Dicuntque aliqui quod adhuc putabat angelos istos homines esse. Verumtamen puto quod ab ea hora qua unus eorum cœpit sibi prædicere de Saræ conceptu infra annum, cœpit conjicere aut sentire quod angeli essent. Nam et ante, idem fuit prænuntiatum per angelum, ut dictum est sæpe.
paras.en: [[18:16|And when the men rose up from thence|Quum ergo surrexissent inde viri]], that is, these angels, who, the meal, the promise and the conversation being over, rose from that place in the manner of men, [[18:16|they turned their eyes towards Sodom|direxerunt oculos suos contra Sodomam]], as though indignant at that most wicked city, and looking upon it to punish it; [[18:16|and Abraham walked with them|et Abraham simul gradiebatur]], that is, with those angels, [[18:16|bringing them on the way|deducens eos]], as it is the custom that guests who are very dear or distinguished are escorted for some distance. Some say that he still thought these angels were men. But I think that from the hour when one of them began to foretell to him Sara's conceiving within the year, he began to conjecture or perceive that they were angels. For the same thing had been foretold before by an angel, as has often been said.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus, utpote angelus iste principalis, qui Isaac conceptionem prædixit: Num celare potero Abraham, quasi diceret: Non decet ut abscondam ab eo, quæ gesturus sum in subversione Pentapolis, quum futurus sit in gentem magnam atque robustissimam, hoc est, quum sit tantus patriarcha, quod innumerabiles ex ejus posteritate nascentur, imo quum sit pater omnium crediturorum, et benedicendæ sint in illo, hoc est in Christo ex ejus semine nascituro, omnes nationes terræ? quæ salvantur per Christum: quæ verba sæpe exposita sunt.
paras.en: [[18:17|And the Lord said|Dixitque Dominus]], namely this principal angel, who foretold the conceiving of Isaac: [[18:17|Can I hide from Abraham|Num celare potero Abraham]], as if he said: It is not fitting that I hide from him [[18:17|what I am about to do|quæ gesturus sum]] in the overthrow of the Pentapolis [that is, the five cities of the plain], [[18:18|Seeing he shall become a great and mighty nation|quum futurus sit in gentem magnam atque robustissimam]], that is, since he is so great a patriarch that countless men will be born of his posterity, nay, since he is the father of all who will believe, [[18:18|shall be blessed|et benedicendæ sint]] [[18:18|in him|in illo]], that is, in Christ who is to be born of his seed, [[18:18|all the nations of the earth|omnes nationes terræ]], who are saved through Christ: words that have often been expounded.

paras.t: Scio enim quod præcepturus sit filiis suis, videlicet Ismaeli quem nunc habet, et Isaac, aliisque quos habebit, et domui suæ post se, id est domesticis suis, ut custodiant viam Domini, id est, Dei præcepta corde custodito observent, et faciant justitiam, reddendo unicuique quod suum est, et judicium, discrete agendo, atque se ipsos ac subditos suos veraciter judicando: ut adducat Dominus propter Abraham omnia quæ locutus est ad eum, id est, universa quæ promisit aut retulit Abrahæ, impleat per merita Abrahæ.
