paras.en: [[18:19|For I know that he will command his children|Scio enim quod præcepturus sit filiis suis]], namely Ismael whom he has now, and Isaac, and the others whom he will have, [[18:19|and his household after him|et domui suæ post se]], that is, his domestics, [[18:19|to keep the way of the Lord|ut custodiant viam Domini]], that is, that they observe God's precepts, keeping them in their heart, [[18:19|and do|et faciant]] [[18:19|justice|justitiam]], by rendering to each what is his, and [[18:19|judgment|judicium]], by acting with discretion and judging themselves and their subjects truly: [[18:19|that for Abraham's sake, the Lord may bring to effect all the things he hath spoken unto him|ut adducat Dominus propter Abraham omnia quæ locutus est ad eum]], that is, that he may fulfil, through Abraham's merits, all that he promised or declared to Abraham.

paras.t: Verumtamen merita Abrahæ non promeruerunt de condigno impletionem omnium Dei promissionum, videlicet incarnationem Filii Dei, et mundi salvationem per ipsum, sed de quodam condecenti seu congruo, quoniam fuit vir præcipue justus et magnus, imo et Dei amicus. Amicis autem, præsertim familiaribus et prædignis, solent revelari secreta, quemadmodum Amos propheta testatur: Non faciet Dominus verbum, nisi revelaverit secretum suum ad servos suos Prophetas: imo viri heroici et perfecti per donum sapientiæ consummatæ, efficiuntur quasi consiliarii ac secretarii Dei, ita quod Deus incerta et occulta sapientiæ suæ eis revelat. Talisque exstitit Abraham, qui quam perfectus fuerit in Dei amore, constat ex hoc, quod sobolem suam atque familiam tam sollicite induxit ad Dei cultum. Nam tanto quisque in Dei amore perfectior perhibetur, quanto plures ad ipsum convertit. Noverat quoque tunc Abraham, quod post multa tempora scripsit Apostolus: Si quis suorum et maxime domesticorum curam non habet, fidem negavit, et est infideli deterior.
paras.en: Yet Abraham's merits did not merit *de condigno* [that is, as a reward strictly owed to merit] the fulfilment of all God's promises, namely the incarnation of the Son of God and the salvation of the world through him, but by a certain becomingness, *de congruo* [that is, as fitting, though not owed], since he was a man eminently just and great, nay, a friend of God. Now to friends, especially intimate and very worthy ones, secrets are wont to be revealed, as the prophet Amos testifies: [[Amos 3:7|the Lord God doth nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets|Non faciet Dominus verbum, nisi revelaverit secretum suum ad servos suos Prophetas]]. Nay, heroic and perfect men, through the gift of consummate wisdom, become as it were the counsellors and confidants of God, so that God reveals to them the uncertain and hidden things of his wisdom[[Ps 50:8||]] [the margin reads Ps. i, 8, that is, Ps. l (50), 8]. Such was Abraham; and how perfect he was in the love of God is clear from this, that he led his offspring and his household so carefully to the worship of God. For each man is held the more perfect in the love of God, the more men he converts to him. Abraham knew too, even then, what the Apostle wrote long afterwards: [[1 Tim 5:8|if any man have not care of his own and especially of those of his house, he hath denied the faith and is worse than an infidel|Si quis suorum et maxime domesticorum curam non habet, fidem negavit, et est infideli deterior]] [the margin note here is illegible; the words are 1 Tim 5:8].

paras.t: Dixit itaque Dominus, scilicet angelus iste in Dei persona jam loquens: Clamor, id est clamorosa seu clamitans pravitas. Sodomorum et Gomorrhorum, per quos et aliarum trium urbium habitatores turpissimi intelliguntur, utpote Adamæ, Seboim et Segor, multiplicatus est, id est, numero et enormitate excrevit; et, pro id est, peccatum eorum, id est multitudo iniquitatum eorum, aggravatum est nimis: quoniam pessima consuetudo vicit et oppressit eos totaliter; imo ad tantam vitiorum voraginem erant prolapsi, quod de nulla turpitudine verecundabantur, ut infra dicetur. De quorum sceleribus in Ezechiele habetur: Ecce hæc fuit iniquitas Sodomæ, superbia, saturitas panis, abundantia, et otium ejus, et manum egeno et pauperi non porrigebant. Unde et Josephus: Sodomitæ, inquit, divitiis elati, hominibus contumeliam faciebant, et erant impii ad Deum, ut nequaquam recordarentur beneficiorum ipsius, aversique sunt a susceptione peregrinorum, et circa eos affectum habere destiterunt. Verumtamen speciale ac gravissimum scelus eorum, fuit vitium contra naturam, quod et specialiter dicitur clamare ad Deum, quoniam sua enormitate expetit ultionem. De quatuor autem peccatis quæ clamant ad Deum, dictum est super illud: Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra. Denique, secundum Gregorium, peccatum cum voce, est culpa interior cum prava actione. Peccatum vero cum clamore, est culpa cum irrefrenata libertate, ut dum quis cum audacia publice peccat ad libitum. Secundum Glossam quoque, clamor iniquitatis, est evidentia publicati flagitii, quæ accusatore non eget.
paras.en: [[18:20|And the Lord said|Dixit itaque Dominus]], namely this angel, now speaking in the person of God: [[18:20|The cry|Clamor]], that is, the clamorous or crying wickedness, [[18:20|of Sodom and Gomorrha|Sodomorum et Gomorrhorum]] [literally, “of the Sodomites and Gomorrhites”], by whom are understood also the most vile inhabitants of the other three cities, namely Adama, Seboim and Segor, [[18:20|is multiplied|multiplicatus est]], that is, has grown in number and enormity; and (put for *that is*) [[18:20|their sin|peccatum eorum]], that is, the multitude of their iniquities, [[18:20|is become exceedingly grievous|aggravatum est nimis]]: for the worst of habits had conquered and overwhelmed them utterly; nay, they had fallen into such a whirlpool of vices that they were ashamed of no foulness, as will be said below. Of their crimes we have in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 16:49|Behold this was the iniquity of Sodom|Ecce hæc fuit iniquitas Sodomæ]], [[Ezech 16:49|pride, fulness of bread, and abundance, and the idleness of her|superbia, saturitas panis, abundantia, et otium ejus]], [[Ezech 16:49|and they did not put forth their hand to the needy, and the poor|et manum egeno et pauperi non porrigebant]]. Hence Josephus too: The Sodomites, he says, puffed up by riches, did insult to men and were impious towards God, so that they in no way remembered his benefits; and they turned away from receiving strangers, and ceased to have any kindness towards them. Yet their special and most grievous crime was the vice against nature, which is also especially said to cry to God, since by its enormity it demands vengeance. Of the four sins that cry to God we spoke on the text: [[Gen 4:10|the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me from the earth|Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra]]. Further, according to Gregory, a sin with a voice is an inward fault joined with a wicked deed; but a sin with a cry is a fault joined with unbridled licence, as when someone sins openly and boldly at his pleasure. According to the Gloss also, the cry of iniquity is the evidence of a crime made public, which needs no accuser.

paras.t: Descendam, et videbo, utrum clamorem qui venit ad me, opere compleverint; an non est ita ut sciam. Jam Dominus per subjectam creaturam stetit in terra, et loquebatur cum Abraham, ac assertive recitavit scelera Sodomorum, quæ et ei certissime nota erant: quomodo ergo nunc ait, Descendam et videbo, etc.? quasi non descendisset, nec vidisset, neque cognosceret Sodomorum facinora. Et respondendum, quod Deus in verbis his loquitur more et affectu humano propter causas condignas: primo, ut instruat judices ac ceteros universos, ne nimis faciliter credant vera esse quæ audiunt, præsertim dum magna de aliis percipiunt scelera, sed personaliter ea pro posse considerent et observent. Ideo dicit Gregorius: Mala hominum non ante credamus, quam probemus; majoraque crimina tarde credantur, et quum veraciter agnita fuerint, citius puniantur. Secundo, ut compescat homines a præcipitanti, temerariaque prolatione sententiæ, imo antequam sententient, causam quam nesciunt, diligentissime investigent. Tertio, ad insinuandum enormitatem vitiorum Sodomiticorum, quæ adeo gravia sunt, quod Deus loquebatur modo præfato, quasi non aut vix credens, et velut admirans quod tam abominabilia scelera possent inter homines inveniri.
paras.en: [[18:21|I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry that is come to me; or whether it be not so, that I may know|Descendam, et videbo, utrum clamorem qui venit ad me, opere compleverint; an non est ita ut sciam]]. The Lord was already standing on earth through a creature subject to him, and was speaking with Abraham, and had declared outright the crimes of the Sodomites, which were most certainly known to him: how then does he now say, [[18:21|I will go down and see|Descendam et videbo]], etc.? as though he had not come down, nor seen, nor knew the crimes of the Sodomites. We must answer that God speaks in these words in a human manner and with human feeling, for worthy reasons. First, to instruct judges and all others not to believe too easily that what they hear is true, especially when they hear of great crimes of others, but to examine and observe them in person as far as they can. Hence Gregory says: Let us not believe the evils of men before we prove them; and let greater crimes be believed slowly, and, when they have been truly known, be punished the more swiftly. Second, to restrain men from a hasty and rash pronouncing of sentence; nay, that before they pass sentence they investigate most diligently a cause they do not know. Third, to suggest the enormity of the Sodomitic vices, which are so grave that God spoke in the aforesaid manner, as though not believing, or hardly believing, and as though wondering that such abominable crimes could be found among men.

paras.t: Itaque dixit: Descendam, non locum mutando, quantum ad incircumscriptibilitatem atque invariabilem deitatis naturam, sed inferiora considerando, vel potius ostendendo me ea perpendere; et videbo per infallibilem sapientiæ ac justitiæ meæ intuitum, utrum clamorem qui venit ad me, id est, an prædictam clamitantem iniquitatem, quæ coram me expetivit ultionem dum facta est, opere compleverint, annon est ita ut sciam, id est, ut per debitam vindictam ostendam me scire excessus illorum.
paras.en: So he said: [[18:21|I will go down|Descendam]], not by changing place, as regards the uncircumscribable and unchangeable nature of the Godhead, but by considering the things below, or rather by showing that I weigh them; [[18:21|and see|et videbo]] by the unfailing gaze of my wisdom and justice, [[18:21|whether they have done according to the cry that is come to me|utrum clamorem qui venit ad me]], that is, whether the aforesaid crying iniquity, which, when it was committed, demanded vengeance before me, is such as they [[18:21|have done|opere compleverint]] [Latin *opere compleverint*, “have fulfilled in deed”], [[18:21|or whether it be not so, that I may know|annon est ita ut sciam]], that is, that by due punishment I may show that I know their excesses.

paras.t: Converteruntque se inde duo angeli, et abierunt Sodomam. Et ita Dominus etiam per duos angelos illos descendit ad videndum vitia Sodomorum, juxta illud Gregorii: Ecce Dominus per angelos ad cognoscenda hominum mala descendit. Abraham vero adhuc stabat coram Domino, id est angelo illo principali, Dei personam repræsentante: Et appropinquans Domino, ut magis adspiceretur et citius exaudiretur ab eo. Ex caritate enim condoluit instanti periculo Sodomorum. Et quoniam caritas est vis unitiva, ex interiori caritatis motu seu affectione etiam corporaliter univit se Domino, appropinquando ad eum, ad ostendendum suæ caritatis affectum, tam ad ipsum Dominum quam ad proximos.
paras.en: [[18:22|And they turned themselves from thence|Converteruntque se inde]], the two angels, [[18:22|and went their way to Sodom|et abierunt Sodomam]]. And so the Lord, through those two angels too, went down to see the vices of the Sodomites, according to that saying of Gregory: Behold, the Lord goes down through angels to know the evils of men. [[18:22|but Abraham as yet stood before the Lord|Abraham vero adhuc stabat coram Domino]], that is, that principal angel who represented the person of God: [[18:23|And drawing nigh|Et appropinquans]] to the Lord, that he might be better seen and more quickly heard by him. For out of charity he grieved with the Sodomites in their imminent peril. And since charity is a uniting force, from the inward movement or affection of charity he united himself to the Lord even bodily, by drawing near to him, to show the affection of his charity both towards the Lord himself and towards his neighbours.

paras.t: Ait: Numquid perdes justum cum impio? quasi diceret: Non decet hoc tuam justitiam. Quocirca sciendum, quod Deus numquam æternaliter damnat justum cum impio, sed in hac vita quandoque permittit justos occidi cum impiis. Unde per Ezechielem ad Jerusalem ait: Occidi in te justum et impium. Quod facit propter majorem justorum mercedem, et quatenus in hac vita pro suis culpis purgentur, eorumque patientia exerceatur, et fides eorum probetur. Interdum vero eripit justos, ne cum impiis trucidentur, sicut et filios Core præservavit, ne cum suo patre absorberentur a terra. Occulta enim et incomprehensibilia, imo et multiplicia sunt Omnipotentis judicia. Unde intelligendum est, quod Dominus non perdit temporaliter, hoc est, corporaliter non occidit, nec occidi permittit justos cum impiis, nisi propter majus bonum justorum, ita quod talis eorum perditio est copiosius lucrum ipsorum. Quidam vero referunt verbum istud ad Lot, quasi Abraham voluerit dicere: Non perdes justum Lot cum Sodomitis. Quumque satis certus esset de hoc, cœpit orare pro Sodomitis communiter. Verumtamen secundum expositores, intentio Abrahæ fuit orare pro tota Pentapoli. Audierat enim a Domino: Clamor Sodomorum et Gomorrhæorum venit ad me; atque a Domino intellexit instare subversionem non Sodomæ tantum, sed et aliis quatuor urbibus ei annexis, subjectis, et in vitiis conformatis.
paras.en: [[18:23|he said: Wilt thou destroy the just with the wicked|Ait: Numquid perdes justum cum impio?]]? As if he said: This does not befit thy justice. Here it must be known that God never damns the just eternally with the wicked, but in this life he sometimes permits the just to be slain with the wicked. Hence he says to Jerusalem through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 21:4|I have cut off in thee the just and the wicked|Occidi in te justum et impium]] [the margin gives Ezech. xxi, 8; the words are in 21:4, and 21:3 is near them]. This he does for the greater reward of the just, and so that in this life they may be purged of their faults, their patience exercised and their faith proved. But at times he rescues the just, lest they be slaughtered with the wicked, as he preserved the sons of Core from being swallowed up by the earth with their father[[Num 26:11||]] [the margin gives Num. xvi, 26, the chapter of Core's rebellion; that his sons did not perish is told at Num 26:11]. For the judgments of the Almighty are hidden and incomprehensible[[Rom 11:33||]], and manifold besides. Hence it is to be understood that the Lord does not destroy the just with the wicked temporally, that is, does not slay them bodily nor permit them to be slain, except for the greater good of the just, so that such a destruction of theirs is their more abundant gain. Some, however, refer this saying to Lot, as if Abraham meant to say: Thou wilt not destroy the just man Lot with the Sodomites. And when he was certain enough of this, he began to pray for the Sodomites in common. But according to the expositors, Abraham's intention was to pray for the whole Pentapolis. For he had heard from the Lord: [[18:20|The cry of Sodom and Gomorrha|Clamor Sodomorum et Gomorrhæorum]] [[18:21|is come to me|venit ad me]]; and he understood from the Lord that the overthrow was at hand not of Sodom only but also of the other four cities joined to it, subject to it, and like it in their vices.

paras.t: Itaque ait: Si fuerint quinquaginta justi in civitate, peribunt simul? hoc est, delebis justos illos tam multos cum injustis? et non parces loco illi propter quinquaginta justos, si fuerint in eo? Interrogative et negative legendum est istud. Tanquam dicat: Omnino decet, ut merito quinquaginta justorum parcas toti illi communitati residuæ: ideo subditur: Absit a te ut hanc rem facias, et occidas justum cum impio, id est tot justos cum impiis ceteris; fiatque justus sicut impius, id est, impio assimiletur in plaga illa a tua justitia. Non est hoc tuum, hoc est, bonitatem, justitiam, et sapientiam tuam non decet, qui judicas omnem terram, id est cunctos habitantes in terra. Nequaquam facies judicium hoc. Sanctissimus iste Patriarcha ex abundantia cordis sui locutus est, et ex ferventissimo cordis sui affectu fiducialiter ista effatus est, atque præ nimia suæ pietatis compassione, quasi argumentando hæc protulit, quasi nitens convincere Deum: et tamen omnia ista per modum orationis sunt intelligenda, ut sit sensus: Spero et oro quod non facies tale judicium. Verumtamen si interdum occidantur justi cum impiis, aut etiam ab impiis, non hoc derogat divinæ justitiæ, quæ ex justis et rationabilibus causis hoc efficit aut permittit: idcirco in tali occisione non fit justus ut impius, quia non ex eisdem causis uterque perimitur. Et mors temporalis uni est janua vitæ æternæ, alteri mortis perpetuæ: uni purgatio, alteri damnationis inceptio. Præterea quidam dicunt, quod Abraham istud oravit non pro solis habitatoribus Sodomæ, sed simul pro eis et habitatoribus aliarum quatuor civitatum, ita quod exoravit ut Deus parceret quinque urbibus illis, si omnes pariter haberent in se quinquaginta justos. Et dicunt quod in verbis præfatis civitas et locus sumuntur pluraliter pro civitatibus illis ac locis. Sed his non videtur consonare quod sequitur.
paras.en: So he says: [[18:24|If there be fifty just men in the city, shall they perish withal?|Si fuerint quinquaginta justi in civitate, peribunt simul?]] that is, wilt thou destroy so many just men with the unjust? [[18:24|and wilt thou not spare that place for the sake of the fifty just, if they be therein?|et non parces loco illi propter quinquaginta justos, si fuerint in eo?]] This is to be read as a question expecting the answer no, as if he said: It is altogether fitting that for the merit of fifty just men thou spare all the rest of that community. And therefore it is added: [[18:25|Far be it from thee to do this thing, and to slay the just with the wicked|Absit a te ut hanc rem facias, et occidas justum cum impio]], that is, so many just men with the other wicked; [[18:25|and for the just to be in like case as the wicked|fiatque justus sicut impius]], that is, that the just be made like the wicked in that stroke from thy justice. [[18:25|this is not beseeming thee|Non est hoc tuum]], that is, it befits not thy goodness, justice and wisdom, [[18:25|thou who judgest all the earth|qui judicas omnem terram]], that is, all who dwell on the earth, [[18:25|wilt not make this judgment|Nequaquam facies judicium hoc]]. This most holy Patriarch spoke out of the abundance of his heart, and uttered these things confidently from the most fervent affection of his heart, and out of the great compassion of his piety he brought them forth as though arguing, as though striving to convince God: and yet all these things are to be understood by way of prayer, so that the sense is: I hope and pray that thou wilt not make such a judgment. Yet if at times the just are slain with the wicked, or even by the wicked, this does not detract from the divine justice, which for just and reasonable causes brings this about or permits it: therefore in such a slaying the just is not made as the wicked, because they do not perish for the same causes. And temporal death is for the one the gate of eternal life, for the other the gate of everlasting death: for the one a purging, for the other the beginning of damnation. Further, some say that Abraham prayed this not for the inhabitants of Sodom alone, but for them together with the inhabitants of the other four cities, so that he obtained that God would spare those five cities if all of them together had fifty just men in them. And they say that in the aforesaid words *city* and *place* are taken in the plural, for those cities and places. But what follows does not seem to agree with them.

paras.t: Dixitque Dominus ad eum: Si invenero in Sodomis quinquaginta justos in medio civitatis, dimittam omni loco, id est habitatoribus totius loci illius, prop[…] hoc est propter merita tot justorum. Ad quod dicunt, quod nomine Sodomæ, quæ fuit metropolis regionis Pentapolis, intelliguntur reliquæ urbes ejus. Et quod Dominus ait, Dimittam omni loco, exponunt distributive pro cunctis urbibus illis. Videtur tamen textum sequendo posse dici, quod Abraham istud oravit formaliter directe et immediate pro Sodoma. Sed quod oravit pro ea, intendebat orare pro qualibet alia quatuor civitatum. Nempe si istud oravit pro quatuor urbibus simul, ergo et quod ultimo oravit, si essent ibi decem, parceretur omnibus propter decem, erit intelligendum de quinque urbibus illis, ita quod Deus pepercisset omnibus illis propter decem justos; et quod non fuerunt in omnibus illis decem justi: quod multis non videtur.
paras.en: [[18:26|And the Lord said to him: If I find in Sodom fifty just within the city|Dixitque Dominus ad eum: Si invenero in Sodomis quinquaginta justos in medio civitatis]], [[18:26|I will spare the whole place|dimittam omni loco]], that is, the inhabitants of that whole place, for […], that is, for the merits of so many just men. To this they say that by the name of Sodom, which was the metropolis of the region of the Pentapolis, its other cities are understood; and what the Lord says, [[18:26|I will spare the whole place|Dimittam omni loco]], they expound distributively, of all those cities. Yet, following the text, it seems it can be said that Abraham prayed this formally, directly and immediately for Sodom; but in praying for it he intended to pray for each of the other four cities. For if he prayed this for the four cities together, then what he prayed last, that if there were ten there all should be spared for the sake of the ten, will have to be understood of those five cities, so that God would have spared all of them for ten just men, and that in all of them there were not ten just men: which many do not think likely.

paras.t: Respondit Abraham: Quia semel cœpi, loquar ad Dominum meum, id est, eadem fiducia, qua semel Dominum invocavi, et quia semel precatus sum eum, adhuc semel orabo eumdem, prosequendo meam […] petitionem, quum sim pulvis et cinis, id est, non obstante mea propria fragilitate et corruptibilitate, qua cineri pulverique assimilor. Sicque humiliando se ipsum in divinæ præsentia majestatis, exaudibilior factus est. Quid si minus quinquaginta justis quinque fuerint, id est, si fuerint ibi quadraginta quinque justi? Delebis propter quadraginta quinque universam urbem? hoc est: Nonne parces universæ urbi propter quadraginta quinque justos? Et ait: Non delebo, si invenero ibi quadraginta quinque justos.
paras.en: [[18:27|And Abraham answered|Respondit Abraham]]: [[18:27|Seeing I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord|Quia semel cœpi, loquar ad Dominum meum]], that is, with the same confidence with which I once called upon the Lord; and because I have once besought him, I will pray to him once more, pursuing my […] petition, [[18:27|whereas I am dust and ashes|quum sim pulvis et cinis]], that is, notwithstanding my own frailty and corruptibility, by which I am like ashes and dust. And so, by humbling himself in the presence of the divine majesty, he was made the more worthy to be heard. [[18:28|What if there be five less than fifty just persons?|Quid si minus quinquaginta justis quinque fuerint]] that is, if there be forty-five just men there? [[18:28|wilt thou for five and forty destroy the whole city|Delebis propter quadraginta quinque universam urbem?]]? that is: Wilt thou not spare the whole city for the sake of forty-five just men? [[18:28|And he said: I will not destroy it, if I find five and forty|Et ait: Non delebo, si invenero ibi quadraginta quinque]] just men.

paras.t: Deinde Abraham orando, descendit usque ad decem. Et Dominus dixit, quod parceret urbi, si essent in ea decem justi. Quo audito, Abraham cessavit orare. Vel, quia putavit quod ad minus essent ibidem decem justi. Vel, quia non audebat magis descendere, nec præsumens pro tanto populo exorare, si esset tam vitiosus quod non esset in eo saltem decem justi.
paras.en: Then Abraham, praying, went down as far as ten. And the Lord said that he would spare the city if there were ten just men in it. When he heard this, Abraham ceased to pray: either because he thought that there were at least ten just men there; or because he did not dare go down further, nor presume to pray for so great a people if it were so full of vice that there were not even ten just men in it.

paras.t: Abiit Dominus, id est, angelus in Dei persona apparens et loquens, repente disparuit, et rediit ad superna, postquam cessavit loqui ad Abraham, et ille, scilicet Abraham, reversus est in locum suum. Circa hæc scribit Lyra, quod Abraham non audebat infra novem descendere, quia considerabat quod octo personæ justæ erant in arca Noe tempore diluvii, et tamen nullus aliorum fuit salvatus propter eorum justitiam; sed ut ex præhabitis patet, Cham unus illorum octo fuit injustus, etiam ante diluvium, et deinceps, et tamen propter sui patris justitiam fuit a diluvio præservatus. Iterum dicit: Abraham non descendit ultra decem, quoniam decem homines, et non pauciores, faciunt populum. Quod autem pro justitia minoris populi, petatur liberatio majoris populi injusti, non videtur irrationabile; sed quod pro justitia tam paucorum quod non constituunt populum, postuletur liberatio populi quinque civitatum, videtur magis extraneum: ideo Abraham non fuit ausus ultra decem descendere.
paras.en: [[18:33|And the Lord departed|Abiit Dominus]], that is, the angel who appeared and spoke in the person of God suddenly vanished and went back on high, [[18:33|after he had left speaking to Abraham|postquam cessavit loqui ad Abraham]], [[18:33|and Abraham|et ille]] [Latin *ille*, “he”, which Denis explains: “namely Abraham”] [[18:33|returned to his place|reversus est in locum suum]]. On this Lyra writes that Abraham did not dare to go down to nine or below, because he considered that there were eight just persons in Noe's ark at the time of the flood, and yet none of the others was saved for the sake of their justice; but, as is clear from what was said before, Cham, one of those eight, was unjust both before the flood and afterwards, and yet for the sake of his father's justice he was preserved from the flood. Again he says: Abraham did not go down beyond ten because ten men, and not fewer, make a people. That for the justice of a smaller people the deliverance of a greater, unjust people should be asked does not seem unreasonable; but that for the justice of so few that they do not make up a people the deliverance of the people of five cities should be asked seems stranger: therefore Abraham did not dare to go down beyond ten.

18.title: De mysticis sensibus, quæstionibus, et objectionibus, concernentibus præsens capitulum octavumdecimum
18.title_en: On the mystical senses, questions and objections concerning the present eighteenth chapter

paras.t: Apparuit ei Dominus in convalle […] Mambre, sedenti in ostio tabernaculi sui in ipso fervore diei. Per convallem designatur humilitas; per fervorem diei, ardens dilectio evangelicæ legis seu temporis gratiæ, de quo ait Apostolus: Dies appropinquavit. Et item: Nos qui diei sumus, sobrii simus. Isaias quoque: In die, inquit, illo erit germen Domini, id est Filius Dei, in magnificentia et gloria. Abrahæ ergo sedenti in convalle Mambre in fervore diei, hoc est viro fideli in humilitate et fervida caritate permanenti ac fixo, Deus apparet. Talem enim virum Dominus copiose illustrat, et radio contemplationis perfundit, atque ad mysticæ theologiæ sacratissimas visiones perducit eumdem, ipsum frequenter præveniendo, validius inflammando, et intra se rapiendo. Porro ostium tabernaculi est fides Ecclesiæ, in qua sedere oportet, seu Christus homo qui contestatur: Ego sum ostium ovium.
paras.en: [[18:1|the Lord appeared to him in the vale|Apparuit ei Dominus in convalle]] […] [[18:1|of Mambre as he was sitting at the door of his tent, in the very heat of the day|Mambre, sedenti in ostio tabernaculi sui in ipso fervore diei]]. By the vale is signified humility; by the heat of the day, the burning love of the law of the Gospel, or of the time of grace, of which the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:12|the day is at hand|Dies appropinquavit]]. And again: [[1 Thess 5:8|let us, who are of the day, be sober|Nos qui diei sumus, sobrii simus]]. Isaias too: [[Is 4:2|In that day|In die]], he says, [[Is 4:2|the bud of the Lord|illo erit germen Domini]], that is, the Son of God, [[Is 4:2|shall be in magnificence and glory|in magnificentia et gloria]]. So to Abraham sitting in the vale of Mambre in the heat of the day, that is, to a faithful man abiding and fixed in humility and fervent charity, God appears. For such a man the Lord enlightens abundantly and floods with the ray of contemplation, and leads him to the most sacred visions of mystical theology, often going before him, inflaming him more strongly, and rapturing him into Himself. Further, the door of the tent is the faith of the Church, in which one must sit; or Christ as man, who testifies: [[John 10:7|I am the door of the sheep|Ego sum ostium ovium]].

paras.t: Quumque elevasset oculos, id est, interiorem visum, tam speculativum quam practicum, elevaverit vir talis ad Dominum, ut eum honoret, non solum credendo et contemplando, sed et præcepta atque consilia adimplendo; apparuerunt ei tres viri, id est, ad superbeatissimæ Trinitatis intuitionem amorosam ac radiosam perducitur, cui occurrit per fidem, desiderans perduci ad patriam, ut quam per fidem nunc intuetur, ibi per speciem beatifice contemplatur; adoratque eam, sciens quod unaquæque divina Persona sit verus Deus. In tribus quoque Personis unitatem essentiæ ac deitatis adorando, colit ac admiratur, et ait: Domine: tres enim supersanctæ Personæ, sunt unus Deus, unusque Dominus: si inveni gratiam in oculis tuis, ne transeas servum tuum, id est, non cito te subtrahas contemplationi animæ meæ, sed fac me tibi perseveranter intentum, et per profectum assiduum requiesce in me.
paras.en: [[18:2|And when he had lifted up his eyes|Quumque elevasset oculos]], that is, when such a man has lifted up his inward sight, speculative as well as practical, to the Lord, so as to honour Him not only by believing and contemplating but also by fulfilling the precepts and counsels; [[18:2|there appeared to him three men|apparuerunt ei tres viri]], that is, he is led to the loving and radiant beholding of the most supremely blessed Trinity, whom he runs to meet by faith, longing to be led to the fatherland, so that what he now beholds by faith he may there contemplate in bliss by sight; and he adores the Trinity, knowing that each divine Person is true God. And adoring also the unity of essence and Godhead in the three Persons, he worships and marvels, and [[18:3|said: Lord|ait: Domine]]: for the three most holy Persons are one God and one Lord: [[18:3|if I have found favour in thy sight, pass not away from thy servant|si inveni gratiam in oculis tuis, ne transeas servum tuum]], that is, do not quickly withdraw Thyself from the contemplation of my soul, but make me intent upon Thee perseveringly, and rest in me through constant progress.

paras.t: Sed afferam pauxillum aquæ, et lavate pedes vestros. Per pedes summæ Trinitatis, intelliguntur fideles, qui Deum per fidem portant in se. Orat ergo vir bonus, ut Deus Trinitas suos purget fideles per aquas contritionis et sapientiæ salutaris. Et requiescite sub arbore. Arbor est homo seu ejus voluntas, sive crux Christi. Oramus ergo, ut Deus in nostra voluntate dignetur pie per caritatem morari, et eos qui Christi passionem in jugi habent memoria, inhabitare. Ponamque buccellam panis, id est, Hostiam sacram altaris proponam et sumam, et confortate cor vestrum, id est, mecum cœnare ac deliciari digneris, qui protestaris, Deliciæ meæ esse cum filiis hominum. Itemque, Si quis aperuerit mihi, cœnabo cum illo. Huic petitioni libenter Dominus acquiescit, Fac, inquiens, ut locutus es.
paras.en: [[18:4|But I will fetch a little water, and wash ye your feet|Sed afferam pauxillum aquæ, et lavate pedes vestros]]. By the feet of the supreme Trinity are understood the faithful, who carry God within them by faith. So the good man prays that God the Trinity may cleanse His faithful by the waters of contrition and of saving wisdom. [[18:4|and rest ye under the tree|Et requiescite sub arbore]]. The tree is man, or his will, or else the cross of Christ. So we pray that God may deign to dwell lovingly in our will through charity, and to dwell in those who keep the passion of Christ in constant memory. [[18:5|And I will set a morsel of bread|Ponamque buccellam panis]], that is, I will set forth and receive the sacred Host of the altar, [[18:5|and strengthen ye your heart|et confortate cor vestrum]], that is, deign to sup and take Thy delight with me, Thou who declarest: [[Prov 8:31|my delights were to be with the children of men|Deliciæ meæ esse cum filiis hominum]]. And again: [[Apoc 3:20|If any man|Si quis]] [[Apoc 3:20|open to me|aperuerit mihi]], I [[Apoc 3:20|will sup with him|cœnabo cum illo]]. To this petition the Lord willingly assents: [[18:5|Do|Fac]], He says, [[18:5|as thou hast spoken|ut locutus es]].

paras.t: Festinavit Abraham in tabernaculum, id est, vir christifidelis ad Ecclesiæ suffragia properat, et ait ad Saram, hoc est ad propriam mentem fecundam: Accelera, et tria sata similæ commisce, et fac subcinericios panes. Tria sata similæ sunt, fides, spes, caritas, per quas Dominus nobis mensurat aliarum incrementa virtutum, et retributionem beatam in patria. Quanto enim in his tribus virtutibus magis proficimus, tanto majora aliarum gratiarum charismata, abundantioremque gloriam in cœlis a Deo participamus. Porro simila est purissima Christi humanitas, seu deitatis suæ immensa sinceritas. Itaque tria sata commiscere, est harum trium virtutum actus et opera contemperare, ut ex caritate credamus atque speremus; ex fide quoque et spe diligamus; ex fide item speremus, et sperando credamus. Caritas quippe omnium virtutum est forma et vertex, sine qua fides et spes exstant informes ac mortuæ. Sed et fides est omnium fundamentum virtutum, et oculus caritatis. Oportet etiam omnia fieri in spe. Ex hac ergo horum trium satorum commixtione et consideratione humanitatis, deitatisque Christi, per aquas devotionis et lacrimas contritionis, fiunt subcinericii panes, hoc est humiles refectiones atque abscondita fercula mentis, quæ igne caritatis coquuntur.
paras.en: [[18:6|Abraham made haste into the tent|Festinavit Abraham in tabernaculum]], that is, the faithful Christian hastens to the suffrages of the Church [suffrages: the prayers and good works of the Church offered for her members], and says [[18:6|to Sara|ad Saram]], that is, to his own fruitful mind: [[18:6|Make haste, temper together three measures of flour, and make cakes upon the hearth|Accelera, et tria sata similæ commisce, et fac subcinericios panes]] [*subcinericios panes*: literally "loaves baked under the ashes"]. The three measures of flour are faith, hope and charity, by which the Lord measures out to us the increase of the other virtues, and the blessed reward in the fatherland. For the more we advance in these three virtues, the greater are the gifts of the other graces, and the more abundant the glory in heaven, that we receive from God. Further, the flour [*simila*, the finest wheat flour] is the most pure humanity of Christ, or the boundless purity of His Godhead. So to temper together the three measures is to blend the acts and works of these three virtues, so that we believe and hope out of charity; love, too, out of faith and hope; and again hope out of faith, and believe in hoping. For charity is the form and summit of all the virtues, without which faith and hope stand unformed and dead [unformed (*informes*): lacking charity, which gives the virtues their form, that is, makes them living and meritorious]. But faith too is the foundation of all the virtues, and the eye of charity. And all things must be done in hope. From this mingling of the three measures, then, and from the consideration of the humanity and Godhead of Christ, through the waters of devotion and the tears of contrition, are made the loaves baked under the ashes, that is, the lowly refreshments and hidden dishes of the mind, which are cooked by the fire of charity.

paras.t: Ipse vero ad armentum cucurrit, et tulit inde vitulum tenerrimum et optimum, deditque puero, qui festinavit et coxit illum. Per armentum designatur quæcumque particularis Ecclesia seu congregatio vere devota, in qua oves et pecora Christi sunt et pascuntur. Vitulus autem tenerrimus et optimus, est vir virtuosus, qui Deo se obtulit, et propter Deum quotidie se ipsum mortificat. Christifidelis igitur pensans sibi non sufficere propria merita, talem virum assumit, ut ejus orationibus meritisque juvetur, quem dat puero ut coquat illum, dum eum committit alicui ad exercitandum. Tulit quoque butyrum, hoc est spiritualem pinguedinem et contemplationis dulcorem; unde cantamus: Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea: et lac, id est christianæ simplicitatis infantiam et innocentiam infantilem, de qua princeps Apostolorum hortatur: Sicut modo geniti infantes, rationabiles, sine dolo lac concupiscite.
paras.en: [[18:7|And he himself ran to the herd, and took from thence a calf, very tender and very good, and gave it to a young man, who made haste and boiled it|Ipse vero ad armentum cucurrit, et tulit inde vitulum tenerrimum et optimum, deditque puero, qui festinavit et coxit illum]]. By the herd is signified any particular church or truly devout congregation, in which the sheep and flock of Christ are, and are fed. The calf very tender and very good is the virtuous man who has offered himself to God and for God's sake mortifies himself daily. The faithful Christian, then, weighing that his own merits are not enough for him, takes such a man to himself, that he may be helped by his prayers and merits; and he gives him to the young man to boil when he entrusts him to someone to be trained. [[18:8|He took also butter|Tulit quoque butyrum]], that is, spiritual fatness and the sweetness of contemplation; whence we sing: [[Ps 62:6|Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness|Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea]]: [[18:8|and milk|et lac]], that is, the infancy of Christian simplicity and childlike innocence, to which the prince of the Apostles exhorts us: [[1 Pet 2:2|As newborn babes, desire the rational milk without guile|Sicut modo geniti infantes, rationabiles, sine dolo lac concupiscite]] [Denis reads *rationabiles*, "rational ones", where the Vulgate has *rationabile*, "rational" milk].

paras.t: Hæc omnia ponit coram Deo, ut per eam misericordiam consequatur, et aliis valeat subvenire: quæ quum comederit Dominus, id est, grata habuerit, promittit homini tali et conjugi, id est menti seu animæ ejus, inopinatam fecunditatem, ita ut vix credat, admirandoque rideat, præsertim dum vires naturæ sibi cernit deficere. Sed hoc redarguit Dominus, hortans ut virtuti suæ gratiæ innitatur, per quam omnia potest, juxta illud Apostoli: Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat. Insuper viro hujusmodi tam fideli ac divino, revelat Deus futura Sodomitarum mollium ac luxuriosorum tormenta, pro quibus nihilominus orat talis vir.
paras.en: All these things he sets before God, that he may thereby obtain mercy and be able to help others; and when the Lord has eaten them, that is, has held them pleasing, He promises such a man and his wife, that is, his mind or soul, an unlooked-for fruitfulness, so that he scarcely believes it and laughs in wonder, especially when he sees the powers of nature failing in him. But the Lord rebukes this, exhorting him to lean on the strength of His grace, through which he can do all things, according to that saying of the Apostle: [[Phil 4:13|I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me|Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat]]. Moreover, to such a man, so faithful and so godly, God reveals the coming torments of the effeminate and lustful Sodomites, for whom such a man nevertheless prays.

paras.t: Amplius, ut tactum est præcedenti articulo, communiter dicitur quod in apparitione trium angelorum, superdignissimæ Trinitatis mysterium sit ostensum; et quod Abraham vidit tunc diem Christi, hoc est, spiritualiter cognovit ejus adventum, et mundi redemptionem per ipsum fiendam. Potest etiam dici, quod Abraham vidit diem Christi, quando promissum est ei: In semine tuo benedicentur omnes tribus terræ.
paras.en: Further, as was touched on in the preceding article, it is commonly said that in the appearing of the three angels the mystery of the most supremely worthy Trinity was shown; and that Abraham then saw the day of Christ, that is, knew spiritually His coming and the redemption of the world that was to be wrought through Him. It can also be said that Abraham saw the day of Christ[[John 8:56||]] when it was promised him: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes tribus terræ]] [Denis has "all the tribes of the earth", the wording of Gen 28:14, said to Jacob; the promise to Abraham is at Gen 22:18, compare 12:3 and 18:18].

paras.t: Insuper ad litteram ex isto capitulo, sancti Patriarchæ hujus exemplo valde commendantur nobis opera pietatis et hospitalitas pia, et ea exercere docemur toto cordis affectu, omni exclusa cupiditate, acedia, ac cura superflua, sanctique Abrahæ alacritatem sectari, humilitatem amplecti, fervore accendi, peccantibus ac pereuntibus condolere, atque pro ipsis cum omni instantia ardentissimo corde orare.
paras.en: Moreover, according to the letter, this chapter, by the example of this holy Patriarch, strongly commends to us the works of piety and devout hospitality, and teaches us to practise them with the whole affection of the heart, shutting out all covetousness, sloth [*acedia*: spiritual sloth, weariness in the things of God] and needless care; and to follow the eagerness of holy Abraham, to embrace his humility, to be kindled with his fervour, to feel for sinners and for those who are perishing, and to pray for them with all earnestness and with a most burning heart.

paras.t: Postremo, circa capitulum istud quæstiones nascuntur. Primo, an angeli sint materiales. Secundo, si non, qualiter assumant corpora, in quibus apparent. Tertio, an in corporibus illis assumptis vere manducent, et quid fiat de cibo quem sumunt. Quarto, an videant per oculos, audiantque per aures corporum quæ assumunt. Quinto, quomodo dixit Deus Abrahæ, velle se parcere populo Sodomorum, si inveniret decem justos in eo, quum dicat per Ezechielem, quod Daniel, Noe, et Job, filium et filiam non liberarent. Sexto, an Dominus pepercisset populo Sodomitico propter pauciores justos, quam decem, si Abraham id orasset. Septimo, an talis ignoscentia fuisset indecens sive extranea.
paras.en: Lastly, questions arise concerning this chapter [a margin note beside this line cannot be read]. First, whether angels are material. Second, if not, how they assume the bodies in which they appear. Third, whether in those assumed bodies they truly eat, and what becomes of the food they take. Fourth, whether they see through the eyes and hear through the ears of the bodies they assume. Fifth, how God said to Abraham that He was willing to spare the people of Sodom if He found ten just men in it, when He says through Ezechiel that Daniel, Noe and Job would not deliver son or daughter[[Ezech 14:20||]]. Sixth, whether the Lord would have spared the people of Sodom for fewer just men than ten, if Abraham had prayed for it. Seventh, whether such pardon would have been unbecoming or foreign to Him.

paras.t: Ad primum breviter respondendum, quod sicut de hoc fuerunt diversæ opiniones inter philosophos, ita et inter theologos. Avicebron enim in libro Fontis vitæ, et multi Platonici, posuerunt ad minus spiritualem materiam in intellectualibus substantiis universis, quod et Proclus Platonicus in Elementatione sua theologica sentire videtur: imo Porphyrius, Apuleius, et alii quidam Platonici dixerunt, dæmones aerea corpora naturaliter sibi unita habere. Peripatetici vero dixerunt, intelligentias, quos angelos appellamus, esse immateriales et incorporales, propter quod vocabant eos substantias separatas. Sic et quidam theologi videntur posuisse ad minus spiritualem materiam, vel aerea quædam corpora in præfatis substantiis, scilicet Augustinus, ut Magister libro secundo allegat. Origenes quoque in libris Periarchon disseruit: Solius Dei est, Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti naturæ id proprium est, ut sine omni materiali substantia et materialis adjectionis societate subsistat. Sed et Damascenus ait libro secundo: Solus Deus essentialiter immaterialis, incorporeusque consistit. Bernardus item super Cantica scribit: Demus soli Deo immortalitatem, sicut et incorporeitatem, cujus natura sola, nec propter se, nec propter aliud solatio indiget instrumenti corporei. Liquet autem, omnem spiritum creatum corporeo indigere solatio.
paras.en: To the first the brief answer is that, as there were different opinions on this among the philosophers, so there were among the theologians. For Avicebron in his book *The Fount of Life*, and many Platonists, held that there is at least a spiritual matter in all intellectual substances, which Proclus the Platonist too seems to hold in his *Elements of Theology*; indeed Porphyry, Apuleius and certain other Platonists said that demons have airy bodies naturally united to them. The Peripatetics, on the other hand, said that the intelligences, which we call angels, are immaterial and incorporeal, for which reason they called them separate substances. So too certain theologians seem to have held that there is at least a spiritual matter, or some airy bodies, in the substances mentioned: namely Augustine, as the Master [Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences] cites him in the second book. Origen also argued in the books *Peri Archon*: It belongs to God alone, that is, to the nature of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, as its property, to subsist without any material substance and without the fellowship of any material addition. And Damascene says in the second book: God alone is essentially immaterial and incorporeal. Bernard likewise writes on the Canticles: Let us grant to God alone immortality, as also incorporeity: His nature alone needs the help of a bodily instrument neither for itself nor for anything else. But it is plain that every created spirit needs bodily help.

paras.t: Alii vero theologi dicunt, quod angeli et dæmones sunt in propria natura simplices formæ et actus in se subsistentes. Unde divinus Dionysius, de Divinis nominibus protestatur quod immateriales et incorporales existant, quod item de angelis in libro de Cælesti Hierarchia frequenter insinuat. Et istud probabilius reputatur, quod etiam Thomas, Albertus et Ægidius assequuntur. Quum enim ex operatione agnoscatur substantia, et propria angelorum operatio sit intellectualis, non dependens a corpore, nec indigens eo, non videntur in sua natura communionem seu conjunctionem habere materiæ. Denique si habent corpus sive materiam, ergo compositi sunt ex forma atque materia. Quæretur ergo de forma ista quæ est pars eorum, an et ipsa composita sit ex forma et materia. Si dicatur, quod sic, quæretur ulterius et procedetur in infinitum, eruntque in eodem plures materiæ. Si autem dicatur, quod non, sequitur quod non solus Deus sit prorsus immaterialis, et item quod aliqua forma creata sit immaterialis, et simili ratione concedendum videtur, quod angelus sit immaterialis. Verumtamen quæstio hæc locum habet circa secundum Sententiarum. Et plurima dici possent de ea, de quibus pertranseo, ista non nisi cursorie tangens.
paras.en: Other theologians, however, say that angels and demons are, in their own nature, simple forms and acts subsisting in themselves. Hence the divine Dionysius declares in *The Divine Names* that they are immaterial and incorporeal, and he often suggests the same of the angels in the book *The Celestial Hierarchy*. And this is held the more probable opinion, which Thomas, Albert and Giles also follow. For since a substance is known from its operation, and the proper operation of angels is intellectual, not depending on a body nor needing one, they do not seem to have in their nature any communion or conjunction with matter. Lastly, if they have a body or matter, then they are composed of form and matter. It will then be asked of this form which is a part of them whether it too is composed of form and matter. If it is said that it is, the question will be asked again and we shall go on to infinity, and there will be many matters in the same thing. But if it is said that it is not, it follows that God is not the only thing altogether immaterial, and also that some created form is immaterial; and by like reasoning it seems we must grant that an angel is immaterial. This question, however, has its place on the second book of the Sentences. And a great deal could be said about it, which I pass over, touching on these things only in passing.

paras.t: Ad secundum quidam dixerunt, angelos nunquam assumere corpora, sed eos tantummodo apparuisse secundum imaginariam visionem, in qua res quæ apparet, non est vere ad extra, sed in interiori imaginatione et visu videntis. Hoc autem salvari non potest, quia Scriptura frequenter testatur angelos sic apparuisse, quod vere extra præsentes fuerunt, atque realia opera exercuerunt: quod in præsenti ac sequenti capitulis apertissime constat: idcirco dicendum, quod interdum assumunt corpora, et frequenter corpora aerea, quæ ad libitum suum possunt consolidare et figurare. Hinc ait Gregorius: Abraham angelos non potuisset videre, hospitio suscipere, eisque cibum apponere, nisi corpora ex aere assumpsissent. Non enim apparerent, et cibos acciperent, nisi solidum corpus ex elemento haberent.
paras.en: To the second, some have said that angels never assume bodies, but that they appeared only by an imaginary vision [a vision in the imagination, as opposed to one seen by the bodily eyes], in which the thing that appears is not truly outside, but in the inward imagination and sight of the one who sees. But this cannot be upheld, because Scripture often testifies that angels appeared in such a way that they were truly present outside and did real works: which is most plainly evident in the present chapter and the next. Therefore it must be said that they sometimes assume bodies, and often airy bodies, which they can condense and shape at their pleasure. Hence Gregory says: Abraham could not have seen the angels, received them in hospitality and set food before them, had they not taken bodies from the air. For they would not appear and take food unless they had a solid body from the element.

paras.t: Ad tertium respondetur, quod manducare et bibere non convenit angelis, proprie atque univoce cum hominibus et ceteris animantibus: quia non habent vim vegetativam ac nutritivam, nec cibus et potus quem sumunt, in eorum substantiam exstat vertibilis; sed quantum ad hoc dicuntur manducare ac bibere, quod cibum ac potum insumunt, ac intus trajiciunt. De quo cibo et potu asserit Augustinus, quod sicut humor a solis calore consumitur, nec tamen in eum convertitur, ita de tali cibo et potu sit sentiendum.
paras.en: To the third the answer is that eating and drinking do not belong to angels properly, nor in the same sense [*univoce*: in exactly the same meaning of the word] as to men and the other living things: for they have no vegetative and nutritive power, nor can the food and drink they take be turned into their substance; but they are said to eat and drink in this respect, that they take in food and drink and pass it within. Of this food and drink Augustine says that, as moisture is consumed by the heat of the sun and yet not turned into it, so we must think of such food and drink.

paras.t: Ad quartum dicendum secundum Thomam et alios multos, quod angeli non uniuntur corporibus quæ assumunt, ut formæ, sed solummodo ut motores, nec habent in se sensitivas potentias: idcirco non vident per oculos, nec audiunt per aures corporum assumptorum, nec per ea sentiunt aliquid, nec corpora ista vivunt.
paras.en: To the fourth it must be said, according to Thomas and many others, that angels are not united to the bodies they assume as forms, but only as movers, nor have they in themselves the powers of sense: therefore they do not see through the eyes nor hear through the ears of the assumed bodies, nor perceive anything through them, nor do those bodies live.

paras.t: Ad quintum dicendum, quod Deus interdum agit secundum rigorem suæ justitiæ, unicuique dando quod meruit, nec uni propter alterius merita propitiando. Sicque per Ezechielem loquitur: Terra quum peccaverit, interficiam de ea hominem et jumentum. Et si fuerint tres viri isti in medio ejus, Noe, Daniel et Job, ipsi in justitia sua liberabunt animas suas, filium autem et filiam non liberabunt. Interdum vero Deus omnipotens agit clementius, parcendo uni propter preces et merita alterius, sicque locutus est Abrahæ. Quemadmodum autem misericordia Dei, ita et justitia ejus diversos habet effectus. Et ipse incomprehensibilis Deus juxta ordinem sapientiæ suæ immensæ omnia operatur irreprehensibiliter atque liberrime, quum ipse sit prima mensura et summa causa universæ justitiæ ac virtutis.
paras.en: To the fifth it must be said that God sometimes acts according to the rigour of His justice, giving each one what he has deserved, and not being propitious to one for the merits of another. And so He speaks through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 14:13|when a land shall sin|Terra quum peccaverit]], I [[Ezech 14:13|will destroy man and beast out of it|interficiam de ea hominem et jumentum]]. [[Ezech 14:14|And if these three men, Noe, Daniel, and Job, shall be in it: they shall deliver their own souls by their justice|Et si fuerint tres viri isti in medio ejus, Noe, Daniel et Job, ipsi in justitia sua liberabunt animas suas]], but [[Ezech 14:20|they shall deliver neither son nor daughter|filium autem et filiam non liberabunt]] [the margin gives Ezech. xiv, 13, 14; these last words are from v. 20]. But sometimes almighty God acts more mercifully, sparing one for the prayers and merits of another; and so He spoke to Abraham. And as the mercy of God, so too His justice has different effects. And the incomprehensible God Himself works all things, according to the order of His boundless wisdom, irreproachably and most freely, since He Himself is the first measure and the highest cause of all justice and virtue.

paras.t: Ad sextum dicendum, quod de hoc certitudo haberi non potest, nisi ex revelatione divina. Posset tamen argui, quod Deus pepercisset Sodomitis propter justos pauciores quam decem, quoniam per Jeremiam ipse Dominus ait: Circuite vias Jerusalem, et quærite in plateis ejus, an inveniatis virum facientem judicium et quærentem fidem, et propitius ero eis, scilicet habitatoribus Jerusalem. Circa hoc scribit Hieronymus: Grandis amor justitiæ, ut non pro decem justis, sicut olim ad Abraham dixit, liberet civitatem, sed si invenerit unum justum in Jerusalem, misereatur civitatis. Præterea per Ezechielem fatetur: Quæsivi de eis virum qui interponeret sepem, et staret oppositus contra me pro terra, ne dissiparem eam, et non inveni, et effudi indignationem meam super eos. Ad ista dicendum sicut prædictum est, quod divina justitia diversis modis agit in peccatoribus, nunc rigorose, nunc quoque clementer. Quid tamen cum Sodomitis egisset, si Abraham orasset, ut parceretur eis pro paucioribus justis quam decem, non constat, quum hoc dependeat ex divina voluntate, quæ in tantum innotescit hominibus, quantum per revelationem et per Scripturas manifestatur. Qualiter vero præinducta Jeremiæ Ezechielisque verba sint intelligenda, super eosdem Prophetas plenius scripsi.
paras.en: To the sixth it must be said that no certainty can be had about this except from divine revelation. Yet it could be argued that God would have spared the Sodomites for fewer just men than ten, since through Jeremias the Lord Himself says: [[Jer 5:1|Go about through the streets of Jerusalem|Circuite vias Jerusalem]], [[Jer 5:1|and seek in the broad places thereof, if you can find a man that executeth judgment, and seeketh faith: and I will be merciful unto it|et quærite in plateis ejus, an inveniatis virum facientem judicium et quærentem fidem, et propitius ero eis]] [Denis reads *eis*, "unto them"], namely to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. On this Jerome writes: Great is the love of justice, that He would free the city not for ten just men, as He once told Abraham, but would have mercy on the city if He found one just man in Jerusalem. Besides, through Ezechiel He declares: [[Ezech 22:30|I sought among them for a man that might set up a hedge, and stand in the gap before me in favour of the land, that I might not destroy it: and I found none|Quæsivi de eis virum qui interponeret sepem, et staret oppositus contra me pro terra, ne dissiparem eam, et non inveni]]; [[Ezech 22:31|And I poured out my indignation upon them|et effudi indignationem meam super eos]]. To these it must be said, as was said above, that divine justice acts in different ways with sinners, now rigorously, now also mercifully. Yet what He would have done with the Sodomites, had Abraham prayed that they be spared for fewer just men than ten, is not known, since this depends on the divine will, which is made known to men only so far as it is shown through revelation and through the Scriptures. But how the words of Jeremias and Ezechiel brought forward above are to be understood, I have written more fully on those same Prophets.

paras.t: Ad septimum breviter respondetur, quod quidquid Deus essentialiter bonus, justus, sanctus ac sapiens facit, eo ipso quod ipse hoc facit, bonum ac decens est: quia ut in libro Sapientiæ scribitur, Virtus ejus justitiæ initium est. Qui etiam ait: An non licet mihi, quod volo, facere?
paras.en: To the seventh the brief answer is that whatever God, who is essentially good, just, holy and wise, does is good and becoming by the very fact that He does it: because, as is written in the book of Wisdom, [[Wis 12:16|thy power is the beginning of justice|Virtus ejus justitiæ initium est]] [Denis has *ejus*, "his power"; the verse number in the margin cannot be read]. And He also says: [[Matt 20:15|is it not lawful for me to do what I will?|An non licet mihi, quod volo, facere?]] [the margin note is partly unreadable and keeps only "15"; these are the householder's words in the parable, Matt 20:15].

19.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli nonidecimi: Veneruntque duo angeli Sodomam vespere
19.title_en: Literal elucidation of the nineteenth chapter: And the two angels came to Sodom in the evening

paras.t: SUBVERSIO Sodomæ et urbium ei subditarum consequenter describitur. Multa autem quæ circa expositionem hujus capituli dici possent, dicta sunt in expositione præcedentis capituli.
paras.en: Next is described the overthrow of Sodom and of the cities subject to it. Many things that could be said in expounding this chapter have already been said in the exposition of the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Veneruntque duo angeli Sodomam vespere. Secundum expositores communiter, isti fuerunt angeli boni, et duo ex tribus qui Abrahæ apparuerunt. Verumtamen in Scholastica historia dicitur, quod secundum quosdam fuerunt alii angeli, utpote mali, secundum quosdam qui aiunt, quod angeli boni non puniunt homines: cujus contrarium constat ex hoc, quod angelus Dei bonus percussit centum octoginta quinque millia hominum in castris Assyriorum. Similiter angelus bonus percussit primogenita Ægyptiorum. Sedente Lot in foribus civitatis, ad videndum an videret peregrinos aut pauperes, quibus hospitalitatem impenderet, quam ab Abraham didicit, et frequentavit.
paras.en: [[19:1|And the two angels came to Sodom in the evening|Veneruntque duo angeli Sodomam vespere]]. According to the expositors generally, these were good angels, and two of the three who appeared to Abraham. Yet the Scholastic History [of Peter Comestor] says that according to some they were other angels, namely evil ones; this according to some who say that good angels do not punish men. The contrary of this is plain from the fact that a good angel of God slew a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp of the Assyrians[[4 Kings 19:35||]]. Likewise a good angel slew the firstborn of the Egyptians[[Ex 12:29||]]. [[19:1|and Lot was sitting in the gate of the city|Sedente Lot in foribus civitatis]], to see whether he might see pilgrims or poor people to whom he might show hospitality, which he had learned from Abraham and often practised.

paras.t: Qui quum vidisset eos, surrexit et ivit obviam eis, ut eos ad domum suam perduceret, et bene tractaret; adoravitque eos pronus in terram adoratione duliæ. Apparuerunt etenim ei in forma honorabili ac humana, quasi homines multum divini. Et dixit: Obsecro, domini, declinate in domum pueri vestri, scilicet mei servi vestri, et manete ibi. Lavate pedes vestros, id est, permittite ut laventur in domo mea: et mane proficiscemini in viam vestram. Et ex omnibus his innotescunt magna pietas, devotio, humilitas, et liberalitas Lot, sicut de Abraham dictum est.
paras.en: [[19:1|And seeing them, he rose up and went to meet them|Qui quum vidisset eos, surrexit et ivit obviam eis]], in order to bring them to his house and treat them well; [[19:1|and worshipped prostrate to the ground|adoravitque eos pronus in terram]], with the worship of dulia [that is, the honour paid to creatures, as distinct from latria, the worship due to God alone]. For they appeared to him in an honourable and human form, as men very godlike. [[19:2|And said: I beseech you, my lords, turn in to the house of your servant|Et dixit: Obsecro, domini, declinate in domum pueri vestri]], namely of me, your servant, [[19:2|and lodge there|et manete ibi]]. [[19:2|wash your feet|Lavate pedes vestros]], that is, allow them to be washed in my house: [[19:2|and in the morning you shall go on your way|et mane proficiscemini in viam vestram]]. And from all these things the great piety, devotion, humility and liberality of Lot are made known, as was said of Abraham.

paras.t: Qui dixerunt: Minime, sed in platea manebimus. Quomodo verum est hoc, quum paulo post ingressi sint domum Lot? Et respondendum, quod dixerunt hoc non simpliciter asserendo, sed more eorum qui invitantur, qui ex curialitate ad tempus non acquiescunt et dicunt se non venire, utpote non tam cito, seu quantum in ipsis est. Cur autem non acquieverunt primæ invitationi Lot, quemadmodum Abrahæ, dictum est in expositione capituli præcedentis. Compulit illos oppido, id est valde, non quod proprie loquendo eos coegerit aut invitos adduxerit, quod nec decuit, nec sibi possibile fuit, sed compulit, id est, per modum quodammodo compellentis opportune et importune ac instantissime eos rogavit, ita quod per caritatem videbatur vincere eos. Ingressisque domum fecit convivium: quia putavit quod homines essent. Coxit azyma, id est panes non fermentatos, qui celeriter fieri poterant, voluitque hospites tantos recenti ac delicato reficere pane.
paras.en: [[19:2|And they said: No, but we will abide in the street|Qui dixerunt: Minime, sed in platea manebimus]]. How is this true, since a little later they went into Lot's house? The answer is that they said this not as a plain assertion, but in the manner of those who are invited, who out of courtesy do not consent for a while and say they will not come, that is, not so soon, or as far as lies with them. Why they did not consent to Lot's first invitation, as they did to Abraham's, was told in the exposition of the preceding chapter. [[19:3|He pressed them very much|Compulit illos oppido]]: *very much*, that is, exceedingly; not that, properly speaking, he *compelled* them [the Latin *compulit* means "he compelled"] or brought them against their will, which was neither fitting nor possible for him; but he *compelled* them, that is, after the manner, as it were, of one compelling, he begged them in season and out of season and most urgently, so that by charity he seemed to overcome them. [[19:3|and when they were come into his house, he made them a feast|Ingressisque domum fecit convivium]]: because he thought they were men. [[19:3|and baked unleavened bread|Coxit azyma]], that is, loaves not leavened, which could be made quickly; and he wished to refresh such great guests with fresh and dainty bread.

paras.t: Prius autem quam irent cubitum, viri civitatis vallaverunt domum illius a puero usque ad senem. Alia littera habet, Ab infante usque ad senem: sicque intelligendum est exclusive, quod dicitur, Ab infante seu puero. Porro, si pueri appellentur omnes qui infra vicesimum annum sunt, sic verisimile quod multi pueri inter illos fuerunt. Quidam dicunt istud intelligendum per modum locutionis hyperbolicæ seu emphaticæ, quia non apparet probabile, quod totus populus Sodomæ confluxerit ad ipsius Lot domum. Sed huic videtur contrariari quod subditur: omnis populus simul. Ideo aliqui dicunt, quod omnes omnino fuerunt ibi, et quod Deus idcirco permisit sic fieri, ut pateret quod omnes habitatores Sodomæ præter Lot fuerunt injusti: et ita sciretur quod Deus complevit, sicut ad Abraham dixerat; quoniam non punivit Sodomitas, donec per angelos suos fuit repertum, omnes communicare in crimine.
paras.en: [[19:4|But before they went to bed, the men of the city beset the house|Prius autem quam irent cubitum, viri civitatis vallaverunt domum illius]], [[19:4|both young and old|a puero usque ad senem]] [literally "from boy to old man"]. Another text has: From infant to old man. And so what is said, From the infant or boy, is to be understood exclusively [that is, as not counting the infants or boys themselves]. Moreover, if all who are under their twentieth year are called boys, then it is likely that there were many boys among them. Some say that this is to be understood as a hyperbolic or emphatic manner of speech, since it does not seem probable that the whole people of Sodom flocked together to Lot's house. But against this seems to stand what is added: [[19:4|all the people together|omnis populus simul]]. Therefore some say that absolutely all were there, and that God permitted it to happen so in order that it might be plain that all the inhabitants of Sodom except Lot were unjust: and so it would be known that God did as he had said to Abraham, since he did not punish the Sodomites until it was found by his angels that all shared in the crime.

paras.t: Vocaveruntque Lot, et dixerunt ei: Ubi sunt viri qui introierunt ad te nocte, id est de vespere? Ex quo constat, quod aliqui Sodomitæ viderunt angelos istos. Et quia in specie juvenili ac pulchra apparuerunt, idcirco qui eos viderunt, nuntiaverunt mox aliis, et magis incitati fuerunt furore libidinis. Educ illos huc, ut cognoscamus eos. Ex hoc patet inverecunda, usitata et vitiosissima turpitudo illorum.
paras.en: [[19:5|And they called Lot, and said to him: Where are the men that came in to thee at night?|Vocaveruntque Lot, et dixerunt ei: Ubi sunt viri qui introierunt ad te nocte]] That is, in the evening. From this it is plain that some of the Sodomites had seen these angels. And because they appeared in a youthful and beautiful form, those who saw them soon told the others, and they were the more stirred up by the frenzy of lust. [[19:5|bring them out hither, that we may know them|Educ illos huc, ut cognoscamus eos]]. From this their shameless, habitual and most vicious filthiness is plain.

paras.t: Egressus ad eos Lot, ut inter eos stans efficacius persuaderet eis, post tergum occludens ostium, ne vitiosi illi domum suam impetuose intrarent, et hospites suos quos homines esse putavit, invaderent, ait: Nolite, quæso, fratres mei, nolite malum hoc facere. Fratres eos vocavit, ex communione habitationis civilis, et propter conformitatem naturæ. Mansuete quoque et amorose eos alloquebatur, ut citius flecterentur. Habeo duas filias, quæ necdum cognoverunt virum: educam eas ad vos, abutimini eis, tamen in membro seu vasculo ad hoc naturaliter instituto, sicut vobis placuerit, dummodo viris istis nihil faciatis mali, quia ingressi sunt sub umbra culminis mei, hoc est, domum meam ingressi sunt, ut ibi protegantur sub tecto meo, quum naturale sit hospitanti hospitatos defendere. At illi dixerunt: Recede illuc, id est, discede a nobis, et redi ad hospites tuos, ut educas eos ad nos. Et rursus: Ingressus es, inquiunt, ut advena, numquid ut judices? hoc est, venisti huc inter nos commorari tanquam extraneus, et non ut judex noster, ita ut audeas nos increpare, et nostra opera reprobare. Te ergo ipsum magis quam hos affligemus, nisi acquieveris nobis in eductione illorum. Vimque faciebant Lot vehementissime, hoc est, violentissime eum tractaverunt, forsitan impellendo, trudendo, trahendo.
paras.en: [[19:6|Lot went out to them|Egressus ad eos Lot]], so that standing among them he might persuade them more effectively, [[19:6|and shut the door after him|post tergum occludens ostium]], lest those vicious men should burst violently into his house and set upon his guests, whom he thought to be men, [[19:6|and said|ait]]: [[19:7|Do not so, I beseech you, my brethren, do not commit this evil.|Nolite, quæso, fratres mei, nolite malum hoc facere.]] He called them brethren because they shared one city as their dwelling, and because of their likeness of nature. He also spoke to them gently and lovingly, that they might the sooner be moved. [[19:8|I have two daughters who, as yet, have not known man; I will bring them out to you|Habeo duas filias, quæ necdum cognoverunt virum: educam eas ad vos]], [[19:8|and abuse you them|abutimini eis]], though in the member or vessel naturally ordained for this, [[19:8|as it shall please you, so that you do no evil to these men, because they are come in under the shadow of my roof|sicut vobis placuerit, dummodo viris istis nihil faciatis mali, quia ingressi sunt sub umbra culminis mei]], that is, they have come into my house to be protected there under my roof, since it is natural for a host to defend those whom he lodges. [[19:9|But they said: Get thee back thither|At illi dixerunt: Recede illuc]], that is, go away from us, and go back to thy guests, to bring them out to us. [[19:9|And again: Thou camest in, said they, as a stranger, was it to be a judge?|Et rursus: Ingressus es, inquiunt, ut advena, numquid ut judices?]] That is: thou camest here to dwell among us as a foreigner, and not as our judge, so as to dare to rebuke us and condemn our doings. [[19:9|therefore we will afflict thee more than them|Te ergo ipsum magis quam hos affligemus]], unless thou yield to us by bringing them out. [[19:9|And they pressed very violently upon Lot|Vimque faciebant Lot vehementissime]], that is, they handled him most violently, perhaps pushing, shoving and dragging him.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, an Lot peccavit, dicendo: Habeo duas filias, educam eas ad vos, etc. Et apparet, quod non, quia dixit hoc pia intentione, ut scilicet impios illos a gravissimis revocaret sceleribus, et hospites suos ab intolerabilibus ignominiis liberaret, et etiam quia non legitur increpatus de isto ab angelis, imo tanquam justus, salvatus est de pereuntium plaga.
paras.en: Concerning these things it is asked whether Lot sinned in saying: [[19:8|I have two daughters|Habeo duas filias]], [[19:8|I will bring them out to you|educam eas ad vos]], etc. And it seems that he did not, because he said this with a pious intention, namely to call those wicked men back from the most grievous crimes and to free his guests from intolerable outrages; and also because we do not read that he was rebuked for it by the angels; rather, as a just man, he was saved from the scourge of those who perished.

paras.t: Oppositum tamen videtur, quia non sunt facienda mala ut eveniant bona, nec debet quis facere contra præceptum, ut a peccatis eruat alium, præsertim quum dicat Salvator: Quid proficit homo, si lucretur universum mundum, se ipsum autem perdat?
paras.en: Yet the opposite seems true, because evil is not to be done that good may come of it, nor ought anyone to act against a precept in order to rescue another from sin; especially since the Saviour says: [[Luke 9:25|For what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world and lose himself|Quid proficit homo, si lucretur universum mundum, se ipsum autem perdat?]]?

paras.t: Circa hujus solutionem pensanda sunt verba Augustini, dicentis: Utrum admittenda sit compensatio flagitiorum, vel quorumlibet vitiorum, ita ut faciamus mala minora, ne fiant graviora, merito quæritur. Ad quod idem sanctus Doctor respondet: Periculosissime compensatio ista admittitur, et quod dixit Lot, non consilio sed perturbationi est attribuendum, quæ mentis perturbatio nullo modo est imitanda. Hinc communiter dicitur, quod Lot ita loquendo, peccavit non venialiter tantum, imo mortaliter, consentiendo in stupra filiarum suarum. Excusatur tamen a tanto, quia ex perturbatione sic corruit, et ex piis quodammodo causis jam tactis, fuerat motus. Si autem dicatur, quod protulit verba illa non ex animo, neque intentione prostituendi filias suas illis, sed solum animo revocandi eos a scelerato proposito: quoniam probabiliter noverat quod non curarent de filiabus suis, neque appeterent eas quas videbant quotidie, nec appetebant, excusari posset a culpa saltem mortali. Est autem inter duo mala minus malum eligendum, ita ut quis faciat levius, ne committat gravius. Verumtamen nemo ita perplexus est, ut malum culpæ nequaquam queat vitare, alioqui culpa non esset culpa.
paras.en: For the solution of this, the words of Augustine are to be weighed, who says: Whether a compensation of crimes, or of any vices whatever, is to be admitted, so that we do lesser evils lest greater ones be done, is rightly asked. To which the same holy Doctor answers: This compensation is admitted at the greatest peril; and what Lot said is to be put down not to counsel but to agitation of mind, and that agitation of mind is in no way to be imitated. Hence it is commonly said that Lot, in speaking so, sinned not only venially but even mortally, by consenting to the defilement of his daughters. Yet he is excused *a tanto* [that is, his guilt is lessened, though not taken away altogether], because he fell so through agitation of mind, and had been moved by causes in a way pious, already touched on. But if it be said that he uttered those words not from his heart, nor with the intention of prostituting his daughters to them, but only with the purpose of calling them back from their wicked design (since he probably knew that they cared nothing for his daughters, nor would desire them, whom they saw every day and did not desire), he could be excused at least from mortal sin. Now of two evils the lesser is to be chosen, so that one does the lighter lest he commit the graver. Yet no one is so perplexed that he can in no way avoid the evil of sin [*perplexus*: caught so that every course open to him is sinful]; otherwise sin would not be sin.

paras.t: Ex præhabitis quoque patet, in quantam criminum profunditatem corruerint Sodomitæ. Unde loquitur Augustinus: Stupra in masculos tanta consuetudine convaluerant apud illos, quantam licentiam aliorum factorum solent præbere leges: atque ut alibi ait: Tantum excæcavit eos pravissima consuetudo, ut magis reprehenderetur ab eis reprehensor flagitiositatis, quam factor.
paras.en: From what has been said it is plain, too, into what depth of crimes the Sodomites had fallen. Whence Augustine says: Outrages upon males had through custom gained as much strength among them as the licence that laws are wont to give to other deeds. And as he says elsewhere: Their most depraved custom had so blinded them that the rebuker of the outrage was blamed by them more than the doer.

paras.t: Jamque prope erat ut Sodomitæ effringerent fores domus ipsius Lot. Et ecce miserunt manum viri, id est, angeli manum exposuerunt, et introduxerunt ad se Lot in domum: quod tamen unus eorum forsitan fecit, quod et facillimum fuit angelicæ potestati: clauserunt […] ostium, et eos qui foris erant, percusserunt cæcitate a minimo usque ad maximum, non omnimoda cæcitate, sed tali, quod non videbant distincte et cum discretione seu notitia id quod quærebant, et cernere cupiebant: quæ cæcitas appellatur […], ab […], quod est sine, et […] quod est visio sive judicium: qua percussi fuerunt qui Elisæum quærebant, et duo discipuli qui ibant cum Jesu in Emmaus. Hinc in Sapientiæ libro scriptum est: Percussi sunt autem cæcitate, sicut illi in foribus justi, quum subitaneis cooperti essent tenebris: unusquisque transitum ostii sui quærebat.
paras.en: [[19:9|and they were even at the point|Jamque prope erat ut]], the Sodomites, [[19:9|of breaking open the doors|effringerent fores]] of Lot's own house. [[19:10|And behold the men put out their hand|Et ecce miserunt manum viri]], that is, the angels stretched out a hand, [[19:10|and drew in Lot unto them|et introduxerunt ad se Lot]] into the house: which perhaps only one of them did, and it was very easy for angelic power: [[19:10|and shut|clauserunt]] […] [[19:10|the door|ostium]] [a word is lost here in the transcription], [[19:11|And them, that were without, they struck with blindness from the least to the greatest|et eos qui foris erant, percusserunt cæcitate a minimo usque ad maximum]]: not with total blindness, but with such that they did not see distinctly, with discernment or knowledge, what they were seeking and longed to make out. This blindness is called […] [evidently the Greek *aorasia*, the Septuagint's word in this verse], from […], which means *without*, and […], which means *sight* or *judgment*: with it were struck those who sought Eliseus[[4 Kings 6:18||]], and the two disciples who were going with Jesus to Emmaus[[Luke 24:16||]]. Hence it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 19:16|But they were struck with blindness: as those others were at the doors of the just man, when they were covered with sudden darkness, and every one sought the passage of his own door|Percussi sunt autem cæcitate, sicut illi in foribus justi, quum subitaneis cooperti essent tenebris: unusquisque transitum ostii sui quærebat]].

paras.t: De hac cæcitate, vel potius semicæcitate, beatus Augustinus effatur: Quum aliquid videtur ab alio, a quo alia quæ adsunt, non videntur, Græce acrisia dicitur, quod nostri interpretes Latine dicere non valentes, in libro Geneseos cæcitatem interpretati sunt, ubi de Sodomitis conscribitur. His verbis in Scholastica historia additur: Forte hoc modo quandoque quærimus, quod in manu tenemus. Verumtamen hoc alio modo potest accidere, utpote ex intensa imaginatione et occupatione circa alia, aut certe ex distractione et inadvertentia.
