Sic ergo percusserunt omnes illos hac cæcitate, ita ut ostium invenire non possent, hoc est, januam domus Lot, non valebant determinate cognoscere, seu ab aliis discernere januis, quamvis illam confuse viderunt; quemadmodum Syri viderunt personam Elisei, et duo discipuli Dominum Jesum, sed absque distincta notitia. Viderunt quippe quod homines essent, sed non cognoscebant distincte eorum personas.
paras.en: Of this blindness, or rather half-blindness, blessed Augustine speaks thus: When something is seen by one person by whom other things that are present are not seen, it is called in Greek *acrisia*; our translators, not being able to say this in Latin, rendered it *blindness* in the book of Genesis, where it is written of the Sodomites [*acrisia* as printed; the Greek word here is *aorasia*]. To these words the Scholastic History adds: Perhaps in this way we sometimes look for what we are holding in our hand. Yet this can also happen in another way, namely from intense imagining and preoccupation with other things, or indeed from distraction and inattention. So then they struck all of them with this blindness, [[19:11|so that they could not find the door|ita ut ostium invenire non possent]], that is, they could not recognise the door of Lot's house definitely, or tell it apart from other doors, though they saw it in a confused way; just as the Syrians saw the person of Eliseus, and the two disciples the Lord Jesus, but without distinct knowledge. For they saw that they were men, but did not know distinctly who they were.

paras.t: Dixerunt autem ad Lot: Habes hic, id est in urbe seu domo hac, quempiam tuorum, generum, aut filios, aut filias? Omnes qui tui sunt, educ de urbe hac; delebimus enim locum istum, hoc est, civitatem hanc cum urbibus sibi adjunctis subvertemus: eo quod increverit clamor eorum coram Domino, id est, clamitans eorum iniquitas, scilicet vitium contra naturam, cum ceteris eorum sceleribus intolerabiliter aucta sit in Dei præsentia, ac justo ejus judicio, ita quod eos ultra tolerare non debuit, sicut ut ad impios Judæos Jeremias locutus est: Non poterat vos Dominus ultra sustinere propter malitiam studiorum vestrorum.
paras.en: [[19:12|And they said to Lot: Hast thou here|Dixerunt autem ad Lot: Habes hic]], that is, in this city or house, [[19:12|any of thine? son in law, or sons, or daughters|quempiam tuorum, generum, aut filios, aut filias?]], [[19:12|all that are thine bring them out of this city|Omnes qui tui sunt, educ de urbe hac]]; [[19:13|For we will destroy this place|delebimus enim locum istum]], that is, we will overthrow this city with the cities joined to it: [[19:13|because their cry is grown loud before the Lord|eo quod increverit clamor eorum coram Domino]], that is, their crying iniquity, namely the vice against nature, together with their other crimes, has grown intolerably great in God's presence and before his just judgment, so that he ought not to bear with them any longer; as Jeremias said to the wicked Jews: [[Jer 44:22|So that the Lord could no longer bear, because of the evil of your doings|Non poterat vos Dominus ultra sustinere propter malitiam studiorum vestrorum]] [the margin's book is lost and only "22" can be read; the words are those of Jer 44:22, where the Vulgate has *portare* for Denis's *sustinere* and lacks *vos*].

paras.t: Quæstio ista angelorum ex ignorantia non processit. Cur ergo dixerunt ad Lot, Habes hic tuorum quempiam, generum, aut filios aut filias, quum Lot non haberet, nisi duas filias virgines? Respondetur, quod hoc dixerunt ad insinuandum, tantam esse justitiam Lot, pietatemque Dei, quod propter merita Lot, Deus paratus fuit parcere omnibus ad ipsum Lot pertinentibus consanguinitate aut affinitate, ita quod cum Sodomitis non disperirent in plaga quæ imminebat.
paras.en: This question of the angels did not come from ignorance. Why then did they say to Lot, [[19:12|Hast thou here any of thine? son in law, or sons, or daughters|Habes hic tuorum quempiam, generum, aut filios aut filias]], when Lot had only two virgin daughters? The answer is that they said this to suggest that so great was the justice of Lot, and the goodness of God, that for the merits of Lot God was ready to spare all who belonged to Lot by blood or by marriage, so that they should not perish with the Sodomites in the scourge that was at hand.

paras.t: Verumtamen ut refert Lyra, Hebræi horum occasione verborum affirmant, quod Lot habebat in Sodoma duas filias maritatas, filiosque habentes, quorum filios asserunt hic vocari filios Lot. Cui dicto objicitur, quod (ut paulo post subditur) egressus Lot ad generos suos, qui accepturi erant filias ejus, dixit: Surgite, egredimini de loco isto. Ex quo videtur, quod si habuisset in Sodoma alias filias, locutus fuisset eis, earumque viris ac filiis eadem verba: quod tamen Scriptura non refert. Rursus post pauca subjungitur: Tolle uxorem tuam, et duas filias quas habes: ex quo apparet, quod non habuit plures.
paras.en: Yet, as Lyra reports, the Hebrews, taking occasion from these words, affirm that Lot had in Sodom two married daughters who had sons, and they assert that it is the sons of these daughters who are here called Lot's sons. Against this saying it is objected that (as is added a little later) Lot [[19:14|went out|egressus]] [[19:14|to his sons in law that were to have his daughters|ad generos suos, qui accepturi erant filias ejus]], [[19:14|and said|dixit]]: [[19:14|Arise: get you out of this place|Surgite, egredimini de loco isto]]. From this it seems that if he had had other daughters in Sodom, he would have spoken the same words to them and to their husbands and sons: which, however, Scripture does not relate. Again, a little after, it is added: [[19:15|take thy wife, and the two daughters that thou hast|Tolle uxorem tuam, et duas filias quas habes]]: from which it appears that he had no more.

paras.t: Porro sanctus doctor Hieronymus circa hæc scribit: Filiæ Lot virgines fuisse dicuntur. Nunc autem dicitur habuisse generos. Sed aliqui arbitrantur eas quæ habuerunt viros, perisse in Sodomis; et eas quæ virgines erant, cum Lot patre suo exisse. Hebraica autem veritas habet: Locutus est Lot ad sponsos qui accepturi erant filias suas: virgines ergo filiæ necdum fuerant maritatæ. In his autem verbis non videtur Hieronymus reprobare, quod aliqui dicunt de filiabus Lot maritatis in Sodomis. Attamen in Scholastica historia scriptum est: Non est credendum (ut ait Hieronymus) his, qui dicunt Lot habuisse duas filias alias præter virgines, viros habentes, et cum viris suis subversas; sed generos vocat Scriptura hic futuros generos, id est, qui futuri erant generi sui, nisi subversio Sodomæ intervenisset.
paras.en: Moreover the holy doctor Jerome writes on this: The daughters of Lot are said to have been virgins; but now he is said to have had sons in law. Some think that those who had husbands perished in Sodom, and that those who were virgins went out with Lot their father. But the Hebrew truth [that is, the Hebrew original] has: Lot spoke to the betrothed who were to have his daughters[[19:14||]] [*sponsos*, "the betrothed", where the Vulgate has *generos*, "sons in law"]: the virgin daughters, then, had not yet been married. In these words, however, Jerome does not seem to reject what some say about Lot's daughters married in Sodom. Yet in the Scholastic History it is written: We must not believe (as Jerome says) those who say that Lot had two other daughters besides the virgins, who had husbands and were overthrown with their husbands; but Scripture here calls sons in law those who were to be his sons in law, that is, who would have been his sons in law had not the overthrow of Sodom intervened.

paras.t: Itaque sicut habetur in textu, Egressus Lot locutus est ad generos suos, qui accepturi erant filias ejus, et dixit: ex quo apparet, quod non habitabant aut tunc non erant in domo Lot: Surgite, egredimini de loco isto, id est, mecum exite, quia delebit Dominus civitatem hanc, id est, urbem istam subvertet. Et visus est eis quasi ludens loqui: hoc est, verba ejus parvipenderunt, et quasi ludicra reputabant, quasi more solito minaretur inaniter. Nam (ut Josephus ait) dixerunt hanc esse consuetudinem verborum ipsius. Vinxerat enim et vicerat illos pessimæ consuetudinis amor. Forsitan tamen non erant tam vitiosi ut ceteri, quibus justus Lot decreverat proprias filias desponsare.
paras.en: So then, as is had in the text, [[19:14|So Lot went out, and spoke to his sons in law that were to have his daughters, and said|Egressus Lot locutus est ad generos suos, qui accepturi erant filias ejus, et dixit]]: from which it appears that they did not live, or were not then, in Lot's house: [[19:14|Arise: get you out of this place|Surgite, egredimini de loco isto]], that is, come out with me, [[19:14|because the Lord will destroy this city|quia delebit Dominus civitatem hanc]], that is, will overthrow this city. [[19:14|And he seemed to them to speak as it were in jest|Et visus est eis quasi ludens loqui]]: that is, they made little of his words and counted them a jest, as though he were threatening idly as usual. For (as Josephus says) they said that this was his customary way of speaking. For the love of a most wicked custom had bound and conquered them. Yet perhaps they were not as vicious as the rest, since the just Lot had resolved to betroth his own daughters to them.

paras.t: Quumque esset mane: nam tota nocte creditur orasse pro civitate. Jamque noverat quod angeli essent, ab ea hora qua dixerunt se missos a Domino ad Sodomam subvertendam. Cogebant eum angeli, dicentes maxime seriose: Surge, tolle uxorem tuam et duas filias, ne et tu pariter pereas cum uxore et filiabus in scelere civitatis, hoc est, ne moriaris in plaga civitatem hanc mox invasura pro ejus sceleribus. Dissimulante autem illo, quia distulit quantum potuit, si forte Deus mitigaret sententiam et preces suas pro populo acceptaret, apprehenderunt manum ejus, et manum uxoris ac duarum filiarum ejus, eo quod parceret Dominus illi. Eduxeruntque eum, et posuerunt extra civitatem, eruendo eum ab imminenti periculo; pepercitque non solum ei pro sua persona, sed et pro uxore et filiabus, meritis ejus. Unde elicitur, quod Deus secundum rigorem suæ justitiæ, potuisset et ipsum Lot cum suis domesticis involvisse periculo civitatis, quia interdum peccaverant.
paras.en: [[19:15|And when it was morning|Quumque esset mane]]: for he is believed to have prayed for the city all night. And he already knew that they were angels, from the hour when they said they had been sent by the Lord to overthrow Sodom. [[19:15|the angels pressed him, saying|Cogebant eum angeli, dicentes]], in all earnest: [[19:15|Arise, take thy wife|Surge, tolle uxorem tuam]] [[19:15|and the two daughters|et duas filias]], [[19:15|lest thou also perish|ne et tu pariter pereas]] with thy wife and daughters [[19:15|in the wickedness of the city|in scelere civitatis]], that is, lest thou die in the scourge that will soon fall upon this city for its crimes. [[19:16|And as he lingered|Dissimulante autem illo]], because he put it off as long as he could, in case God might perhaps soften the sentence and accept his prayers for the people, [[19:16|they took his hand, and the hand of his wife, and of his two daughters|apprehenderunt manum ejus, et manum uxoris ac duarum filiarum ejus]], [[19:16|because the Lord spared him|eo quod parceret Dominus illi]]. [[19:17|And they brought him forth, and set him without the city|Eduxeruntque eum, et posuerunt extra civitatem]], snatching him from the danger at hand; and he spared not only him in his own person, but also his wife and daughters, for his merits. From this it is gathered that God, by the rigour of his justice, could have involved Lot himself and his household in the danger of the city, since they had sometimes sinned.

paras.t: Ibique locuti sunt ad eum, dicentes: Salva animam tuam, id est, te ipsum a plaga hujus interitus erue, nobis obtemperando in præcepto, quo subditur: Noli respicere post tergum tuum, hoc est, non respicias retro, faciem tuam vertendo ad Sodomam intuendam. Istud etiam præceperunt uxori ejus ac filiabus, quamvis scriptura ista non exprimat hoc: sed datur intelligi per hoc quod paulo post scribitur uxor ejus plagata, eo quod retrospexerit. Itaque prohibuit eis Dominus corporaliter retrospicere, et hoc propter mysticam rationem seu moralem doctrinam, quæ tamen est litteralis causa prohibitionis istius, videlicet ad insinuandum, quod non debebant mente reverti ad ea quæ in urbe reliquerant. Erat autem Lot dives, ut habitum est, et tamen videtur sua reliquisse in Sodoma, de quo non debuit contristari. Hinc loquitur Augustinus: Quo pertinet quod prohibiti sunt respicere retro, nisi quia non est redeundum ad veterem vitam, si cogitamus evadere finale judicium Dei? Nec stes in omni circa regione, id est, moram non facias in aliquo loco vallis, in qua est sita regio ista Pentapolis subvertenda; sed in monte salvum te fac, id est, ascende cum tuis montem huic valli propinquum, ut ibi manendo, evadas eversionem Pentapolis situatæ in valle.
paras.en: [[19:17|and there they spoke to him, saying|Ibique locuti sunt ad eum, dicentes]]: [[19:17|Save thy life|Salva animam tuam]], that is, rescue thyself from the scourge of this destruction by obeying us in the command that follows: [[19:17|look not back|Noli respicere post tergum]] [literally "behind thy back"], that is, do not look behind thee, turning thy face to gaze upon Sodom. This they also commanded his wife and daughters, though this scripture does not say so; but it is given to be understood by what is written a little later, that his wife was struck because she looked back. So the Lord forbade them to look back bodily, and this for a mystical reason or moral teaching, which is nevertheless the literal cause of this prohibition: namely, to suggest that they ought not to turn back in mind to the things they had left in the city. Now Lot was rich, as has been seen, and yet he seems to have left his goods in Sodom, over which he ought not to grieve. Hence Augustine says: What is meant by their being forbidden to look back, unless that we must not return to the old life, if we think to escape the final judgment of God? [[19:17|neither stay thou in all the country about|Nec stes in omni circa regione]], that is, make no stay in any place of the valley in which this region of the Pentapolis [that is, the five cities of the plain], due to be overthrown, lies; [[19:17|but save thy self in the mountain|sed in monte salvum te fac]], that is, go up with thine own to the mountain near this valley, so that by staying there thou mayest escape the overthrow of the Pentapolis, which lies in the valley.

paras.t: Dixitque Lot ad eos: Quæso, Domine mi. Singulariter illum alloquitur qui apprehenderat manum ejus, et verbum direxit ad ipsum. Vel in duobus angelis singulariter Deum affatur, quem in suis venerabatur ministris. Quia invenit servus tuus gratiam coram te, et magnificasti misericordiam tuam quam fecisti mecum, id est, effectum pietatis et gratiæ tuæ declarasti magnifice in me, ut salvares animam meam, id est vitam meam, de instanti interitu Sodomorum; nec possum in monte salvari. Jam angeli sibi dixerunt, In monte salvum te fac: quomodo ergo nunc dicit oppositum, Non possum, inquiens, in monte salvari? Respondetur, quod ex perturbatione et humana pusillanimitate non credebat perfecte verbis angelicis, et in hoc fuit culpabilis, sed Deus in tantis angustiis condescendebat eidem. Vel dixit hæc verba, non discredendo aut renuendo, sed ex humana consideratione humiliter persuadendo. Hinc dubitative subjungit: ne forte apprehendat me malum, et moriar; hoc est, ne forte in monte incurram aliquam improvisam adversitatem mortiferam, utpote frigora montium, aut ipse mons tangatur plaga, aut aliqua læsione ex vallis subversione. Hebræi tamen (ut fertur) per montem intelligunt Abraham patriarcham, aut montem in quo tunc ipse manebat, ita quod angelus monuit ipsum Lot, ut iret ad Abraham: quod Lot facere non audebat, ne comparatione tanti Patriarchæ videretur magis culpabilis, et Dei offensam ac plagam incurreret, qui comparatione Sodomitarum justus jam fuerat judicatus. Quod stare non potest, quantum ad hoc quod dicitur Abraham tunc habitasse in monte, quia adhuc habitabat in convalle Mambre, ut elici potest ex dictis, et in exordio expositionis sequentis capituli ostendetur.
paras.en: [[19:18|And Lot said to them: I beseech thee, my Lord|Dixitque Lot ad eos: Quæso, Domine mi]]. He addresses in the singular the one who had taken him by the hand, and directs his words to him. Or, in the two angels, he speaks in the singular to God, whom he venerated in His ministers. [[19:19|Because thy servant hath found grace before thee|Quia invenit servus tuus gratiam coram te]], [[19:19|and thou hast magnified thy mercy, which thou hast shewn to me|et magnificasti misericordiam tuam quam fecisti mecum]], that is, thou hast shown forth magnificently in me the effect of thy kindness and grace, [[19:19|in saving my life|ut salvares animam meam]] [Latin *animam meam*, "my soul"], that is, my life, from the imminent destruction of the Sodomites; [[19:19|and I cannot escape to the mountain|nec possum in monte salvari]] [the Latin has "be saved in the mountain", the angels' own words]. The angels had already said to him: [[19:17|save thy self in the mountain|In monte salvum te fac]]: how then does he now say the opposite, "[[19:19|I cannot|Non possum]]", he says, "[[19:19|escape to the mountain|in monte salvari]]"? The answer is that out of agitation and human faint-heartedness he did not fully believe the angels' words, and in this he was to blame; but God, in such great straits, condescended to him. Or he said these words not disbelieving or refusing, but humbly pleading, out of human reasoning. Hence he adds, doubtfully: [[19:19|lest some evil seize me, and I die|ne forte apprehendat me malum, et moriar]]; that is, lest perhaps on the mountain I meet with some unforeseen deadly misfortune, such as the cold of the mountains, or lest the mountain itself be touched by the plague, or I suffer some harm from the overthrow of the valley. The Hebrews, however (so it is said), understand by the mountain the patriarch Abraham, or the mountain on which he was then living, so that the angel counselled Lot to go to Abraham: which Lot did not dare to do, lest in comparison with so great a Patriarch he should seem the more guilty, and incur the displeasure and the stroke of God, he who in comparison with the Sodomites had already been judged just. This cannot stand, as regards the claim that Abraham was then living on a mountain, since he was still dwelling in the vale of Mambre, as can be gathered from what has been said, and will be shown at the beginning of the exposition of the next chapter.

paras.t: Est civitas hic juxta, ad quam possum fugere, parva, et salvabor in ea a plaga quæ imminet. Numquid non modica est, et vivet anima mea? quasi dicat: Imo permodica est, nec videtur tanta iniquitas esse in ipsa, sicut in Sodomis et ceteris urbibus ejus. Porro quod Lot oravit pro se, oravit quoque pro conjuge sua ac sobole.
paras.en: [[19:20|There is this city here at hand, to which I may flee|Est civitas hic juxta, ad quam possum fugere]], [[19:20|it is a little one, and I shall be saved in it|parva, et salvabor in ea]] from the stroke that threatens. [[19:20|is it not a little one, and my soul shall live?|Numquid non modica est, et vivet anima mea?]] As if to say: Indeed it is very small, nor does there seem to be so great iniquity in it as in Sodom and the other cities of that region. Moreover, what Lot prayed for himself he prayed also for his wife and children.

paras.t: Dixitque ad eum angelus, loquens nunc quasi in Dei persona: Ecce etiam in hoc suscepi preces tuas, ut non subvertam urbem pro qua locutus es. Istud protulit angelus non propria auctoritate, quasi ex suo placito potuerit parcere urbi, quæ fuit una quinque urbium subvertendarum; sed ex inspiratione Omnipotentis, cujus voluntatem esse cognoverat, ut sic exaudiret Lot deprecantem, nec urbem illam subverteret, quamdiu Lot esset in ipsa. Festina ingredi illuc, et salvare ibi ab ultione præfata; quia non potero facere quidquam, id est, nullam vindictam valeo exercere in urbibus vallis istius […] illos. Deus namque præceperat angelo, ut non subverteret urbes illas, nisi ipso Lot existente in loco tuto.
paras.en: [[19:21|And he said to him|Dixitque ad eum]], the angel, speaking now as it were in the person of God: [[19:21|Behold also in this, I have heard thy prayers, not to destroy the city for which thou hast spoken|Ecce etiam in hoc suscepi preces tuas, ut non subvertam urbem pro qua locutus es]]. The angel said this not by his own authority, as though he could spare the city at his own pleasure, which was one of the five cities to be overthrown; but by the inspiration of the Almighty, whose will he had known it to be that He should thus hear Lot's entreaty, and not overthrow that city as long as Lot was in it. [[19:22|Make haste|Festina]] to go in thither, [[19:22|and be saved there|et salvare ibi]] from the vengeance spoken of; [[19:22|because I cannot do any thing|quia non potero facere quidquam]], that is, I can exercise no vengeance on the cities of this valley […] them [words are lost here; the verse goes on "till thou go in thither"]. For God had commanded the angel not to overthrow those cities except when Lot himself was in a safe place.

paras.t: […] est nomen urbis illius Segor, quod interpretatur parva, quia Lot dixit: Numquid non modica est? quæ urbs ante fuit vocata Bala; de qua fertur in Isaia: Usque ad Segor vitulam consternantem; nam instar vitulæ lascivientis, fuit plebs urbis illius lasciva et inquieta. Sol egressus est super terram, ascendendo nostrum horizontem, ita quod videbatur a stante in terra, et Lot ingressus est Segor.
paras.en: […] [the lost words are evidently *Idcirco vocatum*, "Therefore … was called"] [[19:22|the name of that city was called Segor|est nomen urbis illius Segor]], which is interpreted *little*, because Lot said: [[19:20|is it not a little one|Numquid non modica est]]? This city was formerly called Bala; of which it is said in Isaias: [[Is 15:5|unto Segor a heifer of three years old|Usque ad Segor vitulam consternantem]] [the margin note here is unread. Denis reads *consternantem*, "skittish", where the Vulgate has *conternantem*, "three years old"; his gloss follows his reading]; for like a frisking heifer, the people of that city were wanton and restless. [[19:23|The sun was risen upon the earth|Sol egressus est super terram]], rising above our horizon, so that it could be seen by one standing on the earth, [[19:23|and Lot entered into Segor|et Lot ingressus est Segor]].

paras.t: Igitur Dominus pluit super Sodomam et Gomorrham, et etiam super Seboim et Adamam, sulfur et ignem a Domino de cœlo, id est sulfureum ignem a se ipso. Vel, Dominus, id est angelus in Dei virtute hæc ministerialiter exsequens, pluit ignem istum a Domino Deo principaliter hæc agente, de cœlo aereo, puta de aere, in quo virtute divina angelicoque obsequio generabatur seu fiebat hujusmodi ignis, sicut et manna. Et subvertit, hoc est, per ignem istum combussit, et angelo exsequente destruxit atque demersit, civitates has, et omnem circa regionem, id est terram illam Pentapolis, universos habitatores urbium præfatarum, qui fuerunt calidissimo ac fœtidissimo igne isto combusti, ut pœna corresponderet culpæ eorum, quia in Sodomiticis vitiis fuit et est intensissimus ardor libidinis, ac maximus fœtor turpitudinis tam immanis.
paras.en: [[19:24|And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrha|Igitur Dominus pluit super Sodomam et Gomorrham]], and also upon Seboim and Adama, [[19:24|brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven|sulfur et ignem a Domino de cœlo]], that is, sulphurous fire from Himself. Or, *the Lord*, that is, the angel carrying this out as a minister in the power of God, rained this fire *from the Lord* God, who was its principal agent, *out of heaven*, that is, the heaven of the air, namely from the air, in which by divine power and the service of the angel this fire was produced or made, as the manna was too. [[19:25|And he destroyed|Et subvertit]], that is, burnt up with this fire, and, the angel carrying it out, destroyed and sank [[19:25|these cities, and all the country about|civitates has, et omnem circa regionem]], that is, that land of the Pentapolis, [[19:25|all the inhabitants of the cities|universos habitatores urbium]] aforesaid, who were burnt up by this fire, most hot and most foul-smelling, so that the punishment might answer to their guilt; for in the Sodomitic vices there was and is a most intense heat of lust, and the very great stench of so monstrous a filthiness.

paras.t: De hac eversione in Scholastica historia recitatur: Pluit Dominus super terram illam ignem sulfureum, ut terra fieret et maneret sterilis in æternum sine spe germinandi, et versa est regio illa in lacum salsum ac sterilem, qui dicitur mare Mortuum, quia nec pisces nec aves vivere possunt in eo. Navem non patitur, nec aliquam aliam materiam, nisi bituminatam. Si quid non vivens ponatur in eo, statim submergitur; si quid vivum aliqua arte submerseris, superexsilit. Lucerna ardens, in eo supernatat; exstincta, demergitur. In multis locis nigras glebas bituminis evomit, idcirco lacus Asphalti, id est stagnum bituminis, appellatur. Dicitur quoque, quod poma nata in arboribus circumpositis, usque ad maturitatem coloris sunt viridis; si autem ea jam matura scindas, intus favillam invenies. Lacus iste vocatur etiam vallis Salinarum. Forte fit ibi sal, aut lapides salis circa inveniuntur. Hæc in præfata Historia. Denique istud quod dictum est de pomis illis incisis, quod intus favillam habent quasi intus combusta, fidem facit historiæ huic de subversione Pentapolis, ut Josephus contestatur, qui etiam loquitur: Præ nimia levitate, etiam gravissima in lacum projecta, ascendunt. Nam et Vespasianus quosdam, vinctis post tergum manibus, jussit ibi projici in profundum: et omnes, tanquam vi spiritus seu venti sursum impulsi, desuper fluitabant. De hac re scriptum est in libro Sapientiæ: Sapientia justum, videlicet Lot, a pereuntibus impiis liberavit, descendente igne in Pentapolim; quibus in testimonium nequitiæ, fumigabunda constat terra deserta, et incerto tempore fructus habentes arbores. In quibus verbis tangitur aliud signum seu testimonium veritatis præfatæ subversionis, videlicet fumigatio terræ illius irrecuperabiliter, inhabitabiliterque subversæ.
paras.en: Of this overthrow it is related in the Scholastic History: The Lord rained sulphurous fire upon that land, so that the land should become and remain barren for ever, with no hope of bearing growth; and that region was turned into a salt and barren lake, which is called the Dead Sea, because neither fish nor birds can live in it. It does not bear a ship, nor any other material unless it is coated with bitumen. If anything not living is put into it, it at once sinks; if by some device you sink something living, it leaps back up. A lamp floats on it while burning; put out, it sinks. In many places it belches up black lumps of bitumen, and for this reason it is called the lake Asphaltites, that is, the pool of bitumen. It is said, too, that the apples growing on the trees round about are green in colour until they ripen; but if you cut them open when ripe, you will find ashes inside. This lake is also called the valley of the Salt Pits. Perhaps salt is made there, or stones of salt are found round about. So far the History. Lastly, what has been said of those apples when cut open, that they have ashes inside as though burnt within, bears out this account of the overthrow of the Pentapolis, as Josephus attests [the margin gives Josephus, *De Bello Judaico* iv, 27], who also says: Because of its great lightness, even the heaviest things thrown into the lake rise up. For Vespasian too ordered certain men, their hands bound behind their backs, to be thrown into its depths: and all of them floated on top, as if driven upward by the force of a breath or a wind. Of this it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 10:6|She delivered the just man|Sapientia justum]] [Denis has *Sapientia*, "Wisdom", for the Vulgate's "She"], namely Lot, [[Wis 10:6|from the wicked that were perishing|a pereuntibus impiis liberavit]], [[Wis 10:6|when the fire came down upon Pentapolis|descendente igne in Pentapolim]]: [[Wis 10:7|Whose land, for a testimony of their wickedness, is desolate, and smoketh to this day, and the trees bear fruits that ripen not|quibus in testimonium nequitiæ, fumigabunda constat terra deserta, et incerto tempore fructus habentes arbores]]. In these words another sign or testimony of the truth of the overthrow spoken of is touched on: namely the smoking of that land, overthrown beyond recovery and beyond habitation.

paras.t: Respiciensque uxor ejus post se, versa est in statuam salis. Et hoc fecit Deus justo judicio, quoniam contra præceptum angelicum corpore ac mente retrospexit, faciem suam versus Sodomam dirigendo, cum inordinato affectu ad ea quæ ibi reliquit. Sed cur in similitudinem salis potissimum versa est? Respondetur, quod Deus hoc fecit ad innuendum quod sicut sal est condimentum ciborum, sic punitio mulieris illius sit condimentum animarum fidelium: quæ ejus exemplo sic condiuntur sapore sapientiæ, quod non audent similia perpetrare, id est inobedire, et pristina vitia iterare, vel ad ea quæ propter Deum reliquerant, mente reverti. Ideo ait Salvator: Memores estote uxoris Lot. Itemque: Nemo ponens manum suam ad aratrum, et respiciens retro, aptus est regno Dei. Refert Lyra, quod secundum Hebræos, femina ista vespere præcedente noluit suo marito porrigere sal ad condimentum ciborum pro angelis, quoniam instar concivium suorum Sodomitarum, affectum ad peregrinos et hospites non habebat: idcirco in salis statuam est conversa, ut sua punitio corresponderet suo peccato. Hinc in libro Sapientiæ legitur: Incredibilis animæ memoria stans figmentum salis: quod Josephus recitat se vidisse, et hactenus permanere.
paras.en: [[19:26|And his wife looking behind her, was turned into a statue of salt|Respiciensque uxor ejus post se, versa est in statuam salis]]. And God did this by a just judgement, because against the angel's command she looked back in body and in mind, turning her face towards Sodom with a disordered affection for the things she had left there. But why was she turned into the likeness of salt above all? The answer is that God did this to signify that, as salt is the seasoning of food, so the punishment of that woman should be a seasoning for faithful souls: who by her example are so seasoned with the savour of wisdom [in Latin *sapor*, "savour", and *sapientia*, "wisdom", are of one root] that they do not dare to do the like, that is, to disobey, and to repeat their former vices, or to return in mind to the things they had left for God's sake. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Luke 17:32|Remember Lot's wife|Memores estote uxoris Lot]]. And again: [[Luke 9:62|No man putting his hand to the plough and looking back is fit for the kingdom of God|Nemo ponens manum suam ad aratrum, et respiciens retro, aptus est regno Dei]]. Lyra relates that according to the Hebrews this woman, on the evening before, would not hand her husband salt to season the food for the angels, because, like her fellow citizens the Sodomites, she had no kindness for strangers and guests: and so she was turned into a statue of salt, that her punishment might answer to her sin. Hence we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 10:7|a standing pillar of salt is a monument of an incredulous soul|Incredibilis animæ memoria stans figmentum salis]] [Denis's Latin runs: "of an incredulous soul a standing memorial, a figure of salt"]: which Josephus relates that he saw, and that it remains to this day.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, quando et ubi versa sit uxor Lot in statuam salis. Nam juxta ordinem litteræ, videtur id factum post ingressum Lot in Segor, et post descensum ignis in Pentapolim. Et mirum, si uxor Lot non est secum Segor ingressa. Ad hoc dici potest, quod circa ingressum in Segor, antequam urbem illam intravit, ex inordinata affectione et curiositate retrospexit, ut videret quid accidisset Pentapoli, igne mox descendente. Insuper quæritur, ubi manserit anima mulieris illius. Ad hoc respondendum videtur, quod violando præceptum, peccavit mortaliter: et si ante mortem suam non pœnituit, inde damnata est. Si vero in ipso momento conversionis corporis sui in statuam salis, pœnituit, est salvata, et mors ista potuit culpæ suæ esse purgatio.
paras.en: On these things it is asked when and where Lot's wife was turned into a statue of salt. For according to the order of the letter it seems to have happened after Lot's entry into Segor and after the fire came down on the Pentapolis. And it would be strange if Lot's wife did not enter Segor with him. To this it can be said that about the time of the entry into Segor, before she entered that city, she looked back out of disordered affection and curiosity, to see what had befallen the Pentapolis, as the fire was just coming down. It is further asked where that woman's soul went. To this it seems we must answer that in breaking the command she sinned mortally: and if she did not repent before her death, she was damned for it. But if at the very moment her body was turned into a statue of salt she repented, she was saved, and that death could have been the purging of her guilt.

paras.t: Deinde quæritur, qua justitia Deus punivit infantulos Sodomitarum. Respondetur, quemadmodum supra dictum est de infantibus submersis diluvio. Expediebat quippe infantibus illis talis occisio. Filii quoque, quantum ad corpus, interdum puniuntur pro suorum peccatis parentum, ut supra dicebatur diffusius. Præterea quæritur, an habitatores Pentapolis per illam punitionem temporalem et valde acerbam, evaserint damnationem æternam. Et videtur, quod imo, quia non vindicabit Dominus bis in id ipsum. Hieronymus quoque hoc sentire videtur. Et respondendum, quod temporalis pœna, quantumlibet magna, nullum iniquum de culpa purgat, nullum de inferno præservat, nisi pœniteat. Idcirco qui in sua a sulfureo illo igne […]tione non pœnituerunt, ve[…]citer, de temporali incendio ad ignem corruerunt infernl […]. Postremo de celeritate subversionis illius legitur in Propheta: Sodoma subversa est in momento. Pœna etiam Sodomitarum gravior fuit pœna in diluvio submersorum, quia et pœna ignis, præsertim sulfurei, acerbior est submersione in aqua: propter quod multi, ut pœnam ignis evaderent, prosilierunt in gurgitem. Terra quoque quæ fuit operta diluvio, postea viruit, et protulit fructum; non sic terra Pentapolis. Gravius ergo peccaverunt Sodomitæ, quam qui perierunt diluvio, utpote magis contra naturam.
paras.en: Next it is asked by what justice God punished the little children of the Sodomites. The answer is as was said above of the infants drowned in the flood. For such a death was to the good of those infants. Sons too, as regards the body, are sometimes punished for the sins of their parents, as was said more fully above. Further, it is asked whether the inhabitants of the Pentapolis, through that temporal and very bitter punishment, escaped eternal damnation. And it seems that they did, since the Lord will not punish twice for the same thing [a saying drawn from the old reading of Nahum 1:9; the Vulgate has "there shall not rise a double affliction"]. Jerome too seems to hold this. And the answer must be that temporal punishment, however great, purges no wicked man of guilt and saves no one from hell, unless he repents. Therefore those who did not repent in their […]tion [perhaps *combustione*, "burning"] by that sulphurous fire fell ve[…]citer [perhaps *velociter*, "swiftly"] from the temporal burning into the fire of hell […]. Lastly, of the swiftness of that overthrow we read in the Prophet: [[Lam 4:6|Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment|Sodoma subversa est in momento]] [the margin note here is unread; the words are from Lamentations]. The punishment of the Sodomites was also heavier than the punishment of those drowned in the flood, because the punishment of fire, especially of sulphurous fire, is more bitter than drowning in water: for which reason many, to escape the punishment of fire, leapt into the waters. The land, too, that was covered by the flood afterwards grew green again and bore fruit; not so the land of the Pentapolis. Therefore the Sodomites sinned more grievously than those who perished in the flood, inasmuch as they sinned more against nature.

paras.t: Abraham autem consurgens mane, ubi steterat prius cum Domino, id est in loco illo in quo die præcedenti loquebatur cum angelo, qui sibi in Dei persona apparuit, intuitus est Sodomam et Gomorrham, id est versus locum ubi ante suam eversionem steterunt, et universam terram regionis illius, puta Pentapolis, quæ dicitur a πέντε, quod est quinque, et πόλις, civitas. Porro, quod Abraham dicitur adspexisse universam terram illam, per synecdochen accipi potest. Viditque ascendentem favillam de terra illa combusta, quasi fornacis fumum, qui erumpit de clibano in quo saxa coquuntur. Ad istud intuendum exivit Abraham ex pia et caritativa sollicitudine atque compassione.
paras.en: [[19:27|And Abraham got up early in the morning|Abraham autem consurgens mane]], [[19:27|in the place where he had stood before with the Lord|ubi steterat prius cum Domino]], that is, in that place in which on the day before he had spoken with the angel who appeared to him in the person of God, [[19:28|He looked towards Sodom and Gomorrha|intuitus est Sodomam et Gomorrham]], that is, towards the place where they stood before their overthrow, [[19:28|and the whole land of that country|et universam terram regionis illius]], namely of the Pentapolis, which is named from the Greek πέντε, that is, five, and πόλις, city. Further, that Abraham is said to have looked on all that land can be taken by synecdoche [a figure in which the whole is put for a part: he could see only part of it]. [[19:28|and he saw the ashes rise up from the earth|Viditque ascendentem favillam de terra]] of that burnt land, [[19:28|as the smoke of a furnace|quasi fornacis fumum]], which bursts out of the kiln in which stones are baked. Abraham went out to look on this out of loving and charitable concern and compassion.

paras.t: Quum enim subverteret Dominus civitates regionis illius, recordatus est Abrahæ, id est, per pietatis suæ effectum ostendit se memorem esse justitiæ, meritorumque Abrahæ, propter cujus preces et merita liberavit Lot cum conjuge sua ac sobole: ideo subditur, et liberavit Lot de subversione urbium, in quibus, id est in quarum una, habitaverat, vel in quibus successive moratus est. Magis tamen apparet, quod non nisi in Sodoma habitavit. Sic ergo Lot fuit de subversione ista liberatus, non tantum meritis suis, sed et meritis Abrahæ, cujus excellens perfectio per verba hæc commendatur. Hinc asserit Augustinus: Innuit Scriptura Deum liberasse Lot magis meritis Abrahæ quam ipsius Lot. Verumtamen Lot adeo justus fuit, ut princeps apostolus sacratissimus Petrus de ipso testetur: Aspectu et auditu justus erat, habitans inter eos qui de die in diem animam justi iniquis operibus affligebant. Nam et angelus dixit ad Lot: Ecce etiam in hoc suscepi preces tuas, ut non subvertam urbem pro qua locutus es. Si ergo potuit uni urbi veniam seu pœnæ dilationem suis precibus obtinere, quid potuit pro se ipso?
paras.en: [[19:29|Now when God destroyed the cities of that country|Quum enim subverteret Dominus civitates regionis illius]], [[19:29|remembering Abraham|recordatus est Abrahæ]], that is, by the effect of His kindness He showed Himself mindful of Abraham's justice and merits, for whose prayers and merits He delivered Lot with his wife and children: therefore it is added, [[19:29|he delivered Lot out of the destruction of the cities wherein|et liberavit Lot de subversione urbium, in quibus]], that is, in one of which, [[19:29|he had dwelt|habitaverat]]; or, in which he stayed one after another. It seems more likely, however, that he dwelt only in Sodom. So Lot was delivered from this overthrow not only by his own merits but also by the merits of Abraham, whose excellent perfection is commended by these words. Hence Augustine asserts: Scripture intimates that God delivered Lot more for the merits of Abraham than for those of Lot himself. Yet Lot was so just that the prince of the apostles, the most holy Peter, testifies of him: [[2 Pet 2:8|in sight and hearing he was just, dwelling among them who from day to day vexed the just soul with unjust works|Aspectu et auditu justus erat, habitans inter eos qui de die in diem animam justi iniquis operibus affligebant]] [the margin note here is unread; the words are from 2 Peter]. For the angel too said to Lot: [[19:21|Behold also in this, I have heard thy prayers, not to destroy the city for which thou hast spoken|Ecce etiam in hoc suscepi preces tuas, ut non subvertam urbem pro qua locutus es]]. If then by his prayers he could obtain pardon, or a putting off of punishment, for one city, what could he not do for himself?

paras.t: Ascenditque Lot de Segor, et mansit in monte, in quem nolebat prius ascendere, quamvis Dominus hoc moneret; timuerat enim manere in Segor, ne forte subverteretur: nam vidit facinora civium ejus. Et mansit in spelunca, quæ fuit in aliqua parte montis, ipse et duæ filiæ ejus cum eo. Dixitque major ad minorem, id est filia senior ad juniorem: Pater noster senex est, et nullus virorum remansit in terra, qui possit ingredi ad nos juxta morem universæ terræ, id est ducere nos in uxores et fecundare; veni, inebriemus eum vino, dormiamusque cum eo successive; ut servare possimus ex patre nostro semen, hoc est, ut prolem acquiramus ex eo, per quam conservetur genus humanum in terra. Juxta expositores communiter, istæ puellæ ex quadam ignorantia et simplicitate putabant genus humanum per ignem Sodomorum deletum, quemadmodum tempore Noe fuit per aquas consumptum, ita quod sicut tunc nemo remansit in terra præter exsistentes in arca, ita nunc nemo remansisset præter patrem earum et eas in spelunca pariter exsistentes. Nam et a patre suo aliquid didicerunt de consummatione mundi per ignem, quod tamen non intellexerunt perfecte: ideo non libidine, sed posteritatis amore invenerunt istud consilium, ne periret genus humanum, putantes in casu tantæ necessitatis excusari incestum cum proprio genitore, vel in toto, vel a tanto: et utique excusabantur a tanto, non tamen (ut appare[…]) a toto. Debuerant enim potius uti consilio patris sui, qui senex ac sapiens erat, et informationem ab ipso accipere, neque feminea levitate ad tam detestabilem prorumpere commixtionem.
paras.en: [[19:30|And Lot went up out of Segor, and abode in the mountain|Ascenditque Lot de Segor, et mansit in monte]], which he had not wished to go up to before, although the Lord counselled it; [[19:30|for he was afraid to stay in Segor|timuerat enim manere in Segor]], lest perhaps it should be overthrown: for he saw the crimes of its citizens. [[19:30|and he dwelt in a cave|Et mansit in spelunca]], which was in some part of the mountain, [[19:30|he and his two daughters with him|ipse et duæ filiæ ejus cum eo]]. [[19:31|And the elder said to the younger|Dixitque major ad minorem]], that is, the older daughter to the younger: [[19:31|Our father is old, and there is no man left on the earth, to come in unto us after the manner of the whole earth|Pater noster senex est, et nullus virorum remansit in terra, qui possit ingredi ad nos juxta morem universæ terræ]], that is, to take us as wives and make us fruitful. [[19:32|Come, let us make him drunk with wine, and let us lie with him|veni, inebriemus eum vino, dormiamusque cum eo]] one after the other, [[19:32|that we may preserve seed of our father|ut servare possimus ex patre nostro semen]], that is, that we may get offspring by him, through which the human race may be kept alive on the earth. According to the expositors generally, these girls, out of a certain ignorance and simplicity, thought that the human race had been wiped out by the fire of Sodom, as in the time of Noe it was consumed by the waters; so that, as then no one remained on the earth except those who were in the ark, so now no one would have remained except their father and themselves, who were together in the cave. For they had also learnt something from their father about the consummation of the world by fire, which however they did not understand perfectly: therefore not from lust but from love of posterity they hit upon this plan, lest the human race should perish, thinking that in a case of such great necessity incest with their own father would be excused, either wholly or in great part [Latin *vel in toto, vel a tanto*, the schoolmen's terms for an excuse that frees from all the guilt or only lessens it]; and they were indeed excused in great part, though not (as it appe[…]) wholly. For they ought rather to have used the counsel of their father, who was old and wise, and to have taken instruction from him, and not with womanly fickleness to have rushed into so detestable a union.

paras.t: Sed mirum, quod putabant perisse genus humanum præter se, quum paulo ante essent de Segor adhuc stante egressæ. Ad hoc quidam respondent, quod angelus revelavit ipsi Lot Segor esse mox subvertendam, et quod ei præcepit ut inde cum suis filiabus exiret. Quod si verum est, non peccasset Lot inde egrediendo, nec ex infidelitate inde exisset: cujus oppositum multi affirmant. Ait quippe Hieronymus: Quare Lot de Segor transivit ad montem, quum prius prætulerit habitationem Segor refugio montis? Respondemus veram esse Hebræorum conjecturam de Segor, quod frequenter sit obruta terræ motu, propter quod Lot timuit, dicens: Si ceteris urbibus adhuc stantibus, ista sic obruta est, quanto magis in communi ruina seu plaga non poterit liberari? et hanc infidelitatis occasionem, causam incestus fuisse. Qui enim ceteras urbes vidit subversas, et Segor adhuc stare, seque Dei auxilio erutum, non debuit ambigere de eo quod audierat sibi concessum, videlicet se salvandum esse in Segor. His consonat quod Strabus ait: Lot inexcusabilis est. Primum, quia non credidit angelo a quo audierat se posse salvari in Segor; deinde, quia inebriatus est: et fuit in eo unum peccatum causa peccati alterius.
paras.en: But it is strange that they thought the human race had perished except for themselves, since a little before they had come out of Segor, which was still standing. To this some answer that the angel revealed to Lot that Segor was soon to be overthrown, and commanded him to go out of it with his daughters. If that were true, Lot would not have sinned in going out of it, nor would he have left it from unbelief: the opposite of which many affirm. For Jerome says: Why did Lot pass from Segor to the mountain, when before he had preferred dwelling in Segor to the refuge of the mountain? We answer that the conjecture of the Hebrews about Segor is true, that it was often overwhelmed by earthquakes; for which reason Lot was afraid, saying: If, while the other cities still stood, this one was so overwhelmed, how much less will it be able to escape in the common ruin or stroke? And that this occasion of unbelief was the cause of the incest. For he who saw the other cities overthrown, and Segor still standing, and himself rescued by God's help, ought not to have doubted what he had heard was granted him, namely that he was to be saved in Segor. With this agrees what Strabus says: Lot is inexcusable. First, because he did not believe the angel from whom he had heard that he could be saved in Segor; then, because he became drunk: and in him the one sin was the cause of the other.

paras.t: Dederunt itaque patri suo bibere vinum nocte illa, hoc est de sero. Et ingressa est major, dormivitque cum patre. At ille non sensit nec quando accubuit filia, nec quando surrexit. Sicut refert Hieronymus, Judæi istud oppugnant tanquam incredibile, quia natura humana non capit, aliquem coire, et non sentire nec scire hoc: ideo aliqui dicunt quod non sensit, id est, non cognovit nec advertit quod fuit filia sua, sed ebrietate sopitus, et immemor mortis suæ uxoris, putavit se esse cum sua uxore: idcirco Scriptura non dicit, quod non sensit quando cognovit mulierem seu filiam, sed quod non sensit quando accubuit filia sua et quando surrexit, hoc est, quando lectum intravit, et juxta eum se collocavit, nec quando exivit de lecto, quoniam totum hoc fecit patre dormiente. Hinc solutioni objici potest quod paulo post de alia filia subditur: Et ne tunc quidem sensit quando concubuerit, vel quando illa surrexerit. Hinc reor dicendum, quod utique vigilando cognovit filias, et cognoscendo eas, sensit realiter voluptatem, sed non sensit intellectualiter, id est, nec in copula illa, neque post eam discrevit per rationis judicium proprium actum illum, nimia ebrietate prorsus convictus. In omnibus quidem commune est, quod tempore coitus magnitudo voluptatis rationem absorbet, ut Aristoteles, Origenes et Augustinus testantur. Sed Lot fuit tam ebrius, quod nec post actum illum advertit aut discrevit quid egerit.
paras.en: [[19:33|And they made their father drink wine that night|Dederunt itaque patri suo bibere vinum nocte illa]], that is, in the evening. [[19:33|and the elder went in, and lay with her father|Et ingressa est major, dormivitque cum patre]]: [[19:33|but he perceived not, neither when his daughter lay down, nor when she rose up|At ille non sensit nec quando accubuit filia, nec quando surrexit]]. As Jerome relates, the Jews attack this as incredible, because human nature does not allow that anyone should have intercourse and neither perceive nor know it: hence some say that *he perceived not* means that he did not know or notice that it was his daughter, but, stupefied by drunkenness and forgetful of his wife's death, he thought he was with his wife. For this reason, they say, Scripture does not say that he did not perceive when he knew the woman, that is, his daughter, but that he did not perceive *when his daughter lay down* and *when she rose up*: that is, when she got into the bed and laid herself beside him, nor when she left the bed, since she did all this while her father slept. Against this solution may be set what is added a little after of the other daughter: [[19:35|and neither then did he perceive when she lay down, nor when she rose up|Et ne tunc quidem sensit quando concubuerit, vel quando illa surrexerit]]. Hence I think it must be said that he did know his daughters while awake, and in knowing them really felt the pleasure, but did not perceive it with the understanding: that is, neither in that union nor after it did he discern his own act by the judgement of reason, being wholly overcome by excessive drunkenness. It is indeed common to all that at the time of intercourse the greatness of the pleasure swallows up the reason, as Aristotle, Origen and Augustine testify. But Lot was so drunk that not even after the act did he notice or discern what he had done.

paras.t: Altera quoque die dixit major ad minorem: Ecce dormivi heri cum patre meo; demus ei vinum bibere etiam hac nocte, et dormies cum eo, etc. In isto secundo incestu filiæ videntur magis inexcusabiles quam in primo: poterat enim semen servari ex Lot per imprægnationem et partum unius filiæ suæ, nec ob semen servandum necesse fuit ambas a patre cognosci, quum et totum genus humanum ex uno viro, unaque femina est exortum.
paras.en: [[19:34|And the next day the elder said to the younger|Altera quoque die dixit major ad minorem]]: [[19:34|Behold I lay last night with my father|Ecce dormivi heri cum patre meo]]; [[19:34|let us make him drink wine also to night, and thou shalt lie with him|demus ei vinum bibere etiam hac nocte, et dormies cum eo]], etc. In this second incest the daughters seem more inexcusable than in the first: for seed could be preserved from Lot by the conception and childbearing of one of his daughters, and to preserve seed it was not necessary for both to be known by their father, since the whole human race too has sprung from one man and one woman.

paras.t: Conceperunt ergo duæ filiæ Lot de patre suo. Istud rursus mirabile est, quod unaquæque filiarum, quæ virgines erant, concepit ex primo concubitu. Nam ut Scholastica historia protestatur, Dicitur impossibile esse ut in defloratione fiat conceptus. Verumtamen textus non dicit expresse, quod semel dumtaxat utraque sit cognita: sed doctores affirmant, quod non repetebant concubitum, quod sic accipi potest, quod post conceptum non repetebant. Peperitque major filium, et vocavit nomen ejus Moab, quod interpretatur, ex patre: sicque filia ista tanquam impudibunda, per appellationem filii sui publicavit suum cum patre incestum. Ex littera demum sequi videtur, quod Lot non cognovit se cum propriis filiabus esse commixtum, quousque illæ hoc aperuerunt. Erat enim tanta ebrietate oppressus, quod sobrietate redeunte non recordabatur quod in ebrietate commisit. Ipse est pater Moabitarum, etc., quia populus iste a Moab est propagatus.
paras.en: [[19:36|So the two daughters of Lot were with child by their father|Conceperunt ergo duæ filiæ Lot de patre suo]]. This again is a wonder, that each of the daughters, who were virgins, conceived from the first intercourse. For, as the Scholastic History declares, it is said to be impossible for conception to take place at a deflowering. However, the text does not say expressly that each was known only once: but the doctors affirm that they did not repeat the intercourse, which can be taken to mean that they did not repeat it after conceiving. [[19:37|And the elder bore a son, and she called his name Moab|Peperitque major filium, et vocavit nomen ejus Moab]], which is interpreted *from the father*: and so this daughter, as one without shame, made her incest with her father public by the name she gave her son. Lastly, it seems to follow from the letter that Lot did not know he had lain with his own daughters until they disclosed it. For he was overcome by such drunkenness that when he was sober again he did not remember what he had done when drunk. [[19:37|he is the father of the Moabites|Ipse est pater Moabitarum]], etc., because that people was propagated from Moab.

paras.t: Minor quoque peperit filium, et vocavit nomen ejus Ammon, quod interpretatur, filius populi mei. Quasi dicat, Iste est filius quem concepi ex quodam de populo meo: sicque verecundior fuit quam alia, et aliqualiter texit incestum. Ipse est pater Ammonitarum usque hodie.
paras.en: [[19:38|The younger also bore a son, and she called his name Ammon|Minor quoque peperit filium, et vocavit nomen ejus Ammon]], which is interpreted [[19:38|the son of my people|filius populi mei]]. As if to say: This is the son whom I conceived by someone of my people: and so she was more modest than the other, and in some measure covered the incest. [[19:38|he is the father of the Ammonites unto this day|Ipse est pater Ammonitarum usque hodie]].

19.title: De spiritualibus documentis et sensibus ejusdem capituli nonidecimi
19.title_en: On the spiritual lessons and senses of the same nineteenth chapter

paras.t: Ex hujus capituli exordio edocemur, ut […] exemplo Lot opera misericordiæ diligamus, et peregrinis hilariter occurramus, eosque rogemus humiliter ut divertant ad nos, quibus humanitatis officia affectuose sunt impendenda; pauperibus quoque hospitalitas est piissime exhibenda. Domum viri hospitalis ingressi sunt angeli, et liberaverunt eumdem. Domos vero hospitibus non patentes ingressus est ignis, et immisericordes combussit.
paras.en: From the opening of this chapter we are taught that […] by the example of Lot we should love the works of mercy, go cheerfully to meet strangers, and humbly beg them to turn in to us; for the offices of humanity [that is, the kindnesses one man owes another] are to be shown them with affection, and hospitality is to be shown most devoutly to the poor as well. The angels entered the house of the hospitable man and delivered him; but fire entered the houses that were not open to guests, and burned up the unmerciful.

paras.t: Insuper edocemur ex Sodomorum subversione, quantum turpissima vitia ista displiceant Deo essentialiter sancto. Vitanda sunt ergo consortia mollium et omnis carnalis contactus, ac quidquid carnalem provocat motum: et super omnia abominanda ac evitanda est consuetudo pravissima, quæ et pudorem omnem expellit, frontemque meretricis efficit hominis, ita ut de suis non verecundetur spurcitiis, imo ut loquitur Isaias, Peccatum suum prædicet quasi Sodoma nec abscondat, sed glorietur quum impie fecerit; nec æquanimiter correptiones sustineat, sed in corripientem magis consurgat. Vitemus Sodomitarum carnalitatem, inverecundiam, obdurationem, incorrigibilitatem.
paras.en: We are taught besides, from the overthrow of the Sodomites, how greatly these most foul vices displease God, who is holy in his very essence. The company of the effeminate [*molles*: men given to unnatural vice] is therefore to be shunned, and all carnal touching, and whatever stirs a carnal movement; and above all, a most wicked habit is to be abhorred and avoided, for it drives out all shame and gives a man the brow of a harlot, so that he is not ashamed of his own filthiness, nay, as Isaias says, so that he is like those who [[Is 3:9|have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom, and they have not hid it|Peccatum suum prædicet quasi Sodoma nec abscondat]] [the margin's numerals are unread; the words are those of Is 3:9, which Denis puts in the singular], but glories when he has done wickedly[[Prov 2:14||]] [the margin's numerals are unread; Prov 2:14, "who are glad when they have done evil", fits the sense], and does not bear correction patiently but rather rises up against the one who corrects him. Let us shun the carnality of the Sodomites, their shamelessness, their hardness of heart, their incorrigibility.

paras.t: Præterea per generos Lot, quibus ipse Lot videbatur quasi ludens loqui, significantur insipientes, vani et obstinati, qui verba exhortantium et comminantium eis divini districtionem judicii non verentur, imo derident, quemadmodum ad Ezechielem loquitur Dominus de induratis Judæis: Audiunt sermones meos ex te, et non faciunt eos, sed in canticum oris sui vertunt illos.
paras.en: Further, by Lot's sons in law, of whom it is said that Lot [[19:14|seemed to them to speak as it were in jest|videbatur quasi ludens loqui]], are signified the foolish, the vain and the obstinate, who do not fear the words of those who exhort them and threaten them with the strictness of God's judgement, but rather laugh at them; as the Lord says to Ezechiel of the hardened Jews: They [[Ezech 33:31|hear thy words, and do them not: for they turn them into a song of their mouth|Audiunt sermones meos ex te, et non faciunt eos, sed in canticum oris sui vertunt illos]].

paras.t: Amplius, unicuique nostrum dicit quotidie per inspirationem internam angelus custos suus: Salva animam tuam, virtuose vivendo. Noli respicere post tergum tuum, id est, ad pristina vitia tua non revertaris, nec ea quæ propter Deum deseruisti, denuo appetas. Melius namque est non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti, ne tibi contingat illud veri Proverbii: Canis reversus ad vomitum suum, et sus lota in volutabro luti. Nec stes in omni circa regione, hoc est, impiis et iniquis in nullo peccato consentias, nec in aliqua re terrena figas cordis tui affectum: sed in monte salvum te fac. Potest per montem intelligi Christus, et item Ecclesia ac celsitudo virtutum, seu ipsa perfectio aut eremitica vita.
paras.en: Moreover, his guardian angel says daily to each one of us by inward inspiration: [[19:17|Save thy life|Salva animam tuam]] [*animam*, literally "thy soul"], by living virtuously. [[19:17|look not back|Noli respicere post tergum tuum]], that is, do not go back to thy former vices, nor desire again what thou hast forsaken for God's sake. For it [[2 Pet 2:21|had been better for them not to have known the way of justice than, after they have known it, to turn back|Melius namque est non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti]], lest there befall thee that [[2 Pet 2:22|of the true proverb|veri Proverbii]]: [[2 Pet 2:22|The dog is returned to his vomit; and: The sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire|Canis reversus ad vomitum suum, et sus lota in volutabro luti]][[Prov 26:11||]] [the margin gives Prov. xxvi, 11, the proverb of the dog; the words Denis quotes are those of 2 Pet 2:21–22]. [[19:17|neither stay thou in all the country about|Nec stes in omni circa regione]], that is, consent to the wicked and unjust in no sin, and do not fix thy heart's affection on any earthly thing; [[19:17|but save thy self in the mountain|sed in monte salvum te fac]]. By the mountain may be understood Christ, and also the Church and the height of the virtues, or perfection itself, or the hermit's life.

paras.t: Qui autem nondum idoneus est perfectionem amplecti, et contemplativam aut eremiticam assumere vitam, dicat cum Lot: Quæso, Domine mi, non possum in monte salvari, ne forte apprehendat me malum, id est, ne tentationibus vincar, et complere non possim quod inchoavi. Est civitas hæc juxta, ad quam possum confugere, parva. Per civitatem hanc parvam, potest intelligi devotum cœnobium, socialisque vita, seu conversatio activa timentium Deum et custodientium præcepta, sine quorum custodia non est salus: in quibus salvare se debet, qui vitam anachoreticam perfectam seu contemplativam aggredi nequit, sive non audet.
paras.en: But let him who is not yet fit to embrace perfection and to take up the contemplative or the hermit's life say with Lot: [[19:18|I beseech thee, my Lord|Quæso, Domine mi]], [[19:19|I cannot escape to the mountain, lest some evil seize me|non possum in monte salvari, ne forte apprehendat me malum]], that is, lest I be overcome by temptations and be unable to finish what I have begun. [[19:20|There is this city here at hand, to which I may flee, it is a little one|Est civitas hæc juxta, ad quam possum confugere, parva]]. By this little city may be understood a devout monastery and the common life, or the active way of life of those who fear God and keep the commandments, without the keeping of which there is no salvation: in these he must save himself who cannot, or dares not, undertake the perfect anchoretic [that is, solitary] or contemplative life.

paras.t: At vero punitio Sodomorum per ignem sulfureum, fuit figura futuri judicii et exustionis terræ per ignem conflagrationis, ac typus infernalis incendii, quemadmodum sanctus apostolus Judas in sua scribit Canonica: Sodoma et Gomorrha et finitimæ civitates simili modo fornicatæ, et abeuntes post carnem alteram, factæ sunt exemplum, ignis æterni pœnam sustinentes.
paras.en: But the punishment of the Sodomites by fire of brimstone was a figure of the judgement to come and of the burning up of the earth by the fire of the conflagration, and a type of the fire of hell; as the holy apostle Jude writes in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jude 1:7|Sodom and Gomorrha and the neighbouring cities, in like manner, having given themselves to fornication and going after other flesh, were made an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire|Sodoma et Gomorrha et finitimæ civitates simili modo fornicatæ, et abeuntes post carnem alteram, factæ sunt exemplum, ignis æterni pœnam sustinentes]].

paras.t: Per uxorem vero Lot retro adspicientem, et versam in statuam salis, intelliguntur ingrati et recidivantes, atque a Religione apostatantes, qui instar statuæ salis indurantur et amaricantur propriis perversitatibus, ac contra alios faciliter exacerbantur, quorum tamen periclitationis exemplo, electorum ac sapientum corda salubriter condiuntur, ita quod timoratiores, custoditioresque fiunt, et territi plus purgantur.
paras.en: By Lot's wife, who looked back and [[19:26|was turned into a statue of salt|versam in statuam salis]], are understood the ungrateful and those who fall back, and those who apostatize from Religion [that is, from the religious life of an order], who like a statue of salt are hardened and made bitter by their own perversities, and are easily provoked against others; yet by the example of their peril the hearts of the elect and the wise are wholesomely seasoned [*condiuntur*: seasoned, as food is with salt], so that they become more God-fearing and more watchful, and, being made afraid, are the more cleansed.

paras.t: Abraham autem consurgens mane ubi steterat prius cum Domino, intuitus est Sodomam. Sic sapientes et virtuosi cor suum tradunt diluculo ad vigilandum ad proprium Creatorem, maneque adstant Domino, et vident quoniam non Deus volens iniquitatem ipse est. Cujus metuenda pensant judicia, et perpendunt qualiter sæpe punit iniquos, quomodo etiam justo judicio permittit eos quotidie in graviora corruere vitia, quod est maxima ira ac ultio Dei, qui protestatur: Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum, ibunt in adinventionibus suis.
paras.en: [[19:27|And Abraham got up early in the morning, and in the place where he had stood before with the Lord|Abraham autem consurgens mane ubi steterat prius cum Domino]], [[19:28|He looked towards Sodom|intuitus est Sodomam]]. So the wise and virtuous give their heart to watch at dawn for their own Creator[[Ecclus 39:6||]], and in the morning they stand before the Lord, and see that he is not a God that willeth iniquity[[Ps 5:5||]]. They weigh his judgements, which are to be feared, and ponder how often he punishes the wicked, and how also by a just judgement he lets them daily fall into graver vices, which is the greatest wrath and vengeance of God, who declares: [[Ps 80:13|I let them go according to the desires of their heart: they shall walk in their own inventions|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum, ibunt in adinventionibus suis]].

paras.t: Ascendit Lot de Segor, et mansit in monte. Sic aliqui in vita activa et sociali bene exercitati, ascendere possunt aut debent ad apicem vitæ contemplativæ, aut solitariæ ac perfectæ: in qua tamen nisi valde custodite et temperate se habeant, poterunt præcipitari et falli.
paras.en: [[19:30|And Lot went up out of Segor, and abode in the mountain|Ascendit Lot de Segor, et mansit in monte]]. So some who are well practised in the active and common life can, or ought to, go up to the summit of the contemplative life, or of the solitary and perfect life; in which, however, unless they bear themselves very watchfully and with moderation, they may be cast down and deceived.

paras.t: Porro per duas filias Lot, possunt intelligi ratio superior atque inferior, quæ ex patre suo concipiunt, quando a Patre luminum visitantur et adimplentur. Rursus hæ duæ filiæ, accipi possunt appetitus sensitivus et sensus exterior, quæ patrem suum vino inebriant, dum hominem ad gulam præcipitant, a quo tunc pravam concipiunt prolem, videlicet passionum et concupiscentiarum exsecutionem ac sensuum imitationem. Patet denique ex præinductis, quanta vitia oriuntur ex gula.
paras.en: Further, by the two daughters of Lot may be understood the higher and the lower reason [the two parts of reason as the schoolmen distinguish them: the higher looks to eternal things, the lower to temporal ones], which conceive of their father when they are visited and filled by the Father of lights. Again, these two daughters may be taken for the sensitive appetite and the outward sense, which make their father drunk with wine when they drive a man headlong into gluttony; and of him they then conceive a wicked offspring, namely the carrying out of the passions and concupiscences, and the imitation of the senses [a footnote in the edition reads *immutationem*, "alteration", for *imitationem*]. Lastly, it is plain from what has been said how many vices spring from gluttony.

paras.t: Hoc item ex præhabitis innotescit, quam salubre sit urbibus, habere in se cives et habitatores justos, seu vere religiosos, propter quæ Deus omnipotens multa impendit bona civibus ceteris, et urbes a diversis præservat periculis. Nam Sodomæ pepercisset, si decem justi fuissent in ea.
paras.en: It is likewise clear from what has gone before how wholesome it is for cities to have within them just citizens and inhabitants, or truly religious men, for whose sake almighty God bestows many good things on the other citizens and preserves cities from various dangers. For he would have spared Sodom had there been ten just men in it.

paras.t: Postremo per Moab, qui interpretatur, ex patre, intelliguntur reprobi et iniqui, quibus ait Salvator: Vos ex patre diabolo estis. Per Ammon vero, qui interpretatur, filius populi mei, designantur hæretici, qui ex christiano populo prodierunt, et Christi nomine gloriari se jactant, imo se solos veraciter Christianos dici et esse præsumunt.
paras.en: Lastly, by Moab, which is interpreted *from the father*, are understood the reprobate and wicked, to whom the Saviour says: [[John 8:44|You are of your father the devil|Vos ex patre diabolo estis]] [the margin's verse numeral is unread; the words are those of John 8:44]. And by Ammon, which is interpreted [[19:38|the son of my people|filius populi mei]], are signified the heretics, who have come forth from the Christian people and boast that they glory in the name of Christ, nay, presume that they alone are truly called Christians and truly are such.

20.title: Declaratio capituli vicesimi: Profectus inde Abraham
20.title_en: Declaration of the twentieth chapter: Abraham removed from thence

paras.t: Peregrinatio Abrahæ in Gerara, et quid ei acciderit ibi, describitur in præsenti capitulo. Profectus inde Abraham, id est, recedens a convalle Mambre, ut in Scholastica historia exponitur : unde constat quod non habitavit in monte tempore subversionis Pentapolis : in terram australem, hoc est, eundo in terram quæ erat versus austrum, respectu vallis præfatæ, vel simpliciter versus austrum, habitavit inter Cades et Sur, id est inter loca sic dicta, et peregrinatus est in Geraris. Secundum Augustinum, Gerara fuit civitas, cujus rex fuit Abimelech, de quo paulo post subditur, et fuit in Palæstina. Infra vero habetur, quod Abimelech fuit rex Palæstinorum. Denique causam, ob quam Abraham locum suæ habitationis, sicut nunc scribitur, permutavit, aliqui dicunt fuisse, quia subversa Pentapoli, pauci ibant circa vallem in qua morabatur, et ita non poterat ibi hospitalitatem magnam exercere : ideo ivit ad locum præfatum, ut ibi copiosius hospitalitati insisteret. Verumtamen, ut apparet, propter hoc non indiguit ingredi Palæstinam, sed in terra Chanaan, ad quam erat desuper vocatus, potuisset hoc ipsum peragere.
paras.en: The sojourning of Abraham in Gerara, and what befell him there, is described in the present chapter. [[20:1|Abraham removed from thence|Profectus inde Abraham]], that is, departing from the vale of Mambre, as is explained in the Scholastic History: from which it is clear that he did not dwell on the mountain at the time of the overthrow of the Pentapolis [the five cities of the plain]; [[20:1|to the south country|in terram australem]], that is, going into the land that lay toward the south with respect to the aforesaid vale, or simply toward the south, [[20:1|and dwelt between Cades and Sur|habitavit inter Cades et Sur]], that is, between the places so called, [[20:1|and sojourned in Gerara|et peregrinatus est in Geraris]]. According to Augustine, Gerara was a city whose king was Abimelech, of whom mention is made a little after, and it was in Palestine. And further on it is said that Abimelech was king of the Palestines[[Gen 21:33||]] [the margin gives Gen. xxi, 33, where Abimelech returns to the land of the Palestines; he is called king of the Palestines in so many words at Gen 26:1]. Lastly, as to the reason for which Abraham changed the place of his dwelling, as is now written, some say it was that, the Pentapolis having been overthrown, few travelled about the vale in which he lived, and so he could not exercise hospitality there on a large scale: therefore he went to the aforesaid place, so as to give himself more abundantly to hospitality there. Yet, as it seems, he had no need on this account to enter Palestine, but could have done this very thing in the land of Chanaan, to which he had been called from on high.

paras.t: Dixitque de Sara uxore sua, Soror mea est, videlicet ne Palæstini auferrent eam sibi violenter, et interficerent eum, ne viderentur adulterium exercere cum ea. Multa circa hæc scribi possent, de quibus pertranseo, quia in expositione duodecimi capituli sunt inducta.
paras.en: [[20:2|And he said of Sara his wife: She is my sister|Dixitque de Sara uxore sua, Soror mea est]], namely lest the Palestines should take her from him by violence and kill him, so as not to seem to commit adultery with her. Much could be written about these things, which I pass over, because it has been set down in the exposition of the twelfth chapter.

paras.t: Misit ergo Abimelech rex Geraræ, et tulit eam, id est, fecit eam sibi adduci, quia percepit quod esset valde formosa. Mirumque est, quod femina illa tunc nonagenaria, adhuc erat tam concupiscibilis, pulchra, et vivax. Circa quod fertur, quod Hebræi asserunt pulchritudinem et vivacitatem atque teneritudinem suæ carnis, mansisse in ea usque ad ultimum vitæ. Quod si verum est, supernaturale fuisset : ideo credibilius reor, quod ex naturali complexione et bono regimine, et jucunda atque pacifica conversatione cum suo marito, et forsan ex aliqua speciali, occultaque causa seu influentia naturali, permansit in ea tamdiu vigor et speciositas corporis, non tamen modo præclaro usque ad finem vitæ suæ ; sed paulatim decreverunt. Nempe in quibusdam hominibus ex occultis influentiis et naturalibus inexsistentibus fuerunt aliqua valde specialia dona naturæ : de quo plurima dici possent ex astrologorum doctrina.
paras.en: [[20:2|So Abimelech the king of Gerara sent, and took her|Misit ergo Abimelech rex Geraræ, et tulit eam]], that is, had her brought to him, because he perceived that she was very beautiful. And it is a wonder that that woman, then ninety years old, was still so desirable, beautiful and lively. About which it is related that the Hebrews assert that the beauty, liveliness and tenderness of her flesh remained in her up to the end of her life. If that is true, it would have been supernatural: therefore I think it more credible that it was from her natural complexion [that is, the balance of her bodily constitution] and good regimen, and her pleasant and peaceful life with her husband, and perhaps from some special and hidden natural cause or influence, that the vigour and comeliness of her body remained in her so long, yet not in so excellent a degree up to the end of her life; rather they gradually declined. For in certain men, from hidden influences and natural qualities within them, there have been some very special gifts of nature: on which very much could be said from the teaching of the astrologers.

paras.t: Venit autem Deus ad Abimelech per somnium nocte, et ait illi. Ut enim Josephus, expositoresque referunt, statim ut Abimelech tulerat eam, incidit ægritudinem magnam. Desperantibus autem medicis de regis curatione, Deus per angelum apparuit regi in somno, aperiens ei causam suæ infirmitatis. Aliam quoque plagam induxit Deus cunctis mulieribus regis, ut patet in fine hujus capituli. En morieris propter mulierem quam tulisti ; habet enim virum : id est propter culpam quam commisisti, tollendo hanc feminam a suo marito. Istud fuit comminatio, non assertio, vel si fuit assertio, non fuit assertio absoluta, sed conditionata, ut sit sensus : Morieris mox de hac ægritudine, nisi pœnitens restituas feminam istam suo marito. Abimelech vero non tetigerat eam, quia divinitus exstitit impeditus per ægritudinem grandem. Et ait : Domine, num gentem ignorantem, id est, quæ ex ignorantia facti peccasse videtur, sed excusatur, et justam interficies quasi ream ? quasi dicat, Non decet te. Nonne ipse, scilicet Abraham, dixit, Soror mea est : et ipsa ait, Frater meus est ? In simplicitate cordis mei, id est recta et simplici intentione absque palliatione fallaci, et munditia manuum mearum, hoc est innocentia et sinceritate actionum mearum, feci hoc, quoniam intendebam eam uxorem accipere, et maritali affectu accedere.
paras.en: [[20:3|And God came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and he said to him|Venit autem Deus ad Abimelech per somnium nocte, et ait illi]]. For, as Josephus and the expositors relate, as soon as Abimelech had taken her, he fell into a great sickness. And when the physicians despaired of the king's cure, God appeared to the king through an angel in his sleep, disclosing to him the cause of his illness. God also brought another plague upon all the king's women, as appears at the end of this chapter. [[20:3|Lo thou shalt die for the woman that thou hast taken: for she hath a husband|En morieris propter mulierem quam tulisti ; habet enim virum]]: that is, for the fault that thou hast committed in taking this woman from her husband. This was a threat, not an assertion; or if it was an assertion, it was not an absolute assertion but a conditional one, so that the sense is: Thou shalt soon die of this sickness, unless thou repent and restore this woman to her husband. [[20:4|Now Abimelech had not touched her|Abimelech vero non tetigerat eam]], because he was hindered by God through a grave sickness. [[20:4|and he said: Lord|Et ait : Domine]], [[20:4|a nation that is ignorant|num gentem ignorantem]], that is, which seems to have sinned out of ignorance of the fact [that is, not knowing the circumstances of the deed, as distinct from ignorance of the law], but is excused, [[20:4|and just|et justam]] [[20:4|wilt thou slay|interficies]] as though guilty? as if to say: It does not become Thee. [[20:5|Did not he|Nonne ipse]], namely Abraham, [[20:5|say to me: She is my sister|dixit, Soror mea est]]: [[20:5|and she say, He is my brother?|et ipsa ait, Frater meus est]] [[20:5|in the simplicity of my heart|In simplicitate cordis mei]], that is, with a right and simple intention, without deceitful cloaking, [[20:5|and cleanness of my hands|et munditia manuum mearum]], that is, in the innocence and sincerity of my actions, [[20:5|have I done this|feci hoc]], since I intended to take her as my wife and to come to her with a husband's affection.

paras.t: Dixitque ad eum Deus : Et ego scio quod simplici corde feceris. An tota collocutio ista sit in visione et somno completa, an potius in vigilia terminata, quæri potest. Et tota in somno fieri poterat, sicut et tertio Regum legitur Deus Salomoni apparuisse, et facta collocutio inter eos. Deinde subjungitur ibi : Et intellexit Salomon quod somnium esset. Talis vero collocutio fuit intus in anima spiritualis et imaginaria ad aures cordis, non corporis, ad quam homo in somnis est aptior, quia tunc exteriores sensus quiescunt, propter quod in Job scribitur : Per somnium in visione nocturna, quando sopor irruit super homines, aperit Deus aures virorum, et instruit disciplina, ut avertat hominem ab impietate. Ideo custodivi te, ne peccares in me, et non dimisi ut tangeres eam, id est, per istam adversitatem retraxi te ab illicito concubitu, ne me offenderes peccando in proximum. Et istud est donum ac pietas Dei, quod per adversa sic impedit hominem a peccato.
