Abraham autem præceptum hoc Dei nec conjugi suæ, nec servorum alicui manifestavit, ne impediretur per eos, ut Josephus scribit. Quumque conscidisset ligna in holocaustum, hoc est, pro igne holocaustum consumpturo, quod videtur fecisse antequam iter arripuit, abiit ad locum quem præceperat ei Deus accedere. Die autem tertio elevatis oculis vidit locum, videlicet montem, procul, et Deo revelante cognovit, quod ille esset mons, in quo filium immolaret. Dicunt vero nonnulli, quod Bersabee, ubi Abraham habitavit, viginti leucis distabat a monte hoc. Denique sanctus hic Patriarcha habuit gratiam discretionis spirituum, qua cognovit quæ revelationes essent vere a Deo, et quod jussio ista tam mira et inaudita, quæ prima facie videbatur naturali juri ac legi contraria, erat ab ipso veraciter.
paras.en: [[22:3|So Abraham rising up in the night|Igitur Abraham de nocte consurgens]]: in this is plain the fervent readiness of his mind to obey, for he did not wait until dawn. [[22:3|saddled his ass|stravit asinum suum]], that is, he made it ready to carry the wood for the holocaust that was to be wholly burnt. [[22:3|and took with him two young men|Ducens secum duos juvenes]], etc., who (according to the Hebrews) were Ismael and Eliezer. This does not seem true as regards Ismael, who (as we have in the preceding chapter) had already been separated from Abraham's house and had begun to dwell in the desert of Pharan. Abraham made known this command of God neither to his wife nor to any of his servants, lest he be hindered by them, as Josephus writes. [[22:3|and when he had cut wood for the holocaust|Quumque conscidisset ligna in holocaustum]], that is, for the fire that was to consume the holocaust (which he seems to have done before he set out on the journey), [[22:3|he went his way to the place which God had commanded him|abiit ad locum quem præceperat ei Deus]] to go. [[22:4|And on the third day, lifting up his eyes, he saw the place|Die autem tertio elevatis oculis vidit locum]], namely the mountain, [[22:4|afar off|procul]], and by God's revelation he knew that this was the mountain on which he was to sacrifice his son. Some say that Bersabee, where Abraham lived, was twenty leagues from this mountain. Moreover this holy Patriarch had the grace of discernment of spirits, by which he knew which revelations were truly from God, and that this command, so wonderful and unheard of, which at first sight seemed contrary to natural right and law, was truly from Him.

paras.t: Dixitque ad pueros suos: Exspectate hic cum asino. Noluit enim in illorum præsentia filium immolare, ne illi ex compassione reniterentur aut ularent. Pueri isti fuerunt duo servi Abrahæ, ut Glossa insinuat. Ego et puer illuc usque properabimus, postquam adoraverimus, revertemur ad vos. Videtur sanctus vir in hoc esse mentitus, hoc est, contra propriam mentem seu intentionem loquutus, quoniam intendebat filium immolare, nec reverti cum eo. Ad hoc quidam respondent, quod Abraham dixit verba ista prophetice, non tamen advertens quid diceret. Non enim intendebat quod Isaac reverteretur cum eo, idcirco non fuit prophetia proprie dicta, ad quam præcipue pertinet intellectus propheticorum verborum, juxta illud in Daniele, Intelligentia est opus, hoc est principale in visione; sed fuit prophetia large accepta, quoniam Spiritu Sancto movente, sic protulit verba, sicut futurum erat. Verum contra hoc objici potest. Nam Abraham ex deliberatione et proposito protulit verba hæc, ergo sensum eorum advertit, et aliquem sensum intendebat in eis, sicque advertit quid dixit. Aut ergo intendebat pueris insinuare, quod ipse cum filio suo, adoratione completa, rediret ad eos, aut non: si sic, ergo videbatur contra intentionem propriam loqui; si non, ergo nihilo minus fuit ibi falsa et fallax significatio horum verborum. Ad istud videtur posse dupliciter responderi: primo, quod verba Abrahæ vera erant juxta illum loquendi modum, quo duo seu plures dicuntur aliquid facere, quod unus aut quidam eorum efficiunt: juxta quod genus loquendi quidam exponunt, quod discipuli leguntur indignati propter effusionem unguenti super caput Salvatoris, et quod latrones improperabant ei in cruce. Secundo, quod Abraham indubitanter credebat filium suum a Domino suscitandum, si immolaretur: sicque tam se quam filium suum credebat rediturum ad pueros, sive simul et statim, sive seorsum ac successive. Ait quippe Apostolus ad Hebræos: Fide Abraham obtulit, id est, offerre proposuit Isaac, in quo susceperat promissiones, arbitrans quia et a morte suscitare potens est Deus. Hinc loquitur Augustinus: Quum Abraham immolaturus fuisset filium, laudatur credidisse confestim suscitandum eumdem; nec hæsitavit quod sibi reddi poterat immolatus, qui dari potuit non speratus. Alcuinus quoque: Indubitanti, inquit, animo mactare filium Abraham voluit, laudabilis in constantia offerendi, et in fide suscitandi.
paras.en: [[22:5|And he said to his young men: Stay you here with the ass|Dixitque ad pueros suos: Exspectate hic cum asino]]. For he did not wish to sacrifice his son in their presence, lest out of compassion they should resist or wail. These young men were two servants of Abraham, as the Gloss suggests. [[22:5|I and the boy will go with speed as far as yonder, and after we have worshipped, will return to you|Ego et puer illuc usque properabimus, postquam adoraverimus, revertemur ad vos]]. In this the holy man seems to have lied, that is, to have spoken against his own mind or intention, since he intended to sacrifice his son and not to return with him. To this some answer that Abraham spoke these words prophetically, though without heeding what he said. For he did not intend that Isaac should return with him; and so it was not prophecy properly so called, to which above all belongs the understanding of the prophetic words, according to the words in Daniel: [[Dan 10:1|there is need of understanding|Intelligentia est opus]] [the margin gives "Ibid. x, 1", though the note before it is of 1 Kings; the words are Dan 10:1], that is, it is the chief thing in a vision; but it was prophecy taken broadly, since at the prompting of the Holy Ghost he uttered the words as it was to be. But against this it can be objected: Abraham spoke these words with deliberation and purpose; therefore he heeded their sense, and intended some sense in them, and so heeded what he said. Either, then, he meant to give the young men to understand that he and his son would return to them when the worship was done, or not. If so, he seems to have spoken against his own intention; if not, there was none the less a false and deceptive meaning in these words. To this it seems one can answer in two ways. First, that Abraham's words were true according to the manner of speaking by which two or more are said to do something that one or some of them do: by this manner of speaking some explain that the disciples are said to have had indignation at the pouring of the ointment on the Saviour's head[[Matt 26:8||]], and that the thieves reproached Him on the cross[[Matt 27:44||]][[Luke 23:39||]]. Secondly, that Abraham believed without doubting that his son would be raised up by the Lord if he were sacrificed; and so he believed that both he and his son would return to the young men, whether together and at once, or separately and one after the other. For the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 11:17|By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered Isaac|Fide Abraham obtulit]] (that is, he purposed to offer him), in whom he had received the promises, [[Heb 11:19|Accounting that God is able to raise up even from the dead|arbitrans quia et a morte suscitare potens est Deus]] [the margin gives only Heb. xi, 17; these last words are Heb 11:19]. Hence Augustine says: When Abraham was about to sacrifice his son, he is praised for having believed that he would straightway be raised up; nor did he doubt that he who could be given when not hoped for could be given back to him when sacrificed. Alcuin too: With an undoubting mind, he says, Abraham was willing to slay his son, praiseworthy in his constancy in offering him and in his faith that he would be raised up.

paras.t: Tulit quoque ligna holocausti, id est, Abraham deposuit ligna illa de dorso asini, et imposuit super Isaac filium suum: quod factum est ordinante sic Spiritu Sancto, propter mysterium infra tangendum. Ipse vero portabat in manibus suis ignem et gladium. In una etenim manu portavit ignem, ad comburendum corpus filii immolandi; in alia, gladium ad mactandum.
paras.en: [[22:6|And he took the wood for the holocaust|Tulit quoque ligna holocausti]], that is, Abraham took that wood down from the ass's back, [[22:6|and laid it upon Isaac his son|et imposuit super Isaac filium suum]]: which was done by the ordering of the Holy Ghost, because of the mystery to be touched on below. [[22:6|and he himself carried in his hands fire and a sword|Ipse vero portabat in manibus suis ignem et gladium]]. For in one hand he carried fire, to burn the body of the son who was to be sacrificed; in the other a sword, to slay him.

paras.t: Quumque duo pergerent simul, dixit Isaac patri suo: Pater mi. At ille respondit: Quid vis, fili? Ecce, inquit, ignis et ligna hic sunt: ubi est victima holocausti, id est hostia quæ in holocaustum offeretur? Circa hoc loquitur Origenes: Quomodo, putas, filius mox immolandus, per verba hæc viscera concussit paterna? Iterum ait circa verba paulo ante posita, scilicet, Ego et puer, quum adoraverimus, revertemur: Dic mihi, Abraham, vere dicis hoc, an fallis? Si vere, ergo non offers filium; si fallis, hoc tantum Patriarcham non decet. Verum, inquit, dico: et holocaustum offero puerum, et cum ipso redeo ad vos; quoniam fides mea hæc est, quod potens est Deus eum suscitare a mortuis.
paras.en: [[22:6|And as they two went on together|Quumque duo pergerent simul]], [[22:7|Isaac said to his father: My father|dixit Isaac patri suo: Pater mi]]. [[22:7|And he answered|At ille respondit]]: [[22:7|What wilt thou, son?|Quid vis, fili?]] [[22:7|Behold, saith he, fire and wood|Ecce, inquit, ignis et ligna]] are here: [[22:7|where is the victim for the holocaust|ubi est victima holocausti]], that is, the offering that is to be offered as a holocaust? On this Origen says: How, think you, did the son who was soon to be sacrificed shake his father's heart with these words? And again he says, on the words set down a little before, namely, [[22:5|I and the boy|Ego et puer]] … [[22:5|after we have worshipped, will return|quum adoraverimus, revertemur]]: Tell me, Abraham, do you say this truly, or do you deceive? If truly, then you do not offer your son; if you deceive, that hardly becomes so great a Patriarch. I speak truly, he says: I both offer the boy as a holocaust and return with him to you; for this is my faith, that God is able to raise him from the dead.

paras.t: Dixit autem Abraham: Deus providebit sibi victimam holocausti, fili mi. Quidam dicunt, quod Abraham dixit istud prophetice, quia arietem fuerat oblaturus. Verumtamen sicut Abraham putavit se statim oblaturum proprium filium, ita per verba hæc, quibus veritatem caute celavit, intendebat ad litteram dicere, Deus exhibebit mihi, quid immolem ei, utpote te ipsum, inspirando tibi piam voluntatem, qua absque rebellione accedes, ut immoleris in holocaustum.
paras.en: [[22:8|And Abraham said: God will provide himself a victim for an holocaust, my son|Dixit autem Abraham: Deus providebit sibi victimam holocausti, fili mi]]. Some say that Abraham said this prophetically, because he was to offer a ram. But just as Abraham thought he was about to offer his own son, so by these words, with which he prudently concealed the truth, he meant to say in the literal sense: God will show me what I am to sacrifice to Him, namely thyself, by inspiring in thee a devout will by which thou wilt come without rebelling to be sacrificed as a holocaust.

paras.t: Pergebant ergo pariter, et venerunt ad locum, quem ostenderat ei Deus, in quo ædificavit Abraham altare, etc.: in quo loco construxit et Salomon postea altare, secundum Hebræos. Aliqui etiam dicunt, quod Abraham fecit altare illud de terra. Unde in Scholastica historia legitur: Statuit aram de terra. Quumque colligasset Isaac filium suum. Non ideo ligavit filii sui manus ac pedes, ne filius non ligatus, effugeret sive resisteret, quia nec potuisset ligare invitum, et antequam inceperit eum ligare, exposuit ei divinum præceptum de sua immolatione, et cur ligaretur. Cur ergo eum ligavit? Respondetur, ut in hoc servaretur ritus quo et alia animalia quæ in holocaustum immolabantur, ligata offerebantur: et ut per hoc Christi ligatio atque in cruce confixio figurarentur; vel etiam ne Isaac ex naturali mortis horrore se forsitan tempore percussionis moveret. Mortem enim naturaliter refugiebat, quum de beatissimo principe Apostolorum Christus prædixerit: Alius te cinget, et ducet quo tu non vis. Et rursus, quatenus ex ista colligatione magis commendaretur obedientia et constantia Abrahæ, et subjectio ac patientia Isaac. Posuit eum in altare, hoc est super altare illud, videlicet super struem lignorum, id est super ligna illa quæ super altare ordinate composuit, ut super ea filius suus apte jaceret ad occidendum et comburendum.
paras.en: [[22:8|So they went on together|Pergebant ergo pariter]], [[22:9|And they came to the place which God had shewn him, where he built an altar|et venerunt ad locum, quem ostenderat ei Deus, in quo ædificavit Abraham altare]], etc.: in which place Solomon also afterwards built an altar, according to the Hebrews. Some also say that Abraham made that altar of earth; hence we read in the Scholastic History: He set up an altar of earth. [[22:9|and when he had bound Isaac his son|Quumque colligasset Isaac filium suum]]. He did not bind his son's hands and feet lest the son, if not bound, should flee or resist; for he could not have bound him against his will, and before he began to bind him he explained to him God's command about his sacrifice, and why he was being bound. Why then did he bind him? The answer is: so that in this the rite might be kept by which the other animals sacrificed as holocausts were offered bound; and so that the binding of Christ and His nailing to the cross might be prefigured by this; or also lest Isaac, from the natural horror of death, should perhaps move at the moment of the stroke. For by nature he shrank from death, since Christ foretold of the most blessed prince of the Apostles: [[John 21:18|another shall gird thee and lead thee whither thou wouldst not|Alius te cinget, et ducet quo tu non vis]]. And again, so that by this binding the obedience and constancy of Abraham, and the submission and patience of Isaac, might be the more commended. [[22:9|he laid him on the altar|Posuit eum in altare]], that is, upon that altar, namely [[22:9|upon the pile of wood|super struem lignorum]], that is, upon the wood which he had laid in order upon the altar, so that his son might lie fitly upon it to be slain and burnt.

paras.t: Præterea circa hoc Josephus asserit, quod Abraham dixit ad Isaac: Sicut ex voluntate Dei ingressus es mirabiliter mundum, et precibus magnis impetratus a Domino, gaudioseque natus, sic oportet te mirabiliter egredi mundum: ideo Dominus jussit te ei offerri, quasi quem dignum judicavit mori non ægritudine, peste, gladio, aut aliqua passione humana. His verbis (ut recitat Lyra) Josephus dicit Abraham addidisse: Sicque Deus recipiet animam tuam secum perpetuo. Subditque Lyra, quod verba Josephi vera sint, dempta ultima ista particula, quod scilicet Dominus dixerit Isaac animam secum perpetuo permansuram. Nam Deus multa prædixit futura per Isaac, quæ tunc nondum erant impleta. Verumtamen in Scholastica historia verba Josephi aliter, verumque (ut creditur) narrantur, quum dicitur: Deus dignum duxit animam tuam vocare ad se cum sacrificiis et orationibus, et suscitabit te propter promissiones implendas: sicque Isaac libens et promptus accessit ad aram ac mortem. Attamen istam particulam, Suscitabit te, etc., non inveni in Josepho, sed Apostolus in epistola ad Romanos testatur, quod Abraham arbitrabatur Deum posse filium immolatum a morte resuscitare.
paras.en: Moreover Josephus asserts on this point that Abraham said to Isaac: As by the will of God thou didst wonderfully enter the world, obtained from the Lord by great prayers and born amid rejoicing, so must thou wonderfully go out of the world. Therefore the Lord has commanded that thou be offered to Him, as one whom He has judged worthy to die not by sickness, plague, the sword or any human suffering. To these words (as Lyra relates) Josephus says Abraham added: And so God will receive thy soul with Himself for ever. And Lyra adds that Josephus's words are true, except for this last clause, namely that the Lord had said that Isaac's soul would abide with Him for ever: for God had foretold many future things through Isaac which had not yet been fulfilled. But in the Scholastic History Josephus's words are reported otherwise, and (as is believed) truly, where it says: God has thought it fit to call thy soul to Himself with sacrifices and prayers, and He will raise thee up to fulfil the promises; and so Isaac came willingly and readily to the altar and to death. Yet this clause, He will raise thee up, etc., I have not found in Josephus; but the Apostle testifies in the epistle to the Romans that Abraham reckoned that God could raise up his son from death after he had been sacrificed [the margin note here cannot be read; the thought is that of Rom 4:17–21, though the words are closest to Heb 11:19].

paras.t: Insuper Josephus dicit, et communiter sic allegant expositores, quod Isaac erat tunc triginta quinque annorum. Ex quo patet, quod pater suus non colligavit eum invitum. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus his contradicit, quia si sponte accessisset ad immolationem, hoc fuisset maxime meritorium, et non minus quam quod Abraham voluit eum offerre: sicque valde mirabile esset, quod scriptura ista non commendaret Isaac de tantis meritis suis, sicut commendat Abraham de obedientia sua. Hinc Rabbi Paulus allegat, et sequitur quosdam Hebræos, dicentes quod Isaac erat tunc quindecim annorum, et quasi invitus accessit ad aram; nec tamen sit inde culpandus, quia adhuc in puerili fuit ætate, in qua nondum habebat perfecte usum liberi arbitrii, et hoc probat, quia in littera puer vocatur. Non enim habetur in Scriptura, ut homo triginta annorum et ultra vocetur puer. Sed omnia ista Rabbi Pauli verba videntur inepta, et sæpius miror quod loquitur tam indocte. Nam dato quod Isaac non fuisset nisi quindecim annorum, tamen tantæ fuisset ætatis, quod satis compos exstitisset mentis, satisque libero utens arbitrio ad promerendum ac demerendum. Et si invitus accessisset ad immolationem, postquam pater suus vir tam sanctus retulit sibi id esse a Deo præceptum, fuisset ex hoc valde culpandus. Denique consequenter in littera evidenter insinuatur, quantam gratiam Deus præstiterit ipsi Isaac, et benedixerit eum: per quod obedientia ejus manifestatur, approbata ac remunerata a Domino. Josephus quoque narrat, quod Isaac auditis verbis patris sui, delectatus fuit in sapientia ejus, et libentissime ea accepit, dicens se paratum obedire etiam si solus pater suus id sibi præciperet: imo melius sibi esse non nasci, quam non obedire voluntatibus Dei ac patris sui. In Scripturis quoque non solum homines triginta annorum et amplius, imo et plusquam quadraginta annorum, pueri appellantur. Unde in Zacharia habetur, quod angelus unus dixit ad alium: Curre et loquere ad puerum istum, videlicet ad Zachariam prophetam, qui tunc erat grandævæ ætatis. Christus quoque post resurrectionem dixit Apostolis: Pueri, numquid pulmentarium habetis? Inter quos fuit sacratissimus Petrus, qui tunc erat multo plusquam triginta annorum: imo Joannes apostolus tunc erat annorum triginta aut plus; siquidem sexagesimo nono post Christi passionem anno defunctus est, quum centenarius esset.
paras.en: Moreover Josephus says, and the expositors commonly allege it so, that Isaac was then thirty-five years old. From this it is plain that his father did not bind him against his will. Rabbi Paul, however, contradicts this: for if he had come to the sacrifice of his own accord, this would have been supremely meritorious, and no less so than Abraham's willingness to offer him; and so it would be very strange that this scripture should not commend Isaac for such great merits, as it commends Abraham for his obedience. Hence Rabbi Paul alleges, following certain Hebrews, that Isaac was then fifteen years old, and came to the altar as it were unwillingly; yet he is not to be blamed for this, since he was still of a boy's age, in which he did not yet have the full use of free will; and he proves this because in the text he is called a boy. For it is not found in Scripture that a man of thirty years or more is called a boy. But all these words of Rabbi Paul seem foolish, and I often wonder that he speaks so unlearnedly. For granting that Isaac was only fifteen years old, he would still have been of an age to be sufficiently master of his mind, and sufficiently in the use of free will to merit and demerit. And if he had come unwillingly to the sacrifice after his father, so holy a man, had told him that it was commanded by God, he would have been much to blame for it. Then too in what follows the text plainly suggests how great a grace God bestowed on Isaac, and how He blessed him; by which his obedience is shown to have been approved and rewarded by the Lord. Josephus also relates that Isaac, on hearing his father's words, took delight in his wisdom and accepted them most willingly, saying that he was ready to obey even if his father alone had commanded it of him; indeed, that it would be better for him not to have been born than not to obey the will of God and of his father. In the Scriptures, too, not only men of thirty years and more, but even of more than forty, are called boys. Hence it is said in Zacharias that one angel said to another: [[Zach 2:4|Run, speak to this young man|Curre et loquere ad puerum istum]] [the margin reads "Zach." and the rest cannot be read; the words are Zach 2:4; Latin puerum, "boy", which the Douay-Rheims renders "young man"], namely to the prophet Zacharias, who was then of great age. Christ too after the resurrection said to the Apostles: [[John 21:5|Children, have you any meat?|Pueri, numquid pulmentarium habetis?]] [the margin reads "Joann." and the rest cannot be read; the words are John 21:5; Latin pueri, "boys"]. Among them was the most holy Peter, who was then well over thirty years old; indeed the apostle John was then thirty years old or more, since he died in the sixty-ninth year after Christ's Passion, being a hundred years old.

paras.t: Extenditque manum, et arripuit gladium, ut immolaret filium suum. Assumpsit etenim cor virile et constans, ac animum pro fidei efficacia rigorosum, quum tamen sanctus Abraham esset naturaliter valde mansuetus, pius ac dulcis. Et ecce angelus Domini de cælo clamavit, etc. Non extendas manum tuam super puerum, neque facias illi quidquam læsionis aut pœnæ. Nunc satis probata et declarata est fides et obedientia tua, nec innocentis filii tui sanguinem sitit Deus, sed tuarum declarationem virtutum, ad ædificationem aliorum. Dicit autem Hieronymus, et habetur in Glossa præcedentis capituli: Verum est illud linguæ Hebraicæ idioma, quod omnis filius ad comparationem parentis, infans vocatur et parvulus. Romæ quoque usque hodie, omnes filii infantes dicuntur. Hæc Hieronymus. In Scriptura etiam servi ac subditi, communiter pueri nuncupantur. Nunc cognovi, id est, per istum virtuosum effectum jam radicaliter alios cognoscere feci, quod timeas Deum filiali timore, et non pepercisti filio tuo unigenito propter me, id est, paratus eras occidere eum mei intuitu et amore, atque ad majestatis meæ honorem.
paras.en: [[22:10|And he put forth his hand, and took the sword, to sacrifice his son|Extenditque manum, et arripuit gladium, ut immolaret filium suum]]. For he took on a manly and steadfast heart, and a mind made firm by the power of faith, though holy Abraham was by nature very gentle, kind and sweet. [[22:11|And behold, an angel of the Lord from heaven called to him|Et ecce angelus Domini de cælo clamavit]], etc. [[22:12|Lay not thy hand upon the boy, neither do thou any thing to him|Non extendas manum tuam super puerum, neque facias illi quidquam]] by way of hurt or pain. Now thy faith and obedience have been sufficiently proved and declared; God does not thirst for the blood of thy innocent son, but for the declaration of thy virtues, for the edification of others. Jerome says, and it is in the Gloss on the preceding chapter: It is true that it is an idiom of the Hebrew tongue that every son, in comparison with his parent, is called an infant and a little one. At Rome too, even to this day, all sons are called infants. Thus Jerome. In Scripture servants and subjects too are commonly called boys. [[22:12|now I know|Nunc cognovi]], that is, by this virtuous deed I have now made others know thoroughly [[22:12|that thou fearest God|quod timeas Deum]] with filial fear, [[22:12|and hast not spared thy only begotten son for my sake|et non pepercisti filio tuo unigenito propter me]], that is, thou wast ready to kill him out of regard and love for Me, and to the honour of My majesty.

paras.t: Hanc communem hujus verbi, Cognovi, expositionem reprobat aliqualiter Rabbi Paulus, quia per istum effectum ipse Abraham cognoscere fecit se Deum timere: sicque aptius dixisset Scriptura seu angelus, Nunc cognoscere fecisti, etc. Sed ista objectio nullius vigoris est, quoniam Deo jubente, inspirante et confortante, Abraham fecit hoc opus: ideo magis adscribendum est Deo quam Abrahæ. Posset tamen expositio Rabbi Pauli, verbum præfatum metaphorice exponentis, aliquo modo salvari, ut sit sensus: Nunc cognovi, id est, per modum cognoscentis aliquid de novo me habeo, quia viso isto effectu, majora tibi promitto quam ante. Hæc autem verba locutus est angelus in Dei persona.
paras.en: Rabbi Paul in some measure rejects this common explanation of the word *I know*, because by this deed it was Abraham himself who made known that he feared God; and so Scripture, or the angel, would more aptly have said: Now thou hast made known, etc. But this objection has no force, since Abraham did this work at God's command, inspiration and strengthening; therefore it is to be ascribed to God rather than to Abraham. Yet the explanation of Rabbi Paul, who takes the word metaphorically, could in some way be upheld, so that the sense is: [[22:12|now I know|Nunc cognovi]], that is, I behave like one who knows something anew, since, having seen this deed, I promise thee greater things than before. The angel spoke these words in the person of God.

paras.t: Levavit Abraham oculos suos, viditque post tergum arietem inter vepres hærentem cornibus, quem assumens, obtulit holocaustum pro filio, id est loco seu vice filii sui quem obtulisset. Dicunt Hebræi, ut recitat Lyra, quod aries ille fuit ibi paratus a creatione mundi, hoc est, a sexta die, qua primo facta sunt animalia terræ: quod rationi et Scripturis contrariatur, nec dignum est reprobatione. Aliqui autem dixerunt, quod aries fuit ibi de novo formatus: sed verius creditur, quod angelico ministerio fuit ibi de novo adductus, quod et Rabanus protestatur. Præterea dicunt Judæi, Isaac ab immolatione liberatum, et arietem pro eo oblatum prima die Septembris, in cujus rei memoriam tunc solennizant, et cornibus pecorum clangunt, quod vocant festum tubarum.
paras.en: [[22:13|Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw behind his back a ram, amongst the briers, sticking fast by the horns, which he took and offered for a holocaust instead of his son|Levavit Abraham oculos suos, viditque post tergum arietem inter vepres hærentem cornibus, quem assumens, obtulit holocaustum pro filio]], that is, in the place or stead of his son, whom he would have offered. The Hebrews say, as Lyra relates, that that ram had been made ready there since the creation of the world, that is, since the sixth day, on which the animals of the earth were first made: which is contrary to reason and to the Scriptures, and not worth refuting. Some said that the ram was newly formed there; but it is more truly believed that it was newly brought there by the ministry of an angel, as Rabanus also declares. The Jews say, moreover, that Isaac was delivered from the sacrifice and the ram offered in his stead on the first day of September, in memory of which they then keep a feast and sound the horns of beasts, which they call the feast of trumpets.

paras.t: Appellavitque Abraham nomen loci illius, Dominus videt. Vel quia Deus ibi pie et per approbationem adspexit ipsum Abraham et opera ejus; vel quia fecit ibi videri seu cognosci obedientiam ejus ac filii sui. Unde usque hodie dicitur: In monte Dominus videbit: hoc est, ipsi Judæi nomen illud complexum, Dominus videt, traxerunt in verbum vulgare, ita quod quando in angustiis positi sunt, dicunt: In monte Dominus videbit, id est, sicut Deus misertus est Abrahæ et Isaac in monte illo, Abraham revocando ab interfectione carissimi filii, et ipsum filium ab occisione, sic misereatur et nostri.
paras.en: [[22:14|And he called|Appellavitque]] (Abraham) [[22:14|the name of that place, The Lord seeth|nomen loci illius, Dominus videt]]: either because God there looked kindly and approvingly on Abraham and his works, or because He there caused his obedience and that of his son to be seen or known. [[22:14|Whereupon, even to this day, it is said: In the mountain the Lord will see|Unde usque hodie dicitur: In monte Dominus videbit]]: that is, the Jews made that compound name, The Lord seeth, into a common saying, so that when they are in straits they say: In the mountain the Lord will see; that is: as God had mercy on Abraham and Isaac on that mountain, calling Abraham back from killing his dearest son, and the son himself from being slain, so may He have mercy on us too.

paras.t: Vocavit autem angelus Domini Abraham secundo de cælo, dicens: Per meipsum juravi, dicit Dominus. De hoc Dei juramento tractat diffuse Apostolus ad Hebræos, dicendo: Abrahæ namque promittens Deus, quoniam neminem habuit, per quem juraret majorem, juravit per semetipsum.
paras.en: [[22:15|And the angel of the Lord called to Abraham a second time from heaven, saying|Vocavit autem angelus Domini Abraham secundo de cælo, dicens]]: [[22:16|By my own self have I sworn, saith the Lord|Per meipsum juravi, dicit Dominus]]. The Apostle treats of this oath of God at length to the Hebrews, saying: [[Heb 6:13|For God making promises to Abraham, because he had no one greater by whom he might swear, swore by himself|Abrahæ namque promittens Deus, quoniam neminem habuit, per quem juraret majorem, juravit per semetipsum]].

paras.t: Quia fecisti rem hanc, etc., id est, paratus fuisti unigenitum tuum mihi offerre, et multa ad hoc dispositiva egisti, benedicam tibi, augendo in te spiritualia ac temporalia bona, et multiplicabo semen tuum sicut stellas cæli, et velut arenam quæ est in littore maris, hoc est innumerabiliter, ut sæpius expositum est. Tamen quod ait, Sicut stellas, coaptatur ad bonos atque electos, qui splendent instar stellarum, in præsenti per gratiam, et in regno per gloriam. Porro quod ait, Et velut arenam, aptatur malis et reprobis, tam ex Esau quam ex Ismaele, et aliis Abrahæ filiis, natis, cupidis ac terrenis. Nihilo minus, ut in libris Moysis patet, hinc inde utrumque frequenter ad electos refertur.
paras.en: [[22:16|because thou hast done this thing|Quia fecisti rem hanc]], etc., that is, thou wast ready to offer Me thy only begotten, and didst many things that led up to it, [[22:17|I will bless thee|benedicam tibi]], increasing in thee goods both spiritual and temporal, [[22:17|and I will multiply thy seed as the stars of heaven, and as the sand that is by the sea shore|et multiplicabo semen tuum sicut stellas cæli, et velut arenam quæ est in littore maris]], that is, beyond number, as has often been explained. Yet the words *as the stars* are fitted to the good and the elect, who shine like stars, in the present life by grace and in the kingdom by glory; while the words *and as the sand* are fitted to the wicked and reprobate, born both of Esau and of Ismael and of Abraham's other sons, covetous and earthly men. None the less, as is plain in the books of Moses, both are often referred to the elect, now one, now the other.

paras.t: Possidebit semen tuum portas inimicorum suorum, id est, posteri tui adversarios suos debellabunt, eorumque urbes ac patrias possidebunt: quod sub Josue ac postea sæpe constat impletum: et benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terræ, hoc est in Christo, videlicet in ipso credendo, ut supra plenius fuit elucidatum. In fide etenim Christi, et virtute ac merito suæ saluberrimæ passionis, multi ex omni hominum natione consequuntur salutem. Quia obedisti voci meæ. Non est hoc intelligendum, quod obedientia Abrahæ promeruit de condigno, ut in semine suo, puta in Christo, omnes gentes benedictionem consequerentur: imo hoc Christus proprie meruit, cujus meriti meritum obedientiæ fuit figura: sed et de congruo obedientia Abrahæ aliquo modo cooperabatur ad hoc, ut causa meritoria dispositiva. His promissionibus Dei auditis, Abraham et Isaac, qui ambo eas audierunt, osculabantur se invicem cum gaudio magno, et præter spem se amplectebantur.
paras.en: [[22:17|thy seed shall possess the gates of their enemies|Possidebit semen tuum portas inimicorum suorum]], that is, thy descendants shall overcome their adversaries and possess their cities and countries: which is known to have been fulfilled often under Josue[[Jos 14:1||]][[Jos 15:1||]] and afterwards. [[22:18|And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|et benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terræ]], that is, in Christ, namely by believing in Him, as was explained more fully above. For in the faith of Christ, and by the power and merit of His most saving Passion, many of every nation of men obtain salvation. [[22:18|because thou hast obeyed my voice|Quia obedisti voci meæ]]. This is not to be understood as if Abraham's obedience merited *de condigno* [that is, by strict merit, as a reward in justice] that in his seed, that is, in Christ, all nations should obtain blessing: rather Christ properly merited this, and the merit of Abraham's obedience was a figure of His merit; yet *de congruo* [that is, by merit of fitness, not of strict justice] Abraham's obedience did in some way work towards this, as a disposing meritorious cause. When they had heard these promises of God, Abraham and Isaac, who both heard them, kissed one another with great joy, and embraced each other beyond all hope.

paras.t: His itaque gestis, nuntiatum est Abraham, quod Melcha genuisset filios Nachor fratri suo, id est, quod ipsa Melcha soror Saræ uxoris Abrahæ, peperisset suo marito nomine Nachor, qui fuit Abrahæ frater, filios; primogenitum Hus, de quo (secundum Hieronymum) natus est sanctus Job, in cujus exordio libri habetur: Vir fuit in terra Hus, nomine Job, ut plenius scripsi ibidem: et Buz fratrem ejus, de quo natus est Eliu filius Barachel Buzites, qui nimis arroganter ac fervide contra Job disputavit. Circa hæc scribit Hieronymus, et habetur in Glossa: De stirpe Hus descendit Job. Male ergo existimant ipsum Job esse de stirpe Esau. Nam quod in fine libri Job habetur, quod de Syro sermone translatus sit, et quartus ab Esau, et reliqua quæ ibi continentur, in Hebraico non habentur. Post Hus, natus est de Melcha Buz, ex cujus genere fuit Balaam divinus, sicut Hebræi tradunt, qui in Job dicitur Eliu: primo vir sanctus et propheta Dei, qui dum postea per inobedientiam et desiderium munerum, populum Israel maledicere cupivit, divinus vocatus est. Hæc Hieronymus.
paras.en: [[22:20|After these things, it was told Abraham, that Melcha also had borne children to Nachor his brother|His itaque gestis, nuntiatum est Abraham, quod Melcha genuisset filios Nachor fratri suo]], that is, that Melcha herself, the sister of Sara, Abraham's wife, had borne sons to her husband, named Nachor, who was Abraham's brother: [[22:21|Hus, the firstborn|primogenitum Hus]], of whom (according to Jerome) holy Job was born, at the beginning of whose book we have: [[Job 1:1|There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job|Vir fuit in terra Hus, nomine Job]], as I have written more fully there; [[22:21|and Buz, his brother|et Buz fratrem ejus]], of whom was born Eliu the son of Barachel the Buzite, who disputed against Job with too much arrogance and heat[[Job 32:1||]]. On these things Jerome writes, and it is in the Gloss: Job descended from the stock of Hus. They are wrong, then, who think that Job was of the stock of Esau. For what is found at the end of the book of Job, that it was translated from the Syriac tongue, and that he was the fourth from Esau, and the rest that is contained there, is not in the Hebrew. After Hus, Buz was born of Melcha, of whose race was Balaam the soothsayer, as the Hebrews hand down, who in Job is called Eliu: at first a holy man and a prophet of God, who, when afterwards through disobedience and desire of gifts he sought to curse the people of Israel[[Num 22:1||]], was called a soothsayer. Thus Jerome.

paras.t: Camuel quoque patrem Syrorum, qui ab eo exorti sunt. Porro (secundum Hieronymum) Camuel est pater Damasci, pro qua hic ponitur Syria. Et Bathuel. Propter hunc Bathuelem, qui est unus de octo filiis Melchæ, recitatur hic generatio ista, quia de Bathuele nata est Rebecca, de qua infra habetur, qualiter facta sit Isaac uxor. Qualiter autem Thare habuit tres filios, scilicet Abraham, Nachor et Aran, et quod Abraham duxerit Saram filiam fratris sui, nomine Aran, in conjugem: Nachor vero acceperit Melcham filiam Aran in uxorem, ita quod uxores Abrahæ et Nachor fratris sui, fuerunt sorores, quarum frater fuit Lot, scriptum est supra undecimo capitulo.
paras.en: [[22:21|and Camuel the father of the Syrians|Camuel quoque patrem Syrorum]], who sprang from him. Further (according to Jerome) Camuel is the father of Damascus, for which Syria is put here. [[22:23|And Bathuel|Et Bathuel]]. It is because of this Bathuel, who is one of the eight sons of Melcha, that this genealogy is given here, since of Bathuel was born Rebecca, of whom we read below how she became Isaac's wife. How Thare had three sons, namely Abraham, Nachor and Aran; and that Abraham took to wife Sara, the daughter of his brother named Aran, while Nachor took Melcha, the daughter of Aran, to wife, so that the wives of Abraham and of his brother Nachor were sisters, whose brother was Lot: all this is written above, in the eleventh chapter.

22.title: Expositio mystica ejusdem capituli vicesimi secundi
22.title_en: Mystical exposition of the same twenty-second chapter

paras.t: Abraham frequenter designat quemcumque fidelem ac justum. Quemadmodum in exordio hujus capituli tentavit Deus Abraham, de quo scriptum est in libro Judith, Abraham pater noster tentatus est, et per multas tribulationes probatus, amicus Dei effectus est ; et in primo libro Machabæorum, Abraham in tentatione inventus est fidelis : sic et Deus electos suos ac justos in hoc sæculo multipliciter tentat, exercet, flagellat, quemadmodum scriptum est, Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos. Hujus igitur Patriarchæ exemplo conemur in omni tentatione, adversitate et jussione esse fideles, constantes, atque promptissime obedientes.
paras.en: Abraham often stands for any faithful and just man. As at the beginning of this chapter [[22:1|God tempted Abraham|tentavit Deus Abraham]], of whom it is written in the book of Judith that [[Jdt 8:22|our father Abraham was tempted, and being proved by many tribulations, was made the friend of God|Abraham pater noster tentatus est, et per multas tribulationes probatus, amicus Dei effectus est]] [the margin reference here is partly unreadable; the words are Jdt 8:22], and in the first book of Machabees we read of [[1 Mach 2:52|Abraham found faithful in temptation|Abraham in tentatione inventus est fidelis]] [the margin reference here is partly unreadable, but its verse, 52, can be read; the Douay-Rheims puts the words as a question]: so also God, in this world, tempts, exercises and scourges His elect and just in many ways, as it is written: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit]] the elect [the margin reference here is partly unreadable; the words are Wis 3:6, where the Vulgate has *illos*, "them", for Denis's *electos*, "the elect"]. Let us therefore strive, after the example of this Patriarch, to be faithful, constant and most promptly obedient in every temptation, adversity and command.

paras.t: Tolle filium tuum unigenitum, etc. Sic et nos debemus Dei intuitu et amore omnem hominem, quantumcumque nobis dilectum, familiarem aut singularem hortari, ut Deo totum se mancipet : et propter ipsum universa relinquens, caritate succendi, et nil sui sibi relinquere, totusque Dei esse nitatur : et ita se offerat super unum montium, quem Deus sibi monstraverit, hoc est, in aliquo ordine sancto, quem ei inspiraverit Spiritus Sanctus.
paras.en: [[22:2|Take thy only begotten son|Tolle filium tuum unigenitum]], etc. So we too, out of regard and love for God, ought to exhort every man, however dear, familiar or singular to us, to give himself over wholly to God: and, leaving all things for His sake, to strive to be kindled with charity, to leave nothing of himself to himself, and to be wholly God's: and so to offer himself [[22:2|upon one of the mountains|super unum montium]] which God shall shew him, that is, in some holy order to which the Holy Ghost shall inspire him.

paras.t: Insuper Abraham, in quantum obtulit per mentis promptitudinem filium suum carissimum, habet figuram Dei Patris, qui proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum. Sic enim (ut Evangelista testatur) Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret. Per hoc quoque, quod Deus præcepit sibi Isaac immolari in terra Visionis et monte sublimi, præfigurabatur, quod in eadem terra et monte Calvariæ offerendus fuerat Christus.
paras.en: Moreover Abraham, inasmuch as in the readiness of his mind he offered his dearest son, bears the figure of God the Father, who [[Rom 8:32|spared not even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all|proprio Filio suo non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum]]. [[John 3:16|For|Sic enim]] (as the Evangelist testifies) [[John 3:16|God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son|Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret]]. By this too, that God commanded Isaac to be sacrificed to Him in the land of Vision and on a high mountain, it was foreshadowed that Christ was to be offered in the same land and on the mount of Calvary.

paras.t: Rursus per hoc, quod Abraham ducens Isaac ad offerendum, duxit secum et juvenes duos, significatum est, quod Deus Pater duos populos, scilicet gentiles et Judæos, Christo per fidem conjunxit, qui et ejus passione redempti sunt. Et juvenes illos non permisit Abraham interesse immolationi filii sui, per quod significatum est, quod solus Christus pro mundi salute sit passus, et item quod tempore suæ passionis quasi omnes recesserunt ab eo. Vixque perpauci manserunt in fide, propter quod ait in Psalmo : Sustinui qui simul contristaretur, et non fuit : et qui consolaretur, et non inveni.
paras.en: Again, by this, that Abraham, leading Isaac to be offered, took two young men with him as well, it was signified that God the Father joined two peoples, namely the Gentiles and the Jews, to Christ through faith, and they were redeemed by His passion. And Abraham did not allow those young men to be present at the sacrifice of his son: by which it was signified that Christ alone suffered for the salvation of the world, and also that at the time of His passion almost all withdrew from Him[[Matt 26:56||]]. And scarcely a very few remained in the faith; wherefore He says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:21|I looked for one that would grieve together with me, but there was none: and for one that would comfort me, and I found none|Sustinui qui simul contristaretur, et non fuit : et qui consolaretur, et non inveni]].

paras.t: Per hoc vero quod Abraham eis locutus est, Exspectate hic cum asino, ego et puer, etc., revertemur ad vos, præfigurabatur, quod post Christi passionem multi ex eis fuerant convertendi, per quorum asinum potest eorumdem infidelitas et stultitia designari.
paras.en: And by this, that Abraham said to them, [[22:5|Stay you here with the ass; I and the boy|Exspectate hic cum asino, ego et puer]], etc., [[22:5|will return to you|revertemur ad vos]], it was foreshadowed that after the passion of Christ many of them were to be converted; and by their ass their unbelief and folly may be signified.

paras.t: Tulit quoque ligna holocausti, et imposuit super Isaac filium suum. Hoc fuit præfiguratio evidens, quod Deo Patre volente, unigenitus Filius suus propriis humeris crucem suam bajulavit usque ad supplicii sui locum. Nec mirum si Deo Patri adscribatur, quod crudeles perfidissimique Judæi animo fecerunt perverso, quum princeps Apostolorum testetur : Deus qui prænuntiavit per os omnium Prophetarum pati Christum suum, implevit sic. Nempe quod illi fecerunt intentione nequissima, Deus fieri voluit, in quantum per Christi passionem procurata est mundi salvatio.
paras.en: [[22:6|And he took the wood for the holocaust, and laid it upon Isaac his son|Tulit quoque ligna holocausti, et imposuit super Isaac filium suum]]. This was a plain foreshadowing that, by the will of God the Father, His only-begotten Son carried His own cross on His own shoulders to the place of His punishment. Nor is it any wonder that what the cruel and most faithless Jews did with perverse mind should be ascribed to God the Father, since the prince of the Apostles testifies: God, who [[Acts 3:18|before had shewed by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ should suffer|prænuntiavit per os omnium Prophetarum pati Christum suum]], [[Acts 3:18|hath so fulfilled|implevit sic]]. For what they did with most wicked intent, God willed to be done, inasmuch as through the passion of Christ the salvation of the world was brought about.

paras.t: Hinc subditur : Ipse vero portabat in manibus ignem et gladium. Per ignem ardor amoris, per gladium rigor justitiæ datur intelligi. Itaque Pater æternus portavit in manibus, hoc est, in omnipotentia et efficacia sua habebat tantam ad homines caritatem, tantum quoque justitiæ zelum contra eorum iniquitates, quod Unigenitum suum dedit ad patiendum, ut nec genus periret humanum, nec peccatum maneret inultum.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[22:6|and he himself carried in his hands fire and a sword|Ipse vero portabat in manibus ignem et gladium]]. By the fire is to be understood the ardour of love; by the sword, the rigour of justice. So the eternal Father carried them in His hands: that is, in His omnipotence and power He had such charity towards men, and also such zeal of justice against their iniquities, that He gave His Only-begotten to suffer, so that neither should the human race perish nor sin remain unpunished.

paras.t: Insuper per altare quod Abraham ædificavit, intelligitur mons in quo passus est Dominus, vel caritatis sublimitas, in qua et ex qua tanta pro nobis pati dignatus est. Per ligna vero, crux Salvatoris super quam positus et affixus est.
paras.en: Further, by the altar which Abraham built is understood the mount on which the Lord suffered, or the height of charity, in which and out of which He deigned to suffer so much for us. And by the wood, the cross of the Saviour, on which He was laid and fastened.

paras.t: At vero quod non Isaac, sed aries pro eo fuit oblatus, hoc signat, quod caro Christi seu ejus humanitas supplicia toleravit ac mortem, deitate ipsius impassibili permanente. Quemadmodum autem aries ille inter vepres hærebat, sic Christus inter homines ambulans et conversans, ab eis sustinuit multa; imo eorum infidelitas, ingratitudo, perversitas super omnia sibi displicuit, propter quod dixit : O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? quamdiu patiar vos?
paras.en: But that not Isaac but a ram was offered in his stead signifies that the flesh of Christ, that is, His humanity, bore torments and death, while His Godhead remained impassible. And as that ram stuck fast [[22:13|amongst the briers|inter vepres]], so Christ, walking and living among men, suffered many things from them; indeed their unbelief, ingratitude and perversity displeased Him above all, wherefore He said: [[Mark 9:18|O incredulous generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I suffer you?|O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? quamdiu patiar vos?]]

paras.t: Amplius, locus seu lignum in quo passus est Filius Dei, rite vocatur, Dominus videt : quoniam hostia ibi oblata, fuit acceptissima Patri, qui crucem et vulnera Filii sui intuendo, invocantibus se propitiatur, et inspicit eos. Unde usque in præsens dicere possumus, In monte Dominus videbit, hoc est, quando sumus in tribulationibus et tentationibus constituti, ad hoc verba ista proferre debemus, quatenus Deus misereatur nostri in eis, sicut misertus est nostri, quando Filium suum voluit crucifigi pro nobis. Veruntamen (secundum Rabbi Paulum) in Hebræo habetur, Appellavit nomen loci illius, Dominus videat: ut nomen istud sit quasi oratio. Sic enim Christus oravit Patrem, ut merito suæ passionis misereretur hominibus. Secundum Hieronymum quoque, in Hebræo habetur: Unde usque hodie dicitur, In monte Dominus videbitur. Visus est enim Deus incarnatus in monte Calvariæ pendens, atque in monte illo nunc usque per fidem conspicitur: imo per meditationem dominicæ passionis et crucis, ad deitatis contemplationem ascenditur, ejusque beatifica fruitio obtinetur.
paras.en: Further, the place or wood on which the Son of God suffered is rightly called [[22:14|The Lord seeth|Dominus videt]]: since the victim offered there was most acceptable to the Father, who, looking on the cross and the wounds of His Son, is appeased towards those who call upon Him, and looks upon them. Whence even to the present we can say, [[22:14|In the mountain the Lord will see|In monte Dominus videbit]]: that is, when we are set in tribulations and temptations, we ought to utter these words to this end, that God may have mercy on us in them, as He had mercy on us when He willed His Son to be crucified for us. Yet (according to Rabbi Paul) the Hebrew has: He called the name of that place, *May the Lord see*, so that this name is as it were a prayer [*videat*, “may he see”, for the Vulgate’s *videt*, “he seeth”]. For so Christ prayed the Father that by the merit of His passion He would have mercy on men. According to Jerome too, the Hebrew has: Whence even to this day it is said, *In the mountain the Lord shall be seen*. For God incarnate was seen hanging on the mount of Calvary, and on that mount He is beheld by faith even until now: nay, by meditation on the Lord’s passion and cross one ascends to the contemplation of the Godhead, and obtains its blessed fruition.

paras.t: Postremo per hoc, quod Deus promisit cum juramento tam multa et magna Abrahæ patriarchæ, postquam Isaac paratus fuit offerre, utpote quod semen suum innumerabiliter multiplicaret, et in semine suo cunctis benediceret gentibus, suamque posteritatem præponeret ac faceret suis hostibus dominari, quid aliud videtur præfiguratum, nisi quod Christo passo, omnes populi, tribus et linguæ conversi sunt? Tuncque reversus est Abraham ad pueros suos: id est, gentiles ac Judæos invitavit Deus ad Christi communionem, fidem ac legem, illorumque plurimos ac prorsus innumerabiles Christo incorporavit, et simul cum eis habitavit in Bersabee, quia in Ecclesia habitat Deus, et in cordibus demoratur fidelium.
paras.en: Lastly, by this, that God promised with an oath so many and so great things to the patriarch Abraham after he had been ready to offer Isaac, namely that He would multiply his seed beyond number, and in his seed would bless all nations, and would set his posterity above its enemies and make it rule over them, what else seems to be prefigured but that, when Christ had suffered, all peoples, tribes and tongues were converted? [[22:19|Abraham returned to his young men|Tuncque reversus est Abraham ad pueros suos]]: that is, God invited Gentiles and Jews to the communion, faith and law of Christ, and incorporated very many of them, indeed beyond number, into Christ, and dwelt together with them in Bersabee, because God dwells in the Church, and abides in the hearts of the faithful.

23.title: Expositio capituli vicesimi tertii: Vixit autem Sara centum viginti septem annis
23.title_en: Exposition of the twenty-third chapter: And Sara lived a hundred and twenty-seven years

paras.t: Scriptura hic recitat Saræ mortem ac sepulturam. Vixit Sara centum viginti septem annis, et mortua est in civitate Arbee, quæ est Hebron, in terra Chanaan. Quum enim redisset Abraham cum suis a Bersabee ad convallem Mambre, et habitaret ibidem, obiit Sara in urbe Arbee, quæ alio nomine dicitur Hebron. Et dicitur Arbee, secundum Hieronymum, id est quatuor, quoniam ibi prope in agro sepulti sunt quatuor Patriarchæ cum suis uxoribus, scilicet Adam et Eva, Abraham et Sara, Isaac et Rebecca, Jacob et Lia. Unde constat, quod tempore Abrahæ non est urbs illa hoc nomen sortita, saltem ista ex causa, sed postea ex eventu.
paras.en: Scripture here relates the death and burial of Sara. [[23:1|Sara lived a hundred and twenty-seven years|Vixit Sara centum viginti septem annis]], [[23:2|and she died in the city of Arbee which is Hebron, in the land of Chanaan|et mortua est in civitate Arbee, quæ est Hebron, in terra Chanaan]]. For when Abraham had returned with his household from Bersabee to the vale of Mambre, and was dwelling there, Sara died in the city of Arbee, which by another name is called Hebron. And it is called Arbee, according to Jerome, that is, *four*, because near there, in a field, four patriarchs were buried with their wives, namely Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sara, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Lia. From which it is clear that in Abraham's time the city had not yet received this name, at least not for this reason, but afterwards, from the event.

paras.t: Venitque Abraham ut plangeret et fleret eam, id est, mente et corpore de ejus morte lamentaretur, quam tam singulariter ac sincere dilexit. Verumtamen sicut spiritualiter ac sapienter eam amavit, sic moderate eam deflevit. Sed quum Sara fuerat mulier sancta, quare Scriptura non recitat eam obiisse in senectute bona, et plenam dierum, sicut refert de Abraham et aliis sanctis viris quibusdam? Forsitan ideo, quia non est consuetudinis Scripturarum, mortem feminarum quamvis sanctarum, tam solenniter describere sicut virorum.
paras.en: [[23:2|And Abraham came to mourn and weep for her|Venitque Abraham ut plangeret et fleret eam]], that is, to lament her death in mind and body, she whom he had loved so singularly and so sincerely. Yet as he had loved her spiritually and wisely, so he wept for her with measure. But since Sara had been a holy woman, why does Scripture not relate that she died in a good old age and full of days, as it records of Abraham and of certain other holy men? Perhaps because it is not the custom of the Scriptures to describe the death of women, however holy, as solemnly as that of men.

paras.t: Quumque surrexisset ab officio funeris: ex quo patet, quod iste adventus Abrahæ, quo venit deflere Saram, intelligatur de celebri et aperto planctu, quem in ejus fecit exequiis: locutus est ad filios Heth, qui habitabant ibidem, et ab illo Heth, Hethæi sunt appellati. Advena sum et peregrinus apud vos, quia de terra Chaldæorum ac Mesopotamia huc veni ad habitandum, tanquam in terra aliena; date mihi jus sepulcri vobiscum. Non dixit, Vendite mihi jus sepulcri, quia non licet vendere nec emere jus sepulturæ, sicut nec jus primogenituræ, neque jus patronatus, quum inter sacra spiritualia computentur, aut eis annexa sint. Idcirco quod spirituale fuit, petiit Abraham sibi gratis dari, aut si tale quid emit, suam vexationem intelligitur redemisse. Ut sepeliam mortuum meum, id est defunctam conjugem meam, sumendo masculinum pro femineo. Vel, mortuum meum, hoc est exanime corpus seu cadaver conjugis meæ, quod meum est, seu ad meam pertinens curam, quantum ad sepulturam.
paras.en: [[23:3|And after he rose up from the funeral obsequies|Quumque surrexisset ab officio funeris]]: from which it is plain that this coming of Abraham, when he came to weep for Sara, is to be understood of the solemn and open mourning which he made at her funeral rites. [[23:3|He spoke to the children of Heth|locutus est ad filios Heth]], who dwelt there; and from that Heth the Hethites took their name. [[23:4|I am a stranger and sojourner among you|Advena sum et peregrinus apud vos]], for I came hither from the land of the Chaldeans and from Mesopotamia to dwell, as in a strange land; [[23:4|give me the right of a burying place with you|date mihi jus sepulcri vobiscum]]. He did not say, Sell me the right of a burying place, because it is not lawful to sell or to buy the right of burial, any more than the right of the firstborn or the right of patronage [that is, the right of presenting a cleric to a church or benefice], since these are counted among sacred and spiritual things, or are annexed to them. Therefore Abraham asked that what was spiritual be given him freely; or, if he bought anything of the kind, he is understood to have bought himself free of annoyance [that is, he paid only to be spared vexation, not for the spiritual right itself]. [[23:4|That I may bury my dead|Ut sepeliam mortuum meum]], that is, my departed wife, the masculine being taken for the feminine [*mortuum*, "dead", is masculine in the Latin]. Or, *my dead*, that is, the lifeless body or corpse of my wife, which is mine, or which belongs to my care as regards its burial.

paras.t: Responderunt: Audi nos, domine. Ex curialitate vocabant Abraham dominum, quia vir magnus, potens, dives ac sapiens erat; ideo addiderunt: Princeps Dei es apud nos. Alia littera habet: Rex Dei es, id est, vir principalis, ob tuam sapientiam ac virtutem, quasi regio dignus honore, quem tanquam principem honoramus, et cujus prudentia informamur. In electis sepulcris nostris sepeli mortuum tuum, id est in uno sepulcrorum nostrorum honorabiliori: nullusque te prohibere poterit, quin in monumento ejus sepelias mortuum tuum, hoc est in monumento quod amplius decet venerabilem conjugem tuam, sepelias eam. Surrexit Abraham, et adoravit, id est suppliciter honoravit, ac cultu duliæ venerabatur, populum terræ illius, filios videlicet Heth, regratiando eisdem de tanta benevolentia et pietate eorum ad se, et ad mortuum suum. Erant enim inter suos excellentes personæ, ita quod adoratio duliæ poterat eis impendi.
paras.en: They [[23:5|answered|Responderunt]]: [[23:6|My lord, hear us|Audi nos, domine]]. Out of courtesy they called Abraham *lord*, because he was a great man, mighty, rich and wise; and so they added: [[23:6|thou art a prince of God among us|Princeps Dei es apud nos]]. Another text has: Thou art a king of God; that is, a chief man, because of thy wisdom and virtue, worthy as it were of royal honour, whom we honour as a prince and by whose prudence we are instructed. [[23:6|Bury thy dead in our principal sepulchres|In electis sepulcris nostris sepeli mortuum tuum]], that is, in one of our more honourable sepulchres; [[23:6|and no man shall have power to hinder thee from burying thy dead in his sepulchre|nullusque te prohibere poterit, quin in monumento ejus sepelias mortuum tuum]], that is, that thou bury her in the monument that best befits thy venerable wife. [[23:7|Abraham rose up, and bowed down|Surrexit Abraham, et adoravit]], that is, humbly honoured and venerated with the worship of dulia [that is, the honour due to creatures of excellence, as distinct from *latria*, the worship due to God alone], [[23:7|to the people of the land, to wit, the children of Heth|populum terræ illius, filios videlicet Heth]], thanking them for so great kindness and goodwill towards himself and towards his dead. For there were excellent persons among them, so that the adoration of dulia could be shown them.

paras.t: Dixitque ad eos: Si placet animæ vestræ, ut sepeliam mortuum meum, intercedite apud Ephron, id est, ipsum Ephron rogate, ut det mihi speluncam duplicem quam habet in extrema parte agri sui; pecunia digna tradat mihi eam in possessionem sepulcri, etc., id est ad hoc, ut in ea juridice, justoque titulo mortuum meum sepeliam. Noluit enim Abraham sepelire conjugem suam cum infidelibus, aut in eorum sepulcris, sed in primorum sepulcro parentum: nec voluit ut ibi sepelientur infideles cum ea: ideo voluit emere agrum, in quo erat spelunca, ne quis alius haberet interesse ad illam. Denique ex sequentibus constat, quod intendebat emere agrum, non directe speluncam, sed ex consequenti, in quantum pertinebat ad agrum: quod non fuit illicitum. Non enim fuit ager iste consecratus ad mortuorum sepulturam; ideo licite emebatur: sicut nunc licite emitur fundus aliquis, pro construenda ecclesia aut cœmeterio consecrando.
paras.en: [[23:8|And said to them: If it please your soul that I should bury my dead|Dixitque ad eos: Si placet animæ vestræ, ut sepeliam mortuum meum]], [[23:8|intercede for me to Ephron|intercedite apud Ephron]], that is, ask Ephron himself, [[23:9|That he may give me the double cave, which he hath in the end of his field|ut det mihi speluncam duplicem quam habet in extrema parte agri sui]]; [[23:9|For as much money as it is worth he shall give it me|pecunia digna tradat mihi eam]] [[23:9|for a possession of a burying place|in possessionem sepulcri]], etc., that is, to this end, that I may bury my dead in it lawfully and by just title. For Abraham would not bury his wife with unbelievers, or in their sepulchres, but in the sepulchre of our first parents; nor did he wish unbelievers to be buried there with her. Therefore he wished to buy the field in which the cave was, so that no one else should have any claim to it. Lastly, it is clear from what follows that he meant to buy the field, not the cave directly, but in consequence, inasmuch as it belonged to the field; and this was not unlawful. For this field had not been consecrated to the burial of the dead; therefore it was lawfully bought, just as now a piece of land is lawfully bought for building a church or for a cemetery to be consecrated.

paras.t: Responditque Ephron, etc.: Agrum trado tibi, et speluncam quæ in eo est, etc. Adoravit Abraham coram Domino et populo terræ, adorando Deum adoratione latriæ, seu ipsum Ephron reverentia duliæ, tanquam principem inter suos. Et locutus est ad Ephron, circumstante plebe ejus: Quæso ut audias me. Dabo pecuniam pro agro, etc. Responditque Ephron: Domine mi, audi me. Terra quam postulas, quadringentos siclos argenti valet: istud est pretium inter me et te; sed quantum est hoc? Sepeli mortuum tuum. Quasi dicat, Modicum: nec pro tam modico decet me facere difficultatem tantam ad sepeliendum mortuum tuum.
paras.en: [[23:10|And Ephron made answer|Responditque Ephron]], etc.: [[23:11|The field I deliver to thee, and the cave that is therein|Agrum trado tibi, et speluncam quæ in eo est]], etc. [[23:12|Abraham bowed down before|Adoravit Abraham coram]] the Lord and [[23:12|the people of the land|populo terræ]] [Denis's text reads "before the Lord and the people of the land"; the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have only "before the people of the land"], adoring God with the adoration of latria, or Ephron himself with the reverence of dulia, as a prince among his people. [[23:13|And he spoke to Ephron, in the presence of the people|Et locutus est ad Ephron, circumstante plebe ejus]]: [[23:13|I beseech thee to hear me: I will give money for the field|Quæso ut audias me. Dabo pecuniam pro agro]], etc. [[23:14|And Ephron answered|Responditque Ephron]]: [[23:15|My lord, hear me. The ground which thou desirest, is worth four hundred sicles of silver: this is the price between me and thee: but what is this? bury thy dead|Domine mi, audi me. Terra quam postulas, quadringentos siclos argenti valet: istud est pretium inter me et te; sed quantum est hoc? Sepeli mortuum tuum]]. As if to say: It is a small matter; and for so small a thing it does not become me to make so much difficulty about the burying of thy dead.

paras.t: Quod quum audisset Abraham, appendit pecuniam, etc., id est, tantum dedit ipsi Ephron, ut postulavit. Circa quod dicunt Hebræi, et idem videtur sentire Hieronymus et alii multi, quod quamvis Ephron primo se habuit circa Abraham multum liberaliter et honeste, præbendo agrum cum spelunca omnino gratis, postea tamen se habuit cupide, agrum valde care vendendo, quia videbat intensum Abrahæ appetitum ad agrum illum habendum. Vel, quia reprehensibilis fuit, vendendo memorias mortuorum, quamvis quasi coacte: ideoque nomen ejus mutatum est partim, quia quum ante vocaretur Ephron, quod interpretatur perfectus seu confirmatus, postea dictus est Ephran, id est infirmus seu imperfectus. Circa quod ait Glossa: Sciant ergo qui sepulcrorum accipiunt pretium non a cogentibus, sed nolentibus, nomen suum mutari, et aliquid de merito eorum perire, quum reprehendatur et ille qui invitus istud accepit.
paras.en: [[23:16|And when Abraham had heard this, he weighed out the money|Quod quum audisset Abraham, appendit pecuniam]], etc., that is, he gave Ephron as much as he asked. On which the Hebrews say, and Jerome and many others seem to think the same, that although Ephron at first behaved very generously and honourably towards Abraham, offering the field with the cave entirely free, afterwards he behaved covetously, selling the field very dear, because he saw how intensely Abraham desired to have that field. Or else because he was blameworthy in selling the resting places of the dead, though as it were under constraint: and therefore his name was partly changed; for whereas before he was called Ephron, which is interpreted *perfect* or *confirmed*, afterwards he was called Ephran, that is, *weak* or *imperfect*. On which the Gloss says: Let those, then, who take a price for sepulchres, not from those who compel them but from those who are unwilling, know that their name is changed and that something of their merit perishes, since even he is blamed who took it against his will.

paras.t: Confirmatusque est ager quondam Ephronis, id est, ager ille de cetero legitime est translatus ad dominum Abrahæ; in quo agro erat spelunca duplex, respiciens Mambre, etc., hoc est, sita ex opposito vallis Mambre seu urbis Hebron, quæ fuit sita ibidem; atque sic sepeliebat Abraham uxorem suam in spelunca duplici, id est in una speluncarum illarum, de qua in Scholastica recitatur historia: Erat autem spelunca duplex rupes, naturaliter vel artificialiter duas speluncas habens, quam emit Abraham in sepulturam generi suo. In superiori sepeliebantur viri: in inferiori mulieres. Tamen Adam et Eva erant jam ibi sepulti. Hæc ibi. Hinc alii dicunt: Duplex quædam ædificatio fuit ibi, prout solent monumenta apud quosdam ædificari: una superior, alia inferior. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod ambæ speluncæ erant in eadem planitie. Cetera patent.
paras.en: [[23:17|And the field that before was Ephron's|Confirmatusque est ager quondam Ephronis]] was made sure, that is, that field was from then on lawfully made over to Abraham's ownership; [[23:17|wherein was the double cave, looking towards Mambre|in quo agro erat spelunca duplex, respiciens Mambre]], etc., that is, situated over against the vale of Mambre, or the city of Hebron, which stood there. And so [[23:19|Abraham buried Sara, his wife, in the double cave|sepeliebat Abraham uxorem suam in spelunca duplici]], that is, in one of those caves, of which the Scholastic History relates: Now the double cave was a rock having two caves, natural or made by hand, which Abraham bought as a burying place for his family. In the upper the men were buried, in the lower the women. Adam and Eve, however, were already buried there. Thus far the History. Hence others say: There was a sort of double building there, as monuments are wont to be built among some peoples, one upper and the other lower. But some say that both caves were on the same level. The rest is plain.

paras.t: Porro, juxta spiritualem intelligentiam, potest per Saram intelligi, quæcumque fidelis ac virtuosa persona, quæ huic sæculo spontanee moritur, ut Christo quietius vivat. Cujus civilem mortem deplangit bonus prælatus, per Abraham designatus, in quantum talis persona fuit ad aliorum directionem et informationem quodammodo necessaria aut multum idonea: quæ in spelunca duplici sepelitur, dum in sacra religione monastica et vita contemplativa seu solitaria mansione absconditur.
paras.en: Further, according to the spiritual understanding, by Sara may be understood any faithful and virtuous person who of his own accord dies to this world, that he may live more quietly to Christ. His civil death [that is, his death to the world and its affairs on entering religion] is mourned by a good prelate, signified by Abraham, inasmuch as such a person was in some way necessary, or very fit, for the guidance and instruction of others. And such a one is buried in the double cave when he is hidden away in the sacred monastic religious life and in the contemplative life, or in a solitary dwelling.

24.title: Expositio capituli vicesimi quarti: Erat autem Abraham senex, dierumque multorum
24.title_en: Exposition of the twenty-fourth chapter: Now Abraham was old, and advanced in age

paras.t: Consequenter describitur, qualiter Abraham filio suo Isaac procuravit uxorem. Erat autem Abraham senex, dierumque multorum. Erat quippe centum triginta septem annorum quando obiit Sara : nam decem annis fuit senior ea, quæ centum viginti septem annorum exsistens, defuncta est, ut patet præcedenti capitulo : atque triennio post hoc, quum jam esset centum quadraginta annorum, accepit filio suo quadragenario conjugem, prout disseruit Augustinus. Idcirco subjungitur : Dixitque ad servum seniorem domus suæ, id est majorem inter ceteros servos suos domesticos, qui præerat omnibus quæ habebat tanquam procurator et dispensator, qui vocabatur Eliezer, de quo capitulo quintodecimo habitum est : Pone manum […] femur meum, ut adjurem te per Dominum, Deum cœli et terræ.
paras.en: Next it is described how Abraham procured a wife for his son Isaac. [[24:1|Now Abraham was old, and advanced in age|Erat autem Abraham senex, dierumque multorum]]. For he was a hundred and thirty-seven years old when Sara died: for he was ten years older than she, who died at the age of a hundred and twenty-seven, as is plain from the preceding chapter; and three years after this, when he was now a hundred and forty years old, he took a wife for his son, who was forty, as Augustine has set out. Therefore it is added: [[24:2|And he said to the elder servant of his house|Dixitque ad servum seniorem domus suæ]], that is, the chief among the other servants of his household, [[24:2|who was ruler over all he had|qui præerat omnibus quæ habebat]], as procurator and steward, who was called Eliezer, of whom we treated in the fifteenth chapter: [[24:2|Put thy hand|Pone manum]] […] [[24:2|my thigh|femur meum]], [[24:3|That I may make thee swear by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth|ut adjurem te per Dominum, Deum cœli et terræ]].

paras.t: Cur Abraham servum suum adjuraturus, præcepit et manum suam ponere sub femore adjurantis, videlicet Abrahæ ? Respondet Hieronymus : Dicunt Hebræi, quod in sanctificatione Abrahæ, id est per circumcisionem ejus juravit, ideo fecit servum ponere manum sub femore suo, quia circa locum illum fit circumcisio. Nos autem dicimus servum jurasse in semine Abrahæ, hoc est in Christo seu per Christum, qui nasciturus erat ex Abraham. Generatio autem femori solet adscribi, juxta quod infra habetur : Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, nec dux de femore ejus. Itemque : Omnes animæ quæ egressæ sunt de femore Jacob. Itaque servum habentem manum sub femore suo, Abraham adjuravit per Deum cœli, quoniam Deum cœli noverat ex se et femore suo incarnandum ac nasciturum. Hinc ait Gregorius : Manum sub femore jubet ponere, quia per membrum illud descensura fuit caro illius, qui filius Abrahæ esset ex humanitate, et Dominus ejus ex deitate. Quasi dicat : Tange filium meum, et jura per Deum meum. Unde non super femur, sed sub femore manum ponere jussit, quia inde fuerat nasciturus, cujus caro super omnem carnem exstitit exaltanda.
paras.en: Why did Abraham, when he was about to put his servant on oath, command him also to put his hand under the thigh of the one administering the oath, namely of Abraham? Jerome answers: The Hebrews say that he swore by the sanctification of Abraham, that is, by his circumcision, and that Abraham made the servant put his hand under his thigh because it is about that place that circumcision is made. But we say that the servant swore by the seed of Abraham, that is, in Christ or by Christ, who was to be born of Abraham. Now generation is commonly ascribed to the thigh, as we find below: [[Gen 49:10|The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, nor a ruler from his thigh|Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, nec dux de femore ejus]]. And again: [[Ex 1:5|all the souls that came out of Jacob's thigh|Omnes animæ quæ egressæ sunt de femore Jacob]] [the margin notes here are unreadable; Denis's words are closest to Ex 1:5, but since he says "below" he may mean Gen 46:26, "All the souls that went with Jacob into Egypt, and that came out of his thigh"]. So Abraham made the servant, with his hand under his thigh, swear by the God of heaven, since he knew that the God of heaven was to be incarnate and born of himself and of his thigh. Hence Gregory says: He bids him put his hand under the thigh because through that member was to descend the flesh of him who would be the son of Abraham by his humanity, and his Lord by his divinity. As if he were saying: Touch my son, and swear by my God. Wherefore he bade him put his hand not upon the thigh but under it, because from there was to be born he whose flesh was to be exalted above all flesh.

paras.t: Circa hoc quæri potest, an et servus iste juravit. Videtur quod non, quoniam Abraham ipsum adjuravit, ut textus fatetur. Dicendum, quod sicut ex littera mox sequenti habetur, non solum Abraham adjuravit suum ministrum, sed et ille juravit. Quocirca iterum quæritur, an liceat aliquem adjurare. Videtur quod non, quia non licet jurare. Unde et Origenes affirmat : Non oportet ut vir volens secundum Evangelium vivere, adjuret aliquem. Si enim jurare non licet, nec adjurare. Ad hoc Thomas respondet : Qui jurat juramento promissorio per reverentiam divini nominis, se ipsum immobiliter obligat ad solvendum quod promittit. Quemadmodum autem homo se ipsum ordinare potest ad aliquid peragendum, ita et alios : superiores quidem deprecando, inferiores autem jubendo ; sicque superiores propter necessitatem possunt inferiores suos tali genere adjurationis constringere. Porro si quis aliquem sibi non subditum, velit ad aliquid agendum compellere per divini nominis invocationem, usurpat sibi potestatem alienam, et peccat.
paras.en: On this it may be asked whether this servant also swore. It seems not, since Abraham made him swear, as the text declares. It must be said that, as we find in the letter that follows shortly, not only did Abraham put his minister on oath, but the servant also swore. Hence it is further asked whether it is lawful to adjure anyone [that is, to bind another by oath, charging him by the name of God]. It seems not, because it is not lawful to swear. And so Origen affirms: A man who wishes to live according to the Gospel ought not to adjure anyone; for if it is not lawful to swear, neither is it lawful to adjure. To this Thomas replies: He who swears with a promissory oath [that is, an oath confirming a promise about the future] binds himself immovably, out of reverence for the divine name, to fulfil what he promises. Now just as a man can direct himself to do something, so he can direct others too: superiors by entreating them, inferiors by commanding them; and so superiors, when there is need, can bind their inferiors by this kind of adjuration. But if anyone wishes to compel someone not subject to him to do something by invoking the divine name, he usurps to himself a power that is not his, and sins.

paras.t: Itaque, Adjurem te, ut non accipias uxorem filio meo de filiabus Chananæorum, inter quos habito, sed ad terram et cognationem meam proficiscaris, videlicet ad Mesopotamiam, et ad urbem nomine Haran, atque ad consanguineos meos ibi morantes, et inde accipias uxorem filio meo Isaac. Cur Abraham istud præcepit ? Respondetur, quia sciebat quanta bona Deus promiserat filio suo Isaac ac posteris ejus. Quorum bonorum Abraham affectavit suam cognationem participem fieri magis quam alienos.
paras.en: So: [[24:3|That I may make thee swear|Adjurem te]], [[24:3|that thou take not a wife for my son, of the daughters of the Chanaanites, among whom I dwell|ut non accipias uxorem filio meo de filiabus Chananæorum, inter quos habito]]: [[24:4|But that thou go to my own country and kindred|sed ad terram et cognationem meam proficiscaris]], namely to Mesopotamia, to the city called Haran, and to my kinsmen who dwell there, [[24:4|and take a wife from thence for my son Isaac|et inde accipias uxorem filio meo Isaac]]. Why did Abraham command this? The answer is: because he knew how great were the good things God had promised to his son Isaac and to his posterity; and Abraham wished his own kindred, rather than strangers, to come to share in those good things.

paras.t: Respondit servus : Si noluerit mulier venire mecum, quæcumque fuerit illa, hoc est, si puellam filio tuo aptam, et mecum venire volentem, non potero invenire : numquid reducere debeo filium tuum ad locum, de quo tu egressus es, videlicet ad Chaldæam in qua natus es, vel ad Mesopotamiam ex qua huc venisti ? Dixitque Abraham : Cave ne quando reducas filium meum illuc. Hoc idcirco prohibuit Abraham, quoniam promisit Deus posteris suis terram Chanaan, in qua tunc cum Isaac morabatur, in qua noverat Christi mysteria esse implenda.
paras.en: [[24:5|The servant answered: If the woman will not come with me|Respondit servus : Si noluerit mulier venire mecum]], whoever she may be; that is, if I cannot find a maid suitable for thy son and willing to come with me, [[24:5|must I bring thy son back again to the place from whence thou camest out?|numquid reducere debeo filium tuum ad locum, de quo tu egressus es]], namely to Chaldea, where thou wast born, or to Mesopotamia, from which thou camest hither? [[24:6|And Abraham said: Beware thou never bring my son back again thither|Dixitque Abraham : Cave ne quando reducas filium meum illuc]]. Abraham forbade this because God had promised his posterity the land of Chanaan, in which he was then dwelling with Isaac, and in which he knew that the mysteries of Christ were to be fulfilled.

paras.t: Ideo subdit : Deus cœli qui tulit, id est exire fecit, me de domo patris mei, etc., qui juravit mihi, dicens : Semini tuo dabo terram hanc, ipse mittet angelum suum coram te, id est, angelum suum sanctum faciet te invisibiliter præire, dirigere, conservare, et accipies inde uxorem filio meo. Hoc Abraham, Deo revelante, cognovit futurum, et prophetice prædixisse videtur ; vel fuit verbum bonæ spei in Deo.
