paras.t: Duxit ergo aliam conjugem nomine Ceturam. Circa quod scribit Hieronymus: Cetura, Hebraice copulata seu conjuncta interpretatur. Unde Hebræi suspicantur eamdem esse mutato nomine Agar atque Ceturam, ut per hoc etiam ætas Abrahæ excusetur, ne senex novis arguatur nuptiis lascivisse. Hanc refert et Lyra: Dicunt Hebræi, quod Cetura interpretatur thurificata, quia tam munde se habuit postquam cum Ismaele filio suo de domo Abrahæ est egressa, ac si fuisset Deo oblata et consecrata: propter quod, Sara defuncta, misit Abraham filium suum Isaac, ut illam sibi reduceret. Sed istis multipliciter objici posset. Primo, quoniam textus hic dicit, quod Abraham aliam duxit uxorem. Agar autem jam antea fuerat vera uxor sua, quæ quamvis erat separata ab eo ad tempus habitatione, non tamen vinculo conjugali: sicque eam recipiendo, non duxisset aliam conjugem. Secundo, quia paulo post scribitur, quod filiis concubinarum largitus est munera, ubi per concubinas intelliguntur Agar et ista Cetura. Tertio, quia de Abraham ait Apostolus, quod non consideravit corpus suum emortuum, quum fere centum esset annorum: circa quod dicunt expositores, quod corpus suum fuit emortuum, quantum ad vetulam: sed de juniore poterat generare, sicque salvatum est supra, quod de Agar genuit Ismaelem: ergo et Cetura ista fuit juvencula, præsertim quum Abraham esset ad minus centum quadraginta annorum, dum eam accepit. Agar vero tunc vetula fuit. Nam filius ejus Ismael fuit quatuordecim annis senior Isaac, qui circa has nuptias Abrahæ quadragenarius fuit. Verumtamen dicit Lyra, quod nomen hoc concubinarum, in Bibliis Hebraicis correctis, hic scribitur diminute, ad innuendum quod non fuit nisi una. Sed Rabbi Paulus contra hoc dicit: Vocabulum quod hic in Hebraico ponitur, semper significat concubinas in plurali, sive scribatur diminute, sive integre: idcirco ex hoc quod scribitur diminute, non insinuatur quod non fuerit nisi una. Nihilominus Josephus dicit, quod fuit una, et quod Abraham duxit eam, antequam misit pro uxore Isaac filii sui. Quid horum sit verius, nescio.
paras.en: He took, then, another wife [[25:1|named Cetura|nomine Ceturam]]. On which Jerome writes: Cetura is interpreted in Hebrew as *coupled* or *joined*. Hence the Hebrews suspect that Agar and Cetura are the same woman under a changed name, so that by this Abraham's age too may be excused, lest the old man be charged with having played the wanton in a new marriage. This Lyra also reports: The Hebrews say that Cetura is interpreted *perfumed with incense* [*thurificata*: as though offered up like incense], because after she went out of Abraham's house with her son Ismael she kept herself as purely as if she had been offered and consecrated to God: for which reason, when Sara was dead, Abraham sent his son Isaac to bring her back to him. But many objections could be made to these men. First, because the text here says that [[25:1|Abraham married another wife|Abraham aliam duxit uxorem]]. But Agar had already before this been his true wife, who, though she was separated from him for a time in dwelling, was not so in the marriage bond: and so, in taking her back, he would not have married another wife. Second, because a little after it is written that [[25:6|to the children of the concubines he gave gifts|filiis concubinarum largitus est munera]], where by the concubines are understood Agar and this Cetura. Third, because the Apostle says of Abraham: [[Rom 4:19|Neither did he consider his own body, now dead|non consideravit corpus suum emortuum]], [[Rom 4:19|whereas he was almost an hundred years old|quum fere centum esset annorum]]: on which the expositors say that his body was dead as regards an old woman, but that he could beget of a younger one; and so what was said above is upheld, that he begot Ismael of Agar. Therefore this Cetura too was a young woman, especially since Abraham was at least a hundred and forty years old when he took her, while Agar was then an old woman. For her son Ismael was fourteen years older than Isaac, who was forty at about the time of these nuptials of Abraham. Lyra, however, says that this word *concubines*, in corrected Hebrew Bibles, is written here defectively [that is, without its full letters, so that it may be read as a singular], to hint that there was only one. But Rabbi Paul [Paul of Burgos, in his Additions to Lyra] says against this: The word set down here in the Hebrew always means *concubines* in the plural, whether it is written defectively or in full: hence the fact that it is written defectively does not suggest that there was only one. Nevertheless Josephus says that there was one, and that Abraham married her before he sent for a wife for his son Isaac. Which of these is the truer, I do not know.

paras.t: Quæ Cetura peperit ei, scilicet Abrahæ, successive sex filios, qui nominantur in littera. Filii Dedan fuerunt Assurim, etc. Circa hoc dicit Hieronymus: Ab Assurim aliqui putant Syros vocari, et a plerisque filiis Abrahæ dicunt regiones Indiæ occupatas seu habitatas. At vero ex Madian, filio Abrahæ et Ceturæ, ortus est Epha et Apher. Quocirca Hieronymus: Filii, inquit, Ceturæ occupaverunt terram Troglodytarum atque Arabiam usque ad terminos maris Rubri, secundum historicos Hebræorum. Dicitur quoque Apher ex posteris Abrahæ duxisse exercitum adversus Libyam, et ibi victor consedisse, a quo posteri ejus Aphricam nuncupaverunt. Hæc Hieronymus. Cujus verbis in Scholastica historia ex Josepho additur, quod viro illi in Libyam descendenti, Hercules tulit auxilium, et filiam ejus nomine Ethæam Hercules duxit uxorem, genuitque ex ea Dodorim, cujus filius fuit Pnoron.
paras.en: [[25:2|Who bore him|Quæ Cetura peperit ei]], that is, Cetura bore to Abraham, one after another, six sons, who are named in the text. [[25:3|The children of Dadan were Assurim|Filii Dedan fuerunt Assurim]], etc. On this Jerome says: Some think that the Syrians are named from Assurim, and they say that regions of India were occupied or settled by a great many of Abraham's sons. [[25:4|But of Madian|At vero ex Madian]], the son of Abraham and Cetura, [[25:4|was born Epha, and Opher|ortus est Epha et Apher]]. Whereupon Jerome says: The sons of Cetura, according to the historians of the Hebrews, occupied the land of the Troglodytes and Arabia, as far as the borders of the Red Sea. It is said too that Apher [the Douay-Rheims has Opher], of the posterity of Abraham, led an army against Libya and settled there as victor, and that from him his posterity called it Africa. So far Jerome. To his words the Scholastic History adds, from Josephus, that when this man went down into Libya Hercules gave him help, and Hercules married his daughter, named Ethæa, and begot of her Dodorim, whose son was Pnoron.

paras.t: Deditque Abraham cuncta quæ possederat filio suo Isaac, videlicet omnia principalia bona sua, tanquam principali præelectoque filio. Non tamen videtur Abraham habuisse nec ei dedisse hereditaria et immobilia bona, nisi supra præfata, quæ emit aut acquisivit, et pauca fuerunt, videlicet ager in quo erat duplex spelunca, et puteus Bersabee, ac nemus quod ibi plantavit, aut quædam similia. Filiis autem concubinarum largitus est munera. Abraham non erat adulter: idcirco concubinæ istæ fuerunt veræ uxores ipsius, quod et textus apertissime protestatur. Siquidem supra scriptum est, quod Sara dedit Agar ancillam suam viro suo uxorem. De Cetura quoque nunc dictum est, quod Abraham accepit aliam uxorem nomine Ceturam. In Scripturis autem Veteris Testamenti uxor interdum concubina vocatur, ut patet in Judicum libro de uxore Levitæ. Sara demum fuit principalis ipsius Abrahæ uxor, ita quod ejus comparatione, aliæ duæ quasi concubinæ censentur. Abraham tamen cum Cetura non habuit aliam ea principaliorem, saltem eo tempore, quo ita vocata est. Porro qui dicunt eamdem fuisse Agar et Ceturam, affirmant hic plurale poni pro singulari, quum dicitur, Concubinarum: vel ideo Scripturam sic loqui, quoniam eadem quasi bis ducta est.
paras.en: [[25:5|And Abraham gave all his possessions|Deditque Abraham cuncta quæ possederat]] to his son [[25:5|Isaac|Isaac]], that is, all his chief goods, as to his chief and chosen son. Yet Abraham does not seem to have had, or to have given him, any inherited and immovable goods except those mentioned above, which he bought or acquired, and they were few: namely the field in which was the double cave[[Gen 23:17||]], and the well of Bersabee[[Gen 21:30||]], and the grove that he planted there[[Gen 21:33||]], or some such things. [[25:6|And to the children of the concubines he gave gifts|Filiis autem concubinarum largitus est munera]]. Abraham was not an adulterer: hence these concubines were his true wives, as the text too declares most plainly. For it is written above that Sara gave Agar her handmaid [[Gen 16:3|to her husband to wife|viro suo uxorem]]. Of Cetura too it has just been said that Abraham took [[25:1|another wife named Cetura|aliam uxorem nomine Ceturam]]. Now in the Scriptures of the Old Testament a wife is sometimes called a concubine, as is plain in the book of Judges of the Levite's wife[[Judg 19:1||]] [the margin note here could not be read; she is called his wife at Judg 19:1 and his concubine at 19:10 and later]. Sara, then, was Abraham's chief wife, so that in comparison with her the other two are reckoned as concubines, as it were. Yet with Cetura Abraham had no wife more principal than she, at least at the time when she was so called. Further, those who say that Agar and Cetura were the same affirm that the plural is put here for the singular when it says *of the concubines*; or that Scripture speaks so because the same woman was, as it were, married twice.

paras.t: Fuerunt autem dies vitæ Abrahæ, centum septuaginta quinque anni: et ita obiit junior patre suo annis triginta. Nam Thare pater ejus vixit annis ducentis quinque, ut supra legitur. Et deficiens viribus corporis, mortuus est in senectute bona, id est virtuosis actibus decorata, provectaque ætatis, et plenus dierum, id est plenus operibus bonis, quibus usque in finem vitæ suæ inhæsit longævus: per quod insinuatur defunctus in quadam perfectione virtutum. Nam teste Ambrosio, plenitudinem vita justorum habet, inanes vero sunt dies malorum. Congregatusque est ad populum suum, id est, Sanctis in limbo patrum detentis conjunctus, quantum ad animam suam: qui limbus exinde vocatus est Abrahæ sinus. Vel Abrahæ sinus vocatur, secreta requies illa electorum in limbo illo tunc quiescentium. Et sepelierunt eum Isaac et Ismael filii sui, qui tanquam principales nominatim exprimuntur, quanquam et alii interfuerint multi; in spelunca duplici, etc., de qua dictum est copiose. Et post obitum illius benedixit Deus Isaac filio ejus: cui et ante jam benedixit, sed post mortem Abrahæ patris sui, plus quam ante benedixit ei, augendo ei spiritualia ac temporalia bona.
paras.en: [[25:7|And the days of Abraham's life were a hundred and seventy-five years|Fuerunt autem dies vitæ Abrahæ, centum septuaginta quinque anni]]: and so he died thirty years younger than his father. For Thare his father lived two hundred and five years, as is read above[[Gen 11:32||]]. [[25:8|And decaying|Et deficiens]] in the strength of his body, [[25:8|he died in a good old age|mortuus est in senectute bona]], that is, an old age adorned with virtuous deeds, [[25:8|and having lived a long time|provectaque ætatis]], [[25:8|and being full of days|et plenus dierum]], that is, full of good works, to which, living long, he held fast to the end of his life: by which it is suggested that he died in a certain perfection of virtues. For on Ambrose's witness, the life of the just has fullness, but the days of the wicked are empty. [[25:8|and was gathered to his people|Congregatusque est ad populum suum]], that is, he was joined, as to his soul, to the saints held in the limbo of the fathers [that is, the place where the souls of the just who died before Christ awaited redemption]; which limbo was thenceforth called Abraham's bosom. Or else that secret rest of the elect who then rested in that limbo is called Abraham's bosom. [[25:9|And Isaac and Ismael his sons buried him|Et sepelierunt eum Isaac et Ismael filii sui]], who are named expressly as the chief ones, although many others were also present; [[25:9|in the double cave|in spelunca duplici]], etc., of which much has been said. [[25:11|And after his death, God blessed Isaac his son|Et post obitum illius benedixit Deus Isaac filio ejus]]: whom he had blessed already before, but after the death of his father Abraham he blessed him more than before, increasing his spiritual and temporal goods.

paras.t: Hæ sunt generationes Ismaelis, etc., et hæc nomina filiorum ejus, etc. Primogenitus Ismaelis Nabajoth, deinde Cedar, etc; et ponuntur hic duodecim nomina filiorum suorum, qui fuerunt duodecim principes duodecim tribuum suarum: ita quod unusquisque eorum fuit princeps, et caput prosapiæ descendentis ab eo. Circa quod scribit Hieronymus: Duodecim filii nati sunt Ismaeli, primogenitus Nabajoth, a quo omnis regio ab Euphrate usque ad mare Rubrum Nabathæa seu Nabajothæa vocatur, quæ et Arabiæ pars est; et ab aliis filiorum suorum nominibus quædam eorum regiones nomen sortitæ sunt, scilicet Cedar, Duma, Theman, etc.
paras.en: [[25:12|These are the generations of Ismael|Hæ sunt generationes Ismaelis]], etc., [[25:13|And these are the names of his children|et hæc nomina filiorum ejus]], etc. [[25:13|The firstborn of Ismael was Nabajoth, then Cedar|Primogenitus Ismaelis Nabajoth, deinde Cedar]], etc.; and here are set down twelve names of his sons, who were [[25:16|twelve princes of their tribes|duodecim principes duodecim tribuum suarum]] [the Latin reads *twelve princes of their twelve tribes*]: so that each one of them was the prince and head of the line descending from him. On which Jerome writes: Twelve sons were born to Ismael; the firstborn was Nabajoth, from whom all the region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabathæa or Nabajothæa, which is also a part of Arabia; and from the names of his other sons certain of their regions took their names, namely Cedar, Duma, Theman, etc.

paras.t: Et facti sunt anni vitæ Ismaelis, centum triginta septem: deficiensque, mortuus est. Secundum Lyram, in Hebræo non dicitur, Mortuus est, sed, Transivit: quod secundum Hebræos, non dicitur de aliquo moriente, nisi justo: propter quod dicunt eum obiisse in gratia. Verum Rabbi Paulus asserit, in Hebræo non haberi, Transivit, sed, Deficiens mortuus est. Attamen fatetur Ismaelem decessisse in gratia, quia subjungitur: et appositus est ad populum suum, id est, in limbo patrum eis adjunctus. Isti itaque dicunt eum de suis excessibus finaliter pœnituisse. Sarraceni vero dicunt eum fuisse sanctum et vatem Dei. Verumtamen Scriptura ista non dicit de eo, sicut dicit de Abraham, et aliis Patriarchis ac Sanctis quibusdam, quod mortuus sit in senectute bona, et plenus dierum. Habitavit autem ab Hevila usque Sur, id est, ipse et posteritas ejus terras illas incoluit, ab India, quæ ab Hevila nepote Noe vocata est Hevila, usque ad solitudinem, quæ est inter Cades et Barad: quæ solitudo Sur appellatur, et tenditur usque ad mare Rubrum et Ægypti confinia. Ideo additur: Quæ, scilicet solitudo, respicit Ægyptum introeuntibus Assyrios per iter illud. Coram cunctis fratribus, id est filiis et nepotibus suis obiit, seu (ut exponit Hieronymus) in manibus filiorum suorum mortuus est. Per fratres enim intelliguntur quicumque cognati. Unde Jacob infra ait ad Laban: Pone hic coram fratribus meis et fratribus tuis. Ut autem in Scholastica historia tangitur, Ismael fertur dysenteria obiisse.
paras.en: [[25:17|And the years of Ismael's life were a hundred and thirty-seven|Et facti sunt anni vitæ Ismaelis, centum triginta septem]]: [[25:17|and decaying he died|deficiensque, mortuus est]]. According to Lyra, the Hebrew does not say *He died* but *He passed over*: which, according to the Hebrews, is not said of anyone dying unless he is just: for which reason they say that he died in grace. But Rabbi Paul asserts that the Hebrew does not have *He passed over*, but *Decaying he died*. Yet he grants that Ismael departed in grace, because it is added: [[25:17|and was gathered unto his people|et appositus est ad populum suum]], that is, joined to them in the limbo of the fathers. These men therefore say that he repented of his excesses at the last. The Saracens, for their part, say that he was a saint and a prophet of God. Yet this Scripture does not say of him, as it says of Abraham and of other Patriarchs and certain Saints, that he died in a good old age and full of days. [[25:18|And he dwelt from Hevila as far as Sur|Habitavit autem ab Hevila usque Sur]], that is, he and his posterity inhabited those lands, from India, which was called Hevila from Hevila the grandson of Noe, to the wilderness that lies between Cades and Barad: this wilderness is called Sur, and stretches as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt. Therefore it is added: [[25:18|which|Quæ]], that is, the wilderness, [[25:18|looketh towards Egypt, to them that go towards the Assyrians|respicit Ægyptum introeuntibus Assyrios]] by that route. [[25:18|in the presence of all his brethren|Coram cunctis fratribus]], that is, of his sons and grandsons, [[25:18|He died|suis obiit]]; or (as Jerome explains) he died in the hands of his sons. For by brethren are understood any kinsmen whatever. Hence Jacob says further on to Laban: [[Gen 31:37|lay it here before my brethren, and thy brethren|Pone hic coram fratribus meis et fratribus tuis]]. And as the Scholastic History mentions, Ismael is said to have died of dysentery.

paras.t: Deinde describitur generatio Isaac patriarchæ. Hæ quoque sunt generationes Isaac filii Abraham. Abraham genuit Isaac: qui quum quadraginta esset annorum, duxit uxorem Rebeccam, etc. Istud repetitur, ut sequentia aptius inserantur.
paras.en: Next is described the generation of the patriarch Isaac. [[25:19|These also are the generations of Isaac the son of Abraham|Hæ quoque sunt generationes Isaac filii Abraham]]. [[25:19|Abraham begot Isaac|Abraham genuit Isaac]]: [[25:20|Who when he was forty years old, took to wife Rebecca|qui quum quadraginta esset annorum, duxit uxorem Rebeccam]], etc. This is repeated so that what follows may be fitted in more aptly.

paras.t: Deprecatusque est Isaac Dominum pro uxore sua ut conciperet, eo quod esset sterilis. Nam ut infra patebit ex textu, per viginti annos sedit cum Isaac antequam concepit. Denique, quamvis Isaac sciret patri suo Abrahæ esse promissam electi seminis propagationem copiosissimam per se, nihilo minus Deum oravit ut impleretur hoc. Deus etenim multa sic præordinavit, ut per preces obtineantur. Ideo ait Glossa: Quamvis per Isaac promissa erat successio, tamen præfinitio Dei precibus erat implenda. Hinc subditur: Qui exaudivit eum, et dedit conceptum Rebeccæ supernaturaliter, sicut et Saræ, quamvis in Sara fuerat major causa sterilitatis, quia et senium.
paras.en: [[25:21|And Isaac besought the Lord for his wife|Deprecatusque est Isaac Dominum pro uxore sua]] that she might conceive, [[25:21|because she was barren|eo quod esset sterilis]]. For, as will appear from the text further on, she lived with Isaac for twenty years before she conceived. Again, although Isaac knew that a most abundant increase of the chosen seed through him had been promised to his father Abraham, he nonetheless prayed God that this might be fulfilled. For God has foreordained many things in such a way that they are obtained by prayers. Hence the Gloss says: Although the succession had been promised through Isaac, yet God's predetermination was to be fulfilled by prayers. Hence it is added: [[25:21|and he heard him, and made Rebecca to conceive|Qui exaudivit eum, et dedit conceptum Rebeccæ]], supernaturally, as he did Sara too, although in Sara there was a greater cause of barrenness, since there was old age as well.

paras.t: Sed collidebantur in utero ejus parvuli: quando enim vicina fuit partui, cœperunt infantuli in utero ejus collidi, seu invicem se quasi impellere, quasi inter se concertantes, quis eorum primus egrederetur: quod tamen non contingebat naturaliter, sed ex dispositione divina, quia præsagium exstitit futurorum, ita quod Deo volente et movente forte per angelum facta fuit commotio illa infantum, ad præfigurandum quod inter eos natos esset futura contentio propter primogenituram, et etiam inter Judæos et Idumæos ex eis tunc nascituros. Porro Septuaginta transtulerunt, Ludebant et calcitrabant infantes. Symmachus autem, In superficie ferebantur: quasi scilicet in similitudine navis pondere apto carentis. Itaque sicut Deus per verba, ita et per motus istos ostendit futura, quia frequenter per facta prænuntiat aliquid.
paras.en: [[25:22|But the children struggled in her womb|Sed collidebantur in utero ejus parvuli]]: for when she was near her delivery, the little ones in her womb began to struggle, or as it were to push one another, as though contending among themselves which of them should come out first: which yet did not happen naturally but by divine disposition, because it was a presage of things to come; so that by God's will and moving, perhaps through an angel, that stirring of the infants took place, to prefigure that there would be strife between them when they were born, over the birthright, and also between the Jews and the Idumeans who were then to be born of them. Further, the Seventy translated: *The infants leapt and kicked*; and Symmachus: *They were borne about on the surface*, that is, as it were like a ship that lacks fitting ballast. And so, as God shows things to come by words, so too he showed them by these movements, for he often foretells something by deeds.

paras.t: Quæ, scilicet Rebecca, ait: Si sic mihi futurum erat, quid necesse fuit concipere? Timuit enim aborsum, et periclitari in partu, quia ex tali collisione geminorum in utero, solent talia sequi pericula: ideo conceptum suum reputabat infructuose concessum, nisi Deus sibi aliunde succurreret. Vel, quasi admirando locuta est, Si sic mihi futurum erat, etc.; quasi diceret, Si parvuli nondum nati, ita confligunt, quid facient nati? an se invicem destruent? In Scholastica historia legitur: Jacob creditur sanctificatus in utero, et in prædicto motu seu collisione infantum præfiguratum, quod non sit consensus Christi ad Belial. Porro quod Jacob sanctificatus fuit in utero, Augustinus in pluribus locis sentire videtur. Nam super illud ad Romanos, Quum enim nondum nati essent, disseruit: In Jacob nondum nato quid Deus dilexit, nisi gratuitum suæ misericordiæ donum?
paras.en: [[25:22|she|Quæ]], that is, Rebecca, [[25:22|said|ait]]: [[25:22|If it were to be so with me, what need was there to conceive?|Si sic mihi futurum erat, quid necesse fuit concipere?]] For she feared a miscarriage, and danger in childbirth, because such dangers commonly follow from such a collision of twins in the womb: and so she reckoned that her conception had been granted her to no profit, unless God should help her from some other quarter. Or she spoke as if in wonder: [[25:22|If it were to be so with me|Si sic mihi futurum erat]], etc.; as if to say: If the little ones, not yet born, fight like this, what will they do once born? Will they destroy one another? In the Scholastic History we read: Jacob is believed to have been sanctified in the womb, and in the aforesaid movement or collision of the infants it was prefigured that there is no agreement of Christ with Belial[[2 Cor 6:15||]]. Further, Augustine seems in several places to hold that Jacob was sanctified in the womb. For on that text of Romans, [[Rom 9:11|For when the children were not yet born|Quum enim nondum nati essent]], he discoursed: In Jacob, not yet born, what did God love but the free gift of his own mercy?

paras.t: Perrexitque ut consuleret Dominum. Quo vel ad quem perrexit, aut qualiter Deum consuluit, scriptura ista non exprimit. Dicitque Glossa, quod forte ivit ad locum in quo Abraham construxerat aram, seu (ut in Historia scholastica clarius fertur) forsitan transivit ad montem Moria, in quo altare ædificaverat Abraham, et immolatis ibi victimis, deprecata est Deum ut sibi ostenderet, quid sibi atque infantulis esset venturum. Lyra vero refert: Dicunt Hebræi, quod ivit ad consulendum Melchisedech sacerdotem Dei excelsi, et item ad Heber spiritum prophetiæ habentem, tunc usque viventes, ut per eos consuleret Dominum, hoc est, ut ipsi revelationem a Deo acquirerent, Dominum exorando pro certificatione Rebeccæ. Quod autem Melchisedech fuit Sem filius Noe, et quod ipse ac Heber usque post nativitatem Jacob vixerunt, ex superioribus potest patere. Multi quoque Catholici opinantur, quod ad Melchisedech sit profecta. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus hic scribit: Quidam expositores Hebræorum testantur, quod non ivit ad consulendum aliquem Prophetam, sed ad aliquem locum devotum et secretum, in quo pro hac re oraret quietius. Istud quoque tangitur in Glossa, dicente: Forsan ivit ad aliquem locum secretum, in quo magis quiete oraret.
paras.en: [[25:22|she went to consult the Lord|Perrexitque ut consuleret Dominum]]. Where, or to whom, she went, or in what way she consulted God, this scripture does not say. The Gloss says that perhaps she went to the place where Abraham had built an altar; or (as the Scholastic History puts it more clearly) perhaps she went over to Mount Moria, where Abraham had built an altar, and, having offered victims there, besought God to show her what was to come upon her and her little ones. Lyra, however, reports: The Hebrews say that she went to consult Melchisedech, the priest of the most high God, and also Heber, who had the spirit of prophecy, both of them still living then, so that through them she might consult the Lord: that is, so that they might obtain a revelation from God, praying the Lord to give Rebecca certainty. That Melchisedech was Sem the son of Noe, and that he and Heber lived until after the birth of Jacob, can be seen from what was said above. Many Catholics too are of the opinion that she went to Melchisedech. Rabbi Paul, however, writes here: Some expositors of the Hebrews testify that she did not go to consult any prophet, but to some devout and secret place, where she might pray about this matter more quietly. This is touched on in the Gloss as well, which says: Perhaps she went to some secret place, where she might pray more quietly.

paras.t: Qui respondens, ait. Qualiter dederit Rebeccæ istud responsum, textus non docet. Et dicunt nonnulli, quod quum post immolationem et orationem dormiret in monte præfato seu alio loco, revelationem istam a Domino sumpsit per inspirationem occultam seu illuminationem angelicam. Alii putant, quod Deus ei respondit in vigilia per angelum, quemadmodum et per angelum edocuit Agar. Alii dicunt, quod respondit ei per Melchisedech aut aliquem alium Sanctum. Duæ gentes sunt in utero tuo, id est, duo infantuli qui erunt principia et capita duarum gentium, quia ex Esau sunt nati Idumæi, ex Jacob Judæi: et duo populi ex ventre tuo dividentur, id est, præfati duo populi inter se divisi, ex tuis infantulis distinctim nascentur; populusque populum superabit, id est, unus eorum alium vincet, aut sibi subjiciet: quod aliqualiter fuit tempore David impletum, quando Judæi sibi penitus subjugaverunt Idumæam, ut legitur Regum secundo, imo et omne masculinum peremerunt in ea; et major serviet minori, hoc est, populus Idumæorum ex Esau primogenito Isaac natus, Judæis deserviet: quod factum est tempore David, quando Idumæi facti sunt tributarii David regis. Verumtamen Augustinus effatur: Quod dictum est, Major serviet minori, nemo nostrorum aliter intellexit, quam majorem populum Judæorum, minori, id est posteriori populo christiano, serviturum. Et revera quamvis istud aliqualiter videatur impletum in populo Idumæo atque Judæis, tamen convenientius creditur, prophetiam istam aliquid altius intendisse: et quid est hoc, nisi quod in Judæis et Christianis evidenter adimpletur?
paras.en: [[25:23|And he answering, said|Qui respondens, ait]]. How he gave Rebecca this answer the text does not tell. Some say that, as she slept after the sacrifice and the prayer on the aforesaid mountain or in some other place, she received this revelation from the Lord by a hidden inspiration or an enlightening by an angel. Others think that God answered her while she was awake, through an angel, just as he instructed Agar through an angel. Others say that he answered her through Melchisedech or some other holy man. [[25:23|Two nations are in thy womb|Duæ gentes sunt in utero tuo]]: that is, two little ones who will be the beginnings and heads of two nations, for of Esau were born the Idumeans, of Jacob the Jews; [[25:23|and two peoples shall be divided out of thy womb|et duo populi ex ventre tuo dividentur]]: that is, the aforesaid two peoples, divided from one another, shall be born separately of thy little ones; [[25:23|and one people shall overcome the other|populusque populum superabit]]: that is, one of them shall conquer the other, or subject it to itself. This was in some way fulfilled in the time of David, when the Jews wholly subjugated Idumea, as we read in the second book of Kings[[2 Kings 8:14||]], and indeed they even slew every male in it[[3 Kings 11:15||]][[3 Kings 11:16||]]; [[25:23|and the elder shall serve the younger|et major serviet minori]]: that is, the people of the Idumeans, born of Esau the firstborn of Isaac, shall serve the Jews: which came about in the time of David, when the Idumeans were made tributaries of King David. Augustine, however, declares [City of God XVI, 35]: As for the saying, [[25:23|the elder shall serve the younger|Major serviet minori]], none of ours has understood it otherwise than that the elder people of the Jews would serve the younger, that is, the later, Christian people. And truly, although this seems to have been fulfilled in some way in the Idumean people and the Jews, it is more fittingly believed that this prophecy had something higher in view: and what is that, but what is plainly fulfilled in the Jews and the Christians?

paras.t: Jam tempus pariendi, in quo Rebecca pareret, advenerat, et ecce gemini, id est duo infantuli, in utero ejus reperti sunt. Hoc per eorum egressum patuit, quod duo fuerunt in utero, quod tamen et ante innotuit ex infantum collisione ac revelatione divina. Qui primus egressus est, rufus erat; idcirco vocatus est Edom, quod interpretatur sanguineus. Alia quoque ex causa vocatus est sic, ut statim dicitur: et totus in morem pellis hispidus, id est pilosus: ideo dictus est Seir, quod interpretatur pilosus. Hinc ait Hieronymus: Pro hispido seu piloso, in Hebræo habetur, Sear. Unde Esau, sicut alibi legimus, Seir, id est pilosus, dictus est. Vocatumque est nomen ejus Esau, id est fortis, et hoc fuit proprium nomen ipsius. Protinus alter egrediens, plantam fratris tenebat manu: quod Deo sic ordinante sic actum est, ad præfigurandum quod futurus suum fratrem supplantaturus, non violentia, sed jure, ex præordinatione divina. Unde fratris plantam tenendo, quasi ipso facto monstravit, se fratrem suum a jure primogenituræ et privilegio benedictionis, retrahere. Et idcirco appellavit eum Jacob. Quis eum sic appellavit, non habetur ex littera evidenter: tamen de matre ejus dictum videtur, quia paulo ante præhabitum est, Gemini in utero ejus reperti sunt.
paras.en: [[25:24|And when her time was come to be delivered|Jam tempus pariendi]] (the time at which Rebecca was to give birth), [[25:24|behold twins|advenerat, et ecce gemini]], that is, two little ones, [[25:24|were found in her womb|in utero ejus reperti sunt]]. That there were two in the womb became plain when they came forth, though it had been made known before by the collision of the infants and by divine revelation. [[25:25|He that came forth first was red|Qui primus egressus est, rufus erat]]; therefore he was called Edom, which is interpreted 'bloody'. He was so called for another reason too, as is said straightaway: [[25:25|and hairy like a skin|et totus in morem pellis hispidus]], that is, shaggy: therefore he was called Seir, which is interpreted 'hairy'. Hence Jerome says: For 'rough' or 'hairy' the Hebrew has Sear. So Esau, as we read elsewhere, was called Seir, that is, hairy. [[25:25|and his name was called Esau|Vocatumque est nomen ejus Esau]], that is, strong; and this was his own proper name. [[25:25|Immediately the other coming forth, held his brother's foot in his hand|Protinus alter egrediens, plantam fratris tenebat manu]]: which was so done by God's ordering, to prefigure that he was to supplant his brother, not by violence but by right, by divine preordination. So by holding his brother's foot he showed, as it were by the deed itself, that he was drawing his brother away from the right of the firstborn and the privilege of the blessing. [[25:25|and therefore he was called Jacob|Et idcirco appellavit eum Jacob]]. Who called him so is not clear from the letter; yet it seems to be said of his mother, since a little before it was stated: [[25:24|twins were found in her womb|Gemini in utero ejus reperti sunt]].

paras.t: Sexagenarius erat Isaac, quando nati sunt ei parvuli. Ex quo constat quod dictum est, utpote quod viginti annis fuit cum conjuge sua absque prole, siquidem quadraginta exsistens annorum, eam accepit. Hinc etiam patet, stare non posse quod Josephus dicit, Abraham esse defunctum antequam nati fuerunt filii Isaac: imo quindecim annis probatur vixisse post nativitatem eorum: nam Abraham centenarius fuit, quando natus est Isaac, vixitque Abraham centum septuaginta quinque annis. Circa hæc quæritur, cur Isaac infra tot annos infecunditatis suæ uxoris, aliam non accepit, quemadmodum Abraham duxit Agar. Ad hoc (ut fertur) respondent Judæi, quod non licuit Isaac habere conjuges plures, ex quo sponte accessit, ut Deo in holocaustum immolaretur, quia extunc exstitit Deo consecratus. Alii dicunt, quod Isaac specialiter commendatur de continentia conjugali, et castitatis amore non duxit secundam: ita quod sicut Elias ac Jeremias sua continentia virginali, evangelicæ castitatis typum gesserunt perfecte, sic Isaac præsignavit continentiam, quæ in evangelica lege est, conjugalem, in qua unus unius est compar. Unde loquitur Augustinus: Iste Patriarcha nec uxorem habuit aliam, nec aliquam concubinam, sed posteritate duorum geminorum contentus fuit, nec tamen ob hoc patre suo Abraham virtuosior fuit, sed e converso.
paras.en: [[25:26|Isaac was threescore years old when the children were born unto him|Sexagenarius erat Isaac, quando nati sunt ei parvuli]]. From this, what was said above is established, namely that he was twenty years with his wife without offspring, since he took her when he was forty years old. Hence it is also plain that what Josephus says cannot stand, that Abraham died before the sons of Isaac were born: on the contrary, he is shown to have lived fifteen years after their birth; for Abraham was a hundred years old when Isaac was born, and Abraham lived a hundred and seventy-five years. On this the question is asked why Isaac, in so many years of his wife's barrenness, did not take another, as Abraham took Agar. To this (so it is reported) the Jews answer that it was not lawful for Isaac to have several wives, since he had come forward of his own accord to be offered to God as a holocaust, and from then on he was consecrated to God. Others say that Isaac is specially commended for conjugal continence, and out of love of chastity did not take a second wife: so that, as Elias and Jeremias by their virginal continence perfectly bore the type of evangelical chastity, so Isaac foreshadowed the conjugal continence that belongs to the law of the Gospel, in which one is the partner of one. Hence Augustine says [the margin note beside these words could not be read]: This patriarch had neither another wife nor any concubine, but was content with the offspring of the two twins; and yet he was not on that account more virtuous than his father Abraham, but the reverse.

paras.t: Quibus adultis, factus est Esau vir gnarus venandi, id est artificialis venator, et homo agricola; Jacob autem vir simplex: loquendo de simplicitate columbina, quæ dolum et fictionem excludit, et veram includit prudentiam. Sic enim sanctus Job fuit simplex, non simplicitate asinina, quæ caret prudentia atque industria. Hinc alia habet translatio, Jacob sine dolo. Habitabat in tabernaculis. Alia littera continet, Habitabat in domo, et ita est sensus, quod fuit vir quietus, vitans discursus, et remanens domi, nisi rationabilis causa eum egredi quandoque compelleret. Attamen Lyra refert, quod secundum Hebræos, istud intelligatur de tabernaculis Melchisedech et Heber, qui venientes ad se, edocuerunt spiritualia ac divina, ad quos dicunt Jacob venisse, et habitasse ad tempus cum eis, imo quatuordecim annis cum Heber. Unde et Glossa super illud, Habitabat in tabernaculis, ait, Studebat in spiritualibus. Verumtamen in Scripturis veteris Testamenti, domus etiam impiorum tabernacula solent vocari: quanto magis domus Isaac viri justi, qui et filium suum potuit informare? Moyses quippe de Dathan et Abiron loquens: Recedite, inquit, a tabernaculis hominum impiorum. Isaac amabat Esau, eo quod de venationibus illius libenter vesceretur, et etiam quia primogenitus ejus fuit: nec dubium quin amabat etiam Jacob, sed ipsum Esau amplius: nec tamen putandum, quod Isaac patriarcha ex carnalitate aut gulositate talia amabat cibaria, et filium suum propter ea. Potest namque vir bonus ac sobrius moderate uti cibariis delicatis, sicut et pulchra uxore. Et Rebecca diligebat specialiter Jacob propter ejus simplicitatem et sinceritatem, et quia frequentius secum erat in domo, et rursum, ex inspiratione divina, et item, quoniam ex revelatione divina cognovit quod Jacob erat præelectus a Deo, et fratri suo præferendus.
paras.en: [[25:27|And when they were grown up|Quibus adultis]], [[25:27|Esau became a skilful hunter|factus est Esau vir gnarus venandi]], that is, a hunter by art, [[25:27|and a husbandman|et homo agricola]]: [[25:27|but Jacob, a plain man|Jacob autem vir simplex]] [Latin simplex, 'simple'], speaking of the simplicity of the dove, which shuts out guile and pretence and includes true prudence. For it was so that holy Job was simple[[Job 1:1||]] [the margin note here could not be read; Job is called simple in Job 1:1 and 1:8], not with the simplicity of an ass, which lacks prudence and diligence. Hence another translation has: Jacob without guile. [[25:27|dwelt in tents|Habitabat in tabernaculis]]. Another reading has: He dwelt in a house; and so the sense is that he was a quiet man, who avoided running about and stayed at home, unless some reasonable cause at times compelled him to go out. Lyra, however, reports that according to the Hebrews this is to be understood of the tents of Melchisedech and Heber, who taught spiritual and divine things to those who came to them; to them, they say, Jacob came, and dwelt with them for a time, indeed fourteen years with Heber. Hence the Gloss too, on the words [[25:27|dwelt in tents|Habitabat in tabernaculis]], says: He studied spiritual things. Yet in the Scriptures of the Old Testament even the houses of the wicked are commonly called tents: how much more the house of Isaac, a just man, who could also instruct his son? For Moses, speaking of Dathan and Abiron, says: [[Num 16:26|Depart|Recedite]], he says, [[Num 16:26|from the tents of these wicked men|a tabernaculis hominum impiorum]]. [[25:28|Isaac loved Esau, because he ate of his hunting|Isaac amabat Esau, eo quod de venationibus illius libenter vesceretur]] [Denis's text has 'gladly ate'], and also because he was his firstborn: no doubt he loved Jacob too, but Esau more. Yet we must not think that the patriarch Isaac loved such food, and his son on its account, out of carnality or greed. For a good and sober man can use dainty food in moderation, as he can a beautiful wife. [[25:28|and Rebecca loved|Et Rebecca diligebat]] especially [[25:28|Jacob|Jacob]], for his simplicity and sincerity, and because he was more often with her at home, and again by divine inspiration, and also because she knew by divine revelation that Jacob was chosen beforehand by God and was to be preferred to his brother.

paras.t: Coxit autem Jacob pulmentum de quodam legumine, quod vocatur lenticula. Ad quem quum venisset Esau lassus de agro, ait: Da mihi de coctione hac rufa, id est rubicunda seu fulva, quoniam facta erat de lenticula rubea: quia oppido, id est valde, lassus sum. Quam ob causam vocatum est nomen ejus Edom. Circa quod ait Hieronymus: Fulvum seu rubeum, Hebraice dicitur Edom. Ob id autem quod pro rubeo cibo primogenita sua vendidit, nomen Edom seu fulvi accepit: cujus appellationis fuit et alia causa, ut tactum est, quoniam natus est rufus seu rubeus.
paras.en: [[25:29|And Jacob boiled pottage|Coxit autem Jacob pulmentum]], of a certain pulse that is called the lentil. [[25:29|to whom Esau, coming faint out of the field|Ad quem quum venisset Esau lassus de agro]], [[25:30|Said: Give me of this red pottage|ait: Da mihi de coctione hac rufa]], that is, ruddy or tawny, since it was made of red lentils: [[25:30|for I am exceeding|quia oppido]], that is, very, [[25:30|faint|lassus sum]]. [[25:30|For which reason his name was called Edom|Quam ob causam vocatum est nomen ejus Edom]]. On this Jerome says: Tawny or red is called Edom in Hebrew. Because he sold his birthright for red food, he received the name Edom, that is, tawny; and there was another cause of this name too, as was touched on above, since he was born ruddy or red.

paras.t: Cui dixit Jacob: Vende mihi primogenita tua. Secundum Isidorum, primogenita fuit vestis sacerdotalis, qua majores natu cum benedictione patris induti, victimas Deo quasi pontifices offerebant. Porro in Scholastica historia plenius dicitur: Erant autem primogenita, quædam dignitates, quas habuerunt primogeniti in cognationibus suis usque ad Aaron. Habebat enim primogenitus vestem specialem, qua induebatur tantum in sacrificiis offerendis, et quando recepturus erat finalem benedictionem a patre. In solennitatibus quoque et conviviis, benedicebat junioribus, et in his duplam portionem ciborum recepit: sic et in divisione hereditatis habuit duplum, ut fertur. Itaque constat, quod primogenitura inclusit spiritualia aliqua, præsertim sacerdotium et auctoritatem benedicendi. Quomodo ergo petiit Jacob primogenita sibi vendi, quum hoc esse simoniacum videatur? Ad hoc patet responsio ex dictis circa hoc, quod Abraham dicitur jus sepulturæ emisse. Primogenitura quippe jure et præordinatione divina erat ipsius Jacob, qui hoc ipsum ex suæ matris relatione creditur cognovisse: sicque intelligitur suam redemisse vexationem, retrahendo prudenter ad se, quod sibi ex gratia Dei competebat. Alii dicunt, quod sicut jus patronatus partim est spirituale, partimque temporale, propter quod per se vendi non potest, sed cum fundo vendito potest transferri, ita jus primogenituræ cum redditibus ad se pertinentibus transferri poterat per venditionem.
paras.en: [[25:31|And Jacob said to him: Sell me thy first birthright.|Cui dixit Jacob: Vende mihi primogenita tua.]] According to Isidore, the birthright was a priestly vestment, clad in which the elder-born, with their father's blessing, offered victims to God as high priests. The Scholastic History says more fully: Now the birthrights were certain dignities which the firstborn held in their kindreds until Aaron. For the firstborn had a special vestment, which he put on only when offering sacrifices, and when he was to receive the final blessing from his father. At solemn feasts also and at banquets he blessed the younger ones, and at these he received a double portion of food; so too in the division of the inheritance he had a double share, so it is reported. So it is established that the birthright included certain spiritual things, above all the priesthood and the authority to bless. How then did Jacob ask for the birthright to be sold to him, since this seems to be simoniacal? The answer to this is plain from what was said on Abraham's being said to have bought the right of burial. For the birthright, by right and by divine preordination, belonged to Jacob himself, who is believed to have known this from what his mother told him: and so he is understood to have bought off his vexation [that is, to have paid to be rid of an unjust obstacle to a right already his, which is not simony], prudently drawing back to himself what was his due by the grace of God. Others say that, as the right of patronage [the right to present a cleric to a benefice] is partly spiritual and partly temporal, and for that reason cannot be sold by itself, but can be transferred with an estate that is sold, so the right of the firstborn, with the revenues belonging to it, could be transferred by sale.

paras.t: Ille respondit: En morior. Quid mihi proderunt primogenita? quasi dicat, Præ fame et lassitudine, ac desiderio hujus cibi deficio, ita quod primogenitura mihi non prodest. Ait Jacob: Jura ergo mihi, quod venditionem hanc ratam habebis. Juravit ei Esau hoc ipsum, et vendidit primogenita sua cum juramento. Et sic accepto pane et lentis edulio, puta pulmento, comedit et bibit, et abiit, parvipendens quod primogenita vendidisset. Vel quia spiritualia non curavit, quum esset carnalis: vel quia viribus suis confidens, proposuit sibi reservare privilegia primogenituræ per vim, non obstante venditione aut juramento, sciens quod frater suus vir simplex non auderet resistere: sicque multipliciter et graviter valde peccavit, videlicet gula, simonia, illicita juratione, aspernatione spiritualium, ac pravo proposito violentiam atque perjurium committendi. Ideo ad Hebræos ait Apostolus: Ne quis fornicator aut profanus, ut Esau, qui propter unam escam vendidit primogenita sua.
paras.en: [[25:32|He answered: Lo I die, what will the first birthright avail me?|Ille respondit: En morior. Quid mihi proderunt primogenita?]] as if to say: For hunger and weariness and desire for this food I am failing, so that the birthright is of no use to me. [[25:33|Jacob said: Swear therefore to me|Ait Jacob: Jura ergo mihi]], that thou wilt hold this sale valid. [[25:33|Esau swore to him|Juravit ei Esau]] this very thing, [[25:33|and sold his first birthright|et vendidit primogenita]] with an oath. [[25:34|And so taking bread and the pottage of lentils|Et sic accepto pane et lentis edulio]], that is, the pottage, [[25:34|he ate, and drank, and went on his way; making little account of having sold his first birthright|comedit et bibit, et abiit, parvipendens quod primogenita vendidisset]]: either because he cared nothing for spiritual things, being carnal; or because, trusting in his own strength, he purposed to keep the privileges of the birthright for himself by force, notwithstanding the sale or the oath, knowing that his brother, a simple man, would not dare to resist. And so he sinned in many ways and very gravely: by gluttony, by simony, by unlawful swearing, by contempt of spiritual things, and by a wicked purpose of committing violence and perjury. Therefore the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:16|Lest there be any fornicator or profane person, as Esau who for one mess sold his first birthright|Ne quis fornicator aut profanus, ut Esau, qui propter unam escam vendidit primogenita sua]].

paras.t: Sed circa hæc quæstio oritur: Non enim apparet, quod Esau vir humana versutus astutia, qui de cupiditate et gula notatur, vendiderit primogenita sua pro quammodicissimo pretio, utpote una esca, et potissimum si ad primogenituram spectabat ciborum et hereditatis portio duplex. Ad hoc (ut fertur) Hebræi respondent, quod cibus de quo ait ista Scriptura, non fuit pretium emptionis primogenituræ, sed datum fuit ultra pretium istud, eo modo quo in contractibus emptor consuevit ultra pretium dare symbolum aliquod. Si autem objiciatur præallegatum Apostoli verbum, dicentis: Qui propter unam escam vendidit primitiva: respondetur, quod conjunctio, propter, notat ibi causam venditionis motivam, non pretii quantitatem. Huic tamen responsioni objicit Rabbi Paulus, quia si Esau vendidit primogenita sua pro pretio magno, ita quod esca movit eum dumtaxat ad illam venditionem, non vocaretur ab Apostolo ipso profanus. Sed quidquid sit de hujus dicti veritate, ista objectio nullius est ponderis. Nam quantumcumque pretium Esau pro primogenitura per modum pretii accepisset, simoniacus factus fuisset, et ex consequenti, profanatus atque sacrilegus.
paras.en: But a question arises about this. For it does not seem likely that Esau, a man versed in human cunning, who is marked for covetousness and gluttony, should have sold his birthright for so very small a price, namely one mess, and above all if a double portion of food and of the inheritance belonged to the birthright. To this (so it is reported) the Hebrews answer that the food of which this Scripture speaks was not the price paid for the birthright, but was given over and above that price, in the way that in contracts a buyer is accustomed to give some token over and above the price. And if the Apostle's words quoted above are objected, where he says: [[Heb 12:16|who for one mess sold his first birthright|Qui propter unam escam vendidit primitiva]], the answer is that the conjunction *for* [propter, 'on account of'] marks there the cause that moved him to the sale, not the size of the price. Against this answer, however, Rabbi Paul objects that if Esau had sold his birthright for a great price, so that the food only moved him to that sale, he would not have been called profane by the Apostle himself. But whatever be the truth of that saying, this objection is of no weight. For however great a price Esau had received for the birthright by way of price, he would have become simoniacal, and consequently profane and sacrilegious.

paras.t: Amplius, juxta mysticum sensum, sicut Abraham, Sara defuncta, aliam duxit uxorem, quam tamen et ante dicitur habuisse, videlicet Agar; sic Christus nunquam sine spiritualibus nuptiis est, et si una particularis Ecclesia deficiat, aliam sibi procurat, quosdam convertendo ad se. Denique circa finem sæculi, Ecclesia per Antichristum pro maxima parte exstincta, Christus Judæos convertet, et Synagogam quam diu reliquerat, iterum sumet in sponsam. Quemadmodum autem ex Abraham natæ sunt multæ et maximæ nationes infideles et reprobæ: ita ex Christo et Ecclesia renati sunt plures in fonte Baptismatis, qui ad hæreticas pravitates ac varia vitia lapsi, ecclesias malignantium et conventicula hæreticorum, schismaticorum ac impiorum atque carnalium constituerunt: quibus tamen Christus largitus est munera, hoc est, dona gratiæ gratis datæ, bona naturæ ac fortunæ, imo et dona gratiæ gratum facientis in fonte Baptismatis. Isaac autem, hoc est, populo christiano catholico, Christus contulit hereditatem cœlestem, et cuncta quæ habet, quæ eis præparavit ad perfruendum seu participandum: quos nunc separat merito a perversis: deinde separabit eos ab invicem loco et præmio.
paras.en: Further, in the mystical sense: as Abraham, after Sara's death, [[25:1|married another wife|aliam duxit uxorem]], whom however he is said to have had before as well, namely Agar; so Christ is never without spiritual nuptials, and if one particular Church fails, he procures another for himself, converting some to himself. And at last, about the end of the world, when the Church has been for the most part extinguished by Antichrist, Christ will convert the Jews, and will take again as his bride the Synagogue which he had long forsaken. And as there were born of Abraham many and very great nations, unbelieving and reprobate: so of Christ and the Church there are many reborn in the font of Baptism who, falling into heretical depravities and various vices, have set up churches of the malignant and conventicles of heretics, schismatics, the impious and the carnal: to whom Christ nevertheless [[25:6|gave gifts|largitus est munera]], that is, gifts of grace freely given [gratia gratis data: graces given for the good of others, such as prophecy or miracles], goods of nature and of fortune, and indeed the gifts of sanctifying grace [gratia gratum faciens: the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God] in the font of Baptism. But to Isaac, that is, to the Catholic Christian people, Christ has given the heavenly inheritance and [[25:5|all his possessions|cuncta quæ habet]], which he has prepared for them to enjoy or to share; and these he now separates by their merit from the perverse, and hereafter he will separate them from one another in place and in reward.

paras.t: Insuper, sicut post mortem Abrahæ Deus benedixit Isaac filio ejus: sic Christo passo et mortuo, resuscitato et in cœlum levato, Deus benedixit copiosissime ejus discipulis ac filiis. Iterum, sicut per Abraham et Saram, ita per Isaac et Rebeccam designantur Christus atque Ecclesia. Et sicut Isaac rogavit pro Rebeccæ fecundatione: ita Christus pro Ecclesiæ gratiosa fecunditate quam ex se ipsa non habuit. Quumque concepisset Ecclesia, statim cœperunt pullulare et commisceri in ea, et contra se invicem præliari populi duo, videlicet boni et mali, catholici et hæretici: propter quod dolebat Ecclesia, et dictum est ei: Duæ gentes in utero tuo sunt. Christus namque comparavit Ecclesiam sagenæ ex omni piscium genere congreganti; sed populus catholicus et electus hæreticis ac reprobis prævalet.
paras.en: Moreover, as after Abraham's death [[25:11|God blessed Isaac his son|Deus benedixit Isaac filio ejus]], so, when Christ had suffered and died, had risen and been taken up into heaven, God most abundantly blessed his disciples and sons. Again, as by Abraham and Sara, so by Isaac and Rebecca Christ and the Church are signified. And as Isaac prayed for Rebecca's fruitfulness, so Christ prayed for the Church's gracious fruitfulness, which she did not have of herself. And when the Church had conceived, at once two peoples began to spring up and to mingle in her and to war against one another, namely the good and the bad, Catholics and heretics: and for this the Church grieved, and it was said to her: [[25:23|Two nations are in thy womb|Duæ gentes in utero tuo sunt]]. For Christ compared the Church to a net gathering together of every kind of fish[[Matt 13:47||]] [the margin note here could not be read; the passage is Matt 13:47]; but the Catholic and elect people prevails over the heretics and the reprobate.

paras.t: Quemadmodum autem Esau erat totus deformis, rubens et pilosus; sic iniqui ac perfidi mente deformes sunt, sanguinolenti pravisque cogitationibus et iniquis affectibus quasi pilis operti: qui discunt venari, terrenaque colere, quoniam alios venantur ad mortem, et undique evagantur ac temporalibus inhiant. Jacob vero fuit vir simplex, in tabernaculis habitans; sic vere fideles sunt simplices sicut columbæ, et Christi ecclesias visitant, atque in scholis virtutum morantur. Quemadmodum etiam Esau quæsivit pulmentum et terrena a Jacob, et propter ea parvipendit spiritualia bona: sic reprobi et carnales a fidelibus conantur temporalia obtinere, de quibus devoti non curant, dummodo æterna ac spiritualia sortiantur.
paras.en: And as Esau was all misshapen, red and hairy, so the wicked and faithless are misshapen in mind, bloody, and covered as with hairs by depraved thoughts and wicked affections: they learn to hunt and to till the earth, for they hunt others to death, and wander about everywhere, and gape after temporal things. But Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in tents; so the truly faithful are simple as doves, and they visit the churches of Christ and abide in the schools of the virtues. And again, as Esau sought pottage and earthly things from Jacob, and for their sake made little of spiritual goods, so the reprobate and carnal try to get temporal things from the faithful, for which the devout care nothing, so long as they obtain eternal and spiritual things.

paras.t: Caveamus igitur vitia Esau, omnem cupiditatem et gulam, omnem vanitatem et pompam, atque ipsius Jacob virtutes sectemur, quatenus et in nobis populus major minori deserviat, id est, multitudo passionum ac vitiorum, omniumque carnalium appetituum, sensualiumque apprehensionum ac operum subjiciatur cœtui intellectualium sensuum et actuum virtuosorum, imperio rationis, dominio caritatis, rectitudini æquitatis.
paras.en: Let us therefore shun the vices of Esau, all covetousness and gluttony, all vanity and pomp, and follow the virtues of Jacob, so that in us too the elder people may serve the younger: that is, that the multitude of passions and vices, and of all carnal appetites, and of sensual apprehensions and works, may be made subject to the company of the intellectual senses and of virtuous acts, to the command of reason, to the dominion of charity, to the rightness of equity.

26.title: Elucidatio capituli vicesimi sexti: Orta autem fame super terram
26.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-sixth chapter: “And when a famine came in the land”

paras.t: HOC nunc exponendum capitulum, recitat qualiter Dominus benedixit et magnam prosperitatem contulit Isaac patriarchæ. Orta autem fame super terram, id est habitatoribus terræ Chanaan, post eam sterilitatem quæ acciderat in diebus Abraham. Supra duodecimo capitulo legitur Abraham intrasse Ægyptum, propter famem quæ tunc in terra Chanaan erat. Vicesimoque capitulo scriptum est, quod introivit terram Palæstinorum, et habitavit in Geraris: sed ibi non legitur propter famem id accidisse. Porro quando intravit Ægyptum propter famem, nondum genuerat Ismaelem; Isaac vero sexagenarius fuit, dum nati sunt ei Jacob et Esau, qui quum juvenes essent, et forsan plusquam viginti annorum, fecerunt commercium, de quo in fine præcedentis capituli actum est: sicque Isaac videtur tunc fuisse ad minus octoginta annorum; fuit quoque tredecim annis junior Ismaele. Ergo inter famem illam sub Abraham factam, et inter istam sub Isaac ortam, fluxerunt anni nonaginta tres ad minus, si historia ista quæ nunc recitatur de Isaac, contigit post venditionem primogenitorum Esau, ut series textus videtur prætendere. Non est autem verisimile, quod infra tot annos non fuerit in terra Chanaan alia fames, caristia sive sterilitas.
paras.en: This chapter, now to be expounded, relates how the Lord blessed the patriarch Isaac and bestowed great prosperity on him. [[26:1|And when a famine came in the land|Orta autem fame super terram]], that is, for the inhabitants of the land of Chanaan, [[26:1|after that barrenness which had happened in the days of Abraham|post eam sterilitatem quæ acciderat in diebus Abraham]]. Above, in the twelfth chapter, we read that Abraham went into Egypt because of the famine that was then in the land of Chanaan; and in the twentieth chapter it is written that he entered the land of the Palestines and dwelt in Gerara, but there we do not read that this happened because of a famine. Further, when he went into Egypt because of the famine, he had not yet begotten Ismael; and Isaac was sixty years old when Jacob and Esau were born to him, who, when they were young men, and perhaps more than twenty years old, made the bargain spoken of at the end of the preceding chapter: and so Isaac seems then to have been at least eighty years old; and he was thirteen years younger than Ismael. Therefore between that famine which came under Abraham and this one which arose under Isaac there passed at least ninety-three years, if the history now related of Isaac took place after Esau's sale of his birthright, as the order of the text seems to show. Yet it is not likely that within so many years there was no other famine, dearth or barrenness in the land of Chanaan.

paras.t: Præterea supra dictum jam est, quod Abimelech rex Geraræ concupivit et sibi adduci fecit Saram Abrahæ conjugem, Isaac nondum nato. Ergo inter tempus illud, et istud de quo in isto narratur capitulo, quod ipse Abimelech et etiam Phicol princeps militiæ ejus, de quo item vicesimo habetur capitulo, tractaverunt cum Isaac, fluxerunt ad minus octoginta anni: sicque Abimelech fuit tunc ad minus centum annorum, etiamsi non fuisset nisi viginti annorum quando adduxit ad se Saram. Deinde in isto capitulo scribitur Isaac multa egisse in terra Palæstinorum, puteosque fodisse, et loca mutasse, ac succrevisse quousque magnus effectus est vehementer. Post quæ omnia rursus legitur Abimelech cum Phicol venisse ad ipsum, et fœdus amicitiæ percussisse cum illo. Si itaque in recitatione hujus historiæ ordo temporis observatus est, inveniuntur Abimelech iste et Phicol valde diu vixisse, ita ut vix credibile videatur: idcirco Glossa et Scholastica historia dicunt, istam historiam recitari per recapitulationem, ita quod res quæ hic legitur gesta, acciderit ante nativitatem filiorum, Esau et Jacob, aut saltem ante venditionem primogenituræ præscriptam. Verumtamen istud non videtur certum nec necessarium dici, quoniam aliqui tunc vixerunt, imo et multi, quasi ducentis vel centum et quinquaginta annis, sicut et infra patebit de Laban. Nec Isaac videtur fuisse tantæ opulentiæ et sublimitatis, sicut hic fertur, ante mortem Abrahæ patris sui, præsertim quum scriptum sit præcedenti capitulo. Post obitum Abrahæ benedixit Deus Isaac filio ejus. Abraham vero vixit quindecim annis post nativitatem filiorum Isaac, ut in expositione præcedentis capituli est probatum: sicque obitus Abrahæ non præcessit prætactam primogenituræ venundationem, nisi per quinque annos, si filii Isaac non erant nisi viginti annorum tempore venditionis illius. Potius ergo reor ista recitari secundum ordinem temporis quo sunt facta.
paras.en: Moreover, it has already been said above that Abimelech, king of Gerara, desired Sara, the wife of Abraham, and had her brought to him[[Gen 20:2||]], when Isaac was not yet born. Therefore between that time and this, of which this chapter tells that this same Abimelech, and also Phicol the chief of his army, of whom the twentieth chapter likewise speaks [in fact the twenty-first, Gen 21:22], dealt with Isaac, at least eighty years passed: and so Abimelech was then at least a hundred years old, even if he had been only twenty when he took Sara to himself. Next, it is written in this chapter that Isaac did many things in the land of the Palestines, dug wells, changed his dwelling, and grew until he became exceeding great. After all which we read again that Abimelech came to him with Phicol and struck a covenant of friendship with him. If, then, the order of time has been kept in the telling of this history, this Abimelech and Phicol are found to have lived a very long time, so long that it seems scarcely credible: for this reason the Gloss and the Scholastic History say that this history is told by recapitulation [that is, going back to tell what happened earlier], so that the things we read of here happened before the birth of the sons, Esau and Jacob, or at least before the sale of the birthright described above. Yet this does not seem certain, nor necessary to say, since some, indeed many, lived then for about two hundred or a hundred and fifty years, as will also appear below of Laban. Nor does Isaac seem to have been of such wealth and eminence as is told here before the death of Abraham his father, especially since it is written in the preceding chapter: [[Gen 25:11|after his death, God blessed Isaac his son|Post obitum Abrahæ benedixit Deus Isaac filio ejus]]. Now Abraham lived fifteen years after the birth of Isaac's sons, as was shown in the exposition of the preceding chapter: and so Abraham's death came before the aforesaid sale of the birthright by only five years, if Isaac's sons were only twenty years old at the time of that sale. I think rather, therefore, that these things are told in the order of time in which they were done.

paras.t: Itaque abiit Isaac ad Abimelech regem Palæstinorum in Gerara, id est in loco seu oppido sic vocato. Nam propter amicitiam quæ fuit inter Abraham atque Abimelech, habuit Isaac fiduciam confugiendi ad ipsum Abimelech. Apparuitque ei Dominus, per angelum secundum aliquem modorum sæpius prætactorum, dicens: Ne descendas in Ægyptum. Ex quo elicitur, quod intendebat intrare Ægyptum, quæ est regio valde abundans: idcirco Isaac magnam habens familiam, multaque pecora, voluit se illuc tempore sterilitatis transferre, sicut et pater suus Abraham fecerat. Sed quiesce in terra quam dixero tibi, videlicet infra terminos terræ promissionis, et peregrinare ibi, hoc est in terra quæ infra terram Chanaan et Ægyptum est media, puta in Palæstina, quæ ad terram promissionis pertinuit, ut patuit ac patebit: quasi dicat, Esto peregrinus in terra quam in successoribus et posteris tuis possidebis ut dominus.
paras.en: So [[26:1|Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Palestines, to Gerara|abiit Isaac ad Abimelech regem Palæstinorum in Gerara]], that is, to the place or town so called. For because of the friendship there had been between Abraham and Abimelech, Isaac had the confidence to take refuge with this Abimelech. [[26:2|And the Lord appeared to him|Apparuitque ei Dominus]], through an angel, in one of the ways often touched on already, [[26:2|and said: Go not down into Egypt|dicens: Ne descendas in Ægyptum]]. From this it is gathered that he meant to go into Egypt, which is a very plentiful country: and so Isaac, having a great household and many cattle, wished to remove there in the time of barrenness, as his father Abraham also had done. [[26:2|but stay in the land that I shall tell thee|Sed quiesce in terra quam dixero tibi]], namely within the bounds of the land of promise, [[26:3|And sojourn in it|et peregrinare ibi]], that is, in the land that lies between the land of Chanaan and Egypt, namely in Palestine, which belonged to the land of promise, as has appeared and will appear: as if to say, Be a stranger in the land which thou shalt possess as lord in thy successors and descendants.

paras.t: Hinc ratio præcepti hujus subjungitur: Tibi enim, et, pro id est, semini tuo dabo universas regiones has, scilicet Palæstinam, Chanaan, Galilæam, Samariam, etc., complens juramentum quod spopondi, id est firmiter et assertorie feci, Abraham patri tuo, etc., et benedicentur in semine tuo, scilicet Christo, secundum naturam humanam, omnes gentes terræ, id est quidam, imo et multi de omnibus, ut plenius sæpiusque expositum est. Hæc etenim verba eodem sensu promissa sunt Isaac, quo et Abrahæ: per quod patet, quod non Abrahæ tantum, sed et Isaac, imo et Jacob, ut infra clarebit, facta sit ista de Christo promissio.
paras.en: Then the reason for this command is added: [[26:3|for to thee and|Tibi enim, et]] (*and* stands here for *that is*) [[26:3|to thy seed I will give all these countries|semini tuo dabo universas regiones has]], namely Palestine, Chanaan, Galilee, Samaria, etc., [[26:3|to fulfil the oath which I swore|complens juramentum quod spopondi]], that is, made firmly and with assurance, [[26:3|to Abraham thy father|Abraham patri tuo]], etc., [[26:4|and in thy seed|et benedicentur in semine tuo]], namely in Christ, according to His human nature, [[26:4|shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|omnes gentes terræ]], that is, some, nay many, out of all of them, as has been explained more fully and often. For these words were promised to Isaac in the same sense as to Abraham: whereby it is plain that this promise of Christ was made not to Abraham only but also to Isaac, and indeed to Jacob, as will be clear below.

paras.t: Eo quod obedierit Abraham voci meæ, id est jussioni quam ei loquendo præfixi. Verumtamen (ut est dictum) obedientia Abrahæ non promeruit de condigno, sed de congruo, exhibitionem promissionis illius de Christo, videlicet Christi incarnationem, et omnium gentium benedictionem per eum. Et custodierit præcepta, ea videlicet, quæ sunt de dictamine naturalis rationis, ut sunt præcepta Decalogi, quæ omnes respiciebant, et mandata mea, quæ ei specialiter jussi, et cærimonias, legesque servaverit. Cærimoniæ illæ fuerunt certi ritus seu modi colendi Deum, et sacrificandi eidem. Per leges vero nunc possunt intelligi quæcumque institutiones tunc factæ et observandæ, quæ judiciales vocantur, quæ docebant modum servandi justitiam inter homines. Ex his conjicitur, quod ante legem Mosaicam multa præcepta moralia et cæremonialia ac judicialia observabantur a Dei ministris, quæ postmodum in lege Moysis sunt conscripta et ampliata. Per hæc quoque insinuatur excellentia sanctitatis Abrahæ, propter cujus justitiam Dominus dicit se tanta bona filio suo facturum.
paras.en: [[26:5|Because Abraham obeyed my voice|Eo quod obedierit Abraham voci meæ]], that is, the command I laid on him by speaking. Yet (as has been said) Abraham's obedience did not merit *de condigno* but *de congruo* [that is, not as strictly due to it, but as fitting for God's liberality to reward] the fulfilment of that promise of Christ, namely the incarnation of Christ and the blessing of all nations through Him. [[26:5|and kept my precepts|Et custodierit præcepta]], namely those which come from the dictate of natural reason, such as the precepts of the Decalogue, which concerned all men, [[26:5|and commandments|et mandata mea]], which I enjoined on him in particular, [[26:5|and observed my ceremonies and laws|et cærimonias, legesque servaverit]]. Those ceremonies were certain rites or ways of worshipping God and of sacrificing to Him. By *laws*, again, may here be understood whatever ordinances were then made and to be observed, which are called judicial, and which taught the way of keeping justice among men. From these words it is gathered that before the Mosaic law many moral, ceremonial and judicial precepts were observed by the ministers of God, which were afterwards written down and enlarged in the law of Moses. By them also is suggested the excellence of Abraham's holiness, for whose justice the Lord says He will do such great good to his son.

paras.t: Mansit itaque Isaac in Geraris, id est in loco sic dicto. Qui quum interrogaretur a viris loci illius super uxore sua, respondit : Soror mea est, etc. Istud omnino concordat cum his, quæ supra de Abraham dicta sunt, ex quorum expositione patet et sensus istius passus. Quumque pertransissent dies plurimi, prospiciens Abimelech rex Palæstinorum per fenestram, vidit eum jocantem cum Rebecca uxore sua. Secundum Lyram, verbum Hebraicum, pro quo Hieronymus transtulit hic, jocantem, æquivocum est ad ludum et coitum, magisque proprie accipitur modo pro coitu. Verum (ut in expositione vicesimi primi capituli dictum est) Rabbi Paulus affirmat, quod verbum istud nunquam significat coitum, et secundum eumdem, nunc proprie signat jocum seu ludum : ut sit sensus, quod Abimelech vidit ipsum Isaac deosculantem et amplexantem suam uxorem, quod viri boni non faciebant nisi uxoribus propriis. Attamen verba sequentia ad utramque significationem possunt aptari.
paras.en: [[26:6|So Isaac abode in Gerara|Mansit itaque Isaac in Geraris]], that is, in the place so called. [[26:7|And when he was asked by the men of that place, concerning his wife|Qui quum interrogaretur a viris loci illius super uxore sua]], [[26:7|he answered: She is my sister|respondit : Soror mea est]], etc. This agrees entirely with what was said above of Abraham [a margin note here is unreadable in the transcription; compare Gen 12:13 and 20:2], from the exposition of which the sense of this passage too is plain. [[26:8|And when very many days were passed|Quumque pertransissent dies plurimi]], [[26:8|Abimelech, king of the Palestines, looking out through a window, saw him playing with Rebecca, his wife|prospiciens Abimelech rex Palæstinorum per fenestram, vidit eum jocantem cum Rebecca uxore sua]]. According to Lyra, the Hebrew word for which Jerome here translated *playing* is equivocal between play and intercourse, and is here taken more properly for intercourse. But (as was said in the exposition of the twenty-first chapter) Rabbi Paul affirms that this word never means intercourse, and according to him it here properly means sport or play: so that the sense is that Abimelech saw Isaac kissing and embracing his wife, which good men did only with their own wives. Yet the words that follow can be fitted to either meaning.

paras.t: Et accersito eo, id est, Isaac ad se vocato, ait : Perspicuum est quod uxor tua sit. Cur mentitus es eam sororem tuam esse? Secundum quod Abimelech sumpsit hoc nomen, soror, falsum erat Rebeccam esse sororem ipsius Isaac ; non autem secundum quod Isaac sumpsit sororem, utpote pro cognata. Respondit Isaac : Timui ne morerer propter eam, id est, ex timore hoc dixi, et ista sum usus cautela, ne Palæstini me trucidarent, quatenus uxore mea liberius possent uti. Dixitque Abimelech : Quare imposuisti nobis? id est, cur induxisti super nos tantum periculum? In Scholastica autem fertur historia : Imponere est hic verbum absolutum, et designat imposturam seu fraudem, ut sit sensus : Cur imposuisti nobis? id est, cur nos decepisti? Hinc impostor vocatur deceptor, vel secundum Remigium, is qui viliora miscet metalla pretiosis. Potuit coire quispiam de populo cum uxore tua, deceptus ex verbis tuis, putando quod esset soror tua, non uxor ; et induxeras super nos grande peccatum, hoc est, quantum fuit ex parte tui, dedisti nobis occasionem adulterii cum conjuge tua. Verumtamen Isaac non dixit eam esse suam sororem tali intentione, et de Dei providentia sperans, ei commisit exitum rei, sicut de hoc plenius dictum est in exponendo verba et gesta Abrahæ in re pari. Præcepitque omni populo sui dominii, dicens : Qui tetigerit hominis hujus uxorem, morte morietur. Sive hoc exponatur de tactu etiam osculi et amplexus, sive de tactu concubitus, patet quantum gentiles illi adulterium abhorrebant : quantum ergo Christiani id merito abhorrerent?
paras.en: [[26:9|And calling for him|Et accersito eo]], that is, having called Isaac to him, [[26:9|he said: It is evident she is thy wife: why didst thou feign her to be thy sister?|ait : Perspicuum est quod uxor tua sit. Cur mentitus es eam sororem tuam esse?]] In the sense in which Abimelech took this word *sister*, it was false that Rebecca was Isaac's sister; but not in the sense in which Isaac took *sister*, namely for a kinswoman. [[26:9|He answered|Respondit]] (Isaac): [[26:9|I feared lest I should die for her sake|Timui ne morerer propter eam]], that is, I said this out of fear, and used this precaution, lest the Palestines should slay me in order to have freer use of my wife. [[26:10|And Abimelech said: Why hast thou deceived us?|Dixitque Abimelech : Quare imposuisti nobis?]] that is, Why hast thou brought so great a danger upon us? But in the Scholastic History it is said: *Imponere* is here an absolute verb, and means imposture or fraud, so that the sense is, Why hast thou imposed upon us? that is, Why hast thou deceived us? [the Latin *imposuisti* can mean both "thou hast laid upon" and "thou hast imposed upon", that is, deceived] Hence an impostor is the name for a deceiver, or, according to Remigius, for one who mixes baser metals with precious ones. [[26:10|Some man of the people might have lain with thy wife|Potuit coire quispiam de populo cum uxore tua]], deceived by thy words, thinking that she was thy sister, not thy wife; [[26:10|and thou hadst brought upon us a great sin|et induxeras super nos grande peccatum]], that is, as far as lay with thee, thou gavest us occasion of adultery with thy wife. Yet Isaac did not say she was his sister with any such intention, and, hoping in God's providence, he committed the outcome to Him, as was said more fully in expounding the words and deeds of Abraham in a like case. [[26:10|And he commanded all the people|Præcepitque omni populo]] of his dominion, [[26:10|saying|dicens]]: [[26:11|He that shall touch this man's wife, shall surely be put to death.|Qui tetigerit hominis hujus uxorem, morte morietur.]] Whether this is taken of touching even by a kiss and an embrace, or of touching by lying with her, it is plain how greatly those gentiles abhorred adultery: how greatly, then, should Christians rightly abhor it!

paras.t: Seminavit autem Isaac in terra illa, et invenit in ipso anno centuplum, id est inusitate fructum copiosum, ex speciali munere Dei, qui interdum unam terram ultra aliam multum fecundat. Nec oportet ut centuplum designet hic numerum determinatum ac certum ; sed sensus est, quod multo plus accepit de fructu quam consuevit, aut se recepturum putavit : atque ut in Scholastica habetur historia, illud potest intelligi non solum de una specie opum, sed forte in omni genere opum est centuplicatus. Ideo quasi expositorie subditur : Benedixitque ei Dominus, augendo in eo spiritualia ac temporalia bona ; et locupletatus est homo, et ibat proficiens atque succrescens, donec magnus vehementer effectus est, etc. : per quod potissimum designatur in spiritualibus profecisse ; per quod item innuitur, quod temporalis prosperitas donum sit Dei, et ab eo electis aliquando concedatur.
paras.en: [[26:12|And Isaac sowed in that land, and he found that same year a hundredfold|Seminavit autem Isaac in terra illa, et invenit in ipso anno centuplum]], that is, an unusually plentiful crop, by a special gift of God, who sometimes makes one land far more fruitful than another. Nor need *a hundredfold* here signify a fixed and certain number; the sense is that he received much more fruit than he was used to, or than he thought he would receive: and, as the Scholastic History has it, this can be understood not only of one kind of wealth: perhaps he was increased a hundredfold in every kind of wealth. Therefore, as if by way of explanation, it is added: [[26:12|and the Lord blessed him|Benedixitque ei Dominus]], increasing in him spiritual and temporal goods; [[26:13|And the man was enriched, and he went on prospering and increasing, till he became exceeding great|et locupletatus est homo, et ibat proficiens atque succrescens, donec magnus vehementer effectus est]], etc.: by which it is chiefly signified that he advanced in spiritual things; and by which it is likewise hinted that temporal prosperity is a gift of God, and is sometimes granted by Him to the elect.

paras.t: Ob hoc invidentes ei Palæstini, omnes puteos quos foderant servi patris illius Abraham, illo tempore obstruxerunt, implentes humo : invidia namque est dolor de prosperitate alterius: in tantum ut ipse Abimelech diceret ad Isaac : Recede a nobis, quoniam potentior nobis factus es valde. Mirum videtur, qualiter peregrinus in aliena habitans terra, poterat esse fortior rege ac populo terræ illius. Potest hoc verbum intelligi per modum hyperbolicæ locutionis, qua aliquid sine mendacio dicitur per excessum, ad insinuandum insolitam magnitudinem ejus. Vel ideo dixit istud Abimelech, quoniam vidit Isaac divino undique suffultum auxilio, cui se scivit non posse resistere.
paras.en: [[26:14|Wherefore the Palestines envying him|Ob hoc invidentes ei Palæstini]], [[26:15|Stopped up at that time all the wells, that the servants of his father, Abraham, had digged, filling them up with earth|omnes puteos quos foderant servi patris illius Abraham, illo tempore obstruxerunt, implentes humo]]: for envy is sorrow at another's prosperity: [[26:16|Insomuch that Abimelech himself said to Isaac: Depart from us, for thou art become much mightier than we|in tantum ut ipse Abimelech diceret ad Isaac : Recede a nobis, quoniam potentior nobis factus es valde]]. It seems strange how a stranger dwelling in another's land could be stronger than the king and people of that land. This word can be understood as a hyperbolical way of speaking, by which something is said by excess, without lying, to suggest its unusual greatness.
