Or Abimelech said this because he saw Isaac upheld on every side by divine help, which he knew he could not resist.

paras.t: Et ille discedens, tanquam obtemperans regi in propria terra, ut veniret ad torrentem Geraræ, habitaretque ibi : recessit enim a civitate in qua habitavit cum rege, et habitavit non longe in valle, quoniam putavit se ibi aquam et pascua pro suis reperturum pecoribus : rursum fodit alios puteos, quos foderant servi patris sui Abraham, et quos illo mortuo olim obstruxerant Philistiim, id est Palæstini, etc. Illos etenim puteos, eo jubente, servi sui purgabant, ejiciendo humum injectam : quos Philistæi forsitan ideo impleverunt, ne quis ex posteris Abrahæ diceret se ad illos puteos jus habere. Foderuntque in torrente, id est in valle juxta torrentem, vel ubi torrens currere consuevit. Unde in Scholastica historia dicitur : Habitavit Isaac juxta alveum, per quem torrens aliquando influebat. Porro torrens vocatur aqua, quæ ex inundatione imbrium resolutioneve nivium aut glaciei decurrit, nec jugiter fluit : ideo ibi foderunt, quatenus hujusmodi aquam in foveis illis colligerent ac servarent. Et repererunt aquam vivam, id est salientem, quæ instar rerum viventium se movere videtur. Deinde in littera scribitur, qualiter pastores Geraræ contenderunt contra pastores Isaac, propter puteum illum, et similiter propter alium puteum : idcirco, secundum Josephum, Isaac illos puteos imperfectos reliquit, nolens cum indigenis terræ contendere, atque exspectans rationem ac licentiam bonæ voluntatis eorum : ex quibus patet magna humilitas, patientia, et mansuetudo Patriarchæ istius.
paras.en: [[26:17|So he departed|Et ille discedens]], as obeying the king in his own land, [[26:17|and came to the torrent of Gerara, to dwell there|ut veniret ad torrentem Geraræ, habitaretque ibi]]: for he withdrew from the city in which he had dwelt with the king, and dwelt not far off in a valley, since he thought he would find water and pasture there for his cattle: [[26:18|And he digged again other wells, which the servants of his father, Abraham, had digged, and which, after his death, the Philistines had of old stopped up|rursum fodit alios puteos, quos foderant servi patris sui Abraham, et quos illo mortuo olim obstruxerant Philistiim]], that is, the Palestines, etc. For at his bidding his servants cleaned out those wells, casting out the earth that had been thrown in: which the Philistines perhaps filled up so that none of Abraham's descendants should say that he had a right to those wells. [[26:19|And they digged in the torrent|Foderuntque in torrente]], that is, in the valley by the torrent, or where the torrent used to run. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History: Isaac dwelt by the channel through which a torrent sometimes flowed. Now a *torrent* is the name for water that runs down from the flooding of rains or the melting of snow or ice, and does not flow continually: so they dug there in order to gather and keep such water in those pits. [[26:19|and found living water|Et repererunt aquam vivam]], that is, springing water, which seems to move like living things. Then the letter tells how the herdsmen of Gerara strove with the herdsmen of Isaac over that well, and likewise over another well: and so, according to Josephus, Isaac left those wells unfinished, not wishing to contend with the natives of the land, and waiting for their reasonable leave and good will: from which the great humility, patience and meekness of this Patriarch is plain.

paras.t: Profectus inde, fodit, id est, servos suos fodere fecit, alium puteum, pro quo non contenderunt. Itaque vocavit nomen ejus Latitudo, dicens : Nunc dilatavit nos Dominus, id est, ampliavit in bonis, et fecit crescere, id est ditari, super terram, ita quod pecora nostra possunt nunc longe et late hic pasci.
paras.en: [[26:22|Going forward from thence, he digged|Profectus inde, fodit]], that is, had his servants dig, [[26:22|another well, for which they contended not; therefore he called the name thereof, Latitude, saying|alium puteum, pro quo non contenderunt. Itaque vocavit nomen ejus Latitudo, dicens]] [*Latitudo*, breadth: hence *dilatavit*, "hath made broad", in the words that follow]: [[26:22|Now hath the Lord given us room|Nunc dilatavit nos Dominus]], that is, has enlarged us in goods, [[26:22|and made us to increase|et fecit crescere]], that is, to grow rich, [[26:22|upon the earth|super terram]], so that our cattle can now feed far and wide here.

paras.t: Ascendit autem Isaac ex isto loco in Bersabee, ubi et Abraham jam ante habitaverat, ut supra dictum est ; ubi apparuit ei Dominus in ipsa nocte, per angelum in somno seu in vigilia, dicens : Ego sum Deus Abraham patris tui. Ex quo (ut ait Salvator) probatur resurrectio mortuorum, et immortalitas animæ rationalis. Deus namque est Deus eorum qui sunt aut vivunt, ergo Abraham corpore suo exstincto, secundum animam suam fuit et vixit. Noli timere. Hæc consolatio congrue facta est huic Isaac, quando in terra aliena tantam fuit passus injuriam, et a rege terræ depulsus. Itaque, Noli timere timore carnali, mundano, immoderato, quia ego tecum sum. Benedicam tibi et multiplicabo semen tuum propter servum meum Abraham, id est propter merita ejus : per quod rursus eximia sanctitas Abrahæ designatur. Principaliter tamen fecit hoc Deus ex propria misericordia sua, et ad sui ipsius honorem ac gloriam, imo et aliquo modo propter merita Isaac, qui fuit magni meriti apud Altissimum. Nam et hoc piissimum est, quod Deus propter merita unius, alteri miseretur ac benedicit. Itaque ædificavit ibi altare, gratias agens Deo, qui tanta bona sibi jam dedit, et majora promisit : et invocato nomine Domini, quem assidue invocavit, et orando, laudando, obediendo ac immolando venerabatur, extendit tabernaculum ; præcepitque servis suis ut fo[…] Jam enim fuerat animatus ex consolatione et promissione divina, sibi ibidem jam facta. Extenditque ibi tabernaculum : habitavit enim in tabernaculis, tentoriis seu papilionibus, sicut de Abraham dictum est, et ita faciliter poterat locum mutare.
paras.en: [[26:23|And he went up from that place to Bersabee|Ascendit autem Isaac ex isto loco in Bersabee]], where Abraham too had dwelt before[[Gen 21:33||]], as was said above; [[26:24|Where the Lord appeared to him that same night|ubi apparuit ei Dominus in ipsa nocte]], through an angel, in sleep or awake, saying: [[26:24|I am the God of Abraham thy father|Ego sum Deus Abraham patris tui]]. From this (as the Saviour says) the resurrection of the dead is proved, and the immortality of the rational soul [Christ's answer to the Sadducees, Matt 22:31–32]. For God is the God of those who are or live; therefore, though Abraham's body was dead, he was and lived according to his soul. [[26:24|do not fear|Noli timere]]. This consolation was fittingly given to Isaac when he had suffered such injury in a strange land and had been driven out by the king of the land. So: Do not fear with a carnal, worldly, immoderate fear, [[26:24|for I am with thee: I will bless thee, and multiply thy seed|quia ego tecum sum. Benedicam tibi et multiplicabo semen tuum]] [[26:24|for my servant Abraham's sake|propter servum meum Abraham]], that is, for his merits: by which the surpassing holiness of Abraham is again signified. Yet God did this chiefly out of His own mercy, and for His own honour and glory, and indeed in some measure for the merits of Isaac, who was of great merit with the Most High. For this too is most loving, that for the merits of one God has mercy on another and blesses him. [[26:25|And he built there an altar|Itaque ædificavit ibi altare]], giving thanks to God, who had already given him such great goods and promised greater: [[26:25|and called upon the name of the Lord|et invocato nomine Domini]], whom he called upon continually, and worshipped by praying, praising, obeying and sacrificing, [[26:25|and pitched his tent|extendit tabernaculum]]; [[26:25|and commanded his servants|præcepitque servis suis]] to dig […] [the rest of this lemma and what followed it are lost in the transcription, at the top of p. 316]. For he had now been heartened by the divine consolation and promise made to him in that very place. And he pitched his tent there: for he dwelt in tabernacles, tents or pavilions, as was said of Abraham, and so he could easily change his place.

paras.t: Ad quem locum quum venissent de Geraris, Abimelech et Ochozath amicus illius : reges namque solent habere unum specialem amicum, qui antonomastice fertur amicus regis sui, ut patet de David, Salomone ac aliis : verumtamen, secundum Hieronymum, in Hebræo habetur tale complexum, quod significat collegium seu congregationem amicorum regis : ut sit sensus, quod turba amicorum regis venit cum eo propter reverentiam ejus, et Phicol dux militum ; locutus est eis Isaac : qui tamen primo locuti sunt ei ; et inter cetera ipse dixit econverso ad ipsos : Quid venistis ad me hominem quem odistis, et expulistis a vobis ? Interdum enim fuerunt benevoli circa Isaac, interdum malevoli, ut dicit Hieronymus, et nunc constat ex textu. Qui responderunt : Vidimus tecum esse Dominum, et idcirco nunc dicimus : Sit juramentum inter nos, quod amicitiam simul servabimus, et ineamus fœdus pacis, etc. Historia ista quasi eadem est cum ea, quæ capitulo vicesimo primo habetur de juramento et fœdere pacis ac amicitiæ inito inter Abraham et Abimelech.
paras.en: [[26:26|To which place when Abimelech, and Ochozath his friend|Ad quem locum quum venissent de Geraris, Abimelech et Ochozath amicus illius]]: for kings are wont to have one special friend, who is called by antonomasia [that is, by a common name used as if it were his own] the friend of his king, as is plain of David, Solomon and others[[2 Kings 15:37||]][[3 Kings 5:1||]] [the margin gives II Reg. xv, with the verse unreadable, and III Reg. v, 1: Chusai the friend of David, and Hiram, who had always been David's friend]: yet according to Jerome the Hebrew has here a word meaning a college or company of the king's friends: so that the sense is that a crowd of the king's friends came with him out of reverence for him, [[26:26|and Phicol chief captain of his soldiers|et Phicol dux militum]]; [[26:27|Isaac said to them|locutus est eis Isaac]]: though they spoke to him first; and among other things he said to them in turn: [[26:27|Why are ye come to me, a man whom you hate, and have thrust out from you?|Quid venistis ad me hominem quem odistis, et expulistis a vobis]] For at times they were well disposed towards Isaac, at times ill disposed, as Jerome says, and as is now plain from the text. [[26:28|And they answered: We saw that the Lord is with thee, and therefore|Qui responderunt : Vidimus tecum esse Dominum, et idcirco]] now we say [Denis's text has *nunc dicimus*, "now we say", where the Vulgate has *nos diximus*, "we said"]: [[26:28|Let there be an oath between us|Sit juramentum inter nos]], that we shall keep friendship together, [[26:28|and let us make a covenant|et ineamus fœdus]] of peace, etc. This history is almost the same as the one in the twenty-first chapter, of the oath and covenant of peace and friendship made between Abraham and Abimelech.

paras.t: Ecce autem venerunt in ipso die servi Isaac, etc., dicentes : Invenimus aquam : idcirco puteum, in quo aqua illa inventa est, vocavit Abundantiam, et nomen urbi impositum est Bersabee. De hoc nomine et interpretatione, ac rationibus suæ impositionis, dictum est supra in fine expositionis capituli vicesimi primi. Unde aliqui dicunt, quod ista de qua nunc legitur, impositio nominis, non fuit nova institutio, sed prioris impositionis innovatio et confirmatio. Verumtamen, secundum Hieronymum, ex eo quod aqua ibi inventa est, Isaac alludens prioris nominis civitatis, declinavit paululum litteram ; et pro stridulo Hebræorum SIN, a quo SABEE incipit, posuit Græcum sigma, id est Hebræorum SAMECH. Hinc in Scholastica historia apertius dicitur : In modico vocis stridulo et in scriptura, hoc nomen quod nunc impositum legitur, differt a nomine quod Abraham olim imposuerat ei : SABEE enim, scriptum per SIN Hebræum, significat juramentum vel septem, et asperius stridet ; scriptum vero per sigma Græcum, satietatem designat, et mollius sonat. Denique istud videtur magistralius dictum, quam quod scribit alius quidam, dicens : BER in Hebræo significat puteum, SABEE autem significat septem et juramentum ac satietatem. Ex quibus tribus significationibus locus iste ubi erat puteus, vocatus est Bersabee. Primo, propter septem agnas quas ibi statuit Abraham. Secundo, propter juramentum ibi factum inter ipsum et Abimelech regem. Tertio, propter aquæ abundantiam ibi inventam. Quum enim textus hic dicat, quod nomen urbi impositum est Bersabee, videlicet propter abundantiam seu satietatem præfatam, videtur quod nomen istud aliqualiter differat a nomine illo priori.
paras.en: [[26:32|And behold, the same day the servants of Isaac came|Ecce autem venerunt in ipso die servi Isaac]], etc., [[26:32|saying: We have found water|dicentes : Invenimus aquam]]: therefore he called the well in which that water was found [[26:33|Abundance|Abundantiam]], [[26:33|and the name of the city was called Bersabee|et nomen urbi impositum est Bersabee]]. Of this name and its interpretation, and the reasons for which it was given, we spoke above at the end of the exposition of the twenty-first chapter. Hence some say that the giving of the name of which we now read was not a new institution but a renewal and confirmation of the earlier naming. Yet according to Jerome, because water was found there, Isaac, alluding to the city's earlier name, slightly altered a letter; and in place of the hissing SIN of the Hebrews, with which SABEE begins, he put the Greek *sigma*, that is, the SAMECH of the Hebrews. Hence it is said more plainly in the Scholastic History: The name we now read was given differs a little, in the hiss of its sound and in writing, from the name Abraham had once given it: for SABEE written with the Hebrew SIN means oath or seven, and hisses more harshly; but written with the Greek sigma it means fulness, and sounds more softly. Lastly, this seems more masterly than what a certain other writer says: BER in Hebrew means well, and SABEE means seven, and oath, and fulness; and from these three meanings this place where the well was was called Bersabee: first, because of the seven ewe lambs that Abraham set there; secondly, because of the oath made there between him and King Abimelech; thirdly, because of the abundance of water found there. For since the text says here that the name Bersabee was given to the city, namely because of the aforesaid abundance or fulness, it seems that this name differs somewhat from that earlier one.

paras.t: Deinde describitur inconsultum connubium Esau. Esau vero quadragenarius duxit uxores : Judith filiam Beeri Hethæi, et Basemath filiam Elon ejusdem loci. Hi duo viri, quorum filias Esau sumpsit uxores, fuerunt potentes Hethæi seu Chananæi, quas duxit sine consilio suorum parentum, quasi potens et sapiens per se : propter quod, secundum Josephum, fecit se ipsum dominum in potestate uxorum. Quæ ambæ offenderant animum Isaac et Rebeccæ : quia fortassis more Chananæorum fuerunt pompaticæ, curiosæ, immorigeratæ, idololatræ. Displicuit quoque Isaac, quod posteritas sua miscebatur provincialibus ; melius tamen putavit inde silere.
paras.en: Then Esau's ill-advised marriage is described. [[26:34|And Esau being forty years old, married wives, Judith, the daughter of Beeri, the Hethite, and Basemath, the daughter of Elon, of the same place|Esau vero quadragenarius duxit uxores : Judith filiam Beeri Hethæi, et Basemath filiam Elon ejusdem loci]]. These two men, whose daughters Esau took as wives, were powerful Hethites or Chanaanites; and he married them without the counsel of his parents, as though he were powerful and wise in himself: for which reason, according to Josephus, he made himself his own master in the matter of taking wives. [[26:35|And they both offended the mind of Isaac and Rebecca|Quæ ambæ offenderant animum Isaac et Rebeccæ]]: because perhaps, after the manner of the Chanaanites, they were showy, curious, ill-mannered, idolaters. It also displeased Isaac that his posterity was being mixed with the people of the country; yet he thought it better to keep silent about it.

26.title: De spirituali intellectu ejusdem capituli vicesimi sexti
26.title_en: On the spiritual sense of the same twenty-sixth chapter

paras.t: SICUT Isaac ingressus est Palæstinam cum domo sua, orta fame in Chanaan, sic Synagoga indurata, et omni spiritualium alimentorum refectione privata, Christus per Apostolorum prædicationem ad gentilium conversionem processit, atque in eorum demoratus est cordibus, qui evangelicam amplexati sunt legem : et factum est istud post sterilitatem, quæ in diebus Abrahæ contigit, hoc est spiritualem illam inopiam quæ frequenter fuit in cordibus Judæorum, quando Deus Pater in veteri Testamento dicebatur Deus ac Dominus Synagogæ.
paras.en: As Isaac went into Palestine with his house when famine arose in Chanaan, so, when the Synagogue had been hardened and deprived of all refreshment of spiritual food, Christ, through the preaching of the Apostles, went forth to the conversion of the gentiles, and abode in the hearts of those who embraced the law of the Gospel: and this came about after the barrenness that befell in the days of Abraham, that is, that spiritual want which was often in the hearts of the Jews when God the Father was called, in the Old Testament, the God and Lord of the Synagogue.

paras.t: Præterea quæritur, cur juxta mysticum sensum Deus prohibuit Isaac intrare Ægyptum, quod tamen Abrahæ patri ejus non negavit. Respondetur, ad insinuandum quod fideles non debent per vana vagari, sed in meditatione cœlestis patriæ suum cor cohibere, omnemque sæcularem vitare affectionem. Rursus per Abraham multarum gentium patrem, signantur prælati ; per Jacob laboriosum, activi ; per Isaac continentem, et multo tempore in thalamo quiescentem, claustrales et contemplativi. Abraham ergo et Jacob Ægyptum ingredi sunt permissi, ad innuendum quod prælati atque activi possunt sæculares accedere, et per mundum transire ; Isaac vero Ægyptum introire prohibitus est, quoniam contemplativi claustrales et religiosi, debent pro posse vitare discursus, et in abscondito vultus Dei persistere, nec sæcularium conversationi misceri : quia (ut magnus dixit Antonius) sicut pisces si extra aquam tardent, mox moriuntur, sic monachi infrigidantur, si inter sæculares tardaverint.
paras.en: Further, it is asked why, according to the mystical sense, God forbade Isaac to go into Egypt, which He did not refuse to Abraham his father. The answer is: to suggest that the faithful must not wander through vain things, but must keep their heart in meditation on the heavenly fatherland and shun every worldly affection. Again, by Abraham, the father of many nations, prelates are signified; by Jacob, the laborious, those of the active life; by Isaac, the continent, who rested a long time in the bridal chamber, cloistered men and contemplatives. Abraham, then, and Jacob were allowed to go into Egypt, to hint that prelates and those of the active life may go among worldly men and pass through the world; but Isaac was forbidden to enter Egypt, because cloistered contemplatives and religious must avoid going about as far as they can, and abide in the hidden place of God's face, and not mingle in the company of worldly men: for (as the great Antony said) as fish, if they linger out of the water, soon die, so monks grow cold if they linger among worldly men.

paras.t: Seminavit autem Isaac in terra illa, et invenit in ipso anno centuplum. Primo Christus per se ipsum seminavit verbum Dei in populo Judæorum. Unde et dixit : Non sum missus nisi ad oves, quæ perierunt, domus Israel. Deinde per sanctos Apostolos et cæteros prædicatores electos evangelizavit gentilibus in tempore gratiæ, quod est annus benignitatis, et annus acceptabilis Domino : in quo invenit centuplum, quoniam centies, imo innumerabiliter plures ex gentilibus sunt conversi, etiam statim in exordio prædicationis Apostolorum per totum mundum, aut paulo post. Benedixitque ei Dominus : post Christi ascensionem benedixit Deus Trinitas Christo in suis membris, hoc est, ipsis fidelibus copiosissima gratiarum largitus est munera. Habuit quoque possessiones ovium et armentorum, et familiæ plurimum : id est, ex omni genere hominum multi crediderunt in Salvatorem, et subjecti sunt ei, incipientes, proficientes, et perfecti ; rudes, simplices, ac subtiles, activi et contemplativi, diversorumque statuum, graduum, dignitatum ac ordinum homines.
paras.en: [[26:12|And Isaac sowed in that land, and he found that same year a hundredfold|Seminavit autem Isaac in terra illa, et invenit in ipso anno centuplum]]. First Christ by Himself sowed the word of God among the Jewish people. Hence He also said: [[Matt 15:24|I was not sent but to the sheep, that are lost of the house of Israel|Non sum missus nisi ad oves, quæ perierunt, domus Israel]]. Then, through the holy Apostles and the other chosen preachers, He preached the Gospel to the gentiles in the time of grace, which is the year of kindness and the year acceptable to the Lord: in which He found a hundredfold, since a hundred times, nay innumerably more, were converted from among the gentiles, even straightway at the beginning of the Apostles' preaching throughout the whole world, or a little after. [[26:12|and the Lord blessed him|Benedixitque ei Dominus]]: after Christ's ascension God the Trinity blessed Christ in His members, that is, bestowed on the faithful themselves most plentiful gifts of graces. [[26:14|And he had possessions of sheep and of herds, and a very great family|Habuit quoque possessiones ovium et armentorum, et familiæ plurimum]]: that is, out of every kind of men many believed in the Saviour and were made subject to Him, beginners, proficients and the perfect [the three stages of the spiritual life]; the unlettered, the simple and the subtle, the active and the contemplative, and men of divers states, degrees, dignities and orders.

paras.t: Propter quod inviderunt ei Palæstini, hoc est omnes infideles ac reprobi, præsertim indurati Judæi ac tyranni ac multi philosophi ; et omnes puteos quos foderant servi patris illius Abraham, illo tempore obstruxerunt, implentes humo. Per Abraham intelligitur Deus Pater, cujus servi fuerunt Patriarchæ et Prophetæ veteris Testamenti, qui puteos tot foderunt, quot libros sacros conscripserunt ; inter quos Moyses fuit præcipuus. Quumque Salvator et ejus discipuli cœpissent ex libris legis et Prophetarum probare Christi adventum ac ejus mysteria, et ea quæ christianæ sunt fidei roborare, præfati infideles conati sunt omnes hujusmodi libros seu puteos obturare, vel eos litteraliter solum carnaliterque exponendo, ut infideles Judæi, aut eorum veritatem negando, ut pagani et quidam hæretici : qui errores et falsæ expositiones fuerunt quasi humus et sordidum lutum, quo libros istos, quantum in ipsis fuit, sordidarunt.
paras.en: Wherefore [[26:14|the Palestines envying him|Palæstini]] [Denis turns the lemma into his own sentence: *inviderunt ei Palæstini*, "the Palestines envied him"], that is, all unbelievers and reprobates, especially the hardened Jews, and tyrants, and many philosophers; and they [[26:15|Stopped up at that time all the wells, that the servants of his father, Abraham, had digged, filling them up with earth|omnes puteos quos foderant servi patris illius Abraham, illo tempore obstruxerunt, implentes humo]]. By Abraham is understood God the Father, whose servants were the Patriarchs and Prophets of the Old Testament, who dug as many wells as they wrote sacred books; among whom Moses was the chief. And when the Saviour and His disciples had begun to prove from the books of the law and the Prophets the coming of Christ and His mysteries, and to strengthen the things that belong to the Christian faith, the aforesaid unbelievers tried to stop up all such books or wells, either by expounding them only according to the letter and carnally, as the unbelieving Jews did, or by denying their truth, as the pagans and certain heretics did: which errors and false expositions were as it were earth and filthy mud, with which they befouled these books, as far as lay in them.

paras.t: Ita tantum ut ipse Abimelech diceret ad Isaac : Recede a nobis, quoniam potentior nobis factus es valde. Per Abimelech intelliguntur principes sæculares ac perfidi, qui Christi Ecclesiam videntes quotidie numero ac donis Dei multiplicari, nisi sunt Christum excludere, et legem evangelicam eradicare. Ab illorum ergo obstinatorum cordibus Christus discessit, et juxta torrentem Geraræ habitavit in valle, hoc est, in humilium mentibus, atque in his qui gratiarum fluenta gratanter sunt amplexati, dignatus est commorari.
paras.en: [[26:16|Insomuch that Abimelech himself said to Isaac: Depart from us, for thou art become much mightier than we|Ita tantum ut ipse Abimelech diceret ad Isaac : Recede a nobis, quoniam potentior nobis factus es valde]]. By Abimelech are understood the worldly and faithless princes, who, seeing Christ's Church daily multiplied in number and in the gifts of God, strove to shut Christ out and to root out the law of the Gospel. From the hearts of those obstinate men, then, Christ departed, and dwelt in the valley by the torrent of Gerara: that is, He deigned to abide in the minds of the humble, and in those who have gladly embraced the streams of graces.

paras.t: Ibi rursum fodit alios puteos : hoc est, per Apostolos et Evangelistas libros novi edidit Testamenti, de quibus Isaias prædixit : Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris. Hos autem puteos foderunt jam ante servi Abrahæ : quia quod sancti Evangelistæ et Apostoli scripserunt, et docuerunt esse impletum, Prophetæ prædixerunt implendum. In multis quoque conveniunt documentis, ad quod innuendum Ezechiel vidit rotam in medio rotæ, videlicet novum Testamentum in veteri. Foderunt in torrente, et repererunt aquam vivam. Torrens est cor Christi, in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei absconditi : in quo torrente foderunt Evangelistæ et Apostoli, quia ex fonte dominici pectoris hauserunt, quidquid rite intellexerunt et conscripserunt. Idcirco in illo torrente invenerunt aquam vivam, hoc est evangelicæ legis doctrinam, gratiamque cœlestem, atque exuberantiam Spiritus Sancti. Unde dixit Salvator : Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum.
paras.en: There [[26:18|And he digged again other wells|rursum fodit alios puteos]]: that is, through the Apostles and Evangelists He brought forth the books of the New Testament, of which Isaias foretold: [[Is 12:3|Thou shall draw waters with joy out of the saviour's fountains:|Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris]] Now these wells the servants of Abraham had dug already before: for what the holy Evangelists and Apostles wrote and taught to have been fulfilled, the Prophets foretold as to be fulfilled. They agree in many teachings too; to hint at which Ezechiel saw [[Ezech 1:16|a wheel in the midst of a wheel|rotam in medio rotæ]], namely the New Testament within the Old. [[26:19|And they digged in the torrent, and found living water|Foderunt in torrente, et repererunt aquam vivam]]. The torrent is the heart of Christ, [[Col 2:3|In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge|in quo sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei absconditi]] [Denis's text adds *Dei*: "wisdom and knowledge of God"]: in which torrent the Evangelists and Apostles dug, since they drew from the fountain of the Lord's breast whatever they rightly understood and wrote. Therefore in that torrent they found living water, that is, the doctrine of the law of the Gospel, and heavenly grace, and the overflowing of the Holy Ghost. Hence the Saviour said: [[John 4:13|he that shall drink of the water that I will give him shall not thirst for ever|Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum]]

paras.t: Sed et ibi jurgium fuit pastorum Geraræ adversus pastores Isaac, dicentium : Nostra est aqua. Pastores Geraræ fuerunt sapientes sæculi atque philosophi, qui Christi contradixerunt doctrinis, discipulorumque ejus libros reprobare conati sunt, sicut Porphyrius, Celsus, Julianus, Averroes : et quidquid verum ac morale seu utile invenerunt in illis, dixerunt pertinere ad se, seu sumptum esse ex philosophicis libris : imo multi eorum dixerunt, Christum in Ægypto libros didicisse Platonis, et quidquid in Evangelio mirantur Christiani tanquam sublime, ex libris Platonis esse acceptum. Talis ergo puteus vocari potest Calumnia.
paras.en: [[26:20|But there also the herdsmen of Gerara strove against the herdsmen of Isaac, saying: It is our water|Sed et ibi jurgium fuit pastorum Geraræ adversus pastores Isaac, dicentium : Nostra est aqua]]. The herdsmen of Gerara were the wise men of the world and the philosophers, who spoke against the teachings of Christ and tried to discredit the books of His disciples, such as Porphyry, Celsus, Julian, Averroes: and whatever they found in them that was true and moral or useful, they said belonged to themselves, or was taken from the books of the philosophers: nay, many of them said that Christ learned the books of Plato in Egypt, and that whatever Christians admire in the Gospel as sublime was taken from the books of Plato. Such a well, then, may be called [[26:20|Calumny|Calumnia]].

paras.t: Foderunt et alium puteum : pro illo quoque rixati sunt. Alius puteus iste, est supernaturalis Evangelistarum et Apostolorum doctrina, quam constat in libris philosophorum non contineri : idcirco pastores illi increduli rixati sunt, asserendo talem doctrinam esse mendosam. Profectus inde, fodit alium puteum, pro quo non contenderunt. Iste puteus fuit illa doctrina apostolica atque evangelica, naturalem rationem non transcendens, ut quod unus est summus Deus, et consimilia quæ ex naturali ratione probantur : ideo in eo convenerunt et consenserunt, propter quod apte vocatur hic puteus Latitudo.
paras.en: [[26:21|And they digged also another|Foderunt et alium]] well: [[26:21|and for that they quarrelled likewise|pro illo quoque rixati sunt]]. This other well is the supernatural teaching of the Evangelists and Apostles, which, it is certain, is not contained in the books of the philosophers: so those unbelieving herdsmen quarrelled, asserting that such teaching was false. [[26:22|Going forward from thence, he digged another well, for which they contended not|Profectus inde, fodit alium puteum, pro quo non contenderunt]]. This well was that apostolic and evangelical teaching which does not go beyond natural reason, such as that there is one highest God, and the like, which are proved by natural reason: so in it they agreed and consented, for which reason this well is fitly called [[26:22|Latitude|Latitudo]] [*Latitudo*, breadth: the ground wide enough for all].

paras.t: Præcipitque servis suis ut foderent puteum. Isti servi fuerunt posteriores Doctores et Patres Ecclesiæ, qui post Apostolos composuerunt libros catholicos. Insuper quid designet, quod Abimelech rex cum suis venit ad Isaac inire amicitiæ fœdus, constat ex dictis in expositione vicesimi primi capituli.
paras.en: [[26:25|and commanded his servants to dig a well|Præcipitque servis suis ut foderent puteum]]. These servants were the later Doctors and Fathers of the Church, who after the Apostles composed catholic books. Moreover, what is signified by King Abimelech's coming to Isaac with his men to make a covenant of friendship is plain from what was said in the exposition of the twenty-first chapter.

27.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli vigesimi septimi: Senuit autem Isaac, et videre non poterat
27.title_en: Literal explanation of the twenty-seventh chapter: “Now Isaac was old, and he could not see”

paras.t: QUALITER Isaac patriarcha benedixit J […] filiis suis, præsens docet capitulum. Senuit autem Isaac, et caligaverunt oculi ejus, et videre non poterat. Ex naturali et enim causa cæcitatem incurrit, et partim fuit ex senio. Verumtamen diu vixit post ea quæ nunc facta leguntur: quia ut infra habetur, vixit adhuc post reditum Jacob a Mesopotamia. Vocavitque Esau filium suum majorem, id est primogenitum secundum naturam, et dixit ei, etc. : Vides, inquit, quod senuerim, et ignorem diem mortis meæ. Quasi dicat : Quum senex sim, volo adhuc sanus et mente compos peragere, quæ ante mortem facturus sum, ne morte aut sensus defectu præoccupatus, nequeam id explere.
paras.en: The present chapter teaches how the patriarch Isaac blessed J[…] […] his sons. [[27:1|Now Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, and he could not see|Senuit autem Isaac, et caligaverunt oculi ejus, et videre non poterat]]. For he fell into blindness from a natural cause, and it came partly from old age. Yet he lived long after the things that we now read were done: for, as is told below, he was still living after Jacob's return from Mesopotamia. [[27:1|and he called Esau, his elder son|Vocavitque Esau filium suum majorem]], that is, the firstborn by nature, [[27:1|and said to him|et dixit ei]], etc.: [[27:2|Thou seest that I am old, and know not the day of my death|Vides, inquit, quod senuerim, et ignorem diem mortis meæ]]. As if to say: Since I am old, I wish, while I am still sound and in my right mind, to carry out what I am to do before my death, lest, overtaken by death or by the failing of my senses, I should be unable to accomplish it.

paras.t: Sume arma tua, id est venationis tuæ instrumenta, pharetram et arcum, et egredere foras. Quumque venatu aliquid apprehenderis, fac mihi inde pulmentum, id est coctionem, sicut velle me nosti : quia frequenter talem cibum mihi parasti, adjuvante te matre tua aut famula : et affer cibum sic præparatum, ut comedam, et benedicat tibi anima mea, id est ego ipse ex desiderio animæ et cordis affectu, antequam moriar. Cur Isaac filium suum benedicere cupiens, primo ipsi istud injunxit ? Non utique ex carnali affectu aut intemperantiæ appetitu, sed ut filius suus sibi in isto obtemperans, per obedientiam istam magis idoneus redderetur ad benedictionis susceptionem, et item ut ipsemet Isaac ex beneficio atque obsequio sibi a filio exhibitis, magis benevolus efficeretur ad filii sui benedictionem. Rursus, quoniam intendebat filio benedictionem conferre, etiam quantum ad temporalia bona, voluit primo ab eo aliquid temporale, præsertim refectionem, suscipere.
paras.en: [[27:3|Take thy arms|Sume arma tua]], that is, the instruments of thy hunting, [[27:3|thy quiver, and bow, and go abroad|pharetram et arcum, et egredere foras]]. [[27:3|and when thou hast taken something by hunting|Quumque venatu aliquid apprehenderis]], [[27:4|Make me a savoury meat thereof|fac mihi inde pulmentum]], that is, a cooked dish, [[27:4|as thou knowest I like|sicut velle me nosti]]: for thou hast often prepared me such food, with the help of thy mother or of a maidservant: [[27:4|and bring it|et affer]] the food so prepared, [[27:4|that I may eat: and my soul may bless thee, before I die|ut comedam, et benedicat tibi anima mea]]; *my soul*, that is, I myself, from the desire of my soul and the affection of my heart. Why did Isaac, wishing to bless his son, first lay this upon him? Not, surely, from carnal affection or a craving of intemperance, but so that his son, obeying him in this, might through this obedience be made more fit to receive the blessing; and also so that Isaac himself, from the kindness and service shown him by his son, might be made more kindly disposed to bless him. Again, since he meant to confer a blessing on his son with regard to temporal goods also, he wished first to receive something temporal from him, especially refreshment.

paras.t: Quod quum audisset Rebecca, et ille abisset in agrum ut jussionem patris impleret, dixit filio suo Jacob, quem specialius diligebat propter causas in expositione capituli vicesimi quinti introductas : Audivi patrem tuum loquentem cum Esau, etc. Nunc ergo, fili mi, acquiesce consiliis meis, et pergens ad gregem, affer mihi duos hœdos optimos, ut faciam ex eis escas patri tuo quibus libenter vescitur : quas quum attuleris et comederit, benedicat tibi, etc. Istud consuluit Rebecca, quoniam sicut præhabitum est, ex revelatione divina cognovit Jacob esse præelectum a Deo, et ipsi Esau præferendum in benedictione, atque ad ipsum primogenituræ jus pertinere.
paras.en: [[27:5|And when Rebecca had heard this, and he was gone into the field to fulfil his father's commandment|Quod quum audisset Rebecca, et ille abisset in agrum ut jussionem patris impleret]], [[27:6|She said to her son Jacob|dixit filio suo Jacob]], whom she loved more especially, for the reasons brought forward in the exposition of the twenty-fifth chapter[[Gen 25:28||]]: [[27:6|I heard thy father talking with Esau|Audivi patrem tuum loquentem cum Esau]], etc. [[27:8|Now therefore, my son, follow my counsel|Nunc ergo, fili mi, acquiesce consiliis meis]], [[27:9|And go thy way to the flock, bring me two kids of the best, that I may make of them meat for thy father, such as he gladly eateth|et pergens ad gregem, affer mihi duos hœdos optimos, ut faciam ex eis escas patri tuo quibus libenter vescitur]]: [[27:10|Which when thou hast brought in, and he hath eaten, he may bless thee|quas quum attuleris et comederit, benedicat tibi]], etc. Rebecca gave this counsel because, as was said before, she knew by divine revelation that Jacob was chosen beforehand by God and to be preferred to Esau in the blessing, and that the right of the firstborn belonged to him.

paras.t: Cui ille respondit : Nosti quod Esau frater meus homo pilosus sit : fuit enim per totam corporis sui pellem hispidus seu crinitus : et ego lenis, id est corpore tener et tactu mollis. Si attrectaverit me pater meus, et senserit, timeo ne putet me sibi voluisse illudere, et inducat super me maledictionem pro benedictione. Ad quem mater : In me sit, ait, ista maledictio, etc., id est, maledictionis illius periculum accipio super me. Quasi dicat : Certa sum quod non maledicet tibi, sed benedicet : et si malediceret tibi, imputandum esset mihi magis quam tibi, quia induco te ad ista agenda.
paras.en: [[27:11|And he answered her: Thou knowest that Esau, my brother, is a hairy man|Cui ille respondit : Nosti quod Esau frater meus homo pilosus sit]]: for he was shaggy or hairy over the whole skin of his body: [[27:11|and I am smooth|et ego lenis]], that is, tender of body and soft to the touch. [[27:12|If my father should feel me, and perceive it, I fear lest he will think|Si attrectaverit me pater meus, et senserit, timeo ne putet]] I would mock him, [[27:12|and I shall bring upon me a curse instead of a blessing|et inducat super me maledictionem pro benedictione]]. [[27:13|And his mother said to him|Ad quem mater]]: [[27:13|Upon me be this curse|In me sit, ait, ista maledictio]], etc., that is, I take the danger of that curse upon myself. As if to say: I am sure that he will not curse thee, but will bless thee: and if he did curse thee, it would be laid to my charge rather than to thine, since I am leading thee to do these things.

paras.t: Abiit Jacob, et attulit, deditque matri duos optimos hœdos. Paravit illa cibos, et vestibus Esau valde bonis induit eum, id est vestibus sacerdotalibus, quia (ut habitum est) in lege naturæ primogeniti fuerunt sacerdotes, habebantque vestes speciales ac pretiosas, quibus induebantur dum sacrificia offerebant, et quando a patre suo benedictionem acceperunt finalem : pel[…] Jacob, […] : ut videretur habere manus pilosas, et collum Jacob operuit, ne nuda colli ejus caro tangeretur ab Isaac, et sic cognosceretur ab eo.
paras.en: [[27:14|He went|Abiit]] (Jacob), [[27:14|and brought, and gave them to his mother|et attulit, deditque matri]] two kids of the best. [[27:14|She dressed meats|Paravit illa cibos]], [[27:15|And she put on him very good garments of Esau|et vestibus Esau valde bonis induit eum]], that is, priestly garments: for (as was said) under the law of nature the firstborn were priests, and had special and precious garments, which they put on when they offered sacrifices and when they received the final blessing from their father: […] Jacob, […] [the lemma of v. 16 is lost in the transcription]: that he might seem to have hairy hands; and she covered Jacob's neck, lest the bare flesh of his neck should be touched by Isaac, and he so be known by him.

paras.t: Quibus illatis, id est, cibis a Rebecca paratis, ipsi Isaac allatis a Jacob, dixit : Pater mi. At ille respondit : Audio. Quis es tu, fili mi? Dixitque Jacob : Ego sum primogenitus tuus Esau. Feci sicut præcepisti mihi. Videntur in verbis istis duo mendacia contineri, quia non fuit Esau, nec fecit quod Isaac jussit, sumendo arcum et pharetram ad venandum, etc. Respondetur ad primum, quod sicut Christus in Evangelio ait, Joannes ipse est Elias, non utique in persona, sed in similitudine seu conformitate sanctitatis atque officii : sic Jacob dixit veraciter se esse Esau primogenitum, non substantialiter, sed similitudinarie, utpote dignitate primogenituræ : juxta quem modum, quum Christus interrogasset Apostolos, Quem me dicunt homines ? dixerunt : Alii Joannem Baptistam, alii Jeremiam, etc. Ad aliud respondetur, quod Jacob in multis fecerat sicut Isaac sibi præcepit, et ita verificantur verba inducta. Et tamen si Jacob aperte dixisset, Sumpsi arcum et ivi venatum : intelligendum esset, Ego, id est is cujus personam repræsento, et cujus similitudinem gero, jusque possideo, feci hoc, atque tantumdem est quasi personaliter hoc fecissem.
paras.en: [[27:18|Which when he had carried in|Quibus illatis]], that is, when the food prepared by Rebecca had been brought to Isaac by Jacob, [[27:18|he said: My father|dixit : Pater mi]]. [[27:18|But he answered: I hear|At ille respondit : Audio]]. [[27:18|Who art thou, my son|Quis es tu, fili mi]]? [[27:19|And Jacob said: I am Esau, thy firstborn: I have done as thou didst command me|Dixitque Jacob : Ego sum primogenitus tuus Esau. Feci sicut præcepisti mihi]]. In these words two lies seem to be contained: for he was not Esau, nor had he done what Isaac commanded, taking bow and quiver to go hunting, etc. To the first it is answered that, as Christ says in the Gospel of John the Baptist, [[Matt 11:14|he is Elias|ipse est Elias]][[Matt 17:12||]] [the margin gives Matth. xi, 13, 14, xxvii, 12, 13; the second passage is Matt 17:12–13], not indeed in person, but in likeness or conformity of holiness and office: so Jacob said truly that he was Esau the firstborn, not in substance but by likeness, namely in the dignity of the birthright: in which way, when Christ had asked the Apostles, [[Matt 16:13|Whom do men say|Quem me dicunt homines]]? [Denis's wording, *Quem me dicunt homines*, is nearest Mark 8:27] they said: [[Matt 16:14|Some John the Baptist|Alii Joannem Baptistam]], [[Matt 16:14|and others Jeremias|alii Jeremiam]], etc. To the other it is answered that Jacob had in many things done as Isaac commanded him, and so the words brought in are made true. And yet, if Jacob had said openly, I took my bow and went hunting, it would have to be understood: I, that is, he whose person I represent, whose likeness I bear, and whose right I possess, did this; and it is as much as if I had done it in person.

paras.t: Surge, sede, et comede de venatione mea, etc., id est cibum coctum ex hœdis, quos per modum venantis tuli de grege, ut coquerentur. Voluntas Dei fuit, id est effectus divinæ voluntatis, ut cito mihi occurreret quod quærebam : nam, Deo volente, invenit repente hœdos in grege.
paras.en: [[27:19|arise, sit and eat of my venison|Surge, sede, et comede de venatione mea]], etc., that is, the food cooked from the kids which, after the manner of a hunter, I took from the flock to be cooked. [[27:20|It was the will of God|Voluntas Dei fuit]], that is, the effect of God's will, [[27:20|that what I sought came quickly in my way|ut cito mihi occurreret quod quærebam]]: for, by God's will, he found the kids suddenly in the flock.

paras.t: Dixitque Isaac : Accede huc, ut tangam te, fili mi, et probem utrum tu sis filius meus Esau, an non. Videbatur quippe ipsi Isaac ex auditu, quod non esset Esau, ideo voluit certificari per tactum, et experiri palpando an Esau esset. Accessit ille ad patrem, et palpato eo dixit Isaac : Vox quidem, vox Jacob est ; sed manus, manus sunt Esau. Ex quo patet, quod tetigit seu palpavit manus ipsius Jacob, quas dixit esse manus Esau, id est similes manibus ejus in pilositate, vel realiter manus ejus, quia hoc æstimavit. Et non cognovit eum, quod esset personaliter Jacob, quia pilosæ manus similitudinem majoris expresserant, id est, manus Jacob pelliculis coopertæ, ostenderunt eum esse similem, imo et eumdem filio primogenito. Primo namque prætendebant similitudinem, et ex ea Isaac arguit et conclusit identitatem, et in hoc aliquo modo erravit, non tamen peccavit, quia non omnis error est culpa. Aliquo etiam modo non erravit, quia Jacob fuit ille, ad quem jure divino et speciali Dei dono primogenitura ac benedictio pertinebant, et illum Isaac exquirebat, præsentemque esse volebat ac æstimabat, et eumdem benedicere intendebat : quod totum sic fuit seu factum est.
paras.en: [[27:21|And Isaac said: Come hither, that I may feel thee, my son, and may prove whether thou be my son Esau, or no|Dixitque Isaac : Accede huc, ut tangam te, fili mi, et probem utrum tu sis filius meus Esau, an non]]. For it seemed to Isaac from the hearing that it was not Esau; therefore he wished to make sure by touch, and to find out by feeling whether it was Esau. [[27:22|He came near to his father, and when he had felt him, Isaac said: The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob; but the hands, are the hands of Esau|Accessit ille ad patrem, et palpato eo dixit Isaac : Vox quidem, vox Jacob est ; sed manus, manus sunt Esau]]. From this it is plain that he touched or felt the hands of Jacob, which he said were the hands of Esau, that is, like his hands in hairiness, or really his hands, since that is what he thought. [[27:23|And he knew him not|Et non cognovit eum]], that is, that he was Jacob in person, [[27:23|because his hairy hands made him like to the elder|quia pilosæ manus similitudinem majoris expresserant]], that is, Jacob's hands, covered with the little skins, showed him to be like, nay the same as, the firstborn son. For first they gave the appearance of likeness, and from it Isaac argued and concluded identity; and in this he erred in a way, yet he did not sin, since not every error is a fault. In a way, too, he did not err: for Jacob was the one to whom, by divine right and by a special gift of God, the birthright and the blessing belonged; and it was he whom Isaac was seeking, whom he wished and judged to be present, and whom he meant to bless: and all of this was so, and was so done.

paras.t: Benedicens ergo illi, id est, benedicere proponens ipse Isaac filio suo Jacob, ait : Tu es filius meus Esau ? Hoc pro majori certificatione quæsivit. Respondit Jacob : Ego sum, ille qui juste ac merito fuit benedicendus, quem et Isaac benedicere proponebat. At ille : Affer mihi, inquit, cibos de venatione tua, ut benedicat tibi anima mea. Quos quum oblatos comedisset, obtulit ei etiam vinum. Quo hausto, dixit ad eum : Accede ad me, et da mihi osculum, fili mi, ut majori caritate tui accensus, te affectuosius benedicam. Accessit et osculatus est eum.
paras.en: [[27:23|Then blessing him|Benedicens ergo illi]], that is, Isaac proposing to bless his son Jacob, [[27:24|He said: Art thou my son Esau|ait : Tu es filius meus Esau]]? This he asked for greater certainty. [[27:24|He answered: I am|Respondit Jacob : Ego sum]] (Jacob): that is, the one who was justly and deservedly to be blessed, and whom Isaac too proposed to bless. [[27:25|Then he said: Bring me the meats of thy hunting, my son, that my soul may bless thee|At ille : Affer mihi, inquit, cibos de venatione tua, ut benedicat tibi anima mea]]. [[27:25|And when they were brought, and he had eaten, he offered him wine also|Quos quum oblatos comedisset, obtulit ei etiam vinum]]. [[27:25|which after he had drunk|Quo hausto]], [[27:26|He said to him: Come near me, and give me a kiss, my son|dixit ad eum : Accede ad me, et da mihi osculum, fili mi]], so that, kindled with greater charity for thee, I may bless thee more lovingly. [[27:27|He came near, and kissed him|Accessit et osculatus est eum]].

paras.t: Statimque ut sensit vestimentorum illius fragrantiam : vestes enim sacerdotales consueverunt odoriferæ esse, quia cum speciebus boni odoris reponebantur, sive ex alia causa, et hoc propter proprii officii dignitatem ; benedicens illi, ait : Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni, cui benedixit Dominus. Juxta superficiem litteræ, litteralemque sensum primo occurrentem, iste est sensus, quod Isaac percepto odore suavi vestimentorum sacerdotalium, quibus Jacob erat indutus, et delectatus illo odore ex corporali attactu ipsius Jacob, commendavit filium suum ex illo odore, vel potius ex dignitate primogenituræ, quam vestes illæ monstrabant : unde et odorem illum dixit esse odorem filii sui, quia redundabat in eum ; quem etiam odorem comparavit agro pleno fructibus bene redolentibus, cui et Dominus benedixit, magnam ac dulcem fecunditatem ei præstando. Det tibi Deus de rore cœli et de pinguedine terræ, abundantiam frumenti et vini et olei, hoc est copiosum frumentum, abundansque vinum, et oleum multum, quæ ex rore qui generatur in cœlo aereo, et pinguedine terræ causantur. Ad horum quippe productionem, concurrunt corpora cœlestia motu, lumine et influentia, per modum causæ efficientis ; ros et pluvia, per modum causæ disponentis : terra pinguis, ut causa materialis. Solet quoque per tria hæc, tota terræ fertilitas designari : quia per frumentum cibus, per vinum potus, per oleum condimentum signatur.
paras.en: [[27:27|And immediately as he smelled the fragrant smell of his garments|Statimque ut sensit vestimentorum illius fragrantiam]]: for priestly garments were usually fragrant, since they were laid up with sweet-smelling spices, or for some other reason; and this because of the dignity of their office; [[27:27|blessing him, he said: Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field, which the Lord hath blessed|benedicens illi, ait : Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni, cui benedixit Dominus]]. According to the surface of the letter, and the literal sense that first comes to mind, the sense is this: that Isaac, perceiving the sweet smell of the priestly garments in which Jacob was clothed, and delighted by that smell through bodily contact with Jacob, commended his son from that smell, or rather from the dignity of the birthright which those garments showed: hence he also called that smell the smell of his son, since it overflowed upon him; and he compared it to a field full of sweet-smelling fruits, which the Lord had blessed, granting it great and sweet fruitfulness. [[27:28|God give thee of the dew of heaven, and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of corn and wine|Det tibi Deus de rore cœli et de pinguedine terræ, abundantiam frumenti et vini et olei]] [Denis's text adds *et olei*, "and oil"], that is, plentiful corn, abundant wine and much oil, which are caused by the dew that is formed in the airy heaven and by the fatness of the earth. For to the producing of these things the heavenly bodies concur by their motion, light and influence, as the efficient cause; dew and rain as the disposing cause; the fat earth as the material cause. By these three, too, the whole fertility of the earth is commonly signified: for by corn food is signified, by wine drink, by oil seasoning.

paras.t: Et serviant tibi populi, et adorent te, adoratione duliæ, tribus. Esto dominus fratrum tuorum, et incurventur ante te filii matris tuæ. Quando hæc dicebantur, non habuit Jacob nisi unum fratrem, nec mater ejus habuit filios nisi duos, a quorum uno dumtaxat Jacob poterat adorari, a quo tamen nunquam legitur adoratus, sed ipse potius suum fratrem septies adoravit pronus in terram, ut infra habetur : ideo verba ista sunt mystica valde, et prophetico sensu plena, nec sunt impleta in Jacob et Esau, imo Esau fuit ditior et potentior ac dominantior fratre suo Jacob : sed in posteris eorum impleta sunt, quia ex Jacob descendit tribus regalis, et potentissimi reges, præsertim David et Salomon, quibus servierunt ceteri filii Israel ac Idumæi. Maxime vero ista impleta sunt in Christo, cui omnis populus, tribus et linguæ jam servierunt, ac serviunt : et in sanctis Apostolis, quos Deus constituit principes super omnem terram, ut infra tangetur.
paras.en: [[27:29|And let peoples serve thee, and tribes worship thee|Et serviant tibi populi, et adorent te, adoratione duliæ, tribus]] [Denis glosses *adorent* "with the adoration of *dulia*", that is, the honour paid to creatures, not the worship due to God alone]: [[27:29|be thou lord of thy brethren, and let thy mother's children bow down before thee|Esto dominus fratrum tuorum, et incurventur ante te filii matris tuæ]]. When these things were said, Jacob had only one brother, and his mother had only two sons, by one of whom alone Jacob could be worshipped; yet we never read that he was worshipped by him; rather he himself worshipped his brother seven times, bowing down to the ground, as is told below: so these words are very mystical and full of a prophetic sense, and they were not fulfilled in Jacob and Esau; indeed Esau was richer, mightier and more lordly than his brother Jacob: but they were fulfilled in their descendants, since from Jacob came the royal tribe and very mighty kings, especially David and Solomon, whom the other sons of Israel and the Idumeans served[[2 Kings 8:14||]]. But they were fulfilled above all in Christ, whom every people, tribe and tongue has already served and serves[[Dan 7:14||]]; and in the holy Apostles, whom God has made [[Ps 44:17|princes over all the earth|principes super omnem terram]], as will be touched on below.

paras.t: Qui maledixerit tibi, sit ille maledictus, et qui benedixerit tibi, benedictionibus repleatur. Per hæc verba videtur Isaac filio suo Jacob bona spiritualia imprecatus, ut sit sensus : Tantis virtutum ac gratiæ donis repleatis tu et posteritas tua a Deo, ut justo zelo valeat maledici ei, qui maledixerit tibi ; et benedici, qui benedixerit tibi. Hinc Rabbi Paulus ait : Maledicere alicui, communiter importat malum ei optare, quod semper peccatum est, nisi proximus sit peccator, aut saltem peccabilis, ita ut optetur ei aliquod malum pœnæ, quatenus ex ea consequatur aliquod bonum : ex quo constat, quod boni et justi nunquam sunt maledicendi. Ex hoc ergo quod Isaac maledixit prophetice maledicentibus Jacob, intelligitur quod posteritas Jacob, præsertim spiritualis, cui hæc benedictio principaliter dirigebatur, futura erat virtuosa et justa, ita quod ei maledicentes, digni essent maledici.
paras.en: [[27:29|Cursed be he that curseth thee: and let him that blesseth thee be filled with blessings|Qui maledixerit tibi, sit ille maledictus, et qui benedixerit tibi, benedictionibus repleatur]]. By these words Isaac seems to have called down spiritual goods on his son Jacob, so that the sense is: Mayest thou and thy posterity be filled by God with such great gifts of virtues and of grace that, with just zeal, he who curses thee may be cursed, and he who blesses thee may be blessed. Hence Rabbi Paul says: To curse someone commonly implies wishing him evil, which is always a sin, unless the neighbour be a sinner, or at least liable to sin, so that some evil of punishment is wished him in order that some good may follow from it: from which it is plain that the good and just are never to be cursed. From the fact, then, that Isaac prophetically cursed those who curse Jacob, it is understood that the posterity of Jacob, especially the spiritual posterity, to whom this blessing was chiefly directed, would be virtuous and just, so that those who cursed it would deserve to be cursed.

paras.t: Præterea, in Scholastica historia legitur : In benedictione ipsius Jacob quatuor continentur : Primum est abundantia victualium, quum dicitur, Det tibi Deus de rore cœli, etc. ; secundum est excellentia potentiæ, quum additur, Serviant tibi populi, etc. : tertium est præeminentia primogenituræ, quum subditur, Esto dominus fratrum tuorum. Et ista sunt temporalia, præsentisque vitæ. Quartum est spirituale, et circa futura, quum dicitur, Qui maledixerit tibi, etc. Alii dicunt, quod Isaac imprecatus est Jacob seu posteris ejus tria : Primum est, temporalium opulentia ; secundum, honor et excellentia, quum dicitur, Serviant tibi populi, usque ibi. Qui maledixerit tibi : tertium est, aliorum ad eum benevolentia, quum infertur, Qui maledixerit tibi : sic tamen, ut per temporalia ista intelligantur simul et spiritualia ac æterna, tanquam principaliter intenta, quoniam ex sensibilibus atque terrenis, homo erigitur ad cœlestia ac divina.
paras.en: Further, in the Scholastic History we read: In the blessing of Jacob four things are contained. The first is abundance of victuals, when it is said, [[27:28|God give thee of the dew of heaven|Det tibi Deus de rore cœli]], etc.; the second is excellence of power, when it is added, [[27:29|let peoples serve thee|Serviant tibi populi]], etc.; the third is the pre-eminence of the birthright, when there follows, [[27:29|be thou lord of thy brethren|Esto dominus fratrum tuorum]]. And these are temporal, and belong to the present life. The fourth is spiritual and concerns things to come, when it is said, [[27:29|Cursed be he that curseth thee|Qui maledixerit tibi]], etc. Others say that Isaac called down three things on Jacob or his descendants. The first is abundance of temporal goods; the second, honour and excellence, when it is said, Let peoples serve thee, as far as the words, Cursed be he that curseth thee; the third, the good will of others towards him, when there follows, Cursed be he that curseth thee: yet in such a way that by these temporal things spiritual and eternal things are understood together with them, as what is chiefly intended, since from things of sense and of earth man is raised up to heavenly and divine things.

paras.t: Secundum Josephum, Rebecca oravit pro Jacob, ut optatam benedictionem consequeretur a patre. Isaac quoque benedicturus filio suo Jacob, orationem præmisit, dicendo : Domine omnium sæculorum, et creator universæ substantiæ, tu patri meo et mihi abundanter benedixisti, conserva propitius hunc filium meum, et ab omni malo custodi, ac benedic, etc.
paras.en: According to Josephus, Rebecca prayed for Jacob, that he might obtain the desired blessing from his father. Isaac too, about to bless his son Jacob, first offered a prayer, saying: Lord of all ages, and Creator of all substance, Thou hast blessed my father and me abundantly; graciously preserve this my son, and keep him from all evil, and bless him, etc.

paras.t: Vix Isaac sermonem compleverat, id est verba prælatæ benedictionis cum Jacob. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod forsitan plura dixisset ad Jacob, nisi Esau supervenisset ; attamen Deo sic disponente, benedictionis sermonem complevit. Et egresso Jacob foras, de thalamo, in quo cæcus pater quievit : et forsan Jacob sensit adventum Esau, propter quod festinavit exire ; aliter non apparet quod tam repente, et quasi abrupte post patris sui verba exisset : venit Esau, etc. Expavit Isaac stupore vehementi ; et ultra quam credi, id est credendo conjici seu percipi, potest per naturam secundum communem usum et cursum : admirans, quod sic decipi potuit circa notitiam Jacob, vel potius admirans dispensationem pietatis divinæ, et ordinationem sapientiæ Dei, in hoc facto, quod scilicet Deus voluit et præordinavit sic fieri, ut Jacob benediceretur. Hoc etiam in admiratione ista ex revelatione divina cognovit quod ante nescivit. Hinc loquitur Augustinus : Expavit Isaac stupore vehementi, ita ut quædam mentis suæ alienatio sequeretur, quæ raptus aut ecstasis dicitur, et in magnarum rerum revelationibus fieri solet. Unde intelligendum est, ipsum Isaac tunc spiritualiter admonitum esse a Deo, ut confirmaret benedictionem suam in Jacob, cui alias potius potuisset irasci quod patrem fefellerit. Sic et in Adam præcessit ecstasis antequam dixit, Erunt duo in carne una : quod est magnum sacramentum in Christo atque Ecclesia. Hæc Augustinus.
paras.en: [[27:30|Isaac had scarce ended his words|Vix Isaac sermonem compleverat]], that is, the words of the aforesaid blessing with Jacob. From this it seems to follow that he would perhaps have said more to Jacob, had not Esau come upon them; yet, by God's disposing, he completed the words of the blessing. [[27:30|Jacob being now gone out abroad|Et egresso Jacob foras]], from the chamber in which his blind father lay: and perhaps Jacob perceived Esau's coming, and for that reason made haste to go out; otherwise it does not appear why he should have gone out so suddenly and, as it were, abruptly after his father's words: [[27:30|Esau came|venit Esau]], etc. [[27:33|Isaac was struck with fear, and astonished exceedingly|Expavit Isaac stupore vehementi]]; [[27:33|beyond what can be believed|et ultra quam credi]], that is, beyond what can be conjectured or perceived by believing, by nature, according to the common use and course of things: [[27:33|and wondering|admirans]] that he could have been so deceived in knowing Jacob, or rather wondering at the dispensation of the divine goodness and the ordering of God's wisdom in this deed, namely that God willed and foreordained that it should so be done, that Jacob should be blessed. In this wonder he also learned by divine revelation what he did not know before. Hence Augustine says: *Isaac was struck with fear, and astonished exceedingly*, so that there followed a certain going out of his mind, which is called rapture or ecstasy, and which usually comes about in revelations of great things. Hence it is to be understood that Isaac was then spiritually admonished by God to confirm his blessing on Jacob, with whom he might otherwise rather have been angry for deceiving his father. So also in Adam an ecstasy went before, before he said, [[Gen 2:24|they shall be two in one flesh|Erunt duo in carne una]]: which is a great sacrament in Christ and the Church. Thus far Augustine.

paras.t: Itaque Isaac admirans, ait : Quis igitur ille est, qui dudum captam venationem attulit mihi? Non ex ignorantia, sed admirationis abundantia, dixit : Quis igitur ille est ? Jam quippe sciebat quod Jacob fuit. Porro quod addidit, Qui dudum captam venationem, etc., adjecit secundum suam æstimationem, quia sibi revelatum non fuit qualiter Jacob attulit materiam cibi illius non venando, sed ex grege duos hœdos sumendo. Benedixique ei, et erit benedictus : quasi diceret, Benedictionem ei collatam revocare non volo, nec valeo, quoniam Deus sic ordinavit.
paras.en: So Isaac, wondering, [[27:33|said: Who is he then that even now brought me venison|ait : Quis igitur ille est, qui dudum captam venationem attulit mihi?]]? Not from ignorance, but from the fulness of his wonder, he said: Who is he then? For he already knew that it was Jacob. And what he added, *that even now brought me venison that he had taken*, etc., he added according to his own estimation, since it had not been revealed to him how Jacob brought the stuff of that food not by hunting but by taking two kids from the flock. [[27:33|and I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed|Benedixique ei, et erit benedictus]]: as if he said, I neither will nor can revoke the blessing given him, since God has so ordained.

paras.t: Auditis Esau sermonibus patris sui Isaac, irrugiit clamore magno : hoc est, ex intensissimo cordis dolore instar leonis terribiliter exclamavit. Verumtamen non ex vera compunctione aut contritione, neque ex caritate, sed potius ex privato amore et cupiditatis affectu quo ad terrenam prosperitatem valide afficiebatur, atque ex hoc de ejus amissione intensissime tristabatur : idcirco, teste Apostolo, non invenit pœnitentiæ locum, quanquam cum lacrimis inquisisset eam. Et consternatus, id est immoderato mœrore oppressus, ait : Benedic etiam et mihi, pater mi ; quasi diceret, Saltem in temporalibus benedic mihi.
paras.en: [[27:34|Esau having heard his father's words, roared out with a great cry|Auditis Esau sermonibus patris sui Isaac, irrugiit clamore magno]]: that is, out of the most intense grief of heart he cried out terribly like a lion. Yet not out of true compunction or contrition, nor out of charity, but rather out of self-love and the affection of covetousness, by which he was strongly attached to earthly prosperity, and so grieved most intensely at its loss: therefore, as the Apostle bears witness, [[Heb 12:17|he found no place of repentance|non invenit pœnitentiæ locum]], [[Heb 12:17|although with tears he had sought it|quanquam cum lacrimis inquisisset eam]]. [[27:34|and, being in a consternation|Et consternatus]], that is, overwhelmed by immoderate sorrow, [[27:34|said: Bless me also, my father|ait : Benedic etiam et mihi, pater mi]]; as if he said, At least bless me in temporal things.

paras.t: Qui ait, se quodammodo excusando : Venit germanus tuus fraudulenter, hoc est per modum fraudulenti, utpote cum verbis et factis obscuris, et pie circumventivis, et accepit benedictionem tuam, id est, quam tu habuisses, secundum communem legem, in quantum primogenitus, nisi Deus aliter disposuisset ; imo et nisi tu promeruisses ea privari, primitiva tua fratri tuo vendendo. Circa hoc scribit Lyra : Hebræi dicunt, Venit germanus tuus prudenter. Nam dictio Hebraica, interdum dolum, interdum prudentiam seu bonam cautelam significat, pro qua nunc accipi debet. Jam namque Isaac noverat, quod Jacob ex ordinatione divina benedictionem obtinuit : propter quod factum suum non potuit proprie fraudi adscribi. Hæc Lyra. Sed Rabbi Paulus his contradicit, asserens dictionem illam Hebraicam non esse æquivocam, sed fraudem seu dolum tantummodo significare. Sed quia fraus quæ proprie in malo accipitur, quandoque in bono sumitur abusive, juxta illud Apostoli, Quum essem astutus, dolo vos cepi : idcirco hæc dictio fraudulenter, nunc abusive in bono acceptata est.
paras.en: [[27:35|And he said|Qui ait]], excusing himself in a manner: [[27:35|Thy brother came deceitfully|Venit germanus tuus fraudulenter]], that is, after the manner of a deceiver, namely with words and deeds that were obscure and lovingly circumventing, [[27:35|and got thy blessing|et accepit benedictionem tuam]], that is, the one thou wouldst have had by the common law, as firstborn, had not God disposed otherwise; nay, and hadst thou not deserved to be deprived of it by selling thy firstborn's rights to thy brother. On this Lyra writes: The Hebrews say, Thy brother came *prudently*. For the Hebrew word means sometimes guile, sometimes prudence or good caution, and here it should be taken in the latter sense. For Isaac knew already that Jacob had obtained the blessing by divine ordinance: for which reason his deed could not properly be put down to fraud. Thus far Lyra. But Rabbi Paul contradicts them, asserting that that Hebrew word is not equivocal, but means only fraud or guile. But since fraud, which is properly taken in a bad sense, is sometimes taken loosely in a good one, according to that saying of the Apostle, [[2 Cor 12:16|being crafty, I caught you by guile|Quum essem astutus, dolo vos cepi]]: therefore this word *deceitfully* is here taken loosely in a good sense.

paras.t: At ille subjunxit : Juste vocatum est nomen ejus Jacob, quod interpretatur supplantator; supplantavit […] altera vice. Primogenita […], id est, semel me supplantavit, privando me primogenitura per emptionem abreptam. hoc tamen est falsum, tum quoniam Esau sponte et ex proposito vendidit ea, tum quia ex prædestinatione divina pertinebant ad Jacob ; et nunc secundo subripuit benedictionem meam, id est mihi debitam : quod etiam falsum est, quoniam benedictionem illam non subripuit Jacob injuste ut alienam, sed ut sibi debitam, tam ex divina præordinatione, quam ex jure primogenituræ in ipsum translatæ. Verum est tamen, quod supplantavit Esau fratrem suum, id est, ei prævaluit in utraque hac vice, præsertim quum scriptum sit in Osee : In utero supplantavit fratrem suum, hoc est, in utero aliquid fecit sua collisione, per quod futura tunc supplantatio figurabatur.
paras.en: [[27:36|But he said again: Rightly is his name called Jacob|At ille subjunxit : Juste vocatum est nomen ejus Jacob]], which is interpreted *supplanter*; [[27:36|he hath supplanted|supplantavit]] […] [[27:36|lo this second time|altera vice]]. [[27:36|My birthright|Primogenita]] […], that is, once he supplanted me, depriving me of the birthright by a purchase snatched from me. Yet this is false, both because Esau sold it of his own will and on purpose, and because by divine predestination it belonged to Jacob; [[27:36|and now this second time he hath stolen away my blessing|et nunc secundo subripuit benedictionem meam]], that is, the one due to me: which is also false, since Jacob did not steal that blessing unjustly as another's, but as due to himself, both by divine foreordaining and by the right of the birthright transferred to him. Yet it is true that he supplanted his brother Esau, that is, prevailed over him on both these occasions, especially since it is written in Osee: [[Osee 12:3|In the womb he supplanted his brother|In utero supplantavit fratrem suum]], that is, in the womb he did something by his struggling by which the supplanting then to come was prefigured.

paras.t: Rursumque ad patrem ait Esau : Numquid non reservasti et mihi benedictionem? quasi dicat, Adhuc potes et mihi benedictionem aliquam dare. Respondit Isaac : Dominum tuum illum constitui, juxta sensum inductum, et omnes fratres ejus, id est posteros, servituti illius subjugavi, id est subjugandos prophetavi ; frumento et vino et oleo stabilivi eum; hoc est, stabiliter locupletandum prædixi, sicut expositum est : et tibi post hæc, fili mi, ultra quid faciam? quasi dicat, Non possum tibi imprecari majora, præsertim intelligendo sub his temporalibus ac terrenis spiritualia ac æterna. Cui Esau : Num unam, inquit, tantum benedictionem habes, pater? tanquam dicat, Plures benedictiones, quamvis non æque perfectas, potes conferre. Mihi quoque obsecro ut benedicas, etsi non benedictione ad primogenitum pertinente, quam jam fratri meo dedisti, saltem aliqua inferiore.
paras.en: [[27:36|And again he said to his father: Hast thou not reserved me also a blessing?|Rursumque ad patrem ait Esau : Numquid non reservasti et mihi benedictionem?]] as if to say, Thou canst still give me also some blessing. [[27:37|Isaac answered: I have appointed him thy lord|Respondit Isaac : Dominum tuum illum constitui]], in the sense given above, [[27:37|and have made all his brethren|et omnes fratres ejus]], that is, his descendants, [[27:37|his servants|servituti illius subjugavi]], that is, I have prophesied that they are to be made subject; [[27:37|I have established him with corn and wine|frumento et vino et oleo stabilivi eum]] [Denis's text adds *et oleo*, "and oil"], that is, I have foretold that he is to be enriched lastingly, as has been explained: [[27:37|and after this, what shall I do more for thee, my son?|et tibi post hæc, fili mi, ultra quid faciam]] as if to say, I cannot call down greater things upon thee, especially understanding spiritual and eternal things under these temporal and earthly ones. [[27:38|And Esau said to him|Cui Esau]]: [[27:38|Hast thou only one blessing, father|Num unam, inquit, tantum benedictionem habes, pater]]? as if to say, Thou canst bestow several blessings, though not equally perfect ones. [[27:38|I beseech thee bless me also|Mihi quoque obsecro ut benedicas]], if not with the blessing belonging to the firstborn, which thou hast already given to my brother, at least with some lesser one.

paras.t: Quumque ejulatu magno fleret ex causa prætacta, motus Isaac, id est compassione tactus, ex amore et pietate, tam naturali quam supernaturali, dixit ad eum : In pinguedine […] et in rore cæli desuper, veniente erit benedictio tua, id est, in temporalium abundantia, quæ ex pinguedine terræ, et rore seu pluvia oritur, benedictio tua consistet : quod tam in Esau quam in posteris ejus impletum est. Nam et Idumæa sibi ac posteris suis a Deo concessa, pascualis ac fertilis perhibetur. Vives in gladio, id est, vir bellator eris, bellicosaque erit posteritas tua ; et fratri tuo servies : quia Idumæi fuerunt subjecti longo tempore regibus ac populo Judææ. Tempusque veniet, quum excutias et solvas jugum, id est dominium, ejus de cervicibus tuis. Hoc quarto Regum legitur adimpletum sub Joram rege Israel, cui rebellaverunt Idumæi, quamvis semel percusserit eos.
paras.en: [[27:38|And when he wept with a loud cry|Quumque ejulatu magno fleret]], for the reason already touched on, [[27:39|Isaac being moved|motus Isaac]], that is, touched with compassion, out of love and kindness, natural as well as supernatural, [[27:39|said to him: In the fat|dixit ad eum : In pinguedine]] […] [[27:39|and in the dew of heaven from above|et in rore cæli desuper]], coming down, [[27:40|Shall thy blessing be|erit benedictio tua]], that is, thy blessing shall consist in abundance of temporal goods, which spring from the fatness of the earth and from dew or rain: which was fulfilled both in Esau and in his descendants. For Idumea too, granted by God to him and his descendants, is said to be rich in pasture and fertile. [[27:40|Thou shalt live by the sword|Vives in gladio]], that is, thou shalt be a warrior, and thy posterity shall be warlike; [[27:40|and shalt serve thy brother|et fratri tuo servies]]: for the Idumeans were subject for a long time to the kings and people of Judea[[2 Kings 8:14||]]. [[27:40|and the time shall come, when thou shalt shake off and loose his yoke|Tempusque veniet, quum excutias et solvas jugum]], that is, his dominion, [[27:40|from thy neck|ejus de cervicibus tuis]]. We read in the fourth book of Kings that this was fulfilled under Joram, king of Israel [Joram, son of Josaphat, was king of Juda: 4 Kings 8:16], against whom the Idumeans rebelled[[4 Kings 8:20||]], though he once struck them[[4 Kings 8:21||]] [the margin gives IV Reg. viii, 20–22].

paras.t: Oderat ergo semper, id est diu et continue per aliquod tempus, Esau Jacob fratrem suum, pro benedictione, id est propter hoc, quod benedictionem primogenituræ fuit consecutus a patre. Dixitque in corde suo : Venient dies luctus patris mei, et occidam Jacob fratrem meum. Hoc dupliciter potest exponi : Venient dies, etc., id est, fratrem meum citius quo potero interficiam ; et tunc pater meus, qui benedictionem meam illi donavit, lugebit diu ac vehementer, et ita vindicabo me pariter de utroque. Secundo : Venient dies luctus patris mei, id est, quum venerit mors ipsius, et deploraverimus eum, statim occidam fratrem meum : quia ut aliqui dicunt, non audebat hoc facere, patre suo vivente, ne malediceretur seu odio haberetur ab eo.
paras.en: [[27:41|Esau therefore always hated|Oderat ergo semper]], that is, long and continually for some time, Jacob his brother, [[27:41|for the blessing|pro benedictione]], that is, because he had obtained the blessing of the firstborn from his father. [[27:41|and he said in his heart: The days will come of the mourning for my father, and I will kill my brother Jacob|Dixitque in corde suo : Venient dies luctus patris mei, et occidam Jacob fratrem meum]]. This can be explained in two ways. *The days will come*, etc., that is: I will kill my brother as soon as I can; and then my father, who gave my blessing to him, will mourn long and bitterly, and so I shall avenge myself on both alike. Secondly: *The days will come of the mourning for my father*, that is, when his death has come and we have bewailed him, I will at once kill my brother: for, as some say, he did not dare to do this while his father was alive, lest he should be cursed or hated by him.

paras.t: Nuntiata sunt hæc, quæ Esau cogitavit, Rebeccæ a Spiritu Sancto, secundum Glossam. Unde in Scholastica historia fertur : Eodem Spiritu nuntiata sunt ista Rebeccæ, quo ipsa instigavit filium suum Jacob fraudare fratrem suum. Alii dicunt, quod Esau per verba et signa ostendit, quod contra Jacob concepit, et ita Rebecca ab homine hoc audivit. Quæ mittens, et vocans Jacob filium suum, qui jam recessit a præsentia Esau ex timore, dixit ad eum seorsum et secrete : Ecce Esau minatur ut occidat. Nunc ergo, fili mi, audi vocem meam, et consurgens, fuge ad Laban fratrem meum in Haran, id est urbem Mesopotamiæ sic vocatam, habitabisque cum eo diebus paucis, etc. Ita nunc consuluit Rebecca, et filium suum tempore opportuno revocare proposuit. Aliter tamen pro parte evenit, quia Jacob multis annis habitavit cum Laban. Cur utroque orbabor filio in uno die? hoc est, si tu non fugeris, ipse occidet te; et te occidendo, occidi merebitur, aut expelletur seu fugiet de hac terra, et ita vobis ambobus simul privarer: quod totum per istud, quod tibi nunc do, consilium potest vitari.
paras.en: [[27:42|These things were told to Rebecca|Nuntiata sunt hæc]], the things Esau had thought, by the Holy Ghost, according to the Gloss. Hence the Scholastic History says: These things were told to Rebecca by the same Spirit by which she prompted her son Jacob to cheat his brother. Others say that Esau showed by words and signs what he had conceived against Jacob, and so Rebecca heard this from a man. [[27:42|and she sent and called Jacob, her son|Quæ mittens, et vocans Jacob filium suum]], who had already withdrawn from Esau's presence out of fear, [[27:42|and said to him|dixit ad eum]] apart and in secret: [[27:42|Behold Esau|Ecce Esau]] [[27:42|threateneth to kill thee|minatur ut occidat]]. [[27:43|Now therefore, my son, hear my voice, arise and flee to Laban, my brother, to Haran|Nunc ergo, fili mi, audi vocem meam, et consurgens, fuge ad Laban fratrem meum in Haran]], that is, to the city of Mesopotamia so called, [[27:44|And thou shalt dwell with him a few days|habitabisque cum eo diebus paucis]], etc. So Rebecca counselled now, and she purposed to call her son back at a fitting time. Yet in part it turned out otherwise, since Jacob dwelt many years with Laban. [[27:45|Why shall I be deprived of both my sons in one day?|Cur utroque orbabor filio in uno die?]] that is, if thou dost not flee, he will kill thee; and by killing thee he will deserve to be killed, or he will be driven out or will flee from this land, and so I should be deprived of you both at once: all of which can be avoided by this counsel that I now give thee.

paras.t: Dixitque Rebecca ad Isaac: Tædet me vitæ meæ propter filias Heth, id est, tantum affligor de istis uxoribus Esau filii nostri, quæ sunt de genere Hethæorum: de quibus et causis hujus doloris Rebeccæ, dictum est in expositione præcedentis capituli; si acceperit Jacob uxorem de stirpe hujus terræ, hoc est de genere Chananæorum, nolo vivere, id est, tantum inde tristarer, quod quantum in me est, mallem mori.
