paras.en: [[27:46|And Rebecca said to Isaac: I am weary of my life, because of the daughters of Heth|Dixitque Rebecca ad Isaac: Tædet me vitæ meæ propter filias Heth]], that is, I am so afflicted over these wives of Esau our son, who are of the race of the Hethites: of whom, and of the causes of this grief of Rebecca, we spoke in the exposition of the preceding chapter; [[27:46|if Jacob take a wife of the stock of this land|si acceperit Jacob uxorem de stirpe hujus terræ]], that is, of the race of the Chanaanites, [[27:46|I choose not to live|nolo vivere]], that is, I should be so saddened by it that, for my part, I would rather die.

paras.t: Circa quod quæritur: Primo, quare tantum abhorruit hæc Rebecca tale conjugium. Respondetur, quod propter incompositionem, pompam, et alia vitia mulierum Chananæarum, et item quia sciebat promissiones illas magnificas Abrahæ et Isaac factas, in posteris Jacob implendas: ideo voluit ut de sua cognatione duceret conjugem; propter quod etiam Abraham adjuravit servum suum, ut de sua parentela acciperet filio suo Isaac contoralem. Secundo, qualiter excusetur Rebecca, mulier virtuosa, a vitio impatientiæ, in eo quod dixit, Tædet me vitæ meæ propter filias Heth: et rursus, Si acceperit Jacob uxorem de stirpe hujus terræ, nolo vivere. Nempe, quum patientia sit virtus moralis, passionem tristitiæ moderans ac refrenans, videtur ad impatientiam magnam pertinere, sic contristari de adversitate, ut vita vertatur in tædium, morsque optetur. Dicendum, quod de malo culpæ tam proprio quam proximorum, præsertim propriæ sobolis, tristari oportet bona et moderata tristitia; ex quo sequi potest rationabile tædium, quo et Christus passione instante cœpit tædere; et potius appetenda est mors corporalis, quam admittenda culpa mortalis; si convenienter queat vitari: imo et malum pœnæ potest esse occasio appetendi mortem, in quantum est janua vitæ felicis, et sub conditione, videlicet in quantum placuerit Deo, seu quantum est in ipso appetente. Verumtamen memorata verba Rebeccæ intelligi possunt per modum hyperbolicæ locutionis. Nam et tam seriose locuta est suo marito, quatenus induceret eum ad committendum filio suo Jacob quod iret ad Mesopotamiam ob causam præfatam; tamen ut probabile est, non dixit viro suo de odio et comminatione Esau in Jacob, ne ex hoc nimis contristaretur, præsertim quia jam cæcus erat, et quodammodo desolatus. Cæci autem mala quæ audiunt, valde imprimunt suo cordi, quia eorum imaginatio non ita dispergitur circa multa, quum non sint occupati circa diversa, sicut videntes. Augustinus tamen affirmat: Quod habent Latini codices, Vade in Mesopotamiam; Græci habent, Fuge in Mesopotamiam, ut intelligatur et Isaac intellexisse, quod Esau cogitavit de morte Jacob.
paras.en: On this it is asked, first, why Rebecca so abhorred such a marriage. The answer is: because of the unruliness, the showiness and the other vices of the Chanaanite women; and also because she knew that those magnificent promises made to Abraham and Isaac were to be fulfilled in the descendants of Jacob: so she wished him to take a wife from her own kindred; for which reason Abraham too made his servant swear to take a bride for his son Isaac from his own kindred. Secondly, it is asked how Rebecca, a virtuous woman, is excused from the vice of impatience in saying, [[27:46|I am weary of my life, because of the daughters of Heth|Tædet me vitæ meæ propter filias Heth]], and again, [[27:46|if Jacob take a wife of the stock of this land, I choose not to live|Si acceperit Jacob uxorem de stirpe hujus terræ, nolo vivere]]. For since patience is a moral virtue that moderates and bridles the passion of sadness, it seems to belong to great impatience to be so saddened by adversity that life turns to weariness and death is wished for. The answer is that over the evil of guilt, whether one's own or one's neighbours', and especially one's own offspring's, one ought to be sad with a good and moderate sadness; from which a reasonable weariness can follow, such as Christ too began to feel as His passion drew near; and bodily death is rather to be desired than mortal guilt admitted, if it cannot fittingly be avoided: nay, even the evil of punishment can be an occasion of desiring death, inasmuch as death is the gate of the happy life, and under a condition, namely as far as it shall please God, or as far as lies in the one who desires it. Yet the words of Rebecca recorded here can be understood as a hyperbolical way of speaking. For she spoke so earnestly to her husband in order to lead him to send her son Jacob to Mesopotamia for the reason given; yet, as is probable, she did not tell her husband of Esau's hatred and threats against Jacob, lest he should be too much saddened by it, especially as he was now blind and in a manner desolate. For the blind impress deeply on their hearts the evils they hear, since their imagination is not so scattered over many things, as they are not busied about divers things as those who see are. Augustine, however, affirms: Where the Latin codices have, *Go into Mesopotamia*, the Greek have, *Flee into Mesopotamia*, so that it may be understood that Isaac too understood that Esau was thinking of Jacob's death.

paras.t: Insuper quæritur circa præhabita, an Jacob excusetur a culpa mendacii, et a fraude in verbis et factis præhabitis. Et videtur quod non, quia habetur ex verbis Isaac, quod venerit fraudulenter. Exhibendo quoque patri suo manus proprias, pelliculisque coopertas, videtur egisse dolose prætendendo se esse quod non erat. Item dicendo, Feci sicut præcepisti mihi, et, Comede de venatione filii tui, videtur mentitus. Ad istud quidam respondent, quod non oportet Patres veteris Testamenti excusare a veniali peccato, et per consequens, nec a mendacio officioso. Hinc in secundo volumine Collationum Patrum, in Collatione abbatis Joseph asseritur, quod Jacob commisit fraudem atque mendacium; et tamen excusatur ex interiori radice, quia pia intentione et justa ex causa utrumque processit. Porro Augustinus affirmat, quod omnia verba et facta hæc Jacob, mystica erant, et ex occulta inspiratione divina, nec peccavit in eis. Omne autem mendacium est peccatum, similiter omnis fraus proprie dicta. Sed istud dictis Sanctorum plus consonat. In Scholastica vero historia legitur: Excusatur Jacob de mendacio in patrem, et fraude in fratrem per jussionem matris, mater vero per familiare consilium Spiritus Sancti. Attamen non videtur, quod ex sola matris suæ jussione excusaretur, cui non debebat in illicitis (ut sunt mendacium et fraus) obedire, nisi in quantum jussio ista venit ex instinctu Spiritus Sancti. Ex cujus etiam instinctu, credendus est Jacob in his suæ matri obtemperasse.
paras.en: Further, it is asked concerning what has gone before whether Jacob is excused from the fault of lying, and from fraud in the words and deeds related above. And it seems not, since we have it from Isaac's words that he [[27:35|came deceitfully|venerit fraudulenter]]. Also, by showing his father his own hands covered with the little skins, he seems to have acted with guile, pretending to be what he was not. Again, in saying, [[27:19|I have done as thou didst command me|Feci sicut præcepisti mihi]], and, [[27:31|eat of thy son's venison|Comede de venatione filii tui]] [these are Esau's words, v. 31; Jacob said *of my venison*, v. 19], he seems to have lied. To this some answer that it is not necessary to excuse the Fathers of the Old Testament from venial sin, and consequently not from the officious lie either [that is, a lie told to help or to avert harm, not a malicious one]. Hence in the second volume of the Conferences of the Fathers, in the Conference of Abbot Joseph, it is asserted that Jacob committed fraud and a lie; and yet he is excused by the inward root, since both proceeded from a loving intention and a just cause. But Augustine affirms that all these words and deeds of Jacob were mystical, and came from a hidden divine inspiration, and that he did not sin in them. For every lie is a sin, and likewise every fraud properly so called. And this is more in accord with the sayings of the Saints. In the Scholastic History, again, we read: Jacob is excused from the lie to his father and the fraud on his brother by his mother's command, and his mother by the familiar counsel of the Holy Ghost. Yet it does not seem that he would be excused by his mother's command alone, since he ought not to obey her in unlawful things (such as lying and fraud are), except inasmuch as that command came from the prompting of the Holy Ghost. By whose prompting, too, Jacob is to be believed to have obeyed his mother in these things.

paras.t: Amplius quæritur, an Isaac benedixit veraciter ipsi Jacob. Videtur quod non, quoniam non intendebat benedicere ei, sed alteri, imo nec voluit benedicere Jacob. Error quoque personæ, impedit matrimonium, ergo et benedictionem. Ad istud patet ex dictis responsio. Ostensum est equidem, qualiter Isaac istud voluit ac intendit, et qualiter non. In matrimonio tamen est aliter, quia in illo exigitur utriusque consensus: in spiritualibus vero non semper est ita, ut si quis aliquem ordinet aut baptizet, ille est vere ordinatus aut baptizatus, quamvis ordinans aut baptizans, credat illum alium esse, aliumque ordinare aut baptizare intendat. Sufficit namque quod intendit ordinare aut baptizare illum, quem habet coram se. Ex quibus patet, qualiter sit intelligendum quod in prælata narratur Historia: Benedictus est Jacob, secundum verba, non secundum intentionem Isaac; sicut episcopus ordinat alienum, quem putat suum, et est ordinatus.
paras.en: It is asked further whether Isaac truly blessed Jacob. It seems not, since he did not intend to bless him but another; indeed he did not wish to bless Jacob. Also, error of person hinders marriage, therefore the blessing too. The answer to this is plain from what has been said: for it has been shown in what way Isaac willed and intended this, and in what way not. But in marriage it is otherwise, since there the consent of both is required: in spiritual things it is not always so; thus if someone ordains or baptizes another, that man is truly ordained or baptized, although the one ordaining or baptizing believes him to be someone else, and intends to ordain or baptize someone else. For it is enough that he intends to ordain or baptize the man he has before him. From which it is plain how we are to understand what is said in the aforesaid History: Jacob was blessed according to the words, not according to Isaac's intention; as a bishop ordains a stranger whom he thinks to be his own subject, and he is ordained.

paras.t: Denique dicitur esse triplex fraus: Una eruditionis, qua Joseph scyphum suum poni præcepit in sacco fratris. Alia inspirationis, qua filii Israel mutuarunt vasa aurea ab Ægyptiis. Tertia nocivæ deceptionis, quæ est vitiosa, non aliæ duæ. Simulatio quoque quadruplex assignatur: Prima est providentiæ et cautelæ, sicque Josue cum suis simulavit fugam. Secunda doctrinæ, sicut Christus finxit se longius ire. Tertia significationis, qua usus est Jacob, sicut jam patuit. Quarta duplicitatis et calliditatis, et hæc censetur culpabilis.
paras.en: Lastly, fraud is said to be threefold. One is of instruction, by which Joseph ordered his cup to be put in his brother's sack. Another is of inspiration, by which the children of Israel borrowed vessels of gold from the Egyptians. The third is of harmful deception, which is vicious; the other two are not. Pretence, too, is reckoned fourfold. The first is of providence and caution, and so Josue with his men feigned flight[[Jos 8:15||]]. The second is of teaching, as Christ [[Luke 24:28|made as though he would go farther|finxit se longius ire]]. The third is of signification, which Jacob used, as has now appeared. The fourth is of doubleness and craft, and this is judged blameworthy.

paras.t: Postremo quærendum, quomodo dicat Apostolus ad Hebræos, quod Esau non invenit pœnitentiæ locum, et benedictionem cupiens hereditare, sit reprobatus, quum jam scriptum sit, quod Isaac motus et misertus sit ejus, benedixitque ei. Et respondendum, quod reprobatus est quantum ad hoc, quod benedictionem primogenituræ non potuit impetrare, nec quantum ad hoc, invenit pœnitentiæ locum. Reprobatus est quoque a Deo, nec in spiritualibus exstitit benedictus, nec gratiam finalem est consecutus, de quo per Malachiam testatur Dominus: Esau autem odio habui.
paras.en: Finally, we must ask how the Apostle says to the Hebrews that Esau [[Heb 12:17|found no place of repentance|non invenit pœnitentiæ locum]], and that, [[Heb 12:17|when he desired to inherit the benediction, he was rejected|benedictionem cupiens hereditare, sit reprobatus]], when it is written that Isaac was moved and had pity on him, and blessed him. And the answer is that he was rejected in this, that he could not obtain the blessing of the firstborn, and in this he found no place of repentance. He was also rejected by God, and was not blessed in spiritual things, nor did he obtain final grace; of whom the Lord testifies through Malachias: [[Mal 1:3|But have hated Esau|Esau autem odio habui]].

27.title: De spirituali hujus capituli vicesimi septimi intellectu
27.title_en: On the spiritual understanding of this twenty-seventh chapter

paras.t: Juxta doctrinam Apostoli, omnia in figura contigerunt antiquis: potissime vero Patriarcharum verba et gesta, fuerunt mysteriorum Christi atque Ecclesiæ præfigurativa.
paras.en: According to the Apostle's teaching, [[1 Cor 10:11|all these things happened to them in figure|omnia in figura contigerunt antiquis]]; but above all the words and deeds of the Patriarchs were prefigurations of the mysteries of Christ and of the Church.

paras.t: Itaque per Isaac filios duos habentem, intelligitur Deus æternus, qui per creationem possedit populum Judæorum quasi filium seniorem, unde per Jeremiam testatur: Ephraim primogenitus meus; populumque gentilem, tanquam posteriorem. Quod autem Isaac præcepit filio suo Esau, ut sumptis suis armis iret venatum, et de venatione sua sibi pararet pulmentum, significat quod populo Judæorum præcepit prædicare: et prædicando homines ad salutem venari seu capere, sicut per Jeremiam fatetur: Ecce ego mittam ex eis venatores, et venabuntur eos. Ex animabus autem tam salubriter captis, fit Deo quasi suavis refectio, cujus gaudium atque deliciæ sunt nostra conversio ac profectus. Itaque prædicatoribus Judæorum Scribis ac Pharisæis taliter occupatis, Spiritus Sanctus qui per Rebeccam exprimitur, seu divina inspiratio suggessit plebi gentilium, figurato per Jacob, ut pergens ad gregem, id est, ovibus Christi per fidem se socians, et Christi Ecclesiam credendo operandoque intrans, afferret sibi optimos hœdos, id est, tam eos qui idola coluerunt, violata lege naturali, quam eos, qui juxta naturalem legem vixerunt, prædicando converteret: qui optimi erant, id est valde boni bonitate naturæ, seu egregiæ indolis impressione, et quia insigniti erant superbenedictæ Trinitatis imagine. Ex quorum conversione, compunctione, salute, fit cibus quo libenter vescitur Deus Pater, quia de eorum emendatione et salvatione lætatur. Non enim est personarum acceptio apud Deum, sed in omni gente, qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi.
paras.en: So by Isaac, who had two sons, is understood the eternal God, who by creation possessed the Jewish people as his elder son (whence he testifies through Jeremias: [[Jer 31:9|Ephraim is my firstborn|Ephraim primogenitus meus]] [the margin's chapter and verse are unreadable; the words are those of Jer 31:9]), and the gentile people as the later one. That Isaac commanded his son Esau to take his arms and go hunting, and to prepare him a savoury meat of his venison, signifies that he commanded the Jewish people to preach, and by preaching to hunt or catch men for salvation, as he declares through Jeremias: Behold, [[Jer 16:16|I will send them many hunters, and they shall hunt them|Ecce ego mittam ex eis venatores, et venabuntur eos]]. And of souls so wholesomely caught a sweet refreshment, as it were, is made for God, whose joy and delight are our conversion and progress. So, while the preachers of the Jews, the Scribes and Pharisees, were thus engaged, the Holy Ghost, who is expressed by Rebecca, or the divine inspiration, suggested to the gentile people, figured by Jacob, that going to the flock, that is, joining itself by faith to the sheep of Christ and entering Christ's Church by believing and working, it should bring him the best kids: that is, that by preaching it should convert both those who had worshipped idols, breaking the natural law, and those who had lived according to the natural law. These were the best, that is, very good by the goodness of nature, or by the stamp of an excellent disposition, and because they were marked with the image of the most blessed Trinity. Of their conversion, compunction and salvation is made the food which God the Father gladly eats, because he rejoices at their amendment and salvation. [[Rom 2:11|For there is no respect of persons with God|Non enim est personarum acceptio apud Deum]][[Acts 10:34||]]; [[Acts 10:35|But in every nation, he that feareth him and worketh justice is acceptable to him|sed in omni gente, qui timet Deum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi]].

paras.t: Insuper per hoc quod Jacob respondit Rebeccæ: Nosti quod Esau frater meus pilosus sit, et ego lenis. Si attrectaverit me pater meus, etc., designatur quod plebs gentilis aliqualiter illuminata, propriam indignitatem, nuditatem, et vitiositatem attendens, indignam se fatebatur benedictione divina; et præsumptionis argui metuebat, si ad thronum gratiæ Dei auderet per se ipsam accedere, pensans ac confitens quod populus Judæorum, cujus frater fuit per conformitatem naturæ, et ratione unius omnium Creatoris, cœlestisque Patris, et propter eosdem primos parentes, esset pilosus, hoc est, considerationibus et notitiis Scripturarum quasi pilis repletus ac intus opertus; ipsa vero lenis, id est nuda ab actibus virtuosis, et tenera, hoc est imperfecta, et tentationibus cito cedens: ideo timuit, si Pater cœlestis se attrectaret, id est, imperfectionem et indignitatem ejus diligenter inspiceret, putaret quod ipsa voluisset ei illudere, hoc est suas calamitates ipsi Deo abscondere, sicque pro benedictione maledictionem incurreret. At vero Rebecca, id est Spiritus Sanctus seu providentia Dei, humilitatem populi gentilis perpendens, assecuravit eum de tali periculo, dummodo in Deo confidens, et sibi acquiescens, faceret quæ suggessit. Quum ergo populus ille ita egisset, Spiritus Sanctus induit et ornavit eum vestibus Esau valde bonis, quas secum domi habebat, id est diversis gratiarum muneribus, donis ac fructibus spiritualibus, quæ ante fuerunt in Synagoga, et semper fuerunt in potestate Spiritus Sancti; pelliculasque hædorum circumdedit manibus, id est, peccata gentilium conversorum adjunxit operationibus prædicatorum suorum, ita ut pro illis orarent, laborarent, ac satagerent, ut et præterita mala dimitterentur, et præcaverentur futura; et colli nuda protexit, id est, pristinam gentilium elationem virtute humilitatis operuit ac delevit; deditque pulmentum, et panes quos coxerat. Omnia nostra opera bona ac meritoria, dona sunt Spiritus Sancti: quæ tamen quum ipse in nobis et per nos fecerit, dat et imputat ea nobis, in quantum per liberum arbitrium acceptavimus inspirationes suggestionesque Dei, et cooperati sumus eisdem, et vult ut ea Deo Patri quasi per nos facta, offeramus ad laudem et gloriam ejus, ut ipse quasi reficiatur et delectetur in ipsis.
paras.en: Further, by Jacob's answer to Rebecca, [[27:11|Thou knowest that Esau, my brother, is a hairy man, and I am smooth|Nosti quod Esau frater meus pilosus sit, et ego lenis]]: [[27:12|If my father should feel me|Si attrectaverit me pater meus]], etc., it is signified that the gentile people, enlightened in some measure and considering its own unworthiness, nakedness and viciousness, confessed itself unworthy of the divine blessing, and feared to be charged with presumption if it dared to approach the throne of God's grace[[Heb 4:16||]] by itself; weighing and confessing that the Jewish people, whose brother it was by likeness of nature, by reason of the one Creator and heavenly Father of all, and because of the same first parents, was hairy, that is, filled and covered within, as with hairs, with the considerations and knowledge of the Scriptures [a marginal note gives *totus*, "wholly", for *intus*, "within"]; while it was itself smooth, that is, bare of virtuous acts, and tender, that is, imperfect and quick to yield to temptations. Therefore it feared that if the heavenly Father should feel it, that is, examine its imperfection and unworthiness closely, he would think it had wished to mock him, that is, to hide its miseries from God himself, and so it would bring on itself a curse instead of a blessing. But Rebecca, that is, the Holy Ghost or the providence of God, weighing the humility of the gentile people, assured it against such a danger, provided that, trusting in God and yielding to her, it did what she suggested. When, then, that people had so done, the Holy Ghost clothed and adorned it with the [[27:15|very good garments of Esau, which she had at home with her|vestibus Esau valde bonis, quas secum domi habebat]]: that is, with the various gifts of graces, the gifts and spiritual fruits which were before in the Synagogue, and were always in the power of the Holy Ghost. [[27:16|And the little skins of the kids she put about his hands|pelliculasque hædorum circumdedit manibus]], that is, she joined the sins of the converted gentiles [a marginal note reads *prætact…*, perhaps *prætacta*, "the aforesaid sins"] to the works of her preachers, so that they prayed, laboured and strove for them, that their past evils might be forgiven and future ones guarded against; [[27:16|and covered the bare of his neck|et colli nuda protexit]], that is, she covered and blotted out the former pride of the gentiles by the virtue of humility; [[27:17|And she gave him the savoury meat|deditque pulmentum]], [[27:17|bread that she had baked|et panes quos coxerat]]. All our good and meritorious works are gifts of the Holy Ghost; yet when he has done them in us and through us, he gives and imputes them to us, inasmuch as by free will we have accepted God's inspirations and suggestions and have cooperated with them; and he wills that we offer them to God the Father as done as it were through us, to his praise and glory, so that he may be as it were refreshed and delighted in them.

paras.t: Præterea, per hoc quod Isaac dixit ad Jacob, Quis es tu, fili mi? insinuatur quod Deus universos diligenter examinat: et sicut Jacob dixit se Esau esse, similitudine et dignitate primogenituræ, sic conversa gentilitas dixit se esse Israeliticam plebem, imitatione fidei ac virtutum, electionis magnitudine et prædestinatione æterna. Rursus, Patre æterno quasi per modum admirantis habente se de tam celeri gentilium conversione, prædicatores ex gentilitate electi, Deo et gratiæ ejus præcipue adscripserunt hoc ipsum. Et palpato eo, dixit: Vox quidem, vox Jacob est, id est, populus iste adhuc unum Deum confitetur, quemadmodum naturalis ratio dictat; sed manus, manus sunt Esau, id est, opere Deum honorat, Trinitatemque veneratur, sicut ad veros spectabat Judæos.
paras.en: Again, by Isaac's saying to Jacob, [[27:18|Who art thou, my son?|Quis es tu, fili mi?]] it is suggested that God examines all men carefully; and as Jacob said he was Esau, by likeness and by the dignity of the birthright, so the converted gentile world said it was the people of Israel, by imitation of their faith and virtues, by the greatness of its election and by eternal predestination. Again, when the eternal Father showed himself as it were wondering at so swift a conversion of the gentiles, the preachers chosen from among the gentiles ascribed this very thing above all to God and to his grace. [[27:22|And when he had felt him, Isaac said: The voice indeed is the voice of Jacob|Et palpato eo, dixit: Vox quidem, vox Jacob est]], that is, this people still confesses one God, as natural reason dictates; [[27:22|but the hands, are the hands of Esau|sed manus, manus sunt Esau]], that is, in its works it honours God and venerates the Trinity, as belonged to the true Jews.

paras.t: Quum itaque Deus Pater præclara opera bona gentilitatis conversæ misericorditer acceptasset, et de ejus compunctione quasi de vino hausisset, dixit: Accede ad me, et da mihi osculum, fili mi, id est, per contemplationem fervidumque amorem conjunge te mihi immediate: quod conversa gentilitas fecit.
paras.en: So when God the Father had mercifully accepted the excellent good works of the converted gentile world, and had drunk as it were of its compunction as of wine, he said: [[27:26|Come near me, and give me a kiss, my son|Accede ad me, et da mihi osculum, fili mi]], that is, join thyself to me immediately by contemplation and fervent love: which the converted gentile world did.

paras.t: Statimque ut sensit vestimentorum ejus fragrantiam, id est spiritualem dulcedinem et acceptabilitatem ac caritatis suavitatem conversæ gentilitatis, benedicens ei, id est dona gratiæ ac virtutum augens et complens in ea, ait: Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni, hoc est, populus iste gentilis conversus, spiritualiter redolet omni suavitate virtutum, fructuum, ac donorum, ut olim aliquando Synagoga. Potissime quoque Christus omnium solus habens perfectiones, secundum naturam assumptam, suavissimum habebat coram Deo Trinitate odorem; sicut odor est agri pleni, id est universalis Ecclesiæ, donis Dei repletæ: imo ipse solus perfectior ac dulcior ea fuit, quia non ad mensuram Spiritum Sanctum accepit. Det tibi Deus de rore cœli et de pinguedine terræ, abundantiam frumenti et vini et olei. Abundantia frumenti et vini, est copia Sacramenti corporis et sanguinis Christi, de quibus loquitur Zacharias: Quid bonum Domini, aut quid pulchrum ejus, nisi frumentum electorum et vinum germinans virgines? Abundantia olei, est exuberantia spiritualium consolationum et gratiarum, quæ in Sacramento continentur ac percipiuntur. Ista accipiuntur de rore cœli, id est de affluentia liberalitatis divinæ, omnia fecundantis ac reficientis, et de pinguedine terræ, id est de caritate et meritis humanæ naturæ Christi. Serviant tibi populi, et adorent te tribus. Hoc tam in Christo quam in ejus Ecclesia est impletum, quoniam omnes gentes conversæ, Christo obediunt atque Ecclesiæ. Christus quoque est dominus fratrum suorum, id est hominum universorum, præsertim fidelium. Et incurvantur ante eum filii matris suæ, id est conversi ex Synagoga, de qua secundum carnem natus est ipse. In nomine etenim Jesu omne genu flectitur, cœlestium, terrestrium et infernorum: cui qui maledixerit, maledicetur; quoniam juxta Isaiæ oraculum, ad eum veniet, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei: qui vero benedixerit ei ex caritate, benedicetur.
paras.en: [[27:27|And immediately as he smelled the fragrant smell of his garments|Statimque ut sensit vestimentorum ejus fragrantiam]], that is, the spiritual sweetness, acceptableness and charity's delightfulness of the converted gentile world, [[27:27|blessing him|benedicens ei]], that is, increasing and completing in it the gifts of grace and of the virtues, [[27:27|he said: Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a plentiful field|ait: Ecce odor filii mei, sicut odor agri pleni]], that is, this converted gentile people is spiritually fragrant with all the sweetness of virtues, fruits and gifts, as the Synagogue once was. Above all, too, Christ, who alone has the perfections of all, had according to the nature he assumed a most sweet odour before God the Trinity, as is the smell of a plentiful field, that is, of the universal Church, filled with the gifts of God; indeed he alone was more perfect and sweeter than she, for he received the Holy Ghost not by measure[[John 3:34||]]. [[27:28|God give thee of the dew of heaven, and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of corn and wine|Det tibi Deus de rore cœli et de pinguedine terræ, abundantiam frumenti et vini]] and oil [Denis's text adds "and oil", which the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims do not have here]. The abundance of corn and wine is the plenty of the Sacrament of the body and blood of Christ, of which Zacharias speaks: [[Zach 9:17|what is the good thing of him, and what is his beautiful thing, but the corn of the elect, and wine springing forth virgins?|Quid bonum Domini, aut quid pulchrum ejus, nisi frumentum electorum et vinum germinans virgines?]] The abundance of oil is the overflowing of spiritual consolations and graces which are contained and received in the Sacrament. These are received of the dew of heaven, that is, of the overflowing of the divine liberality, which makes all things fruitful and refreshes them; and of the fatness of the earth, that is, of the charity and merits of Christ's human nature. [[27:29|And let peoples serve thee, and tribes worship thee|Serviant tibi populi, et adorent te tribus]]. This has been fulfilled both in Christ and in his Church, since all the converted nations obey Christ and the Church. Christ also is [[27:29|lord of thy brethren|dominus fratrum]], that is, of his brethren, of all men, especially the faithful. And [[27:29|thy mother's children bow down before thee|incurvantur ante eum filii matris]], that is, before him bow his mother's children, those converted from the Synagogue, of which he was born according to the flesh. For [[Phil 2:10|in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those that are in heaven, on earth, and under the earth|In nomine etenim Jesu omne genu flectitur, cœlestium, terrestrium et infernorum]]: and he that curses him shall be cursed, since according to the oracle of Isaias, [[Is 45:25|they shall come to him, and all that resist him shall be confounded|ad eum veniet, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei]] [the margin gives Is. xli, 11; the words are those of Is 45:25]; but he that blesses him out of charity shall be blessed.

paras.t: Vix Isaac sermonem impleverat, et egresso Jacob foras, venit Esau. Quum enim Deus in primitiva Ecclesia copiosissime benedixisset conversis gentilibus, et opera miraculosa operaretur per eos, venit et Synagoga offerens Deo sacrificia et obsequia sua, petens ea a Domino acceptari, et glorians se prælatam olim gentilibus; sed Evangelio divulgato, noluit ea Deus amplius acceptare, dicens eis per Malachiam: Non est mihi ultra voluntas in vobis, et munus non accipiam de manu vestra. A solis enim ortu usque ad occasum, magnum est nomen meum in gentibus, et ubique sacrificatur et offertur nomini meo oblatio munda: ita quod per modum admirantis se habuit de tarditate Synagogæ ad fidem, atque de gentium celeritate ad eam. Auditis Esau sermonibus patris, irrugiit vehementer. Sic et Synagoga jam tam diuturne se relictam a Deo considerans, graviter ingemiscit et benedici precatur, pro adventu Messiæ clamans ad Creatorem, non credens venisse qui jam venit. Porro Deus per libros Prophetarum, per angelicas inspirationes, per Christianorum prædicationem, assidue loquitur Synagogæ, quod populo gentilium benedixit, eaque contulit omnem excellentiam, Synagogæ olim concessam.
paras.en: [[27:30|Isaac had scarce ended his words, when, Jacob being now gone out abroad, Esau came|Vix Isaac sermonem impleverat, et egresso Jacob foras, venit Esau]]. For when God in the early Church had most abundantly blessed the converted gentiles, and was working miracles through them, the Synagogue too came, offering God her sacrifices and services, asking that they be accepted by the Lord, and glorying that she had once been preferred to the gentiles. But once the Gospel had been spread abroad, God would no longer accept them, saying to them through Malachias: [[Mal 1:10|I have no pleasure in you|Non est mihi ultra voluntas in vobis]], [[Mal 1:10|and I will not receive a gift of your hand|et munus non accipiam de manu vestra]]. [[Mal 1:11|For from the rising of the sun even to the going down, my name is great among the Gentiles, and in every place there is sacrifice, and there is offered to my name a clean oblation|A solis enim ortu usque ad occasum, magnum est nomen meum in gentibus, et ubique sacrificatur et offertur nomini meo oblatio munda]]: so that he showed himself as it were wondering at the slowness of the Synagogue to come to the faith, and at the swiftness of the gentiles towards it. [[27:34|Esau having heard his father's words, roared out|Auditis Esau sermonibus patris, irrugiit]] vehemently. So too the Synagogue, considering herself now forsaken by God for so long, groans heavily and prays to be blessed, crying to the Creator for the coming of the Messias, not believing that he has come who has already come. Further, God speaks continually to the Synagogue, through the books of the Prophets, through the inspirations of angels and through the preaching of Christians, telling her that he has blessed the gentile people and has bestowed on it all the excellence once granted to the Synagogue.

paras.t: Quumque ejulatu magno flevit, etc. Quemadmodum Isaac aliquid benedictionis largitus est Esau ejulanti, sic et Deus desolatissimæ Synagogæ temporalia quædam largitur, et rore cœli compluit eos, utpote quadam Scripturarum veteris Testamenti cognitione: quæ vixit gladio, Ecclesiam acriter persequendo, et tamen deinceps servivit eidem; sed veniet tempus, quando collum suum ex hac ejiciet servitute, quando videlicet fuerit ad Christum conversa. Oderat ergo semper Esau Jacob. Sic Judæi implacabile odium habent contra Christianos, propter hoc quod libros legis ac Prophetarum, signa atque miracula Dei, vident translata ad ipsos, et in primitiva Ecclesia nitebantur eos omnino extinguere: propterea Spiritus Sanctus persuasit Ecclesiæ, ut se ad tempus ab induratis elongaret Judæis, et terras gentilium ingrediendo, disseminaret verbum Dei ibidem: postea autem Judæis per Romanos deletis a terra sancta, reducti sunt illuc fideles.
paras.en: [[27:38|And when he wept with a loud cry|Quumque ejulatu magno flevit]], etc. As Isaac bestowed something of a blessing on Esau as he wailed, so God too bestows certain temporal things on the most desolate Synagogue, and rains the dew of heaven upon them, namely a certain knowledge of the Scriptures of the Old Testament. She lived by the sword, fiercely persecuting the Church, and yet afterwards served her; but the time will come when she will cast her neck out of this servitude, namely when she has been converted to Christ. [[27:41|Esau therefore always hated Jacob|Oderat ergo semper Esau Jacob]]. So the Jews have an implacable hatred against Christians, because they see the books of the law and of the Prophets, and the signs and miracles of God, transferred to them; and in the early Church they strove to blot them out altogether. Therefore the Holy Ghost persuaded the Church to withdraw for a time from the hardened Jews, and, entering the lands of the gentiles, to sow the word of God there; but afterwards, when the Jews had been destroyed out of the holy land by the Romans, the faithful were brought back there.

paras.t: Quemadmodum autem displicuerunt Rebeccæ uxores Esau filiæ Hethæorum, nec voluit filium suum Jacob filiabus Chananæorum sociari connubio, sic displicuerunt Spiritui Sancto perfidæ feminæ infidelium Judæorum, nec voluit Christifideles cum infidelibus sociare conjugia, quæ impedit dispar cultus. Nempe, quæ pars fideli cum infideli?
paras.en: And as the wives of Esau, the daughters of the Hethites, displeased Rebecca, and she would not have her son Jacob joined in marriage to the daughters of the Chanaanites, so the faithless women of the unbelieving Jews displeased the Holy Ghost, and he would not have the faithful of Christ join in marriage with unbelievers, which difference of worship [*disparitas cultus*, the impediment that makes void a marriage between a baptized and an unbaptized person] prevents. For indeed, [[2 Cor 6:15|what part hath the faithful with the unbeliever?|quæ pars fideli cum infideli?]]

paras.t: Postremo S. Hieronymus circa istud capitulum, commemorat verba Hippolyti martyris, quæ et in Glossa habentur. Unde Isidorus: Verba, inquit, Hippolyti martyris hoc loco ponenda sunt, sicut ea replicavit Hieronymus vir excellentissimæ scientiæ ac doctrinæ: Isaac portat imaginem Dei Patris, Rebecca Spiritus Sancti, Esau populi prioris et Zabuli, Jacob Christi atque Ecclesiæ; senectus Isaac, consummationem mundi: oculi caligantes, perisse fidem de mundo, et lumen Religionis neglectum esse, significant. Cetera hujus Sancti verba non prosequor, quoniam sententialiter sunt inducta.
paras.en: Lastly, St Jerome, on this chapter, recalls the words of the martyr Hippolytus, which are also in the Gloss. Whence Isidore says: The words of the martyr Hippolytus are to be set down in this place, as Jerome, a man of most excellent learning and doctrine, repeated them: Isaac bears the image of God the Father, Rebecca of the Holy Ghost, Esau of the former people and of the devil, Jacob of Christ and of the Church; the old age of Isaac signifies the consummation of the world; his dim eyes, that faith has perished from the world and the light of religion has been neglected. The rest of this Saint's words I do not follow up, since their substance has already been brought in [*sententialiter sunt inducta*: their sense has been given above].

28.title: Declaratio capituli vicesimi octavi: Vocavit itaque Isaac Jacob, et benedixit eum
28.title_en: Declaration of the twenty-eighth chapter: And Isaac called Jacob, and blessed him

paras.t: Consequenter describitur confirmatio benedictionis Jacob, et revelatio atque promissio ei desuper facta, et qualiter parentibus suis obedivit, Deoque gratus fuit ac votum fecit.
paras.en: Next is described the confirmation of Jacob's blessing, and the revelation and promise made to him from above, and how he obeyed his parents, and was grateful to God, and made a vow.

paras.t: Vocavit itaque Isaac Jacob filium suum, et benedixit eum, juxta formam quæ paulo post subditur; præcepitque ei, dicens: Noli accipere conjugem de genere Chanaan, id est Chananæorum. Hujus rei causæ, præhabitæ sunt in expositione præcedentis capituli. Sed vade, et proficiscere in Mesopotamiam Syriæ, ad domum Bathuel, etc., et accipe tibi inde uxorem de filiabus Laban avunculi tui. Bathuel autem fuit filius Nachor fratris Abrahæ, et pater Rebeccæ ac Laban; fuitque diu mortuus dum ista locutus est Isaac.
paras.en: [[28:1|And Isaac called Jacob|Vocavit itaque Isaac Jacob]] his son, [[28:1|and blessed him|et benedixit eum]], according to the form which is given a little later; [[28:1|and charged him, saying: Take not a wife of the stock of Chanaan|præcepitque ei, dicens: Noli accipere conjugem de genere Chanaan]], that is, of the Chanaanites. The reasons for this were set out in the exposition of the preceding chapter[[Gen 27:46||]]. [[28:2|But go, and take a journey to Mesopotamia of Syria|Sed vade, et proficiscere in Mesopotamiam Syriæ]], [[28:2|to the house of Bathuel|ad domum Bathuel]], etc., [[28:2|and take thee a wife thence of the daughters of Laban, thy uncle|et accipe tibi inde uxorem de filiabus Laban avunculi tui]]. Now Bathuel was the son of Nachor, Abraham's brother, and the father of Rebecca and of Laban; and he had long been dead when Isaac spoke these words.

paras.t: Deinde forma benedictionis subjungitur, quæ etiam per modum orationis profertur, quia a Deo est omnis boni collatio. Deus autem omnipotens benedicat tibi, etc., conferendo et augendo tibi spiritualia ac temporalia bona; et det tibi benedictiones Abrahæ, et semini tuo post te, etc., id est, bona Abrahæ repromissa aut data, largiatur tibi ac posteris tuis.
paras.en: Then the form of the blessing is added, which is also uttered by way of prayer, because every good thing is bestowed by God. [[28:3|And God almighty bless thee|Deus autem omnipotens benedicat tibi]], etc., by bestowing and increasing in thee spiritual and temporal goods; [[28:4|And give the blessings of Abraham to thee, and to thy seed after thee|et det tibi benedictiones Abrahæ, et semini tuo post te]], etc., that is, may he grant to thee and to thy descendants the goods promised or given to Abraham.

paras.t: Quumque dimisisset eum Isaac, profectus pervenit in Mesopotamiam ad Laban filium Bathuel, etc. Illud per anticipationem hic dicitur, quia infra subjungitur qualiter per intermedia loca illuc pervenit. Deinde recitatur in littera, qualiter Esau videns quod Isaac pater suus benedixisset Jacob, et misisset eum ad Mesopotamiam, ut inde acciperet conjugem, et quod Isaac non libenter adspiceret, id est invite haberet filias Chanaan in conjugio filiorum suorum, ivit ipse Esau ad Ismaelem fratrem patris sui, et filiam ejus duxit uxorem, volens per hoc patri suo Isaac complacere, et plana est littera.
paras.en: [[28:5|And when Isaac had sent him away|Quumque dimisisset eum Isaac]], [[28:5|he took his journey and went to Mesopotamia|profectus pervenit in Mesopotamiam]] [[28:5|to Laban, the son of Bathuel|ad Laban filium Bathuel]], etc. This is said here by anticipation, since it is told below how he reached there through the places in between. Then the letter relates how Esau, seeing that Isaac his father had blessed Jacob and had sent him to Mesopotamia to take a wife from there, and that Isaac [[28:8|was not well pleased with|non libenter adspiceret]], that is, was unwilling to have, the daughters of Chanaan as wives of his sons, went himself to Ismael, his father's brother, and took his daughter to wife, wishing by this to please his father Isaac; and the letter is plain.

paras.t: Deinde reditur ad ordinem historiæ. Igitur Jacob egressus de Bersabee: ibi enim habitavit cum suis parentibus in terra Palæstinorum: pergebat Haran, id est versus urbem Mesopotamiæ sic vocatam.
paras.en: Then the order of the story is taken up again. [[28:10|But Jacob being departed from Bersabee|Igitur Jacob egressus de Bersabee]]: for he had lived there with his parents in the land of the Palestines; [[28:10|went on to Haran|pergebat Haran]], that is, toward the city of Mesopotamia so called.

paras.t: Cumque venisset ad quemdam locum. Secundum Isidorum, iste locus fuit ubi Bethlehem nunc vocatur, ubi natus est Christus. Alii dicunt, quod fuit mons Moria, in quo Abraham voluit Isaac immolare, propter quod Jacob reputavit locum illum sacrum, accessitque eum, ut orationi ac devotioni ibi insisteret, et dormiret. Huic concordat quod in Scholastica historia legitur, locum istum fuisse juxta Luzam, id est Jerusalem, ut infra Jacob testatur: Deus omnipotens apparuit mihi in Luza, quæ est in terra Chanaan. Et vellet in eo requiescere post solis occubitum. Quia (ut Josephus ait) noluit urbes provincialium ingredi, aut in eorum domibus hospitari propter eorum malignitatem, et timuit eos, idcirco dormivit sub dio, et interdum in campis. Tulit de lapidibus qui jacebant: et supponens capiti suo, dormivit in eodem loco. Ex quo patet, quod corpus suum rigide satis tractavit, pro pulvinari lapide utens. Refert Lyra, quod secundum Hebræos tulit tres lapides; et tamen apparet ex textu, quod plures acceperat. Isidorus vero effatur, quod supposuit capiti suo lapidem magnum: et hoc probabilius sonat, quoniam saxo pro pulvinari voluit uti; pro tali autem reclinatione magis competebat unus grandis lapis, quam plures parvi: quod et textus infra insinuat, dicens: Surgens mane Jacob, tulit lapidem etc. Recitat quoque Lyra quod secundum Hebræos Jacob evigilans reperit tres lapides illos mutatos in lapidem unum, in signum quod Dominus voluit ipsum Jacob sibi unire, et se ei associare: quod si contigisset, mirum quod Scriptura ista tam solenne non tetigisset miraculum.
paras.en: [[28:11|And when he was come to a certain place|Cumque venisset ad quemdam locum]]. According to Isidore, this place was where Bethlehem now is, where Christ was born. Others say that it was mount Moria, on which Abraham was willing to sacrifice Isaac, for which reason Jacob held that place sacred and went to it, so as to give himself there to prayer and devotion, and to sleep. With this agrees what is read in the Scholastic History, that this place was near Luza, that is, Jerusalem, as Jacob testifies below: [[Gen 48:3|God almighty appeared to me at Luza, which is in the land of Chanaan|Deus omnipotens apparuit mihi in Luza, quæ est in terra Chanaan]]. [[28:11|and would rest in it after sunset|Et vellet in eo requiescere post solis occubitum]]. Because (as Josephus says) he would not enter the cities of the people of that province, nor lodge in their houses, on account of their malice, and he was afraid of them, he therefore slept under the open sky, and sometimes in the fields. [[28:11|he took of the stones that lay there|Tulit de lapidibus qui jacebant]]: [[28:11|and putting under his head, slept in the same place|et supponens capiti suo, dormivit in eodem loco]]. From this it is plain that he treated his body rigorously enough, using a stone for a pillow. Lyra relates that according to the Hebrews he took three stones; and yet it appears from the text that he had taken several. But Isidore declares that he put a great stone under his head; and this sounds more probable, since he meant to use a rock for a pillow, and for lying down in that way one large stone was more fitting than several small ones: which the text also suggests below, saying: [[28:18|Jacob arising in the morning, took the stone|Surgens mane Jacob, tulit lapidem]] etc. Lyra also relates that according to the Hebrews Jacob, on waking, found those three stones changed into one stone, as a sign that the Lord willed to unite Jacob to himself and to join himself to him: if this had happened, it would be strange that this Scripture had not touched on so solemn a miracle.

paras.t: Viditque in somnis scalam stantem super terram, et cacumen ejus tangens cælum. Ista fuit imaginaria visio, in sensu interiori per similitudines sensibiles repræsentata: ad quam visionem et revelationem sequentem, ipse Jacob fuit dispositus per suam devotionem, orationemque præviam, per obedientiam quoque quam parentibus suis exhibuit, et per rigorosam sui corporis castigationem, atque per tribulationem, in qua tunc erat, proprii fratris fugiens persecutionem. Denique, secundum Augustinum, per scalam istam intelligitur Christus, qui etiam ait: Ego sum via. Et, Ego sum ostium. Quæ competunt ei secundum naturam assumptam, quia per ipsum tanquam per mediatorem et salvatorem, ascendunt electi ad regnum cœlorum. Hæc scala stetit in terra, et tetigit cœlum: quoniam Christus per humanitatem cum hominibus convenit, et terram calcavit; per divinitatem vero Patri æterno in cœlis regnanti communicat, imo consubstantialis consistit. Angelos quoque Dei ascendentes et descendentes per eam. Per quod significatum est, quod omnia angelorum ministrantium sacra obsequia, ad insinuanda sacratissima Christi mysteria principaliter ordinantur; et item, quod per Christum pacificata sunt terrena cum cœlestibus, homines cum angelis, imo cum Domino angelorum; et rursus, quod propter Christum angeli sancti libenter ministrant hominibus. Itemque, quod angeli ad Christi obsequium fuerunt semper parati. Hinc ipsemet dixit: Videbitis angelos ascendentes et descendentes super Filium hominis. Et Dominum innixum scalæ. Per quod designatur, quod caput Christi Deus, vel quod deitas unita sit ejus humanitati.
paras.en: [[28:12|And he saw in his sleep a ladder standing upon the earth, and the top thereof touching heaven|Viditque in somnis scalam stantem super terram, et cacumen ejus tangens cælum]]. This was an imaginary vision [that is, one formed in the imagination, neither a bodily sight nor a purely intellectual one], represented in the inward sense by sensible likenesses. For this vision and the revelation that follows, Jacob was disposed by his devotion and the prayer that went before, by the obedience also which he showed his parents, by the rigorous chastisement of his body, and by the tribulation he was then in, fleeing the persecution of his own brother. Lastly, according to Augustine [the margin cites City of God, XVI, 38], by this ladder is understood Christ, who also says: [[John 14:6|I am the way|Ego sum via]]. And: [[John 10:7|I am the door|Ego sum ostium]]. These befit him according to the nature he assumed, since through him, as through the mediator and saviour, the elect ascend to the kingdom of heaven. This ladder stood on earth and touched heaven: for Christ by his humanity met with men and trod the earth, but by his divinity he has fellowship with the eternal Father reigning in heaven, nay, is consubstantial with him. [[28:12|the angels also of God ascending and descending by it|Angelos quoque Dei ascendentes et descendentes per eam]]. By this it is signified that all the sacred services of the ministering angels are ordered principally to making known the most sacred mysteries of Christ; and also that through Christ the things of earth have been set at peace with those of heaven, men with angels, nay, with the Lord of angels; and again that for Christ's sake the holy angels gladly minister to men; and also that the angels were always ready for the service of Christ. Hence he himself said: [[John 1:51|you shall see|Videbitis]] [[John 1:51|the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man|angelos ascendentes et descendentes super Filium hominis]]. [[28:13|And the Lord leaning upon the ladder|Et Dominum innixum scalæ]]. By this is designated that [[1 Cor 11:3|the head of Christ is God|caput Christi Deus]], or that the deity is united to his humanity.

paras.t: Quidam per scalam istam intelligunt gradus et successiones generationum, per quos Christus secundum carnem descendit ab Adam seu Abraham usque ad Virginem gloriosam; per latera quoque scalæ, accipiunt utriusque sexus personas, ex quibus descendit. Potest demum per scalam istam intelligi ordinata virtutum connexio, et spiritualis profectus, per quos ab imis ad summa pertingitur, per quos et Jacob ad tantam gratiæ celsitudinem est perductus.
paras.en: Some understand by this ladder the degrees and successions of the generations through which Christ according to the flesh descended from Adam, or from Abraham, down to the glorious Virgin; and by the sides of the ladder they take the persons of either sex from whom he descended. Lastly, by this ladder may be understood the ordered linking of the virtues, and spiritual progress, by which one reaches from the lowest things to the highest, and by which Jacob too was brought to so great a height of grace.

paras.t: Itaque Jacob audivit interiori auditu Dominum docentem sibi per angelum, cujus obsequio formabatur hæc visio in imaginativa potentia, quam etiam visionem Jacob, angelo intus docente, veraciter intellexit: Ego sum Dominus Deus Abraham, etc. Eritque semen tuum quasi pulvis terræ, id est, posteritas tua instar pulveris erit innumerabilis. Ecce hic tota ejus posteritas pulveri comparatur. Dilataberis ad orientem et occidentem, etc. Quamvis hoc aliqualiter sit impletum in carnali posteritate ipsius Jacob, quæ non solum dilatata est versus quatuor plagas terræ promissionis, sed et in quatuor mundi partibus aucta est et majorata, plenius tamen impletum est in populo christiano, qui sunt spirituales filii Jacob, sicut et Abrahæ, per fidei ac virtutum sectationem. Apostoli namque ex Jacob progeniti, impleverunt mundum spiritualibus filiis per infidelium conversionem, et regenerationem ex aqua et Spiritu. Et benedicentur in te et in semine tuo cunctæ tribus terræ, hoc est in Christo, ut sæpe expositum est: sicque promissio ista facta est non solum Abrahæ et Isaac, sed etiam huic Jacob.
paras.en: So Jacob heard with inward hearing the Lord [[28:13|saying to him|docentem sibi]] [Denis reads *docentem*, "teaching"; the Vulgate has *dicentem*, "saying"] through an angel, by whose service this vision was formed in the imaginative power; and this vision Jacob truly understood, the angel teaching him within: [[28:13|I am the Lord God of Abraham|Ego sum Dominus Deus Abraham]], etc. [[28:14|And thy seed shall be as the dust of the earth|Eritque semen tuum quasi pulvis terræ]], that is, thy posterity shall be countless like the dust. See, here his whole posterity is compared to dust. [[28:14|thou shalt spread abroad to the west, and to the east|Dilataberis ad orientem et occidentem]] [Denis reads "to the east and the west"], etc. Although this was in some measure fulfilled in the carnal posterity of Jacob himself, which was not only spread toward the four quarters of the land of promise but also increased and multiplied in the four parts of the world, yet it was more fully fulfilled in the Christian people, who are the spiritual sons of Jacob, as also of Abraham, by following their faith and virtues. For the Apostles, born of Jacob, filled the world with spiritual sons by converting unbelievers and regenerating them of water and the Spirit. [[28:14|and IN THEE and thy seed, all the tribes of the earth SHALL BE BLESSED|Et benedicentur in te et in semine tuo cunctæ tribus terræ]], that is, in Christ, as has often been explained; and so this promise was made not only to Abraham and Isaac but also to this Jacob.

paras.t: Eroque custos tuus quocumque perrexeris, etc. Magna promissio, ex qua sequi videtur quod Deus in omnibus præservavit eum deinceps a culpa mortali, forsan et ante, maxime quum credatur sanctificatus in utero, sicut præhabitum est.
paras.en: [[28:15|And I will be thy keeper whithersoever thou goest|Eroque custos tuus quocumque perrexeris]], etc. A great promise, from which it seems to follow that God thenceforth preserved him in all things from mortal sin, and perhaps before as well, especially since he is believed to have been sanctified in the womb, as was said earlier.

paras.t: Quumque evigilasset Jacob de somno, ait: Vere Dominus est in loco isto. Quamvis enim dicatur esse ubique, ibi tamen specialius esse asseritur, ubi se ipsum magis gratiose ostendit, et specialius operatur: sicque specialiter fuit in loco hoc per se et suum effectum. Vel dixit hoc, quoniam Deo revelante cognovit mysteria Christi ibi esse complenda pro magna parte, quia in monte illo, tempore Salomonis constructum est templum Salomonis: quo per Chaldæos destructo, ædificatum est rursus ibi templum post reditum a Babylonica captivitate, in quo Christus multoties prædicavit, miracula fecit, et in cœnaculo quod erat templo vicinum, instituit sui corporis et sanguinis Sacramentum. Et ego nesciebam, id est, mysteria ista quæ ex revelatione hac nosco, antea ignoravi.
paras.en: [[28:16|And when Jacob awaked out of sleep, he said|Quumque evigilasset Jacob de somno, ait]]: [[28:16|Indeed the Lord is in this place|Vere Dominus est in loco isto]]. For although he is said to be everywhere, yet he is said to be there more specially where he shows himself more graciously and works more specially; and so he was specially in this place, by himself and by his effect. Or he said this because, God revealing it, he knew that the mysteries of Christ were to be accomplished there in great part: for on that mountain, in the time of Solomon, the temple of Solomon was built[[2 Par 3:1||]]; and when it had been destroyed by the Chaldeans, a temple was built there again after the return from the Babylonian captivity[[1 Esd 5:2||]], in which Christ preached many times and worked miracles, and in the upper room, which was near the temple, instituted the Sacrament of his body and blood[[Luke 22:12||]] [the margin gives Luc. xxi, 10-13; the upper room is at Luke 22:10–13]. [[28:16|and I knew it not|Et ego nesciebam]], that is, these mysteries which I know from this revelation I did not know before.

paras.t: Pavensque, id est reverentialiter metuens Deum, et majestatem ejus ac pietatem, mysteria quoque Christi admirans ex revelatione et visione præfata. Et Habacuc ait: Domine, audivi auditum tuum, et timui; consideravi opera tua, et expavi. Quam terribilis, inquit, est locus iste! Quasi dicat, Valde metuendus est ac venerandus: metuendus, inquam, adversariis potestatibus, et honorandus hominibus, non propter locum seu terram istam secundum se consideratam, sed propter præsentiam Dei in eo exhibitam, et propter opera Dei hic facta, et quoniam templum Dei ædificandum est hic, potissime autem propter præsentiam et opera Christi futura in loco isto. Ideo subditur: Non est hic aliud nisi domus Dei, hoc est, in loco isto templum et tabernaculum Dei erit, in quo ipse specialiter habitabit per copiosum atque multiplicem suæ pietatis effectum: Dominus enim in templo sancto suo. Et porta cœli. Hoc addit, vel quia ab illo loco videbatur sibi cœlum quasi apertum, quando vidit Deum cœli innixum scalæ cœlum tangenti; vel quia per cultum Dei qui futurus tunc erat in templo, meruerunt fideles veteris Testamenti felicitatem cœlestem; vel quia in spiritu vidit Christi passionem circa locum illum futuram, per quam janua regni cœlestis est aperta credentibus. Hinc in Scholastica historia dicitur, quod Jacob per verba hæc prophetavit de lege danda, templo ædificando, et Christi passione.
paras.en: [[28:17|And trembling|Pavensque]], that is, fearing God with reverence, and his majesty and goodness, and wondering also at the mysteries of Christ, from the revelation and vision just described. And Habacuc says: [[Hab 3:2|O Lord, I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid|Domine, audivi auditum tuum, et timui]]; I considered thy works, and trembled [this last clause is not in the Vulgate or the Douay-Rheims; it is the old Latin version made from the Septuagint]. [[28:17|How terrible|Quam terribilis]], he says, [[28:17|is this place|est locus iste]]! As if to say: It is greatly to be feared and revered: to be feared, I say, by the adverse powers, and to be honoured by men; not because of the place or this ground considered in itself, but because of the presence of God shown in it, and because of the works of God done here, and because the temple of God is to be built here, but above all because of the presence and works of Christ that were to be in this place. Therefore it is added: [[28:17|this is no other but the house of God|Non est hic aliud nisi domus Dei]], that is, in this place there will be the temple and tabernacle of God, in which he will dwell specially by the abundant and manifold working of his goodness: for [[Ps 10:5|The Lord is in his holy temple|Dominus enim in templo sancto suo]]. [[28:17|and the gate of heaven|Et porta cœli]]. He adds this either because from that place heaven seemed to him as it were opened, when he saw the God of heaven leaning upon the ladder that touched heaven; or because through the worship of God that was afterwards to be in the temple, the faithful of the Old Testament merited heavenly happiness; or because he saw in spirit the passion of Christ that was to take place near that spot, by which the gate of the heavenly kingdom has been opened to believers. Hence it is said in the Scholastic History that by these words Jacob prophesied of the law to be given, the temple to be built, and the passion of Christ.

paras.t: Surgens ergo Jacob mane, tulit lapidem quem supposuerat capiti suo, et erexit, id est, statuit eum, in titulum, hoc est in memoriale hujus visionis commendabile et condignum, atque in signum rei præteritæ, utpote revelationis sibi ostensæ, in signum quoque rei venturæ, videlicet passionis dominicæ, construendique templi: fundens oleum desuper: quod Deo libavit ac obtulit in signum, quod ab ipso est omnis unctio spiritualis, et quoniam lapis ille Christi figura fuit, qui est petra, angularisque lapis: de quo ait Psalmista: Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ.
paras.en: [[28:18|And Jacob arising in the morning, took the stone which he had laid under his head|Surgens ergo Jacob mane, tulit lapidem quem supposuerat capiti suo]], [[28:18|and set it up|et erexit]], that is, stood it upright, [[28:18|for a title|in titulum]], that is, as a memorial of this vision, worthy and fitting, and as a sign of a thing past, namely the revelation shown to him, and as a sign also of a thing to come, namely the Lord's passion and the temple to be built: [[28:18|pouring oil upon the top of it|fundens oleum desuper]]; this he poured out and offered to God as a sign that from him is all spiritual anointing, and because that stone was a figure of Christ, who is the rock[[1 Cor 10:4||]] and the corner stone[[1 Pet 2:6||]], of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ]].

paras.t: Appellavitque nomen urbis, juxta quam fuit hic locus, Bethel: quod interpretatur domus Dei, quia jam dixerat, Non est hic aliud nisi domus Dei. Postea quoque aucta est civitas ista, ita quod locus iste in ea fuit inclusus; sicque tempore Salomonis in ea constructum est templum, quod Jacob intellexit futurum.
paras.en: [[28:19|And he called the name of the city|Appellavitque nomen urbis]], near which this place was, [[28:19|Bethel|Bethel]]: which is interpreted *house of God*, because he had already said: [[28:17|this is no other but the house of God|Non est hic aliud nisi domus Dei]]. Afterwards, too, this city was enlarged, so that this place was enclosed within it; and so in the time of Solomon the temple was built in it, which Jacob understood was to come.

paras.t: Quæ prius Luza vocabatur. Hæc est Jerusalem, quæ plura nomina est sortita. Nam (ut dictum est) primo a Melchisedech fertur fundata, et Salem vocata: postea dicta est Jebus, quia in ea Jebusæi habitaverunt: ex quibus duobus nominibus post factum est unum nomen, b mutata in r, et Jerusalem est vocata. Dicta est quoque Luza, id est nux sive amygdalus, quia dum cœpit fundari, inventa est ibi radix amygdalina, vel quia arbores amygdalinæ abundabant ibidem. Deinceps a Salomone, qui eam ampliavit et roboravit, appellata est Solyma; atque per compositionem prioris nominis, Jerosolyma dicta est. Est etiam ab Adriano imperatore Ælia vocata, quia ipse Ælius Adrianus appellabatur. In Scholastica demum historia fertur: A Jebusæis qui eam condiderant, prius vocata est Luza.
paras.en: [[28:19|which before was called Luza|Quæ prius Luza vocabatur]]. This is Jerusalem, which has received several names. For (as was said) it is held to have been founded first by Melchisedech and called Salem; afterwards it was called Jebus, because the Jebusites dwelt in it; and from these two names one name was afterwards made, *b* being changed into *r*, and it was called Jerusalem. It was also called Luza, that is, nut or almond tree, because when it began to be founded an almond root was found there, or because almond trees abounded there. After that it was named Solyma by Solomon, who enlarged and fortified it; and by joining this to the earlier name it was called Jerosolyma. It was also called Ælia by the emperor Hadrian, because he himself was named Ælius Hadrianus. Lastly, the Scholastic History says: By the Jebusites, who had built it, it was first called Luza.

paras.t: Vovit etiam votum, id est, Deo promisit, dicens: Si fuerit Deus mecum, et custodierit me in via, etc. Jam ante Deus dixit ad eum: Ero custos tuus quocumque perrexeris. Cur ergo locutus est Jacob de isto conditionaliter quasi incertus de rei eventu? Respondetur, quod forsitan formidavit, ne peccando poneret obicem gratiæ ac beneficiis Dei. Nam tales promissiones divinæ, frequenter sub conditione intelliguntur.
paras.en: [[28:20|And he made a vow|Vovit etiam votum]], that is, he promised to God, [[28:20|saying: If God shall be with me, and shall keep me in the way|dicens: Si fuerit Deus mecum, et custodierit me in via]], etc. God had already said to him before: [[28:15|I will be thy keeper whithersoever thou goest|Ero custos tuus quocumque perrexeris]]. Why then did Jacob speak of this conditionally, as if uncertain of the outcome? The answer is that perhaps he was afraid lest by sinning he should put an obstacle in the way of God's grace and benefits. For such divine promises are often to be understood under a condition.

paras.t: Erit mihi Dominus in Deum. Ista videtur inepta promissio, quia ad Dei cultum tenebatur, etiamsi non dedisset ei necessaria victui atque vestitui. Votum autem debet esse de operibus supererogationis, ad quæ homo aliunde non obligatur, non de necessariis ad salutem. Respondetur, quod non solum vovit quod Dominus esset sibi in Deum, sed et quod coleret eum per actus et hostias specialis devotionis, atque per opera supererogationis. Ideo subditur, et lapis iste quem erexi in titulum, vocabitur domus Dei: id est, in loco isto quum rediero, sacrificia et hostias offeram Domino, ut propono, tanquam in loco sacro, ita quod deinceps domus Dei vocabitur, id est locus divino cultui deputatus, præsertim quia in eo templum Domini construetur. Cunctorumque quæ dederis mihi, decimas offeram tibi. Intelligendum est hoc de decimis, quæ ultra aut præter debitum offeruntur, non de his ad quas ex lege naturali aut divina obligabatur, quas votum proprie non concernit.
paras.en: [[28:21|the Lord shall be my God|Erit mihi Dominus in Deum]]. This seems an unfitting promise, since he was bound to the worship of God even if God had not given him what was needed for food and clothing. But a vow ought to be about works of supererogation [that is, good works beyond what is commanded], to which a man is not otherwise bound, not about things necessary for salvation. The answer is that he vowed not only that the Lord should be his God, but also that he would worship him by acts and offerings of special devotion, and by works of supererogation. Therefore it is added: [[28:22|And this stone, which I have set up for a title, shall be called the house of God|et lapis iste quem erexi in titulum, vocabitur domus Dei]]: that is, when I return I will offer sacrifices and victims to the Lord in this place, as I purpose, as in a holy place, so that thenceforth it shall be called the house of God, that is, a place set apart for divine worship, especially since the temple of the Lord will be built in it. [[28:22|and of all things that thou shalt give to me, I will offer tithes to thee|Cunctorumque quæ dederis mihi, decimas offeram tibi]]. This is to be understood of tithes offered over and above what is owed, not of those to which he was bound by natural or divine law, which a vow does not properly concern.

paras.t: Juxta spiritualem intelligentiam, per Jacob propria ex patris jussione relinquentem, et alienam terram ingredientem, ibique uxorem accipientem, intelligendus est Christus, qui, Deo Patre volente, venit in mundum, et tandem Synagoga relicta, ad gentilitatem se vertit, ad se illam trahens, convertens, et sponsam accipiens, sicut de Abraham dictum est. Insuper, per ejus somnum mors Christi est figurata, ejusque resurrectio per Jacob evigilationem.
paras.en: In the spiritual sense, by Jacob leaving his own home at his father's command, entering a foreign land and taking a wife there, is to be understood Christ, who by the will of God the Father came into the world, and at length, leaving the Synagogue, turned to the Gentiles, drawing them to himself, converting them and taking them as his bride, as was said of Abraham. Moreover, by Jacob's sleep the death of Christ was figured, and his resurrection by Jacob's awaking.

paras.t: Quod autem lapidem capiti suo supposuit, hoc designavit, quod omnes Sancti Christo et ejus gratiæ innituntur. Per scalam vero quam vidit, ultra prætacta, mystice designatur gradus evangelicarum doctrinarum et octo beatitudinum, per quas ad regnum ascenditur sempiternum: per quam scalam angeli, id est sacerdotes boni et contemplativi, omnesque virtuosi ascendunt ad cœlestia adipiscendo atque assidue proficiendo; et descendunt, proximis succurrendo, sua peccata deflendo, se ipsos discutiendo, et suas ærumnas ac defectuositates pensando. Angeli quoque sunt prædicatores et prælati virtuosi ac fervidi, qui in scala quæ Christus est, ascendunt, deitatis sublimia speculando; et descendunt, suæ humanitatis mysteria revolvendo. Sicque per Jacob potest intelligi quicumque vitiorum calcator. Infimum autem scalæ, potest intelligi pœnitentia, fides, timor Dei, sive humilitas. Cacumen autem scalæ, perfecta dilectio, contemplatio pura, mystica theologia. In hac scala homo hujusmodi videt Deum scalæ innixum, id est super omnem virtutum altitudinem elevatum, et ad succurrendum infirmitati humanæ semper paratum, nosque pie hortantem, et grandia promittentem. Latera scalæ dici possunt Scripturæ novi ac veteris Testamenti, intra quas fit ascensus ac spiritualis profectus, dum illis undique admonemur.
paras.en: And his putting the stone under his head signified that all the Saints rest upon Christ and his grace. By the ladder that he saw, besides what has been said already, is mystically designated the degrees of the gospel teachings and of the eight beatitudes, by which one ascends to the everlasting kingdom. By this ladder the angels, that is, good and contemplative priests, and all the virtuous, ascend to heavenly things by attaining them and by constantly advancing; and they descend by succouring their neighbours, by bewailing their sins, by examining themselves, and by weighing their miseries and failings. The angels are also virtuous and fervent preachers and prelates, who on the ladder which is Christ ascend by contemplating the sublime things of his deity, and descend by pondering the mysteries of his humanity. And so by Jacob may be understood anyone who tramples vices underfoot. The lowest part of the ladder may be understood as penance, faith, the fear of God, or humility; the top of the ladder, perfect love, pure contemplation, mystical theology. On this ladder such a man sees God leaning upon the ladder, that is, raised above every height of the virtues, and always ready to succour human weakness, kindly exhorting us and promising great things. The sides of the ladder may be said to be the Scriptures of the New and Old Testament, within which the ascent and spiritual progress take place, while we are admonished by them on every side.

paras.t: Postremo per locum in quo Jacob quievit, intelligitur non solum universalis Ecclesia, sed et quæcumque Ecclesia particularis, imo et materialis basilica Domino consecrata, quæ propter summæ Majestatis præsentiam, propter sacramentorum Christi inexsistentiam, propter divini Officii celebrationem, propter fidelium devotam conventionem et sanctam orationem, terribilis est malignis spiritibus, ac venerabilis etiam angelis sanctis, nec aliud est nisi domus Dei, portaque cœli: quia in ea per sacramentalem confessionem delentur peccata, et infunduntur virtutes, per quas patet janua regni cœlestis.
paras.en: Lastly, by the place in which Jacob rested is understood not only the universal Church, but also every particular church, nay, even a material basilica consecrated to the Lord; which, because of the presence of the supreme Majesty, because Christ's sacraments abide within it, because of the celebration of the divine Office, and because of the devout gathering and holy prayer of the faithful, is terrible to the evil spirits and venerable even to the holy angels, and is no other than [[28:17|the house of God, and the gate of heaven|domus Dei, portaque cœli]]: for in it sins are blotted out through sacramental confession, and virtues are infused, through which the gate of the heavenly kingdom lies open.

29.title: Explanatio capituli vicesimi noni: Profectus ergo Jacob, venit in terram
29.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-ninth chapter: “Then Jacob went on in his journey, and came into the east country”

paras.t: RECITATUR præsenti capitulo, qualiter Jacob ad Laban pervenit, ejusque filias duxit uxores, et ex una earum nomine Lia, quatuor filios generavit; nec est difficultas in textu, ideo immorandum non reor.
paras.en: This chapter relates how Jacob came to Laban and married his daughters, and begot four sons by one of them, named Lia; and there is no difficulty in the text, so I do not think we need dwell on it.

paras.t: Profectus ergo Jacob a loco in quo vidit scalam in somno, venit in terram orientalem, hoc est in Mesopotamiam, quæ respectu Judææ seu Bersabee unde venerat, sita est versus orientem; et vidit puteum in agro, etc., non remote ab urbe nomine Haran seu Charan. Dixitque ad pastores, qui juxta puteum pecora sua custodiebant : Fratres, unde estis? Ex hoc patet humilitas Jacob et caritas, quod ipse tanti filius Patriarchæ, vocavit pastores ovium fratres. Qui responderunt : De Haran, id est de urbe sic appellata, in qua cognati ipsius Jacob commorabantur. Quos interrogans : Numquid, ait, nostis Laban filium Nachor? Dixerunt : Novimus, etc. Laban filius exstitit Bathuelis filii Nachor, sicque Nachor non fuit pater ipsius Laban immediatus, sed avus seu pater mediatus. Nominavit autem Jacob Nachor magis quam Bathuelem, quoniam Nachor fuit caput cognationis illius in loco illo. Dixitque Jacob pastoribus : Adhuc multum diei superest, nec est tempus ut reducantur greges ad caulas, id est ad sua ovilia seu latibula, in quibus de nocte quiescunt ; date ante potum ovibus, hoc est, nunc eas potate, et sic eas ad pastum reducite, etc., quia adhuc longe est a vespera.
paras.en: [[29:1|Then Jacob went on in his journey|Profectus ergo Jacob]] from the place where he saw the ladder in his sleep, [[29:1|and came into the east country|venit in terram orientalem]], that is, into Mesopotamia, which lies towards the east with respect to Judea or Bersabee, from which he had come; [[29:2|And he saw a well in the field|et vidit puteum in agro]], etc., not far from the city named Haran or Charan. [[29:4|And he said to the shepherds|Dixitque ad pastores]], who were keeping their cattle by the well: [[29:4|Brethren, whence are you|Fratres, unde estis]]? From this the humility and charity of Jacob are plain, in that he, the son of so great a Patriarch, called the shepherds of the sheep brethren. [[29:4|They answered: Of Haran|Qui responderunt : De Haran]], that is, from the city so called, in which Jacob's kinsmen dwelt. [[29:5|And he asked them, saying: Know you Laban, the son of Nachor?|Quos interrogans : Numquid, ait, nostis Laban filium Nachor?]] [[29:5|They said: We know him|Dixerunt : Novimus]], etc. Laban was the son of Bathuel the son of Nachor, and so Nachor was not Laban's immediate father, but his grandfather, or mediate father. Jacob named Nachor rather than Bathuel because Nachor was the head of that kindred in that place. [[29:7|And Jacob said|Dixitque Jacob]] to the shepherds: [[29:7|There is yet much day remaining, neither is it time to bring the flocks into the folds again|Adhuc multum diei superest, nec est tempus ut reducantur greges ad caulas]], that is, to their sheepfolds or shelters, in which they rest at night; [[29:7|first give the sheep drink|date ante potum ovibus]], that is, water them now, [[29:7|and so lead them back to feed|et sic eas ad pastum reducite]], etc., since it is still long till evening.

paras.t: Ecce Rachel veniebat cum ovibus patris sui, nam gregem ipsa pascebat. Hæc adhuc apud plures est consuetudo, quod puellæ et filiæ oves pascunt in agris. Ego quoque in pueritia mea antequam cœpi frequentare scholas, custodivi et pavi oves parentum meorum, et etiam puer valde malus, pugnans frequenter in agro contra alios pueros ovium pastores.
paras.en: [[29:9|and behold Rachel came with her father's sheep; for she fed the flock|Ecce Rachel veniebat cum ovibus patris sui, nam gregem ipsa pascebat]]. It is still the custom among many that girls and daughters feed the sheep in the fields. I too, in my boyhood, before I began to attend the schools, kept and fed my parents' sheep, and was moreover a very bad boy, often fighting in the field against the other boys who kept sheep.

paras.t: Quam quum vidisset Jacob, et sciret consobrinam suam esse. Quum enim loqueretur de Laban cum pastoribus, pastores dixerunt ad eum : Puella huc veniens, est filia Laban. Amovit lapidem quo puteus claudebatur : qui lapis magnus fuit. Ex quo expositores eliciunt, quod Jacob non venit solus, sed adjutorio sociorum itineris sui lapidem illum removit. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus dicit contrarium, asserens expositores Hebræorum affirmare, quod solus hoc fecit divina virtute; sed primum verius creditur, nec obstat quod Paulus allegat Scripturam istud singulariter referre de Jacob, quoniam consuetudo Scripturæ est, ut ei factum adscribat, qui principalis causa ipsius est. Et adaquato grege, solito maturius et contra consuetudinem, osculatus est eam, ex naturali amore, tanquam propinquam. Et elevata voce flevit, ex naturali cordis liquefactione, aut quasi præ gaudio, quod post tam longum iter pervenisset tandem ad personam sibi tam proximam : et indicavit ei quod frater, id est nepos, esset patris sui, utpote Laban. Est tamen probabile, quod hoc dixit Racheli ante deosculationem ipsius, imo et ante potationem ovium ejus, ita quod statim accessit eam, dicens se esse filium sororis Laban : alias Rachel forsan ægre tulisset osculum viri ignoti ac peregrini.
paras.en: [[29:10|And when Jacob saw her, and knew her to be his cousin german|Quam quum vidisset Jacob, et sciret consobrinam suam esse]]. For when he was speaking of Laban with the shepherds, the shepherds said to him: The girl coming hither is Laban's daughter. [[29:10|he removed the stone wherewith the well was closed|Amovit lapidem quo puteus claudebatur]]: which stone was a great one. From this the expositors gather that Jacob did not come alone, but removed that stone with the help of the companions of his journey. Yet Rabbi Paul says the contrary, asserting that the expositors of the Hebrews affirm that he did this alone, by divine power; but the first is more truly believed, nor is it an obstacle that Paul alleges that Scripture relates this of Jacob in the singular, since it is the custom of Scripture to ascribe a deed to him who is its principal cause. [[29:11|And having watered the flock|Et adaquato grege]], earlier than usual and against custom [the transcription reads *solito manius*, taken here as *solito maturius*], [[29:11|he kissed her|osculatus est eam]], out of natural love, as a kinswoman. [[29:11|and lifting up his voice wept|Et elevata voce flevit]], out of a natural melting of the heart, or as it were for joy that after so long a journey he had at last come to a person so near to him: [[29:12|And he told her that he was her father's brother|et indicavit ei quod frater, id est nepos, esset patris sui]], that is, nephew, namely of Laban. Yet it is probable that he told Rachel this before he kissed her, and indeed before he watered her sheep, so that he went up to her at once, saying that he was the son of Laban's sister: otherwise Rachel might perhaps have taken it ill to be kissed by an unknown man and a stranger.

paras.t: Lyra refert hic fabulam Judæorum, dicentium quod Jacob in itinere fuit captus et spoliatus ab Eliphaz primogenito Esau, quem pater suus ad hoc misit post Jacob, quem tamen ipse Eliphaz non occidit, sed omnibus bonis suis spoliatum, dimisit solum ac vacuum : ideo Jacob flevit, quod non habuit aliquod clenodium seu jocale quod daret suæ cognatæ. Huic recitationi contradicit Rabbi Paulus, asserens ipsum Jacob solum abiisse a suis parentibus sine comitiva ac copia argenti et auri, tanquam fugitivum ne cognosceretur ab aliquo. Verumtamen verius puto, quod cum honesta servorum comitiva recesserit; nec obstat, quod fugitivus abscessit, imo propter vitanda pericula sibi in via evenire potentia, tutius fuit quod abiit comitatus.
