The word 'hid' here has the force of a past tense: for while Laban was searching the tents of Jacob and of his other wives, Rachel hastily concealed the idols under the furniture, by which some understand the camel's saddle; but it seems doubtful that they could be hidden under the saddle, even though she sat on top of it; so by the camel's furniture may be understood the straw and other things laid under a camel. [[31:34|And when he had searched all the tent, and found nothing|scrutantique omne tentorium, et nihil invenienti]], Rachel said: [[31:35|Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise up before thee, because it has now happened to me according to the custom of women.|Ne irascatur dominus meus quod coram te assurgere nequeo: quia juxta consuetudinem feminarum nunc accidit mihi.]] That is, an unforeseen womanly weakness, the monthly flow, does not permit me to rise. Hence, according to Josephus, she said that her natural purgation was upon her; and this was at the least an officious lie [that is, a lie told to avert harm, not a malicious one]. [[31:35|So his careful search was in vain|sic delusa sollicitudo quærentis est]], because he was deceived by so courteous and plausible a speech.

paras.t: Tumensque Jacob, cum jurgio, id est juste indignans, aut etiam motum aliquem venialiter culpabilem animositatis et iræ atque impatientiæ habens, quoniam contumeliosum fuit ita de furto impeti, reprehendi et examinari, ait: Quam ob culpam meam, etc., sic scrutatus es, etc.? quid invenisti de cuncta substantia domus tuæ? id est, si aliquid de tua substantia invenisti in tabernaculis meis: pone coram fratribus meis et fratribus tuis, etc., hoc est coram filiis et cognatis nostris hic congregatis. Idcirco per viginti annos fui tecum? etc. Quasi dicat: Ingratus es beneficiis meis. Ego damnum omne reddebam, etc., id est, pecora furto ablata, et a bestiis devorata exigebas a me, et satisfeci tibi, ac solvi hujusmodi damna. Die noctuque æstu urebar et gelu, etc., id est, nunc ardore solis, nunc frigore noctis ac hiemis affligebar, circa pecora occupatus. Nisi Deus patris, id est avi mei Abraham, et timor Isaac, hoc est Deus quem super omnia timet Isaac, de quo loquitur Isaias, Dominum exercituum sanctificate, ipse timor vester, et ipse tremor vester (Is. viii, 13): unde ad insinuandum quam summe metuendus sit Deus, et quam specialiter timuit eum Isaac, dictum est quasi in abstracto, Nisi timor Isaac; affuisset mihi, forsitan modo nudum me dimisisses, hoc est utique satis probabile.
paras.en: [[31:36|And Jacob being angry, said in a chiding manner|Tumensque Jacob, cum jurgio ait]]: that is, being justly indignant, or even having some movement of animosity, anger and impatience that was venially blameworthy, since it was insulting to be thus assailed with a charge of theft, rebuked and examined: [[31:36|For what fault of mine|Quam ob culpam meam]], etc., hast thou so [[31:37|searched all my household stuff? What hast thou found of all the substance of thy house?|scrutatus es omnem supellectilem meam? quid invenisti de cuncta substantia domus tuæ?]] That is, if you have found any of your substance in my tents, [[31:37|lay it here before my brethren, and thy brethren|pone hic coram fratribus meis, et fratribus tuis]], etc., that is, before our sons and kinsmen gathered here. [[31:38|Have I, therefore, been with thee twenty years?|Idcirco viginti annis fui tecum?]] etc. As if to say: You are ungrateful for my benefits. [[31:39|I made good all the damage|ego damnum omne reddebam]], etc.: that is, you demanded of me the cattle carried off by theft and devoured by beasts, and I made satisfaction to you and paid for such losses. [[31:40|Day and night was I parched with heat, and with frost|die noctuque æstu urebar, et gelu]], etc.: that is, I was afflicted now by the burning of the sun, now by the cold of night and of winter, while busy about the flocks. [[31:42|Unless the God of my father, Abraham|Nisi Deus patris mei Abraham]] ('my father,' that is, my grandfather), [[31:42|and the fear of Isaac|et timor Isaac]], that is, the God whom Isaac fears above all things, of whom Isaias speaks: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself: and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.|Dominum exercituum ipsum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester.]] Hence, to suggest how supremely God is to be feared, and how especially Isaac feared Him, it is said as if in the abstract, 'unless the fear of Isaac'; [[31:42|had stood by me, peradventure now thou hadst sent me away naked|affuisset mihi, forsitan modo nudum me dimisisses]]: that is, this is certainly quite probable.

paras.t: Circa hoc quærit Rabbi Paulus, cur Jacob distincte ait de Deo et de Abraham ac Isaac, Nisi Deus Abraham et timor Isaac. Ad quod (ut refert quidam) Hebræi respondent, quod Deus non vocatur Deus alicujus singularis personæ, quamdiu vivit in sæculo isto, quia potest mutari de bono in malum; et Abraham jam obierat, et Isaac adhuc vixerat, quando Jacob hæc protulit, ideo ita locutus est. Sed responsio ista non valet, quum supra legatur Eliezer Abrahæ procurator, quum ivisset pro Rebecca, dixisse: Domine, Deus domini mei Abraham, occurre hodie mihi (Gen. xxiv, 12). Deus quoque dixit Abrahæ adhuc viventi, ut sim Deus tuus, et Deus seminis tui (Gen. xvii, 7). Elias quoque in sæculo isto frequenter locutus est, Domine, Deus meus (III Reg. xvii, 20, 21); imo capitulo immediate sequente ait Jacob, Deus patris mei Isaac (Gen. xxxii, 9).
paras.en: On this Rabbi Paul asks why Jacob speaks of God distinctly with Abraham and with Isaac: [[31:42|the God of my father, Abraham, and the fear of Isaac|Deus patris mei Abraham, et timor Isaac]]. To which (as someone reports) the Hebrews answer that God is not called the God of any individual person as long as he lives in this world, because he can be changed from good to evil; and Abraham was already dead, while Isaac was still living, when Jacob spoke these words; therefore he spoke thus. But this answer does not hold, since we read above that Eliezer, Abraham's steward, when he had gone for Rebecca, said: [[Gen 24:12|O Lord, the God of my master, Abraham, meet me today, I beseech thee|Domine Deus domini mei Abraham, occurre, obsecro, mihi hodie]]. God also said to Abraham while he was still living, [[Gen 17:7|to be a God to thee, and to thy seed|ut sim Deus tuus, et seminis tui]]. Elias too, in this world, often said, [[3 Kings 17:20|O Lord, my God|Domine Deus meus]]; indeed, in the very next chapter Jacob says, [[Gen 32:9|God of my father Isaac|Deus patris mei Isaac]].

paras.t: Respondit Laban: Filiæ meæ, scilicet tuæ uxores, et filii, et greges tui, et omnia quæ cernis hic pertinere ad te, mea sunt. Si voluit dicere Laban, quod erant sui juris atque dominii, falsum erat; si autem, quod erant sibi propinqui, seu a se et a pecoribus suis egressa, verum fuit. Quid possum facere filiis et nepotibus meis? Filios Jacob vocat filios suos et nepotes, quasi valde propinquos, tanquam dicat, Non possum rationabiliter eis nocere, quum sit contra jus naturale, et quia a Deo mihi prohibitum est. Veni ergo, et ineamus fœdus, id est pacis et amicitiæ pactum. Tulit itaque Jacob lapidem, et erexit illum in titulum, hoc est, in signum et testimonium confœderationis atque concordiæ, statuit lapidem illum. Dixitque fratribus suis, id est filiis et consanguineis: Afferte lapides. Qui congregantes lapides, fecerunt tumulum magnum, comederuntque super eum, in protestationem quod essent confœderati. Vidit enim Laban Deum esse pro Jacob; propter quod non audebat ei resistere, et etiam emollitus fuit ex commemoratione beneficiorum et obsequiorum, quæ Jacob retulit se illi exhibuisse. Quem vocavit Laban Tumulum testis, id est tumulum qui est testis initæ pacis, et Jacob Acervum testimonii, uterque juxta proprietatem linguæ suæ. Jacob enim imposuit nomen Hebræum, Laban Syrum: et ambo nomina idem significant. Circa quod ait Hieronymus: Acervus, lingua Hebræa GAL dicitur; AAD vero, testimonium. Porro lingua Syra acervus dicitur JEGAR; testimonium, SYNTHA. Jacob ergo acervum illum vocavit Hebraice Galaad, Laban vero Jegarsyntha.
paras.en: [[31:43|Laban answered him: The daughters are mine, and the children, and thy flocks, and all things that thou seest are mine|Respondit ei Laban: Filiæ meæ et filii, et greges tui, et omnia quæ cernis, mea sunt]]: that is, your wives, and the children, and whatever you see here belonging to you. If Laban meant that they were under his right and ownership, it was false; but if he meant that they were his kin, or had come forth from him and from his flocks, it was true. [[31:43|What can I do to my children, and grandchildren?|quid possum facere filiis et nepotibus meis?]] He calls Jacob's children his own children and grandchildren, as being very near of kin, as if to say: I cannot reasonably harm them, since that would be against natural law, and because God has forbidden it to me. [[31:44|Come, therefore, let us enter into a league|Veni ergo, et ineamus fœdus]]: that is, a covenant of peace and friendship. [[31:45|And Jacob took a stone, and set it up for a title|Tulit itaque Jacob lapidem, et erexit illum in titulum]]: that is, he set up that stone as a sign and testimony of alliance and concord. [[31:46|And he said to his brethren|dixitque fratribus suis]], that is, to his sons and kinsmen: [[31:46|Bring hither stones. And they, gathering stones together, made a heap, and they ate upon it|Afferte lapides. Qui congregantes fecerunt tumulum, comederuntque super eum]], in witness that they were allies. For Laban saw that God was on Jacob's side, and so did not dare to resist him; and he was also softened by Jacob's recounting of the benefits and services he had rendered him. [[31:47|And Laban called it, The witness heap|quem vocavit Laban Tumulum testis]], that is, the heap that bears witness to the peace entered upon, [[31:47|and Jacob, The hillock of testimony: each of them according to the propriety of his language|et Jacob, Acervum testimonii, uterque juxta proprietatem linguæ suæ]]. For Jacob gave it a Hebrew name, Laban a Syrian one, and both names mean the same thing. On this Jerome says: 'Heap' in the Hebrew tongue is called GAL, and 'testimony' AAD; but in the Syrian tongue 'heap' is called JEGAR, and 'testimony' SYNTHA. So Jacob called that heap in Hebrew Galaad, and Laban called it Jegarsyntha.

paras.t: Dixitque Laban: Tumulus iste erit testis, id est reale et mutum testimonium, inter me et te hodie, id est pacti quod modo inivimus, imo et de cetero erit signum fœderis hujus; et idcirco appellatum est nomen ejus Galaad, etc., quia Jacob tunc nomen istud imposuit illi acervo. Et adjecit Laban: Intueatur et judicet Dominus inter nos, id est, per effectum suæ justitiæ pandat se inspectorem operum nostrorum, si unquam post hanc horam violaverimus pactum istud, quando recesserimus a nobis, id est unus ab alio, si afflixeris filias meas injuste, et si introduxeris alias uxores super eas, præferendo illas filiabus meis, et eas opprimendo per illas; nullus sermonis nostri testis est absque Deo, qui præsens respicit: hoc est, ego ab obligatione hac ero immunis, nec aliquis hominum poterit me hujus pacti transgressorem ostendere, sed omnium cordium inspector Deus, infallibilis judex ac testis, puniet reum, qui ubique est præsens, et omnia præsentialiter intuetur. Dixitque rursus ad Jacob, repetendo prolata pro confirmatione dictorum: En tumulus hic, et lapis quem erexi in signum rei gestæ inter me et te, testis erit, etc.; ex quo probatur, quod etiam Laban statuit ibi lapidem aliquem grandem, in protestationem et signum verborum et operum ibi mutuo habitorum; si aut ego transiero illum pergens ad te, hoc est, si intentione nocendi tibi pertransiero locum istum versus te, aut tu præterieris illum, malum mihi cogitans, id est, cum proposito nocendi mihi, veneris ultra hunc locum adversus me; Deus Abraham et Deus Nachor fratris Abrahæ, judicet inter nos, castigando iniquum, Deus patris eorum, id est Deus Thare, qui fuit pater Abrahæ et Nachor. Dicitur autem Deus omnium, Deus Nachor et Thare, vel quia coluerunt eum, sicut et Abraham, vel saltem ratione creationis.
paras.en: [[31:48|And Laban said: This heap shall be a witness between me and thee this day|Dixitque Laban: Tumulus iste erit testis inter me et te hodie]], a real and mute testimony, that is, of the covenant we have just made; indeed, it will hereafter also be a sign of this league; [[31:48|and therefore the name thereof was called Galaad|et idcirco appellatum est nomen ejus Galaad]], etc., because Jacob then gave that name to the heap. And Laban added: [[31:49|The Lord behold and judge between us|Intueatur et judicet Dominus inter nos]], that is, may He show Himself the beholder of our deeds by the effect of His justice, if ever after this hour we violate this covenant, [[31:49|when we shall be gone one from the other|quando recesserimus a nobis]]: [[31:50|If thou afflict my daughters, and if thou bring in other wives over them|si afflixeris filias meas, et si introduxeris alias uxores super eas]] unjustly, preferring them to my daughters and oppressing these through them, [[31:50|none is witness of our speech but God, who is present and beholdeth|nullus sermonis nostri testis est absque Deo, qui præsens respicit]]: that is, I shall be free of this obligation, nor will any man be able to show me a transgressor of this pact; but God, the searcher of all hearts, the infallible judge and witness, who is everywhere present and beholds all things as present, will punish the guilty one. [[31:51|And he said again to Jacob|Dixitque rursus ad Jacob]], repeating what had been said, in confirmation: [[31:51|Behold this heap, and the stone which I have set up between me and thee|En tumulus hic, et lapis quem erexi inter me et te]] as a sign of what was done [[31:52|Shall be a witness|testis erit]], etc. From this it is proved that Laban too set up some great stone there, in witness and sign of the words and deeds that passed between them there. [[31:52|If either I shall pass beyond it going towards thee|si aut ego transiero illum pergens ad te]], that is, if I pass beyond this place toward you with intent to harm you, [[31:52|or thou shalt pass beyond it thinking harm to me|aut tu præterieris, malum mihi cogitans]], that is, if you come beyond this place against me with the purpose of harming me, [[31:53|The God of Abraham, and the God of Nachor|Deus Abraham, et Deus Nachor]], Abraham's brother, [[31:53|judge between us|judicet inter nos]], by punishing the wicked one, [[31:53|the God of their father|Deus patris eorum]], that is, the God of Thare, who was the father of Abraham and Nachor. God is called the God of all, and the God of Nachor and Thare, either because they worshipped Him as Abraham did, or at least by reason of creation.

paras.t: Juravit ergo Jacob se servaturum hoc pactum, per timorem patris sui Isaac, juxta sensum expositum, vel ut aliqui dicunt, et Rabbi Paulus tangit, per timorem quem habuit Isaac, quando putavit se offerendum Deo in holocaustum. Consueverunt etenim homines per terribilia quædam jurare, sicut per horam mortis suæ, aut per diem sui judicii. Immolatisque victimis in monte Galaad, quas obtulit Jacob Deo pro gratiarum actione, quod ita protexit se, et de mutua pace providit, poteratque Jacob tanquam sacerdos offerre privilegio et jure primogenituræ ad se devolutæ, vocavit fratres suos, id est filios et propinquos, ut comederent panem, id est cibos ibi paratos, cum gaudio epulan[di] …
paras.en: [[31:53|And Jacob swore by the fear of his father Isaac|Juravit ergo Jacob per timorem patris sui Isaac]] that he would keep this covenant, according to the sense explained above; or, as some say and Rabbi Paul touches upon, by the fear Isaac had when he thought he was to be offered to God as a holocaust. For men were accustomed to swear by certain terrible things, such as the hour of their death or the day of their judgment. [[31:54|And after he had offered sacrifices in the mountain|immolatisque victimis in monte]], which Jacob offered to God in thanksgiving because He had so protected him and provided for their mutual peace (and Jacob could offer as a priest, by the privilege and right of the firstborn which had passed to him), [[31:54|he called his brethren to eat bread|vocavit fratres suos ut ederent panem]], that is, his sons and kinsmen, to eat the food prepared there, feasting with joy […]

31.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-first chapter: “But after that he had heard the words of the sons of Laban”

32.title: Explanatio capituli tricesimi secundi: Jacob autem abiit itinere quo cœperat
32.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-second chapter: “Jacob also went on the journey he had begun”

paras.t: Prosecutio reversionis Jacob ad terram natalem, et solatia sibi a Deo collata, et qualiter ipse se habuit circa fratrem suum, recitantur præsenti capitulo.
paras.en: The continuation of Jacob's return to his native land, the comforts given him by God, and how he bore himself towards his brother, are related in the present chapter.

paras.t: Jacob autem abiit itinere quo cœperat a monte Galaad die sequenti, cum omnibus ad se pertinentibus ibi; fueruntque ei obviam angeli Dei: qui sibi obviaverunt in assumptis corporibus, ita quod sensibiliter eos vidit in illis corporibus. Quos quum vidisset, ait: Castra Dei sunt hæc, id est fortissimi milites Dei, instar castrorum prævalidi, atque ad protegendum me præparati. Et appellavit nomen loci illius Mahanaim, id est castra, ab effectu: quia videlicet angeli apparuerunt sibi ibidem, qui adversariis potestatibus terribiles sunt ut castrorum acies ordinata.
paras.en: [[32:1|Jacob also went on the journey he had begun|Jacob autem abiit itinere quo cœperat]] from Mount Galaad on the following day, with all that belonged to him there; [[32:1|and the angels of God met him|fueruntque ei obviam angeli Dei]]: they met him in assumed bodies, so that he saw them with his senses in those bodies. [[32:2|And when he saw them, he said: These are the camps of God|Quos quum vidisset, ait: Castra Dei sunt hæc]], that is, the most valiant soldiers of God, mighty as an armed camp, and ready to protect me. [[32:2|and he called the name of that place Mahanaim|Et appellavit nomen loci illius Mahanaim]], [[32:2|that is, Camps|id est castra]], from what happened there: because, namely, the angels appeared to him in that place, who are terrible to the adverse powers as an army set in array.

paras.t: Circa hoc refert Lyra: Dicunt Hebræi, quod angeli qui custodiebant provinciam Syriæ, conduxerunt Jacob usque ad finem provinciæ suæ. Deinde obviaverunt ei angeli provinciæ quam consequenter intravit: quod non videtur congrue dictum, quia uni provinciæ non præest nisi unus angelus, generalem totius provinciæ curam habens. Unde in Daniele habetur de principe Græcorum, principe quoque Persarum, qui fuerunt angeli præsidentes toti regno Græcorum et toti regno Persarum, quemadmodum tunc Michael præfuit Synagogæ, qui est nunc princeps Ecclesiæ: et angeli tales sunt de tertio ordine angelorum, qui dicitur Principatus. Ipsi autem Jacob multitudo angelorum occurrit, ut Scholastica ait historia. Et si ei occurrerunt angeli custodientes provinciam, quam post Syriam introivit, quare scriptura ista non exprimit de occursu angelorum custodientium Syriam, sicut de aliorum angelorum occursu? Verius ergo est quod dicunt doctores catholici, quod angeli illi fuerunt missi ad confortandum Jacob contra fratris sui iniqui timorem. Hinc ait Hieronymus: Jacob ad fratrem iniquum iturus, pulchre excipitur angelorum comitantium choris. Glossa quoque testatur: Multitudo angelorum quæ militia cœli vocatur, occurrit: quibus confortatus, non metuat fratrem suum, securus illorum auxilio.
paras.en: On this Lyra reports: The Hebrews say that the angels who guarded the province of Syria escorted Jacob as far as the border of their province, and that then the angels of the province which he next entered met him. But this does not seem fitly said, for over one province only one angel presides, having the general charge of the whole province. Hence in Daniel we read of the prince of the Greeks[[Dan 10:20||]] and also of the prince of the Persians[[Dan 10:13||]], who were the angels presiding over the whole kingdom of the Greeks and the whole kingdom of the Persians, just as Michael then presided over the Synagogue[[Dan 12:1||]], who is now the prince of the Church; and such angels are of the third order of angels, which is called the Principalities. Yet a multitude of angels came to meet Jacob, as the Scholastic History [that is, the Historia scholastica of Peter Comestor] says. And if the angels guarding the province which he entered after Syria came to meet him, why does this scripture say nothing of the meeting with the angels guarding Syria, as it does of the meeting with the other angels? It is truer, then, as the Catholic doctors say, that those angels were sent to strengthen Jacob against the fear of his wicked brother. Hence Jerome says: Jacob, about to go to his wicked brother, is fittingly received by choirs of angels accompanying him. The Gloss also bears witness: A multitude of angels, which is called the host of heaven, came to meet him, so that, strengthened by them, he should not fear his brother, being secure in their help.

paras.t: Misit autem et nuntios ante se ad Esau fratrem suum, qui erat in terra Seir, in regione Edom, etc. Quemadmodum in expositione capituli vicesimi quinti habitum est, Esau etiam appellatus est Seir et Edom, et hæc nomina Seir ac Edom, interdum sumuntur pro illa provincia in qua demoratus est Esau, et ita nunc accipiuntur, estque idem in re, terra Seir et regio Edom. Reversique sunt nuntii ad Jacob, dicentes: Venimus ad Esau fratrem tuum, et ecce properat in occursum tuum frater tuus cum quadringentis viris. Jacob misit nuntios ad Esau, ad explorandum animum ejus, atque ad captandum benevolentiam ejus: et ut in Scholastica habetur historia, nuntii redeuntes dixerunt ad Jacob, quod frater suus occurreret sibi pacifice.
paras.en: [[32:3|And he sent messengers before him to Esau, his brother|Misit autem et nuntios ante se ad Esau fratrem suum]], who was [[32:3|to the land of Seir, to the country of Edom|in terra Seir, in regione Edom]], etc. As was set out in the exposition of the twenty-fifth chapter, Esau was also called Seir and Edom[[Gen 25:30||]], and these names, Seir and Edom, are sometimes taken for the province in which Esau dwelt, and so they are taken here; and the land of Seir and the country of Edom are the same thing. [[32:6|And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying: We came to Esau, thy brother, and behold he cometh with speed to meet thee|Reversique sunt nuntii ad Jacob, dicentes: Venimus ad Esau fratrem tuum, et ecce properat in occursum tuum]], thy brother, [[32:6|with four hundred men|cum quadringentis viris]]. Jacob sent messengers to Esau to sound out his mind and to win his good will; and, as the Scholastic History has it, the messengers on their return told Jacob that his brother was coming to meet him peaceably.

paras.t: Timuit Jacob valde. Mirum quod vir iste tam virtuosus, post promissionem factam sibi a Deo, Ero tecum, etc., et post intuitum angelorum ad ipsius auxilium paratorum, timuit tantum hominem pravum. Ad quod aliqui dicunt, quod timuit, non de Dei promissione et angelorum ope diffidens, sed more hominum perturbatus: quibus objici potest, quod talem perturbationem debuit virtutum constantia, fidei robur, certitudoque spei prævenire atque excludere. Alii dicunt, quod Jacob formidavit se Deum offendisse, diu habitando cum Laban idololatra: quibus rursus objicitur, quod post illam habitationem Deus dixit ei, ut rediret ad terram nativitatis suæ, et quod esset cum ipso, et post omnia illa apparuerunt ei angeli jam præfati. Arbitror ergo dicendum, quod Jacob vir a Deo sublimiter illuminatus, scivit quod judicia Dei sunt incomprehensibilia et occulta, et quod Deus permittit justos ab impiis in hac vita multipliciter tribulari, quod item divinæ promissiones variis modis possunt intelligi: quamvis ergo non formidavit de finali adjutorio Dei, timuit tamen ad tempus a fratre perverso affligi. Ideo loquitur Augustinus: Quæri potest, quomodo Jacob fidem habuit in promissis Dei: sed fieri potuisset ut Esau tabernacula ejus everteret, et tamen post illam eversionem Deus ei rursus adesset, et sua impleret promissa. Quo exemplo monemur, ut quamvis credamus in Deum, tamen faciamus quæ facienda sunt, in salutis nostræ præsidium.
paras.en: [[32:7|Then Jacob was greatly afraid|Timuit Jacob valde]]. It is a wonder that so virtuous a man, after the promise God had made him, [[Gen 31:3|I will be with thee|Ero tecum]], etc., and after seeing the angels ready to help him, should so fear a wicked man. To this some say that he feared, not as distrusting God's promise and the angels' aid, but troubled as men are; against whom it can be objected that the constancy of the virtues, the strength of faith and the certainty of hope ought to have forestalled and shut out such a disturbance. Others say that Jacob was afraid he had offended God by dwelling so long with Laban, an idolater; against whom again it is objected that after that dwelling God told him to return to the land of his birth, and that he would be with him, and after all that the angels already mentioned appeared to him. I think, therefore, it must be said that Jacob, a man sublimely enlightened by God, knew that the judgments of God are incomprehensible and hidden[[Rom 11:33||]], and that God permits the just to be troubled in many ways by the wicked in this life, and likewise that the divine promises can be understood in various ways: so, although he had no fear for God's final help, he feared nevertheless to be afflicted for a time by his perverse brother. Therefore Augustine says: It may be asked how Jacob had faith in the promises of God; but it could have happened that Esau should overthrow his tents, and yet after that overthrow God should be with him again and fulfil his promises. By this example we are warned that, although we believe in God, we should still do what is to be done for the safeguard of our salvation.

paras.t: Et perterritus, divisit populum qui secum erat, greges quoque pecorum, videlicet asinorum et caprarum, et oves et boves et camelos, in duas turmas, ita quod duæ erant turmæ hominum, et duæ pecorum: atque in prima turma erant Bala et Zelpha cum filiis suis: in secunda et posteriori turma erant Lia cum filiis suis et filia sua Dina, et Rachel cum Joseph. Sic tamen, quod Rachel et Joseph tanquam cariores ipsi Jacob, fuerunt in extremitate secundæ turmæ: dicens: Si venerit Esau ad unam turmam, et percusserit eam, videlicet primam turmam, alia turma quæ reliqua est, salvabitur. Quasi dicat, Esau satiatus sanguine primæ turmæ, parcet secundæ: et ista ex causa Jacob fecit has turmas, ne omnes simul occiderentur ab Esau. Itaque quamvis Jacob speravit in Domino, fecit tamen quidquid potuit per humanam industriam. Propter quod dicit Glossa interlinearis: Imminente periculo, faciamus quod habet humana ratio, ne totum Deo committentes, ipsum videamur tentare.
paras.en: [[32:7|and in his fear divided the people that was with him|Et perterritus, divisit populum qui secum erat]], [[32:7|and the flocks|greges quoque]] of beasts, namely of asses and goats, [[32:7|and the sheep, and the oxen, and the camels, into two companies|et oves et boves et camelos, in duas turmas]], so that there were two companies of men and two of beasts: in the first company were Bala and Zelpha with their sons; in the second and hindmost company were Lia with her sons and her daughter Dina, and Rachel with Joseph; yet so that Rachel and Joseph, as dearer to Jacob, were at the far end of the second company: [[32:8|Saying: If Esau come to one company, and destroy it|dicens: Si venerit Esau ad unam turmam, et percusserit eam]], namely the first company, [[32:8|the other company that is left, shall escape|alia turma quæ reliqua est, salvabitur]]. As if he said: Esau, sated with the blood of the first company, will spare the second; and for this reason Jacob made these companies, that all should not be slain together by Esau. So, although Jacob hoped in the Lord, he still did whatever he could by human effort. For which reason the interlinear Gloss says: When danger threatens, let us do what human reason can, lest by committing everything to God we seem to tempt him.

paras.t: Dixitque Jacob: Deus patris mei Abraham, et Deus patris mei Isaac, Domine qui dixisti mihi, Revertere in terram tuam, etc., et benefaciam tibi: minor sum, id est indignus, cunctis miserationibus tuis mihi impensis seu impendendis, et veritate tua quam explevisti servo tuo, hoc est vera et reali exhibitione beneficiorum tuorum. His quippe erat Jacob indignus, considerando eum secundum naturalia sua tantum, per quæ non meruit eadem de condigno. In baculo meo transivi Jordanem istum, id est cum baculo, utpote sine uxore et liberis, quodammodo solus, sine cognatis, solo meo baculo sustentatus: de cujus verbi intellectu dictum est in expositione capituli vicesimi noni ([…] duabus turmis hominum et pecorum regredior.)
paras.en: [[32:9|And Jacob said: O God of my father Abraham, and God of my father Isaac: O Lord who saidst to me, Return to thy land|Dixitque Jacob: Deus patris mei Abraham, et Deus patris mei Isaac, Domine qui dixisti mihi, Revertere in terram tuam]], etc., [[32:9|and I will do well for thee|et benefaciam tibi]]: [[32:10|I am not worthy|minor sum]] [*minor sum*, literally "I am less"; hence the gloss], that is, unworthy, [[32:10|of the least of all thy mercies|cunctis miserationibus tuis]] spent or to be spent on me, [[32:10|and of thy truth which thou hast fulfilled to thy servant|et veritate tua quam explevisti servo tuo]], that is, of the true and real bestowal of thy benefits. For Jacob was unworthy of these, considering him only according to his natural endowments, by which he did not merit them condignly [that is, by a merit owed in strict justice]. [[32:10|With my staff I passed over this Jordan|In baculo meo transivi Jordanem istum]], that is, with a staff, as being without wife and children, in a manner alone, without kinsfolk, supported by my staff alone: on the meaning of which word something was said in the exposition of the twenty-ninth chapter. ([…] [[32:10|with two companies|duabus turmis]] of men and of beasts [[32:10|I return|regredior]].)

paras.t: Quasi dicat: Tu qui tanta bona mihi fecisti, noli me modo derelinquere. Eripe me de manu Esau, etc. Mirum videtur, quod Jacob sciens sibi promissum a Deo totum quod in textu isto commemorat, tam ferventer oravit pro impletione eorum. Et respondendum, quod merito sic oravit, quoniam Deus sic præordinavit electis suis bona conferre, ut tamen velit eos talia orando et laborando acquirere, ita quod media obtinendi gratiam in præsenti, et gloriam in futuro, cadunt sub providentia Dei. Hinc dicitur, quod prædestinatio Dei precibus electorum juvatur, quia prædestinationis effectus orando obtinetur. Itaque Jacob, ne totum opus suum humano consilio tribuat, orationem adjungit: in cujus oratione apparent humana infirmitas et fidei pietas; sicque oravit, quod spem suam moderabatur timore, et timorem suum spe consolabatur, suo nos docens exemplo, ut nobis ipsis ac domesticis rationabiliter consulamus, et tamen Dei auxilium invocemus.
paras.en: As if he said: Thou who hast done me so much good, do not forsake me now. [[32:11|Deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau|Eripe me de manu Esau]], etc. It seems a wonder that Jacob, knowing that all he recalls in this text had been promised him by God, prayed so fervently for its fulfilment. The answer is that he rightly prayed so, since God has so preordained to bestow good things on his elect that he yet wills them to acquire them by praying and labouring, so that the means of obtaining grace in the present and glory in the future fall under the providence of God. Hence it is said that God's predestination is helped by the prayers of the elect, since the effect of predestination is obtained by praying. So Jacob, lest he ascribe his whole work to human counsel, adds prayer; and in his prayer appear both human weakness and the piety of faith. And he so prayed that he tempered his hope with fear and consoled his fear with hope, teaching us by his example to provide reasonably for ourselves and our households, and yet to call upon the help of God.

paras.t: Quumque dormisset ibi nocte illa, separavit de his quæ habebat, hoc est de suis pecoribus, munera Esau fratri suo, ut eum placaret per ea, capras ducentas, etc.: non viliora, sed pulchriora et cariora pecora diversorum generum, abstraxit de gregibus. Et misit per manus servorum, etc., unumquemque gregem ejusdem speciei seorsum, ita quod fuit spatium inter gregem et gregem, quatenus Esau ex munerum oblationibus magis et magis mitigaretur.
paras.en: [[32:13|And when he had slept there that night, he set apart, of the things which he had|Quumque dormisset ibi nocte illa, separavit de his quæ habebat]], that is, of his cattle, [[32:13|presents for his brother Esau|munera Esau fratri suo]], to appease him with them, [[32:14|Two hundred she-goats|capras ducentas]], etc.: he took out of the flocks not the meaner beasts, but the finer and more valuable, of various kinds. [[32:16|And he sent them by the hands of his servants|Et misit per manus servorum]], etc., each flock of one kind by itself, so that there was [[32:16|a space between drove and drove|spatium inter gregem et gregem]], that Esau might be softened more and more by the offering of the presents.

paras.t: Dixit enim ipse Jacob: Placabo illum muneribus quæ præcedunt, et postea videbo illum, etc. Secundum Glossam, istud interpositum est a scriptore, id est libri hujus auctore. Non est enim viri prudentis sua secreta detegere, sicque his cum quibus agitur, suspectum se facere. Itaque Jacob dixit istud in corde suo, et ex cogitatione hac fecit hanc munerum præmissionem.
paras.en: [[32:20|for he said|Dixit enim]] (Jacob himself): [[32:20|I will appease him with the presents that go before, and afterwards I will see him|Placabo illum muneribus quæ præcedunt, et postea videbo illum]], etc. According to the Gloss, this was put in by the writer, that is, by the author of this book. For it is not the part of a prudent man to lay bare his secrets, and so make himself suspect to those with whom he is dealing. So Jacob said this in his heart, and from this thought he sent the presents ahead.

paras.t: Ipse vero mansit nocte illa in castris, id est in uno tentoriorum suorum. Quumque mature, id est ante diluculum, et cum ingenti provisione, nil faciens sine consilio, surrexisset, tulit duas uxores suas et totidem famulas, quæ etiam erant ejus uxores, cum undecim filiis et cum filia una, et transivit vadum Jaboc, id est torrentem seu flumen sic dictum, de quo aliqui putant quod fuit Jordanis, et vitio scriptoris pro Jacob scriptum sit Jaboc. Alii probabilius dicunt, quod fuit alius fluvius. Infra enim habetur, quod Jacob post hæc venit in Phanuel et Socoth, quæ sunt loca ultra Jordanem, ut fertur, quamvis istud non multum convincat. Sed auctoritas quædam testatur, secundo milliari a Jordane in finibus Idumææ esse Jaboc, quem transvadavit Jacob.
paras.en: [[32:21|but himself lodged that night in the camp|Ipse vero mansit nocte illa in castris]], that is, in one of his tents. [[32:22|And rising early|Quumque mature]], that is, before daybreak (and with great forethought, doing nothing without counsel), [[32:22|he took his two wives and his two handmaids|tulit duas uxores suas et totidem famulas]], who were also his wives, [[32:22|with his eleven sons|cum undecim filiis]] and with one daughter, [[32:22|and passed over the ford of Jaboc|et transivit vadum Jaboc]], that is, a torrent or river so called, of which some think that it was the Jordan, and that by a copyist's error Jaboc was written for Jacob. Others say, more probably, that it was another river. For it is said below that after this Jacob came to Phanuel and Socoth, which are places beyond the Jordan, as is reported, although this does not prove much. But a certain authority testifies that Jaboc, which Jacob forded, is at the second milestone from the Jordan, in the borders of Idumea.

paras.t: Traductisque omnibus, etc., remansit solus in ripa fluminis, ut orationi meditationique purius stabiliusque vacaret, et de agendis deliberaret. Et ecce vir luctabatur cum eo usque mane. Ex hoc constat, quod luctatio ista fuit in nocte, et quod Jacob mansit in ripa illa per diem seu partem diei et noctem. Denique, secundum Augustinum, vir iste luctans cum Jacob, id est contra Jacob, fuit angelus bonus in specie viri apparens, qui cum Jacob de Mesopotamia venit: et aliqui dicunt, quod fuit angelus tunc a Deo specialiter missus ad confortandum et consolandum Jacob, qui fratrem suum valde extimuit. Sed cur angelus iste luctabatur cum Jacob? Dicunt quidam quod ideo, quoniam Jacob aliqualiter immoderate timuit fratrem suum, non satis confidens in Domino, qui adsistentiam suam ei promisit, neque in adjutorio angelorum quos vidit: ideo angelus iste finxit se velle a Jacob recedere, ipse vero orationis suæ instantia ac fervore conabatur eum secum tenere: qui conatus vocatur luctatio. In fictione autem illa angelica non fuit falsitas aliqua, quia vere significavit quod mens Jacob aliqualiter recessit per diffidentiam suam a Deo. Unde et Christus post resurrectionem suam cum discipulis ambulans, finxit se velle longius ire. Alii dicunt, quod luctatio ista non fuit propter culpam Jacob, sed quia ipse Jacob desideravit aliquid spiritualis gratiæ obtinere, in quo angelus noluit eum faciliter exaudire, ad innuendum quod majora gratiarum charismata quandoque difficilius obtinentur a Domino.
paras.en: [[32:23|And when all things were brought over|Traductisque omnibus]], etc., [[32:24|He remained alone|remansit solus]] on the bank of the river, that he might give himself more purely and steadily to prayer and meditation, and deliberate on what was to be done. [[32:24|and behold, a man wrestled with him till morning|Et ecce vir luctabatur cum eo usque mane]]. From this it is clear that this wrestling was at night, and that Jacob stayed on that bank through the day, or part of the day, and the night. Further, according to Augustine, this man wrestling with Jacob, that is, against Jacob, was a good angel appearing in the form of a man, who had come with Jacob from Mesopotamia; and some say that he was an angel then specially sent by God to strengthen and console Jacob, who greatly feared his brother. But why did this angel wrestle with Jacob? Some say it was for this reason: because Jacob in some degree feared his brother immoderately, not trusting enough in the Lord, who had promised him his assistance, nor in the help of the angels he had seen, therefore this angel feigned to wish to depart from Jacob, while Jacob by the insistence and fervour of his prayer strove to keep him with him; and this striving is called wrestling. Yet in that feigning of the angel there was no falsehood, since it truly signified that Jacob's mind had in some degree withdrawn from God through his distrust. So also Christ, walking with the disciples after his resurrection: [[Luke 24:28|he made as though he would go farther|finxit se velle longius ire]]. Others say that this wrestling was not on account of any fault of Jacob, but because Jacob desired to obtain some spiritual grace, in which the angel would not readily hear him, to suggest that the greater gifts of grace are sometimes obtained from the Lord with more difficulty.

paras.t: Præterea quæritur, qualis fuerit ista lucta, et dicunt quidam, quod spiritualis dumtaxat. Ait enim Hieronymus super Isaiam: Oratione, non manibus, luctabatur Jacob cum angelo, qui eum custodierat in peregrinatione, et volebat eum relinquere ad cœlum volando, sed Jacob oratione benedictionem obtinuit. Alii dicunt, quod fuit non solum spiritualis, sed etiam corporalis seu manualis, quia paulo post subditur, quod angelus tetigit nervum femoris ejus. Sed quidquid sit de veritate hujus opinionis, argumentum hoc faciliter solveretur, dicendo quod ille fuit tactus virtutis, non manus aut corporis: solo enim virtuali influxu et potestatis suæ contactu potuit angelus hoc, imo et multo majora efficere.
paras.en: It is further asked what kind of wrestling this was; and some say that it was only spiritual. For Jerome says on Isaias: Jacob wrestled with the angel by prayer, not with hands; the angel had guarded him in his wanderings, and wished to leave him by flying to heaven, but Jacob by prayer obtained the blessing. Others say that it was not only spiritual, but also bodily, or with the hands, because a little after it is added that the angel [[32:25|touched the sinew of his thigh|tetigit nervum femoris ejus]]. But whatever be the truth of this opinion, this argument could easily be answered by saying that that was a touch of power, not of the hand or of the body: for by the mere inflowing of his power and the contact of his might the angel could do this, and indeed far greater things.

paras.t: Qui quum videret quod eum, scilicet ipsum Jacob, superare non posset, loquendo de potentia ordinata, id est, quod non deceret, ut ipsum Jacob tam ferventer orantem abjiceret sive relinqueret, juxta quem modum supra Dominus ait ad Lot: Non potero facere quidquam quousque ingrediaris illuc. De Christo quoque in Evangelio scriptum est, quod non poterat ibi virtutem aliquam facere, propter incredulitatem illorum. Unde quidam exponunt sic: Qui quum videret quod eum superare non posset, id est non vellet, et ita in hoc fuit rursus fictio quædam, non falsa, sed dispensativa et figurativa: quia per hoc quod angelus finxit se non posse vincere Jacob, insinuavit quod Esau frater ejus eum superare non posset, imo quod populus nasciturus ex Jacob, superaturus esset posteros Esau ut tempore David impletum est. Rursus dicitur angelus non potuisse superare Jacob, quia non potuit ei persuadere, ut ab invocatione et petitione benedictionis cessaret, et per modum impotentis ad superandum se habuit.
paras.en: [[32:25|And when he saw|Qui quum videret]] that he [[32:25|could not overcome him|superare non posset]] (him, that is, Jacob himself): speaking of ordained power [that is, power as it acts within the order set by divine wisdom, as distinct from absolute power], that is, it was not fitting that he should cast off or leave Jacob while he prayed so fervently; in the way in which, above, the Lord said to Lot: [[Gen 19:22|I cannot do any thing till thou go in thither|Non potero facere quidquam quousque ingrediaris illuc]]. Of Christ also it is written in the Gospel that [[Mark 6:5|he could not do any miracles there|non poterat ibi virtutem aliquam facere]], [[Matt 13:58|because of their unbelief|propter incredulitatem illorum]] [the margin gives Matt. xiii, 58, from which the last words come; the words before them are those of Mark 6:5]. Hence some explain it thus: [[32:25|And when he saw that he could not overcome him|Qui quum videret quod eum superare non posset]], that is, would not; and so in this there was again a certain feigning, not false, but dispensatory [that is, ordered to a purpose of God's providence] and figurative: because by the angel's feigning himself unable to conquer Jacob, he intimated that Esau his brother could not overcome him, and indeed that the people to be born of Jacob would overcome the descendants of Esau, as was fulfilled in the time of David[[2 Kings 8:14||]] [the margin is incomplete, "II Reg. … 14"; David's subduing of Edom is told in 2 Kings 8:14]. Again, the angel is said not to have been able to overcome Jacob because he could not persuade him to cease from calling on him and asking a blessing, and he bore himself as one unable to overcome.

paras.t: Tetigit nervum femoris ejus, utpote latum nervum, seu locum nervosum illius, ex quo vis motiva et progressiva aliquo modo dependet; et statim emarcuit, vim suam perdendo, et aruit. Dicuntque aliqui, quod angelus intulit Jacob illam punitionem pro culpa nimiæ formidinis et aliqualis diffidentiæ suæ. Alii dicunt, quod non pro culpa aliqua ipsius Jacob fecit hoc angelus, sed propter figurativam et mysticam rationem, puta ad insinuandum, quod posteritas Jacob ex femore ejus egressura, esset aliquando lædenda et deprimenda a posteris Esau, non obstante quod primogenitura fuit Jacob collata: et istud (ut Rabbi Paulus refert) dicunt quidam Hebræi doctores, quod probant per hoc, quoniam infra habetur, quod filii Israel non comedunt nervum qui emarcuit in femore Jacob. Nempe si pœna illa accidisset Jacob pro culpa sua, pertinuisset solum ad personam ipsius, et ita propter eam non abstinuissent posteri ejus a nervi comestione.
paras.en: [[32:25|he touched the sinew of his thigh|Tetigit nervum femoris ejus]], namely the broad sinew, or the sinewy place of the thigh, on which the power of moving and walking in some way depends; [[32:25|and forthwith it shrank|et statim emarcuit]], losing its strength, and withered. And some say that the angel inflicted this punishment on Jacob for the fault of his excessive fear and of some distrust. Others say that the angel did this not for any fault of Jacob, but for a figurative and mystical reason, namely to intimate that Jacob's posterity, which was to come forth from his thigh, would at times be hurt and brought low by the descendants of Esau, notwithstanding that the birthright had been conferred on Jacob; and this (as Rabbi Paul [that is, Paul of Burgos, the converted rabbi who wrote additions to Lyra] reports) certain Hebrew doctors say, and they prove it from this, that it is said below that [[32:32|the children of Israel|filii Israel]] [[32:32|eat not the sinew, that shrank in Jacob's thigh|non comedunt nervum qui emarcuit in femore Jacob]]. For if that penalty had befallen Jacob for his own fault, it would have concerned his own person only, and so his descendants would not have abstained from eating the sinew on its account.

paras.t: Dixitque ad eum: Dimitte me, jam enim ascendit aurora: quasi dicat: Hora jam imminet, in qua oportet te circa temporalia occupari, et me insistere laudibus Dei. Aliqui autem dicunt, quod angelus ideo dixit hoc, quia alii non fuerunt digni eum in humana illa effigie sensibiliter intueri. Sed dicendum, quod angeli in assumptis corporibus exhibent se visibiles quibus volunt, ita quod etiam a præsentibus videri non queunt, nisi a quibus volunt.
paras.en: [[32:26|And he said to him: Let me go, for it is break of day|Dixitque ad eum: Dimitte me, jam enim ascendit aurora]]: as if he said: The hour is now at hand in which thou must be busied about temporal things, and I must give myself to the praises of God. Some, however, say that the angel said this because the others were not worthy to look upon him with their senses in that human likeness. But it must be said that angels in assumed bodies show themselves visible to whom they will, so that even by those present they cannot be seen, except by those to whom they will.

paras.t: Respondit: Non dimittam te, nisi benedixeris mihi, imprecando et ministerialiter impendendo mihi dona gratiæ et subventionis optata. Nec Jacob ita loquendo fuit inobediens angelo, sed ex caritatis fervore et sancta devotione hoc dixit. Nec angelus præcipiendo dicebat, Dimitte me: sed hortando, et hoc secundum unam consideratione rationabiliter hortabatur, quia aurora instabat. Jacob vero ex alia consideratione rationabiliter dixit, Non dimittam te etc. Sed cur angelus ait: Dimitte me, qui invito Jacob volebat abire, aut quasi ligatus seu detentus fuisset a Jacob? Respondetur, quod Jacob sua humilitate, caritate, devotione et oratione detinuit angelum: idcirco non decuit angelum invito Jacob disparere. Et quid mirum istud de angelo, quum Dominus locutus sit Moysi, Dimitte me, ut irascatur furor meus contra eos?
paras.en: [[32:26|He answered: I will not let thee go, except thou bless me|Respondit: Non dimittam te, nisi benedixeris mihi]], by praying for me, and by bestowing on me as a minister, the gifts of grace and help I long for. Nor was Jacob disobedient to the angel in so speaking, but he said this out of the fervour of charity and holy devotion. Nor did the angel say [[32:26|Let me go|Dimitte me]] by way of command, but of exhortation; and according to one consideration he exhorted reasonably, since the dawn was at hand. But Jacob, according to another consideration, reasonably said, [[32:26|I will not let thee go|Non dimittam te]], etc. But why did the angel say [[32:26|Let me go|Dimitte me]], as though he wished to depart against Jacob's will, or as if he had been bound or held fast by Jacob? The answer is that Jacob held the angel back by his humility, charity, devotion and prayer; therefore it was not fitting for the angel to vanish against Jacob's will. And what wonder is this in an angel, since the Lord said to Moses: [[Ex 32:10|Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them|Dimitte me, ut irascatur furor meus contra eos?]]?

paras.t: Ait ergo angelus ad Jacob: Quod nomen est tibi? Non ex ignorantia hoc quæsivit, sed ut ex responsione Jacob quam præscivit, aptius inferret quod intendebat. Respondit: Jacob mihi est nomen. At ille: Nequaquam, inquit, Jacob appellabitur nomen tuum, id est, non solum vocaberis Jacob, ut hactenus, sed Israel, hoc est, etiam Israel appellaberis. Cujus nominationis ratio seu interpretatio subditur: quoniam si contra Deum fortis fuisti, id est, quia angelum in Dei persona tibi apparentem vicisti, juxta expositionem præhabitam, quanto magis contra homines prævalebis? hoc est, a fratre tuo non superaberis, neque ab aliis; imo potius in posteris tuis victurus es Idumæos ac alios.
paras.en: [[32:27|And he said|Ait ergo]] (the angel, to Jacob): [[32:27|What is thy name?|Quod nomen est tibi?]] He did not ask this out of ignorance, but so that from Jacob's answer, which he foreknew, he might more fitly bring in what he intended. [[32:27|He answered: Jacob|Respondit: Jacob]] is my name. [[32:28|But he said|At ille]]: [[32:28|Thy name shall not be called Jacob|Nequaquam, inquit, Jacob appellabitur nomen tuum]], that is, thou shalt not only be called Jacob, as hitherto, [[32:28|but Israel|sed Israel]], that is, thou shalt also be called Israel. The reason or interpretation of this naming is added: [[32:28|for if thou hast been strong against God|quoniam si contra Deum fortis fuisti]], that is, since thou hast overcome the angel who appeared to thee in the person of God, according to the explanation given above, [[32:28|how much more shalt thou prevail against men?|quanto magis contra homines prævalebis?]] that is, thou shalt not be overcome by thy brother, nor by others; rather, in thy descendants thou shalt conquer the Idumeans and others.

paras.t: De hujus nominis Israel interpretatione scribit Hieronymus: Josephus putat Jacob ideo Israel appellatum, quoniam contra Deum stetit, ita quod Israel interpretatur stans contra Deum, seu reluctans contra angelum. Ego autem hoc in Hebræo invenire non potui; sed etymologiam hujus nominis angelus posuit, dicens: Quoniam si contra Dominum fortis fuisti, etc.; sicque Israel interpretatur, princeps cum Deo. Quasi angelus dicat: Sicut ego sum princeps, ita et tu. Quod autem in libro Nominum Hebraicorum Israel interpretatur, vir videns Deum, non tam vere quam violenter interpretatum videtur. Hæc Hieronymus.
paras.en: On the interpretation of this name Israel, Jerome writes: Josephus thinks that Jacob was called Israel because he stood against God, so that Israel is interpreted "standing against God", or "wrestling against the angel". But I could not find this in the Hebrew; the angel himself gave the etymology of this name, saying: [[32:28|for if thou hast been strong against God|Quoniam si contra Dominum fortis fuisti]], etc.; and so Israel is interpreted "prince with God". As if the angel said: As I am a prince, so art thou also. But that in the book of Hebrew Names Israel is interpreted "a man seeing God" seems an interpretation more forced than true. Thus far Jerome.

paras.t: Interrogavit eum Jacob: Dic mihi, quo appellaris nomine? Hoc Jacob quæsivit, ut in divinorum cognitione proficeret, atque ut angelum istum proprio nomine invocaret ac honoraret. Unde in Judicum libro, pater Samsonis ait ad angelum: Quod tibi nomen est? ut si sermo tuus fuerit expletus, honoremus te. Respondit: Cur quæris nomen meum? quasi dicat: Nimis altum est tibi, quia angelorum naturam, quantum ad speciem specialissimam, aut non, aut valde difficulter potest homo in hac vita cognoscere: imo juxta Philosophum, sicut oculus noctuæ se habet ad lumen solis, ita intellectus humanus ad manifestissima naturæ, hoc est ad intelligentiarum notitiam. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod ideo angelus dixit, Cur quæris nomen meum? quoniam nomina angelorum qui foris mittuntur, mutantur juxta diversa obsequia ad quæ explenda mittuntur: sicut angelus missus ad purgandum labia Isaiæ, vocatus est Seraph, ex effectu inflammationis, quum tamen non esset de ordine Seraphim, juxta doctrinam divini Dionysii de Ecclesiastica hierarchia: quod quamvis sit verum, attamen angeli saltem nonnulli, aliqua habent nomina fixa, ut Michael, Gabriel, etc.
paras.en: [[32:29|Jacob asked him: Tell me by what name art thou called?|Interrogavit eum Jacob: Dic mihi, quo appellaris nomine?]] Jacob asked this that he might advance in the knowledge of divine things, and that he might call upon this angel and honour him by his proper name. Hence in the book of Judges the father of Samson says to the angel: [[Judg 13:17|What is thy name, that, if thy word shall come to pass, we may honour thee?|Quod tibi nomen est? ut si sermo tuus fuerit expletus, honoremus te]] [[32:29|He answered: Why dost thou ask my name?|Respondit: Cur quæris nomen meum?]] as if he said: It is too high for thee, because the nature of the angels, as to their most specific species [that is, the lowest species, the particular nature of each angel], man in this life either cannot know, or can know only with great difficulty; indeed, according to the Philosopher, as the eye of the owl is to the light of the sun, so is the human intellect to the things most manifest in nature, that is, to the knowledge of the Intelligences [that is, the pure spirits]. But some say that the angel said [[32:29|Why dost thou ask my name?|Cur quæris nomen meum?]] because the names of the angels who are sent out change according to the various services they are sent to fulfil: as the angel sent to purge the lips of Isaias was called a Seraph[[Is 6:6||]][[Is 6:7||]], from the effect of inflaming, though he was not of the order of the Seraphim, according to the teaching of the divine Dionysius on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy [the passage is in fact in the Celestial Hierarchy, ch. 13]; which, though it is true, yet some angels at least have certain fixed names, as Michael, Gabriel, etc.

paras.t: Et benedixit ei in eodem loco. Forma autem hujus benedictionis non exprimitur in hoc textu; sed aliqui dicunt, quod prætacta mutatio nominis Jacob, et interpretatio cur Israel diceretur, fuit benedictio qua angelus ipsum Jacob benedixit, conferendo ei dona optata dispositive seu imprecative.
paras.en: [[32:29|And he blessed him in the same place|Et benedixit ei in eodem loco]]. The form of this blessing is not expressed in this text; but some say that the change of Jacob's name mentioned above, and the interpretation of why he should be called Israel, was the blessing with which the angel blessed Jacob, conferring on him the gifts he desired by way of disposing him for them, or of praying for them.

paras.t: Vocavitque Jacob nomen loci illius, in quo contigit istud, Phanuel, quod interpretatur facies Dei, quoniam vidit ibi faciem ejus. Propter quod subditur: dicens: Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem, id est clare ac facialiter, non in ipsa deitatis incomprehensibili invisibilique natura, quum scriptum sit: Non videbit me homo, et vivet. Et, Deum nemo vidit unquam. Sed ideo dixit hoc Jacob, quoniam oculo exteriori vidit clare angelum in forma humana, qui sibi in persona Dei apparuit atque locutus est. Et salva facta est anima mea, id est, a pristino timore humano erepta, et confortata in Domino, imo et in spe æternæ salutis firmata.
paras.en: [[32:30|And Jacob called the name of the place|Vocavitque Jacob nomen loci illius]], in which this happened, [[32:30|Phanuel|Phanuel]], which is interpreted "the face of God", since he saw his face there. For which reason it is added: [[32:30|saying: I have seen God face to face|dicens: Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem]], that is, clearly and face to face, not in the incomprehensible and invisible nature of the Godhead itself, since it is written: [[Ex 33:20|man shall not see me, and live|Non videbit me homo, et vivet]]. And: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]]. But Jacob said this because with his outward eye he clearly saw the angel in human form, who appeared to him and spoke in the person of God. [[32:30|and my soul has been saved|Et salva facta est anima mea]], that is, delivered from its former human fear and strengthened in the Lord, and indeed made firm in the hope of eternal salvation.

paras.t: Ortus […] sol, postquam transgressus est Phanuel, hoc est, mox ut recessit a loco, quem Phanuel nominavit, facta est clara dies. Ipse vero claudicabat pede, ex arefactione nervi præfati. Expedita namque ambulatio dependet ex multis, videlicet vi motiva, rectitudine tibiæ, vivacitate nervorum, etc.
paras.en: [[32:31|rose|Ortus]] […] [[32:31|the sun|sol]], [[32:31|after he was past Phanuel|postquam transgressus est Phanuel]], that is, as soon as he had departed from the place which he named Phanuel, it became broad day. [[32:31|but he halted on his foot|Ipse vero claudicabat pede]], from the withering of the sinew mentioned above. For walking freely depends on many things, namely the power of movement, the straightness of the shin, the vigour of the sinews, etc.

paras.t: Quam ob causam non comedunt nervum filii Israel, qui emarcuit in femore Jacob, id est nervum femoris, similem nervo qui in femore Jacob obstupuit, et insensibilis factus est: similem, inquam, quantum ad hoc quod est esse nervum femoris, quamvis aliunde ab illo differat, non numero tantum, sed specie quoque; aliorum vero usum nervorum non vitant. Porro in Scholastica historia legitur, quod primo ipsemet Jacob proposuit non comedere de cetero nervum, et id ipsum posteritas ipsius observat: et forte Jacob proposuit hoc in memoriam rei gestæ, et propter mysticam significationem ejus prætactam; posteritas vero Jacob hoc observavit, sectando patris sui exemplum, […] eumque honorando, et in rei gestæ memoriam.
paras.en: [[32:32|Therefore the children of Israel|Quam ob causam non comedunt nervum filii Israel]] [[32:32|eat not the sinew, that shrank in Jacob's thigh|qui emarcuit in femore Jacob]], that is, the sinew of the thigh, like the sinew which in Jacob's thigh grew numb and lost its feeling: like it, I say, in this, that it is the sinew of the thigh, though otherwise it differs from it, not in number only but in species also; the use of other sinews they do not avoid. Further, in the Scholastic History it is read that Jacob himself first resolved not to eat the sinew from then on, and his posterity observes the same; and perhaps Jacob resolved this in memory of what had happened, and because of its mystical meaning touched on above; while Jacob's posterity observed it following their father's example, […] and honouring him, and in memory of what had happened.

paras.t: Præterea de hoc sancti Jacob luctamine cum angelo, scriptum est in Osee: In fortitudine sua directus est cum angelo, et invaluit ad angelum; flevit, et rogavit eum. Ex quibus elicitur, quod Jacob cum fletu deprecatus est angelum, quamvis Hebræi juxta consuetudinem fabularum suarum inanium, dicunt quod angelus qui luctabatur cum Jacob, fuit angelus Esau, cupiens Jacob impedire ab ingressu terræ promissionis, et consecutione primogenituræ ac benedictionum sibi ab Isaac præscitarum, et quod Deus contulit tantam fortitudinem ipsi Jacob, quod angelum illum vicit, in tantum quod angelus victus flevit, et flendo rogavit ipsum Jacob dilationem de obtinendo dominio, seu primogenitura et eminentia super Esau. Quorum omnium falsitas innotescit ex hoc, quod angelus Esau ex divina revelatione et ex rebus gestis cognovit, quod Jacob fuit a Deo ad primogenituram electus, et quod Esau fuit iniquus, ac primatu super Jacob indignus: idcirco noluit divinæ præordinationi taliter reluctari. Perfecta quoque angelorum beatitudo, excludit ab eis omnem miseriam, pœnam, mœrorem, ac fletum.
paras.en: Moreover, of this wrestling of holy Jacob with the angel it is written in Osee: [[Osee 12:3|by his strength he had success with an angel|In fortitudine sua directus est cum angelo]], [[Osee 12:4|And he prevailed over the angel|et invaluit ad angelum]]; [[Osee 12:4|he wept, and made supplication to him|flevit, et rogavit eum]]. From this it is gathered that Jacob besought the angel with weeping; although the Hebrews, after the custom of their empty fables, say that the angel who wrestled with Jacob was the angel of Esau, who wished to hinder Jacob from entering the land of promise and from obtaining the birthright and the blessings that Isaac foresaw for him; and that God gave Jacob such strength that he overcame that angel, so much so that the angel, being overcome, wept, and weeping begged Jacob for a delay in his obtaining the lordship, or the birthright and pre-eminence over Esau. The falsity of all this is plain from the fact that Esau’s angel knew, by divine revelation and from what had come to pass, that Jacob had been chosen by God for the birthright, and that Esau was wicked and unworthy of the primacy over Jacob; and therefore he would not so strive against the divine preordination. Moreover, the perfect beatitude of the angels shuts out from them all misery, punishment, grief and weeping.

32.title: De intellectu spirituali ejusdem capituli tricesimi secundi
32.title_en: On the spiritual understanding of the same thirty-second chapter

paras.t: Jacob autem abiit itinere quo cœperat. Per Jacob vir christifidelis designatur, qui dum in via virtutum stabiliter perseverat ac proficit, abit itinere quo cœpit, cui obviam sunt angeli Dei, qui ad ejus auxilium sunt parati, de quibus loquitur Eliseus: Plures nobiscum sunt quam cum illis, puta iniquis. Hos angelos homo fidelis fide intuens, nominat castra Dei, de quibus spiritualiter accipi potest illud Joel: Multa sunt nimis castra Dei fortia, et facientia verbum ejus.
paras.en: [[32:1|Jacob also went on the journey he had begun|Jacob autem abiit itinere quo cœperat]]. By Jacob is signified the faithful Christian, who, while he perseveres steadfastly and makes progress in the way of the virtues, goes on the journey he had begun; and the angels of God, who stand ready to help him, meet him. Of these Eliseus speaks: [[4 Kings 6:16|there are more with us than with them|Plures nobiscum sunt quam cum illis]], that is, than with the wicked. The faithful man, beholding these angels by faith, names them the camps of God; and of them that saying of Joel may be taken spiritually: [[Joel 2:11|his armies are exceedingly great|Multa sunt nimis castra Dei]], [[Joel 2:11|strong, and execute his word|fortia, et facientia verbum ejus]] [Denis reads *castra Dei*, “the camps of God”, where the Douay-Rheims has “his armies”: the same word as Jacob’s *Castra Dei* at v. 2].

paras.t: Misit autem nuntios ante se ad Esau fratrem suum. Per hoc insinuatur, quod homo virtuosus conatur in bono vincere malum, et non solum eos quos ipse injuste offendit, sed hos quoque qui prorsus injuste contra eum moventur, nititur mitigare, reconciliareque sibi: quod si non potest per se ipsum peragere, studet hoc per alios facere.
paras.en: [[32:3|And he sent messengers before him to Esau, his brother|Misit autem nuntios ante se ad Esau fratrem suum]]. By this it is intimated that the virtuous man strives to [[Rom 12:21|overcome evil by good|in bono vincere malum]], and endeavours to soften and reconcile to himself not only those whom he himself has wronged, but also those who are stirred against him wholly unjustly; and if he cannot bring this about by himself, he is careful to do it through others.

paras.t: Timuit autem Jacob Esau valde, quoniam boni metuunt improbitatem pravorum, magis ne ipsi sua improbitate Deum offendant, seipsosque perdant, ac alios scandalizent, quam ne noceant ipsis bonis, quibus nulla nocet adversitas, imo et plurimum prodest illata injuria, dummodo eis non dominetur propria iniquitas, ita impatientia, aut similis culpa. Verumtamen nullus debet viribus suis ita confidere, ut cesset divinæ pietatis opem necessabilem invocare, ne a fratre suo seu proximo suo lædatur, hoc est, ne ex his quæ videt in aliis, aut quæ suffert ab eis, ad ullum moveatur peccatum, ne aliquem temerarie judicet aut contemnat, aut irrationabiliter indignetur vel contristetur; sed in omni eventu firmiter stet fixus in Domino, quia non contristabit nec perturbabit justum quidquid ei acciderit.
paras.en: Now Jacob was greatly afraid of Esau, because the good fear the wickedness of the depraved, more lest by their wickedness these offend God, ruin themselves and scandalize others, than lest they harm the good themselves, whom no adversity harms; indeed, injury inflicted on them profits them very much, provided that their own sin does not master them, as impatience, or some like fault. Nevertheless no one ought so to trust in his own strength as to cease calling on the needful help of the divine goodness, lest he be harmed by his brother, or his neighbour: that is, lest from what he sees in others, or what he suffers from them, he be moved to any sin, lest he rashly judge or despise anyone, or be unreasonably indignant or saddened; but in every event let him stand firm, fixed in the Lord, for [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|non contristabit nec perturbabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]] [Denis adds “nor trouble him”, *nec perturbabit*].

paras.t: Denique Jacob fecit duas turmas, hoc est, aciem virtutum moralium, aciemque virtutum theologicarum parat fidelis contra malitias perversorum, ut si læsus fuerit in aliqua virtute morali, peccando per iram, impatientiam, aut mœrorem, reliqua turma salvetur, id est, fides, spes, caritas maneant inviolatæ, et per eas damnum animæ suæ recuperet, ad Deum per eas confugiendo, veniam postulando, seque deinceps diligentius custodiendo.
paras.en: Further, Jacob made two companies: that is, the faithful man draws up an army of the moral virtues and an army of the theological virtues against the malice of the perverse, so that if he has been wounded in some moral virtue, sinning through anger, impatience or grief, [[32:8|the other company that is left, shall escape|reliqua turma salvetur]]: that is, faith, hope and charity remain unharmed, and through them he may make good the loss to his soul, fleeing to God through them, asking pardon, and thereafter guarding himself more carefully.

paras.t: In baculo meo transivi Jordanem istum, et nunc cum duabus turmis regredior. Per Jordanem, flumen lacrimarum et saluberrimarum compunctionum accipitur: quod Christifidelis in baculo suo pertransit, quando divinæ pietati per spei suæ sustentationem innitendo, ad spiritualem profectum et complementum præfatarum virtutum per compunctionem et fletum perducitur.
paras.en: [[32:10|With my staff I passed over this Jordan|In baculo meo transivi Jordanem istum]], [[32:10|and now I return with two companies|et nunc cum duabus turmis regredior]]. By the Jordan is understood the river of tears and of most wholesome compunction [that is, the sorrow for sin that pierces the heart]; and the faithful Christian passes over it with his staff when, leaning on the divine goodness with the support of his hope, he is brought through compunction and weeping to spiritual progress and to the fulness of the virtues spoken of above.

paras.t: Amplius, quod Jacob per munera nisus est iram fratris sui exstinguere, docet nos, quod orando et spiritualia aut etiam corporalia beneficia impendendo, debemus irascentium et invidentium ac adversantium passiones, aversiones, ac vitia pro viribus exstirpare. Munus enim absconditum exstinguit iras, et donum in sinu indignationem maximam; atque ut iterum Salomon protestatur, Quum placuerint Domino viæ hominis, inimicos ejus convertet ad pacem.
paras.en: Moreover, that Jacob strove by presents to quench his brother’s anger teaches us that, by praying and by bestowing spiritual or even bodily benefits, we ought to root out as far as we can the passions, aversions and vices of those who are angry with us, who envy us and who oppose us. For [[Prov 21:14|A secret present quencheth anger: and a gift in the bosom, the greatest wrath|Munus absconditum extinguit iras, et donum in sinu indignationem maximam]]; and, as Solomon again declares, [[Prov 16:7|When the ways of man shall please the Lord|Quum placuerint Domino viæ hominis]], [[Prov 16:7|he will convert even his enemies to peace|inimicos ejus convertet ad pacem]].

paras.t: Per hoc demum quod Jacob uxores suas ac filios transduxit per vadum, innuitur quod vir bonus pertinentes ad se, seu subditos sibi, per evenientes adversitates, tentationes et persecutiones, studet ad tranquillitatem, pacem et devotionem suavem perducere. Ipse vero permanet solus, ut Deo simplicissimo expeditius vacet; et ibi luctatur cum Deo ac angelo, dum opportune et importune orando ac laborando, conatur aliquid singularis gratiæ ac virtutis a Domino extorquere, quamvis frequenter ac diu videatur repelli, seu non exaudiri.
paras.en: Lastly, by Jacob’s bringing his wives and children over the ford it is hinted that the good man is careful to bring those who belong to him, or are under him, through the adversities, temptations and persecutions that befall them, to tranquillity, peace and sweet devotion. But he himself remains alone, that he may give himself more freely to God, who is utterly simple; and there he wrestles with God and with the angel, while, praying and labouring in season and out of season, he strives to wrest from the Lord some singular grace and virtue, although he often seems for a long time to be repulsed, or not heard.

paras.t: Quumque frequenter per contemplationem ad Deum se elevat, et rursus ex humana fragilitate evagando infra dilabitur, laboriosum exerceat luctamen; nec Deum dimittit, nisi benedicatur ab eo, concupitam mentis in Deo stabilitatem adipiscendo, ita ut dignus sit, Israel, hoc est vir Deum per fidem et sapientiæ donum contemplans, vocari: quo facto, consolatur eum Altissimus, quod non superabit eum humana malitia, seu aliorum improbitas. Tangit quoque nervum femoris ejus, dum concupiscentias carnis, et pronitatem ad vitiorum itinera in ipso mortificat.
paras.en: And when he often lifts himself up to God by contemplation, and again, wandering through human frailty, slips down below, he carries on a toilsome wrestling; nor does he let God go unless he be blessed by him, by gaining the steadfastness of mind in God that he longs for, so that he is worthy to be called Israel, that is, a man contemplating God by faith and by the gift of wisdom. When this is done, the Most High comforts him, that human malice, or the wickedness of others, shall not overcome him. He also touches the sinew of his thigh when he mortifies in him the concupiscences of the flesh and the proneness to the paths of vice.

paras.t: Locum autem in quo vir contemplativus tanta a Deo consequitur bona, videlicet ecclesiam, cellam, aut aliud quodcumque secretum, nominat Phanuel: quia in eo contemplatus est faciem Dei, hoc est gratiosam præsentiam ejus, viditque eum facie ad faciem, non per speciem, sicut in patria, sed per mysticam theologiam aut anagogicam visionem, sicut testatus est Paulus: Nos autem revelata facie gloriam Domini speculantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a Domini Spiritu. Et tunc salva fit anima a prioribus malis, et Deo familiaris atque carissima redditur; oriturque in ea Sol justitiæ; atque ad ea quæ carnis et mundi sunt, claudicat, sed in via justitiæ recte progreditur.
paras.en: The place in which the contemplative man obtains such great goods from God, namely a church, a cell, or any other secret place, he names Phanuel, because in it he has contemplated the face of God, that is, his gracious presence, and has seen him [[32:30|face to face|facie ad faciem]]: not by sight, as in our heavenly country, but by mystical theology or anagogical vision [that is, the hidden, experiential knowledge of God given in contemplation, which lifts the mind above itself], as Paul testifies: [[2 Cor 3:18|But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord|Nos autem revelata facie gloriam Domini speculantes]] [[2 Cor 3:18|are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord|in eamdem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem, tanquam a Domini Spiritu]]. And then the soul is saved from its former evils and made familiar with God and very dear to him; and the Sun of justice rises in it; and it halts towards the things of the flesh and of the world, but goes forward uprightly in the way of justice.

paras.t: Postremo, secundum Augustinum, et ut plenius tangit Isidorus, per virum qui luctabatur cum Jacob, et se ab eo vinci sponte permisit, intelligitur Christus, qui se a posteritate Jacob, quæ nunc per Jacob significatur, sivit voluntarie crucifigi, atque per suæ meritum passionis etiam his a quibus occisus est, benedictionem promeruit, pœnitentibusque largitus est: ita quod facti sunt veri ac spirituales Israelitæ, qui ante fuerunt carnales Judæi.
paras.en: Finally, according to Augustine [*The City of God*, XVI, 39], and as Isidore touches on more fully, by the man who wrestled with Jacob and of his own accord let himself be overcome by him is understood Christ, who willingly suffered himself to be crucified by the posterity of Jacob, which is here signified by Jacob; and by the merit of his passion he won a blessing even for those by whom he was slain, and bestowed it on those who repented, so that those who before were carnal Jews became true and spiritual Israelites.

33.title: Expositio capituli trigesimi tertii: Elevans autem Jacob oculos suos, vidit venientem Esau
33.title_en: Exposition of the thirty-third chapter: And Jacob lifting up his eyes, saw Esau coming

paras.t: Occursus Jacob electi et Esau reprobi, nunc narratur. Elevans autem Jacob oculos suos, vidit venientem Esau, etc.: divisitque filios Liæ et Rachel, ambarumque famularum: et posuit utramque ancillam et liberos earum in principio, Liam vero et filios ejus in secundo loco, in quo etiam Dina filia Liæ fuit: Rachel autem et Joseph novissimos. Quemadmodum enim præhabitum est, Jacob divisit istos in duas turmas, ita quod Bala et Zelpha cum filiis suis erant in prima, Lia autem et Rachel cum sobole sua in turma secunda, sic tamen, quod Rachel et Joseph erant in extremitate turmæ secundæ. Unde in Scholastica fertur historia, eos errare qui dicunt Jacob fecisse tres turmas. Porro de causa hujus divisionis et collocationis, dictum est præcedenti capitulo.
paras.en: The meeting of Jacob the elect and Esau the reprobate is now related. [[33:1|And Jacob lifting up his eyes, saw Esau coming|Elevans autem Jacob oculos suos, vidit venientem Esau]], etc.: [[33:1|and he divided the children of Lia and of Rachel, and of the two handmaids|divisitque filios Liæ et Rachel, ambarumque famularum]]: [[33:2|And he put both the handmaids and their children foremost|et posuit utramque ancillam et liberos earum in principio]]: [[33:2|and Lia and her children in the second place|Liam vero et filios ejus in secundo loco]], in which Dina too, the daughter of Lia, was: [[33:2|and Rachel and Joseph last|Rachel autem et Joseph novissimos]]. For, as was said before, Jacob divided these into two companies, so that Bala and Zelpha with their sons were in the first, and Lia and Rachel with their offspring in the second company; yet so that Rachel and Joseph were at the far end of the second company. Hence it is stated in the Scholastic History that those are mistaken who say that Jacob made three companies. As for the reason of this division and arrangement, it was spoken of in the preceding chapter.

paras.t: Et ipse Jacob progrediens, id est, duas turmas præfatas præcedens, ut fratrem offensum placaret, ne uxoribus suis ac filiis infligeret malum, adoravit pronus in terram septies, donec appropinquaret frater ejus. Cœpit etenim eum adorare a remotis: et quum semel adorasset illum, surrexit: paululumque progrediens, adoravit secundo: ac denuo surgens, et parum procedens, adoravit tertio: sicque usque ad septimam adorationem, quam exhibuit juxta Esau fratrem suum, quatenus tam frequenti et magna humiliatione fratrem suum provocaret ad pietatem. Nam quamvis Deus promisit ipsi Jacob protectionem, ipse tamen fecit quod in se fuit. Intelligenda quoque sunt hæc de adoratione duliæ, quæ excellentibus exhibetur personis, qualis fuit et Esau, tanto vallatus exercitu, multisque præsidens. Et quod dicitur pronus in terram adorasse, quidam exponunt, quod capite inclinato hoc fecit. Glossa autem interlinearis dicit, quod genua flexit. Litteræ tamen magis consonum reor, ut toto corpore in terram prostrato, hoc fecisse dicatur, præsertim quia consuetudo Scripturæ est, ut per hoc quod dicitur absolute, Pronus in terram, designetur talis prostratio, et quoniam Jacob volebat se maxime humiliare.
paras.en: [[33:3|And he went forward|Et ipse Jacob progrediens]], that is, going before the two companies just mentioned, so as to appease his offended brother, lest he should do harm to his wives and sons, [[33:3|and bowed down with his face to the ground seven times|adoravit pronus in terram septies]], [[33:3|until his brother came near|donec appropinquaret frater ejus]]. For he began to bow down to him from far off: and when he had bowed down to him once, he rose, and going forward a little, bowed down a second time; and rising again and going on a little, bowed down a third time; and so on up to the seventh bow, which he made close by Esau his brother, so that by humbling himself so often and so deeply he might move his brother to kindness. For although God had promised Jacob protection, he nevertheless did what lay in him. These things are to be understood of the adoration of dulia [that is, the honour paid to creatures of eminence, as distinct from latria, the worship due to God alone], which is shown to persons of excellence, such as Esau also was, girt about with so great an army and set over many. And as to its being said that he adored prone upon the ground, some explain that he did this with his head bowed. But the interlinear Gloss says that he bent his knees. Yet I think it more in keeping with the letter to say that he did this with his whole body prostrate on the ground, especially since it is the custom of Scripture that the words "prone upon the ground", said without more, signify such a prostration; and because Jacob wished to humble himself to the utmost.

paras.t: Currens itaque Esau obviam fratri suo, amplexatus est eum, scilicet Jacob fratrem suum. Dicunt quidam, quod ordinante cooperanteque Deo, cor Esau de ira et indignatione ad pietatem et fraternum amorem mutatum sit. Cor enim hominum in manu Dei est: et quocumque voluerit, vertet illud: estque proprium Deo, in ipsam hominis voluntatem immediate agere, et illud ad libitum immutare.
