For it does not seem that Jacob, after his return from Mesopotamia, did not visit his old, blind and most dear father before the things just related, but perhaps long before some of them, and often: but now he is described as having visited his father because Moses wished here to tell of Isaac's death and burial. He came, then, to his father [[35:27|in Mambre, the city of Arbee|in Mambre civitatem Arbee]]. The city of Arbee, or Arbea by name, [[35:27|this is Hebron|ipsa est quæ alio nomine vocata est Hebron]] [the Vulgate has *hæc est Hebron*], which is called by that other name; and, as Jerome writes, the same city was anciently called Mambre, from Abraham's friend named Mambre[[Gen 14:13||]][[Gen 14:24||]], of whom we spoke above. So what a certain writer says here does not appear true, that Mambre is the name of the region in which Hebron was. [[35:27|wherein Abraham and Isaac sojourned|In qua peregrinatus est Abraham et Isaac]], that is, they dwelt in that city as aliens, strangers and newcomers. [[35:28|And the days of Isaac were a hundred and eighty years|Et completi sunt dies Isaac centum octoginta annorum]]: and so he lived five years longer than Abraham. Josephus, however, says that he lived a hundred and eighty-five years, as some report; but I have not found this in Josephus, but as it is in the text.

paras.t: Consumptusque ætate, ita quod naturalem periodum suam implevit, et humidum radicale consumptum fuit in eo a calido naturali : mortuus est, et appositus est populo suo, etc., id est, in limbo patrum et sinu Abrahæ eis conjunctus, quantum ad animam : et sepelierunt eum Esau et Jacob filii sui, qui fuerunt principales inter eos qui sepulturæ interfuerunt. Aderant autem et alii multi, et etiam forsan multi filiorum Jacob et Esau.
paras.en: [[35:29|And being spent with age|Consumptusque ætate]], so that he completed his natural span, and the radical moisture was consumed in him by the natural heat [the medieval account of natural death], [[35:29|he died, and was gathered to his people|mortuus est, et appositus est populo suo]], etc., that is, joined to them as to his soul in the limbo of the fathers and the bosom of Abraham: [[35:29|and his sons Esau and Jacob buried him|et sepelierunt eum Esau et Jacob filii sui]], who were the chief among those present at the burial. But many others were there too, and perhaps also many of the sons of Jacob and Esau.

paras.t: Postremo, quoniam non fit hic mentio de Rebecca, dicunt expositores concorditer, quod fuit defuncta antequam Jacob venit ad Isaac : et Rabbi Paulus dicit, quod secundum Hebræos fuit defuncta ante reditum Jacob a Mesopotamia. Sed tunc quæstio oritur, cur Scriptura non facit mentionem de morte et sepultura Rebeccæ, quum tamen tam solennem faciat mentionem de morte, sepulturaque Deboræ nutricis Rebeccæ. Ad quod (ut recitat Rabbi Paulus) respondent Hebræi, quod Isaac fecit Rebeccam de nocte sepeliri occulte, quoniam ejus sepelitio non potuit honorifice fieri, eo quod ipse Isaac non potuit interesse, tanquam jam valde senex et cæcus. Esau quoque interesse noluit, quoniam mater privavit eum (sua instigatione) benedictione paterna : Jacob vero nondum erat reversus. Ista recitatio videtur incerta et fabulosa. Poterat enim illuc Isaac deduci, poterat quoque multos honorabiles viros illuc dirigere ; nec certum est quod Esau tam pertinax manserit in sua contra matrem propriam indignatione, quod noluit ejus sepelitioni adesse, quod etiam propter humanum decorum (ut puto) vitasset : imo quum fratrem suum tam amorose susceperit, potuit interim pietate et beneficiis suæ matris emolliri, et ei placari. Denique, quamvis fabula illa esset vera, ob hoc tamen non oportuit Scripturam sacram ab enarratione mortis ac sepulturæ Rebeccæ silere : imo absolute loquendo, falsum est quod Scriptura inde conticuit, quia quod hoc loco non refert, infra narrat, quemadmodum moris est Scripturarum, per recapitulationem multa ante omissa describere. Scriptum est equidem infra, præallegato capitulo : Ibi, videlicet in spelunca duplici, sepultus est Isaac cum Rebecca, ibi et Lia condita jacet : ex quo itidem constat, verum non esse, quod dicunt Scripturam non facere mentionem de Liæ sepultura ac morte.
paras.en: Lastly, since no mention is made here of Rebecca, the expositors say with one accord that she had died before Jacob came to Isaac: and Rabbi Paul says that, according to the Hebrews, she died before Jacob's return from Mesopotamia. But then the question arises why Scripture makes no mention of Rebecca's death and burial, when it makes such solemn mention of the death and burial of Debora, Rebecca's nurse. To which (as Rabbi Paul relates) the Hebrews answer that Isaac had Rebecca buried secretly by night, since her burial could not be done with honour, because Isaac himself could not be present, being now very old and blind; Esau too would not be present, since his mother had deprived him (by her prompting) of his father's blessing; and Jacob had not yet returned. This account seems uncertain and fabulous. For Isaac could have been brought there; he could also have sent many honourable men there; nor is it certain that Esau remained so stubborn in his anger against his own mother that he would not be present at her burial, which (I think) he would have avoided for human decency's sake too: indeed, since he received his brother so lovingly, he could meanwhile have been softened by his mother's kindness and benefits and reconciled to her. Lastly, even if that fable were true, it would not be necessary on that account for sacred Scripture to be silent about the death and burial of Rebecca: indeed, absolutely speaking, it is false that Scripture is silent about it, since what it does not tell in this place it tells below, as it is the custom of the Scriptures to describe by recapitulation many things passed over before. For it is written below, in the chapter already cited: There, namely in the double cave, [[Gen 49:31|there was Isaac buried with Rebecca, his wife|sepultus est Isaac cum Rebecca]]: [[Gen 49:31|there also Lia doth lie buried|ibi et Lia condita jacet]]: from which it is likewise plain that what they say is not true, that Scripture makes no mention of Lia's burial and death.

35.title: Spiritualis explanatio ejusdem capituli tricesimi quinti
35.title_en: Spiritual explanation of the same thirty-fifth chapter

paras.t: PER Jacob pium et simplicem designatur quicumque fidelis. Quemadmodum igitur Jacob formidanti invasionem Chananæorum, locutus est Dominus, ut surgens ascenderet Bethel, habitaretque ibi : sic unicuique nostrum invisibilium hostium certamina metuenti, Deus injungit, ut ab immoderata formidine atque ignavia exsurgentes, ascendamus mente per spem et orationem ad domum Dei, ad sanctam matrem Ecclesiam seu congregationem virorum ferventium, audiendo ipsorum consilia, et sequendo Sanctorum exempla, faciamusque ibi altare, hoc est, aram caritatis ac fidei construamus in cordibus nostris, quatenus omnia nostra ex fide procedant, et per caritatem Domino offerantur, quia hoc sacrificium Deus solum acceptat, quod in ara cordis flamma caritatis accendit.
paras.en: By Jacob, devout and simple, any faithful soul is signified. As, then, the Lord spoke to Jacob when he feared an attack by the Chanaanites, that he should arise and go up to Bethel and dwell there: so God enjoins each of us, when we fear the battles of invisible enemies, that, rising up from immoderate fear and sloth, we should go up in mind by hope and prayer to the house of God, to holy mother Church, or to the company of fervent men, hearing their counsels and following the examples of the Saints; and that we should make an altar there, that is, build an altar of charity and faith in our hearts, so that all our doings may proceed from faith and be offered to the Lord through charity, since God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles on the altar of the heart.

paras.t: Jacob vero convocata omni domo sua, ait : Abjicite deos […] et mundamini, ac mutate vestimenta vestra. Sic unusquisque prælatus ac præsidens sibi creditos debet ad caritatem, pacem et profectum assiduum convocare, et sæpe corporaliter congregare, omnesque ferventer hortari, ut deos abjiciant alienos, utpote avaritiam, quæ idolorum est servitus, superbiam, immunditiam, et omne id per quod, seu cui magis adhæret homo quam Deo : se quoque per contritionem, confessionem et satisfactionem emundent, vestimentaque mutent, exuendo veterem hominem cum actibus suis, et induendo novum, qui secundum Deum creatus est, in sanctitate. Prava ac sordida vestimenta, sunt animæ vitiosæ consuetudines, habitus mali, mores et actus perversi, de quibus in Zacharia habetur : Auferte ab eo vestimenta sordida. Hæc vestimenta sunt commutanda in vestimenta pulchra, pretiosa atque fragrantia, quæ sunt virtutes et dona Spiritus Sancti, fructus et beatitudines, ferventes ad Deum affectiones, sinceræ meditationes, virtuosaque vita, quibus anima optime decoratur, ac suavissime redolet coram Deo, eique gratissima redditur. Insuper Jacob convocat domum suam, dum vir timoratus omnia interiora sua examinat, et omnes animæ suæ vires, in quibus vitia et virtutes exsistere queunt, scrutatur quid mali insit, quid boni desit : sicque passiones animæ reformare, universos quoque sensus suos interiores et exteriores rite custodire conetur, ne in aliquo Deum majestatis offendat; et vana ac fœda phantasmata tanquam diabolica simulacra detestatur, et ita coram Altissimo mundum cor gerere elaborat, cum Psalmista decantans : Oculi mei semper ad Dominum. Denique, quando homo sic agit, et ita ad ecclesiasticæ unitatis ac caritatis perfectionem progreditur, omnes invisibilium hostium acies per circuitum conterrentur, in tantum, ut a taliter proficiente diffugiant.
paras.en: [[35:2|And Jacob having called together all his household, said: Cast away the strange gods|Jacob vero convocata omni domo sua, ait : Abjicite deos]] […] [[35:2|and be cleansed, and change your garments|et mundamini, ac mutate vestimenta vestra]]. So every prelate and superior ought to call together those entrusted to him to charity, peace and continual progress, and often gather them bodily, and fervently exhort them all to cast away strange gods, such as [[Col 3:5|covetousness, which is the service of idols|avaritiam, quæ idolorum est servitus]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription], pride, uncleanness, and everything through which, or to which, a man cleaves more than to God: and to cleanse themselves by contrition, confession and satisfaction, and to change their garments, [[Col 3:9|stripping yourselves of the old man with his deeds|exuendo veterem hominem cum actibus suis]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are those of Col 3:9], and putting on [[Eph 4:24|the new man, who according to God is created in justice and holiness|novum, qui secundum Deum creatus est, in sanctitate]] [the margin gives *Ephes.* with the chapter unreadable, verse 24]. The wicked and filthy garments are the vicious customs of the soul, its evil habits, its perverse ways and acts, of which we have in Zacharias: [[Zach 3:4|Take away the filthy garments from him|Auferte ab eo vestimenta sordida]]. These garments are to be changed for fair, precious and fragrant garments, which are the virtues and the gifts of the Holy Ghost, the fruits and the beatitudes, fervent affections towards God, sincere meditations and a virtuous life, with which the soul is best adorned, and smells most sweetly before God, and is made most pleasing to Him. Further, Jacob calls together his household when a God-fearing man examines all that is within him, and searches all the powers of his soul, in which vices and virtues can exist, to see what evil is in it and what good is wanting: and so he tries to reform the passions of his soul, and to guard duly all his senses, inward and outward, so as not to offend the God of majesty in anything; and he detests vain and foul fancies as diabolical images, and so strives to keep a clean heart before the Most High, singing with the Psalmist: [[Ps 24:15|My eyes are ever towards the Lord|Oculi mei semper ad Dominum]]. Lastly, when a man so acts, and so advances to the perfection of the unity and charity of the Church, all the ranks of the invisible enemies round about are terrified, so much that they flee from one who so advances.

paras.t: Tunc etiam talis vir rectius appellatur Israel, tanquam divinorum sincerus expeditusque contemplator, quam Jacob : quoniam vitia, præsertim mortalia ac majora, jam penitus supplantavit, et cadunt a latere suo mille, ac decem millia a dextris ejus.
paras.en: Then too such a man is more rightly called Israel, as a sincere and unhindered contemplator of divine things, than Jacob [*Jacob*, supplanter: see Gen 27:36]: since he has now wholly supplanted the vices, especially the mortal and greater ones, and [[Ps 90:7|A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand|cadunt a latere suo mille, ac decem millia a dextris ejus]] [Denis puts the Psalm in the third person: *at his side … at his right hand*].

paras.t: Amplius, exemplo illius venerabilis Deboræ, tam caritative, humiliter atque concorditer inter proximos conversemur, ut defuncti sic defleamur ab ipsis, quod et locus nostræ sepulturæ, locus fletus digne vocetur. Absit, ut aliquis ita se habeat, quod eo mortuo, alii quasi a gravi onere exoneratos se glorientur. Insuper juxta hortamenta divina, non cessemus cum sancto Jacob spiritualiter crescere ac sanctis operibus multiplicari, quatenus et ex nobis nascantur gentes ac populi, hoc est, nostris verbis, actibus, meritis et exemplis convertantur ac regenerentur per supernorum infusionem charismatum, sicque nostri filii fiant. Reges quoque de lumbis nostris egrediantur, hoc est, aliorum rectores ita gignantur ex nobis, et ita nunc habeamus locum ac partem in Ecclesia militante, deinde in Ecclesia triumphante.
paras.en: Moreover, after the example of that venerable Debora, let us live so lovingly, humbly and peaceably among our neighbours that when we are dead we may be so wept for by them that the place of our burial too may worthily be called a place of weeping. Far be it that anyone should so behave that, when he is dead, others should boast that they are as it were freed of a heavy burden. Further, according to the divine exhortations, let us not cease with holy Jacob to increase spiritually and to be multiplied in holy works, so that from us too nations and peoples may be born, that is, may be converted and regenerated by our words, deeds, merits and examples, through the infusion of heavenly gifts, and so become our sons. Let kings too come out of our loins, that is, let rulers of others be so begotten of us; and so let us now have place and part in the Church militant, and afterwards in the Church triumphant.

paras.t: Egressus inde, venit ad terram quæ ducit Ephratam. Ephrata quæ interpretatur frugifera, designat religionem monasticam, in qua est spiritualium abundantia fructuum : ad quam pergit Christifidelis, dum is qui exemplariter ac honeste inter sæculares se habuit, claustrum ingreditur, ut sicut per viam mandatorum cucurrit in sæculo, sic per viam evangelicorum consiliorum in ipso volet cœnobio. Verumtamen sicut Rachel uxor Jacob, in via illa periclitata est ex partus difficultate, ita interdum contingit in homine religioso, ut caro ejus ex sua fragilitate et difficultate exsequendi quæ fervor spiritus suggerit, cadat sub onere.
paras.en: [[35:16|And going forth from thence, he came in the spring time to the land which leadeth to Ephrata|Egressus inde, venit ad terram quæ ducit Ephratam]]. Ephrata, which is interpreted *fruitful*, signifies the monastic religion, in which there is abundance of spiritual fruits: to which the faithful Christian goes when one who has lived in an exemplary and honourable way among people of the world enters the cloister, so that, as he [[Ps 118:32|I have run the way of thy commandments|per viam mandatorum cucurrit]] in the world, so he may fly along the way of the evangelical counsels in the monastery itself. Yet as Rachel, Jacob's wife, was in danger on that road from the difficulty of her labour, so it sometimes happens in a religious man that his flesh, from its frailty and from the difficulty of carrying out what the fervour of the spirit suggests, falls under the burden.

paras.t: Egressus inde, fixit tabernaculum trans turrem Gregis. Per turrem Gregis potest prælatica potestas intelligi, quæ est altitudo, qua quis gregi Christi præest et præcipere potest. Hoc ergo impletur, dum virtuosus claustralis ad aliorum regimen promovetur, potissimum ad episcopatus fastigium. Potest quoque per turrem Gregis, eremitica ac anachoretica vita signari, quæ est in grege totius Ecclesiæ quasi quædam præclarissima celsitudo, et conversatio angelis proxima ac familiarissima Deo. Tunc ergo fidelis figit tabernaculum trans turrem Gregis, et habitat ibi, dum verus cœnobita efficitur sincerus anachoreta, et solitariam vitam divinam potius quam humanam indefessus prosequitur, ita assidue in Deum absorptus, ut omnium terrenorum prorsus obliviscatur.
paras.en: [[35:21|Departing thence, he pitched his tent beyond the Flock tower|Egressus inde, fixit tabernaculum trans turrem Gregis]]. By the Flock tower can be understood the power of prelacy, which is the height by which one is set over the flock of Christ and can command it. This, then, is fulfilled when a virtuous cloistered man is promoted to the government of others, above all to the summit of the episcopate. By the Flock tower, too, the eremitical and anchoritic life can be signified, which is in the flock of the whole Church as it were a most glorious height, a way of life nearest to the angels and most familiar to God. Then, therefore, the faithful soul pitches his tent beyond the Flock tower, and dwells there, when a true cenobite becomes a sincere anchorite, and pursues tirelessly the solitary life, divine rather than human, so continually absorbed in God that he forgets altogether all earthly things.

paras.t: Præterea ex hoc quod Ruben primogenitus Jacob cum patris sui uxore dormivit, […] ad quam horrenda vitia libido infelicem præcipitet hominem, et quanta sit humana fragilitas, dum tanti Patriarchæ primogenitus, in tam abominabilem ignominiæ fœditatem se ipsum demersit. Ideo qui stat, videat ne cadat. Nemo de se ipso præsumat, alienaque damna faciant nos peritos. Erant autem filii Jacob duodecim : per quos duodecim Apostoli designantur. Et sicut inter duodecim filios Jacob, unus Benjamin nomine, propriam matrem per difficultatem partus peremit : sic unus Apostolorum ex Benjamin tribu natus, nomine Paulus, matrem suam primitivam Ecclesiam ad tempus vastavit, et eam in membris suis occidit.
paras.en: Further, from the fact that Ruben, Jacob's firstborn, slept with his father's wife, […] [the transcription has *amicorum* here, which does not fit; a word such as "we learn" seems lost] to what horrible vices lust drives the unhappy man, and how great human frailty is, when the firstborn of so great a Patriarch plunged himself into such abominable foulness of disgrace. Therefore he that stands, [[1 Cor 10:12|let him take heed lest he fall|videat ne cadat]]. Let no one presume on himself; and let other men's ruin make us wise. [[35:22|Now the sons of Jacob were twelve|Erant autem filii Jacob duodecim]]: by whom the twelve Apostles are signified. And as among the twelve sons of Jacob one, named Benjamin, killed his own mother through the difficulty of his birth: so one of the Apostles, born of the tribe of Benjamin, named Paul, for a time laid waste his mother, the primitive Church, and slew her in her members.

36.title: Expositio capituli tricesimi sexti: Hæ autem sunt generationes Esau
36.title_en: Exposition of the thirty-sixth chapter: “And these are the generations of Esau”

paras.t: MULTIPLICATIO posteritatis Esau, et dominatio posterorum suorum, hoc loco describitur. Hæ autem sunt generationes Esau, ipse est Edom, id est, alio nomine vocatus est Edom. Esau accepit uxores de filiabus Chanaan : Ada filiam Elon Hethæi, et Oolibama filiam Anæ filii Sebeon Hevæi. Supra legitur Esau accepisse duas uxores ex stirpe Chananæorum, quæ ibi aliis exprimuntur nominibus: ideo aliqui putant, quod hic suppleatur quod ibi omissum est, atque quod feminæ istæ fuerunt ab illis diversæ. Aliqui verisimilius dicunt, quod fuerunt eædem, et quod plura nomina habuerunt, sicut et Esau, atque in Evangelio idem vocatur Petrus et Simon ac Cephas. Basemath quoque filiam Ismael, etc. Supra capitulo vicesimo octavo scribitur accepisse Maheleth filiam Ismaelis. Si ergo ista fuit eadem quæ illa, dicendum est quod binomia fuit. Peperit autem Ada uxor Esau Eliphaz, etc., qui (secundum Hieronymum) est primus trium virorum, qui in libro Job inducuntur disputasse cum Job : unde et Glossa interlinearis hoc innuit.
paras.en: Here is described the multiplying of Esau's posterity and the dominion of his descendants. [[36:1|And these are the generations of Esau, the same is Edom|Hæ autem sunt generationes Esau, ipse est Edom]], that is, he was called by another name Edom. [[36:2|Esau took wives of the daughters of Chanaan: Ada the daughter of Elon the Hethite, and Oolibama the daughter of Ana, the daughter of Sebeon the Hevite|Esau accepit uxores de filiabus Chanaan : Ada filiam Elon Hethæi, et Oolibama filiam Anæ filii Sebeon Hevæi]]. Above we read that Esau took two wives of the stock of the Chanaanites, who are there given other names[[Gen 26:34||]] [the margin gives Gen. xxxvi, 34; the place meant is Gen 26:34]: so some think that what was left out there is supplied here, and that these women were different from those. Others say more probably that they were the same, and that they had several names, as Esau also had, and as in the Gospel the same man is called Peter and Simon and Cephas[[Matt 4:18||]][[Matt 16:17||]][[John 1:42||]]. [[36:3|And Basemath, the daughter of Ismael|Basemath quoque filiam Ismael]], etc. Above, in the twenty-eighth chapter, it is written that he took Maheleth the daughter of Ismael. If, then, this was the same as she, it must be said that she had two names. [[36:4|And Ada bore Eliphaz|Peperit autem Ada uxor Esau Eliphaz]], etc., Esau's wife, who (according to Jerome) is the first of the three men who are brought in, in the book of Job, as disputing with Job[[Job 2:11||]]: and the interlinear Gloss also hints at this.

paras.t: Tulit autem Esau uxores suas et filios et filias, et cuncta quæ habere poterat in terra Chanaan, et abiit in alteram regionem, recessitque a fratre suo Jacob. Divites enim erant valde, et simul habitare non poterant ; nec sustinebat eos terra peregrinationis eorum præ multitudine gregum. Non quod ipsi duo soli occupaverint universam terram Chanaan, in qua peregre habitabant, sed quia in illa terra aliunde populosa, non invenerunt sufficientia pascua pro suis pecoribus. Habitavitque Esau in monte Seir, ipse est Edom. Nomina ista Seir et Edom, quandoque accipiuntur prout sunt propria nomina Esau ; quandoque sumuntur pro terra seu regione in qua commoratus est, puta pro Idumæa ; quandoque Seir pro villa accipitur, et ita nunc accipi potest Seir pro villa seu terra illa, et Edom similiter, vel pro ipso Esau, a quo mons ille nomen sortitus est.
paras.en: [[36:6|And Esau took his wives, and his sons and daughters, and every soul of his house, and his substance, and cattle, and all that he was able to acquire in the land of Chanaan|Tulit autem Esau uxores suas et filios et filias, et cuncta quæ habere poterat in terra Chanaan]], [[36:6|and went into another country, and departed from his brother Jacob|et abiit in alteram regionem, recessitque a fratre suo Jacob]]. [[36:7|For they were exceeding rich, and could not dwell together: neither was the land in which they sojourned able to bear them, for the multitude of their flocks|Divites enim erant valde, et simul habitare non poterant ; nec sustinebat eos terra peregrinationis eorum præ multitudine gregum]]. Not that the two of them alone occupied the whole land of Chanaan, in which they dwelt as strangers, but because in that land, populous as it was besides, they did not find enough pasture for their cattle. [[36:8|And Esau dwelt in mount Seir: he is Edom|Habitavitque Esau in monte Seir, ipse est Edom]]. These names, Seir and Edom, are sometimes taken as proper names of Esau; sometimes they stand for the land or country in which he lived, namely Idumea; sometimes Seir is taken for a township; and so here Seir can be taken for that township or land, and Edom likewise, or for Esau himself, from whom that mountain got its name.

paras.t: Sed istis objicitur quia superius dictum est, quod ipso Jacob ex Mesopotamia veniente, Esau habitabat in Seir seu Idumæa, et ex ea venit obviam Jacob, ergo ante mortem Isaac recessit a terra Chanaan, et habitavit in Seir : sicque multitudo gregum ipsius ac Jacob, non fuit causa separationis eorum ab invicem. Ad hoc Strabus respondet : Fieri potuit ut Jacob in Mesopotamiam fugiente, Esau ex dolore præceptæ benedictionis a parentibus suis recesserit, et habitarit in Seir per annos viginti, quibus abfuit Jacob : cui reverso ipse Esau reconciliatus, de Seir reversus, habitavit cum patre suo quamdiu vixit : quo mortuo, recessit a Jacob ex causa præfata. Alii dicunt, quod circa finem vitæ Isaac, rediit Esau ad ipsum, ut bona ejus perciperet, eumque sepeliret : ac deinde mansit ad tempus in terra illa : postmodum vero ad Seir reversus est, non quod ex humilitate cesserit fratri suo Jacob, sed Deo inspirante sic factum est, ut Jacob in terra semini suo promissa maneret. Esau quoque magis afficiebatur ad terram Edom, quia jam diu fuit demoratus in ea.
paras.en: But against this it is objected that it was said above that when Jacob was coming from Mesopotamia Esau was dwelling in Seir or Idumea, and came from there to meet Jacob[[Gen 32:3||]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription]; therefore he left the land of Chanaan before Isaac's death and dwelt in Seir: and so the multitude of his flocks and Jacob's was not the cause of their separation from each other. To this Strabus answers: It may be that when Jacob fled to Mesopotamia, Esau, out of grief at the blessing taken from him, withdrew from his parents and dwelt in Seir for the twenty years that Jacob was away; and that when Jacob returned, Esau, reconciled to him, came back from Seir and dwelt with his father as long as he lived; and when he was dead, withdrew from Jacob for the reason given. Others say that towards the end of Isaac's life Esau returned to him, to receive his goods and to bury him, and then stayed for a time in that land; but afterwards went back to Seir, not that he gave way to his brother Jacob out of humility, but it was so done by God's inspiration, that Jacob might remain in the land promised to his seed. Esau, too, was more attached to the land of Edom, since he had already stayed in it a long time.

paras.t: Postquam in isto capitulo descriptæ sunt generationes Esau seu filiorum ejus quos generavit in terra Chanaan, quorum multi erant binomii, et in libro Paralipomenon primo aliter nominantur quam hic : nunc describitur generatio ejus, seu potius generatio posterorum ipsius in Idumæa : et personæ nunc nominandæ, etiam in primo libro Paralipomenon, aliis exprimuntur nominibus. Hæ autem sunt generationes Esau patris Edom, id est Idumæorum, qui ibi ex ejus semine nati sunt, in monte Seir, etc. Fueruntque filii Eliphaz primogeniti Esau, Theman, Omar, Sepho, etc. Theman quandoque est proprium nomen viri, sicut hic. Interdum vero accipitur pro civitate, quæ fuit metropolis Idumææ, et ab illa Eliphaz iste vocatus est Eliphaz Themanites. Erat autem Thamna concubina Eliphaz filii Esau, quæ peperit ei Amalec, a quo nati et appellati sunt Amalecitæ : unde et populus ille frequenter nomine Amalec designatur. Si autem Eliphaz iste est is, qui disputavit cum Job, credendum est, quod non habuit concubinam postquam duxit uxorem legitimam, nisi sumendo concubinam pro uxore secundaria minus principali. Nam Eliphaz ille fuit vir magnæ prudentiæ, magnam quoque habuit notitiam divinorum, et sanctus Gregorius frequenter testatur tres amicos Job justos fuisse, quamvis disputando cum Job, excesserunt, et hæreticorum tenuerunt speciem, juxta mysticum intellectum. Isti sunt filii Adæ uxoris Esau. Hoc non est referendum ad omnes præfatos, quoniam Amalec non fuit filius Adæ, sed Thamnæ : sed referendum est hoc ad sex illos, qui in littera ante Amalec exprimuntur. Vel si referatur etiam ad Amalec, dici potest quod ipse fuit adoptivus filius Adæ.
paras.en: After the generations of Esau, or of the sons he begot in the land of Chanaan, have been described in this chapter, many of whom had two names and are named otherwise in the first book of Paralipomenon than here[[1 Par 1:35||]], now his generation is described, or rather the generation of his descendants in Idumea: and the persons now to be named are also given other names in the first book of Paralipomenon. [[36:9|And these are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom|Hæ autem sunt generationes Esau patris Edom]], that is, of the Idumeans who were born there of his seed, [[36:9|in mount Seir|in monte Seir]], etc. [[36:11|And Eliphaz had sons: Theman, Omar, Sepho|Fueruntque filii Eliphaz primogeniti Esau, Theman, Omar, Sepho]], etc. [Denis's text adds *primogeniti Esau*, the firstborn of Esau.] Theman is sometimes the proper name of a man, as here. But sometimes it is taken for a city, which was the capital of Idumea, and from it this Eliphaz was called Eliphaz the Themanite. [[36:12|And Thamna was the concubine of Eliphaz, the son of Esau: and she bore him Amalech|Erat autem Thamna concubina Eliphaz filii Esau, quæ peperit ei Amalec]], from whom the Amalecites were born and named: hence too that people is often designated by the name of Amalec. But if this Eliphaz is the one who disputed with Job, it is to be believed that he did not have a concubine after he married a lawful wife, unless *concubine* is taken for a secondary, less principal wife. For that Eliphaz was a man of great prudence, and he had great knowledge of divine things; and Saint Gregory often testifies that the three friends of Job were just, though in disputing with Job they went too far and, according to the mystical understanding, bore the figure of heretics. [[36:12|These are the sons of Ada, the wife of Esau|Isti sunt filii Adæ uxoris Esau]]. This is not to be referred to all those mentioned, since Amalec was not the son of Ada but of Thamna: but it is to be referred to the six who are named in the letter before Amalec. Or if it is referred to Amalec too, it can be said that he was Ada's adopted son.

paras.t: Deinde nominantur duces Idumæorum nati ex semine Esau, per primogenitum ejus nomine Eliphaz. Et hi, qui infra nominatim exprimuntur, fuerunt duces filiorum Esau, non filiorum ejus immediatorum et proximorum, sed remotorum ac posterorum. Filii Eliphaz primogeniti Esau qui duces fuerunt, supple, sunt hi : dux Theman nomine, dux Omar, dux Sepho, etc. Isti septem fuerunt immediati filii Eliphaz, ut in textu habetur : ideo non fuerunt duces totius plebis Idumæorum, sed unusquisque in tribu sua, sicut superius Dominus dixit de Ismaele, Duodecim duces generabit, duces duodecim tribuum suarum. Deinde ponuntur nati ex secundo filio Esau. Hi quoque filii Rahuel filii Esau ex secunda conjuge sua, quam tamen simul tempore habebat cum prima : dux Nahath, dux Zara, etc. Simili modo exprimuntur in littera duces nati ex tertio filio Esau, et intelligendum est de ducibus istis, quod fuerunt duces, unusquisque in tribu sua, ut tactum est.
paras.en: Then the dukes of the Idumeans born of Esau's seed through his firstborn, named Eliphaz, are named. [[36:15|These were dukes of the sons of Esau|Et hi, qui infra nominatim exprimuntur, fuerunt duces filiorum Esau]], who are named one by one below, not of his immediate and nearest sons, but of his remote ones and descendants. [[36:15|the sons of Eliphaz, the firstborn of Esau|Filii Eliphaz primogeniti Esau]] who were dukes, supply, are these: [[36:15|duke Theman|dux Theman]] by name, [[36:15|duke Omar, duke Sepho|dux Omar, dux Sepho]], etc. These seven were the immediate sons of Eliphaz, as is had in the text: so they were not dukes of the whole people of the Idumeans, but each in his own tribe, as above the Lord said of Ismael: [[Gen 17:20|he shall beget twelve chiefs|Duodecim duces generabit]], dukes of their twelve tribes. Then those born of Esau's second son are set down. [[36:17|And these were the sons of Rahuel, the son of Esau|Hi quoque filii Rahuel filii Esau]], by his second wife, whom, however, he had at the same time as the first: [[36:17|duke Nahath, duke Zara|dux Nahath, dux Zara]], etc. In like manner the letter sets out the dukes born of Esau's third son; and it is to be understood of these dukes that they were dukes, each in his own tribe, as has been touched on.

paras.t: Consequenter ponuntur duces, qui ante Esau in terra Idumææ fuerunt. Isti filii Seir Horræi, habitatores terræ. Isti, inquam, Lotan et Sobal et Sebeon, etc. Iste Seir non fuit Esau, sed diu ante eum: fuitque Seir iste Horræus, cujus filii fuerunt habitatores terræ illius, et homines illi cognominabantur Horræi, quos postea posteri Esau expugnaverunt, et possederunt terram eorum, prout in Deuteronomio habetur. Hinc ait Hieronymus: Postquam enumeravit filios Esau, altius repetit qui ante Esau in terra Edom principes exstiterunt ex genere Horræorum. Hi duces Horræi filii Seir, non Esau, sed alterius jam prædicti, qui habitabat in terra Edom, quæ tamen tunc nondum sic vocabatur, quia ab Esau vocata est terra Edom. Erat autem soror Lotan, Thamna. Circa hoc scribit Hieronymus: Hæc est Thamna, ut dictum est, concubina Eliphaz primogeniti Esau. Ideo Scriptura hæc loquitur de Horræis, quoniam primogenitus Esau ex filiabus eorum accepit concubinam, hanc scilicet Thamna.
paras.en: Next are set down the dukes who were in the land of Idumea before Esau. [[36:20|These are the sons of Seir, the Horrite, the inhabitants of the land|Isti filii Seir Horræi, habitatores terræ]]. These, I say: [[36:20|Lotan, and Sobal, and Sebeon|Lotan et Sobal et Sebeon]], etc. This Seir was not Esau, but long before him: and this Seir was a Horrite, whose sons were the inhabitants of that land; and those men were called Horrites, whom Esau's descendants afterwards conquered, and possessed their land, as we have it in Deuteronomy[[Deut 2:22||]]. Hence Jerome says: After he has counted up the sons of Esau, he goes back further to those of the race of the Horrites who were princes in the land of Edom before Esau. [[36:21|These are dukes of the Horrites, the sons of Seir|Hi duces Horræi filii Seir]], not of Esau, but of the other already mentioned, who dwelt in the land of Edom, which however was not yet so called, since it was called the land of Edom from Esau. [[36:22|And the sister of Lotan was Thamna|Erat autem soror Lotan, Thamna]]. On this Jerome writes: This is Thamna, as was said, the concubine of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau. Therefore Scripture says these things of the Horrites, since Esau's firstborn took a concubine from among their daughters, namely this Thamna.

paras.t: Hi filii Sebeon, Aia et Ana. Iste est Ana qui invenit aquas calidas in solitudine, quum pasceret asinos Sebeon patris sui. Pro eo quod translatio nostra habet, Aquas calidas, in Hebræo habetur, Jammum: quod plura significat. Unde beatus Hieronymus: Varia, inquit, apud Hebræos de verbo hoc disputantur. Nam quidam eorum putant, per jammum, maria designari, dicentes hunc Ana, dum pasceret asinos patris sui, congregationes invenisse aquarum, quæ juxta idioma Hebræum maria appellantur, quoniam reperit stagnum seu lacum in eremo, quod ibi difficile reperitur. Quidam putant hoc nomine aquas calidas significari lingua Punica, quæ Hebrææ contigua est seu affinis. Quidam arbitrantur eum primo commiscuisse onagros asinabus, et invenisse hujusmodi concubitum, ut ex eo velocissimi asini nascerentur qui muli vocantur. Alii putant quod equas primus fecit ascendi ab asinis, ut muli contra naturam nascerentur; et istud est melius ac plenius dictum, quam quod circa hunc passum Lyra conscribit, quasi omnes Hebræi idem sentirent de verbo hoc: Hebræi, inquiens, dicunt quod invenit mulas in solitudine; sed dictio Hebraica significat calorem aquarum quam significationem secuta est nostra translatio, sicque exponitur de calidis aquis quæ per modum fontis nascuntur, et fiunt ex terra, ubi sunt venæ sulfureæ, et calorem talem contrahit aqua, cujusmodi fontes reperiuntur in pluribus locis. Hebræi autem dicunt, quod asinos fecit ascendere super equas, sicque invenit modum generationis mularum. Hæc Lyra, qui etiam dicit: Aliqui libri habent Asinas, sed falsa est littera. Circa quod dico, quod secundum ejus expositionem, textus debet habere Asinos, quoniam muli generantur ex equa et asino; sed secundum alias quasdam expositiones, indifferenter legi potest Asinas, et Asinos. Porro, secundum expositionem qua per jammum intelliguntur asini velocissimi, ex onagris asinabusque nati, melius legitur Asinas: idcirco illa sua correctio litteræ, inconsiderata insufficiensque probatur.
paras.en: [[36:24|And these the sons of Sebeon: Aia and Ana|Hi filii Sebeon, Aia et Ana]]. [[36:24|This is Ana that found the hot waters in the wilderness, when he fed the asses of Sebeon, his father|Iste est Ana qui invenit aquas calidas in solitudine, quum pasceret asinos Sebeon patris sui]]. Where our translation has *hot waters*, the Hebrew has *Jammum* [so too the margin]: which means several things. Hence blessed Jerome: Various things, he says, are disputed among the Hebrews about this word. For some of them think that by *jammum* seas are meant, saying that this Ana, while he fed his father's asses, found gatherings of waters, which in the Hebrew idiom are called seas, because he found a pool or lake in the desert, which is hard to find there. Some think that hot waters are meant by this name in the Punic tongue, which is near or akin to the Hebrew. Some judge that he first mated wild asses with she-asses, and discovered such a coupling, so that from it very swift asses might be born, which are called mules. Others think that he first had mares covered by asses, so that mules might be born against nature: and this is said better and more fully than what Lyra writes on this passage, as if all the Hebrews held the same about this word. The Hebrews, he says, say that he found mules in the wilderness; but the Hebrew word means heat of waters, which meaning our translation has followed; and so it is explained of hot waters which spring up as a fountain and come from the earth where there are sulphurous veins, and the water takes on such heat; such fountains are found in many places. But the Hebrews say that he made asses go up on mares, and so found the way of generating mules. Thus far Lyra, who also says: Some books have *she-asses*, but the reading is false. On which I say that according to his exposition the text ought to have *asses* [*asinos*, he-asses], since mules are born of a mare and an ass; but according to certain other expositions one can read indifferently *she-asses* and *asses*. Further, according to the exposition by which by *jammum* are understood very swift asses born of wild asses and she-asses, *she-asses* is the better reading: so that correction of his of the text is proved ill-considered and insufficient.

paras.t: Deinceps describuntur reges de semine Esau, qui regnaverunt in Idumæa post duces præfatos ejusdem stirpis. Reges autem qui regnaverunt in terra Edom, antequam habuerunt regem filii Israel, scilicet ante Saul primum regem Israelitici populi: nam et quamvis Abimelech filius Gedeonis legatur regnasse super quosdam de Israel, non tamen fuit rex divinitus institutus, nec cunctis præfuit Israelitis, sed paucis; fuerunt hi: Balac filius Beor, et ceteri qui exprimuntur in littera, quæ expositione non indiget. Verumtamen pro pleniori horum intelligentia, advertendum est primo quod ait Glossa: Sciendum, quod scriptura ista non commemorat omnes reges qui fuerunt in Edom ante primum regem Israel, sed hos tantum, qui regnaverunt ibi ante Moysis mortem. Secundo pensandum, quod etiam fertur in Glossa, quod iste Balac non est ille qui in libro Numerorum legitur conduxisse Balaam contra filios Israel. Ille enim regnavit in Moab, et fuit filius Sephor; iste in Idumæa, et filius fuit Beor. Tertio intuendum, quod sicut filii Israel primo regebantur per judices usque ad Saul, deinde per reges usque ad transmigrationem Babylonis, et post hoc rursus per principes quosdam seu duces, quorum multi fuerunt pontifices: sic Idumæi ex Esau nati, primo habuerunt duces, deinde reges, quorum primus fuit præfatus Balac, postea redierunt ad ducatum, postmodum tamen rursus regem sibi constituerunt tempore Joram regis Juda, ut legitur quarto libro Regum: Mortuus est autem Balac, et regnavit pro eo Jobab, etc.; quem aliqui vocant Jobab, et secundum Augustinum circa hunc passum, atque Ambrosium super epistolam ad Romanos, iste fuit Job. Hieronymus quoque refert, quod quidam suspicati sunt filium hujus Jobab, nomine Husam, fuisse Job. Hebræi vero dicunt Job natum de stirpe Nachor, non Abrahæ, ut dictum est in expositione capituli vicesimi secundi.
paras.en: Next are described the kings of the seed of Esau who reigned in Idumea after the aforesaid dukes of the same stock. [[36:31|And the kings that ruled in the land of Edom, before the children of Israel had a king|Reges autem qui regnaverunt in terra Edom, antequam habuerunt regem filii Israel]], namely before Saul, the first king of the Israelite people: for although we read that Abimelech the son of Gedeon reigned over some of Israel[[Judg 8:31||]][[Judg 9:6||]] [the margin gives Judic. viii at the end, and ix], yet he was not a king instituted by God, nor did he rule over all the Israelites, but over a few; [[36:31|were these|fuerunt hi]]: [[36:32|Bela the son of Beor|Balac filius Beor]] [Denis's text has *Balac*, where the Vulgate has *Bela*], and the others named in the letter, which needs no exposition. Yet for a fuller understanding of these things it is to be noted, first, what the Gloss says: It is to be known that this scripture does not record all the kings who were in Edom before the first king of Israel, but only those who reigned there before the death of Moses. Secondly, it is to be weighed, as is also said in the Gloss, that this Balac is not the one who in the book of Numbers is read to have hired Balaam against the children of Israel. For that one reigned in Moab and was the son of Sephor; this one in Idumea, and he was the son of Beor. Thirdly, it is to be considered that as the children of Israel were ruled first by judges until Saul, then by kings until the Babylonian captivity, and after this again by certain princes or leaders, many of whom were high priests: so the Idumeans born of Esau first had dukes, then kings, of whom the first was the aforesaid Balac; afterwards they returned to dukedom; yet later they again set up a king for themselves in the time of Joram king of Juda, as we read in the fourth book of Kings[[4 Kings 8:20||]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription]. [[36:33|And Bela died, and Jobab, the son of Zara, of Bosra, reigned in his stead|Mortuus est autem Balac, et regnavit pro eo Jobab]], etc.; whom some call Jobab, and according to Augustine on this passage, and Ambrose on the Epistle to the Romans, this was Job. Jerome too relates that some have supposed that this Jobab's son, named Husam, was Job. But the Hebrews say that Job was born of the stock of Nachor, not of Abraham[[Gen 22:21||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Hus, the firstborn of Nachor, is in Gen 22:21], as was said in the exposition of the twenty-second chapter.

paras.t: Consequenter ponuntur in littera duces Idumæorum, qui præfatis regibus successerunt: quorum regum ultimus fuit Adad, ut habetur in textu. Unde scriptum est primo Paralipomenon: Adad autem mortuo, duces pro regibus esse cœperunt in Edom. Ideo duces hic positi, non præcesserunt tempore reges prædictos. Hæc ergo nomina ducum, id est Idumæorum ex Esau genitorum : dux Thamna, etc. Ex hoc elicitur, quod Thamna quandoque significat proprie virum, interdum vero proprium nomen est mulieris, unde præhabitum est, quod Thamna fuit filii Esau concubina. Sunt etenim quædam propria nomina ad virum et mulierem æquivoca. Hic ergo accipitur Thamna pro viro, sicut et Oolibana, quum subditur, dux Oolibama; quum tamen prædictum sit, quod Oolibama fuit Esau uxor. De ducibus autem hic positis tenetur, quod fuerunt generaliter principes Idumæorum, non unius tantum tribus, sicut de aliis eorum ducibus tactum est. Sed circa hæc difficilis oritur quæstio. Si enim Moyses exprimit reges Edom, qui usque ad tempus suum fuerunt, et duces nunc positi in littera undecim numero, fuerunt post reges illos, qualiter potuit Moyses duces illos cognoscere atque describere? Insuper dictum est, quod non exprimit reges Idumæorum, nisi qui fuerunt usque ad tempus suum; sed oppositum hujus apparet, quia in textu habetur, quod ultimus rex Idumæorum fuit Adad, qui fuit tempore David, et fugit a facie Joab, quando interfecit omne masculinum in Idumæa, ut primo Paralipomenon et tertio Regum libris describitur. Ad primum horum quidam dixerunt, quod Moyses ex revelatione divina per spiritum prophetiæ duces illos præcognovit atque expressit. Alii opinantur, ut in Scholastica historia tangitur, quod Esdras apposuit, textuique inseruit enumerationem ducum illorum. Ad secundum quidam absolute respondent, quod Glossa præallegata, qua dictum est, Moysen non describere reges Edom nisi usque ad tempus suum, sit falsa, quum tamen ex verbis Augustini sit sumpta: idcirco (ut videtur) moderantius dici posset, juxta prætacta ex Historia scholastica, quod enumeratio eorum qui post Moysen exstiterunt, ab Esdra apposita sit.
paras.en: Next the letter sets down the dukes of the Idumeans who succeeded the aforesaid kings: of which kings the last was Adad [the margin notes the reading *Adar*, as in v. 39], as is had in the text. Hence it is written in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 1:51|And after the death of Adad, there began to be dukes in Edom instead of kings|Adad autem mortuo, duces pro regibus esse cœperunt in Edom]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription]. So the dukes set down here did not come before the aforesaid kings in time. [[36:40|And these are the names of the dukes|Hæc ergo nomina ducum]], that is, of the Idumeans born of Esau: [[36:40|duke Thamna|dux Thamna]], etc. From this it is gathered that Thamna sometimes properly means a man, but at times is the proper name of a woman; hence it was said before that Thamna was the concubine of Esau's son. For there are certain proper names common to man and woman. Here, then, Thamna is taken for a man, as also Oolibama, when there follows, [[36:41|Duke Oolibama|dux Oolibama]]; though it was said before that Oolibama was Esau's wife. Of the dukes set down here it is held that they were princes of the Idumeans in general, not of one tribe only, as was touched on concerning their other dukes. But on these things a difficult question arises. For if Moses sets out the kings of Edom who were up to his own time, and the dukes now set down in the letter, eleven in number, came after those kings, how could Moses know and describe those dukes? Moreover, it was said that he does not set out the kings of the Idumeans except those who were up to his own time; but the opposite of this appears, since it is had in the text that the last king of the Idumeans was Adad, who lived in the time of David and fled from the face of Joab when he killed every male in Idumea, as is described in the first book of Paralipomenon and the third of Kings[[1 Par 18:11||]][[1 Par 18:13||]][[3 Kings 11:15||]][[3 Kings 11:16||]]. To the first of these some have said that Moses foreknew and set down those dukes by divine revelation, through the spirit of prophecy. Others think, as is touched on in the Scholastic History, that Esdras added and inserted into the text the list of those dukes. To the second some answer absolutely that the Gloss cited above, in which it was said that Moses describes the kings of Edom only up to his own time, is false, though it is taken from the words of Augustine: so (as it seems) it could be said more moderately, following what was touched on from the Scholastic History, that the list of those who came after Moses was added by Esdras.

37.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli tricesimi septimi: Joseph quum sedecim esset annorum, pascebat gregem cum fratribus suis
37.title_en: Literal explanation of the thirty-seventh chapter: “Joseph, when he was sixteen years old, was feeding the flock with his brethren”

paras.t: Qualiter venditus sit Joseph a fratribus suis, atque ab emptoribus in Ægyptum perductus, ibique denuo venditus, præsens narrat capitulum.
paras.en: How Joseph was sold by his brethren, and brought by his buyers into Egypt, and there sold again, the present chapter relates.

paras.t: Joseph quum sedecim esset annorum, pascebat gregem cum fratribus suis adhuc puer. Adjuvit itaque eos in pastu pecorum. Aliqui dicunt in Hebræo haberi, Quum esset decem et septem annorum : quod concordatur, quia (ut dicunt) habebat sedecim annos plene, et septimumdecimum annum incepit ; sicque translatio nostra computat plenos, quos tunc habuit, annos. Et erat cum filiis Balæ et Zelphæ uxorum patris sui. Porro filii Balæ fuerunt Dan et Nephthali ; filii autem Zelphæ, Gad et Aser. Hi quatuor habuerunt majorem communicationem et societatem ad invicem, utpote in pluribus sibi consimiles, quia filii ancillarum : similitudo namque est causa amoris et communionis ; et ut aliqui dicunt, filii Liæ spreverunt eos, quasi servos ac filios famularum. Accusavitque fratres suos apud patrem eorum et suum crimine pessimo : quod quidam exponunt de coitu eorum in bestias. Nec exprimit textus an de crimine pessimo accusaverit fratres suos omnes, qui erant cum gregibus, an filios Balæ et Zelphæ dumtaxat : magis tamen videtur intelligendum de eis, quia Scriptura immediate præmisit quod erat cum illis. Alii per pessimum crimen, intelligunt odium fratrum quo oderant ipsum Joseph ; quidam vero de mutua fratrum suorum contentione seu rixa, quia (ut dictum est) filii liberæ contempserunt filios Balæ et Zelphæ. Unde ut refert Lyra, in Hebræo habetur, Retulit patri rixam eorum pessimam. Verumtamen Rabbi Paulus contradicit his verbis Lyræ. Cui videlicet Lyræ indecens esse videtur, ut Patriarchis imponatur commixtio talis cum brutis. Ad quod dici potest, non esse incredibile eos sic corruisse, quum primogenitus inter eos proprii patris accesserit conjugem, tam incestuosum adulterium perpetrans. Hinc Glossa fatetur : Crimen pessimum est fraternum odium, vel quod cum pecoribus miscebantur ; vel solum Ruben accusavit de incestu, ut partem a toto accipiamus : non enim omnes accusavit. Sed huic ultimo verbo Glossæ objicitur, quod Ruben potissime restitit venditioni Joseph. Ad quod dici posset, quod forsan eo ignorante accusabatur a Joseph, vel accusationem suam æquanimiter tulit.
paras.en: [[37:2|Joseph, when he was sixteen years old, was feeding the flock with his brethren, being but a boy|Joseph quum sedecim esset annorum, pascebat gregem cum fratribus suis adhuc puer]]. So he helped them in pasturing the cattle. Some say that the Hebrew has: When he was seventeen years old. The two agree because (as they say) he had fully completed sixteen years and had begun his seventeenth; and so our translation counts the full years that he then had. [[37:2|he was with the sons of Bala and of Zelpha his father's wives|Et erat cum filiis Balæ et Zelphæ uxorum patris sui]]. Now the sons of Bala were Dan and Nephthali; the sons of Zelpha, Gad and Aser. These four had closer dealings and fellowship with one another, being alike in many things, since they were sons of handmaids: for likeness is a cause of love and fellowship; and, as some say, the sons of Lia despised them as servants and sons of bondwomen. [[37:2|he accused his brethren to his father of a most wicked crime|Accusavitque fratres suos apud patrem eorum et suum crimine pessimo]] [Denis's text reads "to their father and his"]: which some explain of their lying with beasts. Nor does the text say whether he accused of the most wicked crime all his brethren who were with the flocks, or only the sons of Bala and Zelpha; yet it seems rather to be understood of these, because Scripture has just said that he was with them. Others understand by the most wicked crime the hatred of the brethren with which they hated Joseph himself; and some, a mutual strife or brawl among his brethren, because (as has been said) the sons of the free wife despised the sons of Bala and Zelpha. Hence, as Lyra reports, the Hebrew has: He told his father of their most wicked brawl. Yet Rabbi Paul contradicts these words of Lyra. For to Lyra it seems unbecoming that such intercourse with brute beasts should be laid upon the Patriarchs. To this it can be said that it is not incredible that they fell so low, since the firstborn among them went in to his own father's wife, committing so incestuous an adultery. Hence the Gloss states: The most wicked crime is the hatred of brethren, or that they had to do with cattle; or he accused Ruben alone of incest, so that we take the part for the whole: for he did not accuse them all. But against this last word of the Gloss it is objected that Ruben above all resisted the selling of Joseph. To which it could be said that perhaps he was accused by Joseph without his knowing it, or that he bore the accusation with an even mind.

paras.t: Quæritur, quare Joseph magis associavit se filiis Balæ et Zelphæ. Dici potest, quod ex caritate et humilitate ac pietate hoc fecit, pro eorum solatio, quia vidit eos contemni ab aliis. Potius tamen puto, quod filii Liæ magis ægre ferebant, quod pater eorum tam specialiter dilexit Joseph, et ideo duriores ei fuerunt, quamvis Ruben venditioni ejus magis restiterit : propter quod declinavit ab eis.
paras.en: It is asked why Joseph kept company rather with the sons of Bala and Zelpha. It can be said that he did this out of charity, humility and kindness, to comfort them, because he saw them despised by the others. But I rather think that the sons of Lia took it the more ill that their father loved Joseph so especially, and were therefore harsher to him (though Ruben resisted his sale more than the rest): and for this reason he turned aside from them.

paras.t: Israel autem, scilicet Jacob, diligebat Joseph super omnes filios suos, id est præ unoquoque eorum seorsum accepto, non plus omnibus aliis simul sumptis : sicque Omnes, accipitur hic divisim, non collective ; eo quod in senectute sua genuisset eum. Contra hoc objici potest, quia si illa ex causa maxime eum amavit, magis adhuc amasset Benjamin, quem post Joseph genuerat. Aliqui quoque ex filiis Jacob, vix uno duobusve annis erant ipso Joseph seniores. Respondetur, quod una causa, ob quam magis amavit Joseph, fuit, quod in senectute genuit eum ; sed in hac causa insinuantur et aliæ majoris dilectionis illius causæ, videlicet quod in senectute sua genuerit filium tam elegantem præ aliis in bonitate indolis ingenitæ, honestateque morum et corporis forma, imo et gratia copiosa : solent quippe in senectute generari pueri magis defectuosi, propter naturalem defectum virtutis generativæ in senibus. Benjamin vero erat adhuc infantulus, nec poterant in eo tales amabilitates perpendi ; imo secundum Josephum (ut infra tangetur) necdum fuerat natus. Præterea Rabbi Paulus testatur, in Hebræo non haberi, Eo quod in senectute genuisset eum, sed, Eo quod filius senectutis esset sibi. Quod exponens translatio Chaldaica, ait : Israel diligebat Joseph, eo quod esset filius sapiens : siquidem consideravit, quod filius suus Joseph præ ceteris esset zelator justitiæ contra vitia fratrum, et amator virtutum. Et istud his quæ dixi, satis concordat.
paras.en: [[37:3|Now Israel|Israel autem]], that is, Jacob, [[37:3|loved Joseph above all his sons|diligebat Joseph super omnes filios suos]]: that is, more than each one of them taken singly, not more than all the rest taken together; and so *all* is taken here distributively, not collectively; [[37:3|because he had him in his old age|eo quod in senectute sua genuisset eum]]. Against this it can be objected that if he loved him most for that reason, he would have loved Benjamin still more, whom he had begotten after Joseph. Also some of Jacob's sons were scarcely one or two years older than Joseph. The answer is that one reason why he loved Joseph more was that he begot him in his old age; but in this reason other causes of that greater love are hinted at as well: namely, that in his old age he had begotten a son so excellent above the others in the goodness of his inborn disposition, in uprightness of conduct and comeliness of body, and indeed in abundant grace; for children begotten in old age are commonly more defective, because of the natural failing of the generative power in the old. Benjamin, on the other hand, was still a little infant, and such lovable qualities could not be weighed in him; indeed, according to Josephus (as will be touched on below), he was not yet born. Moreover Rabbi Paul testifies that the Hebrew does not have: Because he had begotten him in his old age, but: Because he was a son of his old age to him. Expounding this, the Chaldee translation says: Israel loved Joseph because he was a wise son: for he considered that his son Joseph, above the others, was zealous for justice against his brethren's vices, and a lover of virtues. And this agrees well enough with what I have said.

paras.t: Fecitque ei tunicam polymitam, id est setaceam, ut in Hebræo habetur, quia erat de panno multis coloribus perornato : idcirco vocatur polymita, a poly, quod est pluralitas, et […] mitos, quod est gutta colorans ; vel ut in Scholastica historia habetur, polymitam, id est plurium mitorum, a poly, quod est pluralitas, et mitos, quod licium est textorum. Hieronymus vero circa hæc scribit : Pro tunica varia, id est polymita. Aquila interpretatus est […] id est tunicam talarem, utpote usque ad talos pertingentem : Symmachus vero, manicatam, id est manibus artificis mira varietate distinctam, seu manicas habentem. Antiqui enim magis colobiis, id est vestibus sine manicis utebantur. Hæc Hieronymus. Hinc alii dicunt, quod ceteri fratres Jacob utebantur colobiis, id est vestibus brevibus sine manicis, ut expeditiores essent ad opera.
paras.en: [[37:3|and he made him a coat of divers colours|Fecitque ei tunicam polymitam]], that is, of silk [*setacea*: of silk or of fine hair], as the Hebrew has it, because it was of cloth adorned with many colours: therefore it is called *polymita*, from *poly*, which means plurality, and […] *mitos*, which is a colouring drop; or, as the Scholastic History has it, *polymita*, that is, of many *mitoi*, from *poly*, which means plurality, and *mitos*, which is the weavers' thread. Jerome, however, writes of this: For *a coat of divers colours*, that is, *polymita*, Aquila translated […], that is, a coat to the heels, as reaching down to the ankles; but Symmachus, *manicata*, that is, picked out by the craftsman's hands with wonderful variety, or having sleeves [*manicata* means "sleeved"; *manibus*, "by the hands", plays on it]. For the ancients wore rather *colobia*, that is, garments without sleeves. Thus far Jerome. Hence others say that Jacob's other sons wore *colobia*, that is, short garments without sleeves, so as to be readier for work.

paras.t: Videntes autem fratres ejus, quod a patre plus cunctis filiis amaretur naturali et paterno amore, et etiam caritate infusa : hoc enim viderunt per signa diversa, et per singularitatem ac pretiositatem præfati vestitus : oderant eum. Invidebant enim eminentiæ ejus in hoc, in quantum eorum judicio redundabat in eorum damnum ac dedecus : timuerunt namque quod pater eorum benediceret ei præ ipsis, et præferret eum omnibus eis, sicut et Isaac benedixerat ipsi Jacob, et prætulit eum Esau prius nato. Reputabant quoque confusibile eis esse, quod pater eorum sic amavit filium juniorem. Nec poterant, id est non valebant, difficulterque poterant ei quidquam pacifice loqui. Habitus enim est quasi altera natura : idcirco qui odio aut alio vitioso habitu sunt repleti, valde difficulter se vincunt.
paras.en: [[37:4|And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons|Videntes autem fratres ejus, quod a patre plus cunctis filiis amaretur]], with a natural and fatherly love, and also with infused charity (for they saw this by various signs, and by the singularity and costliness of the garment just mentioned), [[37:4|hated|oderant]] him. For they envied his pre-eminence in this, in so far as, in their judgement, it redounded to their loss and shame: for they feared that their father would bless him before them and set him over them all, as Isaac too had blessed Jacob himself and set him before Esau, the firstborn. They also thought it a disgrace to them that their father loved a younger son so much. [[37:4|and could not|Nec poterant]], that is, were not able, and only with difficulty could, [[37:4|speak peaceably to him|ei quidquam pacifice loqui]]. For habit is as it were a second nature: therefore those who are filled with hatred or some other vicious habit overcome themselves only with great difficulty.

paras.t: Quæritur, an Jacob recte egit tam specialiter diligendo Joseph. Ad hoc Augustinus respondet, quod quamvis poterat tam præelectum a Deo puerum ac ceteris virtuosiorem, specialiter valde diligere, excessit tamen et aliquo modo peccavit, quod amorem illum specialem tam evidenter monstravit per signa ; quia per hoc dedit aliis filiis suis occasionem multiplicium vitiorum, videlicet indignationis, iræ, tristitiæ et rancoris, imo et tandem sceleratæ venditionis : propter quod etiam Deus permisit ipsum Jacob in hac vita tam dire affligi occasione Joseph, seu ex ejus venditione, ita quod eum putavit a bestia devoratum ; quoniam per quæ quis peccat, per hæc et punitur.
paras.en: It is asked whether Jacob did right in loving Joseph so especially. To this Augustine replies that although he might love very especially a boy so chosen by God and more virtuous than the rest, yet he went too far, and in some way sinned, in showing that special love so plainly by signs; for by this he gave his other sons occasion of many vices, namely of indignation, anger, sadness and rancour, and in the end even of the wicked sale: for which reason God also allowed Jacob himself to be so grievously afflicted in this life on Joseph's account, that is, through his sale, so that he thought him devoured by a beast; since by what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is punished [compare Wis 11:17].

paras.t: Accidit quoque ut visum somnium referret fratribus suis ; quæ causa, id est quæ somnii illius relatio, majoris odii seminarium fuit, etc. Oderant autem eum fratres sui : Primo, quoniam accusavit eorum vitia apud patrem, in quo bene et caritative egit, quia ad patrem pertinebat filiorum suorum correctio, nec correptionem ipsius Joseph voluerunt ad partem accipere. Secundo, propter specialem pretiosamque vestem, quam tulit : ex cujus intuitu, tanquam ex sensibili signo illius tam specialis amoris patris ad eum, incitabantur ad passiones diversas, quasi pater eorum jam transtulisset aut transferre intenderet jus primogenituræ ad Joseph. Tertio, quia pater tam fervide dilexit eum præ ceteris. Quarto, propter somniorum narrationem quæ retulit ipsis, quæ ipsi adscripserunt gravi ambitioni atque superbiæ Joseph, quasi jam ex somniis suis præsumeret vaticinari, eos suæ jurisdictioni ac dominationi esse subdendos.
paras.en: [[37:5|Now it fell out also that he told his brethren a dream, that he had dreamed|Accidit quoque ut visum somnium referret fratribus suis]]; which cause, that is, which telling of that dream, [[37:5|occasioned them to hate him the more|majoris odii seminarium fuit]] [literally "was the seed-bed of greater hatred"], etc. Now his brethren hated him: first, because he accused their vices to their father, in which he acted well and charitably, since the correction of his sons belonged to the father, and they would not accept Joseph's own reproof in private. Secondly, because of the special and costly garment that he wore: at the sight of which, as at a sensible sign of his father's so special love for him, they were stirred to various passions, as though their father had already transferred, or meant to transfer, the right of the firstborn to Joseph. Thirdly, because his father loved him so fervently above the rest. Fourthly, because of the telling of the dreams which he related to them, which they put down to grave ambition and pride in Joseph, as though from his dreams he already presumed to foretell that they were to be made subject to his jurisdiction and dominion.

paras.t: Nam dixit : Putabam nos ligare manipulos in agro, id est, istud in somno apparuit mihi per somnium, seu visionem somnialem in somno per imaginarias formas ostensam : nempe ut Josephus refert, missus fuit a patre cum fratribus ad colligendum messem : et quasi consurgere manipulum meum et stare : recteque dixit, Quasi ; quia visio fuit, non res ; vestrosque manipulos circumstantes adorare manipulum meum. Responderunt fratres ejus : Numquid rex noster eris, aut subjiciemur ditioni, id est jussioni tuæ ? quasi dicant : Nequaquam ; quod tamen somnium tuum videtur evidenter prætendere : idcirco omnino phantasticum est, aut superbe confictum a te. Hæc ergo causa somniorum atque sermonum, id est introductio somnii jam narrati ac enarrandi, et eorundem relatio, vel causa hæc somnialis et sermo prælatus, invidiæ, quæ est tristitia de prosperitate et gratia seu virtute alterius, et odii, etc., quod directe opponitur caritati : estque malitiosa volitio, qua aliquis vult alteri malum, directe odiendo personam ejus secundum se : quod secundum unam considerationem est peccatum gravissimum, quia directe contrariatur summæ virtuti, quæ caritas appellatur ; et sicut odium Dei est absolute gravissimum vitium, sic odium proximi gravissimum perhibetur inter vitia quæ contra proximum sunt.
paras.en: For he said: [[37:7|I thought we were binding sheaves in the field|Putabam nos ligare manipulos in agro]]; that is, this appeared to me in sleep through a dream, or a dream-vision shown in sleep through imaginary forms: for, as Josephus relates, he had been sent by his father with his brethren to gather the harvest; [[37:7|and my sheaf arose as it were, and stood|et quasi consurgere manipulum meum et stare]]; and rightly he said *as it were*, because it was a vision, not the thing itself; [[37:7|and your sheaves standing about bowed down before my sheaf|vestrosque manipulos circumstantes adorare manipulum meum]]. [[37:8|His brethren answered|Responderunt fratres ejus]]: [[37:8|Shalt thou be our king|Numquid rex noster eris]]? [[37:8|or shall we be subject to thy dominion|aut subjiciemur ditioni]], that is, to thy command? as if to say: By no means; and yet thy dream seems plainly to point to it: therefore it is altogether fanciful, or proudly made up by thee. [[37:8|Therefore this matter of his dreams and words|Hæc ergo causa somniorum atque sermonum]], that is, the bringing in of the dream already told and of the one yet to be told, and the telling of them, or this matter of the dream and the speech set forth, [[37:8|ministered nourishment to their envy|invidiæ]], which is sadness at another's prosperity and grace or virtue, [[37:8|and hatred|et odii]], etc., which is directly opposed to charity: it is a malicious willing by which one wills evil to another, directly hating his person in itself; and in one respect it is a most grievous sin, because it is directly contrary to the highest virtue, which is called charity; and as hatred of God is absolutely the most grievous vice, so hatred of one's neighbour is held to be the most grievous among the vices that are against one's neighbour.

paras.t: Aliud quoque vidit, visione imaginaria, non intellectuali, somnium, quod narrans fratribus, ait : Vidi per somnium quasi solem et lunam et stellas undecim adorare me. Hoc somnium idem significat, quod primum, et quodam modo aliquid plus ; fuitque confirmatio somnii præcedentis. Verumtamen ipsemet Joseph non intellexit pro certo significationem somniorum et visionum istarum : idcirco non fuit adhuc propheta, sicut postea quando exposuit somnia Pharaonis, quoniam intelligentia est opus in visione : attamen conjiciebat ipse sapiens puer, quid hæc somnia prætendebant ; sed certus non fuit, an essent ex causa pure naturali, aut fortuita et illusiva, an ex operatione superna et administratione angelica.
paras.en: [[37:9|He dreamed also another|Aliud quoque vidit]], by an imaginary vision, not an intellectual one, [[37:9|dream, which he told his brethren, saying: I saw in a dream, as it were the sun, and the moon, and eleven stars worshipping me|somnium, quod narrans fratribus, ait : Vidi per somnium quasi solem et lunam et stellas undecim adorare me]]. This dream signifies the same as the first, and in a way something more; and it was a confirmation of the preceding dream. Yet Joseph himself did not understand for certain the meaning of these dreams and visions: therefore he was not yet a prophet, as he was afterwards when he expounded Pharao's dreams, since [[Dan 10:1|there is need of understanding in a vision|intelligentia est opus in visione]]. Still, the wise boy guessed what these dreams pointed to; but he was not certain whether they came of a purely natural cause, or of a chance and illusory one, or of a working from above and the ministry of angels.

paras.t: Quod quum patri suo et fratribus retulisset. Jam dictum est, quod somnium istud retulit fratribus suis : et nunc denuo fertur cum additione, quod retulit illud patri suo ac fratribus. Aut ergo primo retulit illud fratribus tantum, et postea simul tam patri quam ipsis ; aut jam suppletur quod ante omissum fuit, videlicet quod a principio retulit illud omnibus eis simul. Potius tamen puto, quod postquam retulerat somnia sua fratribus, ipsi indignantes recitaverunt ea patri, ut provocarent eum contra Joseph, quasi contra phantasticum et superbum : ideoque pater interrogavit eum de somniis suis, et tunc coram eo et fratribus repetiit ea, vel saltem ultimum istud : nec tamen ex levitate aut vanitate recitavit ea fratribus suis, sed ex inspiratione divina, quatenus suo tempore ad memoriam revocarentur, et sciretur quod ex divina providentia evenerunt ea, quæ contigerunt Joseph et fratribus suis. Increpavit eum pater, et dixit : Quid sibi vult hoc somnium quod vidisti ? id est, quid designat ? quasi dicat : Frivolum esse videtur. Ideo subdit : Num ego et mater tua et fratres tui adorabimus te super terram ? quasi dicat : Somnium tuum videtur insinuare, quod ego pater tuus designer per solem, et mater tua per lunam, fratresque tui per stellas, et quod adoratione duliæ simus te adoraturi in vita præsenti, quod apparentia caret.
paras.en: [[37:10|And when he had told this to his father, and brethren|Quod quum patri suo et fratribus retulisset]]. It has already been said that he told this dream to his brethren; and now it is said again, with an addition, that he told it to his father and his brethren. Either, then, he first told it to his brethren only, and afterwards to his father and them together; or what was left out before is now supplied, namely that from the beginning he told it to all of them together. But I rather think that after he had told his dreams to his brethren, they in their indignation repeated them to their father, to provoke him against Joseph as against a fanciful and proud boy; and so his father questioned him about his dreams, and then he repeated them before him and his brethren, or at least this last one. Yet he did not tell them to his brethren out of lightness or vanity, but by divine inspiration, so that in due time they might be called to mind, and it might be known that the things which befell Joseph and his brethren came about by divine providence. [[37:10|his father rebuked him and said: What meaneth this dream that thou hast dreamed?|Increpavit eum pater, et dixit : Quid sibi vult hoc somnium quod vidisti]] that is, what does it signify? as if to say: It seems frivolous. Therefore he adds: [[37:10|shall I and thy mother, and thy brethren worship thee upon the earth?|Num ego et mater tua et fratres tui adorabimus te super terram]] as if to say: Thy dream seems to suggest that I thy father am meant by the sun, and thy mother by the moon, and thy brethren by the stars, and that we are to worship thee with the worship of dulia [that is, the honour paid to a creature, as distinct from the worship due to God alone] in the present life, which has no likelihood.

paras.t: Invidebant ergo ei fratres sui. Pater vero rem tacitus considerabat, id est, secrete diligenter pensavit, quid somnia ista significarent. Quamvis enim sic loquebatur, quasi Joseph ea præsumptuose narraret, et quasi inania essent, ad placandum filios suos contra Joseph accensos : quia interdum licet, ex rationabili causa, uti tali industria, et veritatem celare, et per modum increpantis ad inculpabilem se habere ; nihilo minus intra se cogitavit, somnia illa aliquid secretum prætendere, præsertim quia jam miram probitatem et supernaturalem directionem vidit in Joseph ; imo secundum Josephum, Jacob exposuit ipsi Joseph hoc somnium, et Joseph proposuit illud patri, ut exponeretur ei ab ipso. Præterea intuendum, quod hæc somnia causabantur in eo ex operatione angeli sancti, qui similitudines illas in interiori sensu Joseph formavit ; nec tamen adhuc revelavit eidem significationem visionum illarum, quanquam etiam possent alicui naturaliter talia somnia apparere.
paras.en: [[37:11|His brethren therefore envied him|Invidebant ergo ei fratres sui]]: [[37:11|but his father considered the thing with himself|Pater vero rem tacitus considerabat]]; that is, he weighed carefully in secret what these dreams signified. For although he spoke as though Joseph were telling them presumptuously, and as though they were empty, so as to calm his sons who were inflamed against Joseph (for it is sometimes lawful, for a reasonable cause, to use such skill, to conceal the truth, and to treat a blameless person as one rebuking him), nevertheless he thought within himself that those dreams pointed to something secret, especially because he already saw in Joseph a wonderful uprightness and a supernatural guidance; indeed, according to Josephus, Jacob expounded this dream to Joseph himself, and Joseph had put it to his father so that he might expound it to him. It is further to be observed that these dreams were caused in him by the working of a holy angel, who formed those likenesses in Joseph's inner sense; yet he did not yet reveal to him the meaning of those visions, although such dreams could also appear to someone naturally.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, qualiter verificatum fuerit ultimum somnium Joseph. Aut enim habuit illud ante mortem matris suæ, aut postea : Si ante, ergo Benjamin nondum exstitit natus, ergo non debuit loqui de undecim stellis, sed de decem dumtaxat. Si postea ergo non debuit loqui de luna, per quam sua mater exprimitur, quia jam mortua fuit, nec eum unquam adoravit. Rursus, et si adhuc vixit, numquam tamen legitur eum adorasse, nec intravit Ægyptum, sed ante ingressum Jacob in Ægyptum, fuit defuncta. Nec Jacob unquam legitur suum filium adorasse, imo nec humilis Joseph hoc permisisset.
paras.en: On this it is asked how Joseph's last dream was fulfilled. For either he had it before his mother's death, or after: if before, then Benjamin was not yet born, and so he ought not to have spoken of eleven stars, but of ten only. If after, then he ought not to have spoken of the moon, by which his mother is meant, since she was already dead and never worshipped him. Again, even if she was still alive, yet we nowhere read that she worshipped him; nor did she enter Egypt, but she died before Jacob's going into Egypt. Nor do we read that Jacob ever worshipped his son; indeed the humble Joseph would not have allowed it.

paras.t: Circa hoc quæritur, an mater Joseph fuit ante hanc ejus visionem ac venditionem defuncta. Videtur quod sic, ex ordine recitationis historiæ, quoniam ante hæc describitur mors ipsius, et si ipsa adhuc vixisset, ipse retulisset et ei fortassis somnia sua. Infra quoque in isto habetur capitulo, quod Joseph missus fuit a patre suo de valle Hebron ad fratres suos: ergo Jacob habitavit tunc in Hebron, aut circa, post reditum suum a Mesopotamia: et hoc fuit postquam visitavit Isaac patrem suum, quæ visitatio facta est Rachele defuncta, ut ex præhabitis elucescit.
paras.en: On this it is asked whether Joseph's mother had died before this vision of his and his sale. It seems that she had, from the order in which the history is told, since her death is described before these things; and if she had still been alive, he would perhaps have told his dreams to her too. Further on in this chapter, also, we read that Joseph was sent by his father [[37:14|from the vale of Hebron|de valle Hebron]] to his brethren: so Jacob was then living in Hebron, or near it, after his return from Mesopotamia; and this was after he visited his father Isaac, which visit took place after Rachel's death, as is clear from what has gone before.

paras.t: Oppositum tamen hujus videtur, quia in textu ex verbis Jacob habetur : Numquid ego et mater tua, etc. ? Item quoniam Joseph vidit solem et lunam ac undecim stellas, atque per lunam ejus mater designabatur : ergo vixit adhuc. Insuper, secundum expositores concorditer, Joseph venditus fuit duodecim vel (ut alii dicunt) tredecim annis ante mortem Isaac avi sui : imo, secundum Augustinum, et habetur in Glossa, vivente Isaac, Joseph cœpit esse decem et septem annorum : hoc tamen loquitur Augustinus secundum translationem Septuaginta, cui in hac parte nec nostra translatio, nec Hebraica veritas consonat. Rachel autem non videtur tot annis ante Isaac mortua. Postremo, quando Joseph dominabatur in Ægypto, suisque fratribus loquebatur, videtur primo ignorasse se fratrem uterinum habere, ut infra patebit : ergo ante obitum suæ matris venditus fuit.
paras.en: Yet the opposite seems to be the case, because in the text Jacob is found saying: [[37:10|shall I and thy mother|Numquid ego et mater tua]], etc.? Again, because Joseph saw the sun and the moon and eleven stars, and by the moon his mother was meant: therefore she was still alive. Moreover, according to the expositors with one accord, Joseph was sold twelve or (as others say) thirteen years before the death of his grandfather Isaac; indeed, according to Augustine, and it is in the Gloss, Joseph turned seventeen while Isaac was living: yet Augustine says this according to the Septuagint translation, with which in this matter neither our translation nor the Hebrew truth [that is, the Hebrew original, Jerome's phrase] agrees. But Rachel does not seem to have died so many years before Isaac. Lastly, when Joseph was ruling in Egypt and speaking with his brethren, he seems at first not to have known that he had a brother by the same mother, as will appear below: therefore he was sold before his mother's death.

paras.t: Rursus in contrarium est, quia quando Jacob cum suis intravit Ægyptum, intraverunt cum eo novem filii Benjamin, ut infra continetur, vel potius filii decem.
