Si autem Benjamin natus fuisset post Joseph venditionem, non potuisset habere novem filios quando Jacob intravit Ægyptum, præsertim quia non habuit nisi conjugem unam, et inter venditionem Joseph descensumque patris sui in Ægyptum, non fluxerunt nisi viginti duo anni : et ita si Benjamin, qui matre sua moriente natus est, post Joseph venditionem natus dicatur, non erat adhuc plene viginti duorum annorum, quando pater suus intravit Ægyptum, nec in ea ætate potuit ex una uxore filios novem habere, præsertim quia tunc homines non contrahebant tam mane.
paras.en: Then again, on the other side: when Jacob went into Egypt with his household, nine sons of Benjamin went in with him, as is told below[[Gen 46:21||]], or rather ten sons. But if Benjamin had been born after Joseph's sale, he could not have had nine sons when Jacob went into Egypt, especially since he had only one wife, and between the sale of Joseph and his father's going down into Egypt no more than twenty-two years passed: and so, if Benjamin, who was born as his mother was dying, is said to have been born after Joseph's sale, he was not yet fully twenty-two years old when his father went into Egypt, and at that age he could not have had nine sons by one wife, especially since men did not marry so early in those days.

paras.t: Ad istud dicendum, quod Josephus scribit Joseph venditum esse Rachele matre sua vivente, propter motiva præhabita : et istud auctor Scholasticæ historiæ videtur amplius approbare. Alii vero propter rationes prætactas dicunt oppositum. Itaque in Scholastica historia legitur Joseph duodecim annis venditus ante obitum Isaac, quoniam Isaac sexagenarius erat quando natus est Jacob, ut patuit capitulo vicesimo quinto. Isaac autem vixit in toto centum octoginta annis, ut dictum est capitulo tricesimo quinto : ergo in morte Isaac Jacob fuit centum viginti annorum. In venditione autem filii sui Joseph, fuit centum et octo annorum. Quum enim venit ad Joseph in Ægyptum, fuit centum triginta annorum : sed inter descensum ejus in Ægyptum et venditionem Joseph, fluxerunt viginti duo anni. Joseph enim decem et septem annorum erat, quando venditus est : et triginta novem, quando pater ejus venit ad eum in Ægyptum. Dum ergo rediret Jacob de Mesopotamia, et nondum venisset ad Isaac patrem suum, adhuc vivente Rachel, secundum Josephum, venditus est Joseph, et congrue Jacob dicere potuit : Numquid ego et mater tua adorabimus te ? quia mater ejus adhuc vivebat. Tamen nec mater ejus adoravit eum, quia non descendit in Ægyptum ; nec pater eum legitur adorasse, quia nec Joseph sustinuisset ; sed fratres adoraverunt et parentes in filiis. Hæc ibi.
paras.en: To this it must be said that Josephus writes that Joseph was sold while Rachel his mother was living, for the reasons given above; and the author of the Scholastic History seems rather to approve this. But others, for the reasons touched on before, say the opposite. Thus in the Scholastic History we read that Joseph was sold twelve years before Isaac's death, since Isaac was sixty years old when Jacob was born[[Gen 25:26||]], as appeared in the twenty-fifth chapter. And Isaac lived a hundred and eighty years in all[[Gen 35:28||]], as was said in the thirty-fifth chapter: so at Isaac's death Jacob was a hundred and twenty years old. And at the sale of his son Joseph he was a hundred and eight. For when he came to Joseph in Egypt he was a hundred and thirty years old; but between his going down into Egypt and the sale of Joseph twenty-two years passed. For Joseph was seventeen years old when he was sold, and thirty-nine when his father came to him in Egypt. So while Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia and had not yet come to his father Isaac, with Rachel still living, according to Josephus, Joseph was sold; and Jacob could fittingly say: [[37:10|shall I and thy mother|Numquid ego et mater tua]] [[37:10|worship thee|adorabimus te]]? because his mother was still alive. Yet neither did his mother worship him, since she did not go down into Egypt; nor do we read that his father worshipped him, for Joseph would not have allowed it; but his brethren worshipped him, and his parents in their sons. Thus far the History.

paras.t: Verumtamen non obstantibus his, magis apparet quod Rachel defuncta sit ante Joseph venditionem, præsertim propter ultimam rationem ad hoc inductam de Benjamin : cui adjici potest, quod Joseph qui tam diligenter interrogavit a fratribus suis in Ægypto, an viveret pater eorum, nihil interrogavit de vita aut morte uxorum ipsius, quasi certus de obitu propriæ matris. Porro ad objecta respondetur, quod ideo Joseph vidit solem et lunam, quia parentes ejus adoraverunt eum non in propriis personis, sed in filiis suis, ut Rachel per Benjamin. Apostolus tamen testatur, quod Jacob adoravit fastigium virgæ ejus, videlicet Joseph. Nec absurdum videtur, si dicatur Jacob interdum aliquam duliæ adorationem exhibuisse suo filio in Ægypto, tanquam supremo illius principi terræ post Pharaonem, nec ad hujusmodi adorationem requiritur in terram prostratio aut genuflexio. Porro quod Jacob dixit, Numquid ego et mater tua adorabimus te ? non dixit ad innuendum quod hoc fieri posset, aut mater adhuc viveret, sed ad insinuandum quod hoc fieri non valeret, quasi per hoc insinuans, visionem Joseph reputandam non esse, ad placandum filios suos per modum prætactum. Ad aliud quoque dicendum, quod Joseph in Ægypto fratribus suis primo loquens, scivit se fratrem uterinum ante suam venditionem habuisse : sed an adhuc viveret, ignorabat, præsertim quia non vidit eum cum suis fratribus advenisse : idcirco quæsivit an adhuc alium fratrem haberent.
paras.en: Yet notwithstanding these arguments, it appears more likely that Rachel died before Joseph's sale, especially because of the last argument brought for this, about Benjamin; to which it may be added that Joseph, who asked his brethren in Egypt so carefully whether their father was living, asked nothing about the life or death of his wives, as being certain of his own mother's death. Now to the objections the answer is that Joseph saw the sun and the moon because his parents worshipped him, not in their own persons, but in their sons, as Rachel did through Benjamin. The Apostle, however, testifies that Jacob [[Heb 11:21|adored the top of his rod|adoravit fastigium virgæ ejus]], that is, of Joseph's [Denis takes "his" to mean Joseph's]. Nor does it seem absurd to say that Jacob at times showed his son in Egypt some worship of dulia, as to the highest prince of that land after Pharao; nor does such worship require prostration on the ground or bending the knee. Moreover, when Jacob said, [[37:10|shall I and thy mother|Numquid ego et mater tua]] [[37:10|worship thee|adorabimus te]]? he did not say it to imply that this could be done, or that the mother was still alive, but to suggest that it could not be done, as though suggesting by this that Joseph's vision was not to be taken seriously, so as to calm his sons in the way touched on above. To the other objection too it must be said that Joseph, when first speaking with his brethren in Egypt, knew that he had had a brother by the same mother before his sale; but whether he was still alive he did not know, especially since he did not see him come with his brethren: therefore he asked whether they had another brother still.

paras.t: Quumque fratres illius in pascendis gregibus patris sui Jacob morarentur in Sichem, id est in loco sic dicto prope urbem sic appellatam: et forte interdum erant in urbe illa, interdum in campo et pascuis; dixit ad eum Israel, etc., id est Jacob pater suus, qui alio nomine Israel nuncupatur. Vade, et vide si cuncta prospera sint erga fratres tuos, etc. Missus de valle Hebron, etc., in qua Jacob tunc habitavit, sicut et Isaac ante eum: ex quo videtur, stare non posse quod Josephus scribit, Joseph venditum esse, antequam pater ejus venisset ad Isaac qui habitavit in Hebron. Perrexit ergo Joseph post fratres suos, et invenit eos in Dothain, puta in loco et planitie seu pascuis terræ sic dictæ. Iverunt enim fratres ejus de loco ad locum, secundum quod congruebat eis, ad inveniendum terras aptiores pro suorum pecorum pastu, quæ plurima erant valde, atque unius agri gramina cito carpebant.
paras.en: [[37:12|And when his brethren abode in Sechem, feeding their father's flocks,|Quumque fratres illius in pascendis gregibus patris sui Jacob morarentur in Sichem]], that is, in a place so called near the city of that name: and perhaps they were sometimes in that city, sometimes in the field and the pastures; [[37:13|Israel said to him|dixit ad eum Israel]], etc., that is, Jacob his father, who is called by another name Israel. [[37:14|Go, and see if all things be well with thy brethren|Vade, et vide si cuncta prospera sint erga fratres tuos]], etc. [[37:14|So being sent from the vale of Hebron|Missus de valle Hebron]], etc., in which Jacob then dwelt, as Isaac did before him: from which it seems that what Josephus writes cannot stand, that Joseph was sold before his father had come to Isaac, who dwelt in Hebron. [[37:17|And Joseph went forward after his brethren, and found them in Dothain|Perrexit ergo Joseph post fratres suos, et invenit eos in Dothain]], that is, in the place and plain, or pastures, of the land so called. For his brethren went from place to place, as suited them, to find lands fitter for the feeding of their flocks, which were very many, and soon cropped the grass of a single field.

paras.t: Qui quum vidissent eum procul, antequam accederet ad eos, cogitaverunt illum occidere, ex vehementi invidia, et ad ostendendum vanitatem et falsitatem somniorum ipsius, et ne unquam aliqua occasione eis præficeretur. Verumtamen non omnes, sed major aut magna eorum pars illud concepit et implere proposuit. Et mutuo loquebantur: Ecce somniator venit. Venite, occidamus eum, et mittamus in cisternam veterem, etc., id est, cadaver ejus exstinctum projiciamus in hunc lacum seu puteum exsiccatum, ne unquam inveniatur ab aliquo.
paras.en: [[37:18|And when they saw him afar off, before he came nigh them, they thought to kill him:|Qui quum vidissent eum procul, antequam accederet ad eos, cogitaverunt illum occidere]], out of vehement envy, and to show the vanity and falsehood of his dreams, and lest on any occasion he should ever be set over them. Yet not all of them, but the greater part, or a great part, of them conceived this and purposed to carry it out. [[37:19|And said one to another: Behold the dreamer cometh.|Et mutuo loquebantur: Ecce somniator venit]] [[37:20|Come, let us kill him, and cast him into some old pit|Venite, occidamus eum, et mittamus in cisternam veterem]], etc., that is, let us throw his lifeless body into this cistern, or dried-up well, so that it may never be found by anyone.

paras.t: Audiens autem hoc Ruben, etc., dicebat: Non interficiamus animam ejus, etc., id est ipsum, partem pro toto accipiendo, ut moris est Scripturarum, vel animam, id est animalem et sensitivam vitam ipsius. Unde ex hoc loco probari non potest, animam hominis esse mortalem, ut Sadducæi dixerunt: imo in Prophetis interdum invenitur hic modus loquendi, juxta illud in Jeremia, Ne veniat Ismael et interficiat animam tuam; quum tamen certissimum sit, Prophetas sanctos posuisse quod immortalis sit anima rationalis. Ideo Sadducæi mendaciter imposuerunt Moysi sancto, quod docuerit animam hominis esse mortalem. Sed projicite eum in cisternam veterem, etc. Ruben voluit ut projiceretur vivus in eam, quatenus paulo post fratribus absentibus eum extraheret; idcirco subjungitur: Hoc autem dicebat, volens eripere eum de manibus eorum, et reddere patri suo: imo magis optabat eum eripere absque projectione in cisternam; sed quum non posset hoc, consuluit ut in cisternam projiceretur. Commemoravit quoque Ruben fratribus suis, quam grave facinus esset interficere proprium fratrem, et quantum pater eorum affligeretur de morte Joseph.
paras.en: [[37:21|And Ruben hearing this|Audiens autem hoc Ruben]], etc., [[37:21|and said|dicebat]]: [[37:22|Do not take away his life|Non interficiamus animam ejus]] [the Latin says "let us not kill his soul"], etc., that is, him, taking the part for the whole, as is the custom of the Scriptures; or *soul*, that is, his animal and sensitive life. Hence it cannot be proved from this place that the soul of man is mortal, as the Sadducees said[[Acts 23:8||]]: indeed this manner of speaking is sometimes found in the Prophets, according to that saying in Jeremias, [[Jer 40:15|lest he kill thee|Ne veniat Ismael et interficiat animam tuam]] [the margin gives Jer. xli, 15; the words are from Jer 40:15, where the Latin has "lest he kill thy soul"; Denis words it "Let not Ismael come and kill thy soul"]; though it is most certain that the holy Prophets held that the rational soul is immortal. So the Sadducees lyingly imputed to holy Moses that he taught the soul of man to be mortal. [[37:22|but cast him into this pit|Sed projicite eum in cisternam veterem]] [Denis reads "into the old cistern"], etc. Ruben wished him to be thrown into it alive, so that a little later, while his brethren were away, he might draw him out; therefore it is added: [[37:22|now he said this, being desirous to deliver him out of their hands and to restore him to his father|Hoc autem dicebat, volens eripere eum de manibus eorum, et reddere patri suo]]: indeed he rather wished to rescue him without his being thrown into the cistern; but since he could not do this, he advised that he be thrown into the cistern. Ruben also reminded his brethren how grave a crime it would be to kill their own brother, and how much their father would be afflicted by the death of Joseph.

paras.t: Confestim ergo ut pervenit ad fratres, nudaverunt eum tunica talari et polymita, etc., de qua dictum est. Circa quod dicit Lyra: In Hebræo habetur, Expoliaverunt eum tunica sua et tunica serica: ex quo videtur, quod Joseph indutus fuit tunica duplici, una simplici et alia serica. His contradicit Rabbi Paulus: In Hebræo, inquiens, habetur, Spoliaverunt eum tunica sua tunica serica; ac si dicat, Tunica sua quæ serica fuit: unde ex hoc non habetur, quod habuit duplicem tunicam. Et sedentes, etc., viderunt Ismaelitas viatores venire de Galaad, id est de terra sic appellata, et camelos eorum portantes aromata et resinam, quæ est species odoriferi gummi, et stacten, id est myrrham, in Ægyptum, ad vendendum ibidem. Dixit ergo Judas fratribus suis: Quid proderit nobis si occiderimus fratrem nostrum, etc.: quasi dicat, Enorme crimen esset. Melius, id est minus malum, est ut venundetur Ismaelitis, etc. Acquieverunt fratres sermonibus illius: qui aliquid rationabilitatis continebant in se, idcirco dicuntur sermones: imo comparative loquendo, multo sapientius loquebatur, quam illi qui voluerunt Joseph occidere. Fuit autem Judas inter fratres suos fortior corpore atque prudentior verbis, dempto quod Joseph eo sapientior fuit. Verum ut Salomon loquitur: Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum, qui apprehendit sapientes in astutia eorum, et consilium pravorum dissipat. Judas quippe et fratres ejus vendiderunt Joseph, ut duceretur in Ægyptum, quatenus elongatus ab eis, nequaquam posset eis præferri: sed quod putaverunt esse obstaculum præsidentiæ ipsius Joseph super eos, factum est occasio et adminiculum præsidentiæ hujus.
paras.en: [[37:23|And as soon as he came to his brethren, they forthwith stript him of his outside coat, that was of divers colours:|Confestim ergo ut pervenit ad fratres, nudaverunt eum tunica talari et polymita]], etc., of which we have spoken. On this Lyra says: In the Hebrew we have, They stripped him of his coat and of his silken coat: from which it seems that Joseph was clothed in a double coat, one plain and the other silken. Rabbi Paul contradicts this: In the Hebrew, he says, we have, They stripped him of his coat, the silken coat; as if to say, Of his coat, which was silken: so that it does not follow from this that he had a double coat. [[37:25|And sitting down|Et sedentes]], etc., [[37:25|they saw some Ismaelites on their way coming from Galaad|viderunt Ismaelitas viatores venire de Galaad]], that is, from the land so called, [[37:25|with their camels, carrying spices, and balm|et camelos eorum portantes aromata et resinam]] [Latin *resina*, resin], which is a kind of fragrant gum, [[37:25|and myrrh|et stacten]] [Latin *stacte*], that is, myrrh, [[37:25|to Egypt|in Ægyptum]], to sell them there. [[37:26|And Juda said to his brethren: What will it profit us to kill our brother|Dixit ergo Judas fratribus suis: Quid proderit nobis si occiderimus fratrem nostrum]], etc.: as if to say, It would be an enormous crime. [[37:27|It is better|Melius]], that is, a lesser evil, [[37:27|that he be sold to the Ismaelites|est ut venundetur Ismaelitis]], etc. [[37:27|His brethren agreed to his words|Acquieverunt fratres sermonibus illius]]: which held something of reason in them, and so they are called *words* [Latin *sermones*, reasoned speech, not mere talk]: indeed, comparatively speaking, he spoke far more wisely than those who wished to kill Joseph. Now Judas was, among his brethren, the stronger in body and the more prudent in speech, except that Joseph was wiser than he. But as Solomon says: [[Prov 21:30|There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.|Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum]], [[Job 5:13|Who catcheth the wise in their craftiness, and disappointeth the counsel of the wicked:|qui apprehendit sapientes in astutia eorum, et consilium pravorum dissipat]] [these last words are from Job]. For Judas and his brethren sold Joseph, that he might be led into Egypt, so that, removed far from them, he could never be set over them: but what they thought would be an obstacle to Joseph's rule over them became the occasion and the means of that very rule.

paras.t: Et prætereuntibus Madianitis negotiatoribus, vendiderunt eum Ismaelitis viginti argenteis. Aliqui libri habent, Triginta argenteis, et verba beati Hieronymi in Glossa sic continent, si tamen correcta est Glossa. Ismaelitæ autem et Madianitæ hic pro eisdem accipiuntur. Vel quia Ismaelitæ in terra Madian habitaverunt, vel quia per conjugium aut alio modo facti sunt populus unus, aut quia Agar de qua natus est Ismael et Cetura, de qua Madian genitus est, fuit eadem Abrahæ uxor, ut tactum est supra. Hinc Augustinus: Cur scriptura hæc Ismaelitas vocat Madianitas, quum Ismael sit filius Abrahæ ex Agar, Madian vero ex Cetura? An quoniam teste Scriptura, Abraham dedit filiis Agar et Ceturæ munera, divisitque eos ab Isaac, ideo una gens facti sunt? An vera est Hebræorum opinio, quod Agar et Cetura una fuerunt? Hinc quoque errant Judæi, qui dicunt quod Joseph ter venditus sit, primo Ismaelitis a fratribus suis, secundo Madianitis ab Ismaelitis, tertio magistro militiæ Pharaonis a Madianitis, præsertim quum infra tricesimo nono capitulo scriptum sit, quod Ægyptius ille emit Joseph ab Ismaelitis. Qui duxerunt eum in Ægyptum. Infra habetur, quod Ruben in Ægypto locutus est fratribus suis: Merito hæc patimur quia peccavimus in fratrem nostrum, videntes angustiam animæ ejus dum deprecaretur nos. Ex quibus verbis aliqualiter elici valet, quanta angustia, formido, desolatio, mœror, penetravit animam pii, innocentis, adolescentisque Joseph, quando a fratribus suis sic nudabatur, et in foveam mittebatur, seque ab eis mox occidendum putavit, et quando deinde illis duris atque ignotis vendebatur hominibus, et in terram ducebatur remotam, separatus a suo carissimo patre, quem putavit se amplius non visurum. O quam lacrimose et affectuosissime fratres suos rogabat, ut sui miserentur! Vere multæ tribulationes electorum Altissimi.
paras.en: [[37:28|And when the Madianite merchants passed by|Et prætereuntibus Madianitis negotiatoribus]], [[37:28|sold him to the Ismaelites, for twenty pieces of silver|vendiderunt eum Ismaelitis viginti argenteis]]. Some books have, Thirty pieces of silver, and the words of blessed Jerome in the Gloss run so, if indeed the Gloss is correct. Now the Ismaelites and the Madianites are taken here for the same people: either because the Ismaelites dwelt in the land of Madian, or because by marriage or in some other way they became one people, or because Agar, of whom Ismael was born, and Cetura, of whom Madian was begotten, were the same wife of Abraham, as was touched on above. Hence Augustine: Why does this scripture call the Ismaelites Madianites, since Ismael is the son of Abraham by Agar, but Madian by Cetura? Is it because, as Scripture witnesses, Abraham gave gifts to the sons of Agar and of Cetura and separated them from Isaac, and so they became one nation? Or is the opinion of the Hebrews true, that Agar and Cetura were one? Hence too the Jews are in error who say that Joseph was sold three times: first to the Ismaelites by his brethren, secondly to the Madianites by the Ismaelites, thirdly to the master of Pharao's soldiery by the Madianites; especially since it is written below, in the thirty-ninth chapter, that that Egyptian bought Joseph of the Ismaelites[[Gen 39:1||]]. [[37:28|and they led him into Egypt|Qui duxerunt eum in Ægyptum]]. It is found below that Ruben said to his brethren in Egypt: [[Gen 42:21|We deserve to suffer these things, because we have sinned against our brother, seeing the anguish of his soul, when he besought us|Merito hæc patimur quia peccavimus in fratrem nostrum, videntes angustiam animæ ejus dum deprecaretur nos]] [in Gen 42:21 the brethren say this to one another; Ruben's own words follow in 42:22]. From these words it may in some measure be gathered what anguish, dread, desolation and grief pierced the soul of the devout, innocent young Joseph, when he was thus stripped by his brethren and put into the pit, and thought he would soon be killed by them; and when he was afterwards sold to those hard and unknown men and led into a distant land, separated from his dearest father, whom he thought he would never see again. O how tearfully and how most tenderly he begged his brethren to have mercy on him! Truly [[Ps 33:20|many are the afflictions|multæ tribulationes]] of the elect of the Most High [the Psalm has "of the just"].

paras.t: Reversusque Ruben ad cisternam, non invenit puerum. Ait Josephus, quod in nocte ivit ad lacum. Quumque ei clamanti Joseph non responderet, quem intendebat occulte extrahere ac reddere patri, de mane venit ad fratres. Et scissis vestibus, juxta consuetudinem Hebræorum, qui in præcipuis adversitatibus suas consueverunt scindere vestes, in signum interni et excessivi doloris, pergens ad fratres suos, ait: Puer non comparet, et ego quo ibo? quasi dicat: Non invenio Joseph, ideo nescio quo præ dolore transibo. Putabat namque Joseph a fratribus esse occisum: sed cognito quod adhuc viveret, aliqualiter requievit. Unde constat, quod Ruben venditioni Joseph præsens non fuit. Ivit enim, ut dicit Scholastica historia, ad quærendum pascua meliora, atque (ut alii dicunt) ideo revertebatur, ut fratres suos induceret ad accedendum pascua jam inventa, quatenus eis absentibus extraheret ipsum Joseph, ac redderet eum patri.
paras.en: [[37:29|And Ruben returning to the pit, found not the boy:|Reversusque Ruben ad cisternam, non invenit puerum]] Josephus says that he went to the pit by night; and when Joseph did not answer his call (he meant to draw him out secretly and restore him to his father), he came to his brethren in the morning. [[37:30|And rending his garments|Et scissis vestibus]], according to the custom of the Hebrews, who were wont to rend their garments in great adversities, in sign of inward and exceeding grief, [[37:30|he went to his brethren, and said: The boy doth not appear, and whither shall I go?|pergens ad fratres suos, ait: Puer non comparet, et ego quo ibo?]] as if to say: I do not find Joseph, and so I know not where I shall go for grief. For he thought that Joseph had been killed by his brethren; but on learning that he was still alive, he was in some measure at rest. Hence it is clear that Ruben was not present at the sale of Joseph. For he had gone, as the Scholastic History says, to look for better pastures, and (as others say) he was coming back to induce his brethren to go to the pastures he had now found, so that in their absence he might draw Joseph out and restore him to his father.

paras.t: Tulerunt autem tunicam ejus, et laceraverunt, secundum Josephum, ut putaretur dilaniata a bestia, et in sanguine hædi quem occiderant, tinxerunt, etc. Quam quum cognovisset pater, ait: Tunica filii mei est. Fera pessima comedit eum, etc. Hoc putavit, nec formaliter mentiebatur. Scissisque vestibus, indutus est cilicio, lugens filium suum multo tempore. Sed cur auxit sibi afflictionem induendo cilicium? An ut filio carissimo ostenderet se nimium condolere? vel pro relevamine animæ ejus, aut ut impetraret misericordiam Dei, si forte aliqua spes esset superstes de recuperatione filii prædilecti? Congregatis autem cunctis liberis ejus, etc., noluit consolationem accipere: quum tamen de irremediabilibus malis non sit ita tristandum, sed contra ea valeat oblivio: sed ait: Descendam ad filium meum lugens in infernum, id est ad sinum ac limbum patrum, qui fuit in superiori parte inferni. Ac si dicat: Filium meum usque ad mortem deflebo, flendoque moriar, ut sic filio meo in tali loco inferni secundum animam jungar. Tamen (secundum Augustinum) verba hæc Jacob forsan fuerunt verba perturbati dolentisque animi, et proprias culpas exaggerantis.
paras.en: [[37:31|And they took his coat|Tulerunt autem tunicam ejus]], and tore it, according to Josephus, so that it might be thought to have been torn by a beast, [[37:31|and dipped it in the blood of a kid, which they had killed|et in sanguine hædi quem occiderant, tinxerunt]], etc. [[37:33|And the father acknowledging it, said|Quam quum cognovisset pater, ait]]: [[37:33|It is my son's coat|Tunica filii mei est]]. [[37:33|an evil wild beast hath eaten him|Fera pessima comedit eum]], etc. This he believed, and so he was not formally lying [that is, he said what he thought true, so his words were no lie, though they were false]. [[37:34|And tearing his garments, he put on sackcloth, mourning for his son a long time.|Scissisque vestibus, indutus est cilicio, lugens filium suum multo tempore]] But why did he increase his affliction by putting on sackcloth? Was it to show his dearest son that he grieved with him beyond measure? or for the relief of his soul, or to obtain the mercy of God, if perhaps some hope remained of recovering his best-loved son? [[37:35|And all his children being gathered together|Congregatis autem cunctis liberis ejus]], etc., [[37:35|he would not receive comfort|noluit consolationem accipere]]: though one ought not so to grieve over evils that cannot be remedied, but forgetfulness should prevail against them: [[37:35|but said: I will go down to my son into hell, mourning|sed ait: Descendam ad filium meum lugens in infernum]], that is, to the bosom and limbo of the fathers, which was in the upper part of hell. As if to say: I will weep for my son until death, and die weeping, so that thus I may be joined to my son, as to the soul, in such a place of hell. Yet (according to Augustine) these words of Jacob were perhaps the words of a troubled and grieving mind, and one that exaggerated its own faults.

paras.t: Et illo perseverante in fletu. In Hebræo (ut refert Lyra) habetur sic, Et flevit eum pater suus, quod Hebræi exponunt de Isaac, tunc adhuc vivente, quem dicunt simul cum Jacob ipsum Joseph flevisse. Madianitæ, id est Ismaelitæ, vendiderunt Joseph in Ægypto Putiphari eunucho Pharaonis, magistro militum; sed pro quanto pretio, Scriptura non exprimit. Secundum Hieronymum, quidam dixerunt, Archimagiro, id est principi coquorum. Nam apud nonnullos, dapifer regis honorabilior est minister, princepsque militum. Unde et Josephus ait hic, Principi coquorum. Circa hæc quærit Hieronymus, quomodo Putiphar iste vocetur eunuchus regis, quum infra legatur habere uxorem. Ad quod respondet: Tradunt Hebræi, quod Putiphar emit ipsum Joseph, ob pulchritudinem ejus, in turpe obsequium, hoc est, ut misceretur ei contra naturam: propter quod Deus custodiens Joseph, infrigidavit Ægyptium. Ideo ἱεροφάνται, id est sacerdotes idolorum, elegerunt eum ad pontificatum Heliopoleos, hoc est civitatis solis, ut infra habebitur: fuitque tunc honorabilior auctoritate, quam ante in principatu. Itaque vocatur eunuchus, non sicut qui parvuli castrabantur, sed quoniam instar illorum impotens fuit: vel ut alii dicunt, eunuchi regum ac principum sæpe vocantur, servi eorum honesti et casti: quia et infra princeps pincernarum et princeps pistorum Pharaonis, appellantur ejus eunuchi.
paras.en: [[37:35|And whilst he continued weeping|Et illo perseverante in fletu]]. In the Hebrew (as Lyra reports) it runs thus: And his father wept for him; which the Hebrews explain of Isaac, who was then still living, and who they say wept for Joseph together with Jacob. [[37:36|The Madianites|Madianitæ]], that is, the Ismaelites, [[37:36|sold Joseph in Egypt to Putiphar, an eunuch of Pharao, captain of the soldiers|vendiderunt Joseph in Ægypto Putiphari eunucho Pharaonis, magistro militum]]; but for what price, Scripture does not say. According to Jerome, some have said, To the *archimagirus*, that is, the chief of the cooks. For among some peoples the king's steward is a more honourable minister, and chief of the soldiers. Hence Josephus too says here, To the chief of the cooks. On this Jerome asks how this Putiphar can be called the king's eunuch, since we read below that he had a wife. To which he answers: The Hebrews hand down that Putiphar bought Joseph for his beauty, for a shameful service, that is, to have unnatural intercourse with him; for which reason God, guarding Joseph, made the Egyptian impotent. Therefore the ἱεροφάνται, that is, the priests of the idols, chose him for the priesthood of Heliopolis, that is, the city of the sun, as will be seen below; and he was then more honoured in authority than he had been before in his command. So he is called a eunuch, not as those who were castrated as children, but because he was impotent like them: or, as others say, the honourable and chaste servants of kings and princes are often called their eunuchs: for below too the chief butler and the chief baker of Pharao are called his eunuchs.

37.title: De ejusdem capituli tricesimi septimi mystico sensu
37.title_en: On the mystical sense of the same thirty-seventh chapter

paras.t: De allegoria et tropologia præsentis capituli, a catholicis viris scripta sunt multa. Est enim specialis virtus in verbis hujus materiæ, beatissimum Joseph patriarcham concernentis; et quotiescumque legatur, quantumcumque quoque sciatur, semper tamen cum speciali aviditate auditur, et legentium ac audientium movet et accendit affectum. Est equidem ista materia valde mysterialis et spiritualibus plena sententiis, quæ nunc succinctim dumtaxat, breviterque tangenda sunt, ut vitetur prolixitas, et quæ alibi plenius dicta sunt, non repetantur superflue. Itaque Joseph pene in omnibus figura est Christi.
paras.en: Of the allegory and tropology [that is, the sense concerning Christ and the Church, and the moral sense] of this chapter, much has been written by Catholic men. For there is a special power in the words of this matter, which concerns the most blessed patriarch Joseph: however often it is read, and however well it is known, it is always heard with a special eagerness, and it moves and kindles the affection of those who read and hear it. This matter is indeed full of mystery and full of spiritual meanings, which are now to be touched on only succinctly and briefly, that prolixity may be avoided and that what has been said more fully elsewhere may not be needlessly repeated. Joseph, then, is in almost all things a figure of Christ.

paras.t: Joseph quum sedecim esset annorum, pascebat gregem cum fratribus suis. Sic et Christus Filius Dei, in juventute sua prædicando, miracula faciendo, sanctissime conversando, pascebat populum Synagogæ, non solum cum suis Apostolis, quos per diversa Judææ loca ad prædicandum direxit, sed item cum sacerdotibus, Scribis ac Pharisæis, ex semine Patriarcharum, sicut et Christus, natis. Denique, sicut Joseph ex pietate et humilitate fuit cum filiis Balæ ac Zelphæ: sic Christus Sadducæos, publicanos, ac peccatores admisit piissime; imo incomprehensibili humilitate cum illis conversari ac vesci dignatus est, ut eos sic traheret ad salutem.
paras.en: [[37:2|Joseph, when he was sixteen years old, was feeding the flock with his brethren|Joseph quum sedecim esset annorum, pascebat gregem cum fratribus suis]]. So too Christ, the Son of God, in his youth, by preaching, working miracles and living most holily, fed the people of the Synagogue, not only with his Apostles, whom he sent to preach in various places of Judea, but also with the priests, Scribes and Pharisees, who were born, like Christ, of the seed of the Patriarchs. Further, as Joseph out of kindness and humility was with the sons of Bala and Zelpha, so Christ most lovingly admitted Sadducees, publicans and sinners; indeed, with incomprehensible humility he deigned to keep company and to eat with them, that he might so draw them to salvation.

paras.t: Joseph accusavit fratres suos crimine pessimo apud Jacob: sic et Christus coram Patre æterno accusavit induratos Judæos de infidelitate, quæ pessimum crimen est, dicens: Si non venissem, et locutus eis non fuissem, peccatum non haberent; nunc autem excusationem non habent de peccato suo. Multipliciter quoque et acriter reprehendit Judæos, potissimum sacerdotes, Scribas et Pharisæos, de pessimo hypocrisis vitio, de ambitione, cupiditate ac consimilibus.
paras.en: Joseph [[37:2|accused his brethren|accusavit fratres suos]] to Jacob [[37:2|of a most wicked crime|crimine pessimo]]: so too Christ, before the eternal Father, accused the hardened Jews of unbelief, which is a most wicked crime, saying: [[John 15:22|If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin: but now they have no excuse for their sin|Si non venissem, et locutus eis non fuissem, peccatum non haberent; nunc autem excusationem non habent de peccato suo]]. He also rebuked the Jews in many ways and sharply, above all the priests, Scribes and Pharisees, for the most wicked vice of hypocrisy, for ambition, covetousness and the like.

paras.t: Jacob diligebat Joseph super omnes filios suos, eo quod in senectute sua genuisset eum. Sic et Deus Pater Jesum Christum præ omnibus participibus ejus incomparabiliter diligit, quia in sua æternitate genuit eum, in quantum est Deus, juxta illud, Ex utero ante luciferum genui te; atque in ultima mundi ætate, procreavit eum secundum assumptam humanitatem ex Virgine gloriosa. Unde in baptismo et transfiguratione Christi locutus est ei: Tu es Filius meus dilectus, in quo mihi bene complacui. Jacob fecit filio suo Joseph tunicam polymitam ac talarem: et Deus Pater ornavit Christi humanitatem amictu splendidissimo universarum virtutum, omnique ornatu ac varietate donorum et fructuum Spiritus Sancti, a summa vi animæ ejus usque ad infimam, prout capere poterat. Potest quoque per tunicam istam universitas electorum signari, qua Christus tanquam salvator ac caput eorum venustissime decoratur, juxta illud in Isaia, His omnibus quasi vestimento ornaberis.
paras.en: Jacob [[37:3|loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age|diligebat Joseph super omnes filios suos, eo quod in senectute sua genuisset eum]]. So too God the Father loves Jesus Christ beyond compare above all his fellows[[Heb 1:9||]], because he begot him in his eternity, inasmuch as he is God, according to that saying, [[Ps 109:3|from the womb before the day star I begot thee|Ex utero ante luciferum genui te]]; and in the last age of the world he brought him forth, according to the humanity he assumed, of the glorious Virgin. Hence at Christ’s baptism and transfiguration he said to him: [[Luke 3:22|Thou art my beloved Son|Tu es Filius meus dilectus]], [[Matt 17:5|in whom I am well pleased|in quo mihi bene complacui]] [Denis joins the words of the baptism, Luke 3:22, and of the transfiguration, Matt 17:5]. Jacob made his son Joseph a coat of divers colours, reaching to the ankles; and God the Father adorned the humanity of Christ with the most splendid mantle of all the virtues, and with every adornment and variety of the gifts and fruits of the Holy Ghost, from the highest power of his soul to the lowest, as far as it could receive them. By this coat may also be signified the whole number of the elect, with which Christ, as their saviour and head, is most beautifully adorned, according to that saying in Isaias: [[Is 49:18|thou shalt be clothed with all these as with an ornament|His omnibus quasi vestimento ornaberis]].

paras.t: Insuper, sicut fratres Joseph inviderunt eidem, eo quod a patre plus omnibus amaretur, et quia sic accusavit eos; sic impiissimi sacerdotes, Scribæ ac Pharisæi, videntes quod Jesus eos in omni sapientia, eloquentia, vita, fama, miraculisque excederet, tanquam carissimus Deo, implacabilem contra ipsum conceperunt invidiam, ita quod gravis eis exstitit ad videndum. Nec poterant ei quidquam pacifice loqui, nisi forsan ex simulatione, ut eum caperent in sermone.
paras.en: Moreover, as Joseph’s brethren envied him because he was loved by his father more than all, and because he had so accused them, so the most wicked priests, Scribes and Pharisees[[John 11:47||]], seeing that Jesus surpassed them in all wisdom, eloquence, life, repute and miracles, as one most dear to God, conceived an implacable envy against him, so that he was grievous to them even to behold[[Wis 2:15||]]. [[37:4|and could not speak peaceably to him|Nec poterant ei quidquam pacifice loqui]], unless perhaps in pretence, to ensnare him in his speech[[Matt 22:15||]].

paras.t: Rursus, sicut Joseph vidit somnia præsaga futurorum, quibus suam super fratres suos præsidentiam præsignavit, eisque retulit: sic Christus omnium excellentissimus Prophetarum, præcognovit in Spiritu qualiter præferendus esset universæ Ecclesiæ, atque a cunctis Judæis electis colendus ac adorandus, quod et eisdem sæpe prænuntiavit, Prædicabitur, inquiens, hoc Evangelium in universo mundo. Et, Quum exaltaveritis Filium hominis, tunc cognoscetis quia ego sum. Et, Nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me.
paras.en: Again, as Joseph saw dreams foretelling things to come, by which he foreshowed his rule over his brethren, and told them to them, so Christ, the most excellent of all the Prophets, foreknew in the Spirit how he was to be set over the whole Church, and to be worshipped and adored by all the elect Jews; and this he often foretold to them, saying: [[Matt 24:14|this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in the whole world|Prædicabitur, inquiens, hoc Evangelium in universo mundo]]. And: [[John 8:28|When you shall have lifted up, the Son of man, then shall you know that I am he|Quum exaltaveritis Filium hominis, tunc cognoscetis quia ego sum]]. And: [[John 14:6|No man cometh to the Father, but by me|Nemo venit ad Patrem nisi per me]].

paras.t: Amplius, sicut fratres dixerunt ad Joseph, Numquid rex noster eris? sic perversi Judæi dixerunt de Christo, Nolumus hunc regnare super nos. Et, Non habemus regem nisi Cæsarem. Quumque Salvator dixisset se esse Christum Dei electum; et, Videbitis Filium hominis sedentem a dextris virtutis Dei, ac venientem in nubibus cœli; pontifex insania agitatus, scidit vestimenta sua, et ait ad suos: Quid vobis videtur? Responderuntque omnes, Reus est mortis. Sed Christo a mortuis suscitato, adoravit eum sol, hoc est universalis Ecclesia, et luna, id est quæcumque Ecclesia particularis, congregatioque devota, et stellæ, utpote ecclesiasticæ personæ.
paras.en: Further, as his brethren said to Joseph, [[37:8|Shalt thou be our king?|Numquid rex noster eris?]], so the perverse Jews said of Christ: [[Luke 19:14|We will not have this man to reign over us|Nolumus hunc regnare super nos]]. And: [[John 19:15|We have no king but Caesar|Non habemus regem nisi Cæsarem]]. And when the Saviour had said that he was the Christ, the elect of God, and: [[Matt 26:64|you shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven|Videbitis Filium hominis sedentem a dextris virtutis Dei, ac venientem in nubibus cœli]], the high priest, driven by madness, [[Matt 26:65|rent his garments|scidit vestimenta sua]], and said to his own: [[Matt 26:66|What think you?|Quid vobis videtur?]] And they all answered: [[Matt 26:66|He is guilty of death|Reus est mortis]]. But when Christ had been raised from the dead, the sun worshipped him, that is, the universal Church; and the moon, that is, every particular Church and devout congregation; and the stars, namely the persons of the Church.

paras.t: Jacob misit Joseph ad fratres suos pecora custodientes, ad videndum quid agerent: et Pater misit Christum ad Synagogam, ad instruendum, considerandum, spiritualiterque alendum tam ipsos Judæorum pastores et superiores, quam eorum subjectos.
paras.en: Jacob sent Joseph to his brethren who were keeping the flocks, to see what they were doing; and the Father sent Christ to the Synagogue, to instruct, to look into and to feed spiritually both the shepherds and superiors of the Jews themselves and those subject to them.

paras.t: Rursus, sicut fratres viso a longe Joseph ad eos veniente, locuti sunt, Ecce somniator venit: venite, occidamus eum: sic indurati Judæorum superiores de Christo dixerunt, Insanit, dæmonium habet, seducit turbam; et cogitaverunt interficere eum. Quemadmodum autem Ruben nitebatur eripere Joseph: sic Nicodemus et aliqui boni Judæi nitebantur Christum de manibus eruere Judæorum.
paras.en: Again, as his brethren, seeing Joseph afar off coming towards them, said: [[37:19|Behold the dreamer cometh|Ecce somniator venit]]: [[37:20|Come, let us kill him|venite, occidamus eum]]; so the hardened superiors of the Jews said of Christ: [[John 10:20|He hath a devil and is mad|Insanit, dæmonium habet]], [[John 7:12|he seduceth the people|seducit turbam]]; and [[John 11:53|they devised to put him to death|cogitaverunt interficere eum]]. And as Ruben strove to rescue Joseph, so Nicodemus and some good Jews strove to deliver Christ out of the hands of the Jews.

paras.t: Interim, sicut Joseph a fratribus venditus est Ismaelitis; sic Christus a discipulo Judæis sævissimis, pro triginta argenteis: quemadmodum etiam Joseph venditus ductus est in Ægyptum; ita Judæi Christum emptum mox tradiderunt gentilibus ad interficiendum; et sicut fratres tinxerunt tunicam Joseph in sanguine hædi, et ab ejus venditione voluerunt immunes videri; sic condemnati Judæi, procuraverunt corpus Christi proprio cruore perfundi, et ab ejus interfectione voluerunt reputari immunes, dicentes sanctis Apostolis: Vultis super nos inducere sanguinem hominis hujus. Hinc Christum sciscitati sunt in ascensione sua gloriosi angeli: Quare rubrum est indumentum tuum, et vestimenta tua sicut calcantium in torculari? Præterea, sicut Joseph bis venditus est; ita et Christus: semel a proditore, deinde post resurrectionem suam a principibus sacerdotum et senioribus, qui pecuniam copiosam dederunt militibus Christum resurrexisse narrantibus, ut dicerent corpus ejus a discipulis suis furto sublatum, quatenus per hoc auferrent Christum de cordibus hominum, atque perpetuæ traderent eum oblivioni. Postremo, sicut Jacob inconsolabiliter flevit filium suum; sic Patri æterno quasi implacabiliter displicuit interfectio Unigeniti sui ex parte odii, crudelitatis, et malitiositatis occidentium eum. Unde pervenit super Judæos ira Dei usque in finem, et finis eorum vastitas, et usque in finem eorum desolatio perseverat.
paras.en: Meanwhile, as Joseph was sold by his brethren to the Ismaelites, so Christ was sold by a disciple to the most savage Jews, for thirty pieces of silver[[Matt 26:15||]]; and as Joseph, once sold, was led into Egypt, so the Jews, having bought Christ, soon handed him over to the Gentiles to be put to death; and as his brethren dipped Joseph’s coat in the blood of a kid and wished to seem guiltless of selling him, so the condemned Jews brought it about that the body of Christ was drenched in his own blood, and wished to be reckoned guiltless of his slaying, saying to the holy Apostles: [[Acts 5:28|you have a mind to bring the blood of this man upon us|Vultis super nos inducere sanguinem hominis hujus]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are those of Acts 5:28]. Hence at his ascension the glorious angels asked Christ: [[Is 63:2|Why then is thy apparel red, and thy garments like theirs that tread in the winepress?|Quare rubrum est indumentum tuum, et vestimenta tua sicut calcantium in torculari?]]? Moreover, as Joseph was sold twice, so was Christ: once by the traitor, and then, after his resurrection, by the chief priests and ancients, who gave a great sum of money to the soldiers who were telling that Christ had risen[[Matt 28:12||]], that they should say his body had been stolen away by his disciples[[Matt 28:13||]], so that by this they might take Christ away from men’s hearts and hand him over to everlasting oblivion. Lastly, as Jacob wept for his son inconsolably, so the slaying of his Only-begotten displeased the eternal Father as it were implacably, on the side of the hatred, cruelty and malice of those who slew him. Hence [[1 Thess 2:16|the wrath of God is come upon them to the end|pervenit super Judæos ira Dei usque in finem]], and [[Dan 9:26|the end thereof shall be waste|finis eorum vastitas]], and [[Dan 9:27|the desolation shall continue even to the consummation, and to the end|usque in finem eorum desolatio perseverat]].

38.title: Elucidatio capituli tricesimi octavi: Eodem tempore descendens Judas a fratribus suis
38.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-eighth chapter: “At that time Juda went down from his brethren”

paras.t: In isto capitulo describitur generatio Judæ, quia ex ejus propagine Christus fuerat nasciturus. Eodem tempore descendens Judas a fratribus suis, divertit ad virum Odollamitem, id est de civitate nomine Odolla natum, vel civem ibidem, nomine Hiram. Refert Lyra : Dicunt Hebræi, quod filii Jacob videntes patrem suum inconsolabiliter lamentari, quia credebat mortuum Joseph, cœperunt esse molesti Judæ, eo quod dederit consilium venditionis Joseph, idcirco recessit ab eis. Istud reor incertum aut fabulosum. Potuisset enim se Judas excusare, dicendo : Idcirco consului ut venderetur, quia vos voluistis eum occidere, ideo magis rei estis quam ego. Viditque ibi filiam hominis Chananæi, vocabulo Sue. Circa hoc scribit Lyra : Sue non est nomen uxoris Judæ, sed patris uxoris illius. Huic autem dicto contrariatur quod infra in isto capitulo scriptum est : Evolutis multis diebus, mortua est Sue uxor Judæ. Et accepta uxore, ingressus est ad eam. Quæ concepit et peperit, etc., successive tres filios, ut patet in littera quæ plana est. Quo, scilicet tertio filio, nato, parere ultra cessavit.
paras.en: In this chapter the generation of Juda is described, since Christ was to be born of his line. [[38:1|At that time Juda went down from his brethren, and turned in to a certain Odollamite|Eodem tempore descendens Judas a fratribus suis, divertit ad virum Odollamitem]], that is, born in the city named Odolla, or a citizen there, [[38:1|named Hiras|nomine Hiram]] [Denis's text has *Hiram*]. Lyra relates: The Hebrews say that the sons of Jacob, seeing their father lamenting inconsolably because he believed Joseph dead, began to be troublesome to Juda, because he had given the counsel to sell Joseph; and so he withdrew from them. This I think uncertain or fabulous. For Juda could have excused himself, saying: I counselled that he be sold because you wished to kill him; so you are more guilty than I. [[38:2|And he saw there the daughter of a man of Chanaan, called Sue|Viditque ibi filiam hominis Chananæi, vocabulo Sue]]. On this Lyra writes: Sue is not the name of Juda's wife, but of his wife's father. But against this saying stands what is written later in this chapter: [[38:12|And after many days were past|Evolutis multis diebus]], Sue the wife of Juda died [Denis's text reads *mortua est Sue uxor Judæ*, where the Vulgate has *filia Sue*, the daughter of Sue]. [[38:2|and taking her to wife, he went in unto her|Et accepta uxore, ingressus est ad eam]]. [[38:3|And she conceived, and bore|Quæ concepit et peperit]], etc., three sons in turn, as is plain in the letter, which is clear. [[38:5|After whose birth, she ceased to bear any more|parere ultra cessavit]], namely the third son.

paras.t: Dedit autem Judas primogenito suo uxorem nomine Thamar. Fuitque Her, primogenitus Judæ, nequam in conspectu Domini, id est, abutens vasculo suæ uxoris, et extra illud semen fundens. Quidam vero assignat causam hujus nequitiæ seu abusus, quæ causa videtur apparentiam non habere : quod propter fœditatem materiæ probare omitto. Et ideo ab eo occisus est, id est, Deus repente occidit hunc nequam pro tanta sua nequitia : et fecit Deus hanc ultionem per angelum vel bonum aut malum ; atque (ut in Scholastica historia legitur) inventus est mortuus in lecto juxta uxorem. Quo exemplo terreri debent immundi et molles. Enormitas quoque hujus criminis indicibilis patet, quod etsi execrabiliter fiat cum meretrice, execrabilius tamen fit cum uxore : gravius quoque est quam naturalis cum propria matre concubitus, ut asserit Augustinus.
paras.en: [[38:6|And Juda took a wife for Her, his first born, whose name was Thamar|Dedit autem Judas primogenito suo uxorem nomine Thamar]]. [[38:7|And Her, the first born of Juda, was wicked in the sight of the Lord|Fuitque Her, primogenitus Judæ, nequam in conspectu Domini]], that is, abusing his wife's body and spilling his seed outside it. Someone assigns a cause of this wickedness or abuse which seems to have no likelihood: which, because of the foulness of the matter, I forbear to examine. [[38:7|and was slain by him|Et ideo ab eo occisus est]], that is, God suddenly slew this wicked man for his great wickedness: and God did this vengeance through an angel, either good or bad; and (as we read in the Scholastic History) he was found dead in bed beside his wife. By this example the unclean and the effeminate ought to be terrified. The unspeakable enormity of this crime is plain, too, in that, though it is done execrably with a harlot, it is done more execrably with a wife: it is also graver than natural intercourse with one's own mother, as Augustine asserts.

paras.t: Dixit ergo Judas ad Onan filium suum : Ingredere ad uxorem fratris tui, et sociare illi. Ordo verborum præposterus est : primo enim præcepit filio suo Onan, ut illam acciperet conjugem ; quo facto, cognosceret ipsam. Ut suscites semen fratri tuo, id est filium gignas ex Thamar, qui fratri tuo mortuo adscribatur, et ejus filius sit legalis. Ex hoc elicitur, esse aliqua observata ab Hebræis ante Moysis tempora, quæ ipse deinceps scripsit in lege. Et quæri posset, a quo istud præceptum accedendi uxorem fratris defuncti, primo datum sit et inceperit. De hoc forsitan post dicetur. Ille, scilicet Onan, sciens non sibi nasci filios, id est, quod primus filius quem ex Thamar procrearet, non sibi, sed defuncto fratri suo adscriberetur, introiens ad uxorem fratris sui, semen fundebat in terram, id est, inutiliter et innaturaliter uxorem cognovit, sicut de fratre ejus prædictum est. Idcirco percussit eum Dominus, etc., id est occidit, quemadmodum fratrem suum.
paras.en: [[38:8|Juda, therefore, said to Onan his son: Go in to thy brother's wife and marry her|Dixit ergo Judas ad Onan filium suum : Ingredere ad uxorem fratris tui, et sociare illi]]. The order of the words is reversed: for first he commanded his son Onan to take her as his wife, and that done, to know her. [[38:8|that thou mayst raise seed to thy brother|Ut suscites semen fratri tuo]], that is, beget a son by Thamar who may be ascribed to thy dead brother and be his son in law. From this it is gathered that some things were observed by the Hebrews before the time of Moses which he afterwards wrote in the law. And it could be asked by whom this precept of going in to a dead brother's wife was first given and began. Of this perhaps we shall speak later. [[38:9|He|Ille]], namely Onan, [[38:9|knowing that the children should not be his|sciens non sibi nasci filios]], that is, that the first son he would beget by Thamar would be ascribed not to himself but to his dead brother, [[38:9|when he went in to his brother's wife, he spilled his seed upon the ground|introiens ad uxorem fratris sui, semen fundebat in terram]], that is, he knew his wife uselessly and against nature, as was said before of his brother. [[38:10|And therefore the Lord slew him|Idcirco percussit eum Dominus]], etc., that is, killed him, like his brother.

paras.t: Evolutis autem multis diebus, mortua est Sue uxor Judæ. Secundum Lyram, in Hebræo habetur, Mortua est filia Sue : ex quo infert, quod Sue fuit nomen patris uxoris Judæ. Ego autem credo Hieronymo sæpe dicenti, nihil se mutasse de Hebraica veritate. Hebræi vero perfidi, qui post Christi fuerunt adventum, veritatem litteræ in locis aliquibus corruperunt. Potuit quoque accidere, quod uxor Judæ habuerit nomen multum simile nominis patris sui, ita ut pater vocatus sit Sua, et ipsa filia Sue, quemadmodum in Latino aliquis pater vocatur Joannes aut Jacobus, et filia ejus Joanna aut Jacoba. Unde et Rabbi Paulus insinuat, quod pater uxoris Judæ dictus est Sua. Ita, si Hebraica veritas habet, Mortua est filia Suæ, potest ita intelligi, Mortua est Suæ, quæ fuit filia viri nomine Sua. Qui, scilicet Judas, post luctum quo uxorem suam defleverat, consolatione accepta, ascendebat ad tonsores ovium suarum, ipse et Hiras opilio, id est pastor gregis, qui forte venit pro Juda, ut ovium suarum interesset tonsioni, ac more tunc solito faceret suis grande convivium, prout in libris Regum narratur de Nabal et Absalone: Odollamites, id est de urbe Odolla, de qua in primo Regum libro habetur, Ascendit David ad speluncam Odollam; et Michæas ait, Usque ad Odollam veniet gloria Israel; in Thamnas, id est ad locum circa oppidum sic vocatum, de quo illud Judicum quidam exponunt, Descendit Samson in Thamnatha.
paras.en: [[38:12|And after many days were past|Evolutis autem multis diebus]], [[38:12|the daughter of Sue the wife of Juda died|mortua est Sue uxor Judæ]]. According to Lyra, the Hebrew has, *The daughter of Sue died*: from which he infers that Sue was the name of the father of Juda's wife. But I believe Jerome, who often says that he changed nothing of the Hebrew truth. The faithless Hebrews who came after Christ's coming corrupted the truth of the letter in some places. It could also have happened that Juda's wife had a name very like her father's, so that the father was called Sua and the daughter Sue, as in Latin a father is called Joannes or Jacobus and his daughter Joanna or Jacoba. Hence Rabbi Paul too hints that the father of Juda's wife was called Sua. So, if the Hebrew truth has, *The daughter of Sua died*, it can be understood thus: Sua died, who was the daughter of a man named Sua. [[38:12|and when he had taken comfort after his mourning|consolatione accepta]], namely Juda, after the mourning in which he had wept for his wife, he went up [[38:12|to the shearers of his sheep, he and Hiras|ascendebat ad tonsores ovium suarum, ipse et Hiras]] [[38:12|the shepherd of his flock|opilio]], that is, the shepherd of the flock, who perhaps came on Juda's behalf to be present at the shearing of his sheep, and, after the custom of that time, to give a great feast for his people, as is told in the books of Kings of Nabal and Absalom[[1 Kings 25:36||]][[2 Kings 13:27||]]: [[38:12|the Odollamite|Odollamites]], that is, of the city of Odolla, of which we have in the first book of Kings, [[1 Kings 22:1|and fled to the cave of Odollam|Ascendit David ad speluncam Odollam]] [Denis's text: *David went up to the cave of Odollam*]; and Micheas says, [[Mich 1:15|even to Odollam shall the glory of Israel come|Usque ad Odollam veniet gloria Israel]]; [[38:12|to Thamnas|in Thamnas]], that is, to the place near the town so called, of which some explain that saying of Judges, [[Judg 14:1|Then Samson went down to Thamnatha|Descendit Samson in Thamnatha]].

paras.t: Nuntiatumque est ipsi Thamar, quod socer illius, videlicet Judas, cujus filios habuit maritos, ascenderet in Thamnas ad tondendas oves, per manus servorum suorum. Quæ, depositis viduitatis vestibus. Ex quo verbo perpenditur, quod illis temporibus viduæ portabant specialia vestimenta, utpote humilitatem simplicitatemque prætendentia. Hinc quoque fertur de Judith, quod exuit se vestimentis viduitatis. Multum ergo corripiendæ sunt viduæ christianæ, quæ curiose aut pompatice vestiuntur. Assumpsit theristrum, id est album velamen, seu æstivalem ac lineam vestem, et mutato habitu, utpote meretriculari veste assumpta, sedit in bivio itineris quod ducit Thamnam, id est in compito seu capite duarum viarum, ubi viator diligentius debet considerare quo pergat; eo quod crevisset Sela, videlicet tertius filius Judæ […] […] maritum, etc. Hoc est, idcirco ita ornavit se et tanquam meretrix se exposuit Judæ, non ex libidine, sed desiderio prolis habendæ, quam putabat se non adepturam ex filio Judæ, quia Judas non dedit ei filium illum maritum: ideo ex Juda imprægnari optavit; atque (ut aliqui opinantur) idcirco potius concupivit fecundari ex Juda, quia cognovit Christum ex ejus semine nasciturum; sicque aliqualiter excusatur hæc Thamar de incestu, sicut de filiabus Lot dictum.
paras.en: [[38:13|And it was told Thamar that her father-in-law|Nuntiatumque est ipsi Thamar, quod socer illius]], namely Juda, whose sons she had had as husbands, [[38:13|was come up to Thamnas to shear his sheep|ascenderet in Thamnas ad tondendas oves]], by the hands of his servants. [[38:14|And she put off the garments of her widowhood|Quæ, depositis viduitatis vestibus]]. From this word it is weighed that in those times widows wore special garments, namely ones showing humility and simplicity. Hence too it is said of Judith that [[Jdt 10:2|put away the garments of her widowhood|exuit se vestimentis viduitatis]]. Christian widows, then, are much to be rebuked who dress with curiosity or showiness. [[38:14|and took a veil|Assumpsit theristrum]], that is, a white veil, or a light summer garment of linen, [[38:14|and changing her dress|et mutato habitu]], namely taking a harlot's dress, [[38:14|sat in the cross way, that leadeth to Thamnas|sedit in bivio itineris quod ducit Thamnam]], that is, at the crossroads, or the head of two ways, where the traveller ought to consider more carefully where he is going; [[38:14|because Sela was grown up|eo quod crevisset Sela]], namely Juda's third son, […] [[38:14|and she had not been married to him|maritum]] [some words are lost here in the transcription], etc. That is, she adorned herself so and exposed herself to Juda as a harlot, not out of lust, but out of desire to have offspring, which she thought she would not obtain from Juda's son, since Juda had not given her that son as husband: so she wished to be made with child by Juda; and (as some think) she desired the more to be made fruitful by Juda because she knew that Christ was to be born of his seed; and so this Thamar is in some measure excused of incest, as was said of the daughters of Lot[[Gen 19:32||]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription].

paras.t: Ingrediensque ad eam Judas, ait: Dimitte me ut coeam tecum, etc. Et illa dixit: Patiar quod vis, si dederis mihi arrhabonem, id est pignus pretii quod pro concubitu promisisti. Arrha quippe vocatur pars pretii: inde dicitur arrhabo, quasi arrha bona, et est id quod datur post taxationem pretii loco dandi; sicque Judas dedit ei pro pignore annulum et armillam, scilicet aurium ornamentum, et baculum suum. Ad unum igitur coitum concepit mulier geminos, etc. Misit autem Judas ei hœdum, sicut promisit, per pastorem suum, etc. Quum non invenisset eam, etc., reversus est ad Judam, etc. Ait Judas: Habeat sibi, id est, pignus illud teneat sibi pro hœdo; certe mendacii arguere nos non poterit, etc. Ex hoc verbo Thomas concludit, quod homines interdum faciunt sibi conscientiam majorem de culpa minori, quam graviori: quemadmodum Judas de mendacio, quod non est semper mortale, quam de fornicatione quæ semper mortale peccatum est, loquendo de ea formaliter. Porro, ut recitat Lyra, in Hebræo habetur, Habeat sibi, ut non simus despectui: quod sic exponunt Hebræi, Sit suum quod habet de meo, nec amplius illam quæras, ne hoc factum meum divulgetur ad meam confusionem.
paras.en: [[38:16|And going to her, he said: Suffer me to lie with thee|Ingrediensque ad eam Judas, ait: Dimitte me ut coeam tecum]], etc. [[38:17|I will suffer what thou wilt, if thou give me a pledge|Patiar quod vis, si dederis mihi arrhabonem]], that is, a pledge of the price which thou hast promised for lying with me. For *arrha* is the name for part of the price: hence *arrhabo* is said, as it were *arrha bona*, a good earnest; and it is what is given after the price is fixed, in place of what is to be given; and so Juda gave her as a pledge his ring and bracelet, namely an ornament of the ears, and his staff. [[38:18|The woman therefore at one copulation conceived|Ad unum igitur coitum concepit mulier]] twins, etc. [[38:20|And Juda sent a kid by his shepherd|Misit autem Judas]], as he had promised, etc. [[38:20|not finding her|Quum non invenisset eam]], etc., [[38:22|He returned to Juda|reversus est ad Judam]], etc. [[38:23|Juda said: Let her take it to herself|Ait Judas: Habeat sibi]], that is, let her keep that pledge for herself in place of the kid; [[38:23|surely she cannot charge us with a lie|certe mendacii arguere nos non poterit]], etc. From this word Thomas concludes that men sometimes make themselves a greater conscience of a lesser fault than of a graver one: as Juda did of a lie, which is not always mortal, rather than of fornication, which is always a mortal sin, speaking of it formally. Further, as Lyra relates, the Hebrew has, *Let her have it, that we be not put to shame*: which the Hebrews explain thus: Let what she has of mine be hers, and do not seek her any more, lest this deed of mine be spread abroad to my confusion.

paras.t: Ecce autem post tres menses nuntiaverunt Judæ, dicentes: Fornicata est Thamar, etc. Dixitque Judas: Producite eam ut comburatur. Evidentia etenim facti, probationem majorem non exigit. Sed quæri potest, unde Judæ ista auctoritas, ut eo jubente ducta est ad comburendum : et eo jubente, dimissa est. Rursus, videtur Judas injuste jussisse ut combureretur, quia adulterium non commisit. Non enim pro tunc habebat maritum; et dato quod adulterium perpetrasset, non tamen ob hoc comburi, sed leviori morte puniri promeruit. Ad istud (ut Rabbi Paulus enarrat) quidam Hebræi satis rationabiliter dicunt, quod Judas fuit illo in loco quasi princeps et judex, et quod ex ore ejus fiebant judicia, atque in isto negotio judicavit non secundum leges jam datas, sed juxta suum proprium arbitrium. Posset quoque dici, quod Judas dicitur id fecisse, quod a judice loci illius fieri procuravit ; Scriptura vero cursorie refert istam historiam. At vero Lyra refert, quod Hebræi dicunt hanc Thamar fuisse filiam Melchisedech regis ac sacerdotis, quoniam filia sacerdotis fornicans sive adulterans, erat comburenda : quod dictum reprobat Lyra, eo quod Judas dixit ad Thamar, Esto vidua in domo patris tui : Melchisedech autem mortuus fuit tempore illo. Sed quidquid sit de veritate dicti illius, reprobatio ista infirma est. Nam dicitur aliquis esse et habitare in domo patris sui, patre defuncto. Dicit quoque Lyra, quod Thamar commisit adulterium cum Juda : quod non videtur, quoniam nondum erat matrimonialiter juncta Selæ filio Judæ, quamvis debebat eum accipere, et forte sponsalia erant inter Selam et Thamar contracta. Hinc alii dicunt, quod Judas peccavit adjudicando hanc Thamar morti, quia non meruit hoc.
paras.en: [[38:24|And behold, after three months, they told Juda, saying|Ecce autem post tres menses nuntiaverunt Judæ, dicentes]]: [[38:24|Thamar, thy daughter-in-law, hath played the harlot|Fornicata est Thamar]], etc. [[38:24|And Juda said: Bring her out that she may be burnt|Dixitque Judas: Producite eam ut comburatur]]. For the evidence of the fact does not require greater proof. But it can be asked whence Juda had this authority, that at his bidding she was led out to be burnt, and at his bidding was let go. Again, Juda seems to have commanded unjustly that she be burnt, since she had not committed adultery: for at that time she had no husband; and granted she had committed adultery, yet she did not deserve to be burnt for it, but to be punished by a lighter death. To this (as Rabbi Paul relates) certain Hebrews say reasonably enough that Juda was in that place as it were prince and judge, and that judgments were given from his mouth, and that in this business he judged not according to laws already given but according to his own will. It could also be said that Juda is said to have done what he caused the judge of that place to do; and Scripture relates this history briefly. But Lyra relates that the Hebrews say this Thamar was the daughter of Melchisedech, king and priest, since a priest's daughter who committed fornication or adultery was to be burnt: which saying Lyra rejects, because Juda said to Thamar, [[38:11|Remain a widow in thy father's house|Esto vidua in domo patris tui]]; and Melchisedech was dead at that time. But whatever be the truth of that saying, this refutation is weak. For one is said to be and to dwell in his father's house when his father is dead. Lyra also says that Thamar committed adultery with Juda: which does not seem so, since she was not yet joined in marriage to Sela, Juda's son, though she was to take him, and perhaps a betrothal had been contracted between Sela and Thamar. Hence others say that Juda sinned in condemning this Thamar to death, since she did not deserve it.

paras.t: Quæ quum duceretur ad pœnam, misit ad socerum suum, dicens : De viro cujus hæc sunt, concepi, etc. Qui agnitis muneribus ait : Justior me est, quia non tradidi eam Selæ filio meo, etc. Ex hoc probatur, quod nondum fuit sociata conjugio Selæ. Denique, quamvis Judas locutus sit, Justior me est, ambo tamen peccaverunt mortaliter in hoc facto. Quod si quæratur quis eorum magis peccarit, respondet Hieronymus : Comparatione Judæ, Thamar minus male fecit, quia non vaga turpitudine, sed filios requirendo peccavit. Aliis tamen apparet, quod absolute loquendo Thamar magis peccavit, quoniam scienter commisit incestum, et si Judas scivisset quod nurus sua existeret, non accessisset eamdem. Unde nec postea eam cognovit, sed nec David uxores suas ab Absalon cognitas […].
paras.en: [[38:25|But when she was led to execution, she sent to her father in law, saying|Quæ quum duceretur ad pœnam, misit ad socerum suum, dicens]]: [[38:25|By the man, to whom these things belong, I am with child|De viro cujus hæc sunt, concepi]], etc. [[38:26|But he acknowledging the gifts, said: She is juster than I: because I did not give her to Sela, my son|Qui agnitis muneribus ait : Justior me est, quia non tradidi eam Selæ filio meo]], etc. From this it is proved that she was not yet joined in marriage to Sela. Lastly, although Juda said, *She is juster than I*, yet both sinned mortally in this deed. And if it be asked which of them sinned more, Jerome answers: In comparison with Juda, Thamar did less ill, since she sinned not by wandering lewdness but by seeking children. Yet to others it appears that, speaking absolutely, Thamar sinned more, since she committed incest knowingly; and if Juda had known that she was his daughter-in-law, he would not have gone in to her. Hence he did not know her afterwards either; nor did David [know] his wives who had been known by Absalom[[2 Kings 16:22||]][[2 Kings 20:3||]] […] [the end of this sentence is lost in the transcription].

paras.t: Instante autem partu, apparuerunt gemini in utero ejus, id est, duo fetus inventi sunt in utero Thamar : atque in ipsa effusione, id est egressione, infantium, unus protulit manum, in qua obstetrix ligavit coccinum, id est rubeum filum, ut per hoc discerneretur, quis inter duos gemellos valde consimiles, primogenitus esset, dicens : Iste egredietur prior, hoc est, obstetrix æstimavit quod sic fieri solet. Illo vero retrahente manum simul cum coccino, egressus est alter, manum suam protendens, aliumque nascendo præcedens. Dicitque mulier, id est mater infantulorum, admirans de hac quasi contentione infantum, ut in Glossa exponitur : Quare divisa est propter te maceria ? id est, ob quam causam frater tuus qui primo extenderat manum, rupit membranulam sive pelliculam, qua infans in matrice involvitur, quasi patefaciens tibi viam, ut tu primus exires ac nascereris ? Alter quippe manum suam extendendo, rupit pelliculam illam, quæ in partu dividitur, soletque infantem sequi : imo si post egressum pueri maneat in utero matris, mater ipsa non diu vivit infante egresso. Et ob hanc causam vocavit ipsa Thamar eum, videlicet puerum primo natum, Phares, quod interpretatur divisio, ob hoc quod propter eum divisa fuit pellicula illa a fratre suo. Postea egressus est frater ejus, in cujus manu erat coccinum, qui exivit cum filio illo, quem appellavit Zaram, quod interpretatur oriens, et ita vocatus est, quia primus cœperat apparere, manum extendendo; vel quodam futurorum præsagio, quoniam multi præclari et justi ex eo sunt nati, prout primo libro Paralipomenon scribitur. Quidam dicit, quod Zara interpretatur refulgentia, et quod dictus sit Zara, propter refulgentiam coccini in ejus manu ligati : sed prior interpretatio et ratio nominis hujus est aptior, quam et sanctus assignat Hieronymus.
paras.en: [[38:27|And when she was ready to be brought to bed, there appeared twins in her womb|Instante autem partu, apparuerunt gemini in utero ejus]], that is, two offspring were found in Thamar's womb: [[38:27|and in the very delivery of the infants, one put forth a hand, whereon the midwife tied a scarlet thread|atque in ipsa effusione, id est egressione, infantium, unus protulit manum, in qua obstetrix ligavit coccinum]], that is, a red thread, so that by this it might be told which of two very alike twins was the firstborn, [[38:27|saying|dicens]]: [[38:28|This shall come forth the first|Iste egredietur prior]], that is, the midwife judged that it usually happens so. [[38:29|But he drawing back his hand|Illo vero retrahente manum]] together with the scarlet thread, [[38:29|the other came forth|egressus est alter]], stretching out his hand and going before the other in being born. [[38:29|and the woman said|Dicitque mulier]], that is, the mother of the little ones, wondering at this as it were struggle of the infants, as is explained in the Gloss: [[38:29|Why is the partition divided for thee|Quare divisa est propter te maceria]]? that is, for what reason did thy brother, who had first put out his hand, break the little membrane or skin in which the infant is wrapped in the womb, as if opening the way for thee, that thou mightest come out and be born first? For the other, by stretching out his hand, broke that skin, which is divided in birth and usually follows the infant: indeed, if it remains in the mother's womb after the child has come out, the mother herself does not live long after the infant's coming out. [[38:29|and therefore called his name|Et ob hanc causam vocavit]] (Thamar herself) him, namely the child born first, [[38:29|Phares|Phares]], which is interpreted *division*, because for his sake that skin was divided by his brother. [[38:30|Afterwards his brother came out, on whose hand was the scarlet thread|Postea egressus est frater ejus, in cujus manu erat coccinum]], who came out after that son, [[38:30|and she called his name Zara|quem appellavit Zaram]], which is interpreted *rising*, and he was so called because he first began to appear by stretching out his hand; or by a certain foreshadowing of things to come, since many illustrious and just men were born of him, as is written in the first book of Paralipomenon[[1 Par 2:6||]]. Someone says that Zara is interpreted *brightness*, and that he was called Zara because of the brightness of the scarlet thread tied on his hand: but the former interpretation and reason for this name is more fitting, which Saint Jerome too gives.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, quare et qualiter contigit, quod ille qui manum primo exposuit, eam retraxit et ultimo natus est. Ad quod arbitror respondendum, quod Deo sic moderante ac imperante id accidit, ad præfigurandum quod de Phares Christus fuerat nasciturus. Itemque ad designandum, quod in Christo primi sunt facti novissimi, et novissimi primi : quia Judæi qui erant primi, facti sunt excæcati, et gentiles sunt in Christo illuminati.
paras.en: On this it is asked why and how it came about that he who first put out his hand drew it back and was born last. To which I think it must be answered that this happened by God's so governing and commanding, to prefigure that Christ was to be born of Phares; and also to signify that in Christ the first are made last and the last first: since the Jews, who were first, were blinded, and the gentiles were enlightened in Christ.

paras.t: Postremo, circa capitulum istud movet beatus Augustinus quæstionem non parvam, qualiter scilicet in tempore illo brevi, videlicet viginti duobus annis, aut circiter, quibus Jacob mansit in terra Chanaan post Joseph venditionem, potuerunt omnia hæc narrata impleri, utpote quod Judas accepit uxorem, genuitque ex ea tres filios, quorum seniori conjugem dedit, illoque mortuo eidem conjugi alium suum filium dedit maritum : quo item defuncto, commisit nurui suæ ut in domo patris sui vidua permaneret, quousque cresceret junior filius suus, qui et interim crevit in tantum, quod ad conjugii contractionem fuit idoneus. De hoc Augustinus sic loquitur: Quæritur quando ista fieri potuerint. Si enim post ingressum Joseph in Ægyptum, quomodo infra viginti duos annos fieri potuerunt, ut et filii Judæ fierent tantæ ætatis, quod omnes possent ducere conjuges ? nisi forte dicatur, quod Scriptura velut per recapitulationem intelligi hæc fieri cœpisse per aliquos annos ante Joseph venditionem. Nihilo minus merito quæritur, quot annorum potuit esse Judas quartus filius Jacob, si Joseph sedecim annorum est venditus, quum et ipse Ruben primogenitus Jacob vix sex annis præcedere potuit fratrem suum Joseph ætate. Difficile ergo est videre, qualiter inter annos illos fieri potuerunt omnia, quæ narrantur hic de Juda et filiis ejus ac nuru, nisi forte credamus Judam incidisse in amorem ejus, quam duxit uxorem, statim quum adolescere cœpit, nondum vendito Joseph. Hæc Augustinus. Similiter quoque dicendum de primis duobus filiis Judæ, quod statim in adolescentia sua sint uxorati.
paras.en: Lastly, concerning this chapter blessed Augustine raises no small question, namely how in that short time, namely twenty-two years or about that, during which Jacob stayed in the land of Chanaan after the sale of Joseph, all these things related could be accomplished: namely that Juda took a wife and begot three sons by her, to the eldest of whom he gave a wife, and when he was dead gave the same wife another son of his as husband; and when he too was dead, bade his daughter-in-law remain a widow in her father's house until his younger son grew up, who meanwhile also grew so much that he was fit to contract marriage. Of this Augustine speaks thus: It is asked when these things could have happened. For if after Joseph's entering Egypt, how within twenty-two years could it have happened that Juda's sons were of such age that all could take wives? unless perhaps it is said that Scripture, as it were by recapitulation, means these things to have begun to happen some years before the sale of Joseph. Nevertheless it is rightly asked how old Juda, the fourth son of Jacob, could have been, if Joseph was sold at sixteen years of age, since even Ruben, Jacob's firstborn, could scarcely be six years older than his brother Joseph. It is hard, then, to see how all that is told here of Juda and his sons and daughter-in-law could have happened within those years, unless perhaps we believe that Juda fell in love with her whom he took to wife as soon as he began to grow up, Joseph not yet being sold. Thus far Augustine. So too it is to be said of Juda's first two sons, that they were married as soon as they were youths.

paras.t: Postremo, pensemus in præinductis occulta judicia Dei, et filiorum Judæ vitetur nequitia, nec aliquis conformetur malitiæ Onan, qui maluit fundere semen in terram, ductus invidia, indignationeque pessima, quam suscitare semen fratri suo defuncto : per quem Onan designantur qui aliis prodesse non volunt, etiam quando absque proprio detrimento hoc possunt.
paras.en: Lastly, let us weigh in what has been brought forward the hidden judgments of God, and let the wickedness of Juda's sons be avoided, nor let anyone conform himself to the malice of Onan, who, led by envy and the worst resentment, preferred to spill his seed on the ground rather than raise up seed to his dead brother: by which Onan are signified those who will not profit others, even when they can do so without loss to themselves.

39.title: Expositio capituli tricesimi noni: Igitur Joseph ductus est in Ægyptum
39.title_en: Exposition of the thirty-ninth chapter: “And Joseph was brought into Egypt”

paras.t: HOC capitulo describuntur virtutes Joseph patriarchæ, et quanta pro justitia toleravit, quam gratiose quoque ac dulciter fuit Deus cum eo in adversis. Rediens itaque Moyses ad inchoatam de Joseph historiam, ait : Igitur Joseph ductus est in Ægyptum, etc. Fuitque Dominus cum eo, per providentiam specialem et directionem piissimam ; et erat vir in cunctis prospere agens, etc. Quomodo verum est hoc, quum fuerit adolescens sedecim aut decem et septem annorum, et tanta adversa incurrerit ? Et respondendum, quod paulatim crevit in virum sapientiæ ac virtutum : imo et in adolescentia sua viri fuit, non corpore et ætate, sed probitate morum, constantia mentis, atque prudentia. Porro adversa quæ incurrit, non ex imprudentia ac defectuositate propria incidit, sed et ipsa cooperata sunt ei in bonum, atque in maximam prosperitatem. Fuit quoque in cunctis prospere agens, quantum ad animæ suæ salutem, quæ summa prosperitas est; et quantum ad temporalium rerum domini sui gubernationem, in omnibus prospere egit. Qui, dominus suus, optime noverat Dominum esse cum Joseph : hoc enim consideravit ex actibus virtuosis et prudentissimis verbis ac prosperis ipsius Joseph operibus, atque ut factum est ex verbis Hieronymi, quia Ægyptius ille consideravit se subito infrigidatum a Deo, eo quod decrevit abuti Joseph : et omnia quæ gereret ipse Joseph, ab eo dirigi in manu illius, etc., id est virtute et operatione Dei ad prosperum finem tendere ac moveri. A quo, domino suo Ægyptio, ipse Joseph præpositus omnibus, ceteris qui de familia Ægyptii erant, et temporalibus rebus ejusdem, gubernabat creditam sibi domum, id est domesticos et ea quæ erant in domo, et universa quæ ei tradita fuerant ad custodiendum, dispensandum, seu erogandum. Benedixitque Dominus domui Ægyptii propter Joseph, id est ipsi Ægyptio, pertinentibusque ad domum ipsius, in temporalibus, dando, conservando, et multiplicando ea Ægyptio propter Joseph, sicut benedixit domui Laban propter Jacob, ut scilicet ille Ægyptius esset magis gratiosus et favorabilis ipsi Joseph.
