paras.en: This chapter describes the virtues of the patriarch Joseph, and how much he bore for justice, and how graciously and sweetly God was with him in adversity. So Moses, returning to the history of Joseph he had begun, says: [[39:1|And Joseph was brought into Egypt|Igitur Joseph ductus est in Ægyptum]], etc. [[39:2|And the Lord was with him|Fuitque Dominus cum eo]], by a special providence and a most loving guidance; [[39:2|and he was a prosperous man in all things|et erat vir in cunctis prospere agens]], etc. How is this true, since he was a youth of sixteen or seventeen years, and met with such adversities? And the answer is that he grew little by little into a man of wisdom and virtues: indeed even in his youth he was a man, not in body and age, but in uprightness of conduct, constancy of mind and prudence. And the adversities he met with did not befall him from his own imprudence and failing; rather they too worked together for him unto good[[Rom 8:28||]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription; the words recall Rom 8:28], and unto the greatest prosperity. He was also prosperous in all things as regards the salvation of his soul, which is the highest prosperity; and as regards the management of his master's temporal affairs, he acted prosperously in all things. [[39:3|Who knew very well that the Lord was with him|Qui, dominus suus, optime noverat Dominum esse cum]], namely his master, with Joseph: for he gathered this from Joseph's virtuous acts, his most prudent words and prosperous works; and, as appears from the words of Jerome, because that Egyptian found himself suddenly made cold by God when he had resolved to abuse Joseph [Jerome's tradition that Putiphar was made a eunuch]: [[39:3|and made all that he did to prosper in his hand|et omnia quæ gereret ipse Joseph, ab eo dirigi in manu illius]], etc., that is, they tended and were moved to a prosperous end by the power and working of God. [[39:4|and being set over all by him|præpositus omnibus]], by his Egyptian master, Joseph, over the others of the Egyptian's household and over his temporal goods, [[39:4|he governed the house committed to him|gubernabat creditam sibi domum]], that is, the household and what was in the house, [[39:4|and all things that were delivered to him|et universa quæ ei tradita fuerant]] to keep, dispense or pay out. [[39:5|And the Lord blessed the house of the Egyptian for Joseph's sake|Benedixitque Dominus domui Ægyptii propter Joseph]], that is, the Egyptian himself and what belonged to his house, in temporal things, giving, preserving and multiplying them to the Egyptian for Joseph's sake, as He blessed Laban's house for Jacob's sake: so that the Egyptian might be the more gracious and favourable to Joseph.

paras.t: Erat autem Joseph pulchra facie, et decorus adspectu. In quibus verbis tangitur duplex pulchritudo Joseph : una corporalis, quæ præcipue attenditur et apparet in facie; alia moralis, quæ in compositione apparatus et facetia morum actuumque consistit. Post multos itaque dies injecit domina sua oculos in Joseph, id est, curiose et libidinose eum adspexit, quando jam fuit virilis ætatis, hoc est viginti annorum aut amplius : et ait : Dormi mecum. Probabile est, quod primo per verba et signa habuit se blande procaciterque ad Joseph. Quumque videret se per talia non sortiri intentum, tandem concupiscentiis victa, dixit aperte, Dormi mecum. Qui nequaquam acquiescens operi nefario, dixit ad eam : Ecce dominus meus, omnibus mihi traditis, ignorat quid habeat in domo sua, id est, non scit omnia illa distincte, nec curat, nec advertit hujusmodi, sed commisit omnia mihi. Unde ante hæc verba ait Scriptura, Nec quidquam aliud noverat, nisi panem quo vescebatur, id est proprium cibum ac potum, quia insinuavit dispensatori suo, videlicet Joseph, quid vellet manducare ac bibere. Verumtamen istæ sunt hyperbolicæ locutiones, in quibus aliquid dicitur sine mendacio per excessum, ut magnitudo rei clarius exprimatur. Nec quidquam est in domo ejus, quod non in mea sit potestate, vel non tradiderit mihi ad gubernandum, non ad possidendum : ex quo videtur, quod Ægyptius ille etiam gubernationem sobolis suæ commiserit Joseph ; præter te quæ uxor ejus es. Quomodo ergo possum hoc malum, videlicet adulterium, facere, et peccare in Deum, vel ut alii legunt, In dominum meum? id est, tam verum Deum dominum universorum, quam virum tuum qui est dominus meus temporalis, offendere. Quamvis autem adulterium sit directe peccatum in proximum, cui infert læsionem seu nocumentum, est tamen etiam peccatum in Deum, in quantum est contra præceptum illius. Hujuscemodi verbis per singulos dies loquebatur, et mulier molesta erat adolescenti, quia mulier nitebatur Joseph ad libidinem provocare, et ipse econtrario hortabatur illam ad pudicitiam, fidemque conjugalem ; et ille recusabat stuprum, hoc est adulterium.
paras.en: [[39:6|And Joseph was of a beautiful countenance, and comely to behold|Erat autem Joseph pulchra facie, et decorus adspectu]]. In these words a twofold beauty of Joseph is touched on: one bodily, which is chiefly looked to and appears in the face; the other moral, which consists in the composure of his bearing and the grace of his manners and acts. [[39:7|And after many days, his mistress cast her eyes on Joseph|Post multos itaque dies injecit domina sua oculos in Joseph]], that is, she looked at him curiously and lustfully, when he was now of a man's age, that is, twenty years or more: [[39:7|and said: Lie with me|et ait : Dormi mecum]]. It is probable that at first she behaved coaxingly and wantonly towards Joseph by words and signs. And when she saw that she did not gain her purpose by such things, at last, overcome by her desires, she said openly, Lie with me. [[39:8|But he in no wise consenting to that wicked act said to her|Qui nequaquam acquiescens operi nefario, dixit ad eam]]: [[39:8|Behold, my master hath delivered all things to me, and knoweth not what he hath in his own house|Ecce dominus meus, omnibus mihi traditis, ignorat quid habeat in domo sua]], that is, he does not know all those things distinctly, nor care, nor attend to such things, but has committed all to me. Hence before these words Scripture says, [[39:6|Neither knew he any other thing, but the bread which he ate|Nec quidquam aliud noverat, nisi panem quo vescebatur]], that is, his own food and drink, since he let his steward, namely Joseph, know what he wished to eat and drink. Yet these are hyperbolical ways of speaking, in which something is said without lying by excess, so that the greatness of the thing may be expressed more clearly. [[39:9|Neither is there any thing which is not in my power, or that he hath not delivered to me|Nec quidquam est in domo ejus, quod non in mea sit potestate, vel non tradiderit mihi]] [Denis's text adds *in domo ejus*, in his house] to govern, not to possess: from which it seems that that Egyptian committed even the government of his children to Joseph; [[39:9|but thee, who art his wife; how then can I do this wicked thing|præter te quæ uxor ejus es. Quomodo ergo possum hoc malum]], namely adultery, [[39:9|and sin against my God|facere, et peccare in Deum]]? or, as others read, *against my lord*? that is, offend both the true God, Lord of all things, and thy husband, who is my temporal lord. And though adultery is directly a sin against one's neighbour, on whom it inflicts injury or harm, it is yet also a sin against God, inasmuch as it is against His commandment. [[39:10|With such words as these day by day, both the woman was importunate with the young man|Hujuscemodi verbis per singulos dies loquebatur, et mulier molesta erat adolescenti]], since the woman strove to provoke Joseph to lust, and he on the contrary exhorted her to chastity and conjugal faith; [[39:10|and he refused the adultery|et ille recusabat stuprum]], that is, adultery.

paras.t: Accidit autem quadam die, ut intraret Joseph domum, et operis quidpiam absque arbitris faceret, id est solus nullo præsente, seu absque testibus qui indicare possent et protestari quid accidisset : ex quo conjicitur, quod Joseph sciens improbam consuetudinem dominæ suæ, assumpsit assidue aliquos secum intrando et exeundo ac operando, ne illa auderet sibi inhonesta proponere: et illa, apprehensa lacinia vestimenti ejus, id est ora seu fimbria, vel (ut ait Andreas expositor) cornibus pallii seu mantelli, diceret : Dormi mecum. Qui relicto in manu ejus pallio, fugit, et egressus est foras. Refert Josephus, die illo fuisse præcipuam solennitatem Ægyptiis, in qua omnes ad templa convenerant idolorum, ad quæ etiam feminæ tunc venerunt: sed femina ista persuasit viro suo se esse infirmam, quatenus solitudinem, opportunitatemque captaret alliciendi Joseph ad suum consensum. Quumque sola esset cum eo, cœpit blandiri ac deprecari ejus concubitum, adjiciens minas, videlicet quod eum accusaret apud maritum, si sibi non consentiret. Quumque castissimus Joseph non flecteretur, illa apprehendit eum cum pallio, ut vel sic traheret eum ad stuprum: ipse vero iratus excussit se. Quumque vidisset mulier in manibus suis vestem, scilicet pallium, et se esse contemptam zelo justissimo, quia ut talis, erat prorsus contemptibilis, vocavit ad se homines domus suæ: forte enim aliqui de familia erant in domo, et alii cito redierunt de fano; et ait ad eos: En introduxit virum Hebræum ut illuderet nobis, etc., id est, maritus meus adduxit istum Joseph, qui conatus est dominum suum maxime inhonorare, violando et opprimendo me conjugem ejus, per hoc quod non solum mihi, sed et viro meo ac soboli nostræ ac cunctis ad nos pertinentibus fecisset illusionem atque opprobrium. In argumentum ergo fidei, et in signum et in probationem suæ accusationis, quod vera esset et fide digna : argumentum quippe est ratio rei dubiæ faciens fidem : retentum pallium ostendit marito revertenti domum, et ait: Ingressus est ad me servus Hebræus quem adduxisti, ut illuderet mihi : quasi dicat, Ingratus est tibi et præsumptuosissime egit. Et recte, illicitus adulterinusque coitus, seu concupiscentia prædominans, vocatur illusio, quia per eum ratio penitus superatur, et homo bestialiter agit, ac contumeliose et derisive.
paras.en: [[39:11|Now it happened on a certain day, that Joseph went into the house, and was doing some business, without any man with him|Accidit autem quadam die, ut intraret Joseph domum, et operis quidpiam absque arbitris faceret]], that is, alone, with no one present, or without witnesses who could tell and testify what had happened: from which it is conjectured that Joseph, knowing his mistress's wicked habit, constantly took some people with him in going in and out and working, so that she should not dare to propose shameful things to him: [[39:12|And she catching the skirt of his garment|et illa, apprehensa lacinia vestimenti ejus]], that is, the edge or fringe, or (as Andrew the expositor says) the corners of his cloak or mantle, [[39:12|said: Lie with me|diceret : Dormi mecum]]. [[39:12|But he leaving the garment in her hand, fled, and went out|Qui relicto in manu ejus pallio, fugit, et egressus est foras]]. Josephus relates that that day was a chief festival of the Egyptians, at which all had gathered at the temples of the idols, to which women too then went: but this woman persuaded her husband that she was ill, so that she might seize the solitude and opportunity of enticing Joseph to consent to her. And when she was alone with him, she began to coax him and beg him to lie with her, adding threats, namely that she would accuse him to her husband if he did not consent. And when the most chaste Joseph was not moved, she caught hold of him by his cloak, so as to drag him even so to the deed; but he in anger shook himself free. [[39:13|And when the woman saw the garment in her hands|Quumque vidisset mulier in manibus suis vestem]], namely the cloak, [[39:13|and herself disregarded|et se esse contemptam]] with most just zeal, since such as she was she was altogether contemptible, [[39:14|She called to her the men of her house|vocavit ad se homines domus suæ]]: for perhaps some of the household were in the house, and others quickly returned from the temple; [[39:14|and said to them: See, he hath brought in a Hebrew, to abuse us|et ait ad eos: En introduxit virum Hebræum ut illuderet nobis]], etc., that is, my husband has brought in this Joseph, who has tried to dishonour his master greatly by violating and forcing me his wife, whereby he would have made mockery and shame not only of me but of my husband and our children and all who belong to us. [[39:16|For a proof therefore of her fidelity|In argumentum ergo fidei]], and as a sign and proof of her accusation, that it was true and worthy of belief: for an argument is a reason that makes belief of a doubtful thing: [[39:16|she kept the garment, and shewed it to her husband when he returned home|retentum pallium ostendit marito revertenti domum]], [[39:17|And said: The Hebrew servant, whom thou hast brought, came to me to abuse me|et ait: Ingressus est ad me servus Hebræus quem adduxisti, ut illuderet mihi]]: as if to say, He is ungrateful to thee and has acted most presumptuously. And rightly unlawful and adulterous intercourse, or ruling concupiscence, is called *abuse* [*illusio*, mockery], since by it reason is wholly overcome, and man acts like a beast, insultingly and mockingly.

paras.t: […] domino, et nimium credulus verbis conjugis, iratus est valde. Quæri potest, an Joseph se excusavit, et putant quidam quod non, ne dominam suam dehonestare, diffamareque turpiter videretur. Verumtamen, quia in textu habetur, quod vir fuit nimium credulus verbis suæ uxoris, videtur quod Joseph modeste ac decenter se excusavit saltem seorsum apud dominum suum, aut etiam coram præsentibus ad tollendum scandalum ex parte sui jam instans. Josephus tamen tangit, quod causam suam Deo commisit, neque ad satisfactionem, neque ad integram factorum manifestationem conversus est, sed necessitatem et vincula tacitus ac mansuetus sustinuit. Tradiditque Joseph in carcerem, ubi vincti regis custodiebantur, hoc est qui peccaverunt in regem, ut rei læsæ majestatis: qui carcer erat (ut fertur) intolerabilior carceribus ceteris; et erat ibi clausus.
paras.en: [[39:19|His master hearing these things|domino]] […] [the first words of the lemma are lost in the transcription], [[39:19|and giving too much credit to his wife's words, was very angry|et nimium credulus verbis conjugis, iratus est valde]]. It can be asked whether Joseph excused himself, and some think not, lest he should seem to dishonour his mistress and defame her shamefully. Yet since it is in the text that the husband was too credulous of his wife's words, it seems that Joseph excused himself modestly and becomingly, at least apart before his master, or even before those present, to remove the scandal already arising on his part. Josephus, however, touches on it that he committed his cause to God, and turned neither to giving satisfaction nor to a full disclosure of what had been done, but bore necessity and bonds in silence and meekness. [[39:20|And cast Joseph into the prison, where the king's prisoners were kept|Tradiditque Joseph in carcerem, ubi vincti regis custodiebantur]], that is, those who had sinned against the king, as guilty of high treason: which prison was (it is said) more unbearable than the other prisons; [[39:20|and he was there shut up|et erat ibi clausus]].

paras.t: Fuit autem Dominus cum Joseph. Dominus enim consolatur eos qui propter justitiam affliguntur, nec permittit hominem ultra vires tentari, sed facit cum tentatione proventum, et sperantes in se refocillat : et quoniam sanctus Joseph castitatis amore ac Dei intuitu carnales contempsit delicias, quas tam abundanter poterat habere ad libitum, meruit consolationum affluentiam divinarum. Et misertus illius in tantis adversitatibus, diffamiis, irrisionibus, dejectionibus, catenationibus, seu compeditionibus, quas innocentissime tener et virgineus juvenis toleravit, dedit ei gratiam in conspectu principis carceris. Fecit enim ipsum Joseph sua probitate, verecundia, morigeratione, acceptum principi carceris, mentemque principis illius inclinavit ad compatiendum ac diligendum Joseph, ita quod credidit eum (ut æstimo) innocentem : et forsan jam ante noverat eum, quia famosus erat et omnibus ante carus; fueruntque ejus prudentia et bonitas divulgatæ, quia tam diu rexit domum principis militum Pharaonis. Atque (ut asserit Josephus) subtraxit vincula a Joseph custos carceris, jubens eum meliori vesti cibo, quam vinctis competebat. Qui, princeps carceris, tradidit in manu, id est in dispositione et ministratione illius Joseph, universos, vinctos in carcere illo; et quidquid fiebat in carcere, sub ipso erat. Nec noverat aliquid, cunctis ei creditis, id est, princeps carceris non inquisivit nec scivit quid ageretur in carcere circa vinctos, quoniam omnia illa commiserat ipsi Joseph plenissime, certus de fidelitate ipsius : sicque Joseph vinctis illis diligenter et pie servivit, eundo de uno ad alium, et necessaria apportando ; sicque videtur quod princeps carceris amovit a pedibus Joseph ferramenta, quibus antea erat ligatus : de quibus cantamus in Psalmo. Humiliaverunt in compedibus pedes ejus : ut expedite transiret de uno ad alium.
paras.en: [[39:21|But the Lord was with Joseph|Fuit autem Dominus cum Joseph]]. For the Lord consoles those who are afflicted for justice' sake, [[1 Cor 10:13|who will not suffer you to be tempted above that which you are able|nec permittit hominem ultra vires tentari]], [[1 Cor 10:13|but will make also with temptation issue|sed facit cum tentatione proventum]], and refreshes those who hope in Him: and since holy Joseph, out of love of chastity and in regard of God, despised the delights of the flesh, which he could have had so abundantly at his pleasure, he merited an abundance of divine consolations. [[39:21|and having mercy upon him|Et misertus illius]] in so great adversities, defamations, mockeries, abasements, chains or fetters, which the tender and virginal youth bore most innocently, [[39:21|gave him favour in the sight of the chief keeper of the prison|dedit ei gratiam in conspectu principis carceris]]. For He made Joseph acceptable to the keeper of the prison by his uprightness, modesty and good conduct, and inclined the keeper's mind to pity and love Joseph, so that he believed him (as I judge) innocent: and perhaps he already knew him before, since he was famous and dear to all before, and his prudence and goodness had been spread abroad, since he had so long ruled the house of the captain of Pharao's soldiers. And (as Josephus asserts) the keeper of the prison took the bonds off Joseph, bidding him be given better clothing and food than befitted the prisoners. [[39:22|Who delivered into his hand|tradidit in manu]], the keeper of the prison, that is, into the disposal and ministry of Joseph, [[39:22|all the prisoners|universos, vinctos]] in that prison; [[39:22|and whatsoever was done|et quidquid fiebat]] in the prison, [[39:22|was under him|sub ipso erat]]. [[39:23|Neither did he himself know any thing, having committed all things to him|Nec noverat aliquid, cunctis ei creditis]], that is, the keeper of the prison did not inquire into or know what was done in the prison about the prisoners, since he had committed all that to Joseph most fully, being sure of his faithfulness: and so Joseph served those prisoners diligently and lovingly, going from one to another and bringing them what they needed; and so it seems that the keeper of the prison removed from Joseph's feet the irons with which he had been bound before: of which we sing in the Psalm, [[Ps 104:18|They humbled his feet in fetters|Humiliaverunt in compedibus pedes ejus]]: so that he might pass freely from one to another.

paras.t: Præterea, si quæratur, cur piissimus Deus permisit innocentem Joseph tot et tanta sustinere adversa : respondendum, quod ideo, quia volebat eum tempore præordinato sublimare ad maxima : idcirco primo exercitavit eum adversis, ut in illis et per illa acquireret gratiam ac virtutes, per quas mereretur conservari a Deo in altis ac prosperis, ne caderet et periret in illis : et simili modo eademque ratione exercitavit sanctum David per Saul, antequam promovit eum ad regnum. Non enim est finis sapientiæ Dei, et providentia ejus universa complectitur, atque infinitæ perfectionis consistit.
paras.en: Further, if it is asked why the most loving God allowed the innocent Joseph to suffer so many and such great adversities, it must be answered: because He willed to raise him at the foreordained time to the greatest things: so He first exercised him with adversities, that in them and through them he might acquire grace and virtues, by which he might deserve to be preserved by God in high and prosperous things, lest he should fall and perish in them: and in a like manner and for the same reason He exercised holy David through Saul before He promoted him to the kingdom. For there is no end to God's wisdom, and His providence embraces all things, and is of infinite perfection.

39.title: De spirituali hujus capituli tricesimi noni sensu
39.title_en: On the spiritual sense of this thirty-ninth chapter

paras.t: QUEMADMODUM Joseph ex terra promissionis in Ægyptum perductus est ab Ismaelitis negotiatoribus ; sic Christus, Synagoga relicta, per Apostolorum prædicationem ad gentiles in universum mundum portatus est : et sicut Putiphar eunuchus emit Joseph : sic gentes castæ effectæ, seque propter regnum Dei castrantes, Dominum Salvatorem emerunt, proprium intellectum in captivitatem redigendo in obsequium Christi, hoc est supernaturalibus fidei veritatibus sincere credendo, ad obediendum divinis præceptis. Emerunt itaque Filium Dei fidei sanctæ commercio et obedientiæ nummo, seque ipsos abnegando, ut lucrifacerent Christum. Emerunt eum credendo, orando et superando se ipsos, de qua emptione ipse in Apocalypsi testatur : Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum, probatum, ut locuples fias. Et Isaias : Emite, inquit, absque argento, et absque ulla commutatione vinum et lac. Fuitque Dominus cum eo, et erat vir in cunctis prospere agens. Sic et incomparabiliter plus fuit Deus Pater cum Christo homine ab incarnationis suæ exordio, ejus humanitatem in omnibus incessabiliter, infallibiliter et supergratiosissime dirigens; et fuit Christus vir in universis prosperrime agens, de spirituali prosperitate loquendo : quoniam quidquid egit aut pertulit, saluberrimum et incessabiliter meritorum membris ipsius fuit; sibi ipsi quoque accidentale promeruit præmium. Et habitavit in domo domini sui : quia primo habitavit in medio Synagogæ seu Israelitici populi, quæ fuit tunc domus Dei, qui est Dominus Christi, secundum ejus assumptam humanitatem ; habitavitque in medio electissimorum Judæorum, videlicet discipulorum suorum, quorum unus fatetur : Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis, et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre.
paras.en: As Joseph was brought from the land of promise into Egypt by the Ismaelite merchants, so Christ, leaving the Synagogue, was carried through the preaching of the Apostles to the gentiles throughout the whole world: and as Putiphar the eunuch bought Joseph, so the nations, made chaste, and [[Matt 19:12|who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven|seque propter regnum Dei castrantes]] [Denis: *for the kingdom of God*], bought the Lord and Saviour, [[2 Cor 10:5|bringing into captivity every understanding unto the obedience of Christ|proprium intellectum in captivitatem redigendo in obsequium Christi]], that is, believing sincerely the supernatural truths of faith, so as to obey the divine commandments. They bought the Son of God, then, by the traffic of holy faith and the coin of obedience, and by denying themselves, so as to gain Christ. They bought Him by believing, praying and overcoming themselves; of which buying He Himself testifies in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:18|I counsel thee to buy of me gold, fire tried, that thou mayest be made rich|Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum, probatum, ut locuples fias]] [Denis's text adds *probatum*, tried]. And Isaias: [[Is 55:1|buy wine and milk without money, and without any price|Emite, inquit, absque argento, et absque ulla commutatione vinum et lac]]. [[39:2|And the Lord was with him, and he was a prosperous man in all things|Fuitque Dominus cum eo, et erat vir in cunctis prospere agens]]. So too, and incomparably more, God the Father was with Christ as man from the beginning of His incarnation, guiding His humanity in all things unceasingly, unfailingly and most graciously; and Christ was a man acting most prosperously in all things, speaking of spiritual prosperity: since whatever He did or suffered was most saving and unceasingly meritorious for His members; for Himself too He merited the accidental reward. [[39:2|and he dwelt in his master's house|Et habitavit in domo domini sui]]: since first He dwelt in the midst of the Synagogue, or the people of Israel, which was then the house of God, who is the Lord of Christ according to His assumed humanity; and He dwelt in the midst of the most chosen of the Jews, namely His disciples, one of whom confesses: [[John 1:14|And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us|Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis]] [[John 1:14|and we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father|et vidimus gloriam ejus, gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre]].

paras.t: Præterea cuncta quæ gessit Christus inter homines conversando, dirigebantur in manu illius, hoc est cooperatione et virtute Spiritus Sancti, imo totius superbenedictissimæ Trinitatis. Siquidem anima Christi a suæ creationis primordio fuit summe repleta omni Spiritus Sancti dono, per quod summe ac perfectissime dirigibilis erat a Spiritu Sancto ; propter quod de eo et in ejus persona Isaias prædixit : Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me. Itemque : Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus, etc. Invenitque Joseph gratiam coram domino suo. Sic et Christus acceptissimus fuit Patri suo, quemadmodum in Evangelio profitetur : Pater non reliquit me solum, quia ego quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper. Et ministrabat ei, in quantum homo, quemadmodum protestatur : Sicut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio. Unde per Isaiam Pater ait de Filio incarnato : Ecce servus meus, suscipiam eum : electus meus, complacuit sibi in illo anima mea. A quo præpositus omnibus, gubernabat sibi creditam domum. Sic Christus a Deo universis Judæis prælatus, tanquam verus rex Israel, et summus sacerdos secundum ordinem Melchisedech, direxit Judæos ad veram salutem, prædicando, corripiendo, miracula faciendo, evangelicam legem tradendo ; specialiter quoque gubernavit sibi creditam domum, puta electos ex Israel beatos suos discipulos, de quibus fatetur : Pater, quos dedisti mihi, ego servabam eos, et non perdidi quemquam eorum. Benedixitque Dominus domui Ægyptii propter Joseph. Sic meritis Salvatoris Deus Trinitas benedixit congregationi ipsius, quibus in die Pentecostes misit in signo visibili Spiritum Sanctum, qui corda illorum copiosissime ac ferventissime adimplevit.
paras.en: Further, all that Christ did in His life among men [[39:3|made all that he did to prosper in his hand|dirigebantur in manu illius]], that is, by the co-operation and power of the Holy Ghost, nay of the whole most blessed Trinity. For the soul of Christ from the first moment of its creation was supremely filled with every gift of the Holy Ghost, by which it was supremely and most perfectly guidable by the Holy Ghost; for which reason Isaias foretold of Him and in His person: [[Is 61:1|The spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord hath anointed me|Spiritus Domini super me, eo quod unxerit me]]. And again: [[Is 11:2|And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding|Requiescet super eum Spiritus Domini, spiritus sapientiæ et intellectus]], etc. [the margin gives Psal. xc, 2; the words are those of Is 11:2]. [[39:4|And Joseph found favour in the sight of his master|Invenitque Joseph gratiam coram domino suo]]. So Christ too was most acceptable to His Father, as He professes in the Gospel: [[John 8:29|he hath not left me alone. For I do always the things that please him|Pater non reliquit me solum, quia ego quæ placita sunt ei, facio semper]]. [[39:4|and ministered to him|Et ministrabat ei]], as man, as He declares: [[John 14:31|and as the Father hath given me commandments, so do I|Sicut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio]]. Hence through Isaias the Father says of the incarnate Son: [[Is 42:1|Behold my servant, I will uphold him: my elect, my soul delighteth in him|Ecce servus meus, suscipiam eum : electus meus, complacuit sibi in illo anima mea]]. [[39:4|and being set over all by him, he governed the house committed to him|A quo præpositus omnibus, gubernabat sibi creditam domum]]. So Christ, set by God over all the Jews as the true king of Israel, and the high priest [[Ps 109:4|according to the order of Melchisedech|secundum ordinem Melchisedech]], directed the Jews to true salvation by preaching, rebuking, working miracles and handing on the law of the Gospel; and in particular He governed the house committed to Him, namely His blessed disciples chosen out of Israel, of whom He confesses: Father, [[John 17:12|Those whom thou gavest me have I kept: and none of them is lost|quos dedisti mihi, ego servabam eos, et non perdidi quemquam eorum]] [Denis's wording is nearer John 18:9]. [[39:5|And the Lord blessed the house of the Egyptian for Joseph's sake|Benedixitque Dominus domui Ægyptii propter Joseph]]. So by the merits of the Saviour God the Trinity blessed His company, to whom on the day of Pentecost He sent the Holy Ghost in a visible sign, who filled their hearts most abundantly and most fervently[[Acts 2:2||]][[Acts 2:4||]].

paras.t: Erat autem Joseph pulchra facie, et decorus adspectu. Sic Christus, in quantum Deus, essentialiter et incircumscriptibiliter pulcher, secundum naturam assumptam fuit multiplici pulchritudine excellentissime decoratus ; nec decuit qui humanitatem, nisi omni virtutum donorum, fructuum, beatitudinum ac gratiarum pulchritudine venustissimam, assumi a Verbo æterno. Fuit et corpore speciosus forma præ filiis hominum, et omni morali venustate summe conspicuus ; nec fuit usquam in eo ulla macula culpæ, de quo Sponsa dicit in Canticis : Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi, et rubicundus. Porro, per dominam quæ injecit oculos suos in Joseph, et dixit, Dormi mecum : accipitur Synagoga, quæ aliquando fuit sponsa et uxor Dei, de quo Jeremias disseruit : Non fuit Israel viduatus a Deo suo : qui ait per Isaiam : Quis est iste libellus repudii quo reliqui matrem vestram ? Hæc domina, tempore procedente, facta est spiritualiter meretrix, cui ait Propheta : Et nunc, meretrix, audi verbum Domini. Et Isaias : Quomodo, inquit, facta est meretrix civitas fidelis ? Hæc voluit Christum suis adulteriis, id est erroribus, falsitatibusque involvere, ut sibi in illicitis consentiret, et se esse regem Messiam ac Dei Filium denegaret, nec novam traderet legem : quæ tandem suis passionibus ebria, apprehendit Christum cum vestibus ; ipse autem relicto in manibus adulteræ pallio, fugit et egressus est foras : quia corpus suum permisit ab illa capi, flagellari, et crucifigi, ac eo ab anima sua relicto, descendit in limbum patrum, eodemque die fuit in paradiso. Insuper Synagoga dixit Dominum Jesum ad se ingressum, ut sibi illuderet, id est, per falsas doctrinas deciperet, clamitans coram domino suo Pilato : Seducit turbas, docens per universam Judæam. Itemque : Domine, recordati sumus quia seductor ille adhuc vivens dixit, Post tres dies resurgam. Hinc procuravit Christum sepultum in sepulcro, quasi in carcere custodiri, et lapidem superpositum sigillo signari.
paras.en: [[39:6|And Joseph was of a beautiful countenance, and comely to behold|Erat autem Joseph pulchra facie, et decorus adspectu]]. So Christ, as God essentially and boundlessly beautiful, was adorned most excellently with manifold beauty according to the nature He assumed; nor was it fitting that a humanity should be assumed by the eternal Word that was not most lovely with every beauty of virtues, gifts, fruits, beatitudes and graces. He was also [[Ps 44:3|beautiful above the sons of men|speciosus forma præ filiis hominum]] in body, and supremely conspicuous in every moral grace; nor was there ever in Him any stain of fault; of whom the Bride says in the Canticles: [[Cant 1:15|Behold thou art fair, my beloved|Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi]], and ruddy [Denis's text: *et rubicundus*; the Vulgate has *et decorus*, and comely]. Further, by the mistress who [[39:7|cast her eyes on Joseph, and said: Lie with me|injecit oculos suos in Joseph, et dixit, Dormi mecum]], is understood the Synagogue, which was once the bride and wife of God, of whom Jeremias declared: Israel [[Jer 51:5|have not been forsaken by their God|Non fuit Israel viduatus a Deo suo]] [the margin gives Jer. iii, 5; the words are those of Jer 51:5, *viduatus*, widowed, where the Douay has *forsaken*]: who says through Isaias: [[Is 50:1|What is this bill of the divorce of your mother, with which I have put her away|Quis est iste libellus repudii quo reliqui matrem vestram]]? This mistress, as time went on, became spiritually a harlot, to whom the Prophet says: [[Ezech 16:35|Therefore, O harlot, hear the word of the Lord|Et nunc, meretrix, audi verbum Domini]]. And Isaias: [[Is 1:21|How is the faithful city, that was full of judgment, become a harlot?|Quomodo, inquit, facta est meretrix civitas fidelis]] She wished to entangle Christ in her adulteries, that is, her errors and falsehoods, that He might consent to her in unlawful things, and deny that He was the king Messias and the Son of God, and not hand on the new law: and at last, drunk with her passions, she caught hold of Christ by His garments; but He, [[39:12|leaving the garment in her hand, fled, and went out|relicto in manibus adulteræ pallio, fugit et egressus est foras]]: since He allowed His body to be taken by her, scourged and crucified, and, leaving it by His soul, He went down to the limbo of the fathers, and the same day was in paradise. Further, the Synagogue said that the Lord Jesus had come in to her to abuse her, that is, to deceive her by false teachings, crying out before her lord Pilate: [[Luke 23:5|He stirreth up the people, teaching throughout all Judea|Seducit turbas, docens per universam Judæam]][[John 7:12||]] [Denis: *Seducit turbas*, He seduceth the crowds, as in John 7:12]. And again: [[Matt 27:63|Sir, we have remembered, that that seducer said, while he was yet alive: After three days I will rise again|Domine, recordati sumus quia seductor ille adhuc vivens dixit, Post tres dies resurgam]]. Hence she had Christ, buried in the tomb, kept as it were in prison, and the stone laid over it sealed with a seal[[Matt 27:66||]].

paras.t: Postremo ad Omnipotentis laudem ac gloriam, ædificationemque nostram, vigilantissima mente consideremus omnipotentiam gratiæ Dei, et beatissimi Joseph […] patriarchæ virtutes, qualiter ab infantia mansit in sancta vita, et zelator fuit justitiæ, ac caritativus delinquentium accusator. Deinde in terra aliena idololatriis plena, mansit immobilis in Dei timore, nec ab impiis poterat unquam perverti. Quumque pulcherrimus juvenis esset, et rebus omnibus, honore quoque et gloria abundaret, atque a domina sua, muliere utique secundum sæculum magna, tam diu ac sæpe incitaretur ad voluptatem, insuperabiliter ac virilissime restitit ei. Deinceps ob […] suam inflexibilem æquitatem injustissime incarceratus, nequaquam recessit corde a Domino, nec contra ipsius providentiam murmuravit : sed longanimiter et patientissime tulit, quidquid sapientia Creatoris super se evenire permisit. Itaque comparemus nos ipsos ad virum tantum, et conspiciemus quam infinita sit nostra miseria, nostra defectuositas, nostra malitia : sicque pœniteamus ex intimo mentis affectu, ac sancti hujus Patriarchæ virtutes et castimoniam imitari atque amplecti indefesse conemur.
paras.en: Lastly, to the praise and glory of the Almighty and to our own edification, let us consider with most watchful mind the omnipotence of God's grace, and the virtues of the most blessed patriarch Joseph […], how from childhood he remained in a holy life, and was a zealot for justice and a loving accuser of wrongdoers. Then, in a foreign land full of idolatries, he remained unmoved in the fear of God, nor could he ever be perverted by the ungodly. And when he was a most beautiful youth, abounding in all things, in honour too and glory, and was urged to pleasure so long and so often by his mistress, a woman great indeed according to the world, he resisted her invincibly and most manfully. Then, imprisoned most unjustly for his […] [a word is lost here in the transcription] unbending uprightness, he never withdrew in heart from the Lord, nor murmured against His providence, but bore with long-suffering and the greatest patience whatever the wisdom of the Creator allowed to befall him. Let us compare ourselves, then, with so great a man, and we shall see how infinite is our misery, our failing, our malice: and so let us repent with the inmost affection of the mind, and strive tirelessly to imitate and embrace the virtues and chastity of this holy Patriarch.

40.title: Expositio capituli quadragesimi: His itaque gestis, accidit ut peccarent duo eunuchi
40.title_en: Exposition of the fortieth chapter: “After this, it came to pass, that two eunuchs … offended”

paras.t: Recitatur in isto capitulo, qualiter et ex qua causa cœpit sapientia hujus præinclyti Joseph manifestari regi Ægypti.
paras.en: This chapter relates how, and from what cause, the wisdom of this most renowned Joseph began to be made known to the king of Egypt.

paras.t: His, quæ in præcedenti capitulo sunt narrata, itaque gestis, accidit ut peccarent duo eunuchi, videlicet pincerna regis Ægypti, et pistor, domino suo, videlicet Pharaoni. Tamen quid mali egerint contra regem, aut quid omiserint de agendis, Scriptura non exprimit, nec certum est: quanquam Judæi juxta consuetudinem suarum fabularum, affirmant peccatum pincernæ fuisse, quod in potu regis inventa est musca; pistoris vero, quia in pane regis parvus lapis inventus est. Cur autem isti ministri vocentur eunuchi, dictum est in expositione capituli tricesimi septimi. Iratusque contra eos Pharao: nam alter pincernis præerat, alter pistoribus regis, quæ fuerunt duo magna officia: sicque Pharao tanto acrius fuit contra eos irascens, quanto eos ad officia promovit majora, aut in eisdem servavit; misit eos in carcerem principis militum, in quo erat vinctus et Joseph. Itaque carcer ille fuit sub ditione principis militiæ, qui in eumdem carcerem fecerat Joseph retrudi.
paras.en: [[40:1|After this|His]], that is, when the things narrated in the preceding chapter had thus been done, [[40:1|it came to pass, that two eunuchs|accidit ut peccarent duo eunuchi]], namely [[40:1|the butler and the baker of the king of Egypt|pincerna regis Ægypti, et pistor]], [[40:1|offended their lord|domino suo]], namely Pharao. Yet what evil they did against the king, or what they left undone of what they should have done, Scripture does not state, nor is it certain; although the Jews, after the custom of their fables, affirm that the butler's offence was that a fly was found in the king's drink, and the baker's that a little stone was found in the king's bread. Why these ministers are called eunuchs was said in the exposition of the thirty-seventh chapter. [[40:2|And Pharao being angry with them|Iratusque contra eos Pharao]]: [[40:2|now the one was chief butler, the other chief baker|nam alter pincernis præerat, alter pistoribus]] of the king, which were two great offices; and so Pharao was the more sharply angry with them, the greater the offices to which he had promoted them or in which he had kept them. [[40:3|He sent them to the prison of the commander of the soldiers, in which Joseph also was prisoner|misit eos in carcerem principis militum, in quo erat vinctus et Joseph]]. So that prison was under the authority of the commander of the soldiery, who had had Joseph thrust into that same prison.

paras.t: Sed quæri potest, qualiter Joseph dicatur ibi nunc vinctus, quum ex præcedenti capitulo sit probatum, quod compedes erant depositi. Respondetur, quod vinctus nunc fertur, vel quia jam antea erat ligatus compedibus, vel quia ibidem clausus, vel quia adhuc habebat aliquam ligaturam in crure, cum qua tamen poterat ambulare in carcere. At custos carceris tradidit eos Joseph, etc., ut eis serviret.
paras.en: But it may be asked how Joseph is now said to be a prisoner [*vinctus*, literally "bound"] there, since it was shown from the preceding chapter that his fetters had been taken off. The answer is that he is now called bound, either because he had already been bound with fetters before, or because he was shut up there[[Gen 39:20||]], or because he still had some binding on his leg, with which he could nevertheless walk about in the prison. [[40:4|But the keeper of the prison delivered them to Joseph|At custos carceris tradidit eos Joseph]], etc., to serve them.

paras.t: Videruntque ambo somnium nocte una, id est visionem nocturnam imaginariam, quæ tamen non fuit casualis, aut pure naturalis, sed angelico ministerio in interioribus sensibus eorum exhibita ac formata; nec propter eorum merita fiebat illis repræsentatio talis in somno, sed ut per occasionem expositionis somniorum illorum, manifestaretur suo tempore Pharaoni sapientia Joseph propter commune hominum bonum. Viderunt itaque somnium, juxta interpretationem congruam sibi, hoc est significativum eorum quæ evenerunt eis ambobus.
paras.en: [[40:5|And they both dreamed a dream the same night|Videruntque ambo somnium nocte una]], that is, a nightly imaginary vision [that is, one formed in the imagination, not seen with the bodily eyes], which yet was not by chance or purely natural, but was shown and formed in their inner senses by the ministry of angels; nor was such a representation made to them in sleep for their merits, but so that, by occasion of the exposition of those dreams, the wisdom of Joseph might in its time be made known to Pharao for the common good of men. So they dreamed a dream [[40:5|according to the interpretation agreeing to themselves|juxta interpretationem congruam sibi]], that is, signifying the things that befell them both.

paras.t: Ad quos quum introisset, etc., sciscitatus est eos, dicens: Cur tristior est hodie solito facies vestra? hoc est, Cur nunc majoris tristitiæ ac timoris signa in vultibus vestris apparent? Interior enim dispositio, clarius celeriusque solet in facie apparere. Qui responderunt: Somnium vidimus, hoc est, unusquisque nostrum interiori intuitu aliquid vidit in somno. Erant autem gentiles idololatræ multum intenti somniis suis, visionibus atque oraculis, in quibus a dæmonibus variis modis illudebantur, et quasi semper putabant sibi per talia aliqua designari. Et non est qui interpretetur nobis, hoc est, nullus hic est qui nobis ea exponat. Habebant autem Ægyptii quosdam augures et maleficos ac divinos, a quibus talium expositiones quærebant, qui tunc non fuerunt præsto incarceratis.
paras.en: [[40:6|And when Joseph was come into them|Ad quos quum introisset]], etc., [[40:7|He asked them, saying: Why is your countenance sadder today than usual?|sciscitatus est eos, dicens: Cur tristior est hodie solito facies vestra?]] that is, Why do signs of greater sadness and fear now appear in your faces? For the inner disposition is wont to show more clearly and quickly in the face. [[40:8|They answered: We have dreamed a dream|Qui responderunt: Somnium vidimus]], that is, each of us has seen something in sleep with the inner sight. Now the gentile idolaters were much taken up with their dreams, visions and oracles, in which they were deluded by the demons in various ways, and they almost always thought that something was signified to them by such things. [[40:8|and there is nobody to interpret it to us|Et non est qui interpretetur nobis]], that is, there is no one here to expound them to us. For the Egyptians had certain augurs, sorcerers and diviners, from whom they sought the exposition of such things, and these were not then at hand for the prisoners.

paras.t: Dixitque ad eos Joseph: Numquid non Dei est interpretatio? quasi dicat, Utique a vero Deo, non ab idolis, est somniorum interpretatio requirenda, et a servis ac vatibus Dei, non ab auguribus atque ariolis: quoniam est donum Dei, vere et certitudinaliter exponere, somnia ac secreta; præsertim quoque futurorum pure contingentium veritas per somnium præsignata, non potest certitudinaliter, nisi ex divina revelatione, prænosci. Referte mihi quid videritis.
paras.en: [[40:8|And Joseph said to them: Doth not interpretation belong to God?|Dixitque ad eos Joseph: Numquid non Dei est interpretatio?]] as if to say: Surely the interpretation of dreams is to be sought from the true God, not from idols, and from the servants and prophets of God, not from augurs and soothsayers; for it is the gift of God to expound dreams and secrets truly and with certainty; and above all, the truth of purely contingent future things [that is, things that may or may not come to pass, depending on free causes] foreshown in a dream cannot be known beforehand with certainty except by divine revelation. [[40:8|Tell me what you have dreamed|Referte mihi quid videritis]].

paras.t: Narravit prior præpositus pincernarum somnium suum: Videbam coram me vitem, in qua erant tres propagines, id est frondes seu palmites, crescere paulatim in gemmas, hoc est botros, et post flores vidi uvas maturescere; calicemque Pharaonis, id est scyphum ex quo bibere solet, in manu mea. Tuli ergo, hoc est, de vite deposui, uvas, et expressi, id est, humorem earum premendo effluere feci, in calicem quem tenebam, et tradidi poculum Pharaoni. Non res istas, sed earum similitudines vidit ille in somno, et videbatur ei in somno quod videret, et faceret ea quæ dicta sunt, quia in somno clausa est ratio, et anima similitudines rerum accipit, non ut similitudines, sed pro rebus ipsis, et in hoc ipso decipitur; qui autem in somno habent propheticas visiones, supernaturaliter illuminantur, ad intelligendum earum significationes, nec decipiuntur neque utuntur formis pro rebus per eas significatis, sed accipiunt eas ut similitudines rerum.
paras.en: [[40:9|The chief butler first told his dream: I saw before me a vine|Narravit prior præpositus pincernarum somnium suum: Videbam coram me vitem]], [[40:10|On which were three branches|in qua erant tres propagines]], that is, leafy shoots or tendrils, [[40:10|which by little and little sent out buds|crescere paulatim in gemmas]], that is, clusters, [[40:10|and after the blossoms|et post flores]] I saw it [[40:10|brought forth ripe grapes|uvas maturescere]] [Denis reads *et post flores vidi uvas maturescere*, "and after the blossoms I saw the grapes ripen"]; [[40:11|And the cup of Pharao|calicemque Pharaonis]], that is, the goblet from which he is wont to drink, [[40:11|was in my hand|in manu mea]]. [[40:11|and I took|Tuli ergo]], that is, took down from the vine, [[40:11|the grapes, and pressed them|uvas, et expressi]], that is, made their juice flow out by pressing them, [[40:11|into the cup which I held, and I gave the cup to Pharao|in calicem quem tenebam, et tradidi poculum Pharaoni]]. He did not see these things themselves in sleep, but their likenesses; and it seemed to him in sleep that he saw and did the things said, because in sleep the reason is shut, and the soul takes the likenesses of things not as likenesses but for the things themselves, and in this very thing it is deceived. But those who have prophetic visions in sleep are enlightened supernaturally to understand their meanings, and are not deceived, nor do they use the forms for the things signified by them, but take them as likenesses of things.

paras.t: Respondit Joseph: Hæc est interpretatio somnii: Tres propagines, tres adhuc dies sunt, hoc est, tres rami illi præsignant tres dies, post quos recordabitur Pharao ministerii tui, id est, in sua refectione memor erit, quam decenter consueveras ei porrigere potum; et restituet te in gradum pristinum, etc., quoniam inquisitione de te facta, inveniet, vel jam invenit, te mortem non meruisse. Tantum memento mei, quum bene tibi fuerit, etc. Littera plana est.
paras.en: [[40:12|Joseph answered: This is the interpretation of the dream: The three branches, are yet three days|Respondit Joseph: Hæc est interpretatio somnii: Tres propagines, tres adhuc dies sunt]], that is, those three branches foreshow three days, [[40:13|After which Pharao will remember thy service|post quos recordabitur Pharao ministerii tui]], that is, at his meal he will call to mind how fittingly thou wert wont to hand him his drink; [[40:13|and will restore thee to thy former place|et restituet te in gradum pristinum]], etc., because, inquiry having been made about thee, he will find, or has already found, that thou didst not deserve death. [[40:14|Only remember me when it shall be well with thee|Tantum memento mei, quum bene tibi fuerit]], etc. The letter is plain.

paras.t: Videns pistorum magister, quod prudenter somnium dissolvisset, id est, quod Joseph sapienter exposuisset somnialem apparitionem pincernæ, auferendo ab eo vinculum et velamen suæ difficultatis, quod clausum fuerat et obscurum, ait: Et ego vidi somnium, quod tria canistra farinæ haberem super caput meum: et in canistro quod erat excelsius aliis duobus, tanquam superpositum eis, portare me putabam omnes cibos qui fiunt arte pistoria, avesque comedere ex eo. Somnia horum duorum ministrata sunt eis per similitudines materiarum, eorum officiis satis congruentes. Secundum Glossam in Hebræo habetur, Tres cophinos farinæ. Josephus autem ait: Duo canistra plena panibus, tertium vero plenum obsonio, hoc est cibo delicato, sicut est regius cibus. Unde in Græco habetur, tria canistra χονδριτῶν, id est panum secundorum, puta grossorum; sicque datur intelligi, quod in tertio apparuit esca regalis. Verum de diversitate parva aut nulla est vis, quoniam significatio una est quæ subjungitur.
paras.en: [[40:16|The chief baker seeing that he had wisely interpreted the dream|Videns pistorum magister, quod prudenter somnium dissolvisset]] [*dissolvisset*, literally "had loosed", which Denis's gloss takes up], that is, that Joseph had wisely expounded the butler's dream-appearance, taking from it the bond and veil of its difficulty, which had been shut and obscure, [[40:16|said: I also dreamed a dream, That I had three baskets of meal upon my head|ait: Et ego vidi somnium, quod tria canistra farinæ haberem super caput meum]]: [[40:17|And that in one basket which was uppermost|et in canistro quod erat excelsius]] above the other two, as though set on top of them, [[40:17|I carried all meats that are made by the art of baking|portare me putabam omnes cibos qui fiunt arte pistoria]] [Denis reads *portare me putabam*, "I thought I carried"], [[40:17|and that the birds ate out of it|avesque comedere ex eo]]. The dreams of these two were given them through likenesses of materials well suited to their offices. According to the Gloss, the Hebrew has: Three hampers [*cophinos*] of meal. But Josephus says: Two baskets full of loaves, and the third full of relishes [*obsonium*, the food eaten with bread], that is, of dainty food, such as is the king's food. Hence the Greek has: three baskets χονδριτῶν, that is, of second bread, namely coarse bread [that is, bread of coarse meal, not the finest flour]; and so it is given to be understood that in the third appeared royal fare. But there is little or no weight in the difference, since the meaning that follows is one.

paras.t: Respondit Joseph: Hæc est interpretatio somnii: Tria canistra, tres adhuc dies sunt: post quos auferet Pharao caput tuum, hoc est, decollari te faciet. Porro audito somnio hujus pistoris, Joseph, antequam illud interpretaretur, locutus est, Mallem esse interpres bonorum, ut Josephus dicit.
paras.en: [[40:18|Joseph answered: This is the interpretation of the dream: The three baskets, are yet three days|Respondit Joseph: Hæc est interpretatio somnii: Tria canistra, tres adhuc dies sunt]]: [[40:19|After which Pharao will take thy head from thee|post quos auferet Pharao caput tuum]], that is, will have thee beheaded. Moreover, on hearing this baker's dream, Joseph, before he interpreted it, said: I would rather be an interpreter of good things, as Josephus says.

paras.t: Exinde die tertio natalitius Pharao […] […] erat, id est dies anniversaria nativitatis regis illius. Eratque Pharao nomen commune regum Ægypti, non proprium, sicut Delphinus commune est nomen regum Franciæ. Secundum Hieronymum, nullum invenimus celebrasse diem suæ nativitatis, nisi Pharaonem et Herodem ut quarum par fuit impietas, una esset solennitas. Verumtamen quamvis hoc non legatur in Scripturis sanctis de aliis regibus, aliqui tamen dicunt plurium gentilium regum consuetudinem hanc fuisse. Atque ut tangit Glossa, Pharao et Herodes diem nativitatis suæ celebraverunt, quia ex hora nativitatis, id est ex fato seu influentia horæ illius, se reges factos putabant: vel ad demonstrandum beatitudinem excellentiæ suæ, quasi præclarum bonum acciderit eis ac mundo in hora qua nati sunt.
paras.en: [[40:20|The third day after this|Exinde die tertio]] [[40:20|the birthday of Pharao|natalitius Pharao]] […] [[40:20|was|erat]], that is, the yearly day of that king's birth. Now Pharao was a name common to the kings of Egypt, not a proper name, as Dauphin is a name common to the kings of France [strictly, *Dauphin* was the title of the heir to the French throne]. According to Jerome, we find no one who celebrated his birthday except Pharao and Herod[[Matt 14:6||]], so that those whose impiety was equal might have one solemnity [the margin gives Jerome on Matthew, ch. xiv]. Yet although this is not read in the Holy Scriptures of other kings, some nevertheless say that this was the custom of many gentile kings. And, as the Gloss touches on, Pharao and Herod celebrated their birthday because they thought they had been made kings by the hour of their birth, that is, by the fate or influence of that hour [that is, of the stars at that hour]; or to show forth the blessedness of their own excellence, as though a splendid good had befallen them and the world in the hour in which they were born.

paras.t: Qui faciens grande convivium pueris suis, id est servis et etiam filiis et cognatis, domesticis, aliisque nobilibus quos vocavit, sicut Herodes primis Galilææ, recordatus est inter epulas magistri pincernarum, etc.; fecitque eis sicut Joseph prædixit. Forsan invenit unum illorum præ alio excusabilem: vel ad demonstrandum suæ majestatis ac libertatis potentiam, fecit tale judicium, ostendens se posse exaltare et humiliare, ut amplius timeretur. Ut conjectoris veritas probaretur, id est, ut Joseph ostenderetur verus somniorum interpres, et quod evenit, veraciter prædixisse. Verumtamen quod ait, Ut conjectoris, etc., intelligendum est consecutive seu concomitanter, non directe causaliter. Non enim Pharao fecit illa, ut veritas interpretationis Joseph ostenderetur; sed ad factum Pharaonis, consecuta est illa ostensio præter Pharaonis intentionem, sed non sine præordinatione divina. Denique Joseph vocatur conjector, non quod quasi dubie aut fortuitu verum prædixerit, aut absque certitudine visiones illorum exposuerit; sed nomen conjectoris sumitur hic extense; vel ideo sic vocatur, quia Ægyptii illi putabant eum instar conjicientium esse locutum.
paras.en: [[40:20|and he made a great feast for his servants|Qui faciens grande convivium pueris suis]] [*pueris*, literally "boys", a word used both of servants and of children], that is, for his servants, and also for his sons and kinsmen, his household, and the other nobles whom he invited, as Herod did for the [[Mark 6:21|chief men of Galilee|primis Galilææ]], [[40:20|and at the banquet remembered the chief butler|recordatus est inter epulas magistri pincernarum]], etc.; and he did to them as Joseph had foretold. Perhaps he found one of them more excusable than the other; or, to show the power of his majesty and freedom, he gave such a judgment, showing that he could exalt and humble, so that he might be the more feared. [[40:22|that the truth of the interpreter might be shewn|Ut conjectoris veritas probaretur]], that is, so that Joseph might be shown to be a true interpreter of dreams, and to have foretold truly what came to pass. Yet the words *that the truth of the interpreter*, etc., are to be understood as of what follows or goes along with the deed, not as of its direct cause. For Pharao did not do these things so that the truth of Joseph's interpretation might be shown; but upon Pharao's deed that showing followed, beyond Pharao's intention, though not without divine preordination. Lastly, Joseph is called *conjector* [that is, one who conjectures or guesses, here rendered "interpreter"], not because he foretold the truth as if doubtfully or by chance, or expounded their visions without certainty; but the name *conjector* is taken here in a wide sense; or else he is so called because those Egyptians thought he had spoken in the manner of those who conjecture.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, quando revelavit Deus ipsi Joseph intelligentiam somniorum illorum. Respondendum, quod secundum doctores, gratia prophetiæ est donum actuale magis quam habituale, quia non inest Prophetis fixe ad eorum complacitum, sed prout actualiter tanguntur et illustrantur a Spiritu Sancto: ideo fieri potuit ut Joseph, audiendo recitationem somniorum illorum, acceperit desuper actualem illuminationem, qua sensum somniorum illorum clarissime intellexit; vel forte Deus jam ante revelavit sibi tam somnia illa, quam interpretationem eorum; vel ex inspiratione divina cognovit sibi revelandam somniorum illorum intelligentiam, quum ea audiret aut paulo post.
paras.en: Concerning these things it is asked when God revealed to Joseph himself the understanding of those dreams. The answer is that, according to the doctors, the grace of prophecy is an actual gift rather than a habitual one [that is, a light given in the moment, not a lasting disposition the prophet can use at will], since it is not fixed in the Prophets at their pleasure, but is present as they are actually touched and enlightened by the Holy Ghost. So it could be that Joseph, on hearing those dreams told, received from above an actual illumination by which he understood their sense most clearly; or perhaps God had already revealed to him beforehand both those dreams and their interpretation; or he knew by divine inspiration that the understanding of those dreams would be revealed to him when he heard them, or soon after.

paras.t: Et tamen succedentibus prosperis, præpositus pincernarum oblitus est interpretis sui. Sic multi tempore prosperitatis obliviscuntur pristinæ adversitatis seu paupertatis, imo et beneficiorum quæ eis in adversis exhibita sunt, ac benefactorum suorum. Quocontra in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum, et gratiam fidejussoris tui ne obliviscaris. Denique sicut vexatio dat intellectum, sic prosperatio, inflatio ac voluptas mentem obscurant. Dicunt autem Hebræi id accidisse, quoniam Joseph nimis confidit humano auxilio: quod etiam asseruit Augustinus in homilia de Joseph. Sed potius reor, sine ipsius culpa hoc evenisse ex dispositione divina, quatenus ipse Joseph diutius carcerem sustinendo, gratiam mereretur majorem; ejusque patientia omnibus nobis in exemplum proponeretur, et tempore opportuno desuper præstituto, multo salubrius ab ergastulo eriperetur. Ex præordinatione namque divina non solum contingit tribulatio electorum, sed etiam duratio seu diuturnitas ejus.
paras.en: [[40:23|But the chief butler, when things prospered with him, forgot his interpreter|Et tamen succedentibus prosperis, præpositus pincernarum oblitus est interpretis sui]]. So many in time of prosperity forget their former adversity or poverty, nay, even the benefits shown them in adversity, and their benefactors. Against this it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 11:27|In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils|In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum]], and [[Ecclus 29:19|Forget not the kindness of thy surety|gratiam fidejussoris tui ne obliviscaris]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xxix, 20, the Vulgate's number; the Douay-Rheims numbers this verse 19]. Lastly, as [[Is 28:19|vexation alone shall make you understand|vexatio dat intellectum]] [Denis: *vexatio dat intellectum*, "vexation giveth understanding"], so prosperity, being puffed up, and pleasure darken the mind. Now the Hebrews say that this happened because Joseph trusted too much in human help; and Augustine also asserted this in the homily on Joseph. But I rather think that this came about without any fault of his, by divine disposition, so that Joseph, by enduring the prison longer, might merit greater grace, and his patience be set before all of us as an example, and at the fitting time appointed from above he might be rescued from the dungeon far more profitably. For by divine preordination there comes about not only the tribulation of the elect, but also its duration or length.

41.title: Expositio capituli quadragesimi primi: Post duos annos vidit Pharao somnium
41.title_en: Exposition of the forty-first chapter: “After two years Pharao had a dream”

paras.t: Qualiter Joseph post tribulationem longam et suam extremam dejectionem, sit sublimatus divitiis, deliciis, atque honoribus, præsens refert capitulum. Post duos annos a die quo Joseph exposuit somnium principis pincernarum, seu liberationis illius de carcere, vidit Pharao somnium, id est visionem in somno, videlicet imaginariam apparitionem, sibi per angelum bonum exhibitam tanquam principi communitatis, et propter commune bonum, non propter regis idololatræ meritum. Deus namque frequenter ostendit specialiter providentiam suam circa publicas personas, et aliqua bona eis largitur, ac futura præmonstrat, propter commodum politiæ et utilitatem regni totius, cujus prosperitas magna ex parte dependet a principe.
paras.en: How Joseph, after long tribulation and his utmost abasement, was raised up with riches, delights and honours, the present chapter relates. [[41:1|After two years|Post duos annos]] from the day on which Joseph expounded the dream of the chief of the butlers, or from that man's release from prison, [[41:1|Pharao had a dream|vidit Pharao somnium]], that is, a vision in sleep, namely an imaginary apparition [that is, one formed in the imagination, as distinct from a bodily sight or a purely intellectual vision], shown to him by a good angel as to the head of a community, and for the common good, not for the merit of an idolatrous king. For God often shows His providence in a special way towards public persons, bestows certain goods on them, and shows them the future beforehand, for the benefit of the commonwealth and the profit of the whole kingdom, whose prosperity depends in great part on the prince.

paras.t: Putabat se stare super fluvium, id est, in somno sibi apparuit quod staret super Nilum, videlicet in terra seu ripa juxta Nilum, de quo ascendebant septem boves, secundum apparentiam somnialem, pulchræ et crassæ nimis: sicque boves accipiuntur hic in feminino genere, hoc est pro vaccis, sicut in libro Job: Bos eorum concepit: unde ut Lyra ait, in Hebræo habetur, Septem vaccæ: et pascebantur in locis palustribus, hoc est in paludibus juxta Nilum. Aliæ quoque septem boves emergebant de flumine Nilo post boves crassas, fœdæ confectæque macie, hoc est turpes et macilentæ, et pascebantur in ipsa amnis, id est fluvii, ripa in locis virentibus; devoraveruntque eas, quarum mira species et habitudo corporum erat, hoc est boves priores, valde speciosas ac magnas. Expergefactus Pharao, rursum dormivit: cogitando quippe de somnio suo, denuo obdormivit; et vidit alterum somnium: quatenus geminatio somnii, esset confirmatio et certitudo veritatis præsagii. Septem spicæ pullulabant in culmo uno plenæ granis, atque formosæ; aliæ quoque totidem spicæ tenues, et percussæ uredine, hoc est vacuæ et vento urente læsæ, ita quod grana eorum pauca videbantur corrupta seu elapsa, oriebantur, devorantes omnem priorum spicarum pulchritudinem, id est fructum ac eminentiam.
paras.en: [[41:1|He thought he stood by the river|Putabat se stare super fluvium]], that is, it seemed to him in his sleep that he stood by the Nile, namely on the land or bank beside the Nile, [[41:2|Out of which came up seven kine|de quo ascendebant septem boves]], as it appeared in the dream, [[41:2|very beautiful and fat|pulchræ et crassæ nimis]]. So *boves* is taken here in the feminine gender, that is, for cows, as in the book of Job: [[Job 21:10|Their cattle have conceived|Bos eorum concepit]] [the Latin *bos*, here feminine, "cow", is rendered "cattle" in the Douay-Rheims]; hence, as Lyra says, the Hebrew has "Seven cows": [[41:2|and they fed in marshy places|et pascebantur in locis palustribus]], that is, in the marshes beside the Nile. [[41:3|Other seven also|Aliæ quoque septem]] kine [[41:3|came up out of the river|emergebant de flumine]] Nile after the fat kine, [[41:3|ill-favoured, and lean fleshed|fœdæ confectæque macie]], that is, ugly and lean, [[41:3|and they fed on the very bank of the river|et pascebantur in ipsa amnis]] (*amnis*, that is, of the stream), [[41:3|in green places|in locis virentibus]]: [[41:4|And they devoured them, whose bodies were very beautiful and well conditioned|devoraveruntque eas, quarum mira species et habitudo corporum erat]], that is, the former kine, very comely and large. [[41:4|So Pharao awoke|Expergefactus Pharao]], [[41:5|He slept again|rursum dormivit]]: for while thinking about his dream he fell asleep once more; [[41:5|and dreamed another dream|et vidit alterum somnium]], so that the doubling of the dream might be a confirmation and certainty of the truth of the presage. [[41:5|Seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk full|Septem spicæ pullulabant in culmo uno plenæ]] of grains [[41:5|and fair|atque formosæ]]; [[41:6|Then seven other ears|aliæ quoque totidem spicæ]] [[41:6|thin and blasted|tenues, et percussæ uredine]], that is, empty and harmed by the burning wind, so that their few grains seemed spoiled or fallen out, [[41:6|sprung up|oriebantur]], [[41:7|And devoured all the beauty of the former|devorantes omnem priorum spicarum pulchritudinem]], that is, the fruit and excellence of the former ears.

paras.t: Evigilans Pharao post quietem, et facto mane, pavore perterritus, quia timebat quod somnia illa significarent terribilia et adversa sibi imminentia, nec consuetus erat somnia habere hujusmodi, misit ad conjectores Ægypti, id est ariolos et divinos ac magos, qui intromiserunt se de talibus exponendis, et interdum vere exposuerunt hominum somnia magica arte et ope diaboli, præsertim quando a dæmonibus somnia erant immissa, cunctosque sapientes sapientia Ægyptiorum, quæ potius fuit stultitia, quia superstitionibus plena: potuerunt tamen philosophicam sapientiam quamdam habere. Et accersitis, id est eis ad se adductis, narravit somnium, id est ambo somnia sua, vel forte primum dumtaxat, ita quod videns illos non posse exponere somnium primum, tacuit de secundo; nec erat qui interpretaretur, id est, nullus Ægyptiorum potuit ea exponere. Dicunt tamen Hebræi, ut fertur, quod dabant regi quasdam expositiones, videlicet quod in brevi septem de filiabus suis essent morituræ ac sepeliendæ, et aliæ septem ab eo gignendæ: sed rex non contentabatur de tali expositione, quæ aut parvam aut nullam apparentiam habuit.
paras.en: [[41:7|Pharao awaked after his rest|Evigilans Pharao post quietem]], [[41:8|And when morning was come, being struck with fear|et facto mane, pavore perterritus]], because he feared that those dreams signified terrible and adverse things hanging over him, and he was not used to having dreams of this kind, [[41:8|he sent to all the interpreters of Egypt|misit ad conjectores Ægypti]], that is, to the soothsayers, diviners and magicians, who took upon themselves the expounding of such things, and at times truly expounded men's dreams by magic art and the devil's help, especially when the dreams had been sent by demons; [[41:8|and to all the wise men|cunctosque sapientes]], wise with the wisdom of the Egyptians, which was rather folly, being full of superstitions; yet they could have had a certain philosophical wisdom. [[41:8|And they being called for|Et accersitis]], that is, brought to him, [[41:8|he told them his dream|narravit somnium]], that is, both his dreams, or perhaps only the first, so that, seeing they could not expound the first dream, he kept silent about the second; [[41:8|and there was not any one that could interpret it|nec erat qui interpretaretur]], that is, none of the Egyptians could expound them. Yet the Hebrews say, as is reported, that they gave the king certain expositions, namely that seven of his daughters would shortly die and be buried, and seven others be begotten by him; but the king was not satisfied with such an exposition, which had little or no likelihood.

paras.t: Tunc demum reminiscens eorum quæ sibi acciderant, pincernarum magister, ait: Confiteor peccatum meum, id est ingratitudinem, qua hucusque fui ingratus interpreti meo, vel culpam quam commisi in regem. Iratus rex servis suis, etc., id est, tu Pharao dudum irascens mihi principique pistorum, fecisti nos incarcerari, ubi una nocte uterque vidimus somnium præsagum futurorum. Erat ibi puer Hebræus, etc.
paras.en: [[41:9|Then at length|Tunc demum]] [[41:9|remembering|reminiscens]] what had happened to him, [[41:9|the chief butler|pincernarum magister]] [[41:9|said|ait]]: [[41:9|I confess my sin|Confiteor peccatum meum]], that is, the ingratitude by which I have until now been ungrateful to my interpreter, or the fault I committed against the king. [[41:10|The king being angry with his servants|Iratus rex servis suis]], etc., that is, thou, Pharao, being angry some time ago with me and the chief baker, didst have us imprisoned, [[41:11|Where in one night both of us dreamed a dream foreboding things to come|ubi una nocte uterque vidimus somnium præsagum futurorum]]. [[41:12|There was there a young man a Hebrew|Erat ibi puer Hebræus]], etc.

paras.t: Protinus ad regis imperium eductum de carcere Joseph totonderunt: in carcere namque pili et barba et in longum creverunt: ac veste mutata, obtulerunt ei, id est præsentaverunt regi: quia cum veste vili ac sordida aut pene attrita, non licuit eum coram rege adduci, ne rex horrore affligeretur, aut quasi inhonorari videretur. Cui ille rex ait: Vidi somnia, nec est qui disserat: quæ audivi te sapientissime conjicere, id est interpretari: et hoc relativum, Quæ, non refertur hic determinate ad somnia quæ Pharao se dixit vidisse, sed ad somnia in communi. Nam pincerna dixerat regi, ipsum Joseph esse prudentissimum somniorum interpretem.
paras.en: [[41:14|Forthwith at the king's command Joseph was brought out of the prison|Protinus ad regis imperium eductum de carcere Joseph]], [[41:14|and they shaved him|totonderunt]]: for in prison his hair and beard had grown long: [[41:14|and changing his apparel brought him in to him|ac veste mutata, obtulerunt ei]], that is, presented him to the king; for it was not lawful to bring him before the king in mean and filthy or almost threadbare clothing, lest the king be struck with disgust, or seem, as it were, dishonoured. [[41:15|And he said to him|Cui ille rex ait]] (the king): [[41:15|I have dreamed dreams, and there is no one that can expound them|Vidi somnia, nec est qui disserat]]: [[41:15|Now I have heard that thou art very wise at interpreting them|quæ audivi te sapientissime conjicere]], that is, interpreting. And this relative *quæ* [literally "which"; the Douay-Rheims renders it "them"] does not refer here definitely to the dreams that Pharao said he had seen, but to dreams in general. For the butler had told the king that Joseph was a most skilful interpreter of dreams.

paras.t: Respondit Joseph: Absque me respondebit Deus prospera Pharaoni. Quasi dicat: Etiamsi ego non adessem, seu absque meis meritis et sine meo subsidio, Deus ex sua bonitate per modum sibi placentem manifestaret tibi, et nunc manifestabit expositionem somniorum tuorum, quæ erit pro tua prosperitate, non ad tuum gravamen, ut formidasti. Ex hoc apparet, quod jam ante hæc verba Deus manifestavit ipsi Joseph saltem in generali sensum somniorum regis: alioqui Joseph incaute protulisset hæc verba, vel verba ista erant verba bonæ spei, et consolatoria regis perterriti, quia consuetum est regibus dici quæ libenter audiunt. In Scholastica quoque historia fertur, quod rex apprehensa manu Joseph, dixit ad eum: Vidi somnium, nec timeas edisserere quidquid sit: tuncque Joseph respondit verba prætacta.
paras.en: [[41:16|Joseph answered: Without me, God shall give Pharao a prosperous answer|Respondit Joseph: Absque me respondebit Deus prospera Pharaoni]]. As if to say: Even if I were not here, or without my merits and without my help, God of His goodness would make known to thee, in the way that pleases Him, and now will make known, the exposition of thy dreams, which will be for thy prosperity, not to thy hurt, as thou hast feared. From this it appears that before these words God had already made known to Joseph himself, at least in general, the meaning of the king's dreams; otherwise Joseph would have spoken these words rashly. Or else these were words of good hope, consoling the frightened king, since it is customary to tell kings what they like to hear. In the Scholastic History, too, it is related that the king took Joseph by the hand and said to him: I have seen a dream; do not fear to expound it, whatever it may be; and then Joseph answered with the words already quoted.

paras.t: Narravit ergo Pharao quod viderat, etc., sicut jam recitatum est. De bobus pulchris nunc dicitur, quod erant obesis carnibus, id est carnosæ seu carnibus plenæ, quasi delicate nutritæ ob esum, id est ad hoc ut ederentur; et vireta carpebant, id est, virides herbas ac gramina abradendo edebant.
paras.en: [[41:17|So Pharao told what he had dreamed|Narravit ergo Pharao quod viderat]], etc., as has already been recounted. Of the beautiful kine it is now said that they were [[41:18|full of flesh|obesis carnibus]], that is, fleshy or full of flesh, as though daintily fed *ob esum*, that is, so that they might be eaten [Denis derives *obesus*, "fat", from *ob esum*, "for eating"]; [[41:18|and they grazed on green places|et vireta carpebant]], that is, they ate green herbs and grasses, cropping them.

paras.t: Respondit Joseph: Somnium regis unum est, hoc est, duplex somnium seu duo somnia, quantum ad imaginariam apparitionem distincta, unum est, id est idem significat. Deinde in textu expositio somniorum exprimitur. Septem boves pulchræ, et septem spicæ pulchræ, et plenæ, septem ubertatis anni sunt, etc., id est, significant septem annos fertilissimos, nunc instantes: et convenienter hi fertiles anni, per boves pingues et spicas plenas signantur; quoniam panis, qui fit ex granis spicarum, et carnes bovinæ spectant præcipue ad refectionem humanam, et item quoniam terra per boves aratur ac colitur. Per hoc quoque quod juxta Nilum visæ sunt boves, ostensum est, quod fertilitas et etiam sterilitas terræ, ex diversa dispositione Nili maxime nascituræ fuerunt. Nilus quippe totam Ægypti irrigat terram, ex cujus convenienti irrigatione procedit fertilitas, sicut alibi ex apto pluviarum descensu. Ex irrigationis vero inconvenientia seu defectu, oritur in Ægypto sterilitas terræ, quemadmodum alibi ex pluviarum importuna abundantia, seu vehementi carentia.
paras.en: [[41:25|Joseph answered: The king's dream is one|Respondit Joseph: Somnium regis unum est]], that is, the twofold dream, or the two dreams, distinct as to the imaginary apparition, are one, that is, signify the same thing. Then the exposition of the dreams is set out in the text. [[41:26|The seven beautiful kine|Septem boves pulchræ]], [[41:26|and the seven full ears|et septem spicæ pulchræ, et plenæ]] (beautiful and full), [[41:26|are seven years of plenty|septem ubertatis anni sunt]], etc., that is, they signify seven most fruitful years, now at hand. And these fertile years are fittingly signified by fat kine and full ears, since bread, which is made from the grains of the ears, and the flesh of oxen belong chiefly to man's nourishment, and also since the land is ploughed and tilled with oxen. By the fact, too, that the kine were seen beside the Nile, it was shown that the fertility and also the barrenness of the land would arise chiefly from the differing condition of the Nile. For the Nile waters the whole land of Egypt, and from its fitting irrigation fertility proceeds, as elsewhere from a timely fall of rain; but from unfitting or failing irrigation barrenness of the land arises in Egypt, as elsewhere from an untimely abundance or a severe lack of rain.

paras.t: Sequentur septem anni alii tantæ sterilitatis, ut oblivioni tradatur cuncta retro abundantia: hoc est, omnis victualium copia quæ præcessit in annis fertilitatis, dicitur oblivioni tradita, quia sic periit quasi nunquam fuisset, vel quia homines sic erant circa acquirenda necessaria occupati, quod non cogitabant de aliis rebus. Consumptura est enim fames omnem terram, id est habitatores Ægypti, et aliarum multarum habitatores terrarum, in quibus fames consumpsit pinguedinem, quam præcedens induxit ubertas. Itaque fames eos consumpsit, hoc est maceravit, afflixit, et forte multos occidit.
paras.en: [[41:30|After which shall follow other seven years of so great scarcity|Sequentur septem anni alii tantæ sterilitatis]], [[41:30|that all the abundance before shall be forgotten|ut oblivioni tradatur cuncta retro abundantia]]: that is, all the store of victuals that went before in the years of fertility is said to be forgotten, because it perished as though it had never been, or because men were so busy getting the necessaries that they did not think of other things; [[41:30|for the famine shall consume all the land|Consumptura est enim fames omnem terram]], that is, the inhabitants of Egypt and the inhabitants of many other lands, in whom the famine consumed the fatness that the preceding plenty had brought. And so the famine consumed them, that is, wasted them, afflicted them, and perhaps killed many.

paras.t: Consequenter subjungitur consilium Joseph. Nunc ergo provideat rex, id est prudenter consideret, et eligat sibi virum sapientem in divinis, et industrium, id est prudentem in rebus humanis, in quibus dirigatur a Deo: et præficiat eum terræ Ægypti, qui constituat præpositos per cunctas regiones: erant enim in universo regno Ægypti quædam particulares provinciæ, ad ipsum regnum totale spectantes, in quibus ordinati fuerunt præpositi ad emendum quintam fructuum partem, ut subditur: et quintam partem fructuum per septem annos fertilitatis, qui jam nunc futuri sunt, congreget per illos præpositos aliosque ministros in horrea per singulas urbes et alia loca: et omne frumentum sic collectum, imo et juste emptum, quantum ad blada ab aliis sumpta, sub Pharaonis potestate condatur, etc.; et non consumetur terra inopia, id est, habitatores terræ ex victualium penuria non peribunt, si ita fuerit actum. Placuit Pharaoni consilium Joseph, et cunctis ministris ejus.
paras.en: Next Joseph's counsel is added.
