[[41:33|Now therefore let the king provide|Nunc ergo provideat rex]], that is, let him consider prudently and choose for himself [[41:33|a wise|virum sapientem]] man in divine things, [[41:33|and industrious|et industrium]], that is, prudent in human affairs, in which he may be directed by God: [[41:33|and make him ruler over the land of Egypt|et præficiat eum terræ Ægypti]], [[41:34|That he may appoint overseers over all the countries|qui constituat præpositos per cunctas regiones]]: for in the whole kingdom of Egypt there were certain particular provinces belonging to the kingdom as a whole, in which overseers were appointed to buy the fifth part of the fruits, as is added: [[41:34|the fifth part of the fruits, during the seven fruitful years|et quintam partem fructuum per septem annos fertilitatis]], [[41:35|That shall now presently ensue|qui jam nunc futuri sunt]], let him [[41:34|gather|congreget]], by those overseers and other ministers, [[41:34|into barns|in horrea]] in each city and other places: [[41:35|and let all the corn|et omne frumentum]] thus collected, and indeed justly bought as regards the grain taken from others, [[41:35|be laid up, under Pharao's hands|sub Pharaonis potestate condatur]], etc.; [[41:36|and the land shall not be consumed with scarcity|et non consumetur terra inopia]], that is, the inhabitants of the land will not perish from want of victuals, if it is so done. [[41:37|The counsel pleased Pharao|Placuit Pharaoni consilium]] of Joseph, [[41:37|and all his servants|et cunctis ministris ejus]].

paras.t: Circa hoc quæritur, cur non potius Joseph consuluit reservari mediam, quam quintam fructuum partem. Et videtur quod male. Si enim reliquæ quatuor partes fructuum necessariæ erant in annis fertilitatis, videtur quod quinta pars nequaquam suffecerit pro annis sterilitatis. Respondetur, quod in aliquibus annis sterilitatis fuit aliqualis fructificatio terræ, ut infra patebit. In annis quoque fecunditatis, necessaria fuit magna pars fructuum pro copiosa terræ seminatione, usuque jumentorum: nec æstimandum quod quatuor partes fructuum necessariæ erant in annis fertilibus. Forsitan etiam dici potest, quod non bene poterat plus servari tamdiu, quam quinta pars fructuum, propter corruptionem quæ solet frumento accidere, si in magnis cumulis diu servetur.
paras.en: On this it is asked why Joseph did not rather counsel that half of the fruits be kept back, rather than the fifth part. And it seems that he counselled ill. For if the remaining four parts of the fruits were needed in the years of fertility, it seems that a fifth part would by no means have sufficed for the years of barrenness. The answer is that in some of the years of barrenness there was some fruitfulness of the land, as will appear below. In the fruitful years, too, a great part of the fruits was needed for the plentiful sowing of the land and for the use of the beasts; nor is it to be thought that the four parts of the fruits were needed in the fertile years. Perhaps it can also be said that no more than a fifth part of the fruits could well be kept so long, because of the spoiling that usually befalls corn if it is kept long in great heaps.

paras.t: Insuper, circa præhabita scribit quidam: Pharao non fuit oblitus somnium quemadmodum Nabuchodonosor: quoniam visio Nabuchodonosor fuit respectu futurorum de longe, quæ post ejus mortem impleta sunt: idcirco quia non vidit hujusmodi impletionem, non fuit motus ad honorandum Danielem, nisi Daniel retulisset ei somnium suum oblitum. Visio autem Pharaonis fuit de futuris in proximo: ideo pro ipsius Joseph exaltatione sufficit, quod exposuit somnium. Istud inconsiderate dictum probatur. Primo, quoniam visio Nabuchodonosor, de qua loquitur ille, non solum fuit de futuris in longinquum, sed etiam de futuris in proximo, imo potius de rebus tunc præsentibus. Etenim visio illa fuit de statua grandi, terribili, cujus caput videbatur esse ex optimo auro, ut habetur in Daniele. Et sicut ibidem habetur in textu, expositoresque addunt, per caput aureum intelligitur ipse rex Nabuchodonosor, regnumque ejus, qui tunc tenuit monarchiam, propter quod a Daniele dicebatur rex regum. Secundo, quoniam in Daniele scribitur alia visio Nabuchodonosor, quæ fuit de futuris in brevi, quam rex ille non fuit oblitus, sed eam Danieli narravit: quam quum Daniel regi exposuisset, mox rex Danielem honoravit, antequam impletionem expositionis illius vidit. Similiter quum Daniel exposuisset Balthasar regi visionem ipsius, mox honoravit eum Balthasar valde, et exaltavit antequam expositionis vidit effectum, ut in Daniele habetur. Postremo alia fuit ratio, cur Nabuchodonosor oblitus fuit primum somnium suum magis quam Pharao, prout super Danielem exposui, et nunc breviter tangam. Visio etenim illa, erat Nabuchodonosor terribilior valde quam somnia Pharaonis. Nabuchodonosor equidem vidit statuam altam, terribilem, cujus caput erat ex auro, brachia de argento, venter et femora ex ære, tibiæ ferreæ, pedum vero quædam pars ex ære, et quædam fusilis erat: sicque ex tam monstruosæ statuæ apparitione fuit rex ille perterritus ac turbatus magis quam Pharao ex somniis suis, quæ erant de rebus notis. Vehemens autem formido causat magnam motionem humorum, ex qua turbantur phantasmata, et causatur oblivio.
paras.en: Moreover, on what has gone before, a certain writer says: Pharao did not forget his dream as Nabuchodonosor did[[Dan 2:1||]], because Nabuchodonosor's vision concerned things to come far off, which were fulfilled after his death; and so, because he did not see such fulfilment, he would not have been moved to honour Daniel, had not Daniel told him the dream he had forgotten. But Pharao's vision concerned things soon to come; therefore it was enough for Joseph's exaltation that he expounded the dream. That this was said without consideration is proved. First, because the vision of Nabuchodonosor of which he speaks concerned not only things to come far off but also things to come soon, nay rather things then present. For that vision was of a great and terrible statue whose head seemed to be of the finest gold, as is had in Daniel. And as is had there in the text, and the expositors add, by the golden head is understood King Nabuchodonosor himself and his kingdom, which then held the monarchy; for which reason Daniel called him [[Dan 2:37|a king of kings|rex regum]]. Secondly, because in Daniel another vision of Nabuchodonosor is written, which concerned things to come shortly, which that king did not forget, but told to Daniel[[Dan 4:5||]] [the numbers of the margin's reference are lost here; the king tells this dream to Daniel at Dan 4:5]; and when Daniel had expounded it to the king, the king at once honoured Daniel, before he saw the fulfilment of that exposition. Likewise when Daniel had expounded to King Baltasar his vision, Baltasar at once greatly honoured and exalted him, before he saw the effect of the exposition, as is had in Daniel[[Dan 5:29||]] [the margin gives this reference, Dan. v, 29, beside the previous clause; the verse tells how Baltasar honoured Daniel]. Lastly, there was another reason why Nabuchodonosor forgot his first dream rather than Pharao, as I have expounded on Daniel, and will now touch on briefly. For that vision of Nabuchodonosor's was much more terrible than Pharao's dreams. Nabuchodonosor saw a lofty, terrible statue, whose head was of gold, the arms of silver, the belly and thighs of brass, the legs of iron, and of the feet one part of brass and another part cast [*fusilis*; Daniel has *fictilis*, "of clay"]; and so at the sight of so monstrous a statue that king was more frightened and troubled than Pharao by his dreams, which were of familiar things. Now vehement fear causes a great movement of the humours, by which the images of the imagination are disturbed, and forgetfulness is caused.

paras.t: Insuper advertendum, quod multipliciter atque difformiter Spiritus Sanctus tangat animas Prophetarum. Nam ut in Daniele inducitur, quum rex Babylonis exposuisset Danieli somnium suum de arbore visa in spiritu, Daniel cœpit quasi una hora intra se tacitus cogitare de somnio regis, et intra horam illam accepit a Deo illuminationem ad interpretandum somnium illud; primum vero somnium regis illico exposuit sine mora, imo et ante Deo revelante somnium ejusque significationem cognovit. Joseph vero statim exposuit regi et ejus eunuchis somnia quæ viderunt.
paras.en: Further, it is to be noted that the Holy Ghost touches the souls of the Prophets in many and differing ways. For, as is related in Daniel, when the king of Babylon had set forth to Daniel his dream of the tree seen in spirit, Daniel began to think silently within himself for about one hour on the king's dream[[Dan 4:16||]], and within that hour received from God enlightenment to interpret that dream; but the king's first dream he expounded at once without delay, nay, even before that he knew the dream and its meaning by God's revelation. Joseph, however, expounded at once to the king and to his eunuchs the dreams they had seen.

paras.t: Rursus hic oritur quæstio, cur et qualiter Joseph laudetur de somniorum interpretatione, quum Moyses alibi dicat: Non observabitis somnia: in Ecclesiastico quoque dicatur: Quasi qui apprehendit umbram, et persequitur ventum, secundum hoc visio somniorum. De hac autem materia in diversis locis alibi dictum est, et nunc breviter tangi potest, quod auctoritates illæ loquuntur de somniis quæ generantur ex superflua ventris repletione, aut nimia ejus inanitate, aut dæmonum illusione, aut præviis actibus, aut curis, aut cogitationibus importunis. Quæ autem a Deo vel angelis imprimuntur, sunt attendenda. Similiter ex somniis, quæ ex dispositione corporis ejus qui somniat, vel ex inflictione corporis cœlestis nascuntur, potest quidquid secretum aut futurum prænosci. De his, suis in locis plenius, Deo præstante, tractabitur.
paras.en: Again a question arises here: why and how is Joseph praised for the interpretation of dreams, when Moses says elsewhere: You shall not [[Lev 19:26|observe dreams|observabitis somnia]] [the margin note here is unreadable; the words are those of Lev 19:26, compare Deut 18:10], and in Ecclesiasticus too it is said: [[Ecclus 34:2|like to him that catcheth at a shadow, and followeth after the wind|Quasi qui apprehendit umbram, et persequitur ventum]], after this manner is [[Ecclus 34:3|the vision of dreams|visio somniorum]]? On this matter something has been said elsewhere in various places, and it can now be briefly touched on that those authorities speak of dreams generated by excessive filling of the belly, or its too great emptiness, or the illusion of demons, or preceding acts, or cares, or importunate thoughts. But those that are impressed by God or by angels are to be heeded. Likewise from dreams that arise from the disposition of the body of the one who dreams, or from the impression of a heavenly body, something secret or future can be foreknown. Of these, God granting, we shall treat more fully in their places.

paras.t: Adhuc quoque pensandum, quod somnium et visio atque oraculum inter se distinguuntur, proprie inde loquendo, quamvis extense unum interdum sumatur pro alio. Somnium enim dicitur, revelatio vel apparitio facta in somno per imaginarias formas obscure: et interdum ei cui fit somnium, desuper revelatur significatio seu intelligentia somnii: tuncque talis vocatur Propheta, præsertim quando de futuris est somnium. Interdum vero non ei, sed alteri significatio revelatur, ut patet de Joseph et Daniele: ideo tales sunt Prophetæ, non illi quibus fit solum imaginaria apparitio, ut Nabuchodonosor et eunuchi ac Pharao. Porro visio appellatur revelatio occultorum, sive ostensio futurorum magis clara et intellectualis, tam in vigilia, quam in raptu et ecstasi facta. Hinc Rabbi Moyses ait, quod somnium est casus a prophetia, quoniam prophetia est visio in lumine intelligentiæ; somnium autem est manifestatio futurorum in imagine, ubi cadit lumen intelligentiæ et occumbit. Oraculum vero, secundum Albertum super Danielem, est expressa prænuntiatio seu præcognitio rerum in somno percepta: et ita se habet medio modo inter visionem et somnium, participans cum utraque: puta cum visione, in quantum est manifesta cognitio; et cum somnio, in quantum in somno percipitur.
paras.en: It is further to be weighed that dream, vision and oracle are distinguished from one another, speaking properly, though in a wider sense one is sometimes taken for another. For a dream is the name for a revelation or apparition made in sleep through imaginary forms, obscurely; and sometimes the meaning or understanding of the dream is revealed from above to the one to whom the dream comes, and then such a one is called a Prophet, especially when the dream is of things to come. But sometimes the meaning is revealed not to him but to another, as is plain of Joseph and Daniel[[Dan 2:19||]][[Dan 4:15||]]: therefore these are Prophets, not those to whom only the imaginary apparition is made, such as Nabuchodonosor, the eunuchs and Pharao. Vision, again, is the name for a revelation of hidden things, or a showing of things to come, more clear and intellectual, made either in waking or in rapture and ecstasy. Hence Rabbi Moses [that is, Moses Maimonides] says that a dream is a falling-off from prophecy, since prophecy is vision in the light of the understanding, while a dream is a manifestation of things to come in an image, where the light of the understanding fails and sinks. An oracle, according to Albert on Daniel, is an express foretelling or foreknowledge of things, perceived in sleep; and so it stands midway between vision and dream, sharing with both: with vision, inasmuch as it is a manifest knowledge; with dream, inasmuch as it is perceived in sleep.

paras.t: Locutusque est Pharao, qui valde mirabatur utrumque, hoc est, tam expeditam et claram somniorum suorum expositionem, atque tam providum ipsius Joseph consilium: Num invenire poterimus talem virum, qui spiritu Dei, hoc est illuminatione et gratia Dei, qui spiritus est, plenus sit? Vel, spiritu Dei, id est voluntate seu divinæ voluntatis cognitione de agendis. Potest tamen per spiritum Dei, Spiritus Sanctus intelligi, quanquam Pharao per hæc verba non intellexerit eum. Dixit ergo ad Joseph: Quia ostendit tibi Deus omnia quæ locutus es interpretando somnia mea, et consulendo quid mihi agendum sit, numquid sapientiorem, et consimilem tui invenire potero? id est, nec majorem te in sapientia, imo nec parem tibi in ea valeo reperire. Tu eris super domum meam, id est, palatio meo et ejus domesticis præeris, et ad tui oris imperium cunctus populus obediet in his quæ jurisdictionem tuam concernunt; uno tantum regni solio te præcedam, id est, secundus eris in regno meo, et primus post me, ita quod sola regia dignitate major te ero.
paras.en: [[41:38|And he said|Locutusque est]], Pharao, who greatly wondered at both, that is, at so ready and clear an exposition of his dreams and at so provident a counsel of Joseph's: [[41:38|Can we find such another man, that is|Num invenire poterimus talem virum, qui]] [[41:38|full|plenus sit]] [[41:38|of the spirit of God|spiritu Dei]], that is, of the enlightenment and grace of God, who is a spirit? Or *the spirit of God*, that is, the will of God, or knowledge of the divine will concerning what is to be done. Yet by *the spirit of God* the Holy Ghost can be understood, although Pharao did not mean Him by these words. [[41:39|He said therefore to Joseph: Seeing God hath shewn thee all that thou hast said|Dixit ergo ad Joseph: Quia ostendit tibi Deus omnia quæ locutus es]] in interpreting my dreams and in counselling what I must do, [[41:39|can I find one wiser and one like unto thee?|numquid sapientiorem, et consimilem tui invenire potero?]] that is, I cannot find one greater than thou in wisdom, nay, not even thy equal in it. [[41:40|Thou shalt be over my house|Tu eris super domum meam]], that is, thou shalt be over my palace and its household, [[41:40|and at the commandment of thy mouth all the people shall obey|et ad tui oris imperium cunctus populus obediet]] in the things that concern thy jurisdiction; [[41:40|only in the kingly throne will I be above thee|uno tantum regni solio te præcedam]], that is, thou shalt be second in my kingdom and first after me, so that I shall be greater than thou only in the royal dignity.

paras.t: Dixitque rursus Pharao ad Joseph: Ecce constitui te super universam terram Ægypti, hoc est, plenum et generalem vicarium potestatis meæ te facio, præferendo omni te populo meo. Tulitque annulum de manu sua, et dedit eum in ma[…]u ejus. Annulo enim regum sigillabantur litteræ eorumdem: ideo Pharao cepit annulum de propria manu, et dedit in manu Joseph: ad innuendum, quod quidquid Joseph faceret aut signaret, ratum esset et efficax. Sic et Assuerus rex dederat annulum suum primo Aman, deinde Mardochæo.
paras.en: [[41:41|And again Pharao said to Joseph|Dixitque rursus Pharao ad Joseph]]: [[41:41|Behold, I have appointed thee over the whole land of Egypt|Ecce constitui te super universam terram Ægypti]], that is, I make thee the full and general vicar of my power, preferring thee to all my people. [[41:42|And he took his ring from his own hand|Tulitque annulum de manu sua]], [[41:42|and gave it into|et dedit eum in]] […] [[41:42|his hand|ejus]]. For the letters of kings were sealed with their ring: therefore Pharao took the ring from his own hand and gave it into Joseph's hand, to signify that whatever Joseph did or sealed would be ratified and effective. So too King Assuerus had given his ring first to Aman[[Esth 3:10||]], then to Mardochai[[Esth 8:2||]] [the margin gives Esth. viii, 8, which speaks of letters sealed with the king's ring; the ring is given to Mardochai at Esth 8:2].

paras.t: Vestivitque eum stola byssina, etc., id est candidissima linea veste, quæ subtilissima est in Ægypto. Fecitque eum ascendere super currum suum secundum, id est super pretiosiorem regis currum, uno curru excepto, in quo solus rex sedit; vel ut quidam exponunt, Super currum suum secundum, id est super primum ac regium currum, ita quod Joseph sedebat in illo curru, tanquam secundus a rege, qui interdum permisit ex speciali favore illum qui fuit secundus a se, ascendere currum suum; clamante præcone ante currum Joseph, qui per regiam urbem, et per diversas Ægypti urbes sic vehebatur, ut omnes coram eo genu flecterent, etc., sicut et Assuerus præcepit, ut omnes servi sui coram Aman flecterent genu. Verumtamen secundum Hieronymum et alios, in Hebræo non habetur, Ut flecterent coram eo genu; sed dictio ista, Abrech, sicut et Symmachus transtulit: quod tantum valet sicut, Pater tenerrimus: quasi dicatur, Quamvis Joseph ætate sit tenerrimus, tamen sapientia et virtute meretur pater omnium appellari. Itaque præco hoc nomen clamando, insinuavit ut genua flecterent ipsi Joseph tanquam patri ac principi terræ. Hinc Aquila transtulit, Clamavit in conspectu ejus ad geniculationem.
paras.en: [[41:42|and he put upon him a robe of silk|Vestivitque eum stola byssina]], etc., that is, with a very white linen garment, of the finest kind made in Egypt [*byssus* is fine linen; the Douay-Rheims has "silk"]. [[41:43|And he made him go up into his second chariot|Fecitque eum ascendere super currum suum secundum]], that is, onto the more precious of the king's chariots, one chariot excepted, in which the king alone sat; or, as some expound, [[41:43|into his second chariot|Super currum suum secundum]], that is, onto the first and royal chariot, so that Joseph sat in that chariot as second to the king, who sometimes, by special favour, allowed the one who was second to himself to mount his chariot; [[41:43|the crier proclaiming|clamante præcone]] before the chariot of Joseph, who was thus carried through the royal city and through the various cities of Egypt, [[41:43|that all should bow their knee before him|ut omnes coram eo genu flecterent]], etc., as Assuerus too commanded that all his servants should bow the knee before Aman[[Esth 3:2||]]. Yet according to Jerome and others, the Hebrew does not have [[41:43|should bow their knee before him|Ut flecterent coram eo genu]], but this word, *Abrech*, as Symmachus also translated it; which means as much as *Most tender father*: as if to say, Although Joseph is most tender in age, yet in wisdom and virtue he deserves to be called the father of all. So the crier, by calling out this name, intimated that they should bow their knees to Joseph as to the father and prince of the land. Hence Aquila translated: He cried in his presence for kneeling.

paras.t: Dixit quoque rex ad Joseph: Ego sum Pharao. Quod fuit juramentum regis: quasi dicat, Quam verum est, esse me Pharaonem, qui possum tibi tantam tradere potestatem, tam verum erit quod dicam, videlicet: Absque tuo imperio non movebit quisquam præter me qui major te sum, manum aut pedem in omni terra Ægypti. Hyperbolica locutio est: tanquam dicat, Magna valde erit auctoritas tua, nec aliquis in Ægypto audebit tibi contradicere te sive resistere, nec quidquam notabile contra tuam ordinationem peragere. Porro in Scholastica historia exponitur sic: Neque egredietur hunc sine tuo nutu, nec sine eo publicis fungetur officiis.
paras.en: [[41:44|And the king said to Joseph: I am Pharao|Dixit quoque rex ad Joseph: Ego sum Pharao]]. This was the king's oath: as if to say, As true as it is that I am Pharao, who can give thee so great a power, so true will be what I shall say, namely: [[41:44|without thy commandment no man shall move|Absque tuo imperio non movebit quisquam]], except me, who am greater than thou, [[41:44|hand or foot in all the land of Egypt|manum aut pedem in omni terra Ægypti]]. It is a hyperbolic expression: as if he said, Very great will be thy authority, and no one in Egypt will dare to gainsay or resist thee, nor to carry out anything of note against thy ordering. In the Scholastic History, moreover, it is expounded thus: No one shall go out hence without thy nod, nor without it shall anyone discharge public offices.

paras.t: Vertitque nomen ejus, id est mutando seu aliquid imponendo, et vocavit eum lingua Ægyptiaca, Salvatorem mundi: quia per suam interpretationem atque consilium, liberavit jam quasi mundum a futuro famis periculo. Nomen autem Ægyptium erat; hoc est, Zaphanath, quod (secundum Hieronymum) Hebraice sonat, absconditorum inventor; et tamen quoniam ab Ægyptio impositum est, debet habere rationem linguæ illius. Interpretatur enim Zaphanath Pahaneach, salvator mundi, ut testatur Hieronymus. Deditque illi uxorem nomine Aseneth, filiam Putipharis sacerdotis Heliopoleos. Augustinus quærit, an iste sit Putiphar, de quo dictum est capitulo tricesimo nono, qui fuit emptor ac dominus Joseph. Hieronymus vero absolute respondet quod imo, et idem dicunt Hebræi. Cur autem vocatus sit eunuchus, et cur factus sit sacerdos, id est summus antistes, Heliopoleos, id est civitatis solis, de qua fertur in Isaia, Civitas solis vocabatur una: dictum est in expositione capituli tricesimi septimi. Nullus quippe nisi castratus, aut infrigidatus ac impotens, poterat esse archiflaminus fani illius, forte ob hoc, ut sacris idolorum illius liberius atque integrius esset intentus.
paras.en: [[41:45|And he turned his name|Vertitque nomen ejus]], that is, by changing it or by imposing another, [[41:45|and called him in the Egyptian tongue the saviour of the world|et vocavit eum lingua Ægyptiaca, Salvatorem mundi]]: because by his interpretation and counsel he had already, as it were, delivered the world from the coming danger of famine. Now the name was Egyptian, that is, *Zaphanath*, which (according to Jerome) means in Hebrew *finder of hidden things*; and yet, since it was given by an Egyptian, it must have its meaning in that tongue. For *Zaphanath Pahaneach* is interpreted *saviour of the world*, as Jerome testifies. [[41:45|And he gave him to wife|Deditque illi uxorem]], by name [[41:45|Aseneth, the daughter of Putiphare, priest of Heliopolis|Aseneth, filiam Putipharis sacerdotis Heliopoleos]]. Augustine asks whether this is the Putiphar spoken of in the thirty-ninth chapter, who was the buyer and master of Joseph. Jerome answers outright that it is, and the Hebrews say the same. Why he was called a eunuch, and why he was made priest, that is, high priest, of Heliopolis, that is, of the city of the sun, of which it is said in Isaias, [[Is 19:18|one shall be called the city of the sun|Civitas solis vocabatur una]], has been said in the exposition of the thirty-seventh chapter. For none but one castrated, or frigid and impotent, could be the chief priest [*archiflaminus*, chief of the *flamines* or pagan priests] of that temple, perhaps so that he might attend more freely and wholly to the rites of its idols.

paras.t: Egressus est itaque Joseph ad terram Ægypti. Non quod jam extra terram Ægypti exstiterat, sed sedens in curru, processit de una parte terræ illius ad aliam. Triginta autem erat annorum quando stetit in conspectu Pharaonis taliter sublimatus: et ita fuit circiter tredecim annis in servitute et carcere; et quia nescitur quamdiu in carcere fuit, ignoratur quamdiu ante servierat. Venditus est autem et cœpit servire, quando erat circiter decem et septem annorum. Et circuivit omnes regiones Ægypti, id est particulares provincias quæ ad dominium Pharaonis spectabant, ad videndum urbes et loca et populum, quibus erat prælatus, et ut agnosceretur ac honoraretur ab omnibus: non tamen significavit alicui causam cur ita colligeret segetes, ut Josephus ait. Ex quibus omnibus constat, quanta gratia influxit Joseph, ne in tam repentina et maxima atque multiplici sua exaltatione et honorificentia, inani falleretur lætitia, aut aliqua vanitate. Congregatique successive fertilitas septem annorum, et in manipulos redactæ septem, conditæque sunt in horrea Ægypti, etc., per ministros a Joseph ad hoc deputatos; et intelligendum est istud de quinta parte fructuum, quæ per septennium servabatur.
paras.en: [[41:45|Then Joseph went out to the land of Egypt|Egressus est itaque Joseph ad terram Ægypti]]: not that he had been outside the land of Egypt before, but, sitting in the chariot, he went from one part of that land to another. [[41:46|Now he was thirty years old when he stood before|Triginta autem erat annorum quando stetit in conspectu]] Pharao, thus exalted; and so he had been about thirteen years in servitude and prison; and since it is not known how long he was in prison, it is unknown how long he had served before. Now he was sold and began to serve when he was about seventeen years old. [[41:46|and he went round all the countries of Egypt|Et circuivit omnes regiones Ægypti]], that is, the particular provinces that belonged to Pharao's dominion, to see the cities and places and people over which he had been set, and that he might be known and honoured by all; yet he did not tell anyone the reason why he was so gathering the crops, as Josephus says. From all this it is clear how great a grace flowed into Joseph, lest in so sudden, so great and so manifold an exaltation and honouring he be deceived by empty gladness or any vanity. Then [[41:47|the fruitfulness of the seven years|fertilitas septem annorum]] was gathered in succession, and, [[41:47|being bound up into sheaves|in manipulos redactæ]], was laid up [[41:47|into the barns of Egypt|in horrea Ægypti]], etc. [the Latin of this lemma is printed in a confused form, differing from the Vulgate; it is translated by the sense], by ministers appointed to this by Joseph; and this is to be understood of the fifth part of the fruits, which was kept for seven years.

paras.t: Nati sunt autem Joseph duo filii antequam veniret fames, etc. Hoc (ut quidam scribit) adjicitur quia Hebræi tempore communis tribulationis, ut est fames illa, ab uxoribus abstinebant; sed non est probabile, quod per septem annos famis ita continuerunt. Vocavitque nomen primogeniti Manasses, quod interpretatur oblivio, ideo ratio appellationis subjungitur: dicens, Oblivisci me fecit Deus omnium laborum meorum, et domus patris mei, hoc est, tantam donavit mihi prosperitatem, quod laborum et adversitatum quos pertuli, ac parentelæ meæ recordatio, non ingerit mihi tristitiam, ita quod per modum obliviscentis seu obliti me habeo. Verumtamen constitutis in prosperitate solet esse augmentum solatii, quod multa sustinuerunt adversa, juxta quod scriptum est: Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala. Nomen quoque secundi appellavit Ephraim, quod interpretatur fructificatio seu crementum, ideo subditur ratio nominis: dicens, Crescere me fecit Deus in terra paupertatis meæ, id est in terra Ægypti, in qua in principio venditionis meæ in ea, et tempore incarcerationis pauper fui: in qua nunc crevi in spiritualibus et corporalibus bonis, in prole atque familia, in honore, potestate et gloria.
paras.en: [[41:50|And before the famine came, Joseph had two sons born|Nati sunt autem Joseph duo filii antequam veniret fames]], etc. This (as a certain writer says) is added because the Hebrews, in a time of common tribulation such as that famine, abstained from their wives; but it is not probable that they kept continent in this way for the seven years of famine. [[41:51|And he called the name of the firstborn Manasses|Vocavitque nomen primogeniti Manasses]], which is interpreted *forgetfulness*; therefore the reason for the name is added: [[41:51|saying: God hath made me to forget all my labours, and my father's house|dicens, Oblivisci me fecit Deus omnium laborum meorum, et domus patris mei]], that is, He has given me such prosperity that the remembrance of the labours and adversities I have borne, and of my kindred, does not bring me sadness, so that I behave as one forgetting, or as one who has forgotten. And yet for those set in prosperity it is usually an increase of comfort that they have borne many adversities, according to what is written: [[Ps 89:15|We have rejoiced for the days in which thou hast humbled us: for the years in which we have seen evils|Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala]]. [[41:52|And he named the second Ephraim|Nomen quoque secundi appellavit Ephraim]], which is interpreted *fruitfulness* or *increase*; therefore the reason for the name is added: [[41:52|saying: God hath made me to grow in the land of my poverty|dicens, Crescere me fecit Deus in terra paupertatis meæ]], that is, in the land of Egypt, in which I was poor at the beginning, when I was sold into it, and in the time of my imprisonment; in which I have now grown in spiritual and bodily goods, in offspring and household, in honour, power and glory.

paras.t: Igitur transactis septem ubertatis annis, etc., cœperunt venire septem anni inopiæ, quos prædixerat Joseph; et in universo orbe fames prævaluit. Hoc per hyperbolen aut synecdochen dictum videtur. Non enim absolute in tota terra habitabili fuit caristia, sed ut infra habetur, præsertim in Ægypto terraque Chanaan, in regionibus quoque vicinis, quamvis non tam vehementer. Imo interdum in Scripturis una urbs mundus vocatur, ut quum Dominus ait in Isaia: Visitabo super orbis mala; ubi secundum Hieronymum, aliosque expositores communiter, per orbem ipsa Babylon ad litteram designatur, propter magnitudinem suam. De populo quoque qui venit cum Christo in die Palmarum, dixerunt Scribæ et Pharisæi: Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum. In cuncta autem terra Ægypti fames erat, etc., id est in aliquibus, imo et in multis habitatoribus singularum civitatum Ægypti. Aliqui nihilominus divites erant ibidem, qui in primis annis septem competentiam habuerunt ex propriis, quæ sibi reservarunt de fructibus annorum fertilium; hi præsertim, qui cognoverunt ea quæ Joseph de sterilitate terræ prædixit. Omnesque provinciæ, id est habitatores provinciarum illius climatis, veniebant in Ægyptum, ut emerent escas, etc., id est frumentum et blada ex quibus fit panis.
paras.en: [[41:53|Now when the seven years of plenty|Igitur transactis septem ubertatis annis]], etc., were passed, [[41:54|The seven years of scarcity, which Joseph had foretold, began to come|cœperunt venire septem anni inopiæ, quos prædixerat Joseph]]: [[41:54|and the famine prevailed in the whole world|et in universo orbe fames prævaluit]]. This seems to be said by hyperbole or synecdoche [that is, naming the whole for a part]. For the dearth was not simply in the whole habitable earth, but, as is had below, chiefly in Egypt and the land of Chanaan, and in the neighbouring regions too, though not so severely. Indeed in the Scriptures one city is sometimes called the world, as when the Lord says in Isaias: [[Is 13:11|I will visit the evils of the world|Visitabo super orbis mala]]; where, according to Jerome and the expositors in general, Babylon itself is literally meant by *the world*, because of its greatness. Of the people too who came with Christ on Palm Sunday, the Scribes and Pharisees said: [[John 12:19|Behold, the whole world is gone after him|Ecce totus mundus abiit post eum]]. But [[41:54|in all the land of Egypt|In cuncta autem terra Ægypti]] there was famine, etc. [Denis reads *fames*, "famine", where the Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims have "bread"], that is, in some, nay in many, of the inhabitants of each city of Egypt. Nevertheless there were some rich men there who in the first years of the seven had enough of their own, which they had kept back for themselves from the fruits of the fertile years; especially those who knew what Joseph had foretold about the barrenness of the land. [[41:57|And all provinces|Omnesque provinciæ]], that is, the inhabitants of the provinces of that region, [[41:57|came into Egypt, to buy food|veniebant in Ægyptum, ut emerent escas]], etc., that is, wheat and grain from which bread is made.

41.title: De mystico hujus capituli quadragesimi primi intellectu
41.title_en: On the mystical sense of this forty-first chapter

paras.t: UNA causa, propter quam sancta Ecclesia tam diligenter atque solenniter legit Scripturas veteris Testamenti, est, ut innotescat quod Deus omnipotens semper habuit providentiam actuum humanorum: quod etiam ex hujus capituli historia clarissime comprobatur. Itaque per Pharaonem, qui vidit in somno futura in mundo, intelligitur quicumque princeps terrenus gentilis, qui in exordio fuit primitivæ Ecclesiæ, et tamen prædestinatus fuit a Domino: cui desuper monstrabatur mira et inaudita mundi mutatio: cui Christus per Apostolorum prædicationem exposuit, qualiter tunc instaret jamque inceptum esset tempus gratiæ, in quo toti humano generi exhibenda esset incomparabilis opulentia septem donorum Spiritus Sancti, et supernorum charismatum eis jugiter annexorum, quæ per septem boves pingues, spicasque plenas signantur; deinde tempore procedente, et caritate refrigescente, ventura esset in mundo spiritualis sterilitas, hoc est defectus virtutum, abundantia vitiorum, quæ frequenter ac diu fuit in Christi Ecclesia, atque per boves macras, et spicas exustas exprimitur.
paras.en: One reason why holy Church reads the Scriptures of the Old Testament so diligently and solemnly is that it may be known that almighty God has always had providence over human acts: which is also most clearly proved from the history of this chapter. So by Pharao, who saw in his sleep things to come in the world, is understood any earthly prince of the gentiles who lived at the beginning of the primitive Church and was yet predestined by the Lord: to whom a wonderful and unheard-of change of the world was shown from above; to whom Christ, through the preaching of the Apostles, explained how the time of grace was then at hand and already begun, in which an incomparable wealth of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, and of the heavenly gifts continually joined to them, was to be shown to the whole human race; which are signified by the seven fat kine and the full ears; and then, as time went on and charity grew cold, there would come in the world a spiritual barrenness, that is, a lack of virtues and an abundance of vices, which has often and long been in the Church of Christ, and is expressed by the lean kine and the blasted ears.

paras.t: Porro, sicut Joseph consuluit quintam fructuum partem annorum fertilium colligi ac reponi in horrea ad succurrendum tempore famis: sic Christus durante Ecclesiæ primitivæ fervore, fecit per quosdam viros fideles describi virtutes, sapientiam, miracula, martyria, ac diversa charismata, quæ fuerunt in primitiva Ecclesia, quæ tot tantaque fuere, quod vix quinta pars quibat describi. Descripta vero, in horreis, hoc est in librariis, est condita, in quibus sunt libri cibaria spiritualia continentes, ex quibus subvenitur fidelibus tempore spiritualis inopiæ, qui tunc ex recitatione seu lectione virtutum atque charismatum, ineffabilisque fervoris primorum fidelium ac præcedentium patrum, ædificantur in fide, accenduntur in caritate, roborantur ad bene agendum, sicque salubriter reficiuntur, ne pereant prorsus inopia.
paras.en: Further, as Joseph counselled that the fifth part of the fruits of the fruitful years be gathered and laid up in barns, to give help in the time of famine: so Christ, while the fervour of the primitive Church lasted, had the virtues, wisdom, miracles, martyrdoms and divers gifts which were in the primitive Church written down by certain faithful men; and they were so many and so great that scarcely a fifth part could be written down. And what was written down has been stored in barns, that is, in libraries, in which are the books containing spiritual victuals, from which the faithful are helped in the time of spiritual want: who then, from the reciting or reading of the virtues and gifts and the unspeakable fervour of the first faithful and the fathers before them, are built up in faith, kindled in charity, strengthened to do well, and so are refreshed to their salvation, lest they perish utterly of want.

paras.t: Amplius, ipsius Joseph incarceratio et longa afflictio, figura fuit Domini Jesu Christi passionis: et sicut Joseph post maximam tribulationem subito vehementer est elevatus, Ægypto prælatus, et mundi Salvator vocatus; sic Christus post suam acerbissimam et ignominiosissimam passionem ac sepulturam statim est suscitatus a mortuis, cœlo ac terræ præpositus, atque ubique terrarum vocatus mundi Salvator. Constituitque Deus Pater Christum super domum suam, videlicet universalem Ecclesiam, cujus caput est Christus, et sub eo Romanus Antistes, Domnus apostolicus, generalis, plenus, ac summus Christi in terra Vicarius, in quo est potestatis ecclesiasticæ vertex ac plenitudo.
paras.en: Moreover, the imprisonment and long affliction of Joseph was a figure of the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ: and as Joseph after the greatest tribulation was suddenly raised exceedingly high, set over Egypt, and called the saviour of the world [Denis follows the reading of v. 45, *Salvator mundi*], so Christ, after His most bitter and most shameful passion and burial, was at once raised from the dead, set over heaven and earth[[Ps 2:6||]], and everywhere on earth called the Saviour of the world. And God the Father set Christ over His house[[Acts 10:42||]], namely the universal Church, whose head is Christ[[Col 1:18||]], and under Him the Roman Bishop, the lord apostolic, the general, full and supreme Vicar of Christ on earth, in whom is the summit and fulness of ecclesiastical power.

paras.t: Insuper, annulum fidei dedit Pater in manu Christi, ita ut Christus omnes vocaret ad fidem, animasque fideles sibi per fidem sponsaret. Vestivitque eum stola byssina, id est carnis immortalitate, claritate, impassibilitate, ac subtilitate in sua resurrectione. Auream quoque torquem circumposuit collo ejus, hoc est, ardentissimam caritatem, et splendidissimam sapientiam radicavit in mente ipsius. Fecitque eum ascendere super currum suum secundum, id est supra corda fidelium, potissime Apostolorum et aliorum prædicatorum sanctorum atque pastorum, qui Deum in se portant, circumferunt, retinent, et eum ad aliorum animas vehunt, ac sibi subjectos sustentant, qui sunt currus Dei, sicut ad Eliam dixerat Eliseus, et rex Israel Eliseo : Pater mi, pater mi, currus Israel et auriga ejus! Multi sunt tales currus Altissimi. Etenim currus Dei decem millibus multiplex. Quemadmodum etiam ante Joseph currebat præco clamans, ut omnes et flecterent genu, et dominum eum recognoscerent Ægyptiorum: sic Christum præcessit gloriosissimus sanctissimusque Joannes Baptista, qui prædicavit se esse indignum solvere corrigiam calceamentorum Christi Filii Dei, eumque esse ab omnibus adorandum, dicendo: Qui de cælo venit, super omnes est.
paras.en: Further, the Father gave the ring of faith into Christ's hand, so that Christ might call all to faith, and espouse faithful souls to Himself by faith. [[41:42|and he put upon him a robe of silk|Vestivitque eum stola byssina]] [*byssus*, fine linen], that is, with the immortality, brightness, impassibility and subtlety of the flesh in His resurrection. [[41:42|and put a chain of gold about his neck|Auream quoque torquem circumposuit collo ejus]], that is, He rooted most burning charity and most splendid wisdom in His mind. [[41:43|And he made him go up into his second chariot|Fecitque eum ascendere super currum suum secundum]], that is, upon the hearts of the faithful, above all of the Apostles and the other holy preachers and pastors, who carry God in themselves, bear Him about, keep Him, and carry Him to the souls of others, and support those subject to them; who are the chariots of God, as Eliseus had said to Elias, and the king of Israel to Eliseus: [[4 Kings 2:12|My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the driver thereof|Pater mi, pater mi, currus Israel et auriga ejus]][[4 Kings 13:14||]] [the margin note here is unreadable in the transcription]! Many are such chariots of the Most High. For [[Ps 67:18|The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands|currus Dei decem millibus multiplex]]. And as a crier ran before Joseph, crying that all should bow the knee and acknowledge him lord of the Egyptians: so Christ was preceded by the most glorious and most holy John the Baptist, who preached that he was unworthy to loose the latchet of the shoes of Christ the Son of God, and that He was to be adored by all, saying: [[John 3:31|He that cometh from heaven is above all|Qui de cælo venit, super omnes est]].

paras.t: Præterea, sicut Joseph exaltatus duxit uxorem gentilem, genuitque ex ea filios duos: sic Christus post suam resurrectionem et ascensionem, Synagoga relicta, gentilem plebem convertit, et ex ea sibi collegit Ecclesiam quam duxit in sponsam, ex qua genuit quasi duos filios, hoc est religiosos ac sæculares, seu contemplativos et activos. Ex primitiva quoque Ecclesia, hoc est per sanctorum Apostolorum prædicationem, genuit filios duos, convertendo per eos multa millia Judæorum sed incomparabiliter plura millia paganorum.
paras.en: Further, as Joseph, exalted, married a gentile wife and begot two sons by her: so Christ, after His resurrection and ascension, leaving the Synagogue, converted the gentile people, and gathered from it the Church, which He took as His bride, and from which He begot as it were two sons, namely religious and seculars, or contemplatives and actives. From the primitive Church too, that is, through the preaching of the holy Apostles, He begot two sons, converting through them many thousands of Jews but incomparably more thousands of pagans.

paras.t: Adhuc autem sicut Joseph fuit triginta annorum quando circuivit Ægyptum: sic Christus eadem in ætate exorsus est circuire Judæam ad prædicandum in ea, qui pertransivit benefaciendo, et sanando omnes oppressos a diabolo: et sicut Joseph tempore sterilitatis aperuit horrea, vendiditque frumenta: sic Christus tempore deformationis et conculcationis Ecclesiæ misericorditer auxiliatur, nec unquam in toto relinquet Ecclesiam, sed indesinenter statuit et conservat in ea quosdam electos ac virtuosos, qui mala mundi ac ruinam deplorant Ecclesiæ, clamantes ad Christum pro spirituali refectione ac reformatione populi christiani: quibus pius succurrit Salvator, et spiritualia tribuit alimenta, quæ oratione et subjectione quasi emuntur. Horrea vero sunt libri Scripturæ, sacramenta Ecclesiæ, corda ferventia, imo et ipsa caritas, pietas, omnipotentia, opulentia, liberalitas Dei, in quibus omnia bona supercopiosissime continentur; et tunc quasi aperiuntur, dum nobis ex eis dona gratiæ derivantur.
paras.en: Again, as Joseph was thirty years old when he went round Egypt, so Christ at the same age began to go round Judea to preach in it, [[Acts 10:38|who went about doing good and healing all that were oppressed by the devil|qui pertransivit benefaciendo, et sanando omnes oppressos a diabolo]]: and as Joseph in the time of barrenness opened the barns and sold corn, so Christ in the time of the Church's disfigurement and downtreading helps her mercifully, and will never wholly forsake the Church, but unceasingly sets and keeps in her certain chosen and virtuous men who lament the evils of the world and the ruin of the Church, crying to Christ for the spiritual refreshment and reform of the Christian people: whom the loving Saviour helps, and gives them spiritual food, which is as it were bought by prayer and submission. The barns are the books of Scripture, the sacraments of the Church, fervent hearts, nay the very charity, goodness, omnipotence, wealth and liberality of God, in which all good things are contained most superabundantly; and they are as it were opened when the gifts of grace flow to us from them.
